The 2 official gamemodes are: Survival, and Bomb Escape.
Survival has 2 maps. Both are relativly small, but have plenty of running room to kill some infected. In survival you need to survive waves of zombies with a limited ammo supply and gernades. At the end of every round there is a peace time, with time for your team to resupply health, ammo, some more armor, another gernade, a new gun (gun might be the same or complete downgrade), and time to resume positions. Each wave has increaingly more zombies per wave.
Bomb Deploy has 6 maps. They have you and your team at a starting location, with filled ammo, health, armor, and gernades/crate supplies/sentry health. You and your team have to navigate to the center/end of the map to deploy the bomb. After deploying it, you must return to the start and leave in a military vehicle, or in a room with blast resistant doors.
The pointman has a semi-automatic shotgun, dual pistols, and frag nades. He is the scout and is good at running ahead to land some kills before the team gets there so they dont get overwhelmed my zombies.
The support has an automatic SMG, a pistol, and a supply crate for his friends. He can deploy his supply crate to heal and resupply his friends with ammo. It loses its supplies over time of usage, but is regained when not deployed. It cannot be destroyed by zombies.
The Assault class has an automatic rifle, a powerful pistol, and frag nades. He is pretty much the tank of the group.
The technician has a shotgun, a pistol, and a deployable sentry. He can deploy a sentry with infinite ammo, but not infinite health. The sentry attacks any zombies in its sight and range. While undeployed, its health slowly regenerates. If the sentry is destroyed, it cannot be replaced.
The sniper has a sniper rifle, a pistol, and napalm nades (firebombs). He can scope in with his sniper rifle (and by scoping in I mean using invisible ironsights) and normally one-shot normal/running zombies.
The normal zombie walks normally and has normal health.
The runner zombie moves, attacks more quickly, and has less health.
The soldier zombie moves slowly, attacks more powerfully, and has lots of health.
Also, did I mention you could do a punch that kills and sends zombies flying in one hit?

You'll see a lot of comparisons to Starmade and Space Engineers, and it's true, very similar in this early phase of development.  I played a lot of Starmade early on, and poked around Space Engineers, both were fun in their own respects but lacked something I desperately wanted from a space sim.
Buidling your own ship, station or anything is something I love, but the limits of the game are what ultimately define the experience.  Starmade allowed for fantastically large ships, almost mindbogglingly so and definitely a huge use of time to really get the interior looking good.  Space Engineers really is great if you like the more serious and realistic approach, I wouldn't call it gritty, but ships being torn apart is pretty cool.
Yet neither game really hit that classic space sim feel, sure they simualated some blocky universe of space, or some distant somewhat plausible future, the ships are even quite impressive, with Starmades mining laser crafts eating through asteroids and Space Engineers giant tissue paper cruisers.
I'm not saying Interstellar Rift at this moment does either, surely at it's present state without combat or really anything other to do than fly around a bit and build or stare at non-functioning parts and wonder what the final mechanic will look like.
But in those moments in passing, when you're busily walking through your freshly designed ship, built up with a decent editor(that could use some tweaking and refinement of course) that has more resemblance to a Sims game than it does to Space Engineer's or Starmade's editor, and you stop to notice the Jukebox you had absent mindedly placed for fluff, and you walk up to it.  The screen fades in, and a selection shows up, you hit classical and look out the window.  An asteroid tumbles by silently in the void.
It feels like home.

This little gem just rolled up on the beach out of nowhere! If this game is done right, it will be the future of all space games.
Pros:
- Graphics are pretty dam amazing. When talking about the interior designs and animations of a game, this game is very high quality! The exterior could use some work though....
- Gameplay is smooth and great fun! Yes, there are not many features BUT I STILL FIND MYSELF HAVING A BLAST! If the game this fun at its bare bones then I cannot wait until it is fully implemented
- Ship editor system is on point. Yes, it could use some fine tuning and I would love a way to look at a 3d model of the inside of the ship before having to build it and then scrap it if one part is made incorrectly. OTher than that it is responsive and very detailed.
- Mining done right! YOU FEEL PRODUCTIVE IN THIS GAME! A lot of games have you chopping trees for hours or collecting food. Which is fine, but this game the mining and refining are done in a very interactive and fun way! Keeps you moving and on your feet without it feeling like a drag.
- One of the most immersive space games I've played. You actually are in a station, you have a mining station, you can choose what music plays, and you can walk around your own ship and interact with machines and systems. IT ISNT JUST RANDOM BLOCKS! THEY HAVE MEANING!
- Updates are frequent with hotfixes all the time
CONS
- Resource collecting and ship building and flying are about the only things to do BUT THEY ARE FUN!
- Exterior graphics of the ships are just simply dissapointing...
- Flying mechanics could be improved and more responsive
- Population is low but the game is very early access so it is understandable
Overall, the game is a great game and if done right could easily be a game changer with the graphics and immersiveness they have going. Don't be fooled by my hours in the game. I have been playing this game since before it came to steam! And yes I was one of the lucky few who got the game for free since I started out so early! Early Access Watcher Reviews Gloria Victis (Abridged to fit the review space, check out main site for full review -
-)
Update Version: v.0.6.3.4
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the review, but a review copy was also provided by the developer.
Over the past few years, Black Eye Games has been hard at work and managed to launch Gloria Victis onto Early Access on June 9th. From the 12 hours I have seen of the game I can tell there has been a lot of love put into this medieval island. That being said, it still has a long way to go before it can compete with other products on the market. Gloria Victis, for whatever issues I am about to discuss, does have quite a bit going for it.
While other games with a similar aesthetic go for a more macabre look, Gloria Victis goes for a enlightened and sometimes pessimistic approach with bright lighting effects one moment and gloomy over casts the next. Scenery is plentiful with vast stretches of forest land, muggy swamps, roaring mountains and beaches both sandy and rocky. Huts and small homes are well stocked with furniture (some exceptions apply with abandoned homes) while towns are surrounded by rugged walls and garnered with flags of the nation. Patrols and watch towers litter the map reflecting the colors of the current owner of there region. It isn't the prettiest game to look at, but the unique choice in shading and overall character detail give it the required level of depth to boast a believable Middle Ages environment.
Once I was finished playing this game the first time, I was amazed the music was still playing in the back of my mind. Very few games, especially on Early Access, have the ability to stick with me for long. From the beautiful violin melodies to modest vocal work, it breathes a powerful ambiance into a world pulsing with chivalric vibes. Sounds effects are somewhat of a mixed bag, especially when gathering and walking with heavy armor on. These little details are perfect, but can become massively grating if you don't optimize the volume (which I will get to in a bit). Grunts, opening doors and even the small clink of a drawn weapon are just a small sample of the little touches adding substance to the immersion.
Unlike most MMOs, the combat revolves around a target-less system with every hit depending on range and weapon variants. Melee has a vast selection of pole arms, axes, swords, mauls and daggers along with shields that come in all shapes and sizes. When striking with a melee weapon, you have the ability to charge your attack for a better strike, use a shield to block incoming attacks and have a kick ability to disorient blocking opponents. It plays out similarly to Demons' Souls, but each hit is made without the use of a lock-on system. There is an issue, however, with the strike feedback not matching with the visual or the sound of each attack. Often times I felt many of my strikes were not registering even against something as large as a troll.
Bows are available from the start and add a important role in offensive and defensive positions during attacks. Similar to real world mechanics, each arrow strung adheres to outside factors such as distance and fall off. You cannot expect to hit a target by shooting with the cursor aimed at your target from 100 yards away. This makes archery challenging, but in the best way possible. It makes each hit a bit more satisfying and keeps siege battle rather balanced. A quick note on abilities: there are currently passive abilities and three major stats to pour points into, but nothing along the lines of action based abilities are present yet.
Due to the heavy PvP influence in the game, there is no real PvE content aside from NPCs on the field and some area objectives that act similar to fates in Final Fantasy 14. Thankfully, the PvP system is enjoyable with tournaments and open world territory capture. The primary alternative is in capturing towns and resource locations with a group of people. NPC guards and other players from your opposing faction defend a flag located in the vicinity while you attempt to capture it. Once it is under your control, the region is granted a buff for your faction and you can begin upgrading the area. PvP is an excellent means to level up and a potent method of ensuring control on the island. Just remember, this is a PvP focused game and has very little else outside of it.
The economy is player-driven and thus makes crafting the vital life-line for supplies and upgrades. From weapons and armor; food and ingredients; there is a job for whatever product you need. Crafting levels are based on the amount you make and also provides normal experience, if but a fraction. Recipe books provide the means to make better items and are found from vendors and enemy NPCs. As a full-time crafter in most MMOs, the system felt very basic in design and not in a bad way.
Textures and objects pop in at an alarming rate with enemies sometimes not appearing at all until you have already run into their engagement radius. Upon death, characters can be stuck in a falling motion through the world, which thankfully fixed itself with a few sporadic presses of the movement keys. While more technical than visual, the game has a nasty habit of delaying input commands from selling a simple item to learn recipes. It takes forever to register, sometimes making it difficult to tell if it even went through. Stuttering is probably the worst issue dealing with Gloria Victis and it continually occurs, sometimes forcing me to move forward when I am intentionally trying to turn left or right. This is at every graphic setting with shadows and other intensive settings turned off.
Technical issues are another block of issues that need to be circumvented to play the game properly. Frame rate can be over the place, dropping and spiking from 60 to 40 and even 30 for a couple of seconds before returning to normal. Averaging 55 to 40 normally, this makes movement seem floaty while combat strikes are hard to judge. Loading screen issues are also common place with the screen often becoming unresponsive before finally loading two minutes later.
Bugs are just another part of development, but they need to be addressed. Allocation points are required to level up stats and passive abilities, but whenever I tried to do so, I would confirm my selection and end up losing points (put in 10 when I had 100, then have 90). This is before 130, which then requires two points to level once in a stat. Enemies would sometimes chase after you, only to stop dead in their tracks and not respond after moving only six feet. Economy wise, selling prices are either miss labeled or the game is only paying a fraction of the price promised for selling an item. Some items I tried crafting also fail to be made, using up the materials in the process. These are just a small number of the bugs that are present, some of which can be harmful if not dealt with soon.
Glaring issues from UI, stat lose and performance hiccups make survival rather difficult in an already unforgiving world. It is with a heavy hand I bury the axe into the not recommended side of this table. I will be revisiting this game from time to time and look forward to seeing how it changes within the next six months, where hopefully I can switch my verdict.
Pros
Rough, but truly fitting medieval aesthetic
Music is a real treat and captures the whimsy of the setting
Crafting and territory upgrading creates a stellar player focused economy
PvP is challenging with areas changing sides constantly
Cons
Extremely detrimental lose of upgrade points
Combat provides little feedback with actions often not syncing
Stuttering, random frame rate drops and action delays for most UI commands
Massive pop ins

Blackgaurds is one of the most addicting games I have played and has been a great game to start out 2014 for me. This game has some of the best voice acting and music I've heard and its gameplay feels like it actually melds with the story. Quite a few times you'll be presented with interesting alternatives in combat most wouldn’t think of in a turn based RPG. You could go the classic route and just beat the baddies in a one on one fight, or if you’re feeling creative lure them into hazards that you normally wouldn't think of. For instance lure them into a bush then set it on fire or release a group of prisoners to fight for you. Even some battles have great story elements. Need to collect some mushrooms while a giant troll is guarding them. Distract the troll and gather the mushrooms, then run. It’s these types of options that make you feel like you’re having an impact and cause you to think outside the box. The few problems I do have with the game mostly revolve around a few graphical glitches and sometimes the enemy AI can be a little too slow. Graphical glitches like people suddenly having mouths that stretch way too far when they speak or the amount of a silver currency you earned being blocked has happened to me. While the biggest flaw is probably the AI, I like how you can set traps for them but when an enemy chooses to continually get burned in a bush and not leave it that’s when I call stupid on the AI. These bugs can be annoying but they don't break the game and I recommend this game to any RPG or Turn-Based Strategy fan.

At a glance, Blackguards is a fun foray into the turn-based tactical genre. The system is both simple and overly complex at the same time, but it balances out nicely. The graphics and the storyline certainly aren't anything to write home about, but for a turn-based game they are more than acceptable - after all, the real focus of any turn-based strategy game is going to be the combat, not the sparkling wit or crisp graphics.
Unfortunately, the combat is where things really fall apart.
That's not to say that the combat system itself is at fault. It's passable, and roughly analogous to Dungeons & Dragons. The real problem is that many of the set-piece battles are designed to be inherently unfair. Even on the easiest difficulty, you'll often struggle with scenarios that are designed to be one step short of impossible. You'll often find your character(s) stripped of their equipment and forced to use random items that you don't have the skill to use. You'll often find yourself thrown into insane battlefields filled with literally dozens of hidden traps, endless hordes of respawning opponents, or obtuse victory conditions that require you to interact with five or more scattered pieces of scenery. Somewhere along the line, the designers seem to have gotten just a bit too clever about their level designs, inadvertantly making many encounters more frustrating than fun.
Fortunately, the developers made several adjustments as the game went through early release - so if you can power through the first two chapters (Chapter Two is particularly frustrating), then you'll find that the game opens up a good deal. At that point it becomes a much more enjoyable experience, although still occasionally plagued with annoyingly obtuse map design (one optional "arena" map can easily take an hour or more to finish due to it's maze-like design and infinitely spawning enemies).
If you're a hardcore strategy gamer, then Blackguards is certainly worth buying. For anyone even slightly more casual, though, you should probably give Blackguards a pass.

I had fights like this before, and I got through them by just reloading for two hours until the RNG finally turned into my favor.  Here is an example:
In one fight, turn one, my main character would get shot and fall on his♥♥♥♥♥about 90% of the time. That means the fight is over - I lacked the DPS to win and he would just continually be shot down. There is nothing you can do against this either. You cannot prepare for fights - all spells etc. can only cast once you are IN the fight. So right away 9/10 cases, I had to reload. If my character managed to dodge, I now had to get a very specific spell of to make sure he wont get shot down every single time. However, the spell barely ever got used so it failed in 3/10 cases. If it failed, reload.
So right away I could only progress in 3% of the cases. Of course the rest of the fight also included a lot of luck.
Sure with a different character build that wouldnt have happened - but if the game is only beatable with some very specific builds than either dont give the players the option to build their characters, or rebalance the fights.
This is the main problem of Blackguards - the game is not skillbased, its largely RNG. That means that dicerolls decide outcomes of fights, not your skill or ingenuity. This makes the whole experience hugely frustrating.
And its not frustrating in a good way. In Dark Souls, it is extremely frustrating but you know its your fault, and if you get good enough, if you finally figure all the patterns out, you beat it, and its awesome. In Blackguards, you beat a frustrating fight and the only thing you feel is 'finally its over'. Because its not skill that won the fight, its just that for pure random chance the dice have fallen in your favor.
Almost every fight in the game is like this. The few fights that arent usually have a very simple to figure out environmental danger that you have to activate in order to basically get a free win.
Until this game actually gets balanced, dont buy it.

In the first you started with nothing, got better graphics, controls, music and so on. In the 2nd game you start with like 16-bit graphics or something and already have music. Then go BACK to 8-bit or something (I don't know if these terms are correct), then you go forward again to 3D-graphics. The feeling of progress is lost because of this.

There is no shortage of arcade style twin-stick shooters on Steam, we're all well aware of that.  Furious Angels adds another tally mark to that list.  However, while it doesn't take the genre or the core mechanics very far in any new direction, what it does add makes for a game that feels distinctly different from the thick soup of clunky similar games.
The first thing I noticed after starting up the game, outside of the fact that you're thrown pretty much immediately in to the action, is that the flight mechanics force you to manage your movement with a lot of drift and curve compensation.  Rather than working on a principle of precision control like other twin-sticks, accelerating will create momentum in the corresponding direction, so if you attempt to turn, you won't immediately go that way, but rather make an arching curve dependent on your speed.  While you don't need to be worried about smashing in to the sides of the level like Geometry Wars, you do still need to be able to adjust to avoid the massive amount of enemy fire.  This comes in to play more as you encounter enemies with more damaging and precise weapons, as often a hit or two will be all it takes to bring your run to an abrupt end.  What this mainly did is make the game look much more fluid and play in a way that requires a bit more skill in maneuvering and dodging.
Furious Angels seems as though it was designed with a goal of minimalism beyond all else.  From the very start you're given a menu that exists as text integrated into the game space at an angle, originally aligning itself with the carrier you take off from.  You can even effectively play the game using only a mouse.  There's also little in the way of a UI anywhere on the screen during gameplay.  Score gain floats away from destroyed enemies, upgrade countdowns and other pertinent information floats around your ship.  Even your ship health is a mystery as it is only indicated by some flashing that is incredibly easy to miss in the fast pace and explosive gameplay.  This certainly adds to the unique properties of the game, there are places that it is definitely missed.
While I am a fan of indie arcade games, and I find this game mechanically sound, it's hard to keep playing it solely to climb up the scoreboard.  Especially with how frustrating the upgrade system can be, given that each new upgrade slows you down in the process of giving you more armor and armament, meaning eventually you're just cannon fodder.  Yet, it seems like a game as well crafted as this is mechanically would have more overall content.  Something like permanent upgrades for your ship, or some sort of consumable.   Maybe cosmetic unlocks like new backgrounds, a night mode, skins, special game modes, or even just some variation in the order and components of each wave.  A game that has a gameplay loop that can still manage to keep me challenged and entertained even without the prospect of unlocks or rewards is impressive on its own, but with good additions that include things like that, it would be one I'd have a hard time putting down.  It's clear with the description of the game and the  current design that the developer has no intention of taking the game in this direction – it is as arcade as arcade can be.
Furious Angels joins the elite club of games I can jump in and play for 10 or 15 minutes at a time and feel satisfied having done so.  It may not always be as fun as I wanted, and there's a really high chance I'll die to a random hit when I assumed I had more health than I did, but the simplicity really makes it addicting.  When you couple that with a reasonable price (easily under $5 on sale), Furious Angels earns a recommendation.  It's just one of those games that looks nice
in a video and then you play it and understand why it manages to look fluid and action packed in every snippet.

Pros:

Cons:

A word of warning that learning and getting decent at the game mechanics takes time and practice, try out the demo to see if the game is a good fit for you. A lot of the negative reviews I see are from people buying this, getting wiped and making claims like the enemies have aimbots, or they spawn endlessly, etc. All of that is modular, and only on the absolute highest difficulty does the AI approach feeling like it has an aimbot, and that is because they decide to aim for the head, just like a player would. Another common complaint I see is that stealth is not supported. It is actually, and is one of my favorite ways to play, all you need is to pick up the cloak cyber upgrade from the shop. It is dirt cheap, and affordable after the tutorial level. Between the cloak and using the ghost ability(the one you start with)  to distract guards, you can 100% play it stealthily, but hiding in dark shadows doesn't do anything because you are fighting enhanced soldiers with built in night vision. I love using the cloak to get into a secluded corner, hacking into the cyberbrains of enemies and either making their heads explode, or  forcing them to shoot their allies. Or if psychic powers are more your flavor, you can cloak and run around lifting cars and buses with your mind and slamming them down on your helpless enemies like some sort of vengeful ghost. Or maybe you just want to use your cloak to get your fat♥♥♥♥♥in the middle of a large group of enemies and then reveal yourself all decked out in the heaviest armor and a minigun. The game gives you a ton of fun ways to accomplish the objectives and tear up your enemies, but you need to leave the expectations you are carrying from other games at the door.

I'll be entirely honest.  It's an interesting looking game with an interesting looking world and lore, however, the people who worked on it clearly have no idea what they're doing and it really shows.  The tutorial is basically a series of 144p videos with a little bit of text to tell you what to do.  The mechanics like Psi abilities aren't ever explained, and things like mapping abilities and actions to the action wheel isn't expalined either, making healing an extreme chore in the early game.
Unless you've got a friend who will walk you through exactly how to play the game and teach you ever mechanic that the game refuses to tell you about, then just pass.
If you do manage to get used to the game and figure out the basics, then you'll find that the game is full of different design quirks and features that completely contradict one another.  The Karma system is used to make sure you don't become a complete, mindless, psychopath.  That doesn't really mesh well with the open ended nature of how the game plays.  On top of that, the Karma system punishes the player for killing animals, which are one of the main enemy types.  There are literally missions where you just go insane constantly because of a hilariously bad design flaw.  Compound this with the incredibly linear way the game wants you to play and you end up with an experience that just doesn't keep you engaged.  Why give the player such a huge variety of choices on how to tackle a situation if only one single method of attack leads to success and every other leads to the player getting completely vaporized by every enemy in the map?  One early mission in particular involves the player wandering around a series of canals planting bombs all the while a Fed gunship zips around the map with a deadly arsenal of obscenely accurate weapons.  On top of that, the ship is completely silent and you have no way of seeing it coming becuse there's a dense layer of fog covering the map.  No way to get around it, no way to evade.  If you get caught you just have to eat a resurrector and be on your way (that is if you have the Cloak unlocked.  If you don't, well then good luck).
The entire game feels like it was designed by two opposing forces with two completely different views on how the game should be, and it ends up falling into the players' lap as a mess of brilliant worldbuilding mixed with poor design, and even poorer execution.

I found out about Gloria Victis about a year ago, didn't take much notice at first. I played Mortal online for a long time, and with its many flaws, it was a great concept for a game.
Gloria Victis is exactly what I went to Mortal for, a open world sandbox that I could explore, enjoy, and thrive in.
Gloria gives players a world where they can go out and really feel like a part of a world, with imo great level design, you go out gathering resources for various purposes, crafting goods for various purposes, fight over territory in a simple but great territory control system I can only assume is inspired by planetside. Crafting takes time and effort to become competent, having to learn the system and work towards gathering all the resources to craft the best items.
These developers are some of the best I've ever come into contact. And they really love working with their community to make changes to the game that are gonna make the game fun.
Cuz in end, that's their goal. To make a fun to play, deep, rpg. Where skill really comes into play, and with a big world to explore.
Just to give a comparison, this game is like Planetside and mount and blade had a baby and spit out a low fantasy mmo.

Ok, this is a very good idea for a game but I do feel it needs some work in terms of polish.  It's also not much of a game, really an exam in engineering.
Personally I think a few optimisations would be nice to make this more fun and engaging.
1. Too much language in the initial instance and poorly written.
2. Interface is clunky.  Click to select, click to drop, MMB for selecting wire points which don't snap properly.  Then moving parts around the board don't keep the wires attached.  There is huge room for improvement here - though it is a good start as it does looks nice.
3. Design language.  Perhaps there's a reason I'm missing but why not use the same image for a NOR chip in the inventory as on the board?
4. Game.  Ok, this feels much more like an exam than a puzzle game (though I appreciate this in a way).  However, it is a sudden and sharp learning curve for anyone who is new to the subject.  Consider making the tutorial a series of levels instead of a tutorial with far more problems to solve in a far longer learning curve.
I like this game, but you do need time and plenty of it - no criticism there.  But time spent in a game is usually to enjoy it rather than fight an interface and reach your ability limit before finishing even the tutorial.  Though to be fair I am a bit stupid...

Hardware Engineering is an interesting concept, but unfortunately the execution still needs a little work. The English in the tutorial text/component descriptions are especially distracting and confusing at times, which is
in a game that is trying to teach you the fundamentals of digital logic. Additionally, certain actions (in my case, removing wires) take an unusually long amount of time to perform. It's a shame, too, because the information it teaches is real, accurate, and quite valuable.
This is not to say that it doesn't work at all; it does. It's just quite clunky and awkward in its execution at the moment. The issues I have with the game can be easily fixed (cleaning up the text, and working on some minor hitches); it's just a matter of what the next few patches look like.
Hardware Engineering has the potential to be great, and at $5, it would be a steal if it were a bit more polished, but unfortunately I cannot recommend it as-is at the date of review (September 29th).

Evoland 2 is a much needed improvement to the mediocure original release. It takes you along a fantastic journey and had me hooked from the very beginning and I enjoyed every moment of it!

: The key word for evoland 2 is probably variety. The game has decided to combine elements of tonnes of different other genres into their game. These includes modes like shoot em up, Rhythm, Professor layton style puzzles, platforming, turn based strategy and so many more! Each of these modes aren't half done and just put together really quickly either. There all fully fleshed out with a lot of depth to them and could perhaps make complete games in their own right.
: It features tonnes of references to movies, games and TV shows as well as others. Some are rather obscure and others are very stand out but all of them add a lot to the overall experience. These include things like doctor who, mario, zelda, star trek and probably loads more that I didn't even notice! I believe they even made a reference to themselves at one point by making fun of the random encounters in the first game.
: One of my biggest flaws about the original evoland was the boring story that it had. But this isn't the same with the sequel. The game is a wonderful intriguing story that holds itself well throughout the entire game. It features twists and turns. Each character is unique its own way and there are loads for you to talk to you. The dialog each character gives you is fantastic and it really gives them a personality. The story is set among time periods as you travel backwards and fowards through time.
: Each time period has it's own unique graphics style. They represent different periods in the eras of RPG's. The game styilizes these periods excellently and manages to put so much detail into them. I'm particularly fond of the games present era which I believe to be styilized the best of them all and I was always amazed by the beauty of it whenever exploring the world.
: A wonderfully crafted soundtrack full of so many different songs. Each area you explore seemingly has a different track attached to it. The game even has varients of many of the tracks for different eras of gaming. The tracks perfectly fit the areas you are exploring and greatly and to the experience.
: The main story took me a full 21 hours to complete. A great length and such a difference to the original that only took me 3 hours to complete. There is still tonnes more for me to do in the game as I am currently at 70% progress.
: Some of the best bosses I have seen in a game before. Each are unique and completely different to anything i've seen before. They are all frustrating difficult to complete though. The final boss took me over an hour to complete.
: If you absolutely loved the original then you definitely won't find the same experience here. It doesn't teach you about the eras of RPG's very much at all in this game. It definitely isn't it's main focus. But instead you manage to get a well fleshed out experience. I'm neutral on this because I believe the original concept of the evolution of RPG's was too limiting for them to fill a full game with it.
: I did manage to unfortunately experience a few game breaking bugs throughout. These included getting stuck in the world and a boss fight that froze and wouldn't finish. They hit me a few times meaning I had to restart the game to be able to continue. They were frustrating. But luckily you shouldn't have to deal with these problems. I posted onto the steam forums these bugs and the devs managed to fix them within only a few hours!
: The game features a leveling system when you pick up experience points. When you level up you gain either life, defence or attack statistics. The problem I have with this is that you don't actually get to choose what's upgraded. The game chooses it for you leaving it feel rather pointless. The other problem I have is that the entire world seems to level up and get stronger with you meaning you don't feel the progression. This may be more of a general problem I have with all RPG's though.
: I would strongly recommend a controller for this game. Keyboard has horrible key bindings that can't be changed.
I mean overall evoland 2 is a fantastic well fleshed out RPG with tonnes of variety and a great story. My negatives aren't too big of an issue and won't cause you to have too bad of an experience. So I think this game should appeal to everyone and should definitely be played by everyone! The price may seem a bit steep but for the amount of content you get it is well worth it!

Evoland 2, the spiritual successor to Evoland 1, manages to fuse a whole lot of stuff together in really unique and creative ways. It takes you back through gaming history while providing an deep storyline of its own!
You play as a traditional band of four heroes who eventually travel through time to reach different "resolutions", including 8-bit, 16-bit and 3D! As the group travels throughout these time periods, they discover a variety of conflicts that all lead to an overarching goal.
The story starts quite simple, but becomes very complex by the end of the game. Expect plot holes, which are not necessarily a negative in my view as they create a lot of discussion about the game! One of the strongest parts of the game, though, is its writing! There's a lot of tongue and cheek humor mixed with really great character development. Kuro and the gang will be in my memory for a looong time.
As marketed, there are A LOT of gameplay styles in Evoland 2. Overworld RPG is the predominant style, but expect to see a lot of platforming, puzzle solving and even a good amount of Fire Emblem-like combat! There are sprinkles of DDR, gem-swapping, and Street Fighter gameplay as well, just to name a few! Some of these styles are implemented better than others, but there's a convinient in-game difficulty swap if you find something too hard (or easy!)
The art and soundtrack are beautiful and take hints from Evoland 1 in some cases. It's unfortunate that there aren't different soundtracks for each time period, though. However, the pixel art and 3D modeling is top notch! Look out for gaming culture references - the developers have a particular gripe against Link for some reason xD
I've experienced a few bugs, which including textures not loading and the character getting stuck in an area. They force me to quit and restart the game, but there's an excellent checkpoint system so you'll only lose about 1-2 minutes of gameplay.
I consider Evoland 2 a must-buy for retro gamers and RPG/JRPG players! It's also great for introducing people to gaming, as it covers basically everything gaming has to offer!

TL,DR
Pros:
- Great environment and level design
- Good voice acting and main characters seem to have interesting personalities
Cons:
- Stealth doesn't feel real and breaks immersion
- Autosave trolls you by saving right before your death
- Your stealth indicator is a GLOW (seriously...)
- Reusing the same face and some small outfit variants for all guards I encountered on the first 3 levels
I wanted to love this game after reading the reviews, but although I love stealth games, this isn't stealth. Guards can't see you even when they're looking directly at you as long as you're standing in a shadow zone and your arm is glowing (they decided to make you glow bright when you're stealthed? how does that help the immersion?) The only way I found to effectively kill people without being detected is resorting to invisibility or throwing knives that can one shot. Both are limited so once you run out you can either go back to trying broken stealth, or just find a route where no one will see you and you won't have to kill anyone, which works but is absolutely no fun.
It is a shame because besides the main mechanic of the game being terrible, the game looks very nice. Not in terms of graphics (although they are definitely not bad), but in terms of level design and world building. The levels I played were quite big, with lots of alternative routes and a great sense of verticality, which is great for a stealth game that is all about exploring your surroundings and finding the best strategy.
I wouldn't consider recommending this game unless you don't care about having to break the game to progress. For me personally, playing a stealth game is all about immersion and feeling invisible. Instead here I feel like an elephant in a room, playing with broken mechanics to kill someone. I'm making dodge rolls in plain line of sight of guards and they just keep repeating their line over and over without giving a single ♥♥♥♥. But hey it's normal, since my arm is GLOWING they can't see me!
On top of this, I've had frequent autosave issues where it saved my game 0.1s before me getting killed and if I was lucky enough I could save my♥♥♥♥♥by triggering the invisibility power right about when the loading screen fades out. I've had to restart zones several times because of that and reading through the negative reviews I now see I am far from being the only one. This coupled with the broken stealth system completely broke my immersion and I just couldn't keep on playing.
I want to restate I really wanted to like this game and I still think the level designers did a great job at creating a very cool environment for a stealth game. The problems I encountered were too distracting for me to be able to really enjoy it unfortunately. Maybe later into the game things get more interesting and less tedious, but 2 hours of playtime is all I will give it, at least for now.

Styx: Master of Shadows is pretty cool I guess.
A prequel to the game I never played: Of Orcs and Men, you play as Styx, a runty goblin creature that looks strangely like me to the point that I think I should collect royalties. Styx (the goblin, not the band) has infiltrated the human city-tower of Arkenash in search of the heart of the World-Tree. The heart of the World-Tree is the source of all amber, a substance that, much like LSD, allows the user to do some crazy magical stuff.
Plagued by horrible, unexplainable head aches, our green little friend sets out to free a "friend" and take the heart from the tree from the humans and those smelly hippy elves.
Styx: Master of sneaks was actually a really nice surprise for me. Recommended to me by Dibbin, who also looks like a goblin, he told me that it was a stealth game that returned to form, and how right he was. Styx plays almost like one of the original Thief games, something that caught me off guard after all those "stealth" games that were just action games in a thinly veiled cloak.
To survive, Styx has to remain in the shadows, hide behind and under objects, stick to the high ground, or take the less-trodden, and sometimes more daring, alternative paths.  The game is entirely built around doing so, giving Styx a plethora of abilities, magic spells, and items that allow him to dispatch or flat out avoid patrolling guards. With all this, it's understandable that combat is an after thought, with it becoming just a little timing event where you have to parry your enemies a certain number of times before you can do them in with your giant goblin knife.
Seriously, it's Crocodile Dundee huge.
With the combat being as crummy as it is, I would recommend playing the game at it's highest difficulty, where your options for getting caught is either flight or death, with a few exceptions like having a spare throwing knife at hand. This makes the game punish you for not being sneaky enough and it's not even that much harder than one of the lower difficulties, outside of getting caught, I mean.
There were a few journalists that knocked points off Styx for it's combat. But these people apparently tried to fight their way through a stealth game, so you should listen to me instead because I'm smarter and much more handsome.
The levels in Styx are huge, with each mission making up of 3 to 6 large areas that could each be a mission in their own rights. And the game rewards you for exploring them, with collectibles and even spare items to stock up while you're on your journey. You're also given a handful of secondary objectives to complete that usually does take you off the straight path, forcing you to risk discovery if you're looking for that sweet sweet 100%.
Styx himself is surprisingly likable as well. I can't seem to find his voice actor's name but if anyone knows, I would to know him. While Styx's voice could have just been generic goblin-sounding, instead we get a charming and charismatic tone that goes well with the character. Styx is sarcastic, humorous, determined, and cunning, and all of this is brought to life through his superb voice work. Though I can't say the same for the rest of the cast, going for a generic English accent, but I can't really blame them for that, considering most of them are just generic guards.
But should you play: Styx: Hamster of battles?
I would say yes, though it's not for everyone. My only complaint with the game is that sometimes the platforming has a fart, but most of that can be fixed with a little bit of patience. The game is not accesible to everyone, especially the more combat orientated people. But if you're looking for a good, deep stealth game that will last you a few hours, look no further.

The game has been out for a long time now, and I picked it up in a recent sale. I always saw it flying around but never bothered to pay it any attention. Well this time it was cheap enough to pique my interest, and the game turned out to be not at all what I expected, but in a good way.
I knew it was from the Of Orcs and Men series and as such I thought it would play like it, but it is in fact a really fun and challenging little stealth game with a surprisingly entertaining story. On the story front, the game tries it's best to turn traditional fantasy tropes onto their head and I'd say it does this quite nicely. You play as a Goblin called Styx, who's race in this universe is considered utter vermin and disgusting by Humans, Elves, AND Orcs. You will hear you character called a "creature" and a "monster" for basically the entire game, really driving home that everyone despises your kind. But the catch here is that Styx is blatantly a better individual and more intelligent than anyone you ever encounter for the journey despite looking like a typical, dirty and ugly goblin. It really drives home the fact that Humans and Elves are a disgusting, close-minded pair of races that you honestly never end up feeling bad about butchering. Because the game naturally makes you feel that they deserve it.
The gameplay is very standard for a stealth game but it's a formula that works. The game is by no means AAA and was obviously made on a lowish budget but please don't let this put you off. The level design is great and is semi-open world, and there are plenty of situations where you have to genuinely use your brain to get by certain obsticles. You thankfully have plenty of tools and powers at your disposal, so sky's the limit. The game can be a bit buggy at times which is to be expected. I've had guards unfairly notice me quite a few times and had the odd one or two climbing blunder, and have some abilities/passives not work correctly, but they were such a minor issue that I can't really complain.
Buy this game. Support the smaller companies. There's a second Styx came coming out this year which I myself will definitely be checking out.

Blackguards combines engaging tactical combat with a pretty nifty story. It's pretty much what D&D Tactics wished it could have been, even though I personally liked that as well. The amount of freedom you have when it comes to upgrading your characters is quite welcome as wel, as is the interactive objects on the battlfield. If you're the kind of person who even just thinks this game looks interesting, chances are you'll love it.

I don't write reviews for games often, but i felt the need to review this game being it's getting "mixed" reviews.  Blackguards is one of those games that is not going to give you instant gratification.  After playing it for a couple of hours I initially logged out and went back to another RPG thinking to myself that it was not very fun.  Well after going back to it a few times and progressing through the game I've determined i love the game.  It takes some time to figure out the combat system and how to get a feel for the ebonflow.  It is highly strategic and combat can be approached many different ways using the battlefield, spells, usable inventory and special abilities, this is where the game really shines, it has a difficult and somewhat different system than most RPGs I've played.
If you dislike a true roll based game where you expect to push x spell and it hit your enemy, do not buy.  This game will drive you crazy sometimes in that regard, the battles can be long and having your caster miss twice in a row with your entire party down really brings me back to the Nintendo days of smashing my controller into the screen.  However this is part of the appeal to me.  And yes somewhat less but the enemies do bork their spells ocassionally too so it is a little fair in that regard.
If you dislike having to study a game with a totally different feel than what you are used to, in regards to stats, abilities, and tactics, do not buy.
If you love a good challenge and are willing to spend some trial and error learning the system, it is extremely fun and the play is flawless, i've seen no bugs or problems other than the Head and Foot Icon on the character pane reversed.  I've only put a few days into the game but can say that it has grown on me with each battle and i can see where the replay on it will be high since each battle really is totally different and your tactics are very modifiable.  I'd give this game a 8/10 thus far and believe it's one of the better RPGs on the market right now.  Thanks for reading.

Finding Paradise is an amazing game. It feels like a familiar old friend, but then does something completely different with its narrative structure. Freebird has succeeded in creating something very meaningful and relatable by telling another wonderful story about growing up and looking back.
Now this is an RPG Maker game, and that will turn a few people off of playing it. However, despite the limitations of the engine, the game is able to tell a wonderful story not just through text but through the action of its character, as well as its camera movements. You have to give major props to the developer that they were able to craft a very well put-together audiovisual experience through just sprites.
Speaking of audiovisual, the score and soundtrack is top notch again. The audio is mixed very well with the movement of the game, and the song hits at the perfect spot at the climax to really drive home the narrative.
I would say though that there might be a few too many mini-games that take you out of the narrative, or that there are a few jokes there that is probably out of place within the context of the current scene, but really it just adds to Neil Watts' personality.
Even though the story stands on its own, I really wouldn't recommend playing this before To the Moon. This game pretty much assumes that you are aware of the universe and how it works, and really, this story works better if you already have an expectation on how the operation should go.
Finally and the most importantly, this game is for you if you enjoyed To the Moon or any other bittersweet or tear-jerking stories. Nothing feels like padding. It's all meat here that will make your eyes water as soon by the first bite because it's the best steak you've ever tasted.

Evoland 2, the spiritual successor to Evoland 1, manages to fuse a whole lot of stuff together in really unique and creative ways. It takes you back through gaming history while providing an deep storyline of its own!
You play as a traditional band of four heroes who eventually travel through time to reach different "resolutions", including 8-bit, 16-bit and 3D! As the group travels throughout these time periods, they discover a variety of conflicts that all lead to an overarching goal.
The story starts quite simple, but becomes very complex by the end of the game. Expect plot holes, which are not necessarily a negative in my view as they create a lot of discussion about the game! One of the strongest parts of the game, though, is its writing! There's a lot of tongue and cheek humor mixed with really great character development. Kuro and the gang will be in my memory for a looong time.
As marketed, there are A LOT of gameplay styles in Evoland 2. Overworld RPG is the predominant style, but expect to see a lot of platforming, puzzle solving and even a good amount of Fire Emblem-like combat! There are sprinkles of DDR, gem-swapping, and Street Fighter gameplay as well, just to name a few! Some of these styles are implemented better than others, but there's a convinient in-game difficulty swap if you find something too hard (or easy!)
The art and soundtrack are beautiful and take hints from Evoland 1 in some cases. It's unfortunate that there aren't different soundtracks for each time period, though. However, the pixel art and 3D modeling is top notch! Look out for gaming culture references - the developers have a particular gripe against Link for some reason xD
I've experienced a few bugs, which including textures not loading and the character getting stuck in an area. They force me to quit and restart the game, but there's an excellent checkpoint system so you'll only lose about 1-2 minutes of gameplay.
I consider Evoland 2 a must-buy for retro gamers and RPG/JRPG players! It's also great for introducing people to gaming, as it covers basically everything gaming has to offer!

Nighogg is a lean game hyper focused on one thing, stabbing your enemies. For some games a singular focus like this can be a detriment, but its Nighoggs greatest asset. Death comes quickly and frequently, but is rarely frustrating. The pace is fast and furious, but balanced and easy to navigate visually. The action is easy to pick up, but difficult to master. The music and art are wonderful, minimalist but communicative. On top of all that, the ending of each match results in your character being engufed by the "Nidhogg." The game is pure in such a fundamental way, its a joy to both win and lose.
The goal of Nidhogg is to consistently defeat your respawning opponent, and progress through various screens which serve as both progress markers and battlefields. The refinement of the action, and the strength of the core gameplay loop make every duel a a battle of wits and dexterity. A large array of tactics and tricks are available, from dodging and ducking, to tackling and thrusting, even cartwheeling and catapulting swords are viable techniques, and those are only the beginning. All this murderous depth fuels Nighogg's controlled chaos allowing for a multitude of play styles and strategies further layering the competitive action. I've spent minutes in nail biting stalemates, deadlocked, the balance swinging back and forth. The tension during these moments is palpable, an audience of my friends has many a time erupted with cheering when the stalemate finally breaks. It is endlessly satisfying to win, and horribly crushing to lose, but fun the entire way through.
Another strong point to note is the art style and music. The art is minimalist but meshes well with the pace of the game play. The animation is also very fluid. Its also very exaggerated, which can lead to some very silly moments. The colored viscera and blood staining the floor and walls is a great touch. It adds character to many of the arenas. Overall I really enjoyed the visual aesthetic. Nidhoggs music is fast, loud, and detailed. The layers of instrumentation have a lot of depth on there own, and combined with the wales and cry's from the dying, it builds a wonderful cacophony of sonic violence it layers atop the action. The music, along with the art, helped establish a tone and aesthetic that I've come to really appreciate.
In the way of criticisms, I found a few things disappointing. For one, many of the maps are poorly balanced and not much fun to play on. 'Castle' was really the only consistently viable map, with the others serving as nice distractions, but never really progressing much further then that. In spite of this though, 'Castle' is so well made and wonderfully tuned for death and destruction that it more then makes up for the rest of the map's short comings. Next, I found the online multiplayer to be completely unplayable. The input delay, and general lag completely destroyed any semblance of coherence and quickly showed how poor the online functionality was. Overall, Styx was an incredible experience for me. I would not pay $30, but grabbing it on a sale (it was $7.5 in the last sales) is a great deal

Overall, Styx: Master of Shadows is a solid title.
Pros:
-The level design is fantastic! For any given map, there are almost always 2-3 ways to pass a given section.
-You suck at combat. However, for the purpose of a stealth game, this is actually a great decision, as you have to play the role of a rogue and find creative ways to avoid or kill off your foes.
-The game gives you a wide variety of tools to complete the levels, such as poisoning enemies, dropping chandeliers on their heads, and even creating a clone of Styx.
-Styx is actually a lovable, evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don’t know why, but his constant cursing and death threats are infinitely amusing.
Mixed:
-The plot starts off sounding quite bland and uninspired; you’re given literally zero back story. The game does later justify this, and I found the narrative to be more compelling during the latter half of the game, but the execution in itself is a bit messy.
Cons:
-The biggest issue the game faces is that it backtracks to almost every single map in the game. I found that while the gameplay for the first half of the game, when the maps were new, was utterly fantastic. However, doing the exact same set of maps again, in the exact opposite order and direction that I first completed them detracted from the experience.
-The game's limited dialogue is typically put on repeat, so you'll occasionally hear the exact same exchanges between guards ad nauseam.
-The game automatically makes you automatically climb onto most ledges. I found this to be confusing, as the game clearly has a perk which allows you to kill enemies that are standing on a ledge directly above. Additionally, in the few cases where you don’t automatically climb onto a ledge, there’s clearly an animation for you to crawl sideways along the ledge. It’s not a huge issue, but it can be a bit annoying.
Tips:
-Save often; using the quicksave feature regularly will make your experience infinitely more enjoyable. (This should be the f5 button.)
-If you’re going for a “KILL EVERYTHING!” play through like I did, then I’d highly recommend picking up the “Cover Kill” skill.

A very challenging but interesting tatical RPG with puzzle like battle maps.  And by that I mean the battle map may be unbeatable if you don't figure out which enviornmental trap to use at what time and figuring out how to get the enemy to stand where that trap will be most effective.
While the games tatical battles are quit enjoyable due to this puzzle aspect, at the same time can be frustrating because you can end up spending hours having to try and retry a map to only figure out that in addition to the puzzle you already solved but keep losing at you need to rebalance your attack/parry skill points on your weapon type for the fight in addition to solving the puzzle. Which brings me to the only thing I have come across so far in my play that I have disliked about the game, the combination between having no way to gather more xp since each map seems to be doable only once with the fact that there does not seem to be a way to respec where you allocated your xp. I don't mind that the game does not allow you to grind to over level stuff, infact I like that it prevents you from doing that, but it also means that if you spent all your xp in the wrong areas you can reach a point to where a battle becomes unbeatable because you have all the wrong skills win.  Maybe later in the story it allows you to realocate xp at the cost of gold or something, but currently where I am in the story I can see mismanagment of xp making the game unbeatable.
With that said, despite this one major consern with the games mechanics dealing with xp I would say it is a very enjoyable though sometimes frustrating game. I would say play this game on normal difficulty and if you get stuck on a puzzle don't feel bad having to turn it down to "easy", because some battle maps are hard to complete even on easy unless you have the perfect build where no xp was spent in the wrong place. And as I say this game is definitly worth picking up might I just suggest that for a few of the puzzles do not sell your torches even if your close on weight limits because you will come across some puzzles that become 100x easier to solve with having more then just a mage to use fire damage.
Edit: Also the soundtrack is pretty good, is it $20 of value good, eh, to most people no, but just putting it out there for those debating on picking up the regular edition or the one that comes with the soundtrack.

Evoland 2 for the most part is a throwback JRPG, but throughout the game the gameplay changes. From overhead slasher and turned based fighting to a platformer or even a street fighter style fighter. This may seem like way too much for one game to have, but all of the segments are done well and are tons of fun. Another great part to Evoland 2 is the endless easter eggs and references to other classic games. (Everything from Super Mario to Metal Gear Solid) Throughout the game you get to travel through different time periods trying to figure out who you are as well as helping your friend return to her home. While you are going through the different time zone the games graphics change from SNES all the way to full 3d. I am not the biggest fan of this game genre, but I can really appreciate a good game when I play one. Evoland 2 does almost everything right. The two things that I didn’t like about this game. The first glaring problem is the many glitches, sound and visually. I had many problems with in game sound constantly repeating even when trying to reload the game. (I had to completely close and restart the game to fix the problem) The second issue I had was the fact that the games combat didn’t really become harder after the first 4 hours, but the change of gameplay helped fix this for me. Aside from these two problems I enjoyed every second of my time playing Evoland 2 and would highly suggest picking it up.

10/10! This game is a dream for anyone who has been playing action/adventure games and RPGs since the NES. Picture old school versions of Zelda, Ninja Gaiden, Bomber Man, Chrono Trigger, Raiden, Double Dragon, FF Tactics, and more rolled into one game.
The bulk of the game is similar to Zelda, but certain levels switch to completely different game types, constantly keeping you on your toes. Each game type feels fully fleshed out, not just a mini game. As for mini games: it has a card game in the heart of FF 8 & 9 that is very addicting. There are a few moments where the game can be aggressively difficult (I'm looking at you "Rythm Game" mode), which is true to the games they are paying homage to. This is not just a throwback trying to cash in on gamer nostalgia, this is a game that creatively shifts in ways that help tell the story and keep the gameplay fresh.
Evoland 2 is rife with referrences to other games from most of gaming history: Mario to Bioshock Infinite, and lovingly borrows from them where it can. As an avid console gamer from the late eighties through to the new millenium, this game is equal parts a walk down memory lane and an elegant new gaming experience. If you don't have much experience with the classics Evoland borrows from, this title probably isn't for you.

This game is a refreshing, fun take on stealth games with its flaws.
Pros-
Great stealth
Enjoyable gameplay
Many ways to beat a level
Open to creativity
Cons-
Horrible combat (should not be an issue if you play it as a stealth game....)
Bad voice acting
Story is weak (You are buying the game for the gameplay, not the story)
Clunky controls (especially annoying when you need precision to execute Parkour)
The Pros outweigh the cons. I'd recommend the game only to those that enjoy stealth games. It is great if you can get around the rough edges. I honestly think the game would be benefited by a longer development cycle. It has amazing potential.

If you like the stealth genre then you know good games are hard to come by. Dishonored is one of my favourites and Styx comes close. This is strange because honestly, this game has so much going against it.
Cons -
Terrible combat system (that's fine, because it's a stealth game, but the game still forces you into narrative combat that is unbearably frustrating.)
Really sketchy/buggy platforming
bad controls
an average story that could have been done better
poor quality cut scenes
terrible voice work (other than Styx, who I found entertaining.
Despite all this game has done stealth right. On Goblin difficulty, everything kills you pretty much instantly. There is almost no combat, because you simply die if you're caught. It's a really nice difficulty to put into a game for people who want to play a real stealth game. I also think the entire premise is just really interesting. You are severely underpowered, you are a 3 foot tall Goblin and pretty much everything else towers over you. You really have to use some ingenuity to get around that challenge. On sale this game is an exceptional deal, but I probably would be willing to pay full price now that I know how enjoyable it is.

Phew. What a ride.
I just finished this game maybe... 20 minutes ago, as of writing this review. So there's a lot that I still haven't processed yet. Heck, with To The Moon, I spent at least a couple weeks letting everything sink in. Both of these games have a lot of depth to them, but not so much that you can't follow the narrative or the characters' journeys. It's just that with a game many years in the making from a team that actually cares, a lot of love and a lot of thought goes into it. And so, naturally, I don't think you can appreciate EVERYTHING all at once. It takes a little time. That's been my experience, at least. And I'm certainly not complaining; it's hard to find games that dive this deep into our common shared emotions, worries, desires, and basic humanity - without being pretentious or convoluted.
How effortlessly the story is told, how seamlessly you can jump from heartbreak to hilarity in the blink of an eye, and how subtley this game tugs at your heartstrings... it's amazing. I only cried at the end, and I was almost confused while I was crying. "Why am I crying? But this game hasn't hit me hard enough to make me cry. Oh... wait. Actually, it has. Dang." That was basically my thought process while I was crying. Seriously. I've never had an experience like that in any medium of entertainment or art.
So... if you've actually read this far down, then is this game worth buying? Ummm...
YES.
A thousand times yes. This game had it all: heartbreak, mystery, suspense, laughs, tears, characters worth rooting for, a story worth telling, AMAZING music, and even some out-of-nowhere gameplay mixed in with the narrative. (Nicely done, Kan.) I can't think of a single reason NOT to buy this game.
Please: support everyone who worked on this game and just do it!!!

I've never written any game review before, but I felt obliged to do it with this one. There will be no spoilers whatsoever, cause ti ruin this game for someone is really a crime.
I'll start with little problems with this game to get it out of the way.
- There were little problems with launching, but I was able to launch the game. Maybe it was just Steam error, IDK, really
- Second, the gameplay per se is not really there, the game is more like a movie, but I knew it would be like it, so nothing to complain about here.
- Finally, there's no "Nextgen graphics" to be found. It's not even 3D. However, it doesn't make it any worse (It probably makes it even better).
Now to talk about positive things
+ The game is connected with previous Freebird games products, and it does contain a bit of spoilers
+ The music is absolutely amazing, it'll stay with me long after I finished playing the game
+ The plot is ... breathtaking, to say the least. I enjoy trying to predict what happens next when playing story-driven games, and  don't like when my predictions come true. I couldn't have predicted the ending of this game in my lifetime.
+ The game is messing with your emotions. There are moments when you laugh and 5 minutes later you're about to cry. Nothing compares to this.
In order not to make this a longread, Here's what I've got to say -- If you're up for a cool gameplay, puzzlesolving and drive, you probably won't like it.
"Finding Paradise" is not a movie -- it doesn't have effects and all the heroic stuff.
"Finding Paradise" is not a cartoon -- it touches themes that are really personal - questons of life, happiness, regrets and such;
"Finding Paradise" is a touching story filled with emotions accompanied by sweet music. It's a story about growing up, about dreams and about itself.
I was kinda afraid that it'd suffer from sequel syndrome but it turned out to be just as amazing as To the Moon. It's different, but a masterpiece just the same.
A simple, but remarkabe masterpiece that'll have you saying "Im not crying, I swear" more than you'd probably like.

You know what? This game is a lot of fun! I don't normally go in for simple high score repetitive games, but I really enjoyed this and found myself saying "just one more turn" for easily 20 turns after I thought I'd quit.
There's a lack of meta game or anything, but its price is right. It's really fun to drop in for a few minutes.
There's another key here. There's a variety to the gameplay in the form of upgrades, and temporary "flying tank" bonus sections. The game you're playing from one minute to the next can be quite different, and each variation on your fighter feels different, too.
I really like the enmy design, graphical style, and especially the destruction mechanics on the larger ships. It feels great to blast off the engines on an enemy carrier and watch it topple. That's not to say it's easy. You still have to get to that side of your targeted enemy, which is sometimes impossible to do without dying, so you flee instead.
The game is hard, and one criticism is it basically devolves into circle strafting large groups of enemies eventually, but what game doesn't, frankly?
Another criticism is the sound. It's not bad but a little lacking. The music is great, but the SFX lag behind a little. Still, overall this is definitely worth a go and you'll find you keep coming back.

I wish steam had a maybe option or something in between yes or no, because I would give this game a maybe, depending on how future updates come along.
This game is very simple and that is good in some parts and hurts the game in others. The game resets the leader-boards every day which is an interesting take on a ranking system. The mouse-only control scheme is also pretty interesting and feels great (with the exception of poorly timed upgrades that can send you flying away from where you intended to be). The game has a minimalist UI (to the point of it not being there, really) The problems come with playing the game for too long. There are only seven different enemies, which means the randomized waves every day feature is barely noticeable. You often die because of something randomly firing from off screen and hitting you twice (miners are the most annoying). You'er weak and have no real way of telling how close to death you are (no health bar, your ship flashes when damaged, that's all). Bigger enemies can only be hit on weak spots, which makes sense, but everything that isn't a weak point blocks your shots from hitting other place on enemies (you can't even shoot through destroyed weak spots). There are only two upgrades, one adds missiles that work on a cool-down that you have no indication of (which is annoying because you have to stop shooting and start again to launch them), and the other turns you into a tank. The tank feels nice, it is slow and powerful and can ram a lot of enemies to death, but if it takes too much damage you become even slower and lose the ability to ram anything, wasting some of your time flying slowly waiting to lose the powerup. Then you star back from your base ship. Some achievements are either a grind or require you to be the best at this game, (looking at kill 10,000 jets, play for 10 days, and finish the day at rank #1) which is only really an issue if you are an achievement hunter. But they also feel set up to inflate game time.
At this point, I would only get this game if you really want to compete. I would wait to see what comes in the future or a sale if you really want it.

10/10! This game is a dream for anyone who has been playing action/adventure games and RPGs since the NES. Picture old school versions of Zelda, Ninja Gaiden, Bomber Man, Chrono Trigger, Raiden, Double Dragon, FF Tactics, and more rolled into one game.
The bulk of the game is similar to Zelda, but certain levels switch to completely different game types, constantly keeping you on your toes. Each game type feels fully fleshed out, not just a mini game. As for mini games: it has a card game in the heart of FF 8 & 9 that is very addicting. There are a few moments where the game can be aggressively difficult (I'm looking at you "Rythm Game" mode), which is true to the games they are paying homage to. This is not just a throwback trying to cash in on gamer nostalgia, this is a game that creatively shifts in ways that help tell the story and keep the gameplay fresh.
Evoland 2 is rife with referrences to other games from most of gaming history: Mario to Bioshock Infinite, and lovingly borrows from them where it can. As an avid console gamer from the late eighties through to the new millenium, this game is equal parts a walk down memory lane and an elegant new gaming experience. If you don't have much experience with the classics Evoland borrows from, this title probably isn't for you.

There is some humorous fourth wall breaking comedy and game related comedy which gives a nice subtle nod if you know about the other franchises. But not as much as Evoland 1. This is definitely a different game from what Evoland 1 was and it is dissapointing that I am making a negative review for this title as I was looking forward to progressing through the evolution of the game industry once more.

So this game is  the perfect example of great potential, but unfortunately nothing more.
I found myself getting bored even before you've learned all of the protagonist's basic moves. Some of the upgradable abilities from the skill tree is well executed though and actually makes you feel like your upgrading your hero rather than just spending skill points on a pointless upgrade that barely enhances any of your hero's abilities. I would say that this argument leans towards the best of the bad, but the worst of the bad is without a doubt the poorly executed animations that leaves me feeling completely empty and far from convinced. The voice acting, physics and animations are way off.
In spite of its cheapended graphical- and voiceflaws the game still manages to offer satisfaction in some areas. For instance the fact that you can free roam to a fair extent, and you can drop really far down from edges and still save yourself in different ways. Also some of the kills can be artistically pulled of. Stealth kills are a bit boring and tedious though, and the same goes for lockpicking doors. Take skyrim for instance where you are given a challenge when you lockpick a door and can increase lockpicking skills by leveling up, now that's fun, but here it's just a dull execution which offers you nothing more than a waiting game. You basically end up looking at some poor animation where your hero looks in opposite directions to see if enemies are approaching and a whell in the middle showing the progress of unlocking the door. Boring.
In order for my thumb to point upwards the game needs a serious overhaul. The game's animations and physics needs to be re-polished. This pertains both in-game and during videos. Also less arcade-game vibes and more story-rich vibe. Kill the repetativeness in quests and characters - again referring to the arcade-feel of the game here i guess.
Maybe I could have given the game one more hour of game-play to see if the story unfolds a bit more and/or if I start liking the game-play, but this argument in itself is just another reason to why I would give this game thumbs down again and again.
Long story short:
Good try, but not recommended.

This is one of the greatest releases this year. You don't need to play the first to understand the story, which is nice since this is directly better than the previous one. The first switched between Legend of Zelda puzzles and dungeons, with Final Fantasy overworld and dungeons of its own. This one focuses more on the Legend of Zelda aspect, and having other game types appear as a one - time dungeon with a themed boss.
The transition between them also works a lot better, since your level carries over into everything, where the original Evoland had two different stats for every fight, making it strange to grind for a dungeon and lose the exp after you leave it. There's also a lot more variety; the game keeps it intersting by playing a full different game for an entire fight, and the only one that repeats are the Legend of Zelda dungeons, which add new mechanics each time. It goes from Mario platforming to bullet hell shooters to tactical rpgs, and even an entire boss fight in Street Fighter, with the Ryu inputs and everything. What's important is that it makes since when it changes; you do these different modes not just to take away from the main game, but as an addition, which Evoland struggled with.
There are some negatives though, and these really kill the game for me. The third "world" has a massive frame drop, making it difficult to play and tedious to watch. There are some bugs, but the major one I've encountered is the inability to kill a certain enemy in Slyph Forest, which I need to beat to continue. A walkthrough I watched had no problems with it, but every time I attack it, its invincible. Other people have similar problems here, and I really hope it gets patched soon. The layout of the dungeon means I can't leave until I complete it, meaning I cannot play the game until the next update or start a new game.
For anyone who's got the game, DO NOT enter the Slyph Forest dungeon.
Its possible for this to be the last dungeon before the final boss, so luckily its possible to see everything else this game has, but unfortunately this was the second dungeon for me. The only time I didn't like a boss fight was during the Reno fight, where the hitboxes are picky, and sometimes invisible, plus the first half took way too long. He did little damage, and had way too few openings to attack during the fight, meaning the first half alone was longer than most of the other boss fights in this game, which is dissapointing since the rest of the game paces itself really well.
I hope they add an option to refight some of the bosses, since you only get to see their mechanics once, and the system is really well designed for how short they last. I'd like it if they added some kind of option for this after beating the game, with a boss rush, or even just the ability to the battle.

TLDR: If you are into stealth games and I mean REAL STEALTH games well this game is for you. No way to fight back, if 4 enemies are on you you are dead, being hidden in the dark is the only option and much more...
