Let's be honest...in the first 10 minutes of the game I was like "What the hell am I playing?". I came from FPS and action games mostly. I even played almost all the AC series but this game was frustrating to me in the beginning. When I've started to learn it (and I took the hardest way because in my first and only play, in a moment of madness, I've chose the "Goblin mode" so the hardest difficulty) I really enjoyed it because it is a TRUE STEALTH game with no options if you mess something.
What I mean is...in the normal mode you can fight back in a duel...in the Goblin mode you can't fight back and you will die with a single hit.
The story is incredibly great.
You are a goblin in a prison inside a human fortress that was created mostly to protect "the Tree" that is the main source of Amber. Your mission is to stole the heart of it...but in your way to achive this you will encounter a lot of of plot twist and at a certain point you will think that the game will finish in a certain way but....play it and you will understand what I am talking about :P
The levels are really small and they will be repeated twice (in the beginning and in the end) but with different, and more hard, enemies. This will make them longer due to yourself thinking "HOW IN THE NAME OF GOBLINS I CAN PASS THAT CORRIDOR FULL OF ORCS???!".
Plus there are multiple ways to finish them so you will always find this game different by the choice of gameplay you make.
Gameplay as you should have understood is mostly "hit and hide and do it fast". You can hide yourself in the darkness, into barrels, closets, under the tables etc.
This is really not like AC, if they find you you are 95% dead and you cannot massacre your enemies.
If you want you can even spare the life of everyone (and you will earn bonus points if you do that) or kill them all.
At the end of every level you will gain skill points to use to improve yourself and make your life easier and easier level after level. From fighting skills to hiding ones.
The longevity of the game depends most on how you play it and at which difficulty. Let's say that if you rush and play @ easy mode you can finish it in 10/15 hours.

To get it out of the way, like all Dark Eye computer games this game is built from the ground up to appeal to the "rules lawyers" of the tabletop gaming community. The Dark Eye is like Dungeons and Dragons for people who think that what Dungeons and Dragons really needed was more math and latin.
In keeping with the analogy for Dungeons and Dragons, which I use because as a franchise it is one that most people are more familiar with, the Drakensang games were kind of like Neverwinter Nights. This game, by contrast, is more like Temple of Elemental Evil. The game is almost entirely action, incorporating as much of the nuance of the tabletop game as possible, and takes place within a turn based framework, although with the incorporation of an actual hex grid battlemap rather than the approximation thereof. The combat options are numerous and exceptional in variety, with a number of opportunities to interact with the environment lending additional depth to each of the maps. If it has any weakness, it is perhaps that it is too pure; encumberance limits and limits on the skills offered by trainers and the goods offered by merchants seems inconvenient at times. More than once I wished that I had unlocked a skill at character creation that I can no longer find a trainer for once I discovered that one of my abilities lacked the punch that I expected of it.
This is not a game for everyone, most people will probably find the experience frustrating. For gamers like me, however, it is exactly the sort of game we've been waiting for.

I have a passionate love-hate relationship with this game.
I've been thinking about recommending it forever and here's why I even struggled in the first place: The game's core is great. Some of the different gamemodes are just a blast, I especially digged the tactical rpg part, but some of them (I'm looking at you, Bejeweled) are just -horrible-. I played the entire game on hard, except for this one Bejeweled part that is literally impossible when your enemy just deals 90% of your life in a single swipe.
Apart from that, here's the deal. The game is amazing, yet it manages to annoy you every so often. Some parts are super tedious, occasionally, I just wanted to see if I could re-enter a certain gamemode or stage and then I had to play the entire level again because there's no option to turn back. Same thing with some sort of stealth segment, turns out, if you talk with a certain guard and hit yes (I wanted to see what he replied...) you go straight back into jail. However, even though there a lot of bugs and glitches, it was still super enjoyable. Because the plot is well done, the music is amazing, the gameplay feels (for the most part. ♥♥♥♥ Bejeweled.) good and the controls are tight and responsive. It really sets you back with a bazillion references to older games. I don't even want to spoil a single one, so you can experience it for yourself. So, after this short wall of text, let's review.
+ Amazing Gameplay for the most part.
+ Stunning visuals. (Mostly the Pixel Art though)
+ Amazing humour. Yes, it is THAT good.
+ Stays true to what it does. (Basically, the different gamemodes feel like they should, is what I'm trying to say.)
+ Time Travel Mechanics really add to the plot.
+ Now that I mentioned it, the plot is pretty sweet too, with a satisfying ending. (For me, that is. I did notice some people complain about it being too open ended, which is not really the case.)
- Tedious Mechanics, occasionally.
- Bejeweled
- Bugs/Glitches appear way too often, expect to restart the game or quit to title occasionally. (For example, do not open the treasure radar in the tactical rpg section.♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down.)
- Bejeweled
- Unintentional re-playing of various long and annoying sections, though I guess that was my fault.
- Bejeweled
TL;DR:
Good game, you should give it a shot, ♥♥♥♥ Bejeweled.

This isn't To The Moon 2. Even though the gameplay is still a point and click adventure let's be honest here, both games are basically interactive novels. In fact, I think the game segments hurt the pacing of both games' story.
Reviewing a story driven game without spoiling the story is practically impossible, so I'll just say that it asks some of the questions To The Moon did while also raising some new ones. If you enjoyed To The Moon, you'll probably enjoy this one.

First, if you didn't like the aesthetic of "To the Moon" you probably won't like this.
While the premise of this installment is the same as the predecessor (To the Moon), the story, theme, characters, message, and emotions brought forth are all very much different.  Further separating this from a re-tread (which wouldn't have been too bad of a thing) is differences in how memories are traversed in the first game and this.
The relationship between the doctors of Sigmund Corp are further developed here as are the differences between the previous 2 on how they view the mission and contract.  This is where the meta plot that started to be fleshed out in the previous installment grows, but it does end on a serious cliffhanger if that irks you.
Colin wants his life mostly unchanged, but he wants something just a bit "better".   You encounter past regrets, but some of them are so insignificant (spilled beverage on honeymoon) that one would assume those can't possibly be what was asked of the player characters.   Colin has an unusual motivation and that drives the flow of time in the story.
This was not a tear jerker and I don't think it was meant to be.  Kan Gao always said he never intends his stories to be so.  However, being a good storyteller he will leave you with a sad smile at the end at the beauty of Colin's one true wish. Overall, the story is creepier than the first and the prime plot point is easily discernable, but I do not feel that lessened the impact when the game (mostly) revealed it.
Playtime is I would say about 50% longer than To the Moon.

People often misunderstand what this game is. They think it is a nonsensical, half broken game to be enjoyed ironically while laughing at referances to "brouzouf" (the in game currency), and "My legs are okay."
But when you actually pay attention to the game, and try and understand the story through the occasionally rough writing
(the devs are french), you will find that there is in fact meaning to what may at first seem like madness.
By reading the data terminals at the begining of the game to understand the setting and recieve an introduction to the story, and by reading the dialogue of every character you come across, the (actually rather interesting) story of the game will gradually reveal itself to you.
The characters in the game will often have strange dialogue that may not seem to make sense at times. Unfortunately this leads many people to conclude that the devs are simply idiots and that the dialogue has no meaning behind it whatsoever. This is NOT the case. The comments that characters in this game make are often strange but they are strange FOR A REASON and SHOULD NOT BE IGNORED. The strange comments made by many characters will often give hints as to what is really going on in the game (as in all good stories, not all is as it seems at first glance) but disregarding the in game dialogue as nonsense will lead you to miss important aspects of the plot and will therefore make the story seem confusing and nonsensical.
This is a very unique game, it has one of the best atmospheres of any game I have ever played (probably north of 500 games) and it should be used as an example to level designers everywhere on how to create an atmospheric game enviroment, everything from the lighting to the music to the buildings and clutter on the ground is perfect.
The game is well kown for its strange features, for example, while playing, you may occasionally recieve an achievement notifying you that the soldier or looter you just killed was A loving father, or a vampire, or a videogame censor...
Or a necrophile.
The game is designed to be played through multiple times, and the player will need to complete the primary part of the game at least three times in order to reach the true ending by collecting the three required psychic powers obtained in mutually exclusive paths through the game. Most people who have reviewed this game seem to have a fairly low play time, with only one of them that I could see being more than my own.
From reading what people have said about the game here, I strongly suspect the cast majority of them did not understand one bit of the story, and have not actually finished the game.
The fact that most of them reccomended it anyway despite missing out on what is possibly the game's best feature is testement to how fun this game is, and when played with an actual understanding what is going on is an experience that should not be missed.
TLDR:
The writers were not insane and the game isn't broken. You just need to pay attention and read everything carefully.

A bunch of French nerds took their favorite sci-fi franchises and shamelessly smashed them into a Source engine FPS-RPG with a unique story.
Their English isn't great though so even the updated translation is pretty iffy (which is fun). You can hack a door or get hacked back if you fail. There is a skill that lets you teleport inside of an enemy. It's possible to backstab a helicopter with a hammer. Enemies have no real design consistency and some are basically direct rips from their sources. The map designer may or may not have been taking drugs. Upgrading your stats to the point of being broken is a feature; you can turn invisible, run as fast as a car, and leap over small buildings in a single bound. The singleplayer is short but multiple playthroughs are required to get the true ending. Co-op is the singleplayer but with more players and multiplayer is crazy because everyone is able to use their overpowered singleplayer characters. The backstory is extensive but is never explained in-game so there's a library in the hub that you can spend half an hour at if you so wish. Shooting is about as satisfying as any other Source engine game and some of the guns are particularly amazing.
As a whole this game is packaged chaos. You can get it for as cheap as a dollar or two during sales and it's hard to be disappointed either way for a price like that. Give it a shot.

===
Furious Angels is a top-down 2.5D classic shooter, with strongly competitive-oriented and skill-based gameplay. In this title, the player will be the only pilot left defending his carrier command ship against various hordes of enemies. Luckily, the carrier will give out upgrades every set number of enemies killed, to better fight off the onslaught. The objective, aside from staying alive and protecting the ship, is mostly scoring high combos to get a better position in the daily-resetting leaderboards, to compete with other pilots all over the world.
===
The gameplay of Furious Angels uses a simple but well made and effective formula. There are just two goals, first is staying alive, and the second is to defend the carrier. While you are at it, make as many points as possible, so when you inevitably are overrun by enemies, your legend won't be forgotten!
Combat system is based upon skill and reflexes mostly, you will have to improve after every run and understand the various attack patterns of enemies, to then calculate a good flight trajectory that will enable you to hit while dodging enemy bullets. Since the flight model is inertial, there is no quick turns and shooting, you will have to be more careful than normal or you will end up being a sitting duck and get blasted by a million of shots. There are two upgrades gained by killing enemies at regular intervals, first is Guided Missiles, which you can fire after a few seconds after you stop shooting your gun, and the second upgrade is Heavy Armor, which basically transforms your jet into a flying tank, until you get hit too much, then back to square one, basic jet. Also note that your ship can withstand a few bullet hits and will auto-repair in a short time, but to enable this you will have to hold fire while repairing.
There are resetting leaderboards and new enemy waves each day, a lot of achievements to pursue, though if we speak of content quantity there is not very much to be honest, enemy types are not many just 6 or 7, 2 upgrade types, no progression whatsoever, no other game modes. This game has not been developed with content in mind but with just one thing to do: compete in the global leaderboards, and in that it does pretty well. The main content is, definitely, the competition itself and the skill improvement you get after every run.
The game is fairly balanced, enemies are quite strong but again, skill will matter more than everything in this kind of game, i'd say the learning curve is not too steep, first times you will die after little time but then you will improve. There is nothing too op or too much nerfed, it is well done in this part.
This game is very challenging, both because of the leaderboards and because of the ever increasing difficulty and number of enemies. I'd rate the challenge of this game at High.
===
Graphics style is quite simple and by no means high poly, but it compensates with some quite cool destruction effects, is quite polished and has good details on models of enemies and allied crafts. Too bad the background is quite low res, and also the wrecks of enemy fallen ships do fall on the ground but disappear after some time... would be more enjoyable with all those wrecks around to testify your defiance, but again i suppose it is for performance reasons.
Sound effects are alright, average, some additional soundtracks would have been nice, overall decent.
Smooth, well done, not many elements on screen anyway, should run well on even low spec systems.

I've been playing this game since before the steam EA release and it has a whole lot going for it.
I'm a huge fan of the low fantasy medieval feel and the look of the game. The environments, armor, weapons and structures really add to the atmosphere.
The crafting is fairly robust and complex. Not to mention it's extremely useful, as some of the best items in the game can only be crafted. Make friends with a crafter and develop a good relationship with them, they'll be crucial to your success in the later parts of the game.
Where this game really shines, imo, is the PvP. There are points spread all across the map that are open for capture. The 2 factions (more to be added as the game develops) fight for control and by owning points, you get great exp, crafting and reputation bonuses. When you kill an enemy player, you are assigned a certain number of points and you can loot their items accordingly. For example, at the start of a loot session you're giving 20 looting points. Their weapon costs 10, their boots cost 5 and their helmet costs another 5. Once you've spent all your points, you can no longer loot anything from the enemy. This prevents too much griefing, but also gives the PKer a sense of victory and motivation to keep doing what he's doing.
Alas, because the game is in EA, it is not without its fair share of problems. The most prevalent is the hit detection and lag. In a game where you don't target your enemy but rather aim your weapon, server stability is a key component. Unfortunately, the servers aren't the greatest, and a lot of the time you're struggling to hit the opponent because on their screen they're in a totally different area. Countless times, I'll be blocking my opponent's swings with my shield, yet they'll still be dealing heavy damage. This is worse in certain regions than in others, but overall it really puts a damper on the gameplay experience.
Of course you'll encounter other small bugs as well, but nothing as bad as the aforementioned issue of lag.
Overall, the game is still a lot of fun and has huge potential for the future. With the recent steam release the population has boomed and the world is full of life and action. As with any EA title, I would recommend it if you're willing to stick to the game as the issues are ironed out. If you're expecting a polished. bug free game, turn around and don't look back until the full release.

I have a passionate love-hate relationship with this game.
I've been thinking about recommending it forever and here's why I even struggled in the first place: The game's core is great. Some of the different gamemodes are just a blast, I especially digged the tactical rpg part, but some of them (I'm looking at you, Bejeweled) are just -horrible-. I played the entire game on hard, except for this one Bejeweled part that is literally impossible when your enemy just deals 90% of your life in a single swipe.
Apart from that, here's the deal. The game is amazing, yet it manages to annoy you every so often. Some parts are super tedious, occasionally, I just wanted to see if I could re-enter a certain gamemode or stage and then I had to play the entire level again because there's no option to turn back. Same thing with some sort of stealth segment, turns out, if you talk with a certain guard and hit yes (I wanted to see what he replied...) you go straight back into jail. However, even though there a lot of bugs and glitches, it was still super enjoyable. Because the plot is well done, the music is amazing, the gameplay feels (for the most part. ♥♥♥♥ Bejeweled.) good and the controls are tight and responsive. It really sets you back with a bazillion references to older games. I don't even want to spoil a single one, so you can experience it for yourself. So, after this short wall of text, let's review.
+ Amazing Gameplay for the most part.
+ Stunning visuals. (Mostly the Pixel Art though)
+ Amazing humour. Yes, it is THAT good.
+ Stays true to what it does. (Basically, the different gamemodes feel like they should, is what I'm trying to say.)
+ Time Travel Mechanics really add to the plot.
+ Now that I mentioned it, the plot is pretty sweet too, with a satisfying ending. (For me, that is. I did notice some people complain about it being too open ended, which is not really the case.)
- Tedious Mechanics, occasionally.
- Bejeweled
- Bugs/Glitches appear way too often, expect to restart the game or quit to title occasionally. (For example, do not open the treasure radar in the tactical rpg section.♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down.)
- Bejeweled
- Unintentional re-playing of various long and annoying sections, though I guess that was my fault.
- Bejeweled
TL;DR:
Good game, you should give it a shot, ♥♥♥♥ Bejeweled.

: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an unbiased informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
The original Evoland was somewhat of a surprise gem, utilizing some of the best features and gameplay from RPGs of the past. Expertly blended together, Evoland was a fun unique experience. Evoland 2 does nothing less than the same, crafting a wonderful experience using gameplay elements and mechanics from not only RPGs, but many other genres and series as well. You will see a lot of influences from many games, and many direct references scattered throughout. Even some pop culture references!
==========
Evoland 2 is an action RPG first and foremost, but at times it changes up its style for periods of time. In one segment of the game, you are able to explore the field much like in the classic Secret of Mana style, attacking enemies that wander around the field. In the next segment, you will be platforming through a dark dungeon very reminicent of the old Super Mario titles. This change of style helps keep Evoland 2 fresh, and it lends this feeling of excitement to the game where you press on to see what type of changes come next!
As the style changes, so do the graphics. You will start your adventure with what looks like the classic Game Boy look, black/white/grey pixels makign up your character and the world. This quickly evolves into a better 2D top-down look, in full color and a bit more detailed. Further progression sees full 3D being implemented, increasing the depth and overall look of the game. The original Evoland was all about going through the history of video games, and Evoland 2 still retains some of that feature.
The original Evoland had a traditional turn-based RPG battle system, with a few changes here or there. In Evoland 2, combat is much like Secret of Mana or The Legend of Zelda: enemies are out in the open--you can walk up to them and whack them with your sword while avoiding their attacks. Much like Secret of Mana, you also get a few companions as you progress. But unlike Evoland, they do not join you in battle directly and take their own turns. Instead, you can charge up a Focus Attack that will cause your partner companion to unleash a special attack. After using this, a short cooldown occurs before it can be used again. These Focus Attacks are not only ways to battle enemies, but they are also used to interact with the environment. Menos' attack, for example, can be used to damage groups of enemies or destroy blocks, boulders, or other such obstacles on the field. These abilities can be upgraded as you progress and collect Maana.
==========
The overall look and feel of the game changes as you progress the story. At first, it's very simple: pixelated and colorless. But as you progress, it goes full 3D and filled with color and detail. No matter which stage of the game you are in, even the very beginning, the game looks amazing. It just keeps getting better as you go!
Character sprites at the beginning look nice enough, and when they hit 3D mode you really notice the little details. Attacks looks better, environments look better, everything just looks so much better as you go! It's really amazing how well the art direction of this game was handled.
==========
One of my favorite parts of Evoland 2 is the soundtrack,
. The soundtrack perfectly matches each situation you encounter, the town you are visiting, or the dungeon you are exploring. Cheery, playful tunes for the towns set the mood for them well, and the dark, foreboding songs of each dungeon really make you feel like you are really there in the damp darkness. There is some very light voice acting, at least thus far, in the form of shouts, grunts, and other similar sounds. Swinging your sword is satisfying, as is the sound when hitting an enemy.
==========
Evoland 2 runs flawlessly on my rig, which I like to call a low mid-tier build. 60 FPS at all times, with no lag or slowdown. No frame drops whatsoever were observed. It plays perfectly with my Logitech F310 controller, with no prior setup. The default controls were spot on and easy to acclimate to. That being said, a controller is highly recommended.
==========
If you enjoyed the first Evoland, you will undoubtedly enjoy Evolnad 2 as well. It's a great nostalgic throwback to the games it draws some of its features and mechanics from, and you will surely recognize where a lot of them come from. Tons of easter eggs and references are scattered throughout too, making it an even more nostalgic experience. A must buy for fans of the original Evoland!

This is a fantastic game.
The first Evoland mashed together a bunch of different art and play styles in a sort of 4th wall breaking meta-game. It was entertaining, but it was more of an amusement park filled with a bunch of different rides than a coherent gaming experience.
Evoland 2 is first and foremost a really solid RPG, which uses the changing art and play styles to put together a compelling story. The writing is superb, and the characters manage to be both parodies of classic RPG tropes and well developed and engaging at the same time.
The only knock on the game is that it is a bit buggy at times (including a few soft locks and typos in the dialog), and is really unbalanced at parts, but those are minor things compared to how much of a joy the game was to play.

In a way I would have preferred having to work more for completing the puzzles, but I also appreciate the fact that this isn't a puzzle game and more difficult puzzles could feel out of place and push people away.

As such, I would recommend playing To the Moon and the minisodes before Finding Paradise. I haven't played A Bird Story myself, but I'd assume going through it wouldn't hurt, either. Having said that, I can't help but wonder if playing Finding Paradise before playing To the Moon would make this game stand out more.
Now then, the reasons for saying this game isn't a second To the Moon are fairly simple. However, they all come down to Finding Paradise not having as much of an impact on me.

Arkham City perfects the metroidesque formula of already splendid Arkham Asylum with the inclusion of openworld side-investigations and a doubled array of gadgets, along with a vastly redesigned cobat and predator systems. The engagments, while being more challenging, give the player far more tactical options, with interactive elements like breakable extinguishers and magnetic generators, and expanded goon weaponry, such as detective mode jammers and anti-gargoyle thermal googles.
Of note is far superior plot, still being the best one in the series. The use of Huga Strange as the main (albeit not ultimate) villain allows an in-depth look into Bruce Waynes, as well as his nemesis psyche. A menacing and intelligent enemy, playing in his city-wide experiment heavily mimicking that of Carpenter's "Escape from New York", Strange is propably the most engaging villain in the series, next only to the Joker. The overall array of Batman's foes is also far more interesting then the previous time around, with Hush, Deadshot, Penguin, Mr Freeze and Ra's al Ghul (among several others) all joining the fray to finally deal with the Bat of Gotham.
The challenge system, now renamed "Riddlers Revenge", is also greatly expanded, not only in terms of the ammount of  maps and objectives, but most importantly the campaign system (allowing to play several challenges in a row with several modifiers and mutators) and the ability to play as either Batman, Catwoman, Robin or Nightwing, all with different sets of skills and gadgets.
Overall, it is propably, just propably, the best superhero game on the market and one of the greatest Batman stories ever told.

One of the best stealth games, Styx truely is a master of shadows.
The game focuses entirely on avoiding confrontation. Combat is based
around a one-on-one mechanic, but multiple enemies can attack you at
once, so being sneaky is the way to go. To facilitate this stealthy approach,
the games levels are expertly designed. They are of a non-linear design, with
multiple paths to completing objectives. The game itself is broken up into
severel missions, with one level serving as a hub and base of operations.
Each mission, along with its main objectives, features optional ones to
make things more interesting. Styx, on his part, has several skills, like
enhansed vision that highlights objects of interest, a cloning ability,
limited invisibility, and several different assassinations, to help him
takle objectives. Missions also come with a set of four challanges: no kills, no detection, all collectibles and a speed run.
The only downside of the game is its graphics. It's not bad, just decent.
But don't let that push you away from a great game, especially if you
enjoy the stealth genre.

Furious Angels is a sci-fi arcade shooter focused on score attack mechanics. You try to kill enemy aircraft as it attacks you and your carrier. The concept might be simple enough, but the it’s the execution that gets the prize.
Even if you are not a competitive person – you’ll feel that way because game shows leaderboard and your position in it before every launch. That’s a great design that tries to push “competitive” philosophy to every player. “Go ahead, look how far you can go if you try to survive just a little bit longer!”
-	Great graphics, the game has its own style: not high-poly, but not minimalistic either. The landscape does not have a lot of detail, but the enemies and your own ships do.
-	Good, minimalistic UI
-	Skill based
-	Fun, action-packed gameplay. I mean it.
-	After a while, the game will get repetitive: you always get the same plane and same equipment at the start
-	The controls could be better: the game requires good precision, but it’s really hard to have precise angles on controller. The mouse is OK (I had 35% accuracy with mouse compared to usual 17-18% with controller). Forget about playing with keyboard. Maybe I’m unskilled, but turning the plane on keyboard has really been painful.
-	Music does not fit the game. It’s not bad, it’s just somewhat relaxing and does not put you in “go get em, instant action!” mood.
-	The price is a bit steep for the content offered: if you think about it, the game has less than 10 types of enemies and 3 player upgrades in total.
The game is really fun but it does not have that much content; I think definitely buy it once it’s on 50% discount, but for the current price it seems a bit too expensive to me.

A very neat Castlevania-like game, and the leveling-down part certainly helped with the difficulty curve. I also liked stuff like the multiple endings and more.

If you know this going in, you'll have a great time.  You can sort of get stun locked but whenever that happens it is very fair.  The only real complaints I have is that you can't control what way you face when you have your sword out, and the 2 hardest bosses lag a little bit when there are too many bullets on the screen.  The latter could just be because of my computer, but having S flip your stance would have been great.  I'm also not a fan of losing max health on deaths because I don't like grinding (unless she's hot lol) and you have to grind to get it back up but it's only a tiny bit and it does give you a reason to actually kill the bad guys so it's not a big thing and I could even see some liking it but yeah.
Where this game shines is the bosses.  They all have you do different things and I like that a lot.  Some of them are easier than others, but they're all very fun.  As far as general difficulty is concerned, on my first playthrough I died 160 times but in my most recent run I didn't die at all.  My skill level is ok, I haven't unlocked The Guy in Super Meat Boy but I have beaten the main story line.
I was waiting for this to go on sale, but I finally just payed the 5 dollars and it's the best 5 dollars I've spent in a while.  The levels are also fun when you aren't dealing with the bats.  Those guys are probably the only reason so many people say this game is hard and they die in one hit and I can only think of 7 that are in the game.  They are satisfying to kill and in a normal playthrough you don't think much of them but in speedruns they'll ruin everything.  There's one that prevents you from backtracking through a room, so I went all the way around the world to get back to the room it was guarding because I thought there was a path to the right but there isn't.  And I did that at level 3 so it took forever and was quite hard.
I actually really like the level down system.  It very effectively makes the game harder as you go and does so without inflation.  I don't know if I'd want it in every game but Resin wouldn't be Resin without it and it makes this game special.  It can be seen as a gimmick but it's a fun one so I don't care.  Anyway hope you enjoyed reading this, I'm giving it a thumbs up.

Resin is an interesting game; it’s not good but not bad, just could have better. But let’s start with the story first.
You play as a robot in a dying world, dominated by machines and artificially created lifeforms. Known as Warmth generators, the very last remaining living creatures in the world are used by machines as energy sources. It’s up to you to kill Warmth generators.
Now, what I liked about this game. It’s got some good music and some of the bosses were creepy looking. Combat was not bad, but let’s get into the not bad could have used a lot of work.
First off the story, it’s not bad, but vary, vary bare bones. I mean I am not asking for a big epic story, but some notes about the world and how it got like that, would help make more flushed out.
The enemy’s/bosses, sometimes can be a bit cheap sometimes, and Combat could have been a bit better.
Now for the scenery/background, its bit dull and little bit lifeless. I mean I get what they are trying to do, show a cold dying world, but could have done it a bit better.
So with that, I say only get this game if you’re a Metroidvania fan, but that is a bit pushing it. Its again not but could have been better.

I recommend this game if only because it's basically baby's first Dark Souls.
The combat is simple. That is a good thing in many respects, but it's simple so far as to lack depth. The subtle mechanics aren't exactly told right off the bat or explained unless you simply just experiment in a safe location. Or watch a video of a boss run.
For example, apparently, you are immune while jumping. Or immune to melee or something. Or it behaves like a dodge outside of combat stance. You restore more energy out of stance than in it. Combos cost a varying amount. Sheething sometimes drains energy. Hitbox doesn't EXACTLY line up with the character. Attack range has zero forgiveness and is pretty short.
You MUST take it slow. There are some enemies who you simply just attack relentlessly. Those are the easy ones. The others have a cadence to them. The cadences are not exactly complecated, but they are distinct, especially the bosses. Bosses generally have two attacks. Some only have one. The music and the visuals reinforce this idea of paranoia or adrenaline. It's not scary per se, but when some of the trash mobs are harder than the bosses, it can be nerve wracking, especially if they hit you once and you now have only 2/3s hp.
A lot of the enemies are basically, "hit once, back off." Bosses are a mix. Some follow that pattern. Most do not. Each one has a gimmick that flip flops between "hey, this is cool" to "meh".
Despite what others say, there are plenty of checkpoints. There are in fact one per boss right next to the encounter. The frustration in checkpoint placement comes from trash. Well, git gud.
The game is not "hard". In fact, it really just relies on knowledge instead of timing or reaction. Once you know what to do in a fight and where to place yourself, you can one-shot bosses or no hit easily. Kind of like Ori. It's eyegougingly difficult if you don't know wtf the do. Once you see it, you're like, "oh, that's easy." And it is. That said, there's very little room for innovation. Sure, there are main strategies for bosses in other DS games, but there is flexibility or complete change in tactics depending on class, skills, skill, equipment, etc. Easy to implement combat tactics; no other alternatives for the most part.
The pseudolinear gameflow is a nice break from other DS games. I like exploration, but it's definitely good for such a short game to give you scenery and music instead of having you backtrack.
DO get this game if you want slower gameplay, higher tension, easy-to-execute combat, and linear progression.
DO NOT get this game if you want fast-paced gameplay, a sprawling map, complicated battle cadence, or creative tactics.

I was initially intrigued by Resin.  The bold minimalist visual-style is what initially drew me in, and I was further excited by the reversed progression system.  I found myself very disappointed.
Firstly, the core gameplay is very slow.  The character moves slowly, the environments are large (mostly empty), and every attack the player-character makes lags horribly after the button press.  One must wonder what the point is of having the player-character telegraph it's attacks so much.  Don't get me wrong, slow gameplay is not an inherently bad trait, but I find it almost unforgivable in an action game.
It's also unnecessarely punishing.  The checkpoints are few and far between, meaning death sets you back substantially.   This serves to slow the game down further.  Additionally, you lose max health on respawn.  It can be gained back fairly easily by farming enemies and returning to the checkpoint to refill your health.  This, however, serves to slow the game down further.  When you are hit in combat, you are stunned and lose stanima (which is used to perform combat actions).  These both, of course, serve to slow the game down further.
On a completely unrelated note:  why is there even a jump button at all?  There's effectively no platforming in the entire game, and the jump is pathetic.  It doesn't speed you up, it's not high enough to jump over enemies, and it costs you stamina (which seems ridiculous considering how useless it is).  Your hitbox is also complete garbage.  When you're moving, it juts out past your face.
Ultimately:  Some cool ideas, an awesome visual style, but a frustrating and often dull experience.

The NPC dialogue is pretty basic and I wasn't intrigued by the world much. The music and visuals are captivating, however.
I died once and was like, "naww, this combat isn't interesting enough for me to be interested in the glacial reiteration time." It's the most basic stamina meter management with insane input buffering and a very short range attack. If the camera was zoomed in some, I'd have an easier time playing. If the game didn't have frequent seconds-long periods where I wait for elevators to go up, I wouldn't dread death. This game finds very uninteresting ways to impart challenge and meaningful death.
So... nope. I understand who this game is for and why it's interesting, but considering it's 95% its gameplay, purposefully making that cumbersome AND shallow is... kind of like designing a book about pain with the story of Goodnight Moon but with razor blades in the pages, as opposed to incorporating unpleasant language, imagery, and narrative theme.
This idea of having your health and abilities degrade over time would be brilliant in an immersive sim game or something, but not in this 1-button-to-attack, 1-button-to-dodge-in-1-way combat system. I don't know if this idea fits the scope or minimalism of the game. Also, your character feels horribly stiff initially (doesn't build up momentum with movement, input buffered attacks, an invincibility dodge that makes no sense... etc.).
I'm not too cut about about the price. I'm glad to support an ambitious indie developer. This game isn't for you, though, if you want an art game, a mechanically solid game, or a storytelling game. If you want a 2D Dark Souls-inspired indie game with great presentation, a cool concept, and not much else, that's fine, and you should get it.

It's been months since I've played Resin and general day-to-day business has kept me from writing a heartfelt review about the game.
The concept is awesome. There are a couple negative comments talking about it being unrewarding when you beat a boss because you get even weaker and it becomes more difficult to progress as a result- but that's the entire point of the game. The reward doesn't come with getting stronger after you beat an area- it comes with the timing and precision that constantly needs to be manipulated in order to even beat the game.
Resin is hard but wholly rewarding. The art style, the ambience of it all, it was a great experience, and I'm glad to see more games come out of the box and try and shape gameplay in different ways.
Highly recommend it.

This game has been out long enough that I feel there is little in the way I could add that someone else already hasn't. Still, I enjoyed it enough to finish and even full clear achievement-wise, so why not post a review?
Being a big fan of stealth games, and having played my fair share from as far back as the late 90s, I went into it slightly biased and at first was going to judge it more harshly than the conclusion I ultimately came to. I could parrot all the negative aspects of the game as those previously have done before, it certainly has its fair share. Infact, when I really think about it, I haven't played a game in recent memory that had as many things against it, yet seemed to pull itself together enough for me to recommend. It's not a gorgeous game. It doesn't do anything new. I can't even say for certain it has an actual soundtrack(I only recall one song, that played maybe twice throughout the entire game, save the title screen). The only thing that might
be original, aside from your homely little green protagonist is
. But with such a small team working on this title(you could count the amount of voice actors on one hand), even that isn't surprising.
I will say that despite the lack of AAA game status, they didn't do too bad, when all is said and done. Alot of people complain about the combat, even though it's not a combat-centric game. You're supposed to sneak around, avoid detection, and kill silently, if you feel the need. The stealth kills are amusing enough, albeit I had more fun doing a mercy run second playthrough. I've read people have had issues with wall hanging, and while I certainly came across a few instances of cheap deaths resulting from the character just not being properly aligned with what I was moving toward, all the patches seem to have fixed the majority of this annoyance(it also helps to save often, it makes the game even more manageable). I will say that not being able to go around corners while hanging from a ledge, or even a dedicated button to transition from being atop a ledge to going into the hanging position is my biggest gripe of all, one that I hope will be addressed in future games.
But enough about gameplay, every review should atleast mention the story, right? The story starts off slow, somewhat confusing, and rather sparse at first, with the ending finally fleshing it all out. Despite that, it left me satisfied, even with the rather disappointing final boss. Styx is an origin story for the character of the same name in Of Orcs and Men. That, if nothing else, it does ably enough. It left me cautiously optimistic, looking forward to the upcoming sequel, Styx: Shards of Darkness. And in the end, isn't that what a game
aim to accomplish?
While I enjoyed it enough that I feel the full $30 price tag isn't unreasonable, I recommend getting it at a discount during this year's Steam Summer Sale, if you want a decent stealth/assassination game. It might surprise you. I give it a solid 8/10.

Where to start ?
Updates and Development:
The devs can't seem to be able to prioritise the important stuff in this game and instead publish weekly updates with fancy looking tools such as an auction house, a guild castle or some new armor. But never actually work on fixing the core of the game which is heavily broken and riddled with desync (and has been for 4 years). Just another Dayz in my opinion, keeping you distracted from the real problems with flashy looking gizmo's and events.
The community :
The community is much like any gaming community now a days, You have the players that are friendly, the players that want to help and the players that want to make your every second on the game a miserable experience. Except with this game the devs seem to want to have a massive imput by banning only the Midlander faction players when they step out of line. If you role ismir or azeb its okay, you can get away with whatever you want but if you role midlander , better be careful, even when using the word "fricking" will result you in a weeks ban, whilst the other factions continue to trash talk and alt f4 during combat.
The gameplay, mechanics and world:
The world of gloria victis is a stunning one, I'll give them that. There are some increadibly unique locations on the map which are always a beautiful and calming sight to see. But Sadly the beautiful world and enviroment can only keep you distracted from the Broken physics of the game for so long. When it comes to combat there is a major problem with desync, players are no where near you on your screen but on theirs they are pretty much patting you on the back. This leads to backstabs from 5-7m away, people hitting past your blocks. And shooting with bows at long range near impossible on a moving target. It wouldn't be all that bad if the PvE was really intense and fun but sadly that's just a complete mess to. Npc's are the easiet thing in the world to kill, they have the same predictable attacks and blocks and pathing. You can also solo most events in the game with the exception of a few due to the sheer amount of mobs. Since about 6 months ago the character movement has also felt insanely clunky and "floaty" it's almost like your guy is wearing a pair of roller skates, he continues to glide even when you've stopped taping your keybored.
Verdict:
The game is fun to play for the first few hours until you experience the buggy combat which has only got worse over the years. And the community will either chew you up and spit you out and never make you want to play again, or you'll find the most warm and welcoming guild ever that will alone make you want to keep playing the game even if you hate it. I would say hold of buying this until they fix the real issues and stop posting out pointless updates to keep us distracted.

This is a pretty great, hectic sci-fi shoot 'em up! Set on a rocky planet, you fight increasingly harder and more numerous waves of enemies, which randomizes each day, to defend the mothership and to score points. When you destroy, you unlock upgrades like a space tank.
The gameplay is solid. I thought the keyboard controls were stiff but using your mouse works great though it takes some practice to get the hang of it, which is how it should be! The grafix are simple, but appealing. The distinct shapes and colours of the enemy ships make them easy to identify, though I do not know if I have encountered all of the enemies yet as the game gets pretty gosh darn hard quite early on! The ship physics and destruction are other little great things that add to my enjoyment. Big ships will break apart as they get destroyed and will crash into eachother and the environment below. Better yet, crashing your ship into other ships can destroy them!
The biggest issues with the game is the music and the sound effects. The music does not match with the intense dogfighting that is going on and is somewhat out of place. As another reviewer put it, it does not have the energy that would be suitable for this kind of sci-fi action. Same goes for the sound effects; the massive battles are not accompanied with sounds fitting the explosions and lazers. That is something I hope the developer will improve in the near future. There seems to be room for further expansions to the game, which would probably be pretty nice.
Other than that, great little game. Worth the cash? Sure.

An excellent little shmup with a surprising amount of tactical depth to it. Beginning as a straightforward blastathon, the "upgrade" system gradually introduces new mechanics such as holding your fire to be able to launch missiles and repair yourself, eventually culminating in becoming a "tank in the sky" to rack up enormous scores. You can play with keyboard, mouse or gamepad; for once, I actually preferred the mouse controls to gamepad, since this isn't really a "twin stick" shooter as such.
The music and sound effects are a bit weak -- the music in particular has a very "'90s MIDI" feel to it and doesn't really have the "energy" about it that a game of this type deserves -- but the stylised graphics fit the game well and the way everything explodes into pieces is enormously satisfying.
It'd be nice to see some better music -- or just a bit more variety to it, since there seems to only be one track at present -- in a future update, but for now, this is a solid and enormously addictive shoot 'em up that is a great addition to any score attack junkie's library.

Remember when games were hard? Like really hard? Every jump, attack and movement all had to be precise or you would usually die and have to start over. Games like Ninja Gaiden, Ghouls 'N Ghosts, Castlevenia come to mind. There are some games that have come out these days that attempt to emulate that, like Dark Souls. Games that made you rage on bitter defeat and cheer when you finally struck a killing blow to that one boss.
Enter Resin, a simple looking action side scroller that is all about the fluidity of movement. The idea of the game is rather simple, but incredibly evil genius. You start the game at the height of your powers and as strong as you will ever be. Foes fall before you like dominoes one by one. Your blade slices like a hot knife through butter and you can zig-zag your way around enemies and make them spin in circles. Finally you reach one of the big bad bosses. The battle is fierce but you win the day. Suddenly everything changes and things get a bit colder. Your health/stamina bar shrinks, your movements slightly dulled, the shine on your blade seems slightly tarnished. You are weaker.
Creative writing aside you get the basic idea. Every time you take down a boss your character becomes weaker. This game reminds me of a virtual version of Bruce Lee's Game of Death, all we are missing is a pagoda.
Breaking down the story of Resin isn't really all that simple. Resin story doesn't come off straight forward in its narrative; I found the Steam page to explain more then the actual game did. You are an android lady who kicks robot tail and takes no robot names. Why? Well that is up for you to decide, in a way. The best way to describe the story of Resin is that it is subversive. It is there but more as a means to keep you guessing and keep on going culminating in a huge battle. I am not going to tell you that I was satisfied with the ending, but I was satisfied in the feeling that I made it to the end. There are multiple endings from what I understand. I got the good ending so perhaps there is more to see on the other side. To be fair Resin never really promises you explanations,  so you end up not expecting anything different from the ending. It starts on a weird note and ends on a weird note.
Where the true beauty of this game lies is in its action. When I said fluidity of movement I really want to underline how important that is to this game. Everything in the game is calculated, every enemies lunge, swoop, or attack is crafted. Bosses are no different as you fight against them you will note that the vicious attacks all have a window, an opportunity to strike but you have to be precise or die fast. I was very impressed with how bosses/enemies were crafted and how dynamically things change from beginning, to the middle, and the end. Keep in mind you have to be able to fight at your strongest and weakest. That isn't easy to plan out backwards.
Aside from movement, you only have three buttons that really matter: attack, dodge, and sheath your sword. When you first load into the game you are going to notice two large sets of bars at the top, representing health and stamina. Any fan of Dark Souls is immediately going to recognize this green bar as attacking and dodging are completely dependent on it. Beside those bars is a number. That number represents the number of bosses and what power level you are. Nine being the highest, and yes, it does go down to zero.
You move about a huge map that has multiple paths facing an onslaught of enemies as you hunt down bosses one at time. The bosses are extremely fun to fight and satisfying challenges, from having to shoot ballistas and fend off enemies. Another boss jumps everywhere and wants to pound you into the ground. Like games of old most of them have a pattern that takes a bit of learning to finally overcome them. I died somewhere between five and ten times depending on the boss. About half way through the game though things change dramatically. Suddenly you don't fear facing bosses, but just getting anywhere is a challenge. The once simple enemies you took for granted in destroying, get mean. Real mean. Near the end, any enemy is practically a herculean task to destroy and this is what I loved about Resin. You feel your weakness and miss your strength.
The flip side of that is the way you make progress through the healing stations.(bonfires basically) If for whatever reason you die before getting to the next, you have to retread all that trouble and fight tooth and nail to get there again. This isn't a huge problem for the most part, but did lead to some ragey moments.
There are items that are of a benefit to you that you can find. Scattered around the map are jars of black ooze that provide a smidgen of health. You can find grappling hooks to overcome terrain obstacles and essential items like the respirator that allow you to breath underwater.
Resin has mastered its action, level design, and bosses in very inventive ways. That being said there is one gripe that I have to mention.
Death is annoying, now I know that sounds silly, but bear with me. Every time you die you lose a percentage of health from your health bar. The way to recover this part of your health is to slay a foe, collecting its essence and then head to a healing station. The only problem is, that this becomes rather dull when dying to bosses. It creates this mentality of losing to a boss, go kill a random minion, heal up to 100% and then fight the boss. Why go in with anything less?
Yes I am aware of the argument being "Get gud' noob!" but that is hardly the point here. It's an unnecessary chore that takes away from the pace of the game. Again, a minor gripe, but a gripe but nonetheless.
Moving on, Resin does some impressive work with its pixel art and sprites as well. The game in all has somewhat of a dreary withered robotic vibe that works very well. Bosses are particularly horrifying in ways that remind me of anime monsters. The backgrounds are given quite a bit of detail and in a way tell their own story if you pay attention to them. The game is rather simple looking, mind you, when it comes to the main character and basic enemies but I find it never really holds the game back. I do wonder if the game had a bit more in the graphical department, how much more epic it could've felt.
Resin has a phenomenal soundtrack that elevates the entire game and really brings the tone of the game home. This is one area of the game that is really flawlessly done and I loved the soundtrack. It is quite a shame that the soundtrack isn't available for purchase. I am no musical savant but it has tones of 80's Tron and the type of sci-fi music we see in things like Stranger Things. It creeps you out but its exciting. When the music drops, you know stuff is about to go down. The sound effects on the other hand, do feel uninspired and never really caught my attention.
Game length can vary, as my initial play through took about three hours. If you explore, have troubles with the bosses this can be stretched out. There are multiple endings, which adds replay value to the game as well. What the differences are between those I have yet to discover. One thing to note, is that like Dark Souls or Ninja Gaiden, once you learn how to defeat a boss, it becomes like riding a bicycle; you will never forget how to do it. That initial awe and difficulty isn't as high.
I had a great time with Resin, it brings the old and new together in fun interesting ways. I admit I did rage often and there was times I had to walk away from the game to take a breather. That hardly is a bad thing though when a game aims to be difficult.
Hitting the bullet points: the game does have Steam Achievements/Cards, and features controller support. At the low price of $4.99 Resin is a steal for the amount of gameplay that it is offering. I recommend this title if you are in the market for a unique challenging game that will make you scratch your head.

I didn't play the first Evoland game, but when I had the opportunity to meet up with Shiro Games on gamescom 2015, the first thing they told me was that they took the time, over a year, to analyse what could have been better on Evoland and make sure that their next game would show an improvement. I just finished the game, and I can clearly tell you that they did, all in all, a good job with this new Action-RPG title.
One of the most critical points for Evoland was that it was far too short and it somehow let people empty-handed. My first playthrough, played very casually but still trying to unlock additional content, just clocked at 23 hours, in-game time. Even if some stages or scenes can feel a bit lengthy, there's always something to do in this game: you can progress through the story, you can explore the world and try and find hidden chests or new items or you can spend hours trying to defeat tough opponents in their card game.
You are never bored when you explore the world of Evoland: there is always a hidden reference for you to catch. You will be meeting up with characters from your favorite video games (Elizabeth from Bioshock Infinite, Sakura from Street Fighter, Lara Croft...), you will notice items coming from different universes (mention to the Valley of Wind shop with Captain America's shield on a wall just next to a Buster Sword and Link's Hylian shield). To be honest, at first, I even thought it was too much, all the time, and I had the feeling that this game might even get sued for being just a huge pile of copyrights infringements. But when you decide to play the game for what it is, a sort of homage to past glories like Chrono Trigger or Secret of Mana, you are just having a blast.
Nicolas Decasse, one of the developers, introduced himself as a huge fan of Chrono Trigger, and the scenario of the game clearly shows it: the plot of the game will have you travel through time, using magic stones erected by a now disappeared civilization, while making sure you learn that this power shouldn't be messed around with and that your actions can have dire consequences. As every hero, Kuro, your avatar, will meet new friends on the way, and create special bounds with him. They will help him explore his environment, and he will be able to call on their power to progress through the game, by removing obstacles or creating paths for him. Once their power is fully unlocked, you will be able to use special summons for each of your three partners, like you would be able to in Final Fantasy 6 or 7.
Time travel is represented in a way that a lot of retrogamers are going to enjoy: depending on the era you're in, the more old school the graphics. 8 bits for the past, 16 bits for the present and isometric 3D for the future, you won't be able to forget in which era you're wandering. To explore certain areas, you will have to switch very regularly from one era to another, as some of the puzzles will involve removing obstacles or getting specific items in a different era to progress in the timeframe of your mission. This feature is very nice, but to be honest, from times to times, it just hacks the story telling: backtracking to one of those special stones to change something in another era before going back to the original era you come from and go back where you were is just a pain, at least in the first hours when you have no way of transportation.
However, Evoland 2 always finds a way to renew your interest, by breaking the habit and having the player to explore regularly new video game genres: you will have for instance to defeat a boss in a versus fighting mode, you will try to save an entire civilisation playing a tactical RPG mode, you will have to escape a mountain fighting your way through a bullet hell... You never know what to expect in your first playthrough, and I certainly didn't expect to have to play a mix of Dance Dance Revolution and Guitar Hero in an Action-RPG! My only problem with that is that it reinforces the general impression that the game is just a pot pourri of references and that it lacks a bit of personality: you play a game that talks and shows more of other games than itself.
One of the main criticisms I'll have for this game is that some of the puzzles it offers are just extremely hard to solve, and not because you need a master's degree to solve them.  No, I'm just referring to some tricky hitboxes or silly point of views that actually make you think you're stuck when you just have to move a couple of millimetres to see where you need to go or finally manage to destroy something that was blocking your way. I spent one hour looking for an exit in a forest, knowing where the only exit was, and not managing to open it because of the hitbox of the bush I was supposed to destroy was very tiny and made me think that I couldn't go there just yet. But all in all, the puzzles are kind of tricky in the game and you will have to think for a couple of minutes to solve most of them (just have a look at the discussion boards on Steam and check the numbers of "Blocked in XXX" threads).
All in all, I can only recommend this game to all players who are somehow nostalgic of the golden age of Action-RPGs, who have a massive geek culture or who are just looking for an enjoyable game to entertain them for about 20 hours. It has some downsides, for sure, like the fluctuating rhythm in the action or the fact that allies are reduced to a very supportive role (you never get to fight as one of them), but the diversity in the gameplay and the many references, served with a brilliant soundtrack, are making Evoland 2 a very enjoyable game.

TL;DR: Buy this game to support the devs (and support the devs only), and then get the Japanese version and patch it with the upcoming translation patch!
I would like to recommend this game, I really would. In fact- I do recommend it. However, I don't recommend you bother with this steam version of the game. While the story is pretty good as visual novels go, this particular version is mired with two main issues: heavy censorship and blind-idiot translation.
The censorship is one thing- it's a bit Orwellian in this case how far they've gone to make it completely PG, to the point of completely destroying one character's route (rather famously), but to be honest this is the lesser problem. What the slightly bigger problem is that they haven't done anything to deal with the voices, which sometimes end up saying the uncensored lines instead (I'm pretty sure you don't need any formal education in Japanese to be able to distinguish the words breasts and eyes).
But again, this is fine in comparison to the real reason why I cannot recommend this game: from what I can tell, it was translated by a lot of different people, some of which did not know the characters at all, and their raw translations were mashed together to create the final product. Really, there are points where characters apparently change gender in the middle of a scene multiple times. There are cases I remember where one character's name (which is SPOKEN IN THE DIALOGUE) is replaced by another's. Honorfic translations are inconsistent (if I remember correctly) and this also creates a slight amount of confusion.
You know it's bad when you're reading a visual novel in your native language and you're correcting mistakes in the translation (incorrect nouns for the most part) from listening to the voice track.
APPEND: Wow, I didn't know lots of people agreed with my opinion. To continue what I was saying, the visual novel I would like to recommend is Kono Oozora ni Tsubasa wo Hirogete. However, I cannot say this, as I, as with the majority of people playing the game, cannot read Japanese well enough [or at all] to fully enjoy this game. Therefore I am taking this game for face-value from the Moe-Novel adaptation.
To extend: The Moe-Novel translation is poor, and suffer from very large QC problems. It also has censorship, which unlike many others, I can accept. If it is for the sake of us getting the game on Steam at all, I'd rather have a censored game (see The Fruit of Grisaia) than no game at all. The story is pretty stable enough to support the game without any sexual content, but it is a shame that they decided to set their target audience so low as to have to warp the story of one route to allow for this. Had they only aimed for a 15-17 target audience, then honestly I wouldn't see there being many problems.
As you may know, there is a uncensoring patch available, which also tauts having an improved translation. I have used this patch as well (hence the broken gametime associated with this account) and I can confirm the uncensoring works as intended. However, I cannot say that I found the translation any more consistent and accurate than the original MoeNovel one, even during scenes that weren't in the censored game. If you are looking for a simple hentai fix, then this patch should serve you well, but if you are looking for a game with proper quality controlled translations, then I cannot in good faith say it is any better than the original.
I can appreciate people downvoting my review. I can do this because I have been in your position as well, having a game with a good story that you enjoy that works perfectly well for your standards. But this game is different, so much that I cannot defend it. Having a game this long and the localisation team did not care about it is pathetic. Look at Sekai Project's localisations for an example for how you can have a long visual novel that is translated fairly consistently well. I'm not saying they have no problems, but I can assure you that if I took a shot every time I found a mistake in one of their localisations, I'd be fine by the end of the visual novel. If I did it for this, even for the "patched" version, I'd be hammered in well under half an hour.

I had a LOT of fun with this. The story kind of dragged out in the middle and I got brickwalled by 1 situation trying to leave a level with very little Amber (AKA Mana) left, but otherwise it is loads of fun. In meta, this is more like a puzzle game than anything else, but I relish the fact that there are always multiple ways to approach a level. There is combat - but this is NOT a combat game, it's more about observing covertly and figuring out how you're going to get through a section of the map. You can kill guards, distract them, or go completely unnoticed, and there's a useful and relevant skill-tree to invest in. Every once in a while I was frustrated by Styx not moving like I wanted - but it rarely happened and you can save on-demand - which is pretty fantastic as it really encourages you to just try stuff rather than agonize over a situation; it encouraged me to be creative and try different approaches until I succeeded. I just got done with Normal difficulty, and this game is plenty challenging. Discovery isn't necessarily a death sentence every time, but it usually is... that being said, you can stealthily elminiate almost everyone - and I purposefully played against the grain and tried to do just that, just to see if I could and I had tons of fun trying to figure out how to elminiate as many enemies as possible.
The toolbox you get right out of the gate is very useful and demands skillful use - but boy is it satisfying to pull off a plan once you figure out how to make it work. You can do all kinds of things, like whistling to pull a guard out of position to sneak past or elminiate him, poison food/water to covertly take out enemies without being detected, setup traps with your skills, swipe potions from guards' belts, hang from ledges to avoid detection, throw sand to douse torches and create areas of darkness, all kinds of stuff man! Being able to save at any point really cuts down on what otherwise might have been a frustrating experience - but don't kid yourself it doesn't make the game too easy, it pulls no punches at any point and really rewards smart, attentive, careful play.
You can also replay missions at any point to earn more skill points and unlock more skills, which I'd certainly recommend doing early on once you get some useful skills unlocked.
Overall I'd give this game a 9/10. It only gets -1 because open combat is such an option of last resort against anything, even little bugs, some information is poorly communicated (its '3' to use clone smoke bomb fyi), and I genuinely did get really frustrated trying to get out of that one gate where 7 guards are looking right at it and its the only way to go and I was out of amber... Don't let any of that dissuade you though, it is a fantastic stealth game where detection isn't necessarily guaranteed failure either - that makes for some exhillerating moments where you make a crazy escape after everything goes wrong.

Finding Paradise was a beautiful game.
I've played To the Moon, but that was a long, long time ago. I think it was in the same month it came out, but it always stuck in my head. Like many others, I cried during To the Moon, and even more-so in Finding Paradise. But the point isn't to make you cry, but to tell a beautiful story with meaning. Kan Gao achieved that.
I don't think the game would be the same without the music. It's beautiful. Multiple times I just stopped and listened. Each track was (usually) perfect to the mood of the current scene. I used "usually" because there were one or two times that there was some pretty heavy, bittersweet music while something comedic was happening. It didn't bother me too much, but it was noticable.
The art itself is also very fitting. The pixel art looks very good, but the graphics are improved with the lighting that was used. There were sunshafts in rooms that made some stuff look gorgeous. The backgrounds were very well made too; they were a great accent to the levels.
The story, as previously stated, was fantastic. It had more layers than To the Moon and additional sideplots that helped set up the story for the next episode (admittedly, it's been such a long time since I've played To the Moon that I might be wrong on this, but this was definitely deeper layered and more meaningful than the first to me). Dr. Rosaline and Dr. Watts are a pleasure to see again. There were less jokes than To the Moon, but this time there was a proper build-up to each of them, which made the jokes funnier. I would love to go deeper into the story, but it's something that you should really experience yourself.
I have not played A Bird Story, but it ties in with Finding Paradise. I only looked at screenshots, and I think that people who played A Bird Story previously would have a somewhat deeper understanding of the story than someone, like me, who did not. It didn't really affect me at all though. It's not necessary, just a nice addition.
All-in-all, Finding Paradise is brilliant. I hope that people keep playing this game for a very long time, and I look forward to the next episode.

God ♥♥♥♥ing dammit Steam needs a "mixed" review.
If there is anyone out there who still doesn't own it, I would actually recommend this game to people who like:
- Batman lore
- open-world games
- streamlined reaction time based combat mechanics
My problem is that I like neither.
There are some things that this game does *very* well. Moving around the city by gliding and jumping from roof to roof, listening to the bad guys chatter, swooping in and fighting crime, and the whole being Batman thing feels really good. Graphics-wise it is still pretty impressive. The story is interesting (it depends on how much you like the lore I guess). The production value (world design, voices and dialogue) is insane for a 6 year old game.
I just don't think it's deserving of that 95% rating and those remarks of it being "one of the best games ever" that people keep throwing around. It's actually a simple and linear game, cleverly disguised as an open-world game and with a very well executed Batman skin on top. None of the game mechanics are intrinsically "fun" or valuable on their own. They only make sense once you put the Batman skin on top of them and most of them are fluff, to keep you busy or advance the story line. Combat is basically a very elaborate cut scene, whose outcome is decided through quick time events (see the on-screen prompt, react by pressing the proper button). The combat system is what dissapointed me the most I'd say. "Detective mode" is basically 3D pixel hunting. Stealth is mediocre, feels tacked on and scripted. The "open world" part is just there to keep you busy going from A to B while following the story.  The combat mechanics, gadgets, puzzles are all just thrown at you from the start and will create the illusion of a complex game, but a lot of it is just fluff. There really aren't a lot of mechanics to "master" in the game.
However, everything looks *cool as ♥♥♥♥* and I think that's where the game shines - if you aren't looking for particularly deep mechanics or a sense of challenge, the game is gorgeous and spectacular and is maybe enough to keep you glued. There's a lot of stuff "to do" and achievements to hunt so if that's your thing, you're going to love it.
But if you're looking for something more interesting, deeper mechanics, more complexity layers, look elsewhere. This is definetly not a stealth game - it's no Thief, Hitman, Splinter Cell, Dishonored. It's a linear experience cleverly disguised as an open world game. And it's definetly not one of the best games ever. One of the best produced games ever, yes, but mechanics wise it's very shallow.

First Impressions Video:
I quite enjoyed Resin. It's a game with simple controls, but a good deal of depth to the play.
Fundamentally, you are some sort of ninja dude (apparently an android, but I'm going with ninja) as you run throughout the world and kill stuff. All fun and good. You have an attack which can only be accessed by first going into a stance which completely changes how the character moves. Go out of stance to move around fast, go in stance to hit things. There's also a dodge move.
The game has a good difficulty curve. It starts with super easy enemies so that you can get an idea for the combat and then throws you in against more difficult opponents. The first boss itself just seems to be the proof of knowledge for the game, asking the player whether or not hey know what they're doing. That being said, there is no tutorial until you've already played a bit of the game, so you'll have to check the control scheme.
The art style is interesting. Your character and most of the enemies you fight are very small on the screen. They're not so small as to obscure what's going on. Really, the smallness of the character makes for a much larger looking play area, instilling a sense of vast emptiness in the game. That feeling definitely works to create some good atmosphere.
The control scheme itself is fairly standard. It's a keyboard ZXC set up. Nothing crazy to remark on there.
Overall, the game is quite fun and definitely worth taking a look at if it appeals to you. For five bucks, it's definitely worth a check.

Another game where I wish there was a "neutral" rating. It looks great with nice artwork and style, but the controls are a bit too frustrating at the moment.
Attacks seem to queue up oddly which causes a delay effect at times. Enemies also seem to mimic your movements exactly to camp out at the bottom of elevators which gives them a better chance at the first attack. It's definitely a difficult game but most of the difficulty feels like it's caused by awkward control mechanics. Also, you have a combined limit on the number of attacks and dodges (character jumps away from enemy) which makes all the above even more annoying because often you'll waste attacks or dodges trying to account for the odd control timing which leaves you being a sitting duck. Still though, it has a lot of promise and hopefully they improve some of these control issues so combat feels a bit more fluid (versus the stiffness and awkwardness it is now).
