Have you ever seen a tag line read "a loveletter to the glory days of gaming" or something like that? Usually for a kickstarted indie game with pixel graphics and bleepity bloopity music? Well the first Evoland tried to pull that off, but failed because it focused more on its references and in-jokes than actual gameplay features. Well Shiro is back to right their wrongs, and actually make a game instead of an interactive "Get it?" simulator. And for the most part they do.
The original Evoland had some pretty good ideas behind it, most notably using the evolution of video games (say, from 8 bit to 16 bit) to progress, but Shiro didn't expand on it at all, and the game was mostly references which we've all seen before. Evoland 2 however took the better approach, and built a story and a game to play with the references, instead of having them drive the story and game. It kinda does this Abobo's Big Adventure (which if you haven't played that, google that♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing where it divides itself into different genres and gameplay styles, like shmups and Chrono Trigger for example. Chrono Trigger actually seems to be a pretty heavy influence on the game, what with the time travel and red-haired protagonist. Speaking of, the time travel is one thing the game actually does quite well. Instead of doing the CT thing and letting you choose different time periods, the game's time travel is scripted and advances the story, which I think I prefer. Of course it makes the game so much more linear, and there's little to no exploration to do.
In conclusion, once again i find myself dissapointed in this game, because instead of expanding on previous ideas, it tries to fix what wasn't broken and changes what made Evoland interesting. That said, it is certainly a far surrperior game to the original, and for fans of references that not everyone is going to get, the game is easy to recommend. What Evoland did wrong, this game does right, but at the same time the opposite is also true. I say pick it up durring a sale or if trading cards are ever implemented.

Any reference they throw in, whether it be Professor Layton, Zelda, or Final Fantasy feels surprisingly in place with the type of game this is, and far from forced like in the first one. On top of that, the writing is really enjoyable, and so is the musical score. The only part I didn't really enjoy so far was a stealth section, that lasted a bit too long, and wasn't even that enjoyable to begin wtih. Overall, the game is just a really enjoyable experience so far, and I highly recommend giving it a check, even if you weren't such a fan of the first game.

I'm enjoying it. There are parts that need tightening up, like seeing the console commands on screen, but aside from that it's been a smooth experience for me.
The story is interesting, the world is intriguingly dark and the characters, so far, are all interesting (my favourite being Niam the crackheaded half elf). Combat plays out on small, hex based maps that keep the action from getting bogged down or boring. And, while in combat, that's all you focus on; you can't loot corpses, for example. All of that happens afterwards which I like a LOT.
The combat system is simple, really, but it works. There are enough special abilties to keep it all interesting and to give you a wide variety of tactics (at least when you get the right people to suit your style) but they're not exactly trying to break the mold here. Basically, you've probably seen this all before. It didn't bother me, but I could see it boring some people.
The graphics do their job, though they're nothing to write home about. The voice acting has been surprisingly good for the main characters, although I find the NPCs tend to fall into stereotypes (villains sound like they're about to go "NYAH I'M EVIL"). It's not really distracting, since their lines are short and to the point, but it was something I noticed so take that as you will.
Which is really the best way to sum up this game; to the point. There are side quests and the like, but this isn't an open world game like Skyrim where you can spend a fair amount of time just walking around. You move from battle to battle, taking breathers when you need/want them, and then get right back into the thick of it. It is for this reason that I recommend this game. It's fast, fun but not short. Buy it.

As an avid RPG player, and one who is all about story, I hold any RPG story I play to a high standard. Daedalic have been great storytellers in the past and blackguards is no different. The game is dark and mature, just what I like. Often in RPG's the more morally grey characters are the most enjoyable, relate-able and overall liked characters of a given game. In Blackguards this the type of characters you play, instead of a group of moral paragons, you play a band of rogues, trying to get by in the world and dealing with events that have been thrust upon them.
You start the game as your chosen character hovering above the corpse of princess Elenor who is being eaten by a wolf, after killing said wolf you are blamed for her death, but the strange thing is, you can't quite remember what exactly happened before you saw the wolf. After being tortured and being questioned for a name you know nothing about. Enter the fire loving, fight craving, elf hating dwarf Naurim and you’re soon on a prison break with the intention of finding out just what the hell is going on here.
The Battles in blackguards are very addictive, they tend to be relatively short but by no means easier. The great thing about blackguards combat is its difficulty, some battles require real thought and careful planning. The game is very challenging but by no means overly difficult and while it can be unforgiving at times, the game auto-saves after every battle and even if you die you have the option to start the battle over at any point from the pause menu. Fans of tactical turn based Rpgs will really get a kick out of the challenge blackguards provides. One of the star features of combat is the interactive environments. In certain levels you will have objects placed around that you can use. You can cut a rope causing the hanging chandelier to crush the enemies below it, ignite flammable swamp gas to burn opponents and more. There are over 190 beautifully crafted battlefields in blackguards, these are no mere random maps, these are hand drawn, carefully thought out maps that not only feel unique but really leave a lasting impression.
If your an RPG fan, a turn based strategy fan or you just love a bloody good story, I cannot recommend blackguards enough. It is one of those rare games that I literally lost track of time playing. The story telling is good and engaging. Battles while not lengthy have great solid mechanics and good depth to them. The world is fantastically immersive, Daedalic have envisioned southern Aventuria beautifully. Check out the full video review for a more in depth look.

Bear in mind that I'm unfamiliar with most anime/manga/otaku terminologies. I also have read very few VNs and watched even fewer animes. So here's my review, beginning with the negative points: Aweful translation. I could've done a better job if I knew Japanese. The problem is in the Moenovel's understanding of English and western culture, I can guarantee it. People are talking about how Ageha's route is drastically changed. I wouldn't have minded that if not for the sloppy translation job. I am afraid that it is going to be like the translation, half-baked and full of inconsistencies. The introduction of clearly waaay underage Asa and Yoru as romancable characters freaked me out. I understand that there is an audience for it but cultural differences made it harder for me to continue. That's all the complaints I have with the novel. Everything else, like the plot, music, artwork and assets, is above average. The rough translation job might have butchered some of the cultural references and jokes but I wouldn't have got them anyway. I was specially impressed with the music and art style. The teams behind them are infinitely talented. I can't say much about voice acting as I'm totally Japanese-illiterate, but they did sound authentic and far from melodramatic or dull as with some VNs I've read before. Don't be fooled by typical anime cliches, the rest of it makes the VN so great that you won't even notice them. Go for it and take the soundtrack too, it's lovely.
Update: I have installed the Restoration patch to see what's all the fuss behind it. And oh boy!!! Moenovel has totally butchered the game. It's not that it os bad, it is actually very good as far as the Kotori route goes but that is because the original Japanese material was exceptional, as proven by the restoration patch. Moenovel hasn't just cut the h-scenes which are frankly an important part of the Ageha arc according to many(which is why Moenovel rewrote it), but they also removed any kind of adult jokes and many important plot elements and CGs. The "Restored" version of the game feels like the GOTY edition of the Batman games. The translation job is still as sloppy as ever but a bit better than vanilla Moenovel release. If My Heart Had Wings was originally meany to be a young adult game which is suger-coated due to cultural barriers and taboo and stereotypes circulating japanese media. They should have made an official 18+ patch.

Stealth mechanics are really integrated in the actual videogame landscape, stealth games, not so much. Styx is a pure stealth game, not a game where stealth is an option, but a necessity. This doesn´t mean being spoted it´s an instant game over, but the game certainly doesn´t encourage that you do so, and there´s only a certain amount of enemies and situations that you can handle on combat. And this is one of the stronger aspects of the game, you´re a small goblin and the whole gameplay is based upon that premise. Styx doesn´t become in a killing machine instantly after buying some skills that affect the world but not him, you´re only in control of this small creature and he´ll always be a small creature, more suited to crawl under tables than to take on 4 guards at the same time.
Besides the original main character the game also has an amazing area design, taking full advantage of both horizontal and vertical structures, allowing for multiple ways to tackle most situations. Not all is  gold tough, this game relies heavily on exploration and patience, if you don´t care for those things the game run time plumbers. There´s also some areas that you revisite, and players that don´t  enjoy the previous things wil probably hate this even more.
In the end Styx: Master of Shadow is a passable game for non stealth fans, but if you´re one of them, Styx is def a sleeper title that hooks you up inmidiatly and one of the best current pure stealth experiences.

I am giving this a tentative thumbs up after my initial impressions.
I came in this not from a Kickstarter, but as a purchaser on a half-off discount. I imagine if I backed this, I'd be kinda disappointed.
It's so hard to put it into words.. it's good, but it lacks polish. It also could use more refined controls. Really, if you didn't move so slow, the game might be twice as good. I find myself rolling all the time, and feeling like that's still slow.. it feels like it takes longer than it should to get anywhere, and the jumps even feel like you're kinda floating a bit.
I think all the elements for a good game are here, but the controls could use some tightening, and it could use some more polish in general.
1. Combat feels unfinished with lock-on not facing you towards the enemy, making it annoying to block and do the sort of movements of walking forward and back as you strike that this style of combat system was designed for.
2. Even facing them, it's easy to get hit while blocking, or standing too close for blocking to help.
3. More nitpicky, but the lock-on is unclear; all it does is face the camera, with no clear retina over the enemy; nothing but a cursor change. But if there's any message to my review that I want to get across, it's that small tweaks like these would do worlds of good for this game.
4. Movement feels slow. While that's not a bad thing on its own, once again, the game is based on established mechanics where the player wants to get across spaces fairly quickly. You shouldn't have time to look around your room getting distracted because it takes two minutes to cross the island.
5. Some villagers you can talk to don't have the button prompt, while some who don't talk once you've exhausted their options do. Another nitpicky point, but again, just a small bit of sloppiness..
6. Normally you expect both an in-game pause menu and a main menu.. that being said it was over halfway into my playtime before I figured out that you can switch from the main menu into quest prompts and so on. Just feels unclear, and is out of the norm for most games so I just thought there was ONLY a main menu. In fact, I still don't know what those other menus are, because as a player, I was done once I found the quest prompts. I was planning on critiquing the lack of a minimap or even a regular map until it occoured to me that the map may be in there.
7. I had trouble picking items up. As a player, and as the game is designed very much like Windwaker, I expect to hit the button near an item to pick it up. But you have to have the cursor over the item you want to pick up.. and since equipable items tend to be smaller and blend in with clutter, this means you have to stop and spend a few moments aiming to pick up your sword you dropped because you needed a torch. The crafting system and abundance of supplies make this negligible since you can easily just craft more, but as a player it is incredibly frustrating to have the game be that particular about picking things up, when such precision is completely unnecessary and you just need the character to pick up the closest thing.
I will likely have more to say after I played it some more, but as clunky as it feels, I just can't sit down and give it that time in one go. I want to like it more, but it took me an hour to complete side-quests and open up the other half of the island. While I didn't at first, I figured out the island layout fairly quickly, and where I was going most of the time; that's just how long it took to run from one place to the next and doing what was needed for about four things.
The map size feels good, while unpolished the platforming and level design is fine, you just move.. so slow..
That's why the thumbs-up is tentative. I like it, I want to enjoy it more, but there's more things than I probably noticed in one play session dragging it down. I am glad to have it, but this game needs more work, and I would probably respect it a lot less if I didn't know a few things about game development. But as it stands, exploration and combat are 80% of this game, and both have flaws keeping them from feeling solid. It's close, the systems they need are all there, but it just needs more work to feel right.
So.. I tentatively say that it's good, but should be treated as "early access" level quality, and probably not worth the full price as it is now.

is a third-person 3D adventure RPG.
The game follows the story of Tyrim, a young boy living on a small, Vikingish island.
The cartoony visual style, island-exploring storyline, and
are strongly reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker, but the core gameplay is substantially different. For example, combat is much less important over all, and many hostile situations can be navigated by sneaking, utilizing the environment, or simply running away. Cornerstone is also missing Zelda's epic battles against gargantuan bosses, but given the extent to which combat has been downplayed, that's neither a surprise nor a detriment.
Crafting is a key activity, and basically every usable or equippable item in the game must be crafted and will degrade
with use - instead of collecting gems or mana vials, players will comb the landscape, shredding grass and smashing pots, in order to obtain precious wood, ore, wool, and fuel. New or upgraded items are mainly acquired in blueprint form.
I was pleasantly surprised by
, which had me laughing out loud on several occasions. Another highlight is the windsurfing mechanic on one of the islands - it felt so fun and lifelike that it could have been the focus of an entire game in itself. I must have spent three times as long as necessary exploring Mokaga simply due to that.
All in all, Cornerstone was an enjoyable experience. I spent about ten hours playing through it, including extracurricular windsurfing, and I would recommend that fans of this type of game give it a try.

There aren't enough good stealth games in the world as far as I'm concerned. Now, Styx isn't a 10/10, but if you like stealth games I'd say you're probably not gonna be disappointed.
First off, it's worth noting I was playing this with a 360 controller, so I can't vouch for keyboard controls.
The gameplay is very clutch. You have a decent range of motion through climbable terrain and a set of tools and abilities that suit a plethora of playstyles. The level design is very tight and varied, and altho some maps are re-used for later chapters in the game - progressing through the map backwards, along with new enemy placements and patrols makes it interesting enough.
Each level has some neat side objectives, as well as stipulation bonuses like "no alerts", "no kills", "timed run" etc.
The story won't blow your mind, but it does throw you for a loop and has some pretty interesting twists and turns.
I have two gripes about this game tho, and they are fairly nitpicky. One, there's a noticable lack of voice actors for guard npcs. I've heard, not just the same actor, but the same voice for what must be 5 different characters at this point. There are more voices, but they are being re-used for some cutscenes relentlessly. Two, the facial animations are VERY lackluster. The movement animations are pretty great, which accentuates the flaws in the facial ones even more. Expect blank faces with the bare minimum of lip syncing.
But all in all, very good gameplay, and very good art direction. I'd give it a 8/10.

EDIT: I just finished the game, and while I still recommend it, it really is a very buggy game. Most bugs are small, and are just part of the risks of playing a 3D physics platformer made my an indie dev, but there are some bigger bugs as well. Let's get one thing straight, Cornerstone: The Song of Tyrim is not a Wind Waker clone. It's colorful, and there's a certain amount of sailing, and they're both 3rd person action-adventure games with a young protagonist wearing an unusual hat, but that's where the similarities end. But Cornerstone is a fun game in its own right. It's a physics-based action platformer with crafting, and the physics egine is a bit janky, but in a fun way. Most puzzles have a pretty obvious solution, but there's plenty of times where I found the best solution to be exploiting a glitch, crafting a raft in a tiny pond, or just stacking a pile of boxes on top of each other for some good old-fashioned sequence breaking.
The story is minimal, but what is there is nice and touching. You play Tyrim, the son of a viking who doesn't want to grow up to travel and pillage. He just wants to stay home and craft. But when his father and the rest of the men go missing, he goes on a journey to bring him back.
The main gameplay element of crafting reinforces this. You find crafting recipes for weapons, armor, crates, and other items, and can craft items fairly quickly. Raw materials are scattered everywhere, so you can build to your heart's content.
Weapons and shields degrade over time, and you can occasionally get caught without a weapon in the middle of a fight. It sucks, but once you learn that you have to pay attention and make new weapons before you need them, it adds to the feeling of Tyrim as a craftsman. And like I said, the game throws enough material at you that you can craft as many weapons as you want.
The dialog is cheekily self-aware and pretty clever. One line in particular I love is after someone charges you to "take care" of their bandit problem. After you kill them all, she asks, "what deal did you negotiate with them?" to which Tyrim responds, "Negotiate? Oh no, I just killed them all."
The graphics and music are decent. You won't mistake Cornerstone for a AAA game, but the cartoony style holds up nicely, even if it is a bit rough around the edges. The music is minimal and usually pretty forgettable. But sometimes when I'm out on the open sea, it's really nice just to sail around and listen to the music, even though there's really not much that happens on the way between islands. The game isn't the best optimized, and sometimes there's a very noticeable pause after a dialog closes before the game pops back in.
The game is moderately buggy. Probably the most common one I found is that you can partially jump through some textures. After that, a lot of the buttons stop working. I could still move, but I couldn't jump, roll, or attack. Nearly every bug I encountered was fixed by saving and restarting. Another time, I got stuck behind a fence I wasn't supposed to get behind and didn't have enough wood to craft boxes for an escape. You save automatically when you quit, and you can't make an unlimited number of saves to avoid such problems, so I was afraid I would have to just restart the game from scratch. My solution was to back up in a corner and jump backwards and hope I glitched through the fence, which actually worked. Sometimes two wrongs do make a right.
Even though it's not the most polished game and sometimes feels kind of generic, Cornerstone is very charming and a lot of fun to play. The game really makes you feel like a builder on an adventure, and the physics-based problem solving makes for a lot of fun. Don't mistake it for a Zelda game, and you'll have a lot of fun with it.

It's a little, slightly flawed, gem this game. Its a rather classical  stealth game. Very much in the tradition of Thief 1-3. Even controls feel kind of similar. There is some SKill/Magic system added to it. Which is a nice addition and adds some depth, options and diversity in playstyles.
Nowhere near Dishonored-level, but still....
Story is nice, voice acting is ok, graphics are actually pretty good (Its a stealth game so it tends to be dark  quite often!), Good, not too silly humour.
Even counting, that this is a relatively small budget game by a small developer, there are some problems. The biggest by a mile:  The 2nd half of the game recycles almost completely the locations and areas of the first half. with no changes to their designs. That feels VERY cheap, demotivating - and budget or not, is simply bad/lazy game design.
And while the  ... unusual tower looks amazing at times, all levels are in there, so diversity isnt great in the fist place..
Also the levels are, compared with thief 1-3, a bit on the linear side. (Not as much as Splinter Cell or the last so-called Thief though).
I'd empathise the problems a bit more, were it a full price game, but with its low price in sales and very little real alternatives, its more or less a must buy for classic stealth game fans with reasonable expectations.

God ♥♥♥♥ing dammit Steam needs a "mixed" review.
If there is anyone out there who still doesn't own it, I would actually recommend this game to people who like:
- Batman lore
- open-world games
- streamlined reaction time based combat mechanics
My problem is that I like neither.
There are some things that this game does *very* well. Moving around the city by gliding and jumping from roof to roof, listening to the bad guys chatter, swooping in and fighting crime, and the whole being Batman thing feels really good. Graphics-wise it is still pretty impressive. The story is interesting (it depends on how much you like the lore I guess). The production value (world design, voices and dialogue) is insane for a 6 year old game.
I just don't think it's deserving of that 95% rating and those remarks of it being "one of the best games ever" that people keep throwing around. It's actually a simple and linear game, cleverly disguised as an open-world game and with a very well executed Batman skin on top. None of the game mechanics are intrinsically "fun" or valuable on their own. They only make sense once you put the Batman skin on top of them and most of them are fluff, to keep you busy or advance the story line. Combat is basically a very elaborate cut scene, whose outcome is decided through quick time events (see the on-screen prompt, react by pressing the proper button). The combat system is what dissapointed me the most I'd say. "Detective mode" is basically 3D pixel hunting. Stealth is mediocre, feels tacked on and scripted. The "open world" part is just there to keep you busy going from A to B while following the story.  The combat mechanics, gadgets, puzzles are all just thrown at you from the start and will create the illusion of a complex game, but a lot of it is just fluff. There really aren't a lot of mechanics to "master" in the game.
However, everything looks *cool as ♥♥♥♥* and I think that's where the game shines - if you aren't looking for particularly deep mechanics or a sense of challenge, the game is gorgeous and spectacular and is maybe enough to keep you glued. There's a lot of stuff "to do" and achievements to hunt so if that's your thing, you're going to love it.
But if you're looking for something more interesting, deeper mechanics, more complexity layers, look elsewhere. This is definetly not a stealth game - it's no Thief, Hitman, Splinter Cell, Dishonored. It's a linear experience cleverly disguised as an open world game. And it's definetly not one of the best games ever. One of the best produced games ever, yes, but mechanics wise it's very shallow.

You probably already know if you want this or not based on what you thought of To The Moon. It's a very worthy successor. Stands in its own right as well. Since I found it to be a surprising improved experience, though, it's different enough that other people with their own sensibilities may find it more flawed.
They keep a similar style (visuals, music, "gameplay") but that style has been polished overall too. Visuals are a step up, pacing is smoother sometimes, it all seems more direct. Also, not that TTM necessarily had a problem with this, but there is great chemistry between characters, for the Sigmund crew *and* the people in the patient's memories. This does make the narrative a bit more lighthearted at times, especially in how the "game" medium is utilized, but that doesn't detract from its emotional depth and absolutely stellar plot structuring. If you're going to ask me whether I cried or not, I think a lot of "feels-y" (for lack of a better term) media like this risks either not fulfilling what it builds up to, or making the reader feel something just for the sake of feeling something. Finding Paradise is PERFECT in avoiding both of these. Moreso than its predecessor. The story's progression feels natural, sappy moments do something for the characters, not just the readers. And as a whole these moments touch on broader themes as well, providing substance while still giving closure. Actually, the ending (final 20min or so?) achieves something surprisingly new. How the story wraps up was surprisingly refreshing even in terms of just Kan Gao's works. A couple hints of introspection have me *really* looking forward to where this series goes, or rather whatever is next for Freebird in general.
This team seriously knows how to tell a story.

Episode 1 : To the Moon (2011) = Love & Sadness
Episode 2 : Finding Paradise (2017) = Friendships & Loneliness

Building is simple and fun with a simple drag and drop system with easy to use attachment nodes.
Nitpicks:
The tutorials are presented in a handbook format and teach the mechanics of the game well.
Nitpicks:
Gameplay is the most intuitive, especially if you have prior experience with KSP or similar. The main focus is the nav-ring, which shows prograde, retrograde and target indicators. A lock can be placed on it (using Enter) which the ship will try to point to at all times. When locked attempting to rotate will rotate the lock instead, which is more precise. You can also land on gaseous planets, which is a neat idea, but entirely unrealistic.
Nitpicks:
The map shows information on your apoapsis, periapsis and closest approach/encounter. It's simple and intuitive.
Nitpicks:
The challenges is where the game excels. There are 18 fun and challenging challenges that you can try to beat. There are a couple repeats but the repeats introduce a new hurdle to overcome which keeps the experience fresh.
Nitpicks:
This game is well worth $1.99 when it's 75% off, or even higher. It is fun and has neat challenges. You can build a space station and do whatever. It would be nice if it had a few more features (like mod support) but overall it is a fun and worthwhile game. Do note that the game hasn't received any updates for 2 years, so it is unlikely that these nitpicks will ever be fixed, but that is okay.

E.Y.E Divine Cybermancy is a cool game. You can experience cycles, gain brouzouf, and you don't afraid of anything except breaking your legs.
Though E.Y.E's story is very linear, and only one choice in the game really changes anything, it serves its purpose well enough. In short, you are a member of E.Y.E, and it is your sacred duty to shoot things, and your mentor is a real jerk but so is your commander. Without further investigation, that is about all a player will glean of the story.
Where E.Y.E really shines is the gameplay. Numerous strategies are viable and fun to play. Every single weapon has its own niche, and feels appropriately powerful. Nothing that a cyberpunk game could offer is left off the table: gigantic electronic blades, viscious SMGs, and most importantly, cyberlegs.
E.Y.E has a more-or-less standard cyberpunk setting, but what sets it apart is its mysterious atmosphere. The player will have a tough time getting the whole picture of what is going on in the world as they are assaulted by oddly familiar demons and psionic soldiers, while exploring massive foreign environments, at the request of a strange master. Coupled with the pseudo-philosophical nonsense that is the dialogue (courtesy of a poor translation), the setting as a whole is very interesting.
P.S: This game isn't for everyone. The strange story, setting and gameplay will certainly turn some away, perhaps for a good reason. Because of this, $10 can be a steep asking price, and so if you're uncertain about the game, buy it on sale.

This is a really nice, pure little platformer. It's not difficult; there's no time limit, the only setback for dying is having to restart the level (no "lives") and the levels are short enough that restarting them isn't a big deal. It feels really good to play. The game's a lot bigger than I expected, with lots of surprises. The whole thing is just really relaxing and charming and I liked it a lot.
Only two caveats: First, there's no controller support, but the game feels fine on a keyboard, and if you would really prefer to use a gamepad, the controls are simple enough that setting up JoyToKey only takes a few seconds. Just four directions and a jump button.
Second, the game only runs in either fullscreen or in a very tiny window. It wasn't a big deal for me, but it might be frustrating if you want to stream or record the game, or if there's another reason you need to run the game windowed.
If you like 2D platformers and the above aren't dealbreakers you should absolutely pick it up.

"Demo was great. We'll see how the full game is and whether or not it only likes an XBox controller." --Me
Well, the full game is great. It's an action, beat-'em-up game in the 40k IP. It's fun. It's got Boltguns, chainswords, Orks and Space Marines. You need a game controller. Like so many other games, this one just doesn't function properly with mouse and keyboard. I really hate Microsoft fro making this the norm with action games.
That being said, this is a very good game. The graphics are great, the controls are solid (if a bit odd), and the story is quite good for a licensed scifi vehicle. There's not really much to distinguish it from the horde of other action games out there, except for the XBoxesque slowdown that occurs when the graphics eat up all your rams. Oh, and there aren't any graphics settings. Another big "♥♥♥♥ you" to PC gamers from our friends at Relic.
[UPDATE]
I've been playing the multi-player a lot and I LOVE it. PvP is fairly hectic, and it seems like you're either 733t or a n00b. Exterminatus, on the other hand, is AWESOME. A team of up to 4 marines works together to survive wave after wave of greenskin onslaught. You really have to know how to play the different character classes to be successful individually, and have a good mix of them to be successful as a team. You CAN win with four tacticals, but you better have vox, and you better be prepared to die a lot.
Another great multi-player feature is your character progression. Your account levels as you kill stuff and gain xp. As you level, you unlock equipment and perks for each character class, as well as character slots, which essentially increases the number of builds you can choose from when you join a game.
In my opinion, it's the multiplayer experience that really sets this game apart from other action titles. That and the fact that it's a shooty action game, rather than just a straight swordy action game like most of the others. You'll spend a lot of time in melee combat, but you'll also spend a lot of time with your boltgun.

It's a fun game. You can masterfully plan out your plan of attack, and duck out if caught so you can go right back at it. The controls are smooth and simple to learn, the graphics are the perfect mix of cartoonish and stunning, and the voice acting is pretty good. The downside? If you don't do perfect on a mission, like you miss a token or ruin a perfect stealth run, you have the option to replay it. You can even do it right after the mission ends, when you go back to your hideout. But once you finish that mission and you're back in your hideout, you can't do a damn thing. You can't go on to the next mission. You can't replay the mission again. You are stuck. This kind of thing happens from time to time, but the fact that it's been years since release and this still hasn't been fixed is awful. I may decide to do a non-perfectionist run in the future, since I can't refund this game, but if you want to be perfect on the first try, this is not the game for you.
TL;DR, game breaking bug means you can never replay a mission without having to start over.

A fantastic game for playing with a mate or two, Nidhogg is a skill based game where two players (Or one and an AI) are pit against one another in a vicious bloodsport to reach the edge of the screen that the opponent spawns from. Armed with a rapier and your wit you will roll, jump, throw, stab and grab your way to victory or die repeatedly trying. All in the name of the glorious Nidhogg to which you will sustain!
Each match begins with a face off on equal terms, one will win, one will die. Afterward the victor is allowed to proceed toward their goal and the loser must lay down their life to defend their side. Should the defender score a kill they will be the one allowed to proceed toward their goal. Should you both die in some hilarious fashion likely involving a pit of some sort you will be forced to face off much like the fight at the start of every game.
The controls are responsive and simple to comprehend after some gameplay. However your skill as a player will be the deciding factor in winning or losing, learn to read your opponent and counter accordingly. Learn the nuances of pitched fencing battles to disarm them and skewer their gullets. Or dont and get thrown down pits or worse.
For what it lacks in size Nidhog more than makes up for it in depth and is incredibly fun as a result. You could try jumping over your opponent and making a run for it and they could try throwing their weapon into your back as they frantically chase you down. You might also try rolling past them, while they could counter with a low thrust or a grab if unarmed. You will get into pitched battles of wit and timing and each encounter with your enemy will feel unique and chalenging.
There are 4 varied levels with their own hazards and many different ways to approach or defend them. The level of depth makes for a deeply enjoyable game for two people to play together on the couch. Highly recommended, but only if you have the aforementioned mates as the online can be pretty bad at times.

Age of Chivalry is a first-person medieval combat mod made in 2007 off the game Half Life 2. Upon entering a server, the player would either spectate or choose a team, then pick upon several classes to fight the enemy. The objective could vary depending on the map, but in general you had to kill the enemy and complete your objective. Over many years of playing this game, I will finally give a review to this game to ensure it stays alive as I very much recommend this game.
Before I get into the pro's of this wonderful mod, most of this is based off of memory and by the smallest chances that this mod was updated from me last playing this in 2014, I will ensure it will be updated after I get a response from someone about it.
Pro's:
+ Realistic first person camera angle
+ Different types of attacks and weapons to choose from
+ Good combat style
+ Realistic damage count
+ Chances of getting spawn killed are small
+ A decent community
Con's:
+ Unrealistic interval / amount of stamina
+ Hitboxes don't work as well as they should
+ Limited against choosing certain weapons for classes
Now, people may question why I haven't included graphics in the cons, well thats because the graphics on the mod during the time it was created was perfectly good, and now that it is decently old, it's not getting updated anymore, wether if it was still being updated I would rate the graphics. Although however the graphics seem pretty good compared to other games, so it doesn't bother me as much as the other con's as long as you know the basic model of the enemy and where his hitboxes would be, as if I hit the arm, the arm would be cut off (defaulty with a weapon such as the broadsword).
As a conclusion, I rate this an 8.5 / 10 for a well made mod rewarded by a (hopefully) well reviewed rating.
Thank you for reading my review, I hope it has helped you know what the majority of AOC fan's think of this game, of course this is just my opinion and I can't exactly speak for everyone.

is an adventure game with a similar art style and environment as
.  You play as a young Viking boy going from island to island searching for the men of his village.  I really enjoyed playing this game despite its bugs and the very basic combat.
I loved the Wind Waker art style, so to me this game was pure eye candy.  The performance is very impressive.  I do not have great gaming equipment (I'm looking at you Intel HD Graphics) but still I was able to play this game with high settings and even anti-aliasing without any slowdown in gameplay.   Unfortunately, the book-style cutscenes went to a crawl no matter the settings I chose, but I noticed that a single core was used at full capacity during those, while all of my cores were put to work during gameplay.  The music was also delightful and helped build the overall experience.
In my opinion, the developers have captured the spirit of what is an adventure game to begin with.  The locales are diverse and I always felt excitement when going to or exploring a new place.  New game mecanics are introduced throughout the entire game.  The combat is very basic though.  You wait for an opening, which for most enemies can be done by standing still with your shield raised, land a few blows and repeat.  However, it does not in any way prevent it from feeling as if on an adventure.  There are also some platforming elements.  Unlike in many Zelda titles, you can jump whenever you want.  Puzzle solving is also involved and often mixed with platforming.  I found it to be well executed.
The items you use, such as the weapons, can be picked up or crafted using ressources you acquire.  Ennemies do not respawn when killed, but ressources, spiders and noncritical items such as boxes do.  The state of puzzles and the items linked to them are saved.
There are some physics bugs.  I sometimes "double-jump" when near edges.  I also went a few times through a surface and got stuck when I was going too fast and/or arrived from the wrong angle.  I suggest duplicating your save file just in case something goes wrong.  The dialogs, while not animated, are fairly well written.  They are consistent in showing the personality of the protagonist as a kid with a sarcastic sense of humour determined to achieve his goals.
I recommend this game despite its bugs.  The art style, the exploration and the general feeling of adventure kept me playing.  It is not without flaws, but then again they do not go against the spirit of the game.  I want to thank the developers for supporting Linux, you are awesome!  I finished the game in about 15 hours.  I tried to find every recipe and upgrade, but it looks like I still missed a few.  As a veteran Zelda player who aims to find everything when playing, this is actually a good sign.  I will come back to it shortly to find every secret. ;)

Cornerstone was really a mixed bag for me.

However, I think my experience with those bugs weren't the norm.
So the positive: it's a cute, colourful and interesting little game. You can easily get 20 hours out of the story (based on friends who have completed it), the dialogue is top notch and it really feels like playing an old PS1 type platformer (reminded me of Spyro in a lot of ways).
So I would recommend to pick this up overall, for the sale price. I'll always remember the game, even with not being able to complete much of it. And if you get the same issues, that's why there's refunds.
But overall the game needs more attention paid to it, and more people picking it up, the devs did a great job.

I was surprised by the initial emphasis on crafting and it can get a bit tedious to have to re-craft items as they break. I got used to it quickly, though, and don't really mind.
I'm loving the game in spite of its rough edges. It's a bit buggy; sometimes plants float and the player gets stuck inside of things. But so far, I've been able to get around any such bugs.
The crafting and physics engine combined often give the player multiple ways to overcome challenges and traverse the world. This is part of what makes the game so fun. However, this means that it's possible to find story/quest triggers out of order, and the game doesn't account for that possibility. When sent to find a pair of people early on, I accidentally took the long way around, spawning boxes to climb up one side of a bluff and down the other, saving the girl in distress and then carrying her (literally) to the other person, who proceeded to inform me that the person I'd just rescued was in trouble.
I haven't gotten far enough into the story to know if that will negatively affect my enjoyment later. For now, the exploratory gameplay is fun enough that finding things out of order like that makes me giggle quietly to myself. It helps that the dialogue tends to be amusing in general, with jokes scattered throughout.
I haven't played Dark Souls, only watched a let's play, but while I can see similarities to the Dark Souls combat system, I'm thinking that Cornerstone's combat won't live up to Dark Souls' punishing difficulty. Granted, I'm just about to get off of the starting island, so it could ramp up in difficulty from here.
As for comparing it to Wind Waker... I think that's an apt comparison in terms of the overall feel of the game. It's been a long time since bright, colorful, and lighthearted was common in games. Cornerstone captures that very well without feeling like a Zelda copy.
Edit: Major downside is that keys are not rebindable. :(

Four hours in so far and I'm really anjoying my time with Cornerstone: The Song of Tyrim. As advertised, it has a similar artstyle to Zelda The Wind Waker, which I find quite charming. I don't really think there is much resemblance to Darksouls to be found here frankly: There is a checkpoint-system, which one might argue is similar to the Darksouls-bonfires, and you drop your weapons when you die but that is really about it.
Generally, I don't enjoy the combat very much. It is very basic and feels a little clunky, but it's working and so far isn't too big of a focus of the game. What the game does really well is the exploration. Especially on the first island I had a lot of fun running across the island, searching for things to do, hidden upgrades for the inventory-capacity or new blueprints.
Most interesting I found the crafting-system though: Whereas in most games, the crafting is more a thing you do every now and then outside of combat and inbetween quests, here it is very much the main mechanic. You could start crafting a cannon-turret mid fight if you wanted!
The writing is fine and has a few humourous lines here and there (Sometimes intentionally breaking the fourth wall in a humourous way, but in my opinion the writer didn't overuse it at this point and I did chuckle a few times). I noticed a few spelling-mistakes though, but nothing unfixable. I've seen much worse.
I can't say much about the length of the game yet, since I have yet to complete it. But I'm assuming, in the very least it will be 10 to 15 hours.
I do recommend it if you like the art-direction. It's not a combat-heavy game though and when it comes to puzzles, I haven't found anything very challenging so far. But it has a very nice, bright atmosphere, an interesting world and a story of which I'm curious how it'll continue. I would call it an explorationgame, and a good one too. But you shouldn't expect Darksouls and not even Wind Waker in a sense. It looks like Wind Waker, but it doesn't really play like it. I don't think that's a bad thing though. It's not a Wind-Waker-copy, it's something new, even though the art and the music (The music is very well made actually. It does a great job at enhancing the atmosphere further. Quite like it!) are reminiscent of it. :)

So far, I'm really enjoying Cornerstone: The Song of Tyrim. I pre-ordered it through Humble Bundle weeks before it actually came out, so it's fair to say that I was really anticipating this game. It's similar to games like The Last Tinker: City of Colors, and I enjoyed that one on PC before adding the steam version to my collection.
The graphics are excellent, and the detail in the characters, including facial expressions, is really a showcase of the developer's talent. Parents can also be assured that the content is suitable for a younger audience. If you or your child enjoyed Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas, The Last Tinker: City of Colors, or any of the 3-D Mario or Sonic games, this is definitely one to pick up.
There are multiple areas to explore, well-developed characters and a storyline that includes questing and interacting with members of the viking community. So far, it's evident that the developer put a lot of time and effort into giving these characters unique characteristics and personalities.
There is also a crafting component and a variety of items and weapons that can be crafted. I can see myself spending many hours with this game and definitely intend to do so.
Full controller support, responsive controls, and attainable achievements are always a plus for me, and this game has them all.
There's only one thing I want to point out that detracted from my experience, and that's motion sickness that I've experienced with some 3-D games that have a reduced FOV. I had to take a break once I realized that this was going to be one of those games for me, and the fix, for me, is a cooler, brighter room, sitting further away from the screen, and increasing FOV while reducing screensize. My rig is an ASUS gaming laptop with GTX 970 and G-Sync, so FPS, resolution, and stuttering are not factors for me, though they may be for others who experience motion sickness while gaming.
Overall, I'm intrigued with the game, and I feel that it's worth the price I paid for it. I intend to finish the game and explore to my heart's content. Definitely recommended for younger and experienced gamers looking for a new adventure RPG.

Finding Paradise is the second game and indirect sequel to the excellent, "To the Moon".
It needn't be said that this title like its predecessor delivers when it comes to its insightful and emotional story.
Finding Paradise may not be a complete tear jerker, like "To the Moon", but makes up for this with its overwhelming good writing and story. It is nice to see that freebird games were able to jump off, "To the Moon", rather than feel obliged to make another tear jerker. (This is not to say that there arent any emotional moments in the story)
More importantly, as a fan who has been following the games and minisodes, it is nice that these games are actually being interconnected. Not to give anything away, but i cant wait for the next game in the series.
If you havent played "To the Moon" and its minisodes, i really recommend you do so before playing "Finding Paradise".
In terms of bird story, playing it may hint at some of the more suprising twists in the story, but i still feel it to be an important part of the experience.
Overall, I am glad freebird games were able to recreate their sucess again. "Finding Paradise", will end up being a game i will remember for the years to come. If you enjoy a wonderful story at the cost of deep gameplay, "Finding Paradise" is a must play.

I hated the original Evoland. It was a game that I had high hopes for, seeing how it claimed to be the game exploring why we love video games. Instead, what we got was a joke, a parody. Something that wasn't worth it's price point. There was so much potential in it that just never got realized, and while Evoland II doesn't full realize everything, it still delivered more than what anyone expected. This isn't some kind of parody game, this is the real deal. This is Evoland II.
Evoland II starts out pretty slow, and you'll know that despite the tutorial mimicking the first 2 minutes of the original Evoland, you jump straight into the Present day, which's graphics look a lot like a typical 16-bit JRPG. Evoland II's art style and graphics are a significant step-up from the original, with great pixel-art and it looks a lot more interesting and lively. The 3D areas lack some polish regarding graphics, but they still are nice. The artwork in this game is great, it's clear that compared to the simplicity of the original game, Evoland II strives to make itself presentation-wise much more bigger.
Gameplay-wise, Evoland II is way more bigger in terms of scale and mechanics. There are a lot more puzzles now, some which could take a bit to get through. Compared to Evoland's laughable "puzzles", Evoland II offers some neat challenges. They had a Professor Layton-themed puzzle right at the beginning, and it was pretty cool (and really easy as well). A lot of the combat is still more of the hack-n-slash kind of repetitiveness you'd probably expect, but the game mixes it up with tons of different game modes. Up to the 2 hour mark, I played through your typical Zelda/Secret of Mana gameplay found through the most of the game, 2D platforming (Which to my surprise is probably one of the gameplay styles you'll play a lot), stealth (which will certainly remind you of Metal Gear), and a Diner Dash-themed minigame (Which while a bit ehh, certainly wowed me, because Diner Dash!). There's probably way more different types of gameplay styles and genres to be found here, and they seem to all have different playtime. However, Evoland II is always the Zelda-like RPG it is and these extra game modes simply break up the gameplay when possible.
The emphasis on puzzles in this game is greater. No longer is it pushing boring switches or going to different corridors, they're full-on challenges that's difficulty can be that of Zelda. The game doesn't explain everything traditionally, and you'll most likely figure things out trial-and-error. It's one of those games where you'll walk around for 40 minutes looking for an objective and realize it's right behind you. It's creative with it's puzzles and while they can stump players very, very hard, they are quite unique.
The thing about these genre/styles is that they're down to the core. They all work and are playable, but are very basic and down to the core mechanics. The RPG mechanics (Which is a large part of the game) such as leveling and getting gear just provide simple stat boosts that won't change a lot of things beyond said stat boosts. This means that they all don't have much complexity or depth to it, and this is also compounded by the fact that the game's button layout is basically like the Game Boy. I've only been using the X and A button on my Xbox 360 controller in addition to using the LS to move.
Evoland II's double edged sword is how it explains things. The tutorial does not specify what buttons work, and the game itself generally asks you to figure out things for yourself. This creates a sense of a Zelda game, but because the mechanics in the game (As well as how some gameplay styles work) aren't explained well for the player to make the best of it, it faults those who don't know how to play a lot of these gametypes. The game throws you into something and expects you to know how to play through it. A simple picture depicting the controls would be fine, but Evoland 2 makes the transistion both simple, and confusing. The worst example of this is the Bejeweled-like gameplay mode, which has a lot of complexity to it that isn't explained well, thus making it difficult.
The game is also quite buggy, which is a shame. Graphical errors like a particle effect randomly displaying, things not appearing, and more can happen while playing, which requite a restart. It also doesn't detect a controller while the game is open. If you turn on your controller when the game is already open, it won't detect it. A minor nitpick. The audio stutters, the game struggles to load textures correctly each time you boot up the game, there was a point where the developers made a dungeon impossible to pass through due to trying to fix a bug. Shiro Games should have more communication with us players on the game via Update Notes in the game's announcements or their twitter, because it seems like Evoland II has not been fully patched to be more polished.
Evoland II's story is passable, but it marks a lot of sins by simply not explaining things. The ending is cryptic, weird, and ultimately kinda unsatisfying, and the story likes to drop major events like they never happened. Regardless, the writing makes up to it. Evoland II makes up for this by showing it's confidence through it's writing. While it does play not-so subtle game references everywhere, there's times when the game is just legitimately funny and successfully convey these jokes in a less bothersome manner, like how your main character has this blank, emotionless stare in it's dialogue portrait, like how a lot of your dialogue options are simply "Yes or No", it plays with the aesthetic found in many of these games, but doesn't overplay the joke. It's over the top, but in a way that makes it feel unique on it's own. The game doesn't always have to make jokes or references to make you laugh, sometimes it's just what the characters say or what happens.
So what do I think of Evoland II? It a fantastic redemption of a once-shallow game, and pays a good homage to everything I love about video game.

However we’re here to talk about Evoland 2: A Slight Case of Spacetime Continuum Disorder, and that all matters, because like Evoland 1, Evoland 2 seeks to honor the history of gaming. However, while it does use some technology stuff, it is far from the focus of Evoland 2, and instead it decides to look at the games that have made gaming stand out. It looks to the various generes that have come and some of gaming’s best ideas, and plays with them some, while celebrating everything gaming can be.
The standout thing for Evoland 2 is the writing. Evoland , is quite simply in my opinion one of the smartest and wittiest written games I’ve seen in a long time. While Evoland 2 utilizes a lot of the same Hero’s Journey path you’re used to seeing in games, it executes it incredibly well for the most part and utilizes what is there to the best of its abilities, while surrounding it with a lot of incredibly smart writing.

Omegaland is a coin-collecting platformer reminicent of early 90's cd-rom games. The story is standard save the princess fare with a nice twist mid-way through the game.  Level design is a mixed bag, ranging from downright awful to ingenius.  Some require specific character upgrades to complete, while some are quite trivial. Overall, I had a fun time with it.
+ Story twist is neat and rather well done.
+ There are multiple ways through multiple levels.
+ Does not take itself too seriously.
+ Music and sound design is great.
- No controller support. Keyboard control scheme that is absolutely brutal for left handers. I had to use my right hand for WASD and crossed my left hand over my right to hit ENTER for jump.
- Some levels require specific upgrades to beat, which for story reasons you might not even know is available to you.
- Considering how powerful you are by endgame, the final level is a bit underwhelming.
Have you ever asked yourself "What if Jonas Kyratzes had made Super Mario"? Well, ask no more. Now you can play it, at a bargain price and with many secrets to uncover!

For $3 this is a steal. A neat (if a bit on the easy side) little adventure from the guy who wrote TSWCE and The Talos Principle with some fun twists along the way. Bring the kids!*
*

Before the "few surprises," I liked this game a lot. It took a while to get used to the physics, but the art was cute, the collectibles and other jokes were funny, and figuring out the layouts of the castles was a fun challenge.
After the "few surprises," I loved this game. The music and sprawling levels create a real sense of awe, the sparse dialogue gives me just enough to care about the characters, and the Omegaflow mechanic is a brilliant metaphor for the capricious world Jonas experiences (e.g. cat emergencies). There are also great callbacks to previous games in the Kyratzesverse (a term I coin precisely because Jonas will hate it). Try it out!

If you're thinking about getting this game because it's made by Jonas Kyratzes, and you (rightly) loved his work on Talos Principle and The Sea Will Claim Everything, but you're worried that this game looks really boring/dumb/simplistic and aren't sure if it's worth getting purely based on the developer...
Get this game. It's much more clever than it looks. And no, I'm not just talking about the fact that there *is* a twist, but that it's actually *done* really, really well. This isn't going to reach you as deeply as TTP or TSWCE, but it's unmistakably a product of the same mind. Unquestionably worth $3.

Cover is for the weak!  Kill the heretic, Purge the Xeno!  Hinging on its visceral melee combat against hordes of enemies, Space Marine brings you down to the troop level of the legendary tabletop game.  Though short, and a bit repetitive, fans of the fiction and anyone who loves a good hack and slash will get enjoyment out of Space Marine.

For fans of the Warhammer 40k universe, this game is practically a dream come true. You play as wonderfully badass Captain Titus in a linear romp through war-torn cities of an Imperial planet, and the carnage your reap is endlessly satisfying. I would have liked to keep the assault pack (jump jets) throughout the game but sadly you can only keep it for limited amounts of time. This is too bad because death from above never gets old as you slam into the ground with immense force, killing and maiming dozens of orcs in the process. It's a shame that the game was not a huge seller because it would be great to see the series continue - there are some great ideas here that deserve an improved sequel. This game is a good choiceor non-fans of Warhammer for the fun visceral, meaty combat; for Warhammer fans, this game has incredibly realized Warhammer lore and battles that simply cannot be missed.

All in all I do have to say that I absolutely loved this game and everything about it. I personally had zero problems when it came to this game so for a review this is going to be rather short compared to my normal reviews.
To start off with this game I'm going to talk about the graphics. Now obviously for a game that's almost 6 years old, the graphics are very good, now they aren't as good as Batman Arkham Knight, but they are actually pretty impressive for a 6 year old game. Everything looks actually really damn good for a game that I got for $5 on a Steam sale and I honestly have no complaints for the graphics.
Now for the gameplay. I really liked the combat system in this game. It was overall fun and the controls were easy to get the hang of and were very fluent, now the fact that there were only a few animations, sometimes if you are fighting multiple enemies at once the combat seemed a bit stale but that rarely happened in my case and would be one if not my only criticism for this almost 6 year old game.
Audio was to sum it up amazing. I absolutely loved the voice acting and the music was amazing. I have zero complaints for audio and if anyone does I could argue with them over it all day.
Overall I will have to give this game a 9/10 because the game was honestly very very good. The story was very good, the gameplay was fluent, and the audio was amazing. The only reason I didn't give this game a higher rating is because it is a 6 year old game so there are things that it doesn't do as well as a game that is new such as the open world seems a bit stale for what an open world today is, but thats the only reason why this game didn't get a higher rating.

TLDR: The game was great. If you enjoyed To the Moon, this is a must buy!
First and foremost, although this game can be played as a stand alone without missing any of the story, there are many references and inside jokes scattered throughout the game linking to To the Moon (along with its minisodes), A Bird Story, and I even think I found a couple references to Rakuen for those who played that game. While you won't really miss out much, if you have the extra money and haven't played those other games (Rakuen not required but it is a great game), I highly suggest playing those games first.
The gameplay is fairly similar to To the Moon, in the sense that it is fairly apsent from the game. That is okay though, since the main focus is really on the story. There
some extra gameplay elements over the first game however, but more or less, the gameplay amounts to fairly the same. They had several extra things where you could switch between which character you controlled which was fairly neat. Inconsequential... but neat. Kan Gao also manages to stick with a similar formula to the previous game while keeping it feeling fresh.
As is a trend with Kan Gao's games, the story is very well done. Of course it deals with very different themes than To the Moon and while the story as a whole didn't move me
emotionally as To the Moon did, I thought that it was very well done and heartfelt. We also get some expansion on
The game manages to stick to the main storyline while also expanding on some side plots.
The artwork in this game just feels generally more polished than it was in To the Moon, from the animations, to details, to expressiveness of the characters. It was very well done. The pixel art was used to great effect in bringing this world to life.
The music was phenominal. Kan Gao delivers another great soundtrack to his game and I was so glad that Laura Shigihara came back to do another song. If you enjoyed the music in To the Moon, you will enjoy the music here.
That isn't to say that the game lacks any and all faults. Like I saw online, I will agree that the story drags on a bit in the middle of it, though it isn't too bad. Personally, I wasn't able to get attached to these characters quite as easily as in To the Moon, but that may just be me.
That said, the faults are few and far between and my expectations were definitely met for this game, though I'm not quite sure about exceeded
Finding Paradise is a wonderful addition to the To the Moon series which, while it might not obtain the cult status of its predecesor, stands strong in its own right. That being said, I'm not outright saying which game is objectively better, that is fully due to subjectivity. Some may prefer Finding Paradise while others may prefer To the Moon. I think it all depends on your own experiences which is what makes these games so great! We can all relate to it a different way.

This is not Frog Fractions 2. It is not Alphaland 2, and it most definitely hasn't got anything to do with the rampant love for 8-bit princesses... It is instead an utterly unique, and completely unexpected platformer with clever ideas, cute graphics, excellent writing, and some truly surprising surprises.

+ Usually more than one path through a level, which makes them more fun to return to
+ Full upgrade system is quite fun
+ Cute world that starts to feel a bit like home
- Platforming controls are a little clunky
- No gamepad support yet
- Grinding is optional, but you'll need to do at least a bit of it if you want all those upgrades
* I wouldn't personally call this casual. There's a difficulty spike about a third of the way through. It's never challenging per se, but it's enough that you won't be able to cruise through without some thought.
Similar to the old pixel Mario games, except Omegaland is filled with silly humour and characters in each level who chat with you. It's a charming game that prods you not to take things too seriously; you're even reassured that you're not killing the monsters you stomp on, just throwing them out of the area.
You can revisit every level you play through, which means you're never short on coins (which you use to buy health and other upgrades), and you don't have to stress out if you miss something. It's a nice touch, plus it makes the map feel more like a world you're exploring rather than a series of gameplay objectives.
TL;DR: Fun world to explore, sweet and silly sense of humour, and quite a lot of gameplay for something less than $4. If you tend to avoid stories that appear too twee, this might not be a good fit for you, but if you're in the right mood for it you should find something to love here.

Blackguard is difficult. Blackguard is long. Blackguard is fun.

I'll add on to this as I play more but for right now I have the following:
The first thing I have to say about this is I really, really like these types of games. I really enjoy games like Fire Emblem & Onimusha Tactics on the GBA and XCOM on the PC, which are specifically turn-based games. Blackguards also gives me the vibe/atmosphere of old school RPG games I love like Baldur's Gate I & II, Path of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights + expansions + mods (The old bioware game, not that new MMO). While the games I just listed are not turn based, they do have pause button tactics, and they share the fantasy setting and RPG skill allocation, feats, that sort of thing. The most recent game of this genre was Dragon Age Origins but it has been a while since that came out. To me , Blackguards feels like a true merger of those two types of games I listed above, the action is turn-based, but the environment and customization is very much just like old school RPG.
Anyway, since then, I have been waiting for another game to grab my attention the same way all these massive titles did. I decided to pick up Blackguards, and I will admit that I was scared because it was Early Access. I will tell you now this game has not disappointed me in the slightest, even though it is Early Access. The characters are fun, the gameplay is exactly what I wanted. I have to say they won me over pretty quickly. I wrote down a few pros/cons that were most apparent for me.
Pros:
-I personally love the turn-based gameplay/combat system
-Nice artwork and environments
-Plenty of voiced dialog
-Fun characters
Cons:
-Kind of easy even on hard difficulty, but I like these types of games so.....yea
-Graphics are a tad dated so this might bother some
-Some features are kind of buggy but it is still Early Access so calm down (using bandages ect...)
-I would like some cooler / more tiered armors and weapons
-Seeing the reference tags on characters/objects is distracting
-No in depth character customization (but it is to be added later!)
Verdict:
YES pick it up, if it is on sale (erm Winter Holiday Flash sale) even better. This is a fun game to play even early access. I am glad I did it and I think the RPG community will come together to love it.

If My Heart Has Wings is rather worthy of the awards that it has won. It's a well-executed visual novel that does exactly what it sets out to do. The writing is sharp, the characters well developed and well explored, and the plot is enough to keep even the most monotonous parts at least interesting.
As with many stories out of Japan, it is far more interesting than it has any right to be, and I find myself perplexed as to how to sum up my thoughts about the whole thing. It's just a very well done story that isn't exactly groundbreaking. It's one of the rare instances of a romantic visual novel done just right.
While I'll never praise If My Heart Has Wings as one of the greatest visual novels I've played through, I'm comfortable saying that it'll probably stick in my top ten for a few years to come at least.

Evoland 2 is a great journey through the videogame history! If you have a nostalgic pixelheart then Evoland 2 is the perfect game for you. The game is much longer than the first Evoland and it has many nice references to games you would call "classic". The Legend of Zelda, Final Fantasy, Prof. Layton, Mega Man, Street Fighter, Super Mario and Bomberman are a few examples for that what awaits you in Evoland 2. In spite of everything Evoland 2 is primarily a rpg. But do not expect a serious story with full of emotion. Evoland 2 combines alot of humour with an interesting but shallow time traveling story. Sounds good to you? Then play Evoland 2!

However we’re here to talk about Evoland 2: A Slight Case of Spacetime Continuum Disorder, and that all matters, because like Evoland 1, Evoland 2 seeks to honor the history of gaming. However, while it does use some technology stuff, it is far from the focus of Evoland 2, and instead it decides to look at the games that have made gaming stand out. It looks to the various generes that have come and some of gaming’s best ideas, and plays with them some, while celebrating everything gaming can be.
The standout thing for Evoland 2 is the writing. Evoland , is quite simply in my opinion one of the smartest and wittiest written games I’ve seen in a long time. While Evoland 2 utilizes a lot of the same Hero’s Journey path you’re used to seeing in games, it executes it incredibly well for the most part and utilizes what is there to the best of its abilities, while surrounding it with a lot of incredibly smart writing.

To read the full review, visit the Mouse and Joypad page here;
Improving vastly over the previous instalment, Evoland 2 is a must-play for fans of action RPGs. The game’s world is rich with backstory, the characters are entertaining and the original content is far more enjoyable than I ever imagined. The game is however buggy, and you will need to restart the game a few time. Small patchable flaws aside, this game is a thoroughly enjoyable tale of time travel and destiny. The use of different graphical styles is something truly memorable and engaging, and this time it’s been used as an effective storytelling tool as opposed to a gimmick.
First and foremost, Evoland 2 does almost everything better than the series’ overly disappointing introduction. The use of different graphical designs are now integral to the narrative, representing what era your group of time traveling heroes are currently in. The story has been drastically improved, offering a much deeper lore, with pivotal moments in its history. The characters are engaging, and their dialogue is fun and sometimes even heart-breaking. Simply put, if Evoland was a shoddy attempt at a good idea, its sequel is the redemption.
While the first game felt like it was pandering to its audience, throwing any random gaming reference at them, Evoland 2 pulls back the needless illusions and allows the gameplay to do more of the talking this time around. This pleasant change allowed the developers more creative freedom, and it shows in this instalment.
The story is about a young man who’s discovered in the woods by a girl named Fina. The two of them venture out, seeking his true identity when they end up getting involved in a confrontation between an empire and a group of enslaved demons. They’re suddenly whisked many years into the past, and begin their journey towards discovering your identity, stopping a destructive war and returning everyone home.
While Evoland barely had a story to speak of, Evoland 2 addresses the problem with a vengeance. The plot thickens as you progress through a story clearly inspired by Chrono Trigger, as new twists seem to pop up after every new quest. Themes such as free will, destiny and prejudice are used as a driving force, and it makes the game all the more enjoyable. You constantly want to get to the next quest, and I was delighted when I was rewarded with new exploratory options. There’s something about old RPGs, where something as small as getting a paddle boat is somehow amazingly liberating; something that many modern games don’t seem to get right.
Like the classics mini-games of the past, Evoland 2 nails mixing up the gameplay. In one section, you’ll jump into an Active-Time Battle system ala the Chrono series. These ideas could’ve been phoned in, but the developers at Shiro Games included a nice simple selection of moves and even environmental conditions for this mode. You’ll have to time your attacks, as the lights cut in and out or when you’re avoiding electrified floors that’ll nullify your attacks. These modes are not just RPG inspired either- they also have a space shooter segment, where Galaga fans will feel right at home blasting their way through enemies. There’s even several bosses, all with their own patterns to figure out. There’s a 2.5D fighter segment, side-scroller platforming, Bomberman inspired levels- and it does all of them right. There’s even a card game. Okay- that one does suck, but has there ever been a good card game in an RPG?
One thing I can’t ignore though, are the glitches. Oh man- this is truly heart-breaking. I had to restart this game more times than a thirty dollar android phone. Graphics would simply drop out. Mine carts would randomly appear on the tracks preventing me from progressing. Sound effects would suddenly loop in-game, even when I went back out to the menu. My goodness, what a horrible state this game is being released in. While it was annoying, backing out of the game is fast, and I could always get back to where I was quickly- but I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention these grievous oversights. I will say, the game feels ambitious, so a few glitches can be expected, but these were pretty hard to swallow.
And I think that might be my biggest complaint about the game; all the references. While I laud the developers for running with a ‘parody all the games’ mind-set, they’ve now tuned the machine so well, it’s actually quite good without a gimmick. When you stumble upon a reference, it only pulls you out to remind you that you’re playing what’s ‘pretending’ to be a game. The reference may be light enough, like seeing Sir Dan from MediEvil in a dungeon’s corner- it’s when that reference becomes too obvious or obnoxious that it really hurts the overall mood of the game; like finding a mystery box straight out of the Mushroom Kingdom. In a game packed full of allusions, some are going to work, and some are going to make you shake your head in disappointment. Thankfully, the game has more winners than losers, but those stinkers reared their head in all the wrong places, including a poorly timed Professor Layton reference right at the beginning of the game.
