One of those games that makes you burst out laughing or burst into obscenities.  Or both.  Mostly both.
It's kind of like a love child between Asteroids and Towerfall Ascension.  It has far more options than Astroids.  It has far less options than Towerfall Ascension.
Some random things that some fellow multiplayer retro-gamers might be interested to know:
* 2 to 4 players, local shared screen, small arena, top down 2D space shooter.
* you can add 1 to 3 bots.  There are 2 bot difficulty levels, and each bot can be assigned difficulty levels independently.
* Bots are more of an optional "add some variety when you only have 2 or 3 players" kind of thing,  So 1 player vs bots I'd not recommend.  They are especially stupid regarding proximity mines you drop.  You're going to need 1 to 3 buddies to come over and play with you, because there is...
* no online multiplayer
* full screen or windowed
* Gamepad functions: Turn left, thrust, turn right, fire regular, fire/activate special weapon (pickups), and Dash (short boost/dodge forward).
* Regular weapon and boost each take 1 ammo.  If you don't have ammo, you cannot boost or shoot temporarily.
*Your ammo slowly regenerates, represented as squares orbiting your ship (3 max).  So you (and your opponent) know just how much you can dash or shoot.  Which is good, because it prevents spamming either.
* Joystick bindings and keyboard bindings are not re-mappable in-game.
* game supports 0, 1 or 2 players on the keyboard (but I'd not recommend 2 players unless you have an n-key rollover keyboard)
* Music can be turned off so it won't interfere if you're playing your own.
* PowerUps can be turned off, dashes cannot be turned off.
* Friendly Fire can be toggled (for team DM)
* Turning left or right seems to have some issues on my PS3 (on PC) controller's dpads, so we just use the analog pads.  Move thumb right to rotate ship clockwise, not move thumb up to point ship up.  Up and down serve no function.  Like Asteroids.  And it's digital: there are not different turn speeds.
* The map selection screen shows 13 maps, with a random option.  But it seems the "random" pool of maps leaves a couple out.  This game is just begging for a map designer program for more maps and the ability to toggle which maps are included in "random".
One thing that really sets this game apart is the "pilot hunters".  With pilot hunters, after you blow up a ship (one hit does it) the pilot is left behind, and he's got little thrusters on him to fly around.  He can't shoot or dash.  You must either shoot the pilot or ram him with your ship to actually earn the kill.  If you don't, after 6 seconds, his ship will respawn back on top of him.  The balance is spot on for fun, it's not too difficult, nor too easy to take out the pilots.  Well placed laser shots, or missle shots close to center of the blast will take out the ship and the pilot with one shot, but those are both powerups.
Now if only someone would make a similar 4 player game, with more complexity.  Like 4-player Star Control 2...  I digress.
9/10.
Would be a 10/10 if it had many more customization options like Towerfall Ascension, even if that meant pay for DLC.
Anyway, this is a great game and one of my "go to" games for 2 to 4 player shared-screen gaming fun.  I think I purchased this when it was on sale, but had I paid full price: I would still be very satisfied with the purchase.

...is a hidden object game. Retired from the army, former-priest John is summoned to Africa by his cousin who believes his daughter is possessed and hopes John can exorcise her.
As with other hidden object game, you move from one area panel to another, picking up clues to the stories and items you'll need to interact or unlock further areas, or solving various puzzles to open doors, boxes, or finding objects.
Puzzles consists, of course, of the genre namesake Hidden Object puzzles: you have a scene filled with trinkets and objects of all kinds, and you must find the items described on the list at the bottom of the screen. Other puzzles include connecting dots, moving objects on the screen into a specific pattern, or accomplishing a multi-step task by using items in the right order.
While simple, the story is the usual strange and supernatural style you come to expect from the genre, and the story evolves more as your character slip in and out of dreams, go to additional locations and interact with a few people.
It's always nice to see the hand-drawn style of the panels of each area of hidden object scenes. The objects look indistinguishable from the background, so you can't just figure out which object need to be removed at a glance. For those that are having a harder time, an easier difficulty level is available, as well as a hint system, or the option of skipping some puzzles.
Graphics are based on a 4x3 low resolution that looks pixelated and blurry when stretched over a modern widescreen high-resolution monitor. But cutscenes and animations are what really show the game's age. And while at first the narrator didn't sound too bad, you'll quickly see how awful, dare I say pathetic at times, the voice acting is.
There are very few puzzles, and they are extremely simple. It won't take you long to figure them out, most in a single try. The hidden object scenes have no randomization, nothing special to them. Except perhaps for the last act, almost any item you find are for immediate use, so don't expect to hoard a bunch of items and having to attempt figuring their usefulness out.
Nothing you'll find in this game is unique, it's an extremely bare-bone run-of-the-mill hidden object game. There are very few areas to visit, few puzzles and hidden object scenes at all, and the game will be over before you know it.
This game is way too basic to really stand out. There are so many better games of the genre out there. If you have it in your Steam catalog, take a few hours to get it over with. Otherwise, you should seriously put your money somewhere else if you're shopping for a hidden object game.

This hidden object game had a great premise with the plot about a priest’s haunted niece and the colonial African setting, but it is just too tedious to enjoy.
The Saint: Abyss of Despair manages to present one of the oldest hidden object clichés in an interesting new way: we play as a former soldier and priest, visiting a cousin in colonial Africa to save his little daughter who was seemingly possessed by a demon. From here, the story follows the pacing of a classic British crime novel, with the supernatural and the local belief system (plus bad voice acting) playing a dominant role in the events.
The player has to work hard to watch this story though, because the game is incredibly tedious. You must revisit every area after completing any task, since many hotspots only activate after certain triggers. Some key items do not change the cursor, so it is easy to miss them. The puzzles are easy but take forever, and hit detection during hidden object scenes is wonky at best.
No matter how good the story is, all of these problems are just too great to recommend the game to anyone.

On the other hand, Colin's wish....I'm not even sure how to begin explaining 'it'. 'It' is not something you can just tell everyone about. Many of us definitely wish for 'it' before. A small desire in our heart that wants someone else except yourself to see it at least once.
I had that wish before too, but I know it will never come true no matter what. This is what Colin's wish is like....it is impractical and destructive. There is no way that it will normally work, but that's where our doctors come in. They are here to acknowledge this wish that we had but will never really come true.

A Bizarre game about a warrior cult inspired by Deus Ex, Alien, Warhammer and Blade Runner.
Very confusing at first, but then you play some and its still very confusing, and then you finally beat the game, and still, its confusing. You play as a member of a warrior Cult known as EYE, you wake in a cave with amnesia, and from there you complete missions for the head of the Warrior cult, all the while uncovering a conspiracy with your Mentor.
Its based on the Source engine, and you can feel it, it almost plays like a Half Life 2 Mod, however the missions are all on distinct worlds that have their own feel, which can take away from the Source/Mod feeling. Its strange, the gameplay isnt particularly great, and the story is confusing and does not help new players in any way, but its very compelling, and i felt like i needed to play on.
The first five or so missions are pretty ok, all with their own cyberpunk/sci-fi settings, one of which feels inspired by the ending of Blade Runner. Towards the end, there is a outdoors mission, where you leave the urban setting and are out in a desert, canyon like area. At this point the game became really confusing and felt like a chore to play. This is also the mission where you make a choice, in which the ending of the game forks off in three different ways. Apparently you need to play through the game three times, completing each ending, to get the true ending, i never bothered but apparently the true ending explains everything, whereas the ending i played was confusing and did not really explain anything.
Overall i would give this a reccomendation to anyone that is into the cyberpunk styling of Blade Runner and Deus Ex, and although i have never played or collected warhammer figures, the character design and back story of the main faction seems directly inspired by Warhammer.
Before you play, make sure to watch all the tutorial videos, they will help a lot.

Omegaland calls back to 2010-era Flash games on Kongregate and Newgrounds, games which themselves called back to SNES platformers. Double-retro!
Omegaland is easy to play, and so its rough edges become charming eccentricities. The world map lets you explore in the direction of your choice, so it's quite possible to reach at least two of the "boss" levels before any of the shops that sell powerups - but then it's possible to
the bosses with minimal upgrades. The difficulty curve can be a little schizophrenic, depending on what order you play things in, but if you're struggling with one level then backtracking and trying a different one will usually work.
It's cheap and simple and manages to evoke a huge world in spite of that. One gets the impression that this is the game where Jonas Kyratzes got to do all the things that he wouldn't be allowed to do in a big-budget AAA game. Some levels don't lead anywhere or seem to serve any purpose. Others seem to exist solely to show off some gimmick or joke - like Tiny Hill, a level with no enemies that takes two seconds to finish. Sometimes new game mechanics show up without any introduction. And yet it all works.
In most other games these would be mistakes. Omegaland teaches you to expect them. Omegaland will not hold your hand, will not guide you to the "correct" path, will let you make mistakes and then laugh at you... but you have plenty of hit points and dying only sets you back two minutes, so you're laughing along with it. It is easy and fun and gives you much more leeway than most other games, and then it uses this leeway to indulge in off-the-wall design decisions straight out of a thousand teenagers' first Flash games.
Buy it if you're nostalgic for Flash games ten years ago!
Also buy it if you just like easy and quirky platform games!

Fantastic game with local multiplayer focus, and some solid single player options for if you have no friends. The controls are tight on both keyboard and on game pad (I've only used wired connections for xbox one controllers for gamepad support initially, and it works great). Multiplayer is a complete blast, and is a good way to ruin friendships in a more skill based game than mario party 5000. It runs really well on the surface pro 3, so you can also take it to a (soon to be former) friend's house and humiliate them with your amazing piloting skills. In all seriousness though, it controls super tightly, and causes players to make decisions about ammo conservation, whether or not to rush to a powerup or try to snipe somebody trying to grab one. The game performs great on my surface, and works very well with my minidisplay to hdmi adaptor on my tv. If you have a liking of local vs games like street fighter or tower fall, and enjoy asteroids, or one of those two options separately, this is the game for you.

9/10: Gunpoint is a fun, quick game about espionage, hacking, and corporate sabotage. Play as Richard Conway, freelance spy, as he carries out missions to clear himself after getting wrapped up in murder case involving a pair of gun manufacturing companies.
Gunpoint is a silly, finely-tuned, fun time that left me in a good mood. While the title might suggest gunplay, the revolver was one of the tools I used the least over the course of the game. Instead, most of my time was spent leaping using Bullfrog trousers, crawling about the walls and ceilings, using the Dropshot trenchcoat to survive long falls, and most of all, rewiring electronics to my whim. It's very satisfying using a light switch to open a locked door, or making it so an enemy gun calls an elevator instead of firing. As the game progresses, the game adds separate circuits and tougher enemies, bit it never felt overwhelming thanks to the autosave system. Even so, there was still some challenge in figuring out the route to the objective and secondary laptops, which provides a little extra information about the games story.
Guns had recently been banned in East Point, yet things are heating up as the recent murder of a potential client, Selena Delgado, leaves Richard as a prime suspect. Encouraged by Selena's boss, Melanie Rooke, to wipe the camera footage in order to clear yourself, what ensues are about 20 missions of leaping and intrigue as you resolve the conflict between Melanie's company, Rooke Firearms, and her competitors at Intex, run by Fritz Gessler.
Gunpoint is definitely a stealth game, but it's still active and unstressful. You should take time to case the area, and a single shot will usually kill you. However, instead of slowly crawling around or losing a half hour of time after messing up a mission, you're leaping through windows, pouncing on guards, and hacking security cameras to open doors instead of setting of alarms. It's a real good time, and it says a lot that I leave it wishing it was just a few levels longer.

Styx is an amazing stealth game that requires patience and cunning to play.
Summary:
Choose your own path in a stealthy endeavor to defeat the guards and obtain treasure for your trophy room.
Each room brings a puzzle of its own as you choose how to deal with the guards. You are in trouble if you are caught but you can use powers to help you in most situations. There are some minor issues in regards to map and dropping to a ledge but the pros heavily outweigh the cons.
Pros:
- Choose your own path! You decide how you want to get where you have to go
- You are not spoon-fed the paths. If you want to sneak around then take risks and discover the paths
- Take the time to study the guards, know their paths and use to that to your advantage. Each different room seems like its own puzzle
- Powers help you along but are not the main focus as they cost a lot and potions are tough to find
- Hideout at the end of every level where you upgrade and refill on everything
- If you get caught, you will likely die. This is good in the sense that it motivates you to not get caught but challenging to those who may be coming from an assassins creed style of play where battles are welcome
Cons:
- The map is a little difficult to get used to as it is just a blue print of the area with no layers for floors, just an overtop view where you only see the topmost floor and the lower floors in the gaps. Keep track of where you are or you will likely end up chasing your own tail
- The vision does not seem as helpful as I thought it would be. Everything just gets lit and its too bright to discern from highlighted objects and the walls
- Might be getting picky here but you cannot transfer sideways to another ledge
- The drop to ledge mechanism could use some work. It does not seem guaranteed that you will catch the ledge when walking slow to the edge so it could make for some rage moments
- The character seems a bit vulgar at times, swearing unnecessarily to make his point. I would say leaning towards neutral evil.

Rating: 7.5/10
Overview: Third Person Stealth
The Good:
+ Level design offers multiple pathways to any objective. You can either take a direct approach or a stealthier one depending on how well you explore the levels. Certain levels are linear while others are more open.
+ The story is interesting and offers some nice twists and turns to keep things engaging.
+ The AI finds a nice balance between realistic and fun. Rushing head first into any given room will usually result in death
+ Completing main/side objectives as well as challenges rewards you with experience which can then be used to upgrade skills back at your hideout.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
The art style both on an artistic and technical level is pretty lacking. I wanted more variety with the environments, it feels like a wasted opportunity given the setting.
"Combat" in the game is about parrying enemy attacks until you can kill them. Essentially its 'press the attack button at the right moment" over and over again. Granted this IS a stealth game so combat is a second priority but it would be nice if something better was in place. Getting caught and having to engage with the enemies feels frustrating and boring.
The second half of the game recycles the same levels that you completed in the first half.
The Bad
- The game has a ton of glitches. At first I thought it was cute but the same problems kept persisting throughout the entire game. The biggest offender is enemy guards that walk into each other causing them to end up in weird places there not suppose to be.
- Stealth games always have a difficult time with the final boss encounter and this game is no different. Given the build up of the story the final encounter is anticlimactic and frustrating.
Conclusion
Stealth is a genre that doesn't get much love from big publishers so its nice to see other smaller studios tackle the genre. This is a great stealth but obviously held back by its budget. If you love stealth games this is easily a must have game as it does so much right in regards to the gameplay mechanics.

Styx doesnt break any new ground, but I enjoy it so far. There are some issues, but worth the $8 I paid. You cannot really fight head on; you might be able to kill one guard if he notices you, but not 2 at the same time. I think I am about halfway through the game.
Instead of avoiding interaction, I was aggressive and killed EVERYONE. Much more satisfying. Avoidance is difficult, but trying to kill 3 or even 4 guys all clumped together is harder. Also much more rewarding.
1. Graphics: Looks dated. Some parts have great looking textures and others not so much. Seam lines do not always align. The game looks maybe 7 years old, but I found it good enough.
2. Difficulty: pretty easy, even on hard. Just as easy to avoid as it is to kill everyone. You can save/load at any time so mistakes are not an issue. I have yet to use any health potions. If I did get hurt, it was usually due to a large fall or getting too close to fire. There should be less saves and only a few checkpoints per map, so you would have to be more careful. I heard that the end is difficult so look forward to that.
3. Hiding bodies: There is almost always a place to stash them. Even if there aren't, all you have to do is carry them out of sight. Vials of acid can dissolve bodies. I never used them except on one mission where I was required to.
4. Skills/Items: Invisibility- didn’t use except when you first get it (required). Clones– only used it once or twice for the novelty of it. Whistle- Extremely helpful and all you need to distract a guard. Poison- neat, but never needed it. Amber(vials)- I didn’t use skills that required amber so it seemed like a worthless mechanic. Health potions– havent used any so far. Sand– used to extinguish torches, but I only used it a few times early on. Throwing knives- You can have two. I heard you might have to use them later in the game, but so far, have not bothered with them. You cannot pick up thrown knives. Annoying, but unlimited knives would be too easy. Amber vision- Used only on occasion, feels weak. Not really needed.
5. Skill points. Not used any points so far; they unlock talents that make very little difference. There is little incentive to collect coins or do side quests since it only gains you extra points. The RPG part of the game is weak.
I would prefer more ways to kill or escape; arrows, sleep darts, smoke bombs, ground traps, tripwires, etc. Each level is pretty linear and easy to find the end. You do not have a minimap, but don’t need one either.
You have to be on the same level to kill an enemy (can’t kill while on a table). Enemy AI is predictable and react the same. Jumping and climbing is easy; jump, move left or right etc. Your character automatically grabs onto ledges. I rarely had a problem with falling or navigating around.

9/10: Gunpoint is a fun, quick game about espionage, hacking, and corporate sabotage. Play as Richard Conway, freelance spy, as he carries out missions to clear himself after getting wrapped up in murder case involving a pair of gun manufacturing companies.
Gunpoint is a silly, finely-tuned, fun time that left me in a good mood. While the title might suggest gunplay, the revolver was one of the tools I used the least over the course of the game. Instead, most of my time was spent leaping using Bullfrog trousers, crawling about the walls and ceilings, using the Dropshot trenchcoat to survive long falls, and most of all, rewiring electronics to my whim. It's very satisfying using a light switch to open a locked door, or making it so an enemy gun calls an elevator instead of firing. As the game progresses, the game adds separate circuits and tougher enemies, bit it never felt overwhelming thanks to the autosave system. Even so, there was still some challenge in figuring out the route to the objective and secondary laptops, which provides a little extra information about the games story.
Guns had recently been banned in East Point, yet things are heating up as the recent murder of a potential client, Selena Delgado, leaves Richard as a prime suspect. Encouraged by Selena's boss, Melanie Rooke, to wipe the camera footage in order to clear yourself, what ensues are about 20 missions of leaping and intrigue as you resolve the conflict between Melanie's company, Rooke Firearms, and her competitors at Intex, run by Fritz Gessler.
Gunpoint is definitely a stealth game, but it's still active and unstressful. You should take time to case the area, and a single shot will usually kill you. However, instead of slowly crawling around or losing a half hour of time after messing up a mission, you're leaping through windows, pouncing on guards, and hacking security cameras to open doors instead of setting of alarms. It's a real good time, and it says a lot that I leave it wishing it was just a few levels longer.

A good & fun Top-Down RPG with some RTS game, but no SpellForce
Well first of all I have to say that this isn’t a neutral review, because I’m a SpellForce veteran and play the games of the franchise since 2003. I also did a lot of Modding and Community Maps for SpellForce 2 and 1, because I loved the games and how they were done. Of the Card game that was included in the Collectors Edition of SpellForce 2 I even created a standalone Game for Windows and Android. Anyway I just wanted to make clear that I am not able to give a neutral review of the game, because I will always compare it to the old games. But let’s now start my review:
Overall I give the game a solid 6.5 out of 10
Short Facts (+ Positive, - Negative:
+ good and mature story
+ good graphics
+ way better voice acting
+ good RPG skill point system
+ Main Campaign Coop ready*
+ great music and sound
+ good quest design
+ multiple heroes and custom hero party
+ beautiful world and location map
- No “Free game” Mode
- No 3rd person view
- very small Click & Fight system
- Main Campaign Coop only in “support” role
- Campaign only 30h (I needed 46h because I searched every map for items)
- Nothing to do after campaign except PVP
- RTS (Sector System) does not work in the Campaign (rush & skip always possible)
- Items are skill based, not level based (maxed armor after ~50% of the campaign)
- a lot of loading screens for just a simple location change
- incredible unhandy group management
- character customization is a joke
- only a small handful of character portraits
- a lot of random quest trigger depending on your party (good luck to have the right person at the right time)
Review & Feedback:
Oh was I excited when they said that they will make a SpellForce 3. Finally a continuation of the SpellForce saga! How does it go on after Sf2-DotP? What? It doesn’t? Long time before SpellForce 1? Smells like a reboot… and it is. But let’s get back in time. SpellForce 3 has been in development for 4 years, but they rebooted it after 2 years because they noticed the game back then didn’t make fun and you will notice this reboot in the development. I say how I feel it. This RTS System is exactly an Age of Empires with the “Die Siedler” section system. This RTS system has nothing to do with the system of the other SpellForce games. I have the feeling they wanted to do an other game but needed a name to sell it. So they took it and just added a basic RPG logic to it.
To say that the game didn’t make me any fun wouldn’t be true. But it never gives me the feeling of a SpellForce. More like an Age of Empires with Heroes. EVERY RTS part/map of the game can be skipped/rushed in under 10 min. How you may ask? Just rush with your heroes to the Main Sector of the enemy, destroy the main building and ignore everything else. If this building falls, everything of the enemy drops dead. Everything! Whoever designed that logic hasn’t planned it with RPG heroes. This RTS system does only work in PVP. The RPG part was also only tested on paper but not in game. Because the items are skill based and not level based you can gear up your heroes with end game items at the half of the game. I never had any issues to finish a map in the second half of the game. For these who may wonder, I played it on normal.
What I really dislike about the game is, that there is no “Free Game” Mode and 3rd person view like in the old games. If you don’t play PVP the game has nothing to offer after the campaign. Let me say it how it is, 10 years ago you got a lot more for your 50€/$ as today. These is so much content missing compared to the old ones, that you may think, these was 1 year of development missing.
If you want to play a fun Top-Down RPG with some sort of RTS, you will be happy with this game, but you shouldn’t pay more as 30€/$ at the current state of content. If you want to play a good SpellForce game, then I can recommend my all time favorite SpellForce 2 Dragon Storm.
The Developers said that they will offer Modding tools and map editor for the game in the future. Oh yes the game really needs more content.
But that’s just my opinion.

Spellforce has always been a game in which RTS and RPG meet. Spellforce 3 is no different.
To start with the RPG part. The many different classes, each with their own ability tree, give you enough choices and options to create an unique character every playthrough. Maps can have chests hidden in the every hook and corner so you really have to keep youre eye out. Which doesn't matter, because the graphics are absolutely breathtaking, they've really outdone themselves on that part! In maps you might find hideouts or caves for even more exploration. The only part I didn't like about the RPG part is the limited amount of skills you can carry with you at once. It's a shame that there's such a good choice of abilities yet in combat you can only carry 3 with you for each companion at a time.
Now to the RTS part. There are three races to play, each with their own units and upgrades. They do work all 3 in quite similar ways (1 main barracks building, 1 main upgrade building etc.) so there isn't really any learning curve or huge strategy change required depending on the race. There isn't really a race that has an advantage, the balance is good. Every race has a unit that works well against an other type of unit (aka spears against mounts etc.). Personally I wish there was more blend in the RTS part.  It was handled better in previous Spellforce games.
With that said, the story of the game is just like other Spellforce games really well made. The freedom in where to go and explore maps also feels improved compared to the previous Spellforce game. The game still has some bugs with Steam achievments or mulitplayer sync problems, but not in such a way that its 'unplayable.

The Stalin Subway is a slightly wonky mid-2000s shooter that still manages to be reasonably entertaining due to an under-represented setting and a fair bit of heart. The stereotype of the under-polished slavic game holds true with this one and the voice acting/translation is so bad it starts to get good.
The soundtrack is mostly generic but occasionally somewhat catchy when it actually ♥♥♥♥ing plays. The menu theme and the first level theme (actually a modern version of a fairly well known Cold War era song) particularly stand out.
There was a degree of thought put into the weapons used in the game. They both fit the time period and those of the same calibre
which is a nice touch. The rifles did feel a little underpowered but the rest were fine. Additional features absent from modern AAA shooters like destructible objects and ricochets from missed shots (which can actually hit NPCs or even youself on occasion) were unexpected in such a budget title but also welcome.
Probably worth the price asked and certainly worth picking up on sale it gives 6 hours or so of mildly confusing entertainment. Some degree of challenge can be had if you put it on hard though this will depend on player skill. Bunny-hopping is recommended due to the slow walking speed.
Avoid the sequel (Red Veil) like the plague. You have been warned.

Simple Rockets is a detailed spacecraft building and piloting simulation inspired by games like Kerbal Space Program. The main difference is that Simple Rockets is all 2d. While playing Simple Rockets you’ll get a lot of the same sort of things you’d do in KSP – a trial and error focused experience where the player tries to reach new goals like creating a rocket capable of leaving the atmosphere, then piloting it into orbit.
Overall, Simple Rockets presents itself as a more accessible game than Kerbal Space Program. The interface is organized and easy to navigate, and should you choose to play them, the tutorials teach the player exactly what they need to do for most goals. The art isn’t much to look at, but is perfectly functional with every rocket piece and visual cue being clearly designed and unique.
Check out Simple Rockets if you want a more casual take on the rocket building of games like Kerbal Space Program.

I strongly recommend this visual novel however; in this steam version there is heavy censorship with all sexual jokes and references removed but, you're not all here for that and even if you are, there are ways to restore the game to its original state.
The first and foremost thing to mention about this game is the fantastically touching story about some of the characters. Obviously some of the routes are better written than others (looking at you, whoever translated Ageha's route) but my personal favourite was Kotori's route closely followed by Amane's. Every single character in the main cast has had some sort of significant loss in their past, perhaps even traumatic. And seeing as the main character has had a rather hefty loss himself, Aoi is able to connect on a very strong level with each and every one of these girls. But, for all you people who just got very excited; no, there is no harem ending. Anyway, as the story goes on you encounter more hardships and emotions are evoked several times along the way as the reader. Emotionally evoking stories are often a good read in my opinion.
The music is good in this game, but nothing to write home about. You will probably think of it as really good after you've completed the stories but then after a while you realise that you only feel that way because you're being reminded of certain scenes and dialogues that you liked in the story. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but to repeat myself, the music isn't top notch, but visual novels aren't about the music.
The characters themselves are horrifically stereotypical. The moody handicapped person, the childhood friend, the mysterious senpai, the ditsy twin and the intelligent twin, however; they manage to make it all work. These characters, despite all conforming to stereotpyes actually work and you do get easily emotionally attached to them through the stories.
The artwork is nice, but again, nothing to write home about. Combined with the music there is a nice atmosphere in the game.
There are a number of decisions to make over the course of this long story which is important to some people. I couldn't care less.
Overall, fantastic story, really good characters despite all being stereotypical, decent artwork and music but nothing spectacular about either - a very good visual novel which is going to be retranslated. Hopefully this time around large chunks of Ageha's route aren't an incomprensible mess.
I would recommend this game to anyone who is starting out with VN or is already into VN. I also recommend getting the restoration patch + sweet love ui if you want the "full content."

Styx: Master of Shadows is a really great game and one of my favorite stealth games ever. Don't get me wrong, it's not perfect but it s worth 30 $ but i bought it 5 $ when it is on discount.
There aren't many stealth games around these days and Dishonored is really good but Styx is similar. The gameplay mechanics work really well in this game and there are some that I haven't seen in any other stealth game, such as cloning yourself and booby trapping your clone in a chest or just use it as a distraction for guards. You can even become invisible for short time spans. These things cost you amber which is basically something like mana. You can replenish it with vials you can find during the missions or pickpocket from some of the guards. But those are rare, so don't worry, you can't just walk around the whole level invisibly.
The skill system is also a good thing. It motivated me to get all the insignias and do all the side objectives in the missions, since you get bonus skill points for doing so. With them you can unlock helpful skills such as aerial kills or the aforementioned booby trapping of your clone. You can go for stealthy skills if you like to sneak through the missions or, if you're more into clearing out whole areas, you can invest in more aggressive skills. Every type of player should be able to find some skills they think are cool.
There are also different types of enemies, such as your ordinary guard, crossbowmen, knights, which have plate armor and can only be killed through poisoning or dropping chandeliers on their head, and some more that I won't spoil now. Every enemy has its weak spots and is in his way fun to kill or sneak around.
What I think is really outstanding in Styx is the environment. The level design is just awesome. There are many routes to your destination and you almost always have a choice of how to get there. In synergy with the mostly good graphics (at least good enough for me) and the great lighting effects it often led to me just stopping and looking at the beautiful environments. It's just eye candy to sneak around in the shadows avoiding the bright sun rays falling in a room through a window or climbing a vertical wall in the sunset.
Sadly the fun exploring the levels ends with the exact half of the game. After that you will be back tracked through many levels you have already seen. In most cases this isn't that bad, because there are other guards on other positions with other routes and the levels are still awesome with all the alternative routes. But I have to say that there were one or two areas that just didn't work properly backwards, which was sometimes a little annoying. Nevertheless the back tracking wasn't so bad, although I gladly would have payed 5 or 10 more bucks to just see some more of this really great level design.
The story line was okay for me. It had its suprises and pulled me through the missions and that's all I was expecting from it. The plot is told through voice acting and comic like cutscenes with mostly static pictures of which some were reused a little too often, but that's perfectly fine thinking of the price for the title. The voice acting was good and I personally liked the fact that although the story is set in a fantasy world, the characters swear a lot and talk more like you would expect from real world rogues. That added a special feeling to it and I liked it.
Overall I loved this game and though it has its flaws the whole experience is just great, because every mechanic and every element come together to form a really fun time of stealth gameplay. And since it's worth even the full 30€ in my opinion (i got it 5 dolllars), I recommend this game to every gamer who enjoys stealth games.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Gloria Victis is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was 0.6.3.2 alpha build 0.
Gloria Victis is a MMORPG set in a 'low-fantasy' medieval setting. For anyone a bit confused by that description, that means no magic.
Graphics - Environmental graphics are very pretty. The landscape is suitably diverse, with plains, hills, and treed areas, although I haven't encountered any full-on forests, which would be great.
Character graphics are not quite as nice, although they're functional. Animations seem to be smooth, although I've noticed a bit of 'floating' of peoples' feet across the ground when attacking.
The interface graphics are good, and consistent throughout, although the text used for some of the descriptions doesn't fit within some of the panels.
Sound - Music is very nice and fits the game well. The powerful title music sets the scene and the in-game music, where included, is very nice. I really like the Enya-esque track with haunting female vocals.
Sound effects are mostly good, although the twang of a bow when firing sounds rather metallic. I haven't come across any in-game speech as yet, so I don't know if it's included anywhere.
Gameplay - Gloria Victis is most definitely in Early Access! It's still very buggy, rife with connection issues and not yet feature complete. Character creation only gives you a choice of two of the four different races, and you can only be a male character. You only have a choice of three different facial appearances (+1 scarred version of an existing model), and a number of the higher-level abilities simply say "coming soon". There's a very limited tutorial with no real introduction to the game and a number of grammar errors, and a whole host of features you'd expect such as enemy indicators on the minimap, directional indicators for quests, and a useful indication of what to do next are all missing. But the game is in early access, so all of that can be forgiven for the time being.
The game plays like a typical action RPG MMO. There's no auto aiming, but with the current server issues, there's also no tactical fighting. The game has a real-time combat engine with manual aiming and weapon selection, but what it boils down to is basically a game of sniping for ranged players or hit-and-run for melee players. All enemies that I've encountered so far simply charge or flee, and you have to act appropriately.
Not really feeling like playing a beefed-up warrior type, I chose to specialise in light armour and dexterity, and went out in search of adventure, bow in hand. Unfortunately the ranged combat is not that great, with no real indication of whether an attack is successful or not, and seemingly very little chance of hitting a moving enemy, no matter whether you lead them or not. There also seem to be massive sync issues at the moment, with enemies teleporting around you and the server sometimes failing to register their corpses for looting.
Beyond the somewhat-frustrating PVE combat, the game provides for crafting, which is okay, but nothing new, and progressing towards Steam Achievements, which are a welcome addition, but require a lot of time investment to gain. PVP is an option, but one that I'm not too keen on, so I have't looked into it yet.
Pros:
+ Great environmental graphics
+ Well-realised setting, with no magic; more of a realistic medieval feel
+ Great music
+ Steam Achievements
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Very early access; needs a lot of work!
- Lack of guidance in the early game; it's hard to work out what you should be doing
Gloria Victis is a welcome addition to the MMORPG space: a low-fantasy (i.e. no magic) game in a medieval setting. The current status of the game is very much Early Access, but with the developer interaction and interest gained so far, I believe it will achieve its goals.

Something that needs to be played to be understood, but scratches the itch of wanting a cyberpunk action game and an FPS that goes beyond shooting things to win.
Most criticism is levelled at the game's UI and its unwillingness to guide the player through the complexities of its upgrade system, which include a fairly standard level-up, a cybernetic upgrade purchase system, and a background time-based research system. Each of these are similar to modern, existing gameplay tropes, but done without a great deal of fanfare or constant, blinking notifications.
The gamplay variation is where the game requirs the most investment, but provides the most reward. The game does not outright demonstrate the depth of its gameplay through tutorials or brightly lit menu popups and requires the player to explore the various upgrades, weapons, and abilities in order to understand their function. Enemies can be shot, stabbed, have their minds hacked to make them attack their friends, have cars thrown at them with telekinesis, or be teleported into and blown up. Or everything all at once.
There is no set loadout or defined skilltree, meaning with a few stat increases a player can combine any weapon loadouts or powers they like.
The story is rather complex, as the game takes cues from a tabletop RPG in that every NPC is an attempt at a vibrant charicateur, and the dialogue makes allusions to events occuring elsewhere that add a backdrop to the game's deliberately miserable but campy atmosphere.
It is a game that contains all the tools to be great, and simply requires some investment from the player to shine. The amount of variety in gameplay styles makes it more entertaining than a great deal of FPS's made a decade later, despite the game's obvious age.

Once again, I really enjoy the gameplay. X-Com fans will appreciate the turn based strategy. My earlier concerns regarding the limitations of the trainer system which inhibited true freedom in character development have been lessened however. I still would prefer true freedom to spend my experience points, but the additional content gives you plenty of fights and quests with which to expand your characters, as well as more trainers with the important abilities available to train for. If you are looking for cool loots though, prepare to be disappointed. The emphasis is really more on the characters themselves. As you progress through the story, upgrades of weapons that are marginally better are available, but using merchants to upgrade your characters gear doesn't really feel as fun as beating some monsters or bad guys and finding a cool weapon or magic item.

I am particularly excited for when they add more depth to character creation, as this will allow me to pick some starting skills that will more coincide with how I want to build my character. For example, warriors start with the skill that improves your attack when using a shield. If you want to build a 2-Hand sword wielding warrior, this skill is just a waste. To the Moon Again? Not this time. This story is a little closer to Earth. Or is it?
"Finding Paradise," the next installment of Kan Gao's fantastic series, is everything I hoped it would be and more. With a delightful mixture of old and new characters, this game will expand the horizons of your mind in ways that you could never have imagined. Where the prequel, "To the Moon," explored the mystery of love, "Finding Paradise" instead unravels the mystery of life.
Is it wrong to have regrets? To feel alone? Are the memories we hold closest to us real, or imagined? These are things that every human being wrestles with during their lifetime, and Kan Gao's newest story meets them with the carefulness and wit that his fans have come to expect. Add to that a fanstastic new soundtrack, and "Finding Paradise" is sure to become one of your favorites.
You might cry; you'll probably laugh. But you'll certainly be left with a sad smile and a wellspring of thoughts and emotions that only the best kinds of stories can elicit.

Spellforce is your classic real-time strategy and role-playing series that has been around since 2003. The series is set in a fantasy world called Eo ruled over by near-immortal mages and include various other races including humans, orcs, elves, dark elves, dwarves and trolls.
Like most RPG and RTS games spellforce others complex skill trees to progress through as you level your heroes and get to choose a combination of many skill tree paths to unlock your skills and abilities to make your hero stronger. These include dark and light magic, archery, arcane archery, brutality and others. Gameplay is over the top of the map and giving you an aerial view of Eo’s vast beautiful landscape.
When I began the campaign I was thrown straight in the deep end with 4 heroes at my disposal and had to navigate a labyrinth of corridors leading to an explosive conclusion where one hero was lost with the power of magic the cause of the tragedy. After this battle, there was a long intro leading to your character creation where you could choose your heroes name and attributes you would be using in your battle against the forces of evil. After there were more cinematic sequences followed by a simple tutorial level set in Greyfell keep where you saw the lives of the residents pass by including trials and combat training taken place.
This opened a huge amount of lore in the begging to get us up to speed on the story, so even if you are new to spellforce or a returning fan you will understand the story and the world that you are discovering. You then progress to your first mission where you are shown the ropes of building bases, outposts, claiming territories and all strategies that come with winning a fight. We are tasked to discover a mysterious new disease called the bloodburn in the town of Liannon, however, it is already occupied by the elves who are also studying this new mysterious disease. Disagreements are made, a war begins and results in force, being the only way to get into Liannon.
After pushing the elves out Liannon we are attacked immediately by elf reinforcements who not long after surrender and withdraw from Liannon altogether and tell you that the bloodburn is not a normal disease and that your commander kept from you that Liannon would be purged leaving no survivors. Learning about this vital information you return to your captain who then tells you their true intentions and we refuse to carry out this order. We are then treated as traitors and imprisoned for sentencing and later sentenced to death for high treason to the crown.
The story is very rich and filled with cinematic detail as well as an intense soundtrack to follow the story as you progress through the world of Eo’s. The beauty the game holds is unparalleled in offering vast detail in scenery both during cinematic scenes and during levels. You can easily get lost in the story and forget about time completely while you enjoy such a stunning and exciting storyline.
I awarded the score I did because I believe I can spend hours doing only a few level and still not break the surface of the vast story available. The content available for an RTS is huge and could fill months of enjoyment in just playing the story. All that I found bad with the Spellforce is while razing buildings once 80% is destroyed, the hit points glitch out, but it doesn't hinder the experience of the game too much and for that, i scored 9.

I should lead by admitting I've been a huge fan of Spellforce since Order of Dawn in the early 2000s, with at least a two thousand hours spent finising all the previous titles (even that POS faith in destiny) and playing the multiplayer, so I am somewhat inclined to think fondly of the Spellforce series. I have absolutely loved diving back into the world of Eo in another great game.
In general the game is beautiful, and for once the "in game footage" actually matches what you're buying. The level design and the detail included in these maps, as well as the art style was fantastic. The Spellforce blend of RPG and RTS is always a lot of fun, and waging war with your Orc, Elven or Human forces (and fireballs, lots and lots of fireballs) is fantastic. As far as writing goes, the story was a lot of fun, if a touch predictable at times, and the character writing was very well done.
The multiplayer has been fine since day one as far as I know, and is a lot of fun, though it can be quite a time drain as matches can really last.
Cons
As many of the reviews here indicate, there have been some issues with this release, namely that on release the quests were still buggy as hell. However they have been updating and rectifying these bugs constantly since early december with what felt like a patch a day for the first couple of weeks, and the game is now running very well. There are still issues there, however the only problems I have encountered have been cosmetic and minor nuisance issues, and nothing preventing me from getting on with my game.
So I think if what is stopping you from buying this title are the early reviews then I would highly encourage grabbing this game, and joining the spellforce saga alongside us.
Overall/TLDR
This game was fantastic, a few issues day one now largely resolved. If you think you might be interested then grab it and dive into a wonderful world of magic and fantasy and all that good stuff :)

5 seperate routes. The first choice dosen't come until after the 1st opening movie which takes about 6-7 hours to get to, depending on how fast you can click and read! I was attracted by this game because I enjoy this kind of stealth games. It has a good story and an interesting character. Controls are a little weird at first, but you get used to it as you play more.
The thing I liked most is that there are so many enemies to defeat or avoid, together with accomplishing the different missions makes the game fun to play. On the other side, I didn't like the game re-using repeatedly all scenarios for different primary missions.
The end battle is a little frustrating, especially if you're short on amber or knives. Keep that in mind!

If you enjoy the stealth genre of games, Styx is a good one and worth getting.
The game was made on a fairly small budget, making the results fairly impressive, all things considered. You play a goblin-type character with various primary and optional secondary objectives to meet in each mission, tokens to collect (if you wish), and a relic to find in each mission set.
You gain points from completing the various objectives, which can be used between missions to upgrade your skills and abilities.
The storyline I found to be a bit uninvolved.. there's no lack of it, but I just didn't find it to be that deep or expansive.
Levels are decent in size and usually fairly open, so you have lots of options for taking down guards or evading them. They're not so big that you get particularly lost, but not so small as to have few options.
Difficulty is always a matter of opinion. On the hardest difficulty, I found it a bit easy as someone who games alot, but that's also with the added difficulty of trying to get all the insignia at the end of each mission, which is probably just more about time, patience and reloading. If you weren't doing those, and were living with getting spotted, you'd probably have a harder time in some respects. Depends on your playstyle, but I'm a completionist ;_; You can fight back, but can only defend against one enemy at a time, so you really don't want to have multiple guards hitting on you, as you get locked into a parry/attack timing sequence. The game's really designed for stealth, but with the option to get out of scrapes if you make small errors.
You will find that the second half of the game is pretty much doing the first half's levels again, but backwards. Understandable design choice, as it meant they could put their budget elsewhere, and it means the levels are somewhat familiar, yet different at the same time. guards and items are in different places too. Would have been nice to have more new levels, but I won't hold it against them.
Overall it's a pretty polished game and I enjoyed it. Would recommend it to anyone who likes stealth games, though at the moment it's £25 outside of a sale.. If you're ok paying full price for games, go for it. As someone who only tends to buy sale games, I'd struggle to put that kind of money forward, but then I work for a pittance :P

I don't mind sitting at a game for a while trying to figure out a puzzle or a particularly challenging aspect of gameplay, but I am a firm believer in that while some games should indeed frustrate you and challenge you - they need to give you something to work for, the belief that your efforts aren't going to be in vain. This game does not do that and it is a terrible tragedy because I wanted so badly to love it. A game that focuses entirely on stealth? Yes please! The graphics were nice and the voice acting was good, but the plot was terribly cliche from the start. I have no idea if it gets better because as you may notice, I didn't even finish the whole tutorial on this game.
It was incredibly frustrating and clunky. Playing on keyboard and mouse, I set the camera sensitivity to high and still struggled to get the character to move in the directions I wanted. If I hugged the walls, the camera would derp through walls as I tried to look around me. I had to look up help just to learn how to parry because I died at least six times with no understanding of what I had done wrong. The combat mechanics are hideous and you can't back out of one-on-one combat. But the kicker was learning to take cover. I could see no pattern in the guards' movements no matter how hard I tried, and finally exited in frustration after my tenth death. The game and its plot had given me no reason to want to continue, no hint that there wouldn't be a reward of any kind around the next corner or two. Nothing more than a feeling that I was a rat running around in a maze where there was no cheese. My only consolation is that I purchased this on a sale and did not pay the full price.

Great game all around. It is based on the Pen and Paper game The Dark Eye (TDE or DSA in German) and follows the latest edition rules pretty closely. The combat is turnbased and already (despite early access) very well animated.
The difficulty of this game is rather high. I know the ruleset from my P&P groups and am a very experienced player of turnbased games and I found several battles quite challenging, yet fun. It is not a Fire-Emblem kind of challenge where one wrong move means that your favourite charakter dies, but it is the self-motivation "Hmm if I do this a little different I COULD save the Baroness".
Also this game shows several great ideas and aspects I am missing in many other games. Interactive environment (Cut a rope so a chandelier smashes some guards), diverging story lines, and the possibility to fail (sometimes) and still continue with your story.
Overall this is a great game that I can recommend to everyone with love for Pen and Paper games as well as challenging turn-based games.

After finishing the campaign on hard a few days ago I think the time is right to leave a review of my experience with the game. I'm relatively new to the Spellforce series, but I grew up playing thousands of hours of Warcraft 3, Starcraft, Age of Empires/Mythology, Red Alert, Tiberium Sun, and a dozen other nostalgia-inducing RTS games. I always longed for a game that could tickle my fancy like Warcraft 3 did during my childhood.
Spellforce 3 is a surprisingly good roleplaying game with a horribly mediocre, borderline terrible, real-time strategy aspect tacked onto it. Despite not running into any of the complete gamebreaking bugs like many others, I still encountered far more bugs than any customer should have to deal with, especially for a game with a budget like Spellforce 3. It has a long way to go towards balancing, especially regarding the RTS elements on the game. The AI is not smart and makes up for it by blatantly cheating.
The game has a well written story with fun, unique, and interesting companions who join you along the way. The voice acting was mostly great, with popular voice actors like Doug Cockle (perhaps best known as Geralt of Rivia from The Witcher franchise) and Liam O'Brien (Illidan Stormrage from World of Warcraft) lending their niche vocal range to their respective characters.
I thought it was rather amusing that O'Brien voices an Orc Shaman Warchief that can shapeshift into a bear, and is involved in an unusual  love triangle between a brother and a female childhood friend. Warcraft fans may find his performance a little too on-the-nose for their liking.I personally found it gamebreaking and kept referring to him as "Illidan" to my friends.
I just cannot recommend Spellforce 3 in its current state. The game is a bug-filled, poorly balanced mess, with long loading screens, and what is easily one of the most unenjoyable implementation of an RTS I've ever played.

Do not think that game is easy, Feel-A-Maze is mostly an arcade game with a few puzzle features and you really need to be as fast and accurate as possible. Here's my thoughts on "If My Heart Had Wings"
[Story]
The story is decent but certain elements are a bit long winded. There is a lot of detail pertaining to glider construction and operation, which can be quite distracting. Other than that, this visual novel is what you would expect - your typical high school male is surrounded by females, who (very little effort on his own) is able to attract their attention (player choice depending). The two elements that drew me into playing this visual novel was the prominence of a character with a disability and the concept of a "soaring club" at high school. Combined, these two elements work well together to create a unique story. The individual character story arcs are all really good at allowing the player to connect on one level or another, and you are left feeling somewhat emotionally connected to them (at least, that's how it was for me).
If this particular visual novel isn't to your liking, and you're after a real tear-jerker, I thoroughly recommend CLANNAD (despite its price, it is worth every penny).
[Translation]
I did notice more than several issues with the English translations, some of which are quite big, others are small mistakes (such as missing a letter). Having played only one other visual novel prior to this (that being CLANNAD), the translation absolutely needs some work.
[Graphics]
The native resolution is 1280x720. Having played this in fullscreen mode at a resolution of 1920x1080, I noticed that during certain scenes that had a zoom-in effect, the picture quality becomes a bit blocky on the focused area. However, this isn't often given the length of the visual novel, and doesn't really hurt it overall.
[Sound]
I had no issues with the sound quality. Audio appeared clean, and clear. Since I don't know Japanese, I can't really grade the voice acting.
[Compatibility]
No issues on Windows 8.1 x64.
[Notes regarding Censored Version]
This game has a much merkier past, though a fair number of visual novels do. This game was originally 18+ due to the adult content. This particular version, is throughly censored throughout compared to the original (abeit, there are one or two scenes which some might argue should have got the chop too). It wasn't until after I played the Steam version that I became aware of the missing content. After reading the reviews on Steam, I opted to try out the community patch for purely academic purposes. After playing through at least two character routes, I can say that despite the Steam version being censored, the story does a good job of standing on its own (by which I mean, the removal of the adult content has not created gaps in the story). I feel that the adult content (for the most part) was an unnessecary addition to the game, unless you are specifically looking for a game with those sorts of interactions and depictions.

While I haven't completed all routes on this game yet, with 26 hours of playing (or should I say watching?) and completing 2 routes I think I can write a solid review.
If my heart had wings is a Visual Novel that revolves around gliders and the after school club that wants to build and fly it. I found this a very original subject to base the story lines on. Even though some parts of the story were a bit technical, it didn't bother me. In this VN there are 5 possible girls to date and with the bad ending, this makes 6 possible outcomes. But for some of the options to open, you have to clear the Kotori route.
I started with the Kotori route and that alone took me 20 hours. While I did like her route, I did find it a bit too long, especially because there aren't that many choices to make. The Ageha route I finished in 6 hours, but this is because you can skip all scenes that you have seen before. But you can't skip the new scenes, so this way the game ensures you can't miss anything. Based on these two routes I do think that the game is made for the Kotori route and the other routes are just a nice extra. I think this is true for the Ageha route, at least. While they did try to bring some depth into it, it wasn't nearly as gripping as Kotori's route was. That being said, I have high hopes for the Amane route. I love the music they choose for the intro and ending. The rest is a bit repetitive but it does fit the mood of the moment well.
The one annoying thing about this game were the many spelling errors. For a large part of the game I didn't know if Isuka was a he or a she, because they kept saying it differently and you don't get to meet her in the Kotori route at least. I know there is a pack you can install that fixes this but I didn't do that because I saw it was a bit iffy and a lot of people had problems with the game after that. One other personal dislike for me is that Hotaru wasn't a dating option. Her character was really adorable so that was a bit of a shame.
Overall this is a fun Visual Novel that is worth your time if you like the genre.

I start plotting it out...  As I watched guards patrol I noticed several motion sensors, each of different circuit color.  I quickly notice a purple motion sensor on the bottom floor with a guard trapped in a yellow door.  Above said yellow door on the next floor up is a yellow motion sensor... I then watch my plan unfold, to flash before my eyes, if you will.
A guard tripped the motion sensor which then tripped another motion sensor which opened a door which then caused a guard to trip yet another motion sensor and finally open the yellow door.  The guard inside the yellow door runs out and a purple alarm is raised, which he turns off, which activates the light switch and opens the trap door.  As I was falling through the trap door, I catch a glimpse of a plate glass floor.  "OH SH*T"  I said, before falling through 4 layers of tempered glass in slow motion. First thing first, the game in its current state is EARLY. The gameplay is fun (we'll get to that), but struggling to log in, with every day providing new and exciting challenges to even getting the game up and running, is not. If you are likely to become agitated at the prospect of an infinite loading screen spoiling your plans to play for an evening, you might want to wait a while before picking this up.
But once your in? Glorious. Combat feels very Mount&Blade/Chivalry-esque (directional swinging, hitboxes, etc.), though a little less demanding due to lack of directional blocking. Personally I try to use archery almost exclusively, very satisfying and effective to drop mobs from a mile away :p
Crafting is deep, and frankly a little overwhelming at first with the staggering variety of ingredients and alternate ingredients and craft-specific work stations etc etc etc.... but seems like it will be fun and rewarding once some good guides get up so that I stop wasting all my wood on stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥I don't need instead focus on churning out mass billets :D
The PVP system is almost entirely set in the open world, with the world's two factions (I believe there are plans for 4 ultimately) capturing and reinforcing town and farmsteads across the island. Not only do these locations provide race-wide bonuses to xp, crafting success, etc... they are often valuable locations for crop and resource nodes that may be more spread out or hard to find elsewhere. Even with servers currently seeming to be overwhelmingly viking with fewer midlanders, im seeing locations swap hands a lot, which is a good sign of healthy pvp.
Oh, servers. They're a little weird, since your character can freely play on any of them, and which one you choose has more to do with ping selection than anything else. And global chat in game is really more multiverse chat... you're hearing everyone from all servers all at once, which is weird. I'm not sure whether guilds can as freely swap servers as characters can?
Anyway, there's a great core of gameplay here that looks like its only going to get better. Graphics, meh (my laptop sucks so I run everything on ultra-low anyway), voice acting, hillariously bad, interface, buggy. But the gameplay is pretty special, and definitely will tickle a Mount and Blade MMO feel!

Ok as always, pros/cons:
Pros:
- Plot (it's like watching a really, really good action movie, but you can choose what to do yourself!),
- Characters (both heroes [Batman, Catwoman, Robin] and villians [ex.Joker, Two-Face, Penguin, Mr.Freeze and lost more] was just awesome to play, watch and fight. Characters design was almost lways the best part of Batman's franchise and it's well shown in Arkham City),
- quasi-openworld (we have more free will than we had in Arkham Asylum, but it isn't to many thing to do except Riddlers trophies and some optional missions (which, sadly, most of them unlock time-to-time, so if you don't like to running and waiting something to happen it's can take a while to unlock all of them),
- Fights (best part of Rocksteady's Batman games. Fights are spectacular, you can feel power of the blows as Batman and artistry as Catwoman. These fleshy sounds you can hear while beating "bad guys" give a lot of satisfaction),
- If you like this kind of thing - lots of Riddler trophies to find,
- Graphics and optimization (i was really surprised - game looks awesome and works great at the same time. I had 40-50 stable FPS on a 4 years old laptop - and it the same time look really good. Both in cutscenes and gameplay characters are detailed. City is dirty, dark and decaying - perfect fit for this hellhole),
- Atmosphere (As I said - city is dark, "feeling" of fallen city is overwhelming. Perfect setting for Batman's game).
Cons:
- Usually controls are good, but sometimes i had problems with precise jumping (almost always using Batclav help, but it's kinda annoying - I was using XBOX 360 controller),
- I had mixed feeling at the end. On the one side it should be more stirring, but i couldn't feel that, don't know why,
- Story is little short (took me around 15hrs to complete story, half of optional missions and around 60% or riddler trophies).
Overall it's one of the best "superhero" games i had ever played. Great job Rocksteady!

Styx is a hardcore stealth game where you control a sneaky goblin as he makes his way through a tower full of humans, elves and other baddies looking to kill him. Fortunately, you’ve got a few tricks up your sleeve as Styx eventually learns to throw knives, spawn clones, pull off a series of different kills and even turn (briefly) invisible. Ultimately, Styx is a lot of fun but it’s clearly a game that’s geared towards true stealth fans.
As other reviewers have pointed out, Styx is nothing like other modern “stealth” games like Assassin’s Creed, where stealth is essentially optional and you can choose to play the game as if you’re Rambo if you want. If you don’t hide in Styx, you die. Simple as that. And die you will. I played through the game on normal and I died literally hundreds of times. Auto saves are uncommon, so you need to get in the habit of saving after every guard slain or corner passed unnoticed.
While I found Styx to be a lot of fun, the difficulty and uncompromising nature of the game will put a lot of people off. If we’re going to go off Steam achievements - less than half of players even finish Styx’s prologue, and a mere 8% make it all the way through the game. You’ve been warned. I’ll also admit that there are times in the game when the developers make it a challenge to a point that doesn’t even make sense. For example, there a plenty of areas where the beetles and humans interact freely - why don’t they attack one another? Wouldn’t that add another layer of depth to the game? All that being said, if you love classic stealth games like Thief, look no further than Styx for your next purchase!

Updated impressions to Full Version below:
Blackguards is the first Early Access game i really want to recommend!
First it´s quite well developed already (but surely not without some roughness, especially regarding balancing, texting and bugs), second
because they did two things very well:
Second it actually is a good game in the Realms of Arkania/Das Schwarze Auge universe, since the last ones (Demonicon, Schicksalsklinge HD) were poorest crap.
Secondary it brings a new genre to this rpg system - the strategy (yeah i know, they also did two adventures already, but imo adventure and rpg are not that different).
Also they try to bring a bit of a more grey atmosphere to the normally strictly black and white world of Arkania, you play as a convicted murderer, your party also consists of the strangest fellows like addicts, fanatics and so on.
Though this all Daedalic manages to stay true to the typical rpg feeling as well as presents it with quite some bit of humour as well.
You are somewhat limited in creating your character (three classes only, race and sex are fix) but the skill system (which represents the RoA rules surprisingly well) offers quite some flexibility to process all the characters the further the game progresses.
This mixture of freedom and linear story telling, continues throughout the game, while you visit the locations to progress the main storyline, you have always some options for side quests, which offer a variety of goals.
The battles themself remind me for one of Expeditions:Conquistador, where cover and strategically well placement of your characters is as important as choosing the right means of attack.
They also try to keep the battles different with traps, different obstacles as well as victory conditions.
As the game is still in development i can´t ultimately write about the story, but so far the characters are well done and the development is quite interesting.
So if you either like the realms of arkania universe or are a strategy fan, you can give this one a try.
Update:
In the full version Daedalic has implemented kind of free character generation, since many players wanted this and not only the pre made classes.
Well.. the plus is, Daedalic tried to give the fans what they wanted..
the minus is that they implemented it very half heartedly, it´s an ugly, short creation process, with nearly no explanation about classes or whatever (the only choosing here is a single mage yes/no button?!)
Also you kinda notice that the game was made with a hunter class in mind, if you create some very different hero, you may not find the best stuff/make the most out of it.
Also i still get some stuttering issues/cut off ends of cut scenes, so they didn´t improve this much.
All in all, this may be small points, but they damper a good first impression..

I could say this game is inferior to To The Moon, but I wouldn't really be saying much since that's a hard one to top.
(It's still up there though, when it comes to this little peculiar genre)
I'll instead say that it's a very good continuation of an interesting overarching story and world that also offers an "episode" (the patient/client treated/served) with a more than decent story.
The structure of the game itself isn't much different from the overwhelmingly successful previous chapter, which means you'll  likely laugh and cry with the same frequency as you did with the previous one. You have new jokes, inside jokes and callbacks, as well as new iterations of long running jokes; there's also plenty of lines and situations that might cut deep depending on your current emotional state and where you feel you are in life right now.
The two main character maintain their charm but seem to evolve much less compared to the episode where they were introduced, To The Moon. There seems to be less focus on them and more on moving things forward, both inside the patient's mind and outside. Whether this is a problem of characters, scriptwriting or direction is hard to say. Probably a bit of all.
Still.
One one hand, working with a well-tested formula allows you you as the author to play it safe and satisfy your audience. On the other hand, treading familiar territory also means that you as the audience have certain degree of prescience (which can vary depending on your innate intuition) that might impair the overall effectiveness of the work.
The game, in my opinion, plays it excessively safe, resorting to a few tricks (I'm not using more appropriate words for fear of being too specific and spoiling the game for you) that hide truths you may have seen coming way ahead of time. Trick me once, yatta yatta.
It's by no means a bad game, on the contrary.
Just don't expect the same level of impact and emotional rush.
It's unlikely to happen because you're already acclimated to Freebird Games' style.

While it didn't make me cry quite as much, "Finding Paradise" is as much a beautiful, heart-wrenching story as its predecessor. With gorgeous music, a beautiful world, an enthralling story and intriguing characters (including a pair of familar faces who haven't changed a bit), "Finding Paradise" is everything I could have hoped for in a sequel.
If you enjoyed "To The Moon", you will definitely want to play "Finding Paradise". And if you haven't, play "A Bird Story" before this one. Revolving around the central character, the short ties up some stray memories quite nicely.
All in all, "Finding Paradise" is an excellent game, one I am glad to have experienced. I cannot wait for Episode 3.

I'm really enjoying this game, even in early-access. It still needs some polish, but it is very impressive at its current stage. The characters, while not very deep during Chapter 1 (only chapter available yet, of 5), are still very fun and you get a good sense of their personalities through their dialogue and opinions on the situations. I see a lot of potential with this game. The combat can be a little shallow at the moment, ending up with just moving across the battlefields and attacking/healing as necessary, but I also have not acquired many of the bountiful skills available. Plenty of skills available, but the game does not hold your hand; acquiring and saving the necessary points is definitely part of the challenge and not unwelcome. While it definitely isn't paced to have you being dragonslayers within the first few hours, it isn't overly difficult either. A few battles required multiple tries from me, but only because I was trying to reach bonus objectives in the alloted time. I've burnt through other SRPGs and got bored within the first few hours of playing, but this game has just enough flavor and interest to keep me coming back to the well for more. It is not a AAA title by any means, but an impressive soundtrack, very believable voice-acting and dialogue, and earnest, hard work prove to be more than any flash and bang a mainstream title would use. Once again, very impressed with the quality of this product. I am in it for the longhaul now, and very interested to see where this (and possible future titles) go. Bravo.

With pixels and music, this game manages to convey more emotion and heart than most stories. Naturally, the waterworks came on for me but they might not do for everyone. I just think it's worth stating, and I do so without shame, that I choked up towards the end of the game.
In one word, this game is special.
As a huge fan of To The Moon -- which no doubt alot of the people purchasing this game are -- I came in somewhat sceptical over wherther or not this game would be able to replicate the magic of it's predecessor. I can safely say that it has met expectations and, in some ways, surpassed them. Even if you haven't played To The Moon, this is an episodic experience and, as such, can be played seperately. That said, I'd still highly recommend you buy To The Moon first and play through it to get that proper sense of continuity and some of the 'in-jokes'.
I don't really think I need to say much more -- this game is worth it. No doubt about it.
