I have ~103 hours logged onto this game, but a good chunk of those hours were because my computer was left on at the mnu screen or something; the game does not last that long. My critique:
Music: 10/10. Triumphant and bombastic when it needs to be, slow and serene when it needs to be; it's always fitting.
Story: 8/10. The main reason I kept playing the game for so long. It was compelling enough for me to continue playing but wasn't exactly A++ material. It has quite a few interesting takes on the traditional fantasy tropes and stereotypes as well. The story does change a little bit throughout the game - that is, it's not like you know everything from the get-go... there's always new developments and whatnot to keep it interesting.
Voice Acting and Dialogue: 7/10. The majority of the characters have very fitting voices. There are a few that stand out and really make you want them to shut up. I'm also giving it a lower score because the game is RIDDLED with grammatical errors and inconsistencies.
- At some points, I've noticed some voice actors will refer to person X, then the same voice actor will start pronouncing person X differently half-way through the game.
- The text on screen often does not match what the voice actor is saying, forcing you to either read the text super-fast to catch up to where the voice actor is in the script because they omitted a portion of what's on screen, or force you to pause reading the text until the voice actor catches up to what's on the screen because they're adding something extra.
Gameplay: I honestly have no idea what to say about the gameplay. It's a big, big, big, mixed bag of mixed results. Incoming wall of text for each aspect of the gameplay:
THE RTS ELEMENT: The game boasts that it has "the perfect blend of RPG and RTS". This is not true one bit.
- The game defaults to overworld walking and exploration Diablo 3-style. The game throws you head-first into an RTS-style game at certain checkpoints during main quests.
- Once you destroy the enemy's HQ you lose control of all your troops and buildings as they are no longer needed. After all, you blew up their HQ. But yeah, you can sit there and watch your workers continue to gather resources looking pretty and whatnot.
- The enemy AI has no idea what it wants to do. What it does decide to do, it does so with the coordination of an infant child. For the majority of the maps in the game, they make little to no attempt to expand, giving you little challenge. Conversely, if you spend too much time expanding even after you've created a force strong enough to wipe out their HQ, you are literally wasting your time... that is, unless you enjoy expanding and watching your resources pile up into huge numbers.
- The enemy AI will sporadically send out a single soldier or a single handful of soldiers to different outposts for no reason. My base has 5,000 HP? That Arsonist of theirs deals 8 damage? Better be prepared to hear "Your base is under attack!" for the next twenty minutes unless you send someone back to kill him.
- The RTS is unneccessary beyond the fourth or fifth map once your hero party is strong on their own. Once I progressed to the fifth map, whenever the game threw me into RTS mode, I literally ignored the well-being of my own buildings, never assigned workers, and never built units. I literally send my hero party of four head-first into the enemy base and demolished their HQ, which, by the way, promptly kills and despawns all enemy units and buildings on the map.
- My friend said it best: "The RTS is more of a mini-game than anything." I could not have said it better.
THE RPG ELEMENT: I had little to no issues with the RPG elements in this game.
- The game boasts a "complex and rich" system. This is totally untrue marketing/advertising gibberish. You have Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Wisdom, and Intelligence. Everybody who's ever played an RPG before knows what those do. You get a single point to put into one of those abilities every other level.
- The skill trees are also just as simple. If you've ever seen a skill tree in any other RPG before, you'll be familiar with this one. Put a point here, put a point there, and that's it.
- Your characters can only have three 'present' abilities at a time. Oh, you have more than three abilities/auras that you would like to use at a time? Gotta constantly click this one button or button on your keyboard that flips through different loadouts mid-fight, which is really annoying.
WEAPONS AND ARMOR: The armor in this game is fine for the most part. There isn't a huge amount of variety, but there is. As for the weapons... it just makes me mad. Maybe I couldn't figure it out and somebody else can help me out here, but to me, it's a very broken system. What I type next is what I have found after drinking close to ~30 potions that allow you to reallocate skill tree points and attributes.
- The majority of weapons and armor in this game are sidegrades rather than upgrades.
- Dual-wielding will always deal less damage than 2-handing a heavy weapon.
- STR weapons will always outclass DEX weapons. I'm not joking, I had all my DEX characters chug potions so I can make them spec into STR instead of DEX. Went from dealing 120 DPS to anywhere between 280-400 DPS. It's insane.
- The damage ratings on the weapons hit a plateau very early on the game. You'll find weapons that deal something close to 5 DPS, then, 6 DPS, then 7.5-8 DPS, then 9 DPS, then 10 DPS... then a long period of time before you find any that deal 12-13 DPS... than at one point you find a STR weapon called "Sledgehammer" that deals 21 DPS. What the ♥♥♥♥? Why is there such a huge gap in the quality of the weapons?
- Artifact weapons are a thing in this game. You can do a little treasure hunting and find the pieces to armor/weapons scattered throughout the map. Find all the pieces, put them all together, and bam, you got yourself an artifact. A disappointing number of artifact weapons are simple weapons with 9 DPS that scale with DEX and no bonus stats on it whatsoever. Like, that's the difference between this and a common weapon I can buy off a vendor? Make up your mind, devs.
- A lot of weapons will say "Deal additional Fire/Ice/Black/White/Etc. Damage"... OK... any more info would have been nice. I don't know if I should have this amulet equipped that gives me extra health or the one that gives me "extra ice damage". Same thing with weapons... if I had two weapons that dealt the same damage but one did "extra fire damage" and the other had a chance to bleed... I have no frame of reference for the differences in damage.
It hurts in the best way possible. 10 out of 10, easily one of the best games to have come out this year

Just finished the campaign so it's time for a review!
I bought this game the week after it came out and played through the entire campaign without a single crash to desktop and without a single game breaking bug.  I took my time finishing it as well because I wanted to do all the side quests.  After all things considered here's my verdict:
While not complete polished perfection, this game is was what I've been looking for in the recent void of quality, deeply thought out, RTS games.  I bought this game because I wanted an awesome story that allowed me to progress an interesting storyline and character, set in a stunningly beautiful environment, with massive armies.  In all those aspects, this game delivered.  The hero mechanics are extremely well thought out and simple enough to enjoy while not bogging you down in the middle of an army fight.  I loved each of the teams - while not extremely diverse - still had enough differences to give them a unique play style and fun to experiment with (I would relate the current team diversity to the original supreme commander teams - minus forged alliance updates - I imagine future DLCs/expansions will increase team diversity).
I had a complete blast playing this game through to the end and don't regret a single cent of the $50 I spent on it.    If you're looking for the next Supreme Commander however, you'll be disappointed.  If you're looking for the next KOTOR, you'll also be disappointed.  However, if you're looking for an awesome, top-down RPG game with a compelling story mixed with engaging and extremely satisfying RTS elements, set in the most beautiful world you've seen, this game is for you.
Pros:
-Beautiful environments, sometimes I would catch myself just looking around the landscapes
-Great music, I found myself humming it in my head while not playing the game
-Engaging and original RTS style - I would relate the style to a mixture of Rise of Nations with Battle for Middle Earth
-Compelling story, stayed up multiple nights until 2am to see what would happen next
-Great RTS and RPG integration, I'm exhausted with RTSes that require massive micromanagement (looking at you Blizzard) this game does a great job at both giving you interesting hero abilities while also controlling a massive army without becoming unwieldy
-Any game ending or major bugs, in my experience, have been almost completely resolved and I have full confidence in the publishers that it will only even get more polished with time
Cons:
-Some light bugs (such as inconsistency in voice audio and text) still exist -- First conversation with Andra, whoa, just completely off
-Some RTS aspects in the campaign can be improved.  Some maps you can just rush with your heroes and destroy their capital immediately.  The other option was to try to build up but to eventually get overwhelmingly trashed by the AI.  Can we make it so you can't rush the AI and kill them in the beginning, but also make them defeatable later in the game?
-A little more of a tutorial might have been nice?  There were still some elements of base building and optimization that I still don't understand after completing the whole campaign.  (How do you recreate villagers and how long does it take for each race? What are the benefits and proper ways to stockpile resources?)
-More interesting items?  There were really only two different types of staves.  Since my character was an elementalist, it didn't really give that many options.  The armors and other weapons were cool though.
Final Score -- 8.8/10 After playing through this game, I would have bought it again for $50.  When expansions and DLCs come out, you can bet they'll quickly be in my library.

TL;DR: Half an hour of fun, casual speed mouse dragging but it unfortunately ends too quickly.
Feel-A-Maze is based on the classic concept: drag a mouse (or in this game, a colourful ball) through a maze without hitting any walls or other obstacles.
The title screen looks like it was done with Paint and there's no music - a bad sign. There's a level selection screen on the side and 120 stars to collect from each level.
Once you begin the game, the music starts. It's actually very exciting and works well for the game.
The first levels are simple, containing just immobile blocks. Quickly some interesting features emerge, as the obstacles start to pile on your way. There are blocks moving in several different but always periodic ways, blocks that disappear and blocks that follow you around. There are locked areas that need to be opened with a key to proceed. There are rocks and bouncing balls, and in some levels you have to chase and collect a bunch of stars to finish it instead of the regular exit door. Funny enough, in these levels the stars sometimes run away from you.
The art is mostly just blocks all the way, until you try the Christmas levels that are colourful and decorous, with the expense of sometimes making them slightly messy to look at. The music remains good in Christmas levels as well.
You get one star for completing a level, and at maximum three for completing it in par time, usually really quickly. Nevertheless, I managed to beat many of my best times on the second and third playthroughs even with every level 3-starred in both regular and Christmas levels.
The main disappointment is the short length: the game can be beaten in half an hour. It took me 40 minutes to beat both regular and Christmas levels with 3 stars and I played them through again for fun before this review. While nice and casual, it's just too short.
The game also lacks mouse sensitivity options, rather important for this kind of game. It would be useful to also know where the ball spawns before the level starts, although this is a minor issue.
It's a pleasant game and it could even be challenging for some people (depending on how stable your mouse hand is). That is why I would definitely recommend it. However, because of its short length I can't recommend it at full price - you should certainly wait for a sale.

I honestly think this is where the Arkham series really perfected its formula the best.  It contained many improvements over the original, but didn't deviate too much from the spirit of the original thing.
The gadgets iterated on the ones from Asylum and added a whole new slew of toys for Batman to play with. Batman himself controlled much more fluidly and was very fun to glide over the city with. He still possessed his usual quirks like punching thin air and failing to perform a ground knockout, but a lot of the sluggishness of Asylum was remedied in City.
The city itself is expansive and quite varied in its design. A bit grey and not as fun to look at as the rooms in Asylum, however. I guess that's just how cities look. The atmosphere of the game was still impeccable, but lacked a little bit of suspense and terror.
Bad guys are slightly tougher in this game, but not crazily so. The boss fights were VERY cool and inventive, all the way up to the end. The only gripe I would have with them is that they rely on a single gadget and don't require the player to think of their arsenal as a whole.
Collectibles are numerous and sidequests are interesting and provide background to the universe. The items required to tick off a 100% checklist is a bit ridiculous however. I think the thing that really bogs this game down is a sense of bloating: just a lot of content that isn't particularly rewarding but is just meant to pad out the hours played. For example: the inclusion of Catwoman. An interesting character, sure, but one that isn't nearly as fun to play and who doesn't significantly contribute to the story. Another example: 200+ medals of combat/stealth challenges. Entirely unnecessary, but I guess you're getting your money's worth.
Despite its flaws, I believe City is definitely an improvement on its predecessor.

A very well told touching story.  I thoroughly enjoyed the whole game and, much like with the original game, felt a strong connection to the characters by the climax of the game.  It is, very similar to the first game.  Freebird Studios have clearly found a formula for their games which works and is effective to tell the story that they wish to tell, and I am delighted to see that they stayed true to that.
A few points need to be stressed if you are considering buying this game, however.  The main one being that if you’re looking for a game with breath-taking graphics, visuals or interactivity/impact on the story, this game is the very antithesis of what you are looking for, and you should pass it by.  It is, a story told almost completely in 16 bit graphics, wherein you are constantly given the chance to explore and are expected to find what needs to be found in order to progress, and while the odd choice is given to you in this game, ultimately, the choices have hardly any impact, and what little impact they do have is made irrelevant after a few minutes.
I cannot stress this enough, this a game designed solely to tell a single linear story, and it does that very well.  So, if you’re looking for a story driven game and want it to be a tearjerker, this is the game for you (along with the prequel To The Moon).  The game sets out with that one clear goal in mind and does a fantastic job filling the large boots left by the first game.
Overall, I am very happy with this game, and look forward to the next episode in this series.

Nidhogg boils down competitive gaming to its barest essentials: two diametrically opposed players, endpoints that must be reached, and the pixelated means with which to reach them.
During a match, progress to the endpoints is barred by bounded screens that are unlocked as players slay one another. Skirmishes are quick and deadly, with each player given the ability to duck, roll, cartwheel, jump, dive, stab, or run their opponents through in order to win the encounter. To win consistently, players must learn to make use of positioning, intuiting opponents' rapier movements in order to close in for the kill. Alternately, if one player finds themselves on the wrong side of the arena (or makes the mistake of missing a saber throw, thereby giving the other player a free pass), the other player can circumnavigate them bloodlessly. In any event, the last player to kill the other is rewarded with a flashing "GO" arrow and the ability to bypass the frame, continuing toward the endpoint at the rightmost screen in the level, where a glorious death awaits in the jaws of the Nidhogg, a wormlike serpent.
What makes the game work is its singleminded determination to make you learn its mechanics. First of all, there aren't that many to speak of, so you're forced to quickly learn to chain attacks, dodges, disarms, and executions to make short work of opponents so they are unable to do the same to you. Because its learning curve is so slight, Nidhogg is easy for anyone to jump into, so you'll have no shortage of friends to play against in local multiplayer. In the best situations, the game becomes a raw tug-of-war, a game whose intensity builds alongside the kill count and whose primal quality of skill in combat manifests in the swatches of blood and piles of weapons that accumulate throughout the level. The simple electronic beats and the vivid palette of colors instill matches with a heady trancelike quality that sucks you into your PC's speakers, screen, and keyboard all at once.
Despite these praises, I have to warn anyone interested in Nidhogg that it's a bit anemic in terms of content. There are few maps and only one gametype, so your mileage from the game depends solely on your ability to enjoy the game in short bursts with friends (I recommend that you play locally--online play simply does not capture the glee of some good old-fashioned real-life♥♥♥♥♥♥talking). Still, Nidhogg taps into a special kind of energy, an addictive sense of progress and loss that accompanies the back-and-forth scrolling of the level screens. If you buy the game on the cheap, you're guaranteed to experience some good vibes.
8/10

Yes, somehow, I do recommend this game.
Do not buy it for 4 dollars - get it on sale, or do what I did and sell a lot of useless trading cards and pay for it that way.
I really wanted to try this game because I have an affection for low-budget, early 2000's shooters.  There's just some sort of weird charm to them that makes them interesting to play.
But enough of that: let's get the bad out of the way.
- Crashes at random points.  Seriously: for absolutely no reason at all, the game will crash.  On the other hand, it only takes about 30 seconds to start the game and load your last save, so that's not too big an issue.
- You either have to turn off the music, or replace the .dll file.  There's no way around it.  The cheaply produced, off-European tunes are actually somewhat catchy, so I recommend replacing the file.
- You can't skip through the splash screens, or your game will crash.  Whatever.
- No widescreen support.
- Currently, I'm having some wonky texture glitches that make random parts of the floors and walls just completely black.  Not sure how to fix that.  There is also a plethora of other graphical bugs and glitches as well.
- There's only about three or four enemy character models.
- Not quite sure what the story is about (not that I care).  It appears to be some sort of insurrection inside the post-World War 2 KGB?  You're a KGB agent and you're killing other KGB agents.  Or Chekists.  I don't know.
- Absurdly difficult, even on normal.  However, this is countered by the massive amount of ammo drops in crates everywhere, so you're never short on bullets.
- Speaking of, it takes a lot of bullets to take down enemies.  It's fine, because the cheesy animations and decent physics sort of counteract the fact that you just sank an entire AK magazine into one guard.
- There's probably more I could say, but this is what I dragged up.
Now, the good.
- The voice acting is so terrible that it's hilarious.  Seriously - you'll have a good time listening to cutscenes and whatnot.
- Guns are pretty satisfying.  Decent list of weapons at your disposal.  Sound effects are cheesy and low-budget, but what do you expect.  The Shpagin is probably my favorite: straight up spraying bullets everywhere is pretty fun in this game.
- For an older low-budget game, the graphics aren't too shabby.  You get what you pay for.
- I actually really dig the effects - destruction, physics, etc - in this game.  Sure, it's no Havok or Euphoria or whatever, but the setpieces are pretty nice.  Ricocheting bullets, shattering glass, blowing out portions of the floor and wall, etc.
- Just a good time, Russian shoot 'em up.
So, in short, yes, the game is plauged with technical errors and glitches.  But if you can pick it up for cheap, and you're looking for a straightforward shooter, then this isn't your worst bet.

Styx: Master of Shadows is a fantasy stealth game that has you go through various maps as the plot progresses. You'll be given different tasks and challenges, typically with the formula of primary objectives, secondary objectives, and various collectables. You have multiple paths to choose from, as well as an array of abilities in case you get yourself into a sticky situation. Combat is intentionally difficult and one-sided to make you want to avoid conflict and rely on stealth, which is not a bad thing in the slightest.
Before I really delve into the best parts of this game, I want to focus on some of its flaws. This is for two reasons:
1. The flaws this game does have are VERY obvious and noticeable, so I feel like they're definitely worth mentioning first.
2. I enjoy this game immensely, and honestly it wouldn't be doing it justice if I didn't end the review on a positive note.
When you play Styx, it becomes apparent that the developers didn't have a huge budget to work with. This is no triple A platinum title. This game has its fair share of glitches, poor controls, and clunky AI.
-I've had several instances where I quicksaved when I was safe, reloaded the quicksave, and then got caught immediately by an enemy that didn't even know I existed beforehand. Be careful where you save.
-Climbing up things is a breeze. Climbing down them is another story. One thing that frustrates me to no end is when I try and drop off a ledge to grab the one below, and Styx will just grab the first ledge and climb back up it. This is especially infuriating when you're trying not to get spotted by an enemy coming around the corner.
-The AI is muy estúpido. They have no concept of each others placement. They usually walk in the same looped path, be it around a room, up and down strairs, or from table to table, etc. When you alert them they may stop and look, or even go towards the noise to investigate. During and after this sequence is when you get to enjoy watching them bump into each other. They'll sometimes walk in place towards each other until one of them somehow gets around the other.
-Some of the subtitles need to be proof read. I get the feeling English wasn't the developers first language.
Now that that's done, I can focus on the things this game does well.
-The plot. My god, the plot. The story is surprisingly captivating, intriguing, and well thought out. I won't spoil anything for you, just know that the devs are some creative ♥♥♥♥ers and I admire their story telling ability greatly.
-The stealth portions. Despite what I may have said about the whole climbing down issue, the stealth itself is very well done. I'm sure there are better stealth games out there, but this games sneak mechanics feel nice and balanced to me. I never feel like my ability to sneak is overpowered, nor underpowered. What I'm trying to say is the game itself feels very fair to the player.
-The artwork is lovely. Some cutscenes are done with drawn stills of what is happening with dialogue dubbed over, rather than animated 3D characters like some other cutscenes. I'm sure this would be a complaint for some people, but I really enjoyed it. The art is really well done and it really sets some scenes apart from the others.
-I really love the way the game rewards the player. Essentially you receive skill points when you do primary and secondary objectives, as well as gathering collectables. However, the icing on the cake for me was the insignias. You will also receive skill points for the following:
1. Not being spotted during a mission.
2. No kills during a mission.
3. How fast you managed to complete a mission.
4. Collecting all the treasures. (Collectables, as already mentioned.)
This effectively allows the player to be rewarded and congratulated for things like ghosting or speedrunning, and for me it also allows for more replayability.
In summary, this is not a perfect game. It's riddled with flaws and I understand why people wouldn't care for it, but for me it was fun as hell. I loved playing it and it's admittedly become a personal favourite of mine. I can't recommend it enough, and I implore you to at least give it a shot. It's a real gem and I'm stoked for the upcoming sequel.

Feel-A-Maze is a short game about dragging a ball, avoiding all of the obstacles and reaching the exit. 30 minutes should be enough to complete the 40 levels, getting 3 stars in each of them, which means 100% achievements. This is fun and enjoyable, although not that challeging, except for some levels.
At the current price (4,99€), I think it is too expensive, but if you can find it in a bundle, I recommend it !

What is Feel-A-Maze?
Feel-A-Maze is a dexterity game where you need to navigate a green ball with your mouse through different mazes in a certain time. The time limit is tight, but never unfair - even I was able to finish some levels feeling I had some time left or made a mistake in between and still got three stars.
The game reminds me of the wire-loop game, as in you have that ball and click it with your mouse to navigate it and are not allowed to touch anything except keys you need later to open locks. This "anything" is at first walls, then later moving walls, walls that blend in and out, walls that follow you as well as rocks and balls that fall down and in the case of balls also may bounce.
The biggest minus point of the game is the length. Even at the nice number of 40 levels it brings, you can finish the game in five minutes with perfect play. A realistic estimate to beat it is around 30 to 60 minutes. If you desire so, you can play another 15 christmas themed levels by clicking a button in the main menu. I did not play those since they don't give extra achievements.
Unfortunately I was unable to find how to turn off the music and sound ingame, so a minus point must be given there. The music is okay, but you should not expect anything special.
The graphics are fitting for the type of game it is, with the exception of the final level, but this was most likely done by default.
The controls are - as said before - completely with the mouse. Bad: I would have wished an option where you control the ball always instead of having to keep the mouse key clicked. Regardless of how well that would work for me personally, it would give everyone the preferred playstyle.
The gameplay is varied, but in my opinion some themes are explored not enough. Maybe more levels that screw with visibility would have been nice, or even one where your up and down controls are reversed, but then with a lot more time to complete it.
As it stands, however, it is a solid small title that is reminiscent of the early 1990s in style. It is of course up to your personal taste if you enjoy such games, but for me it was a fun and short experience that had the frust factor nailed right to keep me going - it felt difficult but almost never unfair. Yes, there could be improvements, it is far from perfect. But the developer has apparently invested quite some thought in it. With more levels, more variety, maybe even an editor, this game could improve, but this does not mean it wouldn't already be worth playing.
For achievement hunters: The achievements work fine and can be gotten by getting three stars on all levels, i.e. in the time described above.
Recommended: If you can get it on a good sale, it is definitely worth checking out for fans of dexterity games! There is some potential that is unused, but the base provided here is a solid one. Overall I can give a slightly positive review, or if you prefer numbers I give a 6 out of 10 for the fun but short experience.
It remains to be hoped the developer expands the game or makes a sequel, incorporating a few of my ideas or other ones he can come up with for more variety.

Alright, I have completed the campaign now and felt the time was right to put down a review for the game.
After having to stop on 3 different instances throughout the story due to game breaking bugs I patiently waited for patches that corrected these and let me continue. As I could continue I quickly realised that despite me being able to play along the game was still riddled with bugs. After 20 Patches in roughly so many days, I still couldn't recruit one follower, could not complete 3 quests with followers I had already recruited, wasn't able to complete several side quests and encountered about 20 to 30 instances in the game where certain event triggers wer broken. Either resulting in me having to play a map again or having to put up with ever repeating dialogues throughout the whole map because something was stuck.
I actually really wanted to like this game and saw a lot of potential. I finished it because I wanted to be thorough and give it more chances than it deserved, mostly because I love Spellforce 1. But in the end the RTS part is alright, the Roleplaying part and especially the loot is underwhelming. Roughly 5 hours into the game and you ahve seen nearly everything lootwise that there is. Then you end up finding a lot of parts to artifact weapons and armor, yet the game does not provide a single way of combining them or giving you any clues what is missing to make use of those parts. There are NPCs you can recruit for your city that never arrive (architect, scholar, smith, etc.) and the whole upgrading system for units is completely pointless. Roughly halfway through the game the heroes become strong enough to simply punch through any enemy resistance and kill their capital building thus defeating every unit on the map.
On top of that: The story is at best mediocre. The references towards Spellforce 1 are nice, but there is nothing in there that is well written.
But after all the developers seem to try to fix their game. The problem with that is that they simply sold a completely broken game that, even in a state where it isn't broken, is just okayish at best. For those that enjoy Spellforce 1: Play that and don't bother with this one. For everyone else I would recommend watching a rather detailed review video first before making any decisions. It's a tough game to enjoy and like.

Nidhogg is a fast paced, local multiplayer focused fencing game developed by Messhof. In Nidhogg you take up fencing and fight one on one matches against AI or other players through local or online multiplayer. The aim of the game is to make it past your opponent and run to the other side of the map.
+Awesome pixel graphics
+Simple gameplay, all you have to do is stab your opponent and run to the other side of the map, it might sound boring but it's actually really entertaining, especially when playing with friends
+The different maps are very different to each other which provides some nice variation for the game
+Nidhogg can be enjoyed in Singleplayer, Local Multiplayer and Online Multiplayer/Matchmaking
+The fast-paced side-scrolling nature of Nidhogg makes it perfect for playing in Local Multiplayer and things get pretty intense, making Local Multiplayer pretty exhilirating and the best way to enjoy the game
+Nidhogg features a tournament mode which allows 3-8 players to play Local Multiplayer
+The soundtrack is great and fits with the game well
+The fighters in the game are all brightly coloured and blood basically acts like paint for the maps so you end up with some pretty cool designs on the floor if one area of the map gets particularly bloody
+Both the KB&M controls and the 360 Gamepad controls are very good and very responsive
-Nidhogg has a severe lack of content due to only having four maps, for £10.99 that kind of content really isn't good enough
-Singleplayer gets repetitive (thanks to the lack of content) very quickly
-Until recently Online Multiplayer wasn't very good (due to lag mainly) but it has been fixed, sadly it would seem not many people who own Nidhogg know that it was fixed since the game's Online Multiplayer remains pretty much dead
Verdict:
Highly Recommended, but Only When Discounted (6.5/10)
Nidhogg is a great, fast paced fighting game with awesome graphics and simple gameplay, sadly the game is very much let down by its lack of content and high asking price. If you're looking for what is one of the best Local Multiplayer games on Steam and you don't mind paying the high price then give Nidhogg a go, if not, wait for a sale.

Nidhogg is a side scrolling fighting game which was released in early 2014. You duel against another sword wielding foe.  You have to get to the other side of the map before your opponent. In order to do so, you must run, jump, throw your sword and slide past the other enemies.
The actual gameplay is very simple, just kill the other guy really. This can be done in a number of ways, the most common is just to kill the enemy in a sparing match. You can also disarm your opponent by knocking their weapon out of their hands leaving them very vulnerable with just their fists to fight back with. You can get quite technical if you want though, by wall jumping, dive kicks and knocking down enemies by sliding their feet out.
Nidhogg has a single player mode, which is quite enjoyable, but can be completed in about two hours if you have any sort of skill at the game. The single player is essentially the four different levels repeated over and over increasing in difficulty. While I did have fun playing this mode, the real fun from Nidhogg comes out of the local multiplayer mode. This will pit you against your friends in a duel with the same mechanics as previously mentioned, things get competitive very fast, so watch out!  We also have an online multiplayer options available, however there were no players online every time I checked so I would class this as a no go zone.
The graphics are a very simplistic style, which actually have a nice look to them; this is the type of game that doesn't need fancy textures and shadows to make it more appealing, as you hardly pay any attention to the graphics due to how fast paced the gameplay is.
The single player mode of Nidhogg is about two hours long, so if you are purely looking for a single player experience, this may not be for you since there is not much replay-ability for single player. If you have friends who you can hook up a second controller with, Nidhogg really shines there. The majority of my time on Nidhogg was spent in a local multiplayer mode and it's an absolute blast.
Whilst I think the price of £10,99 is quite steep for this game given the lack of single player and online multiplayer content available, the amount of fun you can have in local multiplayer redeems it slightly. So I am going to recommend Nidhogg, but only when it is on sale for anything under £5.  This is certainly a game I will be keeping installed for when friends come round.

EPILEPSY WARNING: THIS GAME HAS FLASHING LIGHTS
It has potential, but I can't recommend it game right now.
First things first, if you wanna understand this game, you need to know his shenanigans (google "bob's game").
Despite all that, the game is... Interesting.
The game is basically a "crossover" of several puzzle games, like Puyo Puyo, Columns, and Super Puzzle Fighter. You can either select them individually or play it on a set order, each game being its own "stage". That's a quite solid concept, but there are quite a few tecnical problems in this game
First, visuals. The neon pieces are quite nice, but the problem lies outside the puzzle grid. There is a huge cluster of information concentrated outside of the grid on the left side of the screen. These  are huge lines of text (for an UI) with precise statistics. Things for a casual viewer, like number of lines, whith also numbers I've only heard being used by hardcore puzzle players, like current gravity and lock delay. I don't mind the quantity of information presented on screen, but I can see someone having a problem with that not being presented in text. It kinda looks like a debug build, Just text, mind you, nothing even remotely close to the aesthetics of the rest of the game. It's ugly and distracting. It is completely possible to have these statistics displayed in a more aesthetical way than this games shows right now. There there is so much text and information that,  if you're playing in the default windowed mode, four of those options will be hidden (I'll get to that in a second).
My second biggest problem is actually ironic, considering the last paragraph. This game has the habit to not telling what are you supposed to be doing in each segment. It probably helps that I played most of these puzzles, but there are a few games that are not self-explanatory (notably Super Puzzle Fighter). There are items on the game that I don't have the slightest clue on how they work. For example, the Pacman icon. What does it do? I have no clue. It doesn't work like in Pac Attack, because I can eliminate all the blocks present, and even then Pacman doesn't move (btw, Namco might sue you for using a Pacman, there's precedent for that). There are a few items on the first puzzle that I took a while to understand what they were doing, because the name of the information flashes rapdily on screen, giving me not enough time to process.
There's also no training mode, or any other outside of "marathon" or "endless", which... Actually, I have not that much of a problem with that, the quantity of games inside Bob's Game is a lot of content already (I kinda wish there was a "random" mode, with a randomly generated order of "stages").
And I will not try to use multiplayer because... Come on, Pelloni, you're asking too much from me. People are questioning the validity of this game enough, and you're asking people to register for online multiplayer? Come one, man.
But I would urge the author to not worry with extra features right now. Because this game is, above all,  collection of tecnical misteps. The game behaves differently based on the size of the windows, with information either missing or being relocated (and, need I remind you, this game opens in a small window by default). The transitions between games are very clumsy, without any kind of warning. The game loves using flashing lights as substitutes for more elaborate animations, which oh boy do I have a headache right now. Trying to vote basically softlocks the game with an error informing me the game cannot connect into the server. The menus are clumsy and look really bad. There's a wall of text on the title screen, with the author shilling his Patreon and other information (I'm not against Patreon, I'm against wall of texts polluting the UI). Scrolling is a mess, most notably in the tetris attack segment.
With all that said, this game has a lot of potential. The game sure needs a lot of work into it, but it is very possible to turn itself into a excellent puzzler.
And its playable at least. That's a lot more than I can say about, for example, Tetris Ultimate.

Well, I saw the name bob's game® pop up in my recommended games and almost jumped out of my pants. Then I saw that it was some weird puzzle game and not the RPG game some dude locked himself in a room for.
Doing some looking into it, apparently now bob's game® (the rpg) is about making bob's game® (this puzzle game) and is still slated to come out soon®. So yes, this is the bob's game® you're thinking of, but not totally the bob's game® you're thinking of.
Barring that confusion, I think bob's game® (the puzzle game) is a pretty cool idea wrapped in this weird half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥veil. But not the kind of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥where it feels like the developer didn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about it, the kind where that same dev who's passionate about his game ran out of time, money, or inspiration, and instead of canning the project just decided to randomly release it 65% complete.
I played through an entire "run through" of bob's game. The premise is this: you play a puzzle game in a screen space that's sort of similar to tetris, but whenever you "level up" by getting enough points, you change the rules of the puzzle game completely into another puzzle game. This is all happening while words and random sentences are flying at the screen like "Wow, I've never gotten this far before!" and "SEQUENCE LINE BREAK"
I played some sort of weird campaign because it was the default option- it basically was the core premise of the game but randomly after I played long enough it yanked the controls away from me and said "YOU WON!". It's not even like that was the point I cycled through every game, as I saw repeats. I have absolutely no clue how multiplayer on this game could even work, and couldn't find anyone to play with (not surprising).
I think the idea is that people create minigames, petition to get them added to the base game, and they get added through popularity vote. It's kind of similar to the game "Move or Die", but if the minigames were automatically patched into the game but the artist took the day off and just made everything spheres. This forces the players to constantly try and figure out how to play these user made games and score the best for leaderboard purposes.
I actually really love that base idea.
The major problem with this is that your creativity is locked to the format of a falling block game, and there really isn't much room left for interesting or new falling block games as all of the good sane ones have already been made. This is backed up with the fact that I recognized 85% of the games that came packaged with bob's game®, and that makes me assume the other 15% is just stolen games I don't recognize. I'll say that you are not all that wrong that this game is "so deep yet so shallow" and you're concerns that this is mostly a co-op ,and I would add random non-campaign single-player, platform are not entirely incorrect either.
However, I'll also have to say what may or may not be a bit more bad news depending on who you are. Issues that are obviously bugs aside, the way E.Y.E. is paced and how it plays are not really a "mistake", in that sense the game is the way it's supposed to be.
If that's a problem then there's a good chance this game isn't what you think it is.
To try to clarify what I mean by this, I'll give a slightly shortened version of a an explanation I've posted elsewhere.
If you really really want to understand why E.Y.E. is the way it is and have time to spare then I would recommend the following:
-Re-install Half-Life 1 and install Sven Co-op and play a few maps of that.
-After that install another Half-Life 1 mod called Syndicate Black Ops, which is from the developer of E.Y.E. and is pretty much its prequel, and play a few levels of that as well.
-After that go play some E.Y.E. again. There’s a good chance that E.Y.E. "design" will then suddenly make sense, and its intentions will probably turn out to be not quite as lofty as you might have thought.
That's probably a lot of trouble to go through so here's a quick summary of sorts.
E.Y.E. is NOT a Deus Ex, STALKER, or Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines and it was never meant to be. It sort of reaches in that direction but it starts from a very different place.
Instead, E.Y.E. sort of "evolved" out of an odd subset of old FPS co-op mods that were sort of environment where aggressive respawning enemies and constantly being under attack are commonplace. Some people genuinely liked that sort of play, and for better or worse that's sort of why E.Y.E. has inherited that mentality.
I suppose the best way I can try to describe E.Y.E. without the above mentioned context is that it’s “like a Serious Sam from an alternate world where games like Deus Ex, System Shock 2, and STALKER became really big and sold as as much as Call of Duty does in our world”.
It has RPG mechanics, various tools, a hacking system, inventory management, leaning, and all sorts of mechanics we associate with more "deep and sophisticated” games, but these are just means to an end and in this case they are not matched with “deep and sophisticated” ends, and that can be somewhat confusing at first.
In this case they’re all there to enhance the end objectives of “killing tons of enemies” and “being a badass”.
E.Y.E. has respawning enemies because if they didn’t respawn you’d run out of things to fight.
Stealth is not that fleshed out because stealth is not intended as a gameplay approach by itself, it’s just another tool to help you kill more dudes and for that the game’s version of stealth works quite well.
Hacking lets you do a lot of interesting things, but it’s also meant to be yet another tool you use to be a badass killing machine and not a completely separate play-style.
The cybernetic and magic themes are not there to provoke deep thought, they’re just there for flavor and to justify giving you more abilities that you then use in combat.
If that’s not enough “gameplay” for you by itself then you’re probably going to hate the game or have to make some adjustments to get the game to do what you want, because that’s what the “gameplay” is.
This game was made by and for people who genuinely find this sort of play to be satisfying.
The confusing plot that people like to speculate about is mostly icing on the cake and excuse to have the sorts of weird locations and maps the game has. It has a story of course and it does have a lot of interesting bits to it, but again it’s mostly there to justify sending the player to odd places. Everything else is mostly “Rule Of Cool”.
The game has magical space werewolves, space stoner hippies, and a king of the dead who kills you if you want to join his army for pete’s sake, that should be a clue in that while the plot and setting have some serious elements, overall this isn’t a super-serious plot or setting.
Anyway, there’s my explanation of E.Y.E..
Interpret that how you will.

Stalin Subway comes to us from Orion Games, the same people who gave us the "gem" that was Dusk-12. And because of that, The Stalin Subway comes with all of the same technical issues of Dusk-12. Fortunately, this time around the games forums were very helpful in providing fixes and I could enjoy this game without too much hassle.
Speaking of which, enjoy this game I did! The Stalin Subway is a great classic shooter.
Graphics:
Nothing too amazing here, but nothing awful either. In comparison to their other effort, Dusk-12, The Stalin Subway actually looks better. None of the models look too stiff and the game runs fine without too many hiccups. However, in some of the Metro levels the games engine has some... interesting ways of showing shiny reflective surfaces.
Gameplay:
Classic FPS like Quake/Doom etc. You got health/armor meters (though it seems armor drops are extremely rare) and a plethora of guns to use. You can't sprint in the game, but if you want to get across the level quickly you can just jump strafe to victory for a lightning quick way to get down long corridors.
Sound:
Re-used gun sounds from DUSK-12 so all the guns sound pretty weak and rather unsatisfying to shoot. With a new Audiere.dll file, I actually got to hear some music while I played this, and it wasn't bad at all.
Story:
You play as Gleb Suvorov, a KGB liutenant. On a routine shift in a secret base, KGB Officers begin an insurrectection against Stalin. The plan on blowing up Moscow with an atomic bomb. It's your job to track down the traitor of the Motherland and stop the bomb!
Pretty simple, and enjoyably shlocky. Stalin himself appears in FMVs but, he doesn't seem to have any idea whats going on or even when he does, not all that concerned about it. The voice acting is pretty brutal here, and a lot of mistranslated lines which kind of adds some charm to it.
Other Stuff:
Back on the armor thing.. I find it weird that you have an armor meter and start the game 100 Armor, but I only once found any armor thoughout the game. It's like the devs just forgot about armor drops. Either way, it's not a hassle since most enemies drop health items and you shouldn't have too much trouble getting through the game.
Overall:
The Stalin Subway is a rootin' tootin' Soviet shootin' good time.. GET IT.
It's like John Chaser in Russia 1950's XD.

The games combat is a bit wonky, when you start an attack, a bar comes up, I guess its supposed to be a charge meter or something, but the game doesnt tell me. Hitting your target is also pretty hard, so far I have only used melee weapons like axes, daggers, and small swords. Bigger swords might give me a bit more of a hitbox to hit, but i don't know yet. RPG:

You get stats from leveling and apparently just doing stuff? Hard to say exactly what, but I notice sometimes I get extra points before I have even leveled up. There is also passive abilities that gives you low bonuses early, don't know about late game, but early its stuff like "1%+ more damage with backstabs" "1% less taken damage from backstabs" and etc.
Crafting:
Pretty interesting but also confusing, you get resources by gathering from resources nodes around the world, or from dead bodies. Inventory fills up quickly as theres a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of materials. Crafting is pretty straightforward, get resources, press craft, and done. For weapons theres small chances of getting bonus damage from +1 to +6, higher level and using a "workshop" increases the chances for higher bonuses. Right now theres not many weapons in game, like 3 different bows, 2 of them have the same stats as far as I see. about 5 different 2 handed weapons, and etc. You can buy recipes from merchants but I haven't seen any new ones for weapons. theres a lot of steps in crafting something like a bow, you would have to go like
kill wolf -> butcher corpse -> clean tendons -> \
chop wood -> craft planks -> \
= craft bow
PvP:
Haven't seen much PvP in the game yet, only thing I encountered was a random guy just chopping my back for some reason (his reason later was explained as "I was lost"). In the game world theres currently 2 empires you can join, attacking players from the enemy empire will probably not give you any demerits. But attacking your own people marks you, which allows the attacked player to attack back, and guards from cities will hunt you down. Attacking enough of your own people will make you exiled, and you will be transported to an island where you have to get your reputation back by killing bandits, this is what I have heard happens from the in game chat, I am not sure if thats the exact steps, but thats how it was explained to me.
Performance:
Eh, worked pretty alright for a long while yesterday, today this morning it worked a bit worse, might just be situational or depending on where I am.
Summary:
Its an alright game, with lots of promise, I still haven't gotten into tournaments or capturing towns that people seem so hyped up about in the game, but so far I have been having quite a lot of fun just playing as a bowman, hunting down wolves and the occasional bear.
This is a pretty fun game, although there are still a lot of bugs. For how cheap it is, it's definitely worth picking up.

As someone that's not followed the game and came into it here's my thoughts so far (Early Access First Impressions)
- Gloria Victis is set in a beautiful open world with nice graphical fidelity and an art style that feels fitting for a medivel game, shortly after logging in you'll feel a sense of immersion from the music and enviromental consistency as you explore many diverse areas with different types of terrain and buildings.
- The bow and arrow combat feels realistic and fun, I really enjoyed having to lead my shots based on how far away my target was, it feels really skill based and impactful.
- Gloria Victis is a game that gives you a heavy feeling of faction pride, currently there's only two factions in the game but eventually when the game is finished the world will be much larger and you'll be able to fight for one of 4 factions to enguage in mass scale PVP where you'll capture towns and castles in reward for faction wide buffs and glory
- Crafting in Gloria Victis is a pretty huge part of the game and will enable you to make some of the best armor and weapons you can get, for someone that tends to ignore crafting and professions in MMOs I found the interface and crafting in general with this game very easy to get my head around yet interesting and totally worth doing, I did encounter a lot of bugs that prevented me from crafting a few things though but the games in Alpha so i'm sure that'll be fixed soon
- The game has a nice clean user interface that didn't♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, many parts of the UI could be moved and I like how damage numbers and health bars aren't displayed over the top of a mobs head like in most MMOs as I think that would break immersion, instead this information is displayed in your combat log which I feel makes sense in this game, basically I feel like the game does a good job in displaying all the relivent information to you without taking up too much space on the screen, that being said I think it'd be nice to be able to resize certain things such as the crafting window, character window and world map.
- Upon release the game will apparently have a content limited trial with the possibility to unlock everything through gameplay, owners of the early access version of the game will be given access to all the content so basically the game will be free to play to a certain point however you'll need to put in extra effort to unlock everything if you don't wanna pay, as long as there's no pay to win micro transactions then I'm fine with this
- Gloria Victis seems to have classless combat in which changing your gear essentually changes your class, I absolutely love this idea and found myself switching between using a bow at long range and a melee weapon at close range, giving players this freedom to change their equipment, weapons and armor on the fly allows for some interesting and dynamic encounters that don't get boring as you can just change up your build and role to suit the situation.
- As this is mostly a PVP game killing another player will give you a short period of time when you can loot their body, I think this is a good idea as it makes the world feel dangerous and keeps you on your toes against the enemy however I like how they've designed the player loot system to not be overly punishing, instead of being able to take everything a player has you're given a limited amount of loot points, more valuble items and gear cost more loot points so if you do die it's not the end of the world as you'll only lose one or two items, this is vastly different to games such as runescape where dying can cause you to lose everything you have sometimes taking days, even weeks to recover.
- The Soundtrack in Gloria Victis is absolutely stunning and buying into the early access will give you a the full digital soundtrack which is a nice bonus, expect music with a similar vibe to The Witcher 3, the games Main theme tune is actually composed by the same guy that composed the witcher 3 soundtrack, I think the other tracks are composed by different artists but are still upto the same standard
- As much as I do like the UI in this game I feel like it needs to be more responsive, it doesn't feel overly polished and there's usually a short delay between clicking something and getting a response from the game.
- I mentioned earlier that I think it'd be nice if you could resize the in game map but I also think it should be more helpful, currently it doiesn't give you much information other than a vague overview of the world, I think it'd be helpful to get more detail by clicking on towns, citys and specific zones, possibly allowing you to set waypoints too, currently it just lacks functionality
- As much as I enjoyed the ranged combat I feel like the melee combat is a long way off, the sound effects are lacking, the animations don't feel convincing and it just doesn't feel overly fun at the moment, I'm not sure specifically how to fix this but I'd love to see a melee combat system that feels similar to dark souls in this game, I feel like that could possibly work well
- Gloria Victis seems like it won't have much PVE content outside of killing mobs for exp, personally I don't mind this at all as the mass scale PVP is the main selling point of the game for me however I know that many gamers only play MMORPGs for PVE raids and dungeons and hate PVP, from what I can tell it doesn't look like this game will have that

The goal of this game is very simple - in every level you need to move a ball to the exit through a maze without touching the edges of the maze and avoiding all other obstacles. There is a time requirement for every level - you get 1 - 3 stars per level according to your time performance; these stars are needed for unlocking all the levels.
This is considered to be one of the games in which you can obtain 100% achievements very easy – some do it in 30 minutes – 1 hour. For me, the experience of obtaining 100% was a quite frustrating because I had to retry each level several times and push myself to do it faster and faster to the point in which my wrist started to hurt like hell. Depending on your mouse type and mouse grip or maybe depending on your coordination skills and quick reactions that have been trained or not by extensive session of FPS – this might be a fun game for you or not.
Despite this, I decided to give this game a positive review – I enjoyed the concept but I think that the required times might be a bit too strict - it's that kind of game in which 1 millisecond counts a lot. I also liked a lot the extra Christmas levels, which had innovative ideas and were very fun to play.

At the price that it is originally posted as, $4.99, this game is definitely not recommended.  However, I did pick this up for $0.49 at 90% off and at that price this game is a good game.  The basic concept is that you click on a ball and walk it through a maze or an obstacle course.  If you touch a wall or any other object other than the exit, you will start the level over.  There are 40 levels and the types of obstacles from standard walls to ghosts to lasers to bouncing balls changes as the game progresses.  The graphics are not anything spectacular, but then again the game doesn't require them to be.  The game is really short and easy to complete, but yet you will go through your frustrations as the sensitivity of the mouse can easily slam you into walls again and again and again.  Overall, if the price is as low as the one I got it for, then I recommend it since there is no other game like it that I'm aware of on Steam.

Earth Space Colonies
Released
Persona and Pixel Studio
Persona and Pixel Studio
3D Colony Simulation
1st of July, 2016
Singleplayer
Ever since playing Startopia in 2001, I became fascinated by video games which portray the hardships of outer space colonization. Earth Space Colonies (ESC) does not feature playable alien races or a giant donut-shaped space station, but Startopia’s principles and general gameplay, remain firmly in place. Survival has a steep cost and resource management is paramount. For a Steam debut, the developer left quite an impression on me. I had been following this game’s progress for several months and I contacted the developer asking for a review copy. It’s not something I do often nowadays, but some games most certainly deserve my undivided attention. A mixed Steam rating spells a polarizing subject, but you shall find more details below.
The campaign underwent the most radical changes from the one present in Earth Space Colonies’ Early Access stage. You can still find several YouTube clips showcasing the initial lack of polish in both the User Interface and voice acting along with a limited space on which structures were built from the start. Once fully released, ESC now truly looks like a 3D colony sim worthy of being reviewed by yours truly. The story per se, is farily simple. You’re the nameless administrator of humanity’s colonization efforts on Mars, Ceres (dwarf planet) and Ganymede (Jupiter's largest moon).
Ah, the
Subject of so many video games and films, that it should come as no surprise that Mars is the focal point of your expedition. Your ultimate goal is to somehow transform that obviously inhospitable environment into the ultimate tourist destination. Or just terraform it enough until the red sand and gravel get replaced by green pastures. As you can imagine, it’s still a Sci-Fi topic since Mars shall probably take a few more decades until humanity attempts to colonize it.
Unity Engine 5 in all its glory. The assets look great and the attention to detail is obvious. It’s a shame that some structures still have flickering textures to them, the closer you zoom in. Biggest culprit seems to be the hydroponics facilty, but the shadows cast by most buildings also seem a bit jagged around the edges. Disappointing, since playing at 4K res should have eliminated those annoying artefacts, even without further antialiasing settings. I still like the graphical diversity on most of the structures you shall build and the fact that you may rotate before placing them, improves the visual variety of the prospering colony.
The astronauts themselves can be distinguished by the different colors they wear, corresponding to their jobs. Cyan for scientists, Green for maintenance workers, Yellow for miners and a few more categories which you have to unlock later in-game. Sadly, you may not interact with the colonists at all and clicking on them is pointless. A wasted opportunity in ESC, if you ask me. They are just nameless NPCs that cannot even be issued any commands and whose AI isn’t anything noteworthy.
Soundtrack is decent, albeit repetitive. The sound effects and voice acting are pleasant enough and as a result I wasn’t entirely unimpressed. There are even a few attempts at humor through the interaction between your AI assistant, Sinclair and a few subordinates that offer you advice from time to time, in the campaign mode.
Since we’re not gonna focus only on Mars, you can actually agree with the game’s title that states “colonies” instead of just one. Your Martian exploits shall have to be supplemented by similar efforts on the mining facilties of Ceres or the colonial exploration & defense of Ganymede, from alien threats. How you design and manage each of those three colonies is up to you. In all honesty, it takes some time getting used to the building layout and the many pathfiding issues encountered by the maintenance crews you shall have to train fast enough.
These colonial structures seem even more flimsy than the ones in Red Faction: Guerrilla (I’ll let you guess where that game’s action takes place). Unless they constantly receive the attention of your astronaut grease monkeys, they will explode within 15-20 minutes. That is a serious issue considering the not so stellar (pun intended) Artificial Intelligence which has your spacemen wait in front of the very buildings they should be repairing. I had to restart the campaign and colony designing several times until I realized that the key to success, is to leave avenue-sized spaces between anything you erect.
The AI really takes away a lot of the charm from this otherwise entertaining simulation, but at least after you spend several hours perfectly planning and crafting the necessary materials, you can trigger all sorts of disasters to test your colonists’ mettle. Everything from earthquakes, deadly meteor showers and even hovering UFOs that blast several buildings in one shot. You can’t complain from a lack of activities in Earth Space Colonies since you’ll have to micromanage a lot, even if some of the crafting resources can be given an automated process of harvest and trading. It’s best to keep a constant eye and expand across the large maps, instead of building each structure close to one another. Soon enough you’ll be employing rovers and drones, instead of just relying on snail-paced astronauts.
Yes, I know what you’re thinking. The game has a few lingering technical issues and then there is also Planetbase on the Steam Store. A more polished 3D planetary colony sim that is also priced slightly higher than ESC. You have your answer right there. For better or worse, Earth Space Colonies’ is a title quite decently marketed for what it offers and its developer deserves all the support it can get since creating simulations with Unity Engine assets is neither that common or as easy as developing yet another platformer. Steam surely features enough of those already. Colonial simulations on the other hand? Keep them coming!
+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
+ Implementation of disasters and alien threats.
+ Complex colonial simulation and crafting system.
- Serious pathfinding issues for the colonists/astronauts.
- Limited sound selection.
- Several texture glitches.

Nidhogg embodies the aggressive, intoxicating thrill of competition. Through hazily defined personas and their ethereal exacting movements, a simple duel is transformed into a bustling frenzy of close saves, impossible luck, and overlapping cries of victory and defeat. It only took one match for me to fall in love with Nidhogg – to be hooked by the overwhelming energy that erupts both inside and outside the game – and hours later each round continues to bring with it that same feeling that I’m discovering something incredible for the first time and desperately need someone to share it with.
In the most concise and direct of terms, Nidhogg is a two-player fencing game which calls back to the simpler times of 80’s arcade classics like Joust and Pong, but bridges the generational gap with a precision and adrenaline that would have melted the insides of the quarter devouring machines which have grown extinct over the last 30 years. Nidhogg’s indirect heritage doesn’t define it so much as provides a sense of place for Nidhogg where so many other games are quickly lost and forgotten. Already it feels like a classic I’ve loved for years and a staple game that is kept installed eternally as part of an evergreen collection of multiplayer games.
Nidhogg works so immensely well because it’s the sort of game you stop thinking about almost immediately. Controlling your swordsman in Nidhogg is impeccably intuitive as they move and react contextually and clearly, causing you to forget about how your controlling them as you focus all your attention on what you’re actually doing. Nidhogg feels much like a spontaneous dance between two people attempting to kill each other. It’s not about executing a particular move or performing a perfect counter block, but allowing yourself to be taken by the moment as you and your opponent flow together in a blur of kicks and stabs as you fight against each other in a deadly tug of war.
The organic interplay which develops over the course of a match helps keep Nidhogg from ever feeling one-sided the way many multiplayer games do. Everything which takes place during a match is the dual result of two players colliding and reacting with one another, which forms a dynamic that feels cordial and joyful. Even during my worst matches I often found myself erupting in laugher over my own mistakes and haphazard attempts to regain ground, because even when I’m losing Nidhogg’s ridiculous pace and explosions of pixels are still ludicrously fun to be a part of.
To me the lifespan of a multiplayer game is almost entirely based on whether or not it’s enjoyable to the person losing, and I’ve never played a competitive game where me and my supposed competitor have fallen into such fits of laughter precisely because we’re losing. Nidhogg is a brilliantly tactical and engaging beast of a fighting game, but that it can also allow for a much friendlier mood and feel satisfying even when you’re outmatched is a remarkable achievement very few other games can boast.
I suppose it has to be mentioned though that there is one rather enormous qualifier to recommending Nidhogg, that being the requirement of another local player. Though there is a single player mode it feels like a lifeless shell of its multiplayer counterpart, only potentially worth venturing into as a means of practicing advanced strategies against increasingly tough AI opponents. The online mode as well, despite being fairly functional, can’t compete with the feeling of having another person in the room with you (even more so if you are playing against random players). It will suffice if you have absolutely no other options, but I found myself growing tired of it fairly quickly and wishing the person I was playing with was sitting next to me instead of on the other end of the internet.
I desperately hope that whoever is reading this won’t be hamstrung by a lack of local competition though, as with another person in the room Nidhogg is a phenomenal experience that takes only moments to sell itself but has had me repeatedly stuck in place for hours at a time, always shocked when I finally look at the clock and realize how long we’ve been playing. It’s a finely tuned machine you won’t notice and a catalyst for the delightful multiplayer mayhem that few other games have come anywhere close to matching for me.
Developer Messhof understands that multiplayer means more than putting two players on the screen; that making sure multiple people are having fun isn’t as simple as letting them play together, and that creating a friendly competition in a space where there can be only one winner is perhaps the easiest thing to screw up and the most imperative to get right. Nidhogg doesn’t assume what it’s doing is easy the way a lot of similar games seem to, but knows if it can get it right that the end result is an atmosphere and enthusiasm that can’t be matched. Wow, did they ever follow through on that one.

Nidhogg is a very simplistic representation of fencing where the goal is to reach the opponent's start point and get eaten by some giant creature presumably called the Nidhogg. The gameplay has a bit of a tug-of-war feel to it as dead players respawn a bit further back from where they were slain meaning you have to continuously battle all the way to the end without failing to win. Combat consists of moving your blade up/down, thrusting, rolling, throwing the blade, and jump kicks, combinations of which can be used to confuse and disable your opponent, setting them up for the kill. Once you kill an opponent, you gain the right of way and place him on the defensive, meaning that if you were to jump over him and continue towards his start, he would have to pursue you or allow himself to be scrolled off and respawn in front of you.
Due to the overall simplicity of the game and small number of levels, it seems to suit itself more towards multiplayer than single player which is unfortunate because the multiplayer can get downright unplayable due to latency causing your inputs to get ignored or delayed. Additionally the controls can be awkward when shifting between stances not to mention you risk throwing your sword when shifting to stab high from a mid-stance. I originally had a bit more positive of a review for this game but after re-playing it I decided to drop my recommendation since the content is really lacking and not worth the base price (or really even the sale price).

A triumph of literature, art, and music, If My Heart Had Wings takes the reader on a bold adventure of love, hope, and achievement. Telling the story through the eyes of our wounded protagonist, IMHHW delivers a heart-wrenching tale complete with loveable characters, visual beauty, and a soundtrack that ranges from bliss to despondency. The reader embarks on an emotional roller-coaster, travelling across the entire spectrum of thoughts and feelings, leaving them to ask, "How is it possible to become so attached to fictitious characters?" Much like a good novel, there is a certain melancholy readily apparent for the player when the tale is finished. "Why couldn't our story continue on forever?" Nonetheless, it is impossible not to smile meekly in hindsight at the trials and experiences of our protagonist, and wish him the best on his continued adventures in the cosmos of our imaginations.
IMHHW is, of course, a visual novel, so the reader is not expected to interract within the game beyond passing through the dialogue provided by the story. There are a few critical questions asked of the player, which influence how the game proceeds; they are rare, but their importance cannot be understated. The characters themselves are deep, well established, and loveable; in fact, it is truly a forlorn sense of disappointment when some decisions in the game must be made between them. Beyond the literary exposition provided by the game's text, the characters are also aided by a gorgeous series of artwork. I was shocked by the detail and beauty presented in the story's art, and it added an additional dimension of presentation to not only the novel itself, but also to the development of the characters. Completing the triumverate of sensation is the music provided with the game; while certain events of the game, and the accompanying artwork, provide enough of an emotional pull, the music really brings the story to another level of excellence. We laugh with the characters; we cry with the characters; and together, we are immersed into this tale of young love and boundless expectation colliding with the sometimes cruel advacement of reality. I cannot speak too much on the quality of the voice acting, because I am not a fluent speaker, but each of the voices of the characters fit into their character archetypes and gave another level of realism to them.
The story itself is very long, but not too long; never is the reader left idle in a state of boredom. I took more than ten hours to finish the story, and I am an extremely quick reader; do not make my mistake of beginning this game after 4 PM, because if you find the story as engrossing as I did you will not be able to leave until it concludes (a long time into the next day!) I daresay it may be impossible for the average reader to finish this story in one sitting; I would recommend pausing after each chapter is completed (I believe the chapters are called "Movies" in the game itself).
There are a few grammatical errors in the dialogues, which I attribute to the translation efforts for the game. Most of them aren't significant issues; in fact, I am surprised that, over the course of literally thousands of lines of dialogue, there are only several mistakes that I noticed. The only egregious mistakes I noticed were in the gender of the pronouns; twice or three times, I noticed that a character is incorectly assigned a gender pronoun. This was only a major issue in one of the lines of dialogue (because it references an unmet character, so you are confused as to that character's gender). These complaints, however, should not factor into the consideration to purchase this story.
There is only one facetious complaint I will make. The authors of this novel have constructed a tale so emotionally engrossing that it will leave you thoroughly invested into the plot's outcome. Dare I say, the worst part of this visual novel is the fact that it had to end; that I had to bid goodbye to the characters I had grown so attached to; I had to face the sudden realization that none of the events of this story had actually happened. That fundamental attribute of this novel makes it comperable to any other literay work, such as a printed novel; and, despite the fact that I am saddened to have to leave this tale behind for now, I will thoroughly recommend it to any reader who wishes to enjoy such a story.
I cannot make this final claim for certain, because I have only read through the novel once, but I am willing to believe that the ending will change fundamentally depending on the choices made in the game. If I had to guess (again, I have not played it through multiple times, so this is only conjecture), there may be as many as five endings to the game, which adds an incentive to return to the mythos of IMHHW. Thankfully, if that is the case, I am provided a reason to play through the story once again, and return to visit my fictional friends once more.
