Earth Space Colonies is a building outer world pods simulator. I recommend the game for the reason I was enjoying such things right from the Moonbase Commander (which is quite old now). But - I see some mishaps so far which is why not everyone happy about this project, so - I urge you to think before getting yourself into.
Generally, there you build some structures, and then build more. And more. Some of them are very basic for survival (giving your colonists energy, water, fresh air and so on). Other will be gathering materials for the further growing, and once you'll have enough - you get more structures to build (like bigger powerplant or even a factory to build stuff from another stuff). That's it! Build - wait to collect some materials - build further. There will be other tasks, like maintenance of your buildings in the unfriendly environment - but those elements are quite crude at moment. In theory, you can build military base, and even fight some foes there... But principally, it's about building and developing, and not raging wars. And that's a good feature! Too many games are theming bloodbaths now and too few - prosperity and well-being of the all humankind.
What I liked was the overall atmosphere, which returns us to the romantic novels, like Ray Bradbury used to write. You know, about blooming gardens on the Mars surface...
What I didn't liked is the lack of content - but the developer promises to make more. What I didn't like even more is the unfriendly interface. Considering the facts that your buildings wears off quite fast, you need to build new ones and hire maintenance stuff even faster, right? But to build new pods you'll need materials. Which of existing structures produces them - you'll learn only when click all of them. If you'll need more stuff later - again, you should manually find that specific building and make an order of producing. Even on the point, where you'll be managing dozens of materials, you'll be doing the very same basic moves by finding the producer, ordering him to do some work, and controlling all such producers... Jeez, I need "yellow pages" there!
In the bottom of the hud there are 5 special buttons to Destroy your colony. I'll not be arguing, that they can be of some use... yet I don't need them so often, even if I forget about Bradbury completely. I'd preferred to see on that place some other, much more useful elements, like special buttons for producing all aviable materials from one place!
To make a final statement, this is a building sandbox simulator, which is not quite good with the building so far... and considering its sandbox nature, not so much fun. Yet... it is still early access, so there is still hope. You know, of the better future. So far, it is just another indie game made by one man, where you need to tune with the developer's logic - like Zigfrak, for example. I'll mark it as 6/10. Certainly not a sleep-taker. Yet it deserves to be on Steam much more than many other scumming junk pieces, which people buying only for cards. As of price, though... Sol 0 is two times cheaper and delivering more fun at moment. Think, people.

Batman: Arkham City is the sequel to Batman: Arkham Asylum.
The game begins a while after Batman: Arkham Asylum. Arkham City is a big section of Gotham City which has been turned into a large-scale prison for its criminals, all constructed by Hugo Strange. Very early in the game Bruce Wayne is campaigning to demolish the institution when he himself is incarcerated under Strange's orders.
While Strange prepares to commence "Protocol 10", Wayne obtains his equipment via airdrop from Alfred, allowing him to become Batman. Now it is up to him to find out what Protocol 10 is. Along the way he fights several famous villains, among them Joker, Riddler, Penguin and Two-Face.
The story is pretty well done. Many recognizable characters on both sides of the Batman mythos are along for the ride.
Batman: Arkham City plays and controls much like Arkham Asylum. But one thing you will notice is that the game takes place in an open city, rather than in a single area. Arkham Asylum was by no means a small game, but in Arkham City the player is able to get the full Batman experience by gliding around the city in a much larger scale.
The combat system is pretty much the same as in previous game. You punch, counter, and use gadgets and finishing moves to subdue large amounts of enemies.
Besides of the main story and side quests you also have a lot of other stuff to do like solving Riddler secrets, Catwoman Missions, challenge maps and more. This game will last you a long time if you are trying to go for 100% completion.
The graphics are stunning and all the characters look really good. Faces and facial expressions are brilliantly made.
The soundtrack is literally Hollywood movie quality. The voice acting is incredible and everything else sounds great as well.
Batman: Arkham City is a great experience for anyone who likes Batman or who wants to discover his universe. It is definitely worth to buy and to play.

You're probably here looking answers to the question: "Did it make you cry?"
I can only speak for myself, but the answer is yes, although not as much as To the Moon did. Keep in mind, however, that I appreciate these games not just for being emotional, but because they give insight into people's inner selves and desires, what makes us what we are, and how complicated the sum of what makes us, 'us', is.
And approaching Finding Paradise from this direction, I can say it's a great success like its predecessor was.
Everything about Finding Paradise is amplified and refined compared to To the Moon. Its visuals are prettier and more detailed, with more expressive and animated character sprites that really bring the world to life. Soundtrack is amazing, and rearranged leitmotifs from To the Moon makes me feel at home, being in the company of the doctors.
Storyline is also expanded: intrique is built up very well, and there's more story happening outside the actual job this time around. The story beats feel familiar, while also building up its mystery in a less straightforward, more ambiguous manner. It isn't totally unpredictable, but Kan Gao has certainly improved in making things have more than meets the eye.
While the good parts of To the Moon are amplified, the same applies to the flip side. There are still some tonal inconsistencies, accompanied by Watts' signature video game riffing. At one point it goes to new heights in a very jarring way that feels completely redundant. The puzzle-solving gameplay is still just kind of there, but it doesn't get in the way of the narrative, so I digress. There's also some missed potential with the game's themes, but I won't go in-depth with it. Most of my issues with the narrative cluster in the final act of the game, so they're not persistent problems, but they keep me from singing very high praises of the game.
In the end I still think Finding Paradise stands tall next to To the Moon, even if it might not gain the same cult status. If you have any love for To the Moon or an appreciation for video game narratives, don't miss out.
It's definitely a worthy experience and a legitimate expansion of the original's worldbuilding and ethical musings.

Occasionally, there are corny scenes, and one felt a bit longer than I'd like (thanks a lot Neil). I would say that A Bird Story is an important part of understanding the patient. It hints at the patient's secret more than one might think.
Although the game is slightly shorter than To the Moon, it is just as meaningful, or more meaningful for those who can relate to Finding Paradise. I enjoyed it all the way through, despite one of Neil's scene and the cliffhanger.

Ok, so I've finally played this game after several months in my library. First, quick and dirty: it's hard. I'm a veteran of stealth games since the first Metal Gear Solid, Splinter Cell, and Hitman and I have gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by this game. It is fair, however: the controls are fairly expressive and the responsive--and a lot of the aspects that make it difficult are truly beneficial to the experience: observant enemies, intricate, complicated levels, a "sound" mechanic beyond how gentle you are with the stick (land on carpets for less sound, debris and odds and ends scattered around to accidentally kick) and a good amount of differentiation between enemy types can be quite surprising.
On the bad-hard side, the jumping is not very polished, which you'll be doing a lot of. You've got sticky grip to edges, and specific environment points to jump at and... that's about it. It's responsive, but kind of violent and difficult to control. Which is ok for a platformer but less ok for a control-fest like a stealth game, where precision is pretty important. Related, the hanging system is not developed. It's quite difficult to drop into a ledge grab, you have to edge off the ledge until you fall and then it's a mysterious 80% of grabbing it. You can move back and forth, but not around corners while hanging, and if ANYTHING disrupts the rail, there's not way to jump across or even just reach. It's a little frustrating.
Little things I liked: the clone mechanic, which seems like it could be a huge game changer that even after 10 hours I haven't mastered, and the skillpoint-based growth system. Also the first game I've played where poisoning food or water sources really feels rewarding--you gotta work hard to get in there, but it pays off. All the components feel pretty rewarding, actually. Even resource management--I'm a hoarder in games, I always think "can't use this here, it'll be useful somewhere else" until some boss or section where realize I'm almost done and I could actually settle down and become and NPC shopkeeper for the next hero that comes along I have some many items, so I spend a bunch to just cheese through. In Styx, I really did need to make hard decisions about items. Eg: there's a guard with an amber potion on his belt and I have almost no amber left and only one in stock-- but getting it off him involves a series of intricate moves down the corridor, including spending at least a sandball to distract him, and like six save reloads to do it perfectly to leave unseen--just for the item so that down the line somewhere I can get through a pair of well-positioned guards with invisibility instead of searching for another method.
Minor annoyances: the collecting. Urg. There's a "Sigil" which you earn by collecting all of the little tokens in each stage--and results in skill points, so you have some skin in the game. There are an unfriendly amound of sigils in some seriously unfriendly places, and you need to get the full set to get anything. Can be 30-40 in a level, tiny little gold tokens lying on tables, on top of pipes, occasionally even more eccentric places. An enormous pain for very little pay-off. Would have much prefered if they were used to buy something so you didn't need to comb the whole level with a fine toothed comb to get a relatively small amound of skill points. Miss one, no sigil, and the next replay everything resets.
Also, the levels are SUPER LONG. They're broken into numbered chunks but the first time playing through it will take HOURS to get back to your base. A speed run (another "sigil") is 25 minutes if you know exactly where you're going. That's not bad, necessarily, but it can be exhausting. Especially because this is definitely a "just one more section, just one more area" kind of game. They go down like popcorn. Well, like popcorn kernals because they are ♥♥♥♥ing hard, but still.
THE SEXY TAKEAWAY: Styx teaches you to savor little victories and eat a lot of defeat. It puts you in enormous, gorgeous set pieces and says "make that your home and learn to live in it so deeply that you can move unseen and unheard and prove to your victims that their house was never their own, it was just waiting for you to find it." A lot of games talk in grandiose terms, "bust into a prison! steal his keys! plan your escape!" and then show you a movie of someone else doing it. Styx doesn't gild the lily at all, just "Get in there and do it," and two hours later after your crawled through♥♥♥♥♥♥and killed with every desperate means you can eek out and slunk through the shadows and climbed up crumbling masonry and cowered in what you desperately hoped would be an unseen cranny, you KNOW what it is to break into a prison, to take those keys, to escape and you ♥♥♥♥ING did it and you're the greatest thief there ever was.
I recommend it.

This is a great game. Nidhogg is a game where you battle an opponent by sword fighting, or fist fighting. First off, I really like this games controls. You can roll, duck, wallrun, jump, divekick, throw your sword and all sorts of things using a joystick, and only two buttons. Second reason why I reccomend this game is that the local multiplayer (keep in mind I said local) is really fun to play with a friend. Third reason why I reccomend this game is that the music is well done, and it's very unique in its own way. Now, onto the cons. This game has a online multiplayer, which is what you basically play after beating the game. The problem with it is that there is no one ever playing multiplayer to match up with. If you do, sometimes you have a LOT of control lag, and that is a REALLY horrid thing because you need precice controls to even play the game, so there is a big of disadvantage to you. Another thing why this game lacks, not enough content. This is a very simple game, and there is nothing much to it. The most content you will get out of it would be in the local multiplayer, where you can modify the game rules. But, it's not the same as like, Super Smash Bros, where you can have an overwhelming amount of rule changing, its more fun stuff, like baby mode, or speed trails. If there were more options in the multiplayer, or more content overall, that would sit in my stomach better. EDIT: I have played a bit of the Steam configuration of the game, and I have decided that I cannot recommend the game in its current state. The review below assumes you have fully modded the game with the restoration patch. This review, and the unrecommendation, assume the game as Steam installs it. I cannot recommend a game that requires modding to be decent.
The censoring is not the issue. I don't really have a problem of the removal of the sex scenes. I have read that some of the story is butchered a bit to avoid such scenes, but I haven't actually reached that point. I don't need to, to update this review.
The problem is the translation. It isn't as halting and awkward as I was lead to believe (though I'm only a few days into the game at this point), but there are some truly glaring errors in the translation.
The worst example is the use of the word "grade" where they ought to be using the word "year". For instance, there is a part where the main character and his friend are discussing the awesome time the main character took third in a bicycle race when he was in "first grade". I'm a great big weeaboo, so I know what they were trying to say: his first year at that school (likely fourteen or fifteen years old). But it just brings to mind the sight of a teenage guy still proud about how his athletic career peaked at six years of age.
Then there's the girl at the dorm, who is apparently the oldest one there. She's in fourth grade, apparently. (I swear, officer, she didn't look that young!) Of course, that means she's in her fourth year of this specialist high school (most Japanese high schools only go three years). Severely problematic for someone who's not already deep in the fan community.
A lesser issue I'd like MoeNovel to revisit is the attempt to translate "sempai" and "kohai". This translation uses the word "senior" and "junior", respectively, in contexts that would suggest to an American reader that they are in their third and fourth year at the school, when it reality it just means one is older than the other. Current practice is to leave those words untranslated (as they have no English equivalent), and just trust that the information is readily availble, because it is.
Finally, most of the reviews it will complain to the swallowtail route. When I wrote the part of before that, I'm for about playing in the middle of the Asaruto, and the translation was not great. But I have to play the final in the Ageha route, someone, translated into Japan took the English Google again, is the it through to it ran Such translated it I feel. Japanese, and back again.
Thus, I cannot recommend the game in its current state. But if you want to play it, read the review below, and then look for installation instructions for the Restoration Patch.
It took me a while to decide whether or not I was going to recommend this game. On the one hand, the story was fun and rewarding. On the other hand, it isn't "gamelike" enough. Just before this one, I played Clannad; this is no Clannad.
To be honest, this would, in my opinion, make a better manga than visual novel. There are a few places where the soundtrack and visual effects add to the experience, but for the most part, the entire story could be conveyed well through images on a page. The alternate stories are few enough, and the choices needed to choose between those stories few enough, that simply releasing an alternate story in another volume would work.
That said, it was a great story, and given that I got it for $4.94 (on sale as of this writing), the only real expense was the time. Visual novels generally aren't for busy people, I don't think, but I'd say it was worth my time.
A word about the Restoration Patch. I decided to have the entire game here for my first playthrough, and so I have the patch installed. This restores the nudity... full (slightly censored) nudity, and full-on sex scenes. I plan to play through the Korori route a second time with the game at Steam's standard configuration and edit this later on, to see the differences and edit this review to give my own analysis of the differences between the two. That said... they're pretty hot.
So if you've got a lot of time on your hands and you don't have a manga you'd rather put a few bucks toward, I can recommend If My Heart Had Wings. As to the soundtrack, it doesn't cost that much more, but while there are a few decent tracks, it's mostly what I would call "below par" where video game music is concerned. If you need to not spend a couple extra bucks, you can safely pass it up.

Quick Review December 2017:


The controls and keybindings are decent. I kept wishing for a mix of the two schemes that were proposed. But overall, they are good enough for casual players. "Competitive" players might want to use their own keybinds however.
Nothing serious here to mention. The quality of the soundtrack is great. A bit repetitive sometimes, but it's manageable. The voice acting is also pretty solid. Every lines are there and well acted. Some NPCs might sound a bit "unrealistic" sometimes. But very rarely.
The game is gorgeous. It is impressive actually. Though you will need a pretty good computer in order to run the game maxed out. The shadows are incredibly demanding. If you want to play this game competitively, you might want to consider keeping the graphic settings lower. But really, it's a beautiful game.
While I did love the overall game, I think the RTS part of the game is lacking. The RPG side is solid if you ask me, but the RTS one is very "thin". Which is quite a big deal considering the multiplayer is mostly RTS. Campaign wise, I played the game on the hardest difficulty and had a fun time with it. Although every RTS missions ended up by me rushing straight to the capital center to stop the endless attacks coming from everywhere. But as I said, it was a pleasure to play!
The story is excellent. I definitely did not expect the game to be this long and well written. It reminded me of Dragon Age Origins at times. Unfortunately, the game needs optimization really bad. The FPS drop like crazy from time to time for no reasons. And also the camera made me dizzy sometimes. Especially in the first areas of the game. And well, the game's buggy sometimes unfortunately. Can't click on certain NPCs, enemies not spawning, quest items not dropping, chests unopenable. Now this might seem a lot, but it's not that bad. Not anymore atleast.
Overall this game shocked me! I was not expecting much from it at first. I was thinking the campaign would last about 10 hours and I would be done, but it's actually a pretty long a game! Which is a very good thing for me. The RPG side of the feels really good. It actually feels like Pillars of Eternity, Baldur's Gate, Tyranny, etc. The RTS side however... Meh, It's decent enough to be fun and actually be an RTS. But it's missing things in order to be great. The story is great, especially if you are an old veteran of the old Spellforce games. It really deepens the lore of Spellforce. Otherwise, do keep in mind that the game needs optimization and is buggy at times.

Cricket Captain 2015, the same game every year with given a tiny application of makeup and making no progress whatsoever.
The thing is, Cricket Captain is basically a Cricket Manager game, minus 90% of management features that are needed to make the game interesting. But let me get the pro's out of the way with first;
The match engine is brilliant, the statistical information available to the player is brilliant. The one-day and 20-20 match engines have been tweaked and are better than previous instalments. Graphics have finally gotten a facelift, but animations remain the same as in previous versions pretty much, thus edges mostly go in the same areas and not always to shots that make sense.
To demonstrate the laziness; the animations for the umpires to signal 'byes' is the real life signal for leg byes, this has been like this for the past three or four instalments, it can't be that hard to fix surely?
Outside of the match engine, there is almost nothing for an aspiring manager to do. Yeah, there is team building from the transfer market, and the promotion of youth players. You also get to adjust the budgets a little, but the initial funding doesn't change (aside from prize money), there's no opportunity to build the club up as you become more successful. There's no chance to look more in depth at a youth or reserve team, and you can't hire a specific number of physios or coaches. Training is limited, staff numbers are linked to the budget but never anymore than numbers rather than actual personalities themselves - a batting coach who is aggressive for example, or a bowling coach with his own philosophy - nope, they're just generic numbers.
And that, really is the problem with the game. It's a spreadsheet game, with all your time spent looking at statistical averages. Best batsman number 1 will always be replaced by generic youth product number 51, because there are no personalities in the game, nothing to indicate ability (outside of averages), nothing to indicate talent (outside of averages) because there's no staff to talk to, no youth team to develop and team to mould in line with bigger games such as Football Manager.
The whole thing, is just a numbers game without any real flavour to it. The hardcore fans and cricket nuts will pick it up as usual, but aside from reading the numbers and possibly playing around with tactics in the admittedly decent match engine there's nothing outside to keep things interesting, no media, no discussions, no personalities, training events or anything that adds spark and interest. Nothing but your imagination and the bland numbers popping up as each match goes by.
For a series that has been around for a long while now, they really need to get with the times and produce something more than a match engine.

I've played every Cricket Captain game since it's inception many years ago and I've thoroughly enjoyed the series.  I probably don't need to get each edition as some have been nothing more than a databse update with a few minor additions, but this is clearly the best cricket management game on the market.  Nothing comes close.
So should you buy it?  The short answer is yes.  The three major leagues in England, India and Australia are all well covered and there are plenty of options to play both in and out of the game.  You can be a hands on coach and play every ball, go a little less with every over or even sim through games you don't feel you need to play.  It really is good stuff and you can get hours of enjoyment out of it.  With a few seasons under my belt I've been able to build a very handy side in all three formats as the contract system works well.
There are, however, a few things that need to be mentioned that haven't been fixed in years.
1. - There is no true way to see just how good a player is or the potential they have.  The only way you can tell is at the end of the season when you sign their contract - if they ask for a higher amount (eg. above $50,000) then you can be assured you are generally getting a good player.  However outside of this it's hit and miss.  I've signed players for big bucks that have been a huge disappointement.  Why?  I don't really know.  Adding in a system like this would be sensational and help decide the make up of your team better.
2. - There are some incosistencies with the AI.  There seem to be far too many LBW's and often when you change a batsman's aggressiveness they can go out in the next over.  The AI is generally pretty good but be prepared for the odd frustration here and there.
3. - The training system is only decent.  There are plenty of options to choose from but there is no way to tell how well things are working.  This ties into being able to see how good a player is or the potential of how good they CAN be with the right training.  Fixing this would be excellent.
Outside of those criticism's this is an excellent game and if you can sink some time into it you'll thoroughly enjoy it.

Sure, nothing will ever be To The Moon. But nothing else needs to be To The Moon.  We've experienced it and grown from it. It's done its job.
This game is the natural progression from that. While in some ways To The Moon taught us about love and finding strength in someone else, Finding Paradise shows us the importance of loving yourself and finding strength within, along with other lessons about life, regrets, and what-ifs.
Of course I could just be taking out of my♥♥♥♥♥here, but that's what I get from it. Maybe you'll get something completely different.
Wherever you are in your life, these games speak to you in ways that other games can't.

So much more.

Simple Rockets is a rather straightforward game, which I picked up for about $8.00 USD during the steam summer sale. A steam port of a mobile game, the game title is quite accurate. You assemble and launch rockets using in a 2D world with a basic physics model and interface. It actively pays homage to KSP, which the author explicitly credits for some inspiration, and the build interface in particular is quite reminiscent of it.
That said, one should not expect the same level of detail as one would from KSP. There is a limited selection of components, the physics model is quite simple, and the interface is quite barebones, having been designed for use on phones and tablets. Manuever plotting doesn't quite exist, which can make it somewhat hit or miss. The upside, however, is that it is simple enough to get into, and there is no resource, part, or limits other the physics themselves, so messing up a launch won't set you back anything other than time.
Which is part of the fun, after all, watching your contraptions randomly explode into a billion pieces. It does come with some missions, but they are mostly for training and orientation. The sandbox mode is a welcome departure rom KSP, in that it allows you to build and launch from any planet.
It could use some additional polish, however that may not be plausible unless the developer is willing to make a PC only game version. In addition to aforementioned manuever plotting, the game currently lacksmany components, and adding RCS components to your vehicles can be a pain as there is no way to show the center of gravity for vehicles. The lack of these features doesn't detract from the game or its pricetag, however, so you can get by without them.
Overall, I would give this game a 7.5 out of 10, rating it as a good way to play away an afternoon, thus passing the movie ticket test.

Earth Space Colonies is a space colony management game developed and published by Persona and Pixel Studio. The game itself is similar to Planetbase and Sol 0: Mars Colonization. At first glance Earth Space Colonies looked quite interesting to me since I haven’t really played a management game for quite a while, especially a space one. That said, I was somewhat drawn out due to the graphics because from the screenshots on the Steam Store page, it looked like a game for mobile devices but once I was inside the game, it wasn’t that bad and I grew fond of them after a while.
Right now the point of the game is pretty simple, even though, from what I’ve played I still couldn’t figure out if what I’ve gone through was part of the tutorial or if there was no tutorial at all. What I can say is that you always have atleast one objective given to you by one or more of the game’s characters and that is one of things that interests me most in Earth Space Colonies. The fact that it has characters and a narrative driven story, which I assume is still being worked on. According to the developers, the game will have three different campaigns and I only played one of them.
After around four hours of gameplay, I still have mixed feelings about Earth Space Colonies but I can say for sure that the game has the potential to become a very good game. But, right now I feel like it still needs some work, optimizing the AI and polishing the interface, because I can imagine some people would get somewhat confused while playing it at the moment since it can be somewhat unintuitive.
That said, I do think the game might be worth your time if you’re into space exploration or if you’re just a fan of management games in general with a little bit of micromanagement thrown into the mix . The three different campaigns make the overall game much more interesting Since each one of them focuses on different aspects,
Unlike other games from this genre, in Earth Space Colonies you always have some sort of guidance throughout the game, the objectives. These help you progress not only on game mechanics and unlocking new craftable items and resources but also allow you to progress through the story.
So, if you like what I mentioned and if the game interests you, I say go for it. It seems the developers are currently working on the pathfinding AI and hopefully, soon enough, all campaigns will be complete.

Where he meets up with old childhood friends, and meets new friends, one of them being Kotori Habane, a beautiful, wheelchair bound girl.
The general story of the game is that Aoi and friends wants to fly above the clouds in what is called a glider.
As I don't want to spoil anything I will leave it at that.
If you do want to know everything that this game offers, you'll have to play it yourself, but I can assure you, any fans of Visual Novels will
be disappointed, people new to Visual Novels will likely love it aswell.
Characters are great, they have personality, and you get to see them grow up emotionally as you progress, it's a joy to play through this, just the characters make it a great VN.
The voice actors that make the characters are superb, people who have played their fair share of VN's or watched a lot of anime will likely recognize the voices.
Soundtrack is a joy listen to, this is one of the few VN's where I have the background music actually playing, the tunes that usually plays are soothing and easy to listen to while reading and listening to the voice actors.
Artstyle aswell, the use of CG (Computer Graphics) for certain scenes doesn't intrude at all like CG often does, though I can't say it looks really good either.
Artstyle for backgrounds, characters and scene pictures are great however.
Sadly, like with everything, a game always has their downsides.
Rest assure that in the case of this game, it's not the games fault, rather, it's the poor translation.
If you know Japanese there's actually some pretty comedic moments, laugh at how bad they translated this.
If you don't know Japanese then sadly, there's gonna be scenes where you might be lost.
This isn't the worst translation I've seen, but sadly it's up there.
Some scenes are so poorly translated that what is written makes 0 sense.
Personally I'm fine, as I can understand what the girls say most the time, but the main character is silent, making some scenes just laughably bad.
Therefore, do I recommend this game? Hell yes, all my yes, it's an adorable story and the characters just as adorable.
But sadly, due the the poor translation, it could be hard for some to follow at times.
It's still playable, a lot of the translation is fine, but a re-translation project is in the works by fans of the game so either play now and re-play it (totally worth doing) once the re-translation is finished, or wait for the re-translation project to finish, and buy it then.
So, skip the Sakura games and pick this up, this game is worth your money far more than all of them combined.

Very buggy but they're releasing patches frequently. On my second playthrough I'm noticing a huge difference. The Gameplay is a pretty unique combination of a well thought out RTS and a pretty good RPG. Together these offer a very interesting game. Many RTS these days don't put much thought into the key element of RTS gameplay which is the economy and logistics. Spellforce 3's Logistics system is amazing. Want to build something accross the map from your base? You have to cart the resources over there to do it and if your carts are attacked on the way you lose the resources. My suspension of disbelief is not broken by the way you use resources in this game unlike nearly every other RTS title in existence. I think the factions could be a bit more diverse in how they fight though and I'm hoping to see more factions in the future.  I'm really glad this game is a prequel because I've tried to play the previous games in the series and the first one suffers from some horrifying voice acting and repetive gameplay. The second seems to be allergic to my computer. So yeah I'm really glad to not need the context of the first two games to get the third.

I've played Life is Feudal and pretty much every other MMO out there since 2001. Gloria Victis has promise but not polish.  I love the focus on realism (although "realism" is limited. For example your inventory is HUGE and in no way realistic. But the combat physics are realistic.)
Now that there is a decent population in the game, I'm excted to see how territory control will look and how big the batles will be. The PVP in this game is really quite fun and rewarding and the devs are always tweaking it and improving it.  But "lone wolf" pvp will be tough I think unless you're incredibly talented and resourceful (managing stamina and hp regen is a HUGE thing in PVP). There is a sense that something is really on the line when you go out into the world because you can be killed and looted, but you could also kill and loot others.
speaking of looting. Let me explain:
It's a PARTIAL LOOT SYSTEM. This means that there is a 30 second window after someone dies in which they can be looted (so if you're fighting nearby your friend who dies, if you can keep the enemy off of him for that time period, he won't get looted at all!). If they are looted in that time, the person looting  has only a certain number of points they can "Spend" looting stuff off the dead player. So let's say the player has 48 points worth of stuff on him and you have 10 points to spend. You see how they would not be able to take all your stuff? Also only ONE PERSON CAN LOOT A BODY. So no loot trains. I feel like this is a really fantastic system to keep PVPers happy by providing incentive for PVP and to keep other players happy knowing that they won't lose all their stuff. Also, can't loot money at all.
PVE is better than in some games because the devs are working on making the AI for mobs more intelligent. They aren't super intelligent right now, and there are no ranged mobs, but I'm looking forward to Darkfall-esque mobs that really move almost like players. There is some differentiation in them now and I'm excited for that to grow. Ther are some real challenges out in the wilds too. Bosses and group and camps you can take on.
I think my favorite thing about the game is that it is a true MMO and the servers are not run by GMs who can ban you if you kill them (what up Life is Feudal).
Right now all characters can play on all servers and your bank is global which makes things a LOT easier in terms of keeping up with your friends. In the future, the devs are looking to have 1 global server as the land mass increases. you should see the ful map for this game! It's like 100x as big as the map we have now and is a bastartized version of Europe.
The game looks nice at highest settings and I enjoy the ambience of the music and atmosphere.
I love the crafting system. Normally I'm more of a gatherer than a crafter, but man, something about this gmae makes me want to craft. It's a very detailed system and I found myself writing things down to keep track of the flow of component parts to make things. It can be overwhelming if you just look at the crafting menu because it does NOT hold your hand, but it is actually fairly intuitive and is based on (apparently) real life midieval craftmanship.
Looking forward to supporting the game as it develops, and just since I've been playing the past couple months there have been HUGE changes for the better. These devs are for real and they are making a great little game.

Edit: No matter what I write, I know I cannot do this game justice just by my own words, because it's just that great. But still, I really feel like I should at least give an analysis/comparison of this, especially for the sake of people who have previously played To The Moon. Keep in mind that this will contain no spoilers.
In To The Moon, the feeling of sadness is more distributed throughout the whole series kind of equally, by that I mean the parts where you travel from memory to memory, each memory had it's own "aww" moment that makes you feel sad, if that makes any sense to you.
In Finding Paradise, the sad parts are more isolated from the happier ones.
To The Moon had a great sense of humor, but in Finding Paradise you'll probably see yourself laughing even more often. Yeah, I guess this game has more parts that are funny than parts that are tragic compared to To The Moon. But still reminding you, both are pretty sappy stories.
A finale with a great tearjerker potential -> checked. Exists in both games.
Both games have this mystery surrounding the patients at the start of the game. While playing Finding Paradise, even though you'll find yourself scratching your head and trying to come up with many different possibilities and scenarios in your head early on, but soon you'll probably guess what is going on before the game tells straight to your face. To the Moon nailed the mystery part much better and was much harder to predict, at least that's my opinion of it.
I know very few people didn't enjoy To The Moon as much for it being "too pretentious". While I don't share their sentiments (I liked To The Moon very much), I still can see where they are coming from. I mean, 8 year old children philosophizing about the meaning of stars and the loneliness and stuff, and a main character whose emotions and actions are incredibly hard to understand (River).
Finding Paradise keeps it less pretentious in that aspect, while not losing any depth. For most of the time, you will understand the actions and motivations of all characters involved, and it will make sense.
The patient in Finding Paradise has a much more interesting character and a great sense of humor compared to Johnny from To The Moon (at least in my opinion :P )
Finding Paradise has more "gameplay" moments, though I personally found that a little bit too distracting from the main story, even though they were generally comedic moments more than anything, take this as however you will.
How could I forget this? This should go without saying anyways. Both have equally amazing, hauntingly beautiful soundtrack.
All in all, there's no reason you wouldn't love this if you loved To The Moon. Both are very great, and a must play if you are into story driven indie games.

I feel as though it's safe to say that
has been highly anticipated for a number of years. For me, I've waited 3 years and I can honestly say it did
leave me disappointed.
may be the second episode of the
... series...? but it's able to function as a standalone title. There are a handful of jokes that might go over your head if you haven't played the first installment (I'm looking at you, squirrel), but nothing that takes away from the enjoyment of the game. In fact, you have the choice of skipping through the dialogue of how the Sigmund Corp. works if you don't want or don't need it. If you have played it before, you'll definitely get a few extra laughs out of the dialogue and one or two familiar locations.
I initially thought the story was going to be predictable, but boy was I wrong. About halfway through the game, I sat there proudly thinking I'd solved the problem and was just waiting for Neil and Eva to confirm everything for me. Needless to say, they did not. In fact, the only thing I was able to guess correctly was the significance of the green book. I truly appreciated the game's ability to keep me guessing; I kept flipflopping between what I thought was actually going on with the technology, and with Colin's memories.
I also found the story narrative to be believable. It was able to maintain its futuristic elements while still somehow being grounded firmly in reality, especially the emotional aspects of the game. I recall a lot of negative criticism on Neil's poor comedic timing in the first installment, and I think that's been addressed here. The humor is appropriate and we're able to appreciate the more somber scenes without interruption from jokes or puns. Moreover, the dialogue itself feels a more natural and not quite as stilted as it sometimes came off in the first installment.
Even though I loved
, I was worried that a similar gameplay idea would make the game stale or boring, but thankfully that's not the case. You still have to find mementos, but breaking the barrier is a bit easier (and more challenging, depending). The patient is a unique individual, which also helps the games from being too similar.
One more gameplay aspect is the idea of choice. While the opportunities to make decisions are few in number, they are, for the most part, pretty meaningful. They allow the player to see the morality of Neil and Eva, especially Neil who has opportunities to break protocol and handles such times in a unique manner.
As expected, the music was phenomenal. I enjoyed the remixes of familiar songs from
, but the new songs were just as amazing. They all fit the mood and the settings, and for those who have played the first game the music will definitely be nostalgic. As I expected, Laura Shigihara made a return to sing another beautiful piece.
Overall, I feel this game is an absolute gem. It's reasonably priced for a game that's a little over 5 hours long with decent replayability, and if you enjoyed
you'll probably enjoy
. While I'm glad my 3 year wait didn't end in disappointment, I'm definitely not looking forward to a years long wait for the next installment.

Anyhow, to the review. As others have said this is like KSP but in 2D. Prior to obtaining this game on Steam I have played this game for several months off and on.  This is probably among my top few favorite games.  I would endorse this without reservation and encourage it for everyone.
Although this game couldn't be said to have the best graphics of any space game, I beleive it reasonable to claim that this has some of the best and simplest gameplay of all realistic space games.  It is easiest to learn and has a sprawling potential for the imaginative soul who loves to understand how spaceflight really works.
This game puts real spaceflight physics (or a reasonable facsimile) into a sidescrolling 2d solar system and allows one to design rocket ships of all sorts and sizes and shapes using components that lock together.  If one builds their rocket ship correctly and it does not explode (a good portion of the pleasure in starting out in the game, as I recall, is building one ship after another and seeing all the things that lead to catastrophic failure and the presumed death of any presumably present pilots in a firey explosion) then one can go into orbit (whatever orbit one choses), fly to other planets or the sun (if one builds enough rocket stages to change one's velocity appropriately) and land on them with parachutes and rockets and sometimes water landings).
There are in-game instructions for how to manage various feats and there are challenges in the game to keep one interested.  I have completed all but one of those challenges.
There are mods for this game--at least the non-steam version--but they do not appear to be entirely compatible with the latest update.  I look forward to the possibility of mods for this game through Steam.
I have seen in various updates an improvement in the types of ship components available and I always hope for more to become available.
This game is endorsed by the website AtomicRockets and I think that is a strong endorsement as they validly criticize so much that is presented as science fiction.  I would endorse this without reservation and encourage it for everyone.
The planets are out there in this game and only in understanding what it really takes to get to the planets in our solar system can one truly appreciate the value and accomplishment of the real space missions that have been acheived.

E.Y.E.: Divine Cybermancy is a game created by Streum On Studio, their first full release. The aesthetics and story are heavily designed around Streum On's old RPG "AVA" from 1998, a derivative tabletop game based on Warhammer 40k. The game's internal operations reflect upon this, as the damage of weapons and chance of a player succeeding with certain skills is directly tied to the stats from this original system. E.Y.E. is self-described by Streum On as an experience akin to the original Deus Ex, integrating the styles and themes of Warhammer 40k and Ghost in the Shell. The game runs off a heavily modified Source Engine, though the stylizing makes it very hard to tell sometimes.
I find it very difficult to properly recommend E.Y.E. objectively. For all intents and purposes, it should be a bad game for its huge array of faults. Missions can be constantly broken by player interactions with the AI, meaning that someone has to die enough times to fail the mission, costing EXP (there is no way to stop someone from killing mission-essential characters, and no kick system). There are weapons immediately available in the early game that directly outclass others available, rendering them useless. Learning how to do basic functions of the game -even with its in-game video guide- absolutely requires an external guide/wiki do properly explain the complexities of the simplest actions. The translation of the game itself is incredibly rough and messy. High level players are essentially able to teleport inside lower level ones and instantly kill them with a high change for fatal wounds. The fatal wounds system (taking permanent stat disadvantages for strange deaths) allows for a completely overpowered method of leveling in the late game, though the chance of even doing this is barred behind a multi hundred thousand brouzouf research tree. Even the main character himself acknowledges that "nothing makes any sense".
E.Y.E. is a total and absolute hellscape of a game. It is madness incarnate. But for myself, and many others, that's what makes it such an incredible and almost mantric experience. No single aspect of the game excels in any real sense, but the sum of these many and very disjointed parts creates one of the most insane games available on the market today.
At its core, E.Y.E. is essentially the midpoint between Deus Ex, Half Life 2, and a Warhammer 40k tabletop game. Sword and gun combat dominates most of the game, and two subsystems -CyberTech implants and PSI powers- allow for a mix of play styles. There is also a very strange hacking subsystem that functions as a real-time action menu minigame against the defending AI, almost like a text-based Final Fantasy battle. All of these elements allow for a multitude of different builds; a sniper that uses Targeting System to take down his foes without a scope while moving, a lightweight shotgun-rogue that can jump high into the air to get behind enemies, a Priest-warrior that has completely abandoned guns in favor of PSI powers that turn enemies into monsters and a sword that explodes upon contact, a hacker that sits in a corner and takes over enemy AI, etc. The game itself has a large degree of replayability, especially considering that it needs to be beaten in 4 unique ways to unlock its true ending.
However, building towards these playstyles is dependent upon three different in-game subsystems that control stats. First, there is standard leveling, capped at 250 (though most end-game builds are possible by level 50). Then, there is a procedurally-blocked array of CyberTech implants that also directly effect stats and actions, though it is sectioned off by the third subsystem, the research tree. The research tree itself is its own independent function that requires unique human enemy drops as a base, and slowly increases in expensiveness and time to achieve the highest-tier items (Metastreumonic Complimentarity, the highest possible research besides Necrocybermancy, takes 50 days to research, the real world equivalent of 3.75 hours). In all honesty, all builds gravitate at high levels towards a god-like character that can spam high-tier instant-death PSI powers, though even getting to this point can be difficult.
E.Y.E. is primarily progressed through a main, mission-controlled storyline (which can be completed in SP or co-op). In E.Y.E., you play as an amnesiatic member of of the Culter Dei, one of the two subsections of E.Y.E., a religious warrior-priest collective that are part of the larger Secreta Secretorum, who are trying to fight the Federation (an oppresive military regime), who are all trying to fight the Metastreumonic Force, an enigmatic energy that is able to create monsters from nothing. Also, the Culter Dei hate the Jian Shang Di. There is no real reason for this, and your experience will be a lot less confusing if you just acknowledge this and move on.
The story itself is just as a confusion mess as the gameplay can be. Missions are played chronologically out of order, individuals that die in one will be present in another, and practically nothing is explained. In the fair defense of E.Y.E., the true ending of the game somewhat justifies this.
Aside from the main narrative, it is possible to revisit old missions, either via the Temple HQ, or via special dedicated online servers that cyclically run random missions. Among the other game types are Battle Royale, TDM, and a very strange CTF-like gamemode; each will restrict a player's weapons, stats, abilities, and implants, maintaining some degree of balance. By far the most populated games are individual servers running through the entire E.Y.E. campaign. The community for the game is extremely small, never amounting to higher than 20 people playing at any given time, save after Steam sales (this is mostly due to the high barrier to entry and generally confusing mess E.Y.E. can be for a new player).
My best piece of advice for a new player is to religiously read and consult guides if you're confused. Learn how fatal wounds work before you even get them. Read the research tree and footnotes to understand how important it is. Get the Bearkiller before Mars. Always make sure your legs are okay. Don't make waves.
As I mentioned before, I have a lot of difficulty recommending E.Y.E. despite the fact that I enjoyed it so much. Strangely enough, the game reminds me of the old PS1 game Drakengard in this respect. Nothing makes sense. Subsystems are confusing and downright undocumented in some cases. The presentation for the game is either confusing or completely non-existent occasionally. Every aspect of the game clashes with another, creating a confusing, difficult, and unexplained mess.
But all of this unyielding chaos comes together to make one of the most insane and interesting games I've ever played.

Earth Space Colonies, developed and published by Persona and Pixel Studio, is a Steam Early Access title that fits within the resource management simulation-strategy genre. The ultimate object of the game is to terraform space colonies and to save the human race. The first planet that you have to work your magic on is Mars. You have been selected to create the first self-sustaining colony on the red planet. You must terraform it into a natural, fertile wonderland that is beaming with life. Getting there will not be easy as you’ll have to manage your resources expertly and balance between growth and development and maintaining the stations, buildings and equipment that you already have at your disposal lest you kill off your colony.
I have to suggest that for an early access title the game is already at a very playable level. There are three planned zones but the current game is limited to Mars. There is more than enough content to satisfy your gameplay needs for at least several hours and I’d suggest that there would be a lot of room for replayability. I know that with my first playthrough that I wasn’t necessarily happy with a few things that I did, for example I should have utilized my space much better, and doing things differently would likely have provided me with different outcomes. Most importantly what is there absolutely works. It shows off its potential, ultimately leaving you wanting more but allowing you to have a taste of what is to come. It’s exactly how I would hope an early access title should be.
The level of micromanagement in this game is something to be praised. I feel that many games within this subgenre fall short in the accessibility of micromanagement. While I know that not everyone is a fan because it can become tedious I can appreciate when a developer puts the work in to find the right balance. I believe that that balance is met extremely well here. Of course, balances can change throughout the development of a game but for now its a major pro.
I quite enjoyed the objective structure of the game. There’s always something new to build and develop towards and there is seemingly many ways of doing that thanks to what appears to be a very diverse marketing system. The research into how many of each structure do you build to amass a colony that suits your needs will leave those who like to build data sheets spellbound for a long time. Do you target experience points rather than finances or vice versa? Is there a way to capitalize on both targets at the same time? What is the quickest and best way to attain your next actual objective? There is room for a ton of strategies that could work. Some will fall short, obviously, but therein lies the beauty of the genre.
The game is currently priced at $13.99 and is going to be raised as many early access titles are when it is released. If you’re a fan of city and base builders and resource managers then I would highly recommend jumping in now. It’s already what I would consider to be a good game and knowing that more is to come makes me very eager for its retail release.  A wholehearted recommendation.

This is a shame. I had high hopes for this one. The issue isn't it's early stage in development, it's the glaring lack of design work. The main thrust of the game is producing saleable products to fund your colony's growth. There is no support in the UI for this, however.
Each building is seperate, so you have to click on each building to view its status. Then for each unit of raw materials you want to produce, you have to click once per unit to add it to the production queue. There's no way to say "I want to produce these until I say otherwise"; you just have to click hundreds of times. And if it finishes, then you don't get a notification, so make sure you click more times than you need, or resign yourself to checking back periodically. Then, you have to click each manufacturing building to view its status, and if it's not currently manufacturing, you can tell it to produce one manufactured item. No queue there, so just remember to check each factory periodically to see if it's finished with its one item. Then to sell the items, you go into that building and click once for each item you want to sell. If you want to sell fifty units, that's fifty clicks. If you think all that sounds pretty tedious, you'd be right.
That the game has reached a playable state with no thought given to how it's going to be played makes me very doubtful that the game will ever fully mature. I'd love to be proven wrong. I am not going to hold my breath, however.

I payed retail for this game at release on a hunch as the core gameplay appealed to me.  I don't regret it; however there are some things they need to add for lategame quality of life.
Legitimate post-launch support is the reason I'm posting this review.  I've experienced around 7 game-breaking or at least highly irritating bugs during my play-through.  This is, itself, not terribly surprising for a launch and should be layed aside as a data point.  More importantly, ALL of them were fixed within 24h of my (and others) posting bug reports.  This is impressive.  Most of the issues I had were literally fixed by the time I next launched the game.
Positives:
The game looks and (now after a couple patches) performs beautifully in 4k.  The upper zoom level is perfect for 4k and the game runs great on a 1080 Ti with everything turned up.  There were memory leaks and optimization issues but not anymore for me at least.  The UI has native scaling options and a very slick option for running the game UI at full resolution and lower for the 3d component.  This would allow, for example, 4k UI and 1080p 3d behind it if your rig isn't quite up to it yet.
Gameplay is paced well and production quality is solid.  That is the powers are on high enough cooldowns or otherwise gated so as to not require high APM click/hotkey ninja mode to enjoy and succeed in even higher difficulty.  There aren't too many quests going on at any given time and also there really isn't that much loot to clock on which is nice.  You still end up looking at everything you pick up.  Voice acting is good, if a little too obvious they were in a sound booth reading lines, but still 'good' and given that most of the time you're adventuring I'll take it.
Negatives:
Inventory and party management haven't been implimented really at all.  For example, late game you end up with a ton of items... there isn't even a 'sort'...  It's not terrible, as you tend to collect only a few really strong items and ditch the rest anyway, but it needs a look.  Similarly, there isn't a way to edit the gear of your heroes other than taking them to a map and then stripping them naked before going back to the main city and taking the other guy you wanted to  move his armor to.  I believe this will be patched in, they are focusing on the game breaking stuff first, but it should be mentioned as lategame is a bit of a chore in this regard.
Nothing is explained.  While tooltips are great, most items, powers, etc don't actually tell you numbers.  For example, it took a ton of experimenting to find out that the third level aura from the white tree is like 10x as good as the healing aura from the leadership tree.  I should have been able to figure this out from numbers in the UI.  It's really difficult to know if you are getting what you are intending in a build for this reason.  Specifically, you will see things like 'improved resistances' or 'a chance to X' without any idea what the ratios are, any diminishing returns, stacking limitations, etc etc.  The developers need to go look at the Riot patch notes from League of Legends and take a page back home.  Does it break the game?... No but it's annoying.
There aren't nearly enough items.  I had 3 copies of the same shield until all the way till the end of the game.  Similar with weapons and helmets.  There are maybe 15% the number of items there need to be, and as a result its difficult to build the way you want because a logical combination of item stats isn't available to craft or buy.  I have a feeling this will also be a quality of life patch at some point, but it bears mentioning.
I still recommend the game, as I've had a great experience trapsing around adventuring because the core gameplay fantasy and pace are so good; but they need a little more time to polish the endgame experience and give a little more info for the nerdy RPG folks who are their core audience and like to understand the game mechanics.
Oh, and I still have no idea why mages need STR to increase damage on magic weapons just because they are 2-handed when they will be stacking INT or WIL anyway.  But I digress.  Support this developer, they are actually doing what we want.

Styx: Master of Shadows is one of the best hidden gems of 2014.
While the lacklustre story is completely forgettable and the combat system leaves much to be desired, Styx absolutely nails every other aspect that makes a great stealth action title. Its absolutely superb environments, with great use of verticality, are breathtakingly well designed. The music, overall sound and all other aesthetics fit the game perfectly.
It is, however, a very difficult game. You’ll find yourself using quicksaves on every small section you manage to pass through, especially because autosaves are scarce. Trigger an alarm – reload. Tumble – reload. Accidentally kick over a bucket – reload.
All of this makes Styx a great title for the veterans of the stealth genre. You’re free to go for a careless run towards the exit, you could slaughter everyone on the map, but nothing beats the sense of accomplishment for completing the huge levels without ever being seen.
It is a low budget game, but don’t let this scare you away. Sure, I could fill this review with plenty of negative comments about small glitches and poor voice acting, but I knew what to expect. It’s not without its flaws, but none of those break the immersion Styx has to offer. If you’ve been looking for a solid stealth game, look no further.
8.5/10

The entire game is riddled with problems.
First, elves. These are enemies you can only kill with throwing knives or aerial attacks as they detect you based on distance rather than on anything you've learned to avoid up to that point. They appear at the very end of the game meaning you have no controlled environment to learn how to kill them, and aerial attacks are locked behind a skill. So one of your only two methods of dealing with them is locked away for... reasons?
Second, every enemy in the game. The AI is just terrible. There are times when I placed a clone in a chest and whistled from the other side of the room. Where does the enemy look for the source of the noise? Well obviously the chest! The chest 10 meters away from the whistling. Because logic. And that's when they're not walking into each other, messing up their patrol routes and making it impossible to sneak past them without invisibility or slaughter.
Third, the controls. Everything in this game is extremely finnicky. Some of the jumps you have to make are obstructed by objects over your head that you can't avoid. You just have to hope that Styx understands from your instructions to avoid smashing his head into the chandlier. Sometimes he will, sometimes he'll fall to the ground and get tramped by guards. It's also up to luck whether or not you'll pull off things like aerial assaults or covered kills in certain areas.
Fourth, there are very few autosave points per level. And considering how finnicky a lot of the controls and jumps can be in this game that means you're going to die and go right back to the start of the level a lot. It's a little sad when Half Life Source has better autosave than a game released in this modern age.
Finally, the final boss is disappointingly pathetic. As in the only way they could think of to ramp up the difficulty was to make the final boss near impossible without a full bar of amber plus several amber potions. Yes, it's that type of boss. Not a boss that tests everything we've learned and used up to that point but a boss that ramps up the difficulty by being a specific type of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t while you play the adventure game logic of figuring out how the developers wanted you to beat this guy. It's frustrating to the point that I'm almost certain most of the reviewers giving this a high score never actually played the game to completion before giving it their glowing recommendation. It's worth docking 2-3 points off any score for.
Instead of a score I'll just say this. Styx: Master of Shadows is worth around $15.00 USD. There's enough to like about the game to enjoy it if you get it at that price but not anything close to the base price.

Here is a short and honest one.
- The game is in deep alpha state and full of bugs. Those with no patience should stay away (and that would be 99.9% of Steam population)
- There is nothing much to do yet ingame, again due to it being alpha, besides some crafting and some combat. Since wipes are going happen there is no point in doing anything serious and dedicated
- A sandbox without player housing? No. Just my 2 cents.
And now for the game elements:
- Graphics - okish. Nothing spectacular but for a sandboxy game ok.
- Sound - rudimentary
- Animation - Not good
- Combat - Trying to be good but very clunky. Reminds a bit of some other games in the market which is good but still a long way from publicly sellable product
- Crafting - Looks good-ish. What I'm missing is the quality of the ingredients, an oakenwood weapon should be a bit better than pinewood weapon in my opinion. It is trying to be complex but it is in fact simple, grindy and luck based. Level 10 can make item X, gather items Y and Z to make X, click hundred times to get a result. Many of the recipes are still bugged like bags for example (which are more important than steel armor for new starters if I may add). But one can have some fun and be pleased about wearing the armor he or she personally made
Gathering - node based. Just no! Node based gathering is for theme parks and not for sanboxes. My 2 cents.
And that is it! Its early alpha state, pretty playable when servers are not on strike and sandbox fans might get their money's worth (20$ only) over the next few weeks of fun. But without player housing and clan owned territories (which is what I consider main elements of medieval sandboxes) the fun might be of short breath. And node based gathering is simply a letdown.
I'm not going to ask for a refund, I'm sticking with them to see what they will come up with in the next year. But I cannot recommend this game at the moment to anyone except the ones with most patience and with very low expectations. Good luck.

Death is something that every one of us will have to face one day. In most video games, we are supposed to avoid death to win. In Finding Paradise and To the Moon, we explore this issue of death instead, as well as the struggles that a dying person may have when they realize their life is almost over. Both games have meaningful messages, that have made me a better person.
While To the Moon gave huge emotional impact to most people who played it, I think Finding Paradise will have bigger emotional impact on lonely people,
. To me, the last few scenes really hit home, and I couldn't help but got very emotional and broke down in tears. Such a beautiful and inspiring story! Definitely worth the price, even more. Every minute spent in the game was meaningful. And I definitely will replay this game when I need to be reminded that life is beautiful and our struggles in life are worth fighting.

SimpleRockets is a 2D spacecraft building sandbox game developed by Jundroo, LLC. SimpleRockets is effectively a simplified and 2D version of KSP (the dev even says on the store page it's heavily influenced by KSP) so as you would imagine you build spacecraft of all different shapes and sizes and send them on their way into the dark expanse we know as Space. Blast off from Smearth and travel to Smercury, Smars, the Smoon, Smenus, Smupiter, Smaturn, Smuranus and Smeptune.
+Simple graphics, they do look more akin to something you'd find in a flash game but they fit the game well
+Simple building mechanics, you get a list of parts and they all have highlighted areas to show where they can be attached to other objects
+Despite being such a simple game you can make some rather complex things as can be seen in the Store page screenshots though I'm not really good enough to make such things
+Being a simplified version of KSP makes this a useful tool for practising things, particularly orbital mechanics, before trying them in KSP
+As well as a sandbox mode there are a number of challenges with varying levels of difficulty to try out
+The controls are great (basically the same as KSP as well which is nice)
+You can choose what planet to launch from in Sandbox mode which is really cool
+You can split the screen down the middle, one half displaying your spacecraft and the other half displaying the map of the solar system
+The plants (and Smoon) all feel very different to each other
-There's not a huge amount of parts available to use but from what I understand the game is easy to mod so perhaps we'll see some mod packs soon
-The camera centers on the planet and can't be moved which is a little annoying upon re-entry as you often have to watch your rocket descend from an odd point of view
-Sound effects don't play for anything that isn't attached to your command module, for example if you detatch a stage too early and your rockets are still firing you can't hear them. Not a major issue but something I found irritating
-Parts only have very brief descriptions giving you a basic idea of what they do but there's no specifications for them
Verdict:
Worth Purchasing (7.5/10)
SimpleRockets provides a more accesible experience than Kerbal Space Program while maintaining the essence of spacecraft building. If you're a fan of KSP but aren't overly good at it, like myself, chances are you'll enjoy this one.

It's a mix between Gears of War and Devil May Cry.  It looks and feels like Gears of War, but then feels like Devil May Cry as enemies barge in screaming at you by the hundreds, only to be splattered as quickly as they came with satisfying gun and melee mechanics, rather than stick yourself behind bits of wall and play whack-a-mole.  Regardless of the aforementioned foes being very much kill-able, the campaign still presents a challenge, and while it is indeed only a 7 hour one, it's still fun, even for those who never touched the Warhammer lore in his life like myself.  The multiplayer, while a touch frustrating at first with spam and a leveling system that withholds equipment, quickly becomes addicting with well balanced, variable combat, and best of all, it's very easy to kill campers.  I heard that in October 2011, Steam users will get a free co-op campaign mode, but at the time of writing this, there is no co-op.  Still, a fun and very well optimized experience well worth it.

Finished 'If My Heart Had Wings' - or rather finished the Common Route - 19 hours in. Obtained 'Bad Ending' (no routes) 21 hours in.
I have next to no desire to re-read content just to play specific routes. I appreciate this is common for VNs, However the 'choices' for IMHHW were so anodyne re: who looks best in a bikini, whom do you wish to accompany to the supermarket, and were so few and far between, that I find it hard to retain any sense of credulity that such choices presented a potential route.
Perhaps I'm playing in the mind-set of an early 40s British guy which is the issue, and one who is not completely au-fait with VNs. But I'll be damned if I will spend hours re-reading the same dialogue, especially narrative that wasn't terribly enthralling in the first place. Except for Armane (for obvious reasons), I never really felt a connection with the characters: Aoi felt like a diluted Murakami protagonist (minus the ubiquitous cat) , whilst Kotori had annoying mannerisms, especially her frequent open mouth - jabbing finger expression.
I get that the game pushes you down the main [Kotori] route, but to such an extent that with the exception of Ageha, the relationships with other characters were hardly developed beyond the usual harem tropes.
What it boils down to is that excellent production values and musical score aside (the standard to which all VNs shall be judged production wise), the actual narrative itself was fairly soporific. I did enjoy IMHHW otherwise I wouldn't have persisted. That said, it is pretty much standard high-school angst / shojo, unless you have a fascination with the technical detail for gliders.

If My Heart Had Wings is a visual novel, more than a gal-game in a lot of senses.
You are a guy who, depends on whichever route you choose, will help the girl in the route to accomplish her wish.
The main route, Kotori route is the main focus of the series, and you'll be able to help her to fly with her own and regain her confidence.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The game spends a hefty of time on making and maintaining glider, and the rest on daily-life, or nichijou.
Might get boring if you find the extra information is heavy and simply want a gal-game.
