The RPG part is not particularly original or outstanding, but not too bad either. I would have enjoyed the game if it didn't attempt to have a full-blown RTS aspect to it.
But I like RTS and since RTS games are so rare nowadays that was the main part that I wanted to play. Unfortunately, it is not very good. It feels like an RTS straight out of the 90s in the sense that the AI doesn't give a crap about resources  or losses or anything at all, it will just keep mindlessly throwing units at you, and you can keep killing 10x or 100x or 1000x more units than they do and it changes absolutely nothing because the AI cheats and never runs out of resources.
And while that is not necessarily bad on its own and can still be enjoyable, other aspects of the design make it very annoying.
Units are very slow and unresponsive and tend to disperse, chase random targets and die, so they require constant babysitting.
Every expansion has its own independent pool of workers and every building needs to be manually assigned workers to function, including watch towers. So every time the AI decides to suicide another bunch of units you need to deallocate workers from production buildings, assign them to the towers, wait until the enemy units die, remove them from towers and assign back to production, and because this game is very expansion happy and the AI likes to attack random expansions you end up doing A LOT of that, turning the game into an endless whack-a-mole.

Until they optimized how  the camera works in this game, don't even bother buy the game, it's atrocious. Most of the time you are playing, it's you against the camera. Never I play any RTS/RPG game with this kind of horrible camera control.
At the moment, no, don't buy it. I'll change the review once they optimize the camera operation.
Also it's full of bugs, even the dev need to update the client on daily basis.
Wait for 2-3 months later if you want to buy the game.

Game Tycoon 2 is a tycoon game, developed by Sunlight Games, about making your own game with your own video game company. Sounds super fun right? Because you know, you're a gamer, so that means you gotta have the game about making games for gamers, right, right? Well, not with this game. If you really want a game development game that's good, five dollars less, and more polished, get Game Dev Tycoon.
Game Tycoon 2 has interesting concepts. You have your office, development office and the accessibility to a bank, lawyers, an advertisement agency, the local university, a shopping mall, your own home, and also a production warehouse to create box art and ship the games. You better look at the tutorials because I didn't on my first play-through and had no idea what I was doing. I assumed they'd teach you through out the game, like other tycoon games do, but they didn't. Aside from the tutorials, they have a “campaign”, and an endless mode. Now, I say “campaign”, because it's a “mission” where you have to achieve one goal. There is no way of telling you that you've failed either, you just have to go bankrupt.
I think the main problem with this game is that it's very unclear on what to do because it's not like other tycoon games I've played. The different offices and places available are cool, in concept, but don't really execute well. You can sign a contract to have a company publish or distribute your game and it has a deadline, but you can't make your workers work faster unless you make them stop or train them, which already takes too long. I don't get the process of researching technologies, they still cost the same when you're trying to develop your game. And the main thing that bugged me was the UI. I don't get how it could be that buggy. It was the most difficult thing to assign members of your staff to projects. They made it so complex, for some reason.
The graphics weren't a big deal to me in this game, but I think the character art is pretty weird. Just saying. Now, I sound like I hate the game but I think it could definitely be a good game. The concepts of being able to make your own box art, sign up employees from the local university, advertise your company or game, make contracts, get a loan and buy shares of other companies, surprised me. It has the concepts that could make a great game. But, it's just so hard to get things done with the UI, to me. It makes the game hard to navigate.
The sound of this game is, whatever, average. I can't see myself buying this game for 15 dollars either. Maybe 5. This game just needs to be easier to learn, easier to navigate and have some extra functionalities like speeding up the process of creating the game, despite the quality of the game worsening like in Game Dev Tycoon. With that and other things, this game could definitely be something worth 15 dollars and have good replayability.

Gambling on investments is cool, but stock market is too shallow. Apartment is a feature from the previous part of the game and I still don't see it's purpose.
At the end, despite all the flaws, I still recommend this game for true fans of the genre. I will continue to play it, because I saw that under "gimmicky" front, there is solid tycoon game inside.

I would Highly Recommend anyone who plan on playing this game to play bird story right before it.
So it finally arrived. I was literally counting date before this game was released, purchased as soon as it got onto the store, finished it just now. To start off, as always, writing review about this game is hard just like To the moon, simply because I do not want to spoil anything, and so much things are floating on my head and I am not sure if I can really write it too well about it.
I am planning on re playing this game sooner or later simply because there are many things that I felt like I missed and some stuffs I couldnt fully understand, so I will have to give a second run for this game.
For Music, as always I would like to give 10/10. To the moon made an awesome music pieces, very repetitive, but very addictive. Compare to To the Moon series, I would say that I liked To the moon music bit more (I started playing Piano after playing To the moon as well), but that is only in comparison to To the moon. Compare to other games of this genre, I would give 10/10 without hesitation.  Especially the main theme, "Time is a place" is such an awesome piece.
For story, story of finding paradise is very different from To the Moon. I wouldnt approach this game thinking we will have some kind of heartbreakening love story that will make you shed with tears. Rather, this is story about man, story about his life.
How should I put it... Playing To the Moon feels as if you are watching well made drama or novel about love story. It isnt story about us. It is story about River and Johnny. It is story about them. However, Finding Paradise is bit different. It feels as if it is a story about me, story about you, and story about all of us. There is no such thing as heartbreakening love story. Rather,  it is story about our life. Our past, present, future, regrets, dreams, fulfillment, friends, lovers, children, and goes on.
Playing to the moon made me shed a tear. After playing Finding Paradise, however, I find myself sitting on a chair at 4am, with so many thoughts about myself, my past, my present, my future, and about my life. I do not know, or I cannot say whether playing this game has any impact about my own life or not, but what I can say for sure is that playing this game has changed how I view about who I am.
Is this game better than To the Moon? I do not know, you may love To the Moon but may say meh, story of finding paradise was so-so. Simply because To the Moon makes you much more emotional, whereas finding paradise makes you feel tranquil.
Thanks Ken Gao for creating such an awesome game.
Just piece of advice for people who are planning on playing this game, do not rush it, just take it slow and read each lines slowly and do not miss anything out. Give yourself whole day, and just play from Bird story to Finding Paradise. If you take this slow, it will give you unforgettable moment after you finish the game.
And lastly, dont try to judge this game. Dont try to judge meh compare to To the Moon, its not that emotional, it is not as "new" as it is. Just take the story slowly and go with the flow. I think a lot of time we miss good things because we are too busy judging them.
Thank you and have fun.

A.V.A. can be most accurately be described as a faster-paced Counter-Strike. The TTK (time to kill) on most weapons is extremely short, coupled with a relatively slower movement speed of players when they aren't sprinting. Weapons and loudouts are separated between 3 classes:
- Pointman (SMGs/shotguns, fastest movement, weak armor)
- Rifleman (AR's, medium speed, strong armor)
- Sniper (SR's, medium speed, regular armor)
Each are set to the F1, F2, and F3 keys respectively. You can technically have multiple loudouts per character, but that'll only change your primary weapon, which can be done mid-game or before you respawn.
Your standard Team Deathmatch and Demolition are here, along with Escape (kinda reminiscent of ZM in CS:S), Escort (on team leads tank to objective while other stops tank), and others. There's also a PVE channel, though I've never been able to find people playing, so either its dead or I just don't come on at that channel's peak hours.
There are multiple currencies in this game, so I'll summarize each below:
- Euros: standard currency earned by playing the game. You'll usually get very few per match in truth, but this can be greatly boosted by completing daily missions, of which you select based on gamemode before playing. You'll gain them from leveling up, as well as earning 2000 Euros for every hour you play. The weapons in the shop range from 15,000 to 70,000 Euros, equating to about 2-3 Daily Missions depending on gamemode, not factoring in boosters/leveling/etc.
- Red Tickets: Earned from opening Capsules (basically Supply Drops) or login rewards. You'll earn anywhere frrom 1-20 on certain days when logging in (not the most consistent) with weapons usually at 120 RT or up.
- EMP (En Masse Points): The game's premium currency. Only available through use of real money, and can be used to spend on premium Capsules, skins, boosters, etc. Pretty self explanatory, really.
Now I can't give a definite answer on what capsules are available as the list can change whenever the game's updated or if there's a rotation for what's available, but you are able to view all possible items including the amount of time you'll get them (most weapons are permanent, but there are a few that are not). At the time of writing there are only two capsules that can be bought with Euros, so if you wanna win that cool gun you want you'll have to fork over real money. From what I've seen these weapons in the capsules are not inherently Pay-To-Win, and just have differing stats to the defualt weapons.
some of the premium weapons do have an extra damage bonus that stacks with the more kills you get with it in a match.
Shortly after En Masse acquired A.V.A., the game became plagued with issues as the servers couldn't handle the load, causing people to quit.
Now there are only a few bugs, such as stuttering during gameplay.
I found that this could be fixed by disabling fog, setting sound quality to either the "16 Channel", or 32 Channel options, and generally customizing the settings to your preference/rig from then on. I along with others experienced these issues even with nice rigs, which means it is an issues with the game.
The game's graphics, while not next-gen by any means, do hold up. Enemies can easily be told apart from allies, maps are well-lit and visually easy on the eyes. Sound design is very good: footsteps are clear and can hepl locate enemies, weapons sound very cool and powerful (a sniper sounds like a sniper instead of a pistol sort of thing), and callouts are said in the language of the team (either English or Russian) dependent on side.
Out of a lot of these kinds of games, A.V.A. actually feels like it takes skill to play, and is rewarding when you win. You'll see this in the absolutely insane clutches some people pull off (probable due to the ESL players for this game) and the F2P model isn't as bad as it could be. The game can only benefit from more players so more support will come to it.

I was considering recommending this game because, if I did, this review will be considered more credible in regards the flaws it points out. Seriously, though, I can't honestly recommend this game. If you're buying it with a 75% discount like I did, then I ALMOST recommend this. It's definitely not worth its full price, though, and of that I can't be more sure.
I can't think of anything good to say about this game. Honestly, not every part of it is bad, but I can't think of anything good enough that I consider worth noting, either. Maybe a couple of moderately cool stuff, like the ability to turn invisible for a very limited amount of time using a very limited and precious source of energy? You can earn new skills or enhance the ones you have as you play along, too, which is at least something that will motivate you throughout the game. This is hardly worth noting, though, since tons of other games have this feature and they tend to do it considerably better.
I remember when I first played this, I left a rage-filled review after only two hours. In my case, I started the game on an infuriating note, as the controls are not properly explained. I kept losing to the first guy I was supposed to fight with. It took me about 15 minutes to beat him. Apparently you can only counter attacks, and normal attacking doesn't do anything. It was very simple, in the end, but I needed to check a playthrough in order to know what to do.
This game is quite repetitive. You move from room to room, or area to area, trying to get past guards undetected. This game is a bit outdated, so the guards' senses tend to be unrealistic. You will immediately get used to being spotted or heard from unrealistic distances. This is excusable at times, since certain wooden things like chairs are thrown into the air with the slightest touch, alerting the guards, which also sucks.
There tend to be different options in regards paths you take, but none of them will ever make you feel sly. It's not as much a challenge of wit as much as it is you trying to see whether you can make an awkward jump, or whether a guard will keep his head turned long enough for you to tip-toe past. It's a stealth game, but it doesn't require you be creative. It requires you to be patient and to be weary of your surroundings. It's quite simple, but it can also be frustrating at times, not to mention repetitive. It's made very clear early on that you are supposed to be stealthy, as fighting more than one guard at once will get you killed in a matter of seconds. Also, don't get too confident about fighting a single guard unless you do it stealthily or there are no other guards in the area that he can alert.
Speaking of fighting, whether your opponent knows of your presence or not, I hope you don't mind doing the same moves over and over again. One move for opponents on the defence, and another move for unsuspecting opponents. That's it as far as I'm concerned. To be honest, I'm not sure whether you can get new fighting skills and I don't feel like checking, but I doubt it. I think I'd remember if that were the case.
The graphics are outdated. The outside looks like Columbia from Bioshock Infinite, if BSI was in third-person and it came out in 2006. The inside areas tend to look like houses/dungeons from Elder Scrolls: Oblivion (third-person view).
You have an option to find some treasure/s in every level, but the hints that are given to you in the map are very vague and I haven't found one yet. If this was a really good game that I'm really into, I would try harder at this, but I really don't feel like it's worth the time.
I don't really care about the characters as I don't find them appealing at all, and I'm yet to encounter someone with a hint of depth. The story is cliche, too, not much thought went into it.
Styx doesn't make sense at times. I remember being ganged up on and dying within 2 seconds, and I kept respawning in the same spot, with the same guards beating and shooting arrows at me, a second before dying. I had to start over with that level because the autosave was not strategically timed.
The worst part of all, the thing that ultimately makes the above even less worth doing is the fact that this game is very boring. If it was at least a little interesting, I'd get myself to play it despite all the bad features and the features that are barely average at best. Alas, it's not the case. I'm not half-way through and I'm going to have to stop, the reason being that it feels like a chore to play this game. I almost want to procrastinate from playing by doing coursework. This is the reason why I'm writing this review even though I haven't beaten the game, since I'm not going to beat it, ever.
*Sigh*, what a waste of money.

The game keeps upping up the challenge with new enemy types that really counter your skills and options. Do you like rolling around fast? There's an enemy type that can hear very well. Do you like climbing on top of things? They introduce an enemy later on that can counter that. Do you like killing everything? Some enemies are unkillable. I got the opportunity to try this out at PAX East, and I'm glad I did-- I found a fun game, I learned about a sale price, and I was able to pick up a copy for myself. The game is very straightforward and fairly easy to pick up, and leaves no illusions as to what you're supposed to do. You shoot things. You shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of things, and you do it
. I tend to shy away from shoot-em-up platformers out of habit, but this is honestly a fun one.

It's at this point where I note that this is, as stated, Early Access, so I wasn't expecting this to be a 10-hour playthrough. It's fast-paced, quick restart, high octane arcade gameplay. The "Bounty" system (the coin payout at the end of a match) is a little slow at first, but if you rack up good combos and dedicate a few minutes, you'll get thousands. I'm not kidding-- thousands. And at the moment, the only thing to do is buy accessories, worth 20 coins apiece.
There are a couple of little bugs (Hats disappear when you crouch, the game froze up when I chose Quit, small hiccups) that aren't much of a bother for an Early Access. They come with the territory. For a five dollar game (or three on sale!) with more to come than what it's got, it's a GREAT timekiller and I look forward to seeing what's next.

This was such an incredibly frustrating game. For every neat aspect that drew me in, there is another poorly designed or badly explained one to push me away. I played about 1 1/3 playthroughs (it seems that 3 playthroughs equals game completion). The first playthrough I did with a friend. I used a minigun, and my co-op partner used a sniper rifle. This combination was able to handle just about everything we saw on the normal difficulty, me taking out close to mid-ranged enemies and him mopping things up at long range. There was always plenty to shoot, as the game continually respawns enemies. Though I suppose some might find this a way to keep the game engaging and keep you on your toes, I just found it to be tedious and it made me feel somewhat ineffective. We liked the ability to hack and possess bots and enemies, though this system is somewhat poorly explained. Hacking was very time-consuming, and it never feels good to be harassed by the continually-respawning enemies while in the middle of a hacking battle. We wanted to use different weapons, but it never seemed clear exactly how to unlock some of them. The research system has quite a bit of potential, but it too just ending up being frustrating to me. You don't know exactly what researching something will give you (sometimes it actually gives you nothing at all), and you are only able to research things for which you've received the appropriate random briefcase drop. This makes it difficult to plan a "build," and because the research can take a bit of time, you only can get so much done playing the game at a moderate pace. The "Cybertech" tree seems like another missed opportunity: it's difficult to figure out where exactly to spend your money, as you also are attempting to save up for weapons and research. Each point put in a "Cybertech" discipline is very expensive. Lastly, I have to comment on the simply absurd story. We couldn't figure out what was going on - the game was tonally inconsistent, and sometimes seemed cryptic for no particular reason.
I attempted to begin another playthrough where I used resources online to plan my build: I wanted to use a little floating robot to help me fight (think ED-E from Fallout New Vegas). I planned my research to give me the strength I needed to buy the weapon at the weapon shop, and completed the "Drone Forcefield" and "XSP345" research to maximize the robot's effectiveness. I finally reached the prerequisites and bought him, only to find that I couldn't get him to fight with me. I went into the menu and clicked the button to summon him, I saw him briefly, and then he seemed to disappear. I looked for an option to give him orders. There was an option called "Drone and Slave commands" that was unbound in the keybindings. I bound a key to this option, and found that when I hit the key I heard a dull noise seemingly indicating that nothing was happening. So, I gave up on my "build" experiment and deleted the game.

When I started this game, I was very confused. After one playthrough, I am still confused. I don't understand this game, and I don't think I ever will. Maybe that's why I like it so much. Here is a sample of the questions this game has left me with:
-Who am I?
-What is Cybermancy, and what is divine about it?
-What is E.Y.E., and why did I join it?
-What does E.Y.E. stand for?
-What is my position within the organization?
-What caused my amnesia?
-Who is my Mentor, and what is his position in E.Y.E.?
-Why is E.Y.E. divided into Culters and Jians?
-What is a Culter?
-What is a Jian?
-Why do I instantly gain Brozoufs when I kill something?
-What is a Brozouf?
-If Brozoufs are the currency, why can I dump thousands of them into myself to upgrade my cyborg body?
-Why are fetch quests only ever half a fetch quest? (seriously, "bring me this object" objectives only actually mean pick the thing up and instantly get paid without ever returning it to the person who asked for it)
-Why can I jump off a 10 storey cliff and get the notification "my legs are OK" but getting shot in the legs for a few seconds means "my legs are broken"?
-Why is there a video tutorial about the video tutorial menu?
-Why is the video tutorial menu bound to a hotkey?
-Why do none of the video tutorials contain much (if any) coherent or useful information?
-How does one "buy to a seller"?
-Why do I sometimes start a mission from the beginning, but sometimes start at a random point? (for some reason I bypassed the entire final level and started it at the final boss. I died and had to redo the level and actually started at the beginning, but it was a strange experience that wasn't unique to that level.)
-Why do I have to go to great pains to protect one of my comrades only to see him killed and get the dramatic announcement that the mission is failed and I have to blow up the building to contain the demon threat inside if that very same comrade shows up the VERY NEXT MISSION alive and well (though he gets killed again, of course)?
-Why do I have to go through the very same tiny dream world level every time I start the game or die too many times?
-What is Klaadum's ladder, and what does "my note" on it mean?
-What is the karma system, and what does my ranking on it mean?
-What is going on with the mental balance system? I don't see a pattern to what does or does not make me insane.
-If my superiors keep telling me that I should be stealthy in missions, why are my loadout options 1 silenced weapon and a whole mess of other non-silenced weapons?
-Why does one of my swords make people or monsters explode?
-Why is my medkit nearly as heavy as a pistol?
-If my medkit has unlimited charges to heal me to full health, why doesn't everyone in the universe also have one and use it regularly?
-Why do I have personal access to so many scientists to research things for me?
-Why are there ancient stone ruins on Mars?
-What language are people speaking? The text is English, signs alternate between English, Chinese, and a language that as far as I can tell is just a made up fantasy language to put on carvings, and the spoken language I cannot identify whatsoever.
-Why are my dialogue options generally 1. Insult person and agree, 2. Insult person and leave, 3. Insult person and threaten to kill them, thereby initiating combat?
-Why are there armouries all over the place for me to fully restock my ammunition and weapons?
-Who are the Federation, and why do they hate E.Y.E.?
-Why are there encyclopedias worth of lore and backstory information in the hub world that make nearly no sense?
-Why is the hub world so gigantic? It takes me 5 minutes to get from one end to another at a dead sprint the entire time.
-Why should I care about anything or anyone in this world?

This is a nice little stealth game with a fun mechanic in being able to rewire the level.  It was a good game with some fun dialogue and decision-making.  I was surprised that I actually cared about the choices I was making in the meta-game.
I have a few complaints though.  I feel like the game was a good concept which hadn't been fully fleshed out.  There's a lot more that could be done with this mechanic.  There should be more to wire up than just switches, lights, and doors.  I wish there had been more complicated systems to navigate and control.  It didn't take long to completely master the game.
I also noticed a few glitches where the game would occasionally freeze briefly or kinda wig out.  It always recovered, but it was definitely annoying.  I think it may have had something to do with playing the game in windowed mode on a Mac.  Beats me.
Lastly, the game is not particularly long.  I wasn't bothered by the length, especially since the mechanics were somewhat limited as I mentioned before.  But it's short enough that I would have felt cheated had I spent very much on the game.

Kan Gao and his team have done it again. They have managed to tell a story that is witty, warm, and in some ways educational. Without spoiling details from either To The Moon or this game, I can say that both titles work wonders in exploring the concepts of mind, memory, and mental health. They do not shy away from the rougher edges of the human condition, and in doing so tell genuine and heart-tugging tales.
In short, if you like narrative driven games, buy this and To The Moon( and, should you feel so inclined, A Bird Story, though I actually recomend this after playing the other two). They are both masterpieces in their own right.
Be aware that these games are not so much "games" as they are interactive novellas( though this one does have a few refreshing gameplay tweaks here and there) That's about all I can say if you're new to the franchise.
Now, I will talk to the home crowd, the ones that have been waiting for this for ages. I will be frank: this is not the same kind of story as To The Moon, and does not hit as universally as the romance between Johnny and River. What we get, in my opinion is no less powerful, even if it isnt as universal. I still felt endeared to all of the characters, and it was nice to see Niel and Eva developed even further. There are also tons of refrences to To The Moon if you pay attenton, and even a well crafted nod to A Bird Story( note that our patient here is the boy in A Bird Story as an adult). There's also a TON on intrigue that leads me to believe that this franchise will be around for a while longer, and I for one am quite excited for whats to come.
TL:DR
Get the game if you liked To The Moon. Gao deserves it.

I tried to restart the first one, but since I'd completed it, I guess the game thought I had mastered all the skills available in that tutorial, and wouldn't want a refresher course.  Oh well, I guess I'll just work on 2 through 5.  So I did.  I made it through 4 more tutorials, all of which were just as bad as the first.  I didn't learn anything.
It took about 35 minutes to complete the remaining tutorials, at which point I was released to the world of Game Tycoon 2 to do as I please.  I choose a character, which I assume I'll never need to see again.  I pick a company name, NME something or other.  Then a company logo...I chose the H8 logo, because I H8 this game.
Then, because I'm super confident in my skills from all the excellent information given to me by the tutorial, I choose hard mode and start my game.
I lay out the groundwork for my game.  A brilliant piece of work.  Truly, a masterpiece of it's time.  It's called Bang!, and it's a shooter.  But it's not just any shooter.  This is 1980, we don't have fancy things like graphics.  It's a text based shooter.  I can clearly see this will be a hit.  Just imagine with me...
/fire at grue
SYNTAX ERROR
/shoot grue
>>You can't see <GRUE>, it's dark.
/shoot north
>>You hit the <GRUE> in the leg.  <GRUE> Eats you.  You are dead.
Thrilling, right!?  Now, don't go stealing my ideas or anything, because I've already filed the paperwork to make this a reality.
So, we start developing Bang!, but I run in to a problem.  I don't have staff!  How dare I make the assumption that a beginning developer start their first game on their own.  No!  I need a programmer and a graphic artist.  I don't know why, because there are no graphics.  Maybe he's also a writer, because he's a creative type.  This is where the one point of realism I liked came in though, because I deliberately didn't want sound in my game, so I wasn't required to hire a sound guy.  Nice touch, 1 single point to Game Tycoon 2 for that.
Now, let's go back to my office and watch the little Newton's cradle on my desk.  Yes, there is a semi-functioning Newton's cradle!  If you hover over it, the balls go back and forth.  Well, the ones on the end do anyway, the 3 in the middle just sit there transferring energy.  Lazy good for nothing...wait a minute.  Something is missing.  Apparently I wasn't the only one to not hire a sound guy, because Sunlight Games didn't bother to put that little clacking sound these things make in the game.  I'm taking back that point I gave you in the last paragraph.
Finally, the time has come.  I made my game!  Bang!  It's here, it's done!  I rush over to the production and distribution area, where I design a box.  In the tutorial, I just went with the standard poor quality box, and it showed.  Man that thing was ugly.  Not for my pride and joy though.  Nothing but the best for Bang!.  I go with the Noble option.  Yeah, the scale is Normal, High Value, and Noble.
Oh, I also skipped Copy Protection, because A. I don't believe in it, and B. it's 1980, what options were there?  A sticker that says "Please do not make illegal copies of this software" as the Simple option, and Complex is a copy of the music video "Don't Copy That Floppy" that is mandatory to watch every time you load the game.
Back to production, we don't get an option for a manual, which is odd to me, since the developer of this game is really invested in making sure the player sees the tutorial.  Maybe all games just come with a built in guy that talks you through everything in an unintelligible language.
I make 1,000 copies of the game, since that's the minimum, and I have no idea what the market is like.  I'll play it safe, assuming I can make more later, I just might miss a sales window if I have a hit.  I get my 1,000 games, and...are you kidding me?  This is Noble quality box making?  Not a single edge on this box is a straight line!  I'm all for artistic design here, but come on, be practical.  How is this supposed to sit on a shelf?  I guess consumers are forced to lay it on it's back.  Although, for all I know, the box isn't big enough for all the disks, and it starts to bow outward a bit.
Well, let's get to business.  All this work is about to pay off.  Time to sell these games.  I need to determine a price.  Well, I vaguely remember it costing over $1.00 to manufacture each game, but I don't know if that price includes development costs or not.  Let's assume not.  I suppose $3.00 is a fair price to ask, but I want to make sure.  I'll just drive down to the local game store in the mall, and price check other games.
I make it to the game store, which doesn't sell erotic games by the way.  They made a point of specifically mentioning that in the tutorial.  The only thing here is a list of hit games.  But because it's before any games have been released, it's empty.  Why does an entire store exist that doesn't sell anything yet?  I'm feeling my immersion start to fade.  Everything is falling apart and nothing makes sense in this world.  Just then, a black hole emerges from the empty game store, sucking everything into it, where I die and it's game over.
Then I woke up, and I was still playing this game!  I angrily drive back to the distribution center, where I say screw it, sell it for $3 a game, I don't care.  But I don't have a distribution contract.  Now I have to drive to the lawyer, negotiate a contract, drive back, ship my game, and repeat the process.  When I make it to the lawyer though, there isn't anyone interested in distributing my game.  No one wants a text based first person shooter.  I guess there's a lesson to be learned there.
Make sure a market exists for the game before you make it.  Because no matter how much you defend how great a game it is, if no one wants it, you've just wasted a bunch of time and money.
To anyone who does like this game, fantastic!  I'm beyond thrilled that you found something in this world that brings you joy.  But for the general public, and those on the fence, and those who think this is a sequel to Game Dev Tycoon, I would advise against buying this game.  It's just not fun.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here from Universal Gaming Reviews to bring you a summary of our review for Game Tycoon 2 by Sunlight Games and Kiss Ltd. You can read our full review for the game here:
To start the summary I'll be honest and say that I wasn't really sure if I was going to enjoy the game going into the review because I'm pretty skeptical of post 2005 Tycoon games and have played very few that really wowed me. I still don't think the game matches up to the likes of Zoo Tycoon 2, The Movies or Rollercoaster Tycoon but what's available is quite fun if you're a fan of micromanaging type games.
The game puts you in the role of a game developer trying to reach the top of the market starting in 1980 and going all the way to 2050. The game's main mode is endless mode which allows you freely create games, manage your development studio and keep track of everything. The game has a suprirising amount of depth to it and there's a ton of stuff to manage. It took me a couple games to get the hang of things initially through trial and error.
The game is surprisingly addictive and I had quite a lot of fun playing it even though I don't think it's the best tycoon game I've ever played. With some improvement it could be excellent and if you're a fan of management style games it's worth checking out but it might not be something everyone will enjoy.
Thanks a lot for reading our summary and full review folks, happy gaming!

The game is a Real Time Strategy, with the most notable feature being that instead of training individual dudes, you train whole squads of dudes at a time. So instead of "oh no, those thirty guys look really tough" you get "oh no, those ten squads are terrifying."
The other thing making it different is the lack of resources. You only have one resource: population. To be trained, the village you are trying to train them from needs to have enough citizens in it to become your new unit. They repopulate overtime. So capturing villages is essential so you can have more guys, but there are times where you may instead want to burn down an enemy village to completely remove it from the game as opposed to capturing it.
The main problem, and we are still playing to figure this out, but the Romans appear to just suck. The Barbarian equivalents of their units are just that much better. We haven't tried Egyptians, maybe the Barbarian vs Egyptian match up is balanced, but as it stands the Romans are most likely bottom tier. They are the only three races, and all of them have the same equivalent units, except for their three super units which you can only train if you've gotten enough "honour points" - which you get by killing dudes.
Getting multiplayer to work required us to go through Gameranger instead (hence the low playtime), but we did get it to work and it is very worth it. Especially at the moment at only 49 cents.

For those having problems on Windows 7 what worked for me was opening the game's folder and running "trobleshoot compatability" on the Praetorians application. Be sure however to launch it from steam and not from in the folder. Hope this helps.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy is a weird, crazy, broken mess of a game that awkwardly mixes an incredibly strange world, heavy RPG mechanics and FPS combat. And I utterly love it.
This game isn't for everyone - its tutorials are so terrible I didn't know half of what I could do until 20 hours of play - but if you can persevere through its flaws you will find an incredibly engaging and unique experience. The gunplay is exceptionally rewarding, the stat systems have powerful effects on how you play, the Psi Powers are all fun to play with, implants like the Cloak add new depths of stategy to combat and movement, and no feeling beats the first time you hack one of those blasted Interceptors to turn on your foes.
For any new players I have two essential words of advice: Get a Medkit ASAP, and the Power Conversion implant soon after. The two together will save you innumerable minutes of waiting crouched in a corner for your stamina to refill.
Finally, this game is even more fun with friends. Battle Royale is like a souped up callback to old days of competing in DOOM, though it locks away special abilities in the interest of balance, and co-operative missions can be insanely satisfying as you blow away hordes of enemies.
To me this game is like the incredible pie your grandmother baked for a picnic that someone kicked over in the car - it's crushed and broken, the pastry strewn everywhere, but if you get past its appearance and give it a taste you'll find it's more delicious than you ever hoped. I love this game, and when the open worlds and grand vistas of newer games get stale E.Y.E is where I return for a few fun hours of hacking doors and smashing heads.

I find that sequels to games like To the Moon are a bit difficult to pull off. How can one not only capitalize on the humor, mystery, and comfiness of the first one, but expand upon it?
This question should be asked to Freebird Games Developer Kan Gao, because Finding Paradise is an exceptional sequel and definitely gets my recommendation. The humor is wonderful, the story is gripping, and the game has several emotional moments that really make this a must play if you enjoyed To The Moon.
The game isn't too long, I beat it in a single playthrough of 5 hours, but it's just as long as it needs to be to tell a good story. If you're looking for that then look no further than Finding Paradise. Let's just hope they don't take as long with the next sequel!

The Good:

The Not So Good:
-story is convoluted

-doesn't answer many questions and raises too many new ones.
Honestly, I didn't connect with the characters in this game.  I enjoyed Eva and Neil well enough.  I could not build an emotional connection with Colin.  He really felt bland as a character.  he really didn't have any trauma or real struggles to deal with.  I feel as though the story had to get a little crazy to counter this, but as a result, Colin really was lost in the mix.  By the end of it, I forgot the story was even about him in the first place.  When you have a story driven game like this, you need more interesting and flawed characters (like River and Johnny).  The story and new characters fell flat for me, which is a major shortcoming in a story based game.
It's also a pet peeve of mine to have so many unanswered questions.  I understand you need some,  but none of the overall mysteries were answered at all.  Then on top of that, a ton of new mysteries were piled on.  I feel this game suffers from middle book syndrome, where it really just exists to set up stuff for the next entry.  I'm to the point in my life where I don't want to wait around for years just to get some (if any) answers.  I get impatient and do not want to bother waiting around. I've been burned by too many series I suppose.
Congratulations to Freebird Games, on what seems to be a very successful entry.  But sadly, this was a miss for me.

Alchemist's Castle is a 2-D side-scrolling Metroidvania-style game with a lot of heart and atmosphere.  It's light on combat complexity (you have one type of attack - thrown vials that explode on contact), heavy on exploration, and priced extremely fairly.  The game is relatively short, moreso if you're well-versed in these types of mechanics, but even then odds are good that you'll find yourself pleased at being left wanting more at the end.  The jumping mechanics feel very fluid and satisfying to me.  I realize that I've been playing games for so long that sometimes I'm invested in really nitpicky features, but I have to formally declare that I LOVE the ability to utilize your jump and double-jump while falling.  It feels fantastic every time I do it, and it allows for more interesting challenges within the layouts of the different rooms.  It's just one of those little gameplay quirks that you see more often in the crazy score/time-rush platformers and not so often in the Metroidvania sub-genre, so I need to show it some love here.
The graphics are atmospheric, there are some light puzzle-solving elements involving getting from Point A to Point B within some of the rooms, and there are some optional/extra power-ups to be discovered.
On top of all this, the devs are active on the game's discussion board and quick to address bugs.  The game has already had updates to address some gamepad issues and add achievements, and as of 11/29/2017 it is still actively being improved.
If you have a gamepad and $0.99, what are you waiting for?  You could be exploring that castle right now.

This game is surprisingly well made considering the low sales price. It’s a fun little metroidvania with platforming and puzzle elements, but lacking in combat. The controls are responsive and precise, I especially like the grace period when jumping off a ledge and the natural movement speed. You don’t experience cheap deaths because of bad controls, it’s your fault if you die. The graphics are pretty good and the soundtrack is nice. The level design has some good points and some flaws. Although every room is unique in its design and I enjoyed the variety, there aren’t that many different platforming and puzzle challenges, which I attribute to the low amount of abilities. What I really like about the level design is the connection between all the rooms and that a lot of the rooms have a fast route for backtracking. Backtracking doesn’t feel tedious. In addition, the level design is really well-thought-out. Although you can explore areas you can’t advance in yet, getting permastuck isn’t possible as far as I can tell. I can’t say anything about the story because I didn’t read the notes you find throughout the game, which I probably should have but realised too late. The platforming, combat and puzzle elements aren’t particularly challenging, depending on your skill.
This game was fun but short. I hope the developers will expand on this game, it has way more potential. They have a solid foundation to make a really great game. Expand the world, introduce new abilities for more platforming and puzzle elements, improve the combat system, include some boss fights and raise the sales price because it will be worth it. Although the current game is short, it’s definitely worth a purchase for this low price.

EDIT AFTER MORE PLAYTIME
I tried to give the game a second chance since the developer responded to the review.  I still would not reccomend it.
The tool tips and gameplay cues about what happens when you say advertise with your game, versus advertise for the company as a whole are not remotely clear.  The lack of save functionality is crippling in realtime game with poor and non customizable autopause features.  Trying to get the information about say what games are popular is on a totally different screen than the one that offer syou contract and it 3 or 4 clicks away.
The whole bank makes little sense, the loan terms are all wrong.  You ae only charged interest once, it is not amortized.  So you can get a $100k loan for 1 year for a one time 7%, or over 25 years for a one time 30%...which do you think is a better deal?  Loans don't actually work that way.  A 1 year 7% loan indeed costs you ~$107k, but a 25 year 30% loan costs you $750k NOT $130.
There is a good game here somewhere with a better interface and so more clear tool tips and fat cutting of needless features and more focus on the game development portion of game, but uggh what a chore to play right now.

This is a nice little stealth game with a fun mechanic in being able to rewire the level.  It was a good game with some fun dialogue and decision-making.  I was surprised that I actually cared about the choices I was making in the meta-game.
I have a few complaints though.  I feel like the game was a good concept which hadn't been fully fleshed out.  There's a lot more that could be done with this mechanic.  There should be more to wire up than just switches, lights, and doors.  I wish there had been more complicated systems to navigate and control.  It didn't take long to completely master the game.
I also noticed a few glitches where the game would occasionally freeze briefly or kinda wig out.  It always recovered, but it was definitely annoying.  I think it may have had something to do with playing the game in windowed mode on a Mac.  Beats me.
Lastly, the game is not particularly long.  I wasn't bothered by the length, especially since the mechanics were somewhat limited as I mentioned before.  But it's short enough that I would have felt cheated had I spent very much on the game.

Having loved the first two installements and all of its DLCs, I was really looking forward to SP3.
However, I'm sorry to say that if you expected SP3 to follow in the footsteps of its predecessors, you'll be as disapointed as I was.
SP3 isn't BAD.  It's just a bad Spellforce title.  The game is mostly now an RPG with some RTS campaigns spread out on SOME maps.  If you were looking for a nice evening of base and army building, SP3 isn't the game for you.  I played 30 hours so far and maybe 5 of those were spent playing the base building part.  The rest was spent exploring dungeons with my heroes, doing fetch quests, talking to NPCs and rotating the camera to find loot.
Like mainstream RPGs, you can customize your hero and its skills, talk to your companions, build a relationship with them, ask them about their past and motivations, talk to NPCs and do endless fetch quests.  You know... the BORING part of an SP title, which mostly occupies 70% of your time in SP3.  I usually love doing these things in games like Dragon Age but in SP3, the plot and characters just aren't interesting enough for me to invest in them.
It'll even take a few hours of gameplay until you reach your first point in the game where you can build your base and your army unlike previous titles where you pretty much started doing just that... and never really stopped doing it, map after map.
As far graphics go, it's very very very very cluttered.  It also doesn't help that your heroes and all of the NPCs are tiny little ants on your screen and that all of these tall buildings hide everything in sight.  In dungeons, you'll spend a LOT of time trying to rotate the camera to see what the hell is going on.
As for the plot, it's pretty much a mashup of all 3 Dragon Age games.  Mages are bad, they're persecuted, the chantry (err, Purity) want them either dead or serving the Maker (errr, Aonir, the all father).  There's a blight (hur hur) of a plague going on and you're supposed to fix it.  You then go into the deep roads (err, Mulandir) to search clues among the Sheparate (err, Shapers).
I'll keep on playing it until I'm done with it ('cause I can't just NOT finish a game) but I end up pausing often out of boredom or frustration.  I think after that I'll go replay SP1 for the 10th time to cleanse my gaming palet.  Or play Dragon Age.

I really like this game.
Gunpoint is a game in which you play a private detective who specializes in hacking who delves deep into a strange mystery about a murder.
I really like the game's mechanics, and not just the hacking mechanics in which you hack stuff like a light switch, a door, security camera, trap door, and if you upgrade a guards gun. My favorite mechanic is the high jumping mechanic. One of the first gadgets you are introduced to is this pair of high-jump pants, in which you just jump around high and fast like that one scene in Man of Steel where Superman is constantly jumping around and eventually learns to fly (I am sorry for comparing this game to a mediocre movie, this was the only way I can best describe the high jump mechanic). It also adds to the fun of the stealth.
Oh yeah this is also a stealth game, meaning don't be seen by enemies. In addition you also get more rewarded for not killing enemies, making less noise as possible, and hacking extra laptops.
One thing I didn't really like about the game was the story. It wasn't bad, I was just like "ok" at every dialogue segment that gives me a mission briefing and tells whats going on in the story. I read through it, but I just immediately forgot about it. Hence why I kind of described the plot of this game a bit vaguely. One thing I did like about the dialogue segments was that you can pick how you can respond to them. You can either be snarky and witty, or all around series. They do however affect the story and missions so pick wisely.
One criticism I hear about the game is that it is too short, in to which that I say. Yeah it is kind of short. About 3-2 hours at best.
There is still some good replay value though like a level editor, community made levels, and the achievements.
Overall, Gunpoint is a really fun game. I enjoyed it despite it's length and kind of forgettable story (not saying the story was bad, I just skimmed past it just to get to play the levels). Gunpoint is a bit flawed but none of the less still worth checking out. However I highly recommend getting it when it is on sale. None of the less, still a great game.

Gunpoint is a 2-D stealth puzzle/action game about a for-hire spy, and is probably one of the best games about stealth that I've played to date.
The mechanics are solid, the story is quite good, and while the game is sort of short, workshop integration makes the fun last longer with player-made levels.
The game's first mechanic involves how the player can traverse the enviorment. You can cling onto walls and the ceiling and move around on them, and can also perform massive leaps that can latch you onto said walls, smash you through windows, and tackle stuff, all with adjustable power and a trajectory displayed.
The major focus of the game is how you can rewire electrical systems to change their behavior, making a lightswitch open a door, or an elevator arriving at a floor cause a power outlet to shock someone, knocking them out. You can do it from anywhere on the map, meaning that you don't need to actually be there to mess with systems. There are also different colors of systems, and while red is always available at the start, the blue, green, yellow, and pink systems (the ones actually accessible depending on the number of systems and their chosen colors) must first be compromised through a terminal that corresponds to their type. Systems may not intermingle, so a red-system door cannot be opened by a blue-system switch, forming the foundation of a puzzle as the player works out what switches must be pressed to accomplish which goals, and in what order, and at what time.
However, this is not all that the game has to offer. The mechanics of the hacking system are intertwined with the NPCs that patrol each level. Getting caught by an NPC almost always means instant death, so the player must work around the NPCs to solve the puzzles presented by each level. For example, an NPC walking through a motion detector can be exploited by connecting it to a door, which opens the door as the NPC patrols through the detector, granting the player entry.
This is, however, not the only viable strategy that the game offers. You can tackle 2/3 types of guards and punch them, rendering them unconcious, or killing them to eliminate a witness. You can drop any guard type down pits, killing them, or push them off of buildings or out of windows, also killing them. However, each mission has a set of optional missions that may force you to consider a different playstyle, such as leaving no witnesses or causing no harm, including knocking people out. However, flexibility still exists. Leaving no witnesses either means don't get caught, or kill everyone, and causing no harm doesn't mean you can't get caught, just don't get shot.
After each mission, you gain an upgrade point and some money to use to purchase new equipment. This equipment can help you to alter your playstyle to revolve around being more agressive, such as using the quite expensive gun, being more sneaky, such as being able to silently break glass, or being more manipulative, such as being able to rewire the guns of NPCs to trigger things instead of firing.
The game has dialogue sections at the start and end of missions, and the player is presented with three choices of response, one of which is usually very snarky and sarcastic.
Speaking of humor, this game has a good sense of it. Dialogue can sometimes be humorous, the achievements are quite funny, and the game tries not to take itself TOO seriously, but can, when needed, do just that.
It's hard to describe Gunpoint without saying that it's just great. The combination of stealth and puzzles is done beautifully, and the story and humor work well together and separately. In conclusion, stop reading and buy the damn game.

What happens when a game is developed and instead of focusing on a core idea, it puts all the ideas into the game.
Answer:  E.Y.E. Divine Cybermancy.
Now let me get this out of the way.  This is a fantastic achievement for 10 people, it has an amazing level of design and programming included, more systems than most people even attempt to conquer, and some very novel ideas.
And yet it doesn't work.  Instead of just a typical game like Bioshock where you can shoot or use plasmids, in EYE you have cyber attacks, gun attacks, psiotics, drones, inventory management, hacking, and stealth.   And that there is both the benefit and negative.
Yes you can play this game your way (Though it appears you need to be able to hack)  Which is an interesting idea.  However there is so much going on the player will be overwhelmed quickly in this game.
Every system is overly complicated as well.  Let's just look at the shooting system, there's many different types of weapons, each with it's own bullet type... well here's the problem with that system, it is also completely realistic.  Reload? You lose your ammo.  Want 10 magazines? you better have 10 slots.   And you WILL go through that ammo fast.  Want to pick up an item of a specific size? Better have the slot for it.   All this goes on at a breakneck speed as well.
The real problem of the game is every system is like this, overly complicated, overly deep, and the player is expected to deal with these systems as fast as possible from the first moment.   What's worse is there's a bare bones tutorial system.  That means there IS a tutorial, but at the same time, the tutorial really doesn't have enough to help the player get comfortable in the system.  The fact is there's enough systems in the game to support 4 games, but because it never is delivered in a clear way, the player is left floundering.
If you're willing to spend a long time learning how to play this game, you'll find a deep and engrossing world... but it's kind of hard to get over that initial hump.
Of course all that ignores one final fact.. this is a source engine game.  Which means the UI is horrific... And that's really off putting.   A shame, because I think a good UI might have actually helped this game more than everything, and the developers REALLY try to make the UI work...I just don't think it really is there yet.

Alchemist's Castle is an exploratory platformer that tries to channel Metroidvania titles, and at least for its price does a decent job doing so.
The artwork is quite decent, which is why I picked it up. Upon playing it, I found several flaws (as documented below), but the developers are open to criticism and have made changes based on the issues I encountered with the game.
While there's still a few flaws within the game, such as the nondescript rooms mentioned below, I think that if you like exploration platformers, it's worth picking up for its price of a buck.
-----------------
Original review here for archival purposes:
Alchemist's Castle is an exploratory platformer that tries to channel Metroidvania titles but kind of fails doing so.
While I understand that this is a very low budget title, I would not recommend playing it, as there are some fatal flaws that make the game fairly uninteresting.
Given its price, the art is surprisingly decent (and was the main reason I picked this up), but beyond that it kind of falls apart.
I'll start with the map: It's pretty hard to decipher, doesn't have a "you are here" marker - at least as far as I could tell.
Moving along, the font used makes reading the plot scrolls unbearable, at least to me.
There is no indicator that you took damage. Occasionally I think I took fall damage but I'm not sure if that is true or if I grazed an enemy/trap. There is no way to tell.
The progression and level design are... lackluster. These two tie together because whenever I got a powerup, I still didn't know where to go, since the rooms all are so nondescript, and the maze-like construction of the world makes it very hard to remember which path to take for areas where you may have been stuck in before - the map of course doesn't help.
For now, I would recommend you to skip this game, though if some of the issues are cleared up, it definitely has potential as a low budget title.

I've only played about an hour so far but that is enough to know that it is a good game, especially for the price.
It is mostly an exploration game, with block pushing puzzles, tricky jumps and some light (so far) combat against enemies that are more obstacles than threats. You have to explore to find the power-ups that let you reach places you couldn't before. There will be a lot of back-tracking within the maze of inter-connected screens.
Note: When starting a game, selecting "Dynamic" map will only show screens you have visited, and highlight the one you are on. Selecting "Static" will show you the whole map and where all the power-ups are, but not show you the screen you are on. This makes it very difficult to navigate with the map, so I'd recommend "Dynamic".
You pick up scrolls along the way that piece together the story, which I am admittedly not paying much attention to yet, partly because the font is hard to read. It does keep all the text of the scrolls in a journal so you can read it any time.
It uses checkpoints, and they seem to be spaced fairly well.
The controls, graphics and sound are surprisingly good, compared to your average lower-priced platformer.

This game deserves a more in depth review than it has had yet, so I'll do my best.
Between the campaign and the puzzles there is some good content that will make you think hard.
The Campaign's final battle was suitably epic.  Unfortunately, beating the campaign and trying all of the puzzles and only failing on 2 out of 17 puzzles, both of which I think were bugged, only took me 13.8 hours.  paying the 6 USD sale price for 13.8 hours of good fun, I think I got my money's worth, but I've had better deals.
what would give this endless hours of fun would be if the multiplayer or offline vs. CPU modes were good.  Unfortunately I've tried searching for multiplayer games without being able to find any.  It seems like this game got buried in mass of games being produced nowadays and noone bought it, so unless you have a steam friend you can buy this game for and convince to play it with you or this game shocks everyone with a second wind of sales then multiplayer just isnt going to happen.  Multiplayer also lacks a menu where you could potentialy see what other players games are going on and have an option to observe those games if those players allowed observers into their games.
the Offline VS. CPU mode didn't impress me either.  This and multiplayer are the only modes where you can build your deck from the full complement of cards in the game.  The Campaign, while fun, doesnt even use a deck in 6 of the 9 missions, and when it does use a deck, your card choices are heavily limited.  Unfortunately, the CPU AI is pretty bad, so I can't realy test what cards are good or bad effectively in the VS. CPU mode.  Another feature I would have liked to see for the VS CPU mode would have been the ability to play with or give the CPU a random deck.  there is no random deck option, you have to pick your opponents deck, so you know what they have.
One thing that disappointed me from Steam's side is that in the window for "similar to games I play" on this game's store page, it didn't list Pox Nora.  This game is infact similar to Pox Nora and less buggy than that game.  Last I played Pox Nora was like 2 years ago though but I have over 390 hours in that game.
Overall I'll give this game a 6.8/10  I wanted to give it a higher score, and I still do reccomend it.  It is good fun and takes a good amount of thinking hard for about 13.8 hours.  Understand that if you do buy it, chances are you probably wont find yourself playing it much longer than that.

Edit; Crap. You put me on the front page, here is a real review.
Let me start this honestly. I am totally biased. If My Heart Had Wings is the first Visual Novel I ever played, and I love it with all of my little heart. Also in case you didn't notice I've played this game for more than 900 hours, and only 20 of those hours were idle. I've run through each route in this game at least 15 times, and I can actually speak really crappy Japanese because of this game. In addition, I've spent more money on this game for the badges, emoticons, cards, extra cards and backgrounds.
So yeah, I am biased.
If you chose to continue thanks, and here's the review;
The good parts of this game are extremely good, and the bad parts of this game are extremely bad.
So here is the good.
1. The characters are well fleshed out, being both fully voice acted and having logical lives and choices. Sure each of them are anime tropes, but the tropes are presented so well that they work here. Ageha is the generic tomboy, Kotori is trapped in a wheel chair, Amane is the innocent genius, the twin's are polar opposites of eachother that rarely agree. Ageha's suggestive dialogue makes you smile, and Kotori's fears are understandable. Even Amane's childlike innocence is presented in conjunction with her hopes for the future, and living up to what it means to be an adult.
2. Next is the art, it's not the crazy excess.....of certain areas.....of the Sakura series, or the strange realism of more "American" anime. Here the character's are mostly normal. This is a personal preference, but I certainly appreciate it.
3. The routes are also well done. Kotori's, of course, is the main route and does have the most story, and in the words of most reviewers "it got da feels". But, personally, Kotori is not my favorite route. I enjoy Ageha's more, as a matter of fact Ageha's route was the first I completed. Her personality develops as much as Kotori's on the route and becomes as complex as Kotori's. The same happens with Amane's route. The twins' routes are probably the least interesting, but still work well.
There is more good like the soundtrack, the dialogue, and the story itself but it's time to move onto the bad stuff.
1. Moenovel, and censoring. These are probably the most obvious problems. The game was originally published in Japan, and was translated by Moenovel. They did a pretty crappy job of it. Not only are their many horrible typos, and brutal censorship, they also directly detract from the story. One moment in particular always breaks the immersion. At one point Ageha is explaing that a women can control any man with her big, bouncy, round....eyes. Now, we all know that "eyes" is definetely not the right word. This comment which could have gotten a laugh without censorship really crushes me. I have played this game with the fan-created restoration patch, but it is agony to install.
Overall, I think this game gains a solid 8/10 for most people and a 9.5/10 for me, mostly due to nostalgia. Definetely worth the purchase at full price, and a steal for less than $5.

If my heart has wings, winner of several visual novel game awards, is an all-ages visual novel that is available on Steam. If My Heart Had Wings is a romance title centering around a high school glider club known as the “Soaring Club.” It is a touching story about loss, love, and passion which is an enjoyable read from start to finish. There are 5 routes in total and all of them had happy moments and depressing moments. It’s hard not to get invested in a character emotionally when they have so much detail put into them.
If My Heart Had Wings had several explicit sex scenes upon its original release in Japan. However, all of these scenes have been cut wholesale from the game and additional nude scenes have been heavily edited in the Western version. Therefore I will not be talking about the adult version.
Aoi Minase returns with shattered dreams to his hometown of Kazegaura. There, atop a hill lined with windmills, he encounters a wheelchair-bound girl, Kotori Habane, and a beautiful, white glider soaring through the sky. Together, they decide to revive their school’s Soaring Club in order to ride the “Morning Glory”, a cloud known to appear once in a blue moon on the wind that blows across Kazegaura.
The characters has a diverse and well-rounded cast. There is Ageha, the childhood best friend character who is transitioning from tom boy into a popular girl; Amane, an eccentric genius who has repeatedly failed her senior year in order to remain in the Soaring Club; Asa, the cute, excitable freshman; and Yoru, Asa’s twin sister, seemingly polar opposite; and Kotori the main girl of the story, Kotori, is by far the most interesting character. She is your typical tsundere but have a physical disability,of not being able to use her legs and much of the story focuses on her dealing with her disability of overcoming it and while dealing with the psychological effect of her being a teenage girl not being able to walk on her own.
I generally enjoyed the overall art and
of the game, the background art is really beautiful with vibrant colors being used and the environment is absolutely stunning. Character designs are top-notch too with beautiful CG’s.
The
i really loved it has a full Japanese audio for all of the girls, and side characters combined with a well fitting soundtrack sets the mood and feel like it belongs in the situation and the environment.
Overall i feel that there is not many flaws i can find in this visual novel other than it gives way too much information about gilders that turn some point of the story from interesting to boring and some “typo” plus bad translation.
I would definitely recommend this great title from MOE novel, it’s a title not to be missed as this is something that will be a deep, engaging experience.

Don't care if friends see this review.
If My Heart Had Wings was the second visual novel I ever read, and it's the only one I've re-read multiple times. The visuals, the music, the characters and the story always have me coming back for more. The story, spoiler free, is that of Aoi (lol girl's name) returning to his hometown to find that many things have changed. He takes on a job as the caretaker of an all female dorm and [skipping a bit] gets sexy with lots of waifu material.
I can't say it's my favorite romance story of all time, as the story in each of the 5 routes tends to focus a lot on the state of the glider and everyone's shared dream of reconstructing and flying above a rare natural phenomenon. There's just enough romance to call it a romance game, and yet the relationships seem more real for the fact that it's a by-product of coming together with a shared goal in mind. It doesn't deal with any social issues, nor does it strive to leave some deep message ingrained in your subconscious that is intended to change your life somehow. It's just pure, fun storytelling.
I'm aware of some issues using the (highly recommended) restoration patch on Win8, but it's been solved on Win10.
PROS
-LONG, can spend upwards of 15 hours per route if you listen to all the audio
-Visuals are (mostly) top notch
-Soundtrack (buy it)
-It's a feel-good novel. Minimal tragedy, happy endings
-Duck with tophat

-Sexy times, if you download the patch.

CONS
-Some minor disply issues with non-background images and motion, relics left (got cockblocked by Hat on my first playthrough, was on screen for 2 different... "encounters")
-Not much focus on romance, more about Soaring Club narrative
-Bunch of censored, unintelligble Engrish bull spit in the vanilla

In conclusion. the visuals and soundtrack are 10/10, the story is 9/10. This game has me coming back for more every few months, and I wouldn't want it any other way.  Download this if you call yourself a VN fan: you'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll have a lot of spare tissues in the trash can, you'll get a warm fuzzy feeling. If only my heart had wings...

This is a review for the single player campaign.
RTS:
- Your own units are dumb as bricks and need to be microed constantly while the AI attacks on all fronts all day, every day.
- There is no defensive posture. It's either hold or attack, in which case your units will scatter across the map and die.
- There are no formations or otherwise tactical mechanics. Build more units = you win.
- The resource and outpost system is interesting, but base building is an afterthought otherwise. There is no variety in build order whatsoever. There are no walls or interesting defensive structures. People who like to turtle up and/or build good looking bases are out of luck. This game is about rushing only.
- The AI seems to cheat even at normal difficulty, churning out troops much faster than possible. Even when the player controls almost all outposts (which gives the player access to resources and workers), they just keep on coming.
- Uninteresting tech.
- Boring units.
- The AI spams the map full of buildings. Since you need villagers to crew them and you only have a limited amount per outpost, most of them are pointless.
RPG:
- Meagre hero skill trees, with lame spells and abilities.
- An annoying active skill system that limits the heroes to three active skills at a time. Changing the active skill set is possible via hotkey, but this is just bad game design. There's no auto casting either, which would've helped since literally everything needs to be micro managed.
- Targetting individual units is a pain in large battles.
- Some skills, like elemental infusion, just don't work.
The game was launched riddled with bugs. Many things have been patched, but it wasn't launched in an acceptable state.
I wanted this to be good, like its predecessors. It's not. It does neither RPG, nor RTS well.
The graphics are gorgeous and the story is interesting, but gameplay-wise Spellforce 3 falls flat on its face.
I regret buying it.

Gunpoint is a 2-D stealth puzzle/action game about a for-hire spy, and is probably one of the best games about stealth that I've played to date.
The mechanics are solid, the story is quite good, and while the game is sort of short, workshop integration makes the fun last longer with player-made levels.
The game's first mechanic involves how the player can traverse the enviorment. You can cling onto walls and the ceiling and move around on them, and can also perform massive leaps that can latch you onto said walls, smash you through windows, and tackle stuff, all with adjustable power and a trajectory displayed.
The major focus of the game is how you can rewire electrical systems to change their behavior, making a lightswitch open a door, or an elevator arriving at a floor cause a power outlet to shock someone, knocking them out. You can do it from anywhere on the map, meaning that you don't need to actually be there to mess with systems. There are also different colors of systems, and while red is always available at the start, the blue, green, yellow, and pink systems (the ones actually accessible depending on the number of systems and their chosen colors) must first be compromised through a terminal that corresponds to their type. Systems may not intermingle, so a red-system door cannot be opened by a blue-system switch, forming the foundation of a puzzle as the player works out what switches must be pressed to accomplish which goals, and in what order, and at what time.
However, this is not all that the game has to offer. The mechanics of the hacking system are intertwined with the NPCs that patrol each level. Getting caught by an NPC almost always means instant death, so the player must work around the NPCs to solve the puzzles presented by each level. For example, an NPC walking through a motion detector can be exploited by connecting it to a door, which opens the door as the NPC patrols through the detector, granting the player entry.
This is, however, not the only viable strategy that the game offers. You can tackle 2/3 types of guards and punch them, rendering them unconcious, or killing them to eliminate a witness. You can drop any guard type down pits, killing them, or push them off of buildings or out of windows, also killing them. However, each mission has a set of optional missions that may force you to consider a different playstyle, such as leaving no witnesses or causing no harm, including knocking people out. However, flexibility still exists. Leaving no witnesses either means don't get caught, or kill everyone, and causing no harm doesn't mean you can't get caught, just don't get shot.
After each mission, you gain an upgrade point and some money to use to purchase new equipment. This equipment can help you to alter your playstyle to revolve around being more agressive, such as using the quite expensive gun, being more sneaky, such as being able to silently break glass, or being more manipulative, such as being able to rewire the guns of NPCs to trigger things instead of firing.
The game has dialogue sections at the start and end of missions, and the player is presented with three choices of response, one of which is usually very snarky and sarcastic.
Speaking of humor, this game has a good sense of it. Dialogue can sometimes be humorous, the achievements are quite funny, and the game tries not to take itself TOO seriously, but can, when needed, do just that.
It's hard to describe Gunpoint without saying that it's just great. The combination of stealth and puzzles is done beautifully, and the story and humor work well together and separately. In conclusion, stop reading and buy the damn game.
