In any discussion about art, you’re almost destined to find someone who proudly declares that true art is subjective. This is the argument that one man’s trash is another man’s treasure; that what is a Picasso to one, is a crude finger painting to another. It's also most likely the argument The Path's defenders have ready to deploy, for when you finally stumble to its conclusion and begin to wildly question everyone as to why it’s so terrible... It’s all “subjective”, they'll proudly declare. You just don’t get it. The reality, however, is that this couldn’t be further from the truth – put simply, The Path’s a really bad game.

It’s a total mess of ideas from the very beginning. Pick a character, and you’re thrown into the wild with instructions to visit your Grandmother and – crucially – to stay on the path. If by some chance you actually like following instructions and adhere to this command, all the game ever entails is walking in a straight line and then slowly plodding through a house. Do this, and the ending screen promptly screams “FAILURE” at you without ever explaining why, leaving you with nothing but a mix of confusion and boredom to slowly try and make sense of in your head.

Things don’t get much better in the much more likely scenario that you defy orders and wander off into the woods. You’re faced with a bland and repetitive landscape, desperately trying to seek one of the sparse points of interest that are scattered within. All the while, things happen around you seemingly without rhyme or reason. To list; Cryptic text and images flash on the screen seemingly at random, with the camera spinning around erratically the moment you find anything that might be remotely interesting.  There’s 144 collectables dotted around that truly and honestly serve no purpose whatsoever. Sometimes a girl appears and sometimes she doesn’t. Add on top of that a soundtrack that aims to be unsettling but just proves annoying, and you've got a cacophony of ideas that - put simply - combine together in a way that made me want to cry out in physical pain.

It’s only via finding a guide online that I actually achieved a semblance of what I was meant to be trying to do, which says a lot as to how vague this game really is with its concept. The aim, you see, is to use each girl to track down something that represents their “wolf”. Do so, and you’ll be treated to a scene whereupon… Uh… Things happen. Then you wake up outside your grandmother’s house, walk up to it at a pace which is so criminally slow it made me want to toss my computer out the window, then wander through its interior as… Well… More stuff occurs, I guess?

I’m not just joking around here. I honestly had no real idea what was meant to be going on most of the time. Never mind what it meant - half the time I couldn't even work out what the heck I was supposed to be looking at in the first place. Manage to complete this torment with one character and you’re simply looped back to the start to do it with someone else. And, with only another mess of random imagery to look forward to, it’s going to take a herculean effort to power playing through everyone and reaching the actual ending. It’s never fun, never interesting, and only achieves the lofty goal of being confusing on a never-ending basis.

This, as you may have guessed already, creates a situation whereupon it’s impossible for your journey to have any sort of meaning to it. Trying to pick apart a deeper meaning to all of this is incredibly difficult; the astute among you may have picked up on the parallels between this game and the tale of Little Red Riding Hood, with the mentions of wolves and grandmothers, but to be honest that’s by far the easiest thing to pluck from the chaos. The real Aesop seems to be that you shouldn’t stray from the path of innocence and virtue into sin… Yet it was only by deciphering the few pieces of content I could possibly hope to understand, as well as reading way too much discussion about the game online, that I ever really reached this conclusion. Before that, I simply didn’t have a clue.

And that’s the biggest problem, in the end. The Path is just too vague, too buried within its own pretentiousness and artistic beliefs, to even begin to qualify as anything that has actual emotional impact or – more importantly – simply be fun to play. Just don’t buy this. There are so many other indie games out there which manage to be more powerful or entertaining than this by a country mile; and it’s those paths that you should really be setting your sights on to walk down in the future.

"Styx: Master of Shadows" is a good game.  It's got its issues (see below), but in general I enjoyed it.  The graphics and voice acting are good (though I see that some people don't much care for Styx's voice), the plot is tolerable (though it falls down a bit by the end), and the stealth is well done.   My listing of the problems looks like a lot, but I still felt that the game was well done and definitely worth the price (60.8 hours to finish the game with all Achievements).  My complaints (not problems) are:
- I wish we had an option for non-lethal take downs.  Change the environment depending upon the body count (see Dishonored)
- My biggest complaint with the game is the highly prevalent swearing.  It's unnecessary, incongruous, and childish.  Heck, it's embarassing.  Other people in the house can hear those f-bombs and s**ts echoing down the hall.  I've seen comments that the swearing is necessary to set the tone.  But, I say horse-puckey.  The developers have total control over the graphics, sound, storyline, text, etc..  They've spent millions of dollars producing this.  If they need language from any high-school locker room in the country to set the tone, they're in the wrong business.  If they need someone to swear, put it into cultural context.  Say something like "by the Tree's big hairy root" or something.  Tolkien managed to set the tone of his evil-doers without a potty mouth and all he had was paper and ink.
- The placement of the tokens we need to find needs improving.  It gets annoying to have to grab a token from right under a guard's nose time and time again.  Put those things in odd places throughout the environment to promote full exploration instead.
Actual problems:
- In the Deliverance 2 mission, the developers use a very high frequency tone either for music or for background noise.  It's utterly horrible and pain inducing.  People have been complaining about it for over a year and it's still there.  It needs to be removed.
- In the Architect 3 mission, the secondary mission resets itself to "not done" when you talk to your main objective.  The only way to keep that secondary mission "done" is to do it AFTER talking to the main objective.
Again, that looks like a big list.  But, those issues aren't big enough to detract all that much from the game.  So, I'm definitley recommending it.

Story: The story isn't much neither is it well developed. With a lot of flaws and only partly out characters it's not really interesting to follow. However a few parts were quite entertaining but not worth following the rest of it.
Gameplay: As a game that focuses completely on stealth the stealth mechanics aren't good enough. The half decent mechanics were playable but not at all acceptable. Some weren't quite thought through and others not enough developed.
The combat mechanic was more or less awful due to the lock-on system which made combat unnecessarily difficult as the camera keeps spinning around and it completely disrupts the flow of the stealth which easily could have been fixed by removing the lock on system or putting more effort into it. Otherwise the combat mechanics are decent even though in my opinion not every enemy should have an unlimited amount of range attacks when a special unit/enemy exist for this purpose.
Graphics: The visuals are good, not nearly any triple A title but still good. The video sequences and animations are often asynchronous or wrong, but still acceptable. However during my gameplay many visual bugs occurred where some sequences wouldn't be played at all or be played wrong, which didn't really bother since the content of such was irrelevant and I only noticed it while looking up a walkthrough.
Level-Design: The level design is great, A+, many possible path as it should be for a stealth game. Sometimes some parts were to difficult or bad initialized and some a little bit too difficult to understand due to visual problems. However only a little bit more work on that one and it reaches it's best.
More: The hitboxes of many objects are wrong which led to many bugs (positiv and negativ). Though some of the bugs were funny and quite amusing they should be fixed (for example the character starting to fly when trying to engage certain walls). Enemies often attacked through supposedly solid walls or saw the character in spots where they weren't supposed to. It also felled wrong to walk around certain objects (barrels for instance) in a square whilst the visual shows a circle.
In short: The game does not seem to be ready to be sold yet and isn't worth anything near it's original price. I recommend not buying it unless it is on sale for 5€, maybe 10€ maximum. However I recommend the developers to continue their work and put more effort into precise programming and further story development.

Spellforce 3 has potential but in its current state it is a failed attempt to merge RPG with RTS.
Pros:
1. Astonishing visuals. There is detail in every pixel.
2. Well written campaign. It keeps you entertained and most of the time you are not bored of character conservation.
Cons:
1. Too much visual detail presented in a window. Paths, hallways are obstructed and collectibles are hard to see and find. You quickly get lost in the map. After an hour of gameplay I get a headache because of overstressing my eyes.
2. No tactical pause feature implemented which is a must for any real-time RPG. There is no way to pause the game when you swap equipment of your characters. Also tactical positioning of your characters is a requirement on higher difficulties. But since there is no pause you have to micromanage everything in real-time. RTS controls does not let you do that so you have to move every single one of your characters one by one to different  locations within 2 seconds to avoid the whirlwind of the enemy hero. The game tests only your micromanaging skills.
3. Minimap is poorly implemented. You cannot enlarge it without pressing M (which creates a window). The terrain is also rendered on the minimap so you cannot see the pathways between points of interest clearly. Different unit and building types are not presented on the minimap. Everything on the minimap is basically a blue square. It is really hard to find your way around on the minimap and also in game.
4. Units&minions are ridiculously weak. The game turns itself from an RTS to a spawn unit festival because there is no tactics left within it. The lifetime of an average unit (a recruit, a scout etc) is usually 0.5-1 seconds in battle so empowering your units with auras or even healing them will not extend this duration more than half a second plus your characters lose focus by doing so. It is usually a better idea to reserve your focus for massive aoe attacks to clean-out enemy minions rather than empovering your own. Or for taking down enemy heroes with burst damage skills. Minions are basically meat-shields for your heroes nothing else.  Basically whoever spawns more units (hotkeyed barracks for unit spawning) and keeps the meat-shield running wins the game.
5. There is only one unit formation in the game which is the rectangular formation. Basically you drag your mouse with RMB pressed for this. Other than that there is no formation support. You cannot say for instance that you want you archer hero to follow your melee heroes at a distance behind them. This can be done in all RPGs starting from Baldur's Gate to Pillars of Eternity.
6. The game does not provide enough information about the attributes or skills. For instance you cannot see the explainations of 2nd levels' of the attributes you pick without picking the first level. You cannot know what weapons you can use and what you can't before assigning your strength and dexterity. I.e. all greatswords in the game require some dexterity. But the explanations mislead you.
7. There is no fast-run feature in the game. Seriously... You have to wait for your characters to go from one location to another doing nothing for minutes of time. Most of the time this constitutes at least one third of the game play time. This is not a requirement for the skirmish mode but for campaign it is a must to have feature. Worse than this you cannot event alt+tab to read about the recent news on your browser while you wait for your characters to get to their destinations.
8. The fun ends once you complete the campaign. There is no free sandbox mode or anything in which you can progress through while you level and gear up your characters. Once you consume the campaign the game turns into a regular RTS. And acquiring gear and leveling up in an RTS style skirmish breaks the purpose of the game being half RPG. This is because the skirmish will not take more than an hour and your characters will not be persistent.
9. Area loading times in the campaign are insane for a 2017 game. And I have the game on a 1 TB Samsung SSD drive. Even that can't reduce the loading times to a sane time.

Mmm... okay, I better get this review over with.
This is a dating sim, essentially. Though chances are you already figured it out. I ended up grabbing this on a whim at one point and eventually got around to playing it. As far as these sorts of games go, much is as you expect: high school, male lead with no voice acting, and a bunch of female leads that are some personality archetype with some added twists (like the Tsundere being bound to a wheelchair). What is new is the sheer volume of info this game throws at you about aerodynamics, and while that was interesting... its more info than the game needed.
Actually, having "too much" is something I can throw at this game in a general way. It takes ~15 hours or so to go through one of the routes, but it feels longer than that as it is slow paced and has huge gaps where little of interest happens. This is not helped by the game having so few choices (and very simple ones at that) it almost feels like a Kinetic Novel (please be one or the other). In truth, I didn't even read all the text in this game because after the first playthrough (Kotori) I started skipping large amounts of dialogue that I hadn't seen yet because I knew nothing interesting was going to end up happening in a particular scene. Or rather, since basically every route of this game ultimately ends up in the same place, the "new" scene was basically the exact scene again with perhaps some slightly altered text. A VN that does this... has a pretty serious problem.
Another thing this VN has too much of is drama. Now... drama is good, and some of my favorite VN's live off of it (Steins;Gate, Clannad, Little Busters!). But unlike those games, the drama here feels... fake somehow. The biggest story problems come from scenes that involve this teacher who has a MASSIVE petty grudge against your club and its long-standing member, Amane. He has "reasons", but he comes across as the most petty of fools desperately trying to cling to what little authority they might have in a feeble attempt to try to seem relevant. It does not help that, aside from Amane's storyline, you never find out what his weak excuses for being a massive jackass are. Unfortunately, since one of the most recent  "new" anime/VN's i've watched/played was Higurashi... I spent much of my time while playing this game thinking of all the fun ways I wish this teacher would die horribly. And it never happened. Where is Sonozaki Shion when you need her? :(
Up to this point, you probably think I'm going to give this game a negative review. And trust me... this game is a hair away from me having done so. However, for much of what this game gets wrong, it gets too many other things right for me to do that and feel confident in doing so. Either that or I'm just sick of getting my negative reviews panned simply for being negative.
So what does this game do right? Well, the characters can be quite interesting and some of them are better than average. Kotori, while far from my favorite character, has a rather serious and memorable storyline about overcoming her personal tragedy (being unable to walk due to an accident) and what that does to a young girl psychologically who had lived a normal life up until that point. The other routes are a mixed bag: Ageha's was hard to enjoy, Amane's was filled with drama but ultimately heartwarming, Asa's was nice and huggly, and Yoru's was... weird. It was Yoru who ended up being my favorite character simply by being a snarky genius (she kinda reminded me of Makise Kurisu from Steins;Gate) that was a massive breath of fresh air in the second half of the game. In a game filled with airheads or the often-depressed, Yoru was entertaining and made me laugh quite alot. Sad that she and her twin Asa are lolis and that her route was... what it was.
The side characters tend to be pretty good too, except for that teacher and the idiot male tsundere Masatsugu. Kanako was fun too, though having her being the fan service girl by walking around half-dressed for much of her screentime was lame. Another character worth mentioning is Tatsuya, or A-chan, who sadly doesn't get much screen time but would have been great if he did. He kinda reminded me of being an older grown-up version of Natsume Kyousuke from Little Busters!, though Kyousuke is still better. Also the art was pretty good. Mostly.
Ultimately, if it wasn't for Yoru, story moments that were genuinely heartwarming, and the pretty art, I would have given this game a bad review. Maybe i've just played too many VN's lately and seen too many similar but better things that I am being much more mean to this game than I otherwise would have. My two recent VN's were Higurashi (woohoo paranoid terror) and Eden (;_;), both of which were quite good (Higurashi especially). This game just does not compare well compared to those, but I can't call it bad without feeling a little dishonest. But just barely.
One last thing: the translation is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Also this game has very heavy (and uneven) censorship, but I don't want to get into that issue because its been brought up plenty by other people elsewhere. Before playing this game, I had expectations, theories, and some general idea of how certain characters would be unraveled. After my first playthrough, all of these expectations were blown away, and in a very good way.

Whether you have or have not played the other titles, you won't be disappointed experiencing this wonderful journey for a dying person.

I recieved this game as a gift to get my opinion on it. I am very pleased with what I see and would buy it if Steam still allowed storing games in your inventory :/.
*Update: I have now bought the game via the Storefront. I will leave the box checked however, as that is how I had innitially recieved the game.
Celestial Creator is an innovative approach to block-building games, with currently odd controls. They're probably arranged for a foreign keyboard but I still managed to build a Minecraft-style house and some furniture (Look in the Screenshots tab).
How it differs from other block-builders is that you can apply any texture to any block or shape (there are more than simply cubes), with advanced options such as resize, rotate, move, and texture options for lighting, detail and scale. You can change all textures of the same group too. So if you decide your building should have a different look you can swap out the entire structure's texture at once.
Another neat feature is the inclusion of meteors, which fall towards your current position from all sides. You must shoot these down with varying amounts of bullets else they will destroy the blocks around you. For instance you could build a castle, bring the rain, then run around defending it.
Each wave is activated using PgUp to start the next and PgDn to go back. Hammering the button before a wave starts will advance the levels quicker so you can get some real action.
In its current state it's more akin to a lite 3D editor with character and vehicle interaction, however if you're looking for a block-builder with advanced options for shape, texture, and a guy with a gun to shoot sh-- up in violent debris-filled explosions, this may be something to follow.
I will be posting a video with commentary in the next few days showing the features and some furniture I put together on my first try :). You can see them in the Screenshots tab, along with a stunt track I built on my second go. The track is available for download by visiting the Discussions tab and looking into the Creations thread. There you will also find a video of the track to see how it plays.
Instructions on using player maps can be found in the Guides section.

First off, I highly recommend you check out my
on this game as that delves into more of the "behind the scenes actions" that have been occuring with the game, this review will mainly focus on the game it's self and if it has any redeeming qualities.
Celestial Creator's premise is primarily to act as a form of construction based game where you're placed in a world with over 300 materials at your disposal to create what you want. The game also has a number of asteroid belts that you can toggle that can come and destroy builds that you've made and as an extra challenge, the player can protect the builds they've made with the protector build of the main character. On the topic of character builds, there are different types of character builds that can be toggled with the numerical keys, there is protector mode, explorer mode, fly mode, buggy mode and big buggy mode. Protector mode as described before is used if you toggle the asteroid attacks, you're given a gun and you have to shoot them before they come into contact with anything. Explorer mode is basically a build of the character where you can run around the map and basically do nothing. There is additionally contruction mode which is the build in which you can place down different material blocks. The other modes are self explanatory in which you're given the applicable vehicle and you get to drive that around the map.
One big huge flaw of a construction based game is when you're extremely limited in the ways that you can actually construct something, and this is where Celestial Creator mostly falls flat. Now, like I said, there are over 300 materials at your disposal, but here's the thing, if you try and place a material ontop of something else, it will simply mirror the material that you placed it ontop of, regardless of what material you're holding. For example, if you want to place a stone block ontop of a grass block, you can't, instead when you try to place the block down, all you will end up with is a grass block ontop of a grass block. As you can imagine, with this being apparent, the game becomes extremely limited in what it is that you can construct. As a result of you basically being unable to construct much towards your desires (unless you like creating towers of grass blocks) you can't really construct much, taking a lot of the possible fun out of the protector mode as well, since there is not much of a risk as a result of any failures you may have.
As for the vehicle modes, they're incredibly glitchy, especially the jeeps as there is a good 80% chance that when you hit certain speed limits on the vehicles, the vehicle will glitch out and throw you off the map and will cause a reload behind a really long load screen (and yes, all load screens in this game are very long.)
Additionally, something else that I want to bring up is the control scheme in the game, as this was probably the best part of the whole game, and you might be thinking how can a control scheme be the stand out feature of the game? When the control scheme makes no sense at all and the sheer inexperience with the control scheme actually makes you laugh with confusion as to why someone would think this was a good control scheme. Here are a few stand out hotkeys that the game has to perform certain actions:
This game has no real redeemable qualities, and is definitely not worth the £10 base price.
Final verdict: 1/10

I've read a number of reveiws of this game, mostly negative. Quite frankly I don't understand why. I've owned the disk version of this game for some time now and have played it nearly a dozen times. It is what I like to call one of my "perennial favorites", or more specifically, one of those games I play every couple of years. Now having picked it up on Steam for a mere $1.03 I'm enjoying it yet again.
Iron Storm has immersive atmosphere, cool weapons and satisfying, challenging combat. The story, while nothing particularly original manages to drag me in and keep me there. You embark on a seemingly simple objective but circumstance makes the goal anything but simple. There are some tricky parts that leave you wondering what you are supposed to do or where to go but they are few and once figured out pose no problem.
The level design is quite good for a straight forward shooter with some good indoor and outdoor combat. Graphics are dated but pleasing enough. Sound, especially ambient noises are quite good, as is the voice acting, what little there is.
One of the biggest complaints was the ending, I won't spoil it for you but I felt it was one one of the best conclusions to a game I've had the pleasure to experience, one that fit aptly the somber and dark mood that prevails throughout the game.

In a nutshell:
For Ten bucks, you get a fully fleshed out RPG that plays like a FPS and delights itself in obfuscating the storyline and scenario design to the point of mockery.
Oh and your legs will be ok.
On paper this looks like someone's dream game in raw form, and to be quite honest once the gameplay clicks, it's actually a rather enjoyable experience. Don't get me wrong, you'll be stumbling through the dark on this one and eventually you'll give up making any sense that this game's plot has (and some mechanics and Scenarios). However, this is the first time in a LONG time I've "beaten" (I think?) a game and wanted to go again immediatley after.
This is a game where you can get killed by a door hacking you, your legs will inexplicably be the only limbs that need maintenance (and will be OK for the most part), and for some reason you end up killing your Mentor. It makes no sense half the time and it's oddly delightful in that way.
It helps that the gunplay is still rather satisfying (despite being somewhat dated). On top of just shooting all the things, your character has all of these cool Deus-ex-ey cyber upgrades, weird psychic powers, and Ghost in the Shell style hacker-possessions, which are all legitimate ways to deal with most situations.
If there are any other downsides besides it's delight in confusing the heck out of you, it is that while some avenues of approach are rewarding if you pull off, they are often times more trouble than they are worth.
EDIT 3/27/17: Actually Not really if you invest in it (Cloak, Cyber legs, Cyber Eyes, Motra SMG, and Stregnth/Agilityfrom memory) With some skill you can pop in and out of invisibility nailing soldiers left and right or getting into position to hack
Hacking is oftentimes tedious and pace killing, and you often will be doing it under fire unless you are constantly checking the menu*. Plus it's useless against
Metastreumatic Force.
Finally, Melee is rather inneficient, as you can usually deal with a threat better with guns (and not lose as much blood or energy doing it).
Still even with modest investments in any of these will give you a viable build 99% of the time. You can still fight, sneak, or hack your way out, even if it isn't as efficient. It's still a lot of fun
*As an aside: For some odd reasion  ventilation shafts are far better protected than Federation Special forces units who have some of the LOWEST cyber stats in the game.
EDIT 3/27/17: A couple additional flaws that surfaced, Nothing that makes me regret buying this but good to know
Another knock against it is that some optional scenarios feel impossible. The most infamous being the New Eden (Wurster Corp, the "Green fog" level early in the game) opening, I had some pretty hefty stealth investments, and despite being cloaked, sneaking around the side sewer, and moving VERY SLOWLY. I was still spotted. There are only two of these that come to mind (The other is the infamous "Dont make waves" one) The rest are difficult but with some foresight are completley doable.
The last issue I have with it is that multiplayer over internet is a bit of a pain to set up. LAN is fine but me and a friend have had issues getting it set up. It's doable  but more painful than nessecary.

War... war never... ends?
"Iron Storm" is great example of alternative history, which has qualitatively-performed details of "turning point" and aftermath  Little portion of lore - it takes the real history of baron Nikolai Robert Max Baron von Ungern-Sternberg (in-game - baron Nikolai Aleksandrovitch Ugenberg) and uses it to turn story of First World war in another way - Revolution in Russian Empire was crushed, new regime smashed Deutsches Kaiserreich and was ready to reach shores of Atlantic. Entente was reformed to United States of Western Europe to resist new Russian-Mongolian Empire for fourty years. Endless war is source of capital - there's stock-market, which is functioning on weapon-trade, so every event in the warfront (and in the rear) affect on stock indexes. Investments, advertising - all of these become "gears of war"... or its fuel. Paradoxal sutuation, when even soldiers can make investments in company, which produces arsenal of their elimination.
Fabula of game's storyline is simple - Empire is ready to start produce fundamentally new type of weapon - not infantry weapon, but weapon of mass destruction
. Main character, as veteran of this war (fighting practically for 21 years) and professional commando, get order to destroy manufacture of this weapon and get its sample. So, lieutenant Anderson must pass frontlines and reach military object in the deep of enemies rearward.
First World war in 1964 is kilometers of trenches, crossing former Reich and full of infantry with semi-automatic and full-auto weapon, hunting snipers, pillboxes with machinguns, roaring artillery, barraging helicopters and crawling tanks. And infiltration behind enemy lines means breaches through trenches, assaults of heavy-guarded positions, cleaning of bunkers, hide-and-seek with heli's and assymetric duels with awkward tanks.
In gameplay-terms that means variety - variety of situations, which we can solve with variety of arsenal - technical progress of this war help us to react on all types of threats, using knife or silenced pistole for careless soldiers, automatic rifle and trench-gun for CQC, semi-automatic rifle or sniper rifle for long range contacts, RPG's for war machines and sorts of special weapon and grenades for special situations (as tribute to essence of real WWI here exist grenades with mustard gas). Role of commando helps player to meet face to all faces of this war. And this role obliges him to be careful too - enemy is dangerous and even one soldier (and even cook!) can kill you, if you're not ready to kill him - you must be ready to shoot, cover, find ways to victory. Game uses health-system, but there're enough amount of medkits to not turn game in S/L-carousel.
There're different quasi-realistic details, that pretty good work for game's atmosphere - first of all, that's one of games, where you can see your body in FPS-mode - trifle, but pleasant trifle! Furthermore, inventory of character is not a black hole, where player can hide crate of machineguns and pair of RPG's - it consists of knife, pistol (silenced or machine-), trenchgun, sniper rifle and sort of heavy weapon (automatic/semi-automatic rifle, heavy machinegun or RPG/grenade launcher). And you can see all arsenal on model of your character - behind back, on hip, in holster and scabbard. Health-system is simple, without delineation of damage, but it's compensated by ability of your enemies to bring that damage. Well, abilities of enemies - their AI - are good. That's no level of "F.E.A.R.", for sure, but they can suppress you with fire, use grenades, retreat and cover.
Returning to the storyline as part of game - well, this is game of great atmosphere. Little dialogues of soldiers, that can uncover some sides of life in the world of endless war, transmitters with TV-broadcasting, that help to understand situation around you, terminals with orders, cautions or diaries... all of that make "Iron Storm" not just simple meat-shooter, but ticket to another world with it own life. And yeah, separate gratitude to developers for game's sound! When they had given voices to game's characters, they used authentic languages, so soldiers of Ugenberg's Empire speak on good russian and deutsch - there're no grammar or context mistakes, no accent. What about ambient sound - exploding shells, echo of gunfire - well, there're no problems.
Simple fabula of storyline will blossom with few intriguing twists. And yes, what I said about variety of in-game situations, means variety of game locations too. It's not only about trenches and bunkers (despite of fact, that these trenches are good made) - there are streets of german town, large scientific complex, wagons of armored train and... something more. Somebody can call them linear, but there's fact, that often enough you must find way to your goal, trying different variants.
Well, it looks, that I must draw a line to all this massive of different objective and subjective facts. "Iron Storm" feels differently: there are rough of fire contacts, cold of silent slicing of enemy's throat, rage of machine gun fire, fear of meeting with steel beasts - and of all of these is mixed of joy, which is called by delicious execution. It's game of great story, that gives you opportunity to breathe smoke of fire, devouring world, which could be our world.
At least, this is game, where you can meet face to face with german sturmpioneers, siberian elite specialists or heavy tank UG-III - and win.

I'll be honest, it's a good game, but it has MANY flaws. My biggest complaint is the simple fact that it relies on one uninterresting key concept. "The Gem", I'll call it. All it does is you can toss in on the ground or walls, and it creates a beam that pushes you in the opposite direction of the floor/wall it lands on. You can slow or speed up your movement in the beam, but that's about it. Now the game does have other abilities. Items you can carry in your backpack, and equip and use at any given time. There are simple items like bombs and a more powerful beam that blasts you away about double the height of a normal beam, but also a few more unique ones such as the slingshot. Unlike most other items, it gives you the ability to launch your  a Gem in any direction in a straight line, provided you're standing on a stable surface. The problem with these unique items, is that I never really get to use them. They all have a carry limit, which can be expanded with pickups sometimes hidden. However, it is difficult to regain your items. You rarely find some extras for free unless you're searching for every little secret, or you just have to buy more at vending machines. But that's only when you come across one. Most of the time I either find myself never using my items unless I have to, or running out of them so quickly I regret ever even equiping it. These are the important reasons as to why I dislike the game.
However the game isn't all negative. I really enjoy the stylistic aspects of the game. The 2D-3D aspect is very well done, with all the art being 3D but the gameplay is solely 2D. The characters seem like they could be better, but I understand that they're simple machine looking people. The main character, Kurt, is very intelligently done in my opinion. Kurt is the one the player controls. He has a small blue cap and some simple clothing, but not much facial features. This, in my opinion, is a smart choice. It gives the feel of being more attached to the character, like you can simply implant yourself into his role. That leads me to the story aspect of the game.
The games story is a nice one, although not very interresting in my opinion. You start by being dropped of on a random planet after passing out on a sort of bus ride, and once you regain concionceness, talk to some people waiting at the bus stop. They say the bus will soon arrive, but you quickly find out that they've been waiting for over 300 years. You learn of a possible way to get home, although it happens to be a long ways away. Kurt, needing to get home before another 300 years passes, does his best to make it to The City. Not long after leaving the bus station,  he uncovers The Gem hidden in a chest. It appears to be guarded, but the guard is busy reading a magazine. You take it but quickly realize that it's not coming off your hand. This leads you to be hunted by an unknown enemy your whole journey home. I won't spoil too much for anyone wanting to play the game themselves.
My final point is it's difficulty. Yes, I know one of it's tags is difficulty, but let me explain. The game is difficult in ways it shouldn't be. The difficulty seems to be a bit sporadic like it can't decide how hard it wants the game to be. Enemies are more like obstacles. They're very hard or sometimes impossible to kill without using your items, and some tend to be more like an annoyance. The moths are an enemy that head towards your beam, like moths do to light. It's a simple concept, but they sometimes don't seem to want to follow it. They're placed in ways that make them insanely hard to pass without taking 5 minutes to move them out of your way, or sometimes decide they just don't want to follow your beam anymore. The only time the difficulty is well done is during the puzzles. Navigating around areas without much enemies, with a few neat mechanics like pipes and platforms moved by your beam.
All in all, it's not the worst game for sure, but has it's problems. It would definately be worth a few dollars, but not much more. If I was to give any constructive critisism, I would say to focus more on the puzzle aspect of the game, and not so much the enemies or bosses. The bosses however we're really good most of the time.

I like tower defenses games but in this game some parts ruining this for me. First some positives I love visuals of this game and amount of upgrades but there are lots of things I don't like. Upgrades are not very well designed, first of all you need upgrade one part of technology to upgrade another bot often you ended up looking from one icon to another and compare to see what you need do first to make another step closer to thing you want to do, tree based upgrade system would solve this in no time. Another thing is that you don't have enough information what upgrade give you, some give you only option to upgrade another items but some give you +1 damage, armor or something like that but you din't know it until you actually get this upgrade and get some more information with this.
Gameplay- well this is not classic tower defense, you can place tower anywhere and enemies also coming from general directions of pointer not exact point and can walk freely. not on specific path, so this make it harder to make strategic decisions and you have to react quickly to what is happening on map and you don't have active pause to do so. Camera shakes, glitches and other visuals effects sometimes make chaos on screen and I turned it off quite quickly. You can zoom out and in bigger maps this would be very, very helpful to see better situation on battlefield especially when you can pause and move to different parts of map.  Another thing is adaptive difficulty setting and transferring money from one level to another, this is interesting, in theory sound good but in real life scenario not always work as should, if you do good in one level your reward will be that next one will be harder, sometimes much harder than it should be. And money transfer from one level to another can cause that in next level you will have barely any money if you do exceptional bad in last one but still finished it.
And lastly after some time it all feel the same, levels are generated randomly but due its random nature and way you can place towers and how enemies can walk freely it feel very similar and repetitive. Ans there are some more tings I can complain but I think this is enough to decide if this is game for you or not.

I've played a LOT of local multiplayer games, and I think this is a little gem.
Almost every level introduces a new gameplay mechanic, which causes three things to happen. First: Utter chaos and confusion. Second: Some people figure out what's happening, and start yelling at everyone else. Third: A collective "Aha!" moment.
But after figuring out the puzzle, you still need to DO it. This is always harder than it looks, due to the madness caused by 5+ characters moving around. The most difficult levels demand a near-telepathic degree of synchronization. Winning those levels feels amazing.
It's a short game, but it barely repeats any ideas. The designer could have built 40 more levels by recycling stuff, but chose quality over quantity. (Actually, I'd happily play more levels which recycle the idea from level 13.)
Highly recommended if you want a ridiculous teambuilding activity for 5 or more people. The world needs more games like this.

Ironstorm is one of these games that really annoys me.
Mostly because of how it's just a lot of wasted potential. It's a game with an extremely original premise, and it's bogged down by convoluted objectives and forced stealth missions.
Ironstorm takes place in an alternate history 1964, where World War 1 never ended. So you have things like trenches and mustard gas, but you also have automatic weapons and nukes. This premise is very good and I've never seen a game attempt something like this. Indeed the action segments of the game are passable and remind you a great deal of Return to Castle Wolfenstein.
Unfortunately the designers ruined this by having convoluted objectives like forced stealth segments. Ones where you require a strategy guide to get past. Or nearly impossible objectives like luring a tank to a prior area without getting instantly killed by it's gun.
The game is okay if you're particularly masochistic and don't mind looking a lot of the solutions up. But if you're looking for a quality fps experience that feels tested and polished look elsewhere.
Also note the screenshots for this game on the Steam store are misleading. They're screenshots from the later PS2 port. If you wish more accurate screenshots check out the Gog version.

If someone would ask me to name an example of an "uncut diamond" among games, E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy would be my answer. Not only that, but I would even call it the very
of it. It has massive amounts of content, ideas, lore and features, all crammed together to a confusing, unpolished and clunky mess that is very rough around the edges. This game somehow manages to be both amazing and awful at the same time. It doesn't hold your hand and includes many things that aren't properly explained.
E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy (subsequently called EYE) is a FPS/RPG hybrid. You'll spend most of your time going around sending your enemies to the game's equivalent of an afterworld. Through occasional dialogue, usually between missions, you can catch glimpses of the story, which you can try to put together yourself if you're up for a headache.
Killing enemies rewards experience and currency that can be used to upgrade your character's stats and CyberTech (mechanized bodyparts), as well as to unlock new weapons, PSI powers and cybernetic implants. As you progress through the game, you can really feel how all the tiny upgrades come together for a huge boost in power. When you start out, your character can panic at the mere sight of a monster and gets his legs broken in almost every gunfight. After many hours of progress, you control an unstoppable death machine that jumps and teleports through the world, leaving even the strongest enemies at his mercy.
One of EYE's strongest points is the visual design. Set in a futuristic cyberpunk world, the artstyle looks surreal and mysterious. It's easy to see that this game took inspiration from works such as Blame! and numerous others.
The leveldesign is great. EYE has a rather small number of maps you'll encounter during the single-player campaign and can revisit for side missions at any time. They are large and nonlinear, with many different paths and corridors, and have unique themes and styles. The maps play more like "arenas" than traditional maps. When you're dropped into one of these for a mission, you're often required to find a far away objective while fighting off an endless number of constantly respawning enemies. This can be very annoying and even frustrating for newer players, but for the more experienced, it keeps the gameplay fresh and adds a lot of replay value. The detail put into these maps is impressive, especially given their size.
However, the size and nonlinearity of certain maps can make them difficult to navigate. New players may find themselves aimlessly wandering in circles while fighting off the respawning enemies for an hour or more while trying to find that one mission objective with no idea how to get there.
The game gives you access to a vast arsenal of tools to deal with your enemies. You start out with a number of weapons, and can unlock more from vendors after you've upgraded the necessary stats or completed certain research projects. Most weapons feel and sound satisfying and are fun to use, but once you progress to the later levels and start encountering enemies with armor, you'll notice an imbalance towards the few armor-piercing weapons. EYE does have some kind of bullet physics, which doesn't seem to be particularly consistent and can make it very hard to hit moving targets at a distance. Even close up, enemies strafing around you can be a challenge to hit. It feels more like lag and affects just you, but not NPCs.
Once you've sufficiently upgraded your stats and arsenal of PSI powers, you can deal with enemies like a spellcaster, making them explode with your mind. You can also buy a number of implants for support skills that let you cloak, increase weapon accuracy, see through walls, reduce incoming damage and more.
Unfortunately, both PSI powers and cybernetic implants require energy to use, the same energy that is also consumed by running and jumping, and you lack the means to reliably restore this energy on characters that aren't highly upgraded. What that means in practice is that you can use these tools only sparingly for a major part of your character's life while playing similar to a run-of-the-mill FPS, until you get certain powers, implants and CyberTech upgrades, after which you can spam these abilities as much as you want.
When you're tired of killing your enemies, you can start hacking. Hacking is one of the game's main features in the form of a minigame, and you can do a lot of things with it. It lets you open doors, steal money or energy, make enemies explode, turn hostiles into allies to kill each other, and more.
Personally, I found the hacking minigame to be annoying, frustrating even without a high stat in it. And the game forces you to hack on multiple occasions to open doors, or you cannot progress further. Although dependant on your hacking stat, it is still somewhat random in nature, and sometimes the enemy has much higher stats than you, which leads to unwinnable scenarios. Even defeating evenly matched opponents in the minigame can take quite some time, and while you're stuck in the menu, you are fully vulnerable. Since most maps have respawning enemies, you can (and most probably will) be interrupted by an attacker at any time. This is likely to happen even if you find some remote corner before your attempt. A character highly skilled in hacking has the potential to horribly mess with his enemies, but you're almost required to do all hacking before your cloak runs out of energy.
The single-player campaign consists of a number of levels you can count on your fingers. If you only do the strictly necessary objectives, the game is pretty short. An experienced player with an upgraded character can complete the campaign in under an hour, while a new player should be done within a handful of hours, provided he/she doesn't get horribly lost on Noctis aka Mars.
Where EYE really shines is the replay value, thanks to the large arena-like maps with respawning enemies and side missions that can add countless hours of fun. It also is said to be a great co-op and multiplayer experience, though I cannot comment on that because I've never done anything but single-player.
EYE has plenty of both good and bad things about it. However, the bad stuff is mostly of the "newbie-crusher" type, that makes this game somewhat hard to get into because you don't know anything about how it works, or can't find your way around the nonlinear levels, or get obliterated by enemies you don't know how to deal with. Once you learn the mechanics and memorize the maps, many of the issues become nonexistant, while you grow accustomed to others. For someone just picking EYE up, the bad might outweight the good, but the longer you play and the more you learn about the game, the more this balance will shift towards the good. After a few dozen hours I have come to terms with most of the shortcomings and accepted them as features that ultimately make EYE to what it is as a whole.

Hello guys =), ( my english is not as good as it should be, but i hope my review can reach and help, more people)
Styx, oh Styx...
Basic Data:
I played Styx around 27.5 hours from the Intro to the ending cutscene.
Difficulty: Goblin [hardest one].
Kills: I did not kill a single person! (recommended when it is supposed to be even more difficult [you will cry and rage])
Shadow: No guard had seen me in the whole game! [recommended if you want to become frustrated]
Level: 7, one of which is made up of 3-5 smaller levels.
Story  ~  5/10 Points
I don't want to talk to much about the Story, because its not the best. The Story is really strange. You will get thrown into the story, not really knowing why and what is the heart of it. But later in the game it will all make sense. But in my opinion the story is a little bit too shallow.
Gameplay ~ 8/10 Points
Climbing: It's nothing very special in the climbing actions, we can see this in so much other games too. Like ac. And sometimes it has the same problems! You want to drop, and he will climb and will stop in front of a guard. You jump on a hook and he will not grab it.
Skills: You have so much Skills but in my opinion nothing overpowered. I think the best Skill is the invisibility Skill but its not time related its movement related. You can stand 10h on the same position but you only can run up to 10-15 meters. You can spawn mirror images and control them to kill, activate or simply take the whole attention to them. You have the Amber Vision which allows you to see people behind walls and its highlight items and interactive elements.
Items: You have 5 Items. 3 Elixiere and 2 Throw items. The first Elixiere recovers health. The second the very important Amber (what you need to use your skills!). With the third you can get rid of a dead body. The two throw items are sand to put out the torches, and the knives that kill fast, silent and over distance.
AI: The guards moving on prepared ways, so you can watch them, and make your plans. Sometimes there are trigger events and a guard will come straight to your position. In this situation it's important to know whats around you, tables, hooks or maybe a big jar. If there is nothing, you only can hide using your invisibility skill, but if they step on you they instantly know you are here. The Elves are the hardest ones they can feel your presence (over, behind, below, right, left, behind walls,jars, and in front of them ... horrible!!!). But think not the guards are stupid guys... they nearly see everything and interact really good together to find you in the area.
Level Design ~ 10/10
Awesome. You can't say anything else. I think it's impossible to find every single way to the goal! The Levels are sooo big and there are so many ways to get to the destination you want. The ways also related to your kind of playing it, because if you don't want to kill somebody you may should search sometimes for an other way.
Conclusion  ~  26/30 Points  (22+4 Points because its sooooo hard, and give me that awesome feeling after finisch)

Revenge of the Titans has excellent art design, is really challenging, and the towers and units have a pretty solid feel to them in gameplay and animation terms. It took me a long time to get around to finishing it due to the fact that the campaign used to allow you to corner yourself in a bad part of the tech tree, but this has since been patched out. What's left is a game that's suitably challenging and open-ended to be quite fun - for the most part.
Of the complaints worth mentioning, some of the levels are so dark that even with my screen brightness turned all the way up I can barely read the terrain. It's also not always clear which objects block construction or obstruct the firing arc of which turrets (but to be safe, assume almost all objects block your turrets from firing).
My biggest problem, though, is with ghostly enemy types that can only be attacked by manually using a Capacitator turret against them. This rips you away from the high-level strategic game into click-driven micro instead, and I think that really interrupts what is otherwise an exciting and challenging high-level planning experience, much to the game's detriment. If the ghost/capacitator system wasn't a part of the game, you'd have a much more cohesive experience overall that really lets you get into the flow of things.
That said, it's still a good game, one of the most engaging tower defense games I've ever played. Give it a shot and just keep your eyes on those damned capacitators (which, incidentally, are a good way of defeating bosses).

Very pretty, with a variety of enemies and an interesting and large research tree, but ultimately ruined due to poor balance and bad gameplay decisions by the developers.
At it's core, it's tower defense with funds and research carried between levels. You can replay old levels in order to improve your funds or undo research choices...but going back is permanent, losing your progress after that level. Essentially this makes the game about creating a single, perfect, optimized run...which most people would find incredibly tedious anyway, assuming the gameplay was interesting enough to support constant replays - which it isn't. At the very least, you'll be replaying every level at least twice: once to learn what you're up against and where everything spawns, plus at least one run to beat it with minimal losses. This gets tedious real quick.
The big problem with this is that the game *also* penalizes doing well. Difficulty scales to your funds (= how well you've done so far), and it's not a minor correction, either; monsters get significantly harder (up 3x life and speed) and more numerous and crystals ($) actually stop spawning at all after a certain point. That's ridiculous, and what's more it doesn't go back down unless you lose the game repeatedly and let the monsters wreck your base. In a game whose mechanics practically mandate replaying levels in order to get perfection, this is ENRAGING.
There are plenty of other problematic design decisions (extremely large damage ranges for some weapons, easier difficulty requiring losing to access, lack of a sandbox mode, most Research being useless, etc.), but this is the big one. Ultimately, the game encourages you to play one way, and when you do, it punishes you for it.

Hello All,
Finding Paradise is the followup to To The Moon and follows the character in A Bird Story.
I am a To The Moon addict. I love discussing the many different objects, the music, the story, the characters, etc. with everyone who plays games. (I have a 100% success rate in referal turnover to fans for that game XD) I also enjoyed A Bird Story for what it's worth.
Now, this is a Finding Paradise review so I'd best stop talking about other games and talk about this one!
Finding Paradise is another journey full of suspense and emotion like its predecessor To The Moon. There was much crafty humor implemented in this game that had me laughing frequently. There are suspenseful moments in the story where I was unsure of what outcomes were going to be. There were also a few moments that were presented well to draw sadness out of the player.
Kan Gao continues his witty humor in Finding Paradise. I think this game had the most humor out of the three I have mentioned thus far and it isn't just reusing jokes that everyone has heard. Finding Paradise's humor is unique in that you don't see it coming, but anticipate the next bit of humor that is assuredly going to occur at some point. The use of mechanics and names from other games and movies as jokes is also a nice touch (Loved the mafia Kan, lol).
Finding Paradise improves most on the previous games in aspects of gameplay. Gameplay isn't the most important thing in a story-driven game and I get that, but Finding Paradise added new game mechanics at regular intervals to keep it interesting (I just was sad that my shoe attack did NOTHING, lol).
At this moment if I were to rate the three games I have mentioned I would give Finding Paradise a 9/10. It really is a different type of game than To The Moon in my opinion. I think that each will appeal more to seperate groups though both will be enjoyed alot. My ratings of the Freebird games:
Finding Paradise- 9/10
To The Moon- 10/10
A Bird Story- 8/10
I highly recommend everyone to play all three and though it is said that Finding Paradise is a standalone game (It is), you will miss out on ALOT of references if you do not complete the other two games first. Do yourself a favor and pickup all three of these amazing games.
(Amazing work once again Kan Gao. This was my most anticipated game this year and I am glad to have got to play it. Tell the team to keep making great games like this, the gaming industry needs these kind of games that focus on story. Gameplay is good in its own right, but the majority of my favorite games lack alot of gameplay and excel heavily in story. Thanks once again).

Thanks Gaben for making the summer sale and I managed to buy this game on discount at an EXTREMELY low price ($2.99). This game is generally fun and you can play with your friends in a party, or whatever. I would recommend you to use a controller and play it on bigscreen as it is generally more fun and easier to control.
The goal of this game, is to reach the goal sides set on teh side of both sides. You can repeatedly kill each other, until one reaches the end. (And you get a dragon to eat you for winning)
There is a range of levels where you can entertain yourself and your friends with and have a good laugh. If you don't have friends or if they are too busy doing something else, you can play against the bot (singleplayer). The bot was also decent to play against. It wasn't too hard and it wasn't too easy. The online mode is messed up.
Each map was fun to play with unique features. For example the map Mine, had transportation belts which either brings the player forward to allow him to reach the goal side quicker or push him/her back and make the progress slower. And the map Wild, had tall grass for the players to hide in.
The graphics is good for a game like this. I'd prefer it to be pixelated and it gives it an arcade feel. The truth is, it doesn't need detailed graphics.
For player movement, it was great. You can stab your opponent, throw swords, roll underneath players, disarm players from their swords and if you got disarmed yourself, you can punch the other player to death. If you fell down a pit and managed to grab a wall, keep on wall-kicking and get yourself out.
And lastly, it gives a player tutorial which helps you learn about the controls, how to stab, throw, disarm, etc.
Overall, this game is great and if you want a good laugh and have an enjoyable time by yourself or with your frieds, I'd definitely get it as it is on discount. Get 1 copy for your friends too!

If someone would ask me to name an example of an "uncut diamond" among games, E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy would be my answer. Not only that, but I would even call it the very
of it. It has massive amounts of content, ideas, lore and features, all crammed together to a confusing, unpolished and clunky mess that is very rough around the edges. This game somehow manages to be both amazing and awful at the same time. It doesn't hold your hand and includes many things that aren't properly explained.
E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy (subsequently called EYE) is a FPS/RPG hybrid. You'll spend most of your time going around sending your enemies to the game's equivalent of an afterworld. Through occasional dialogue, usually between missions, you can catch glimpses of the story, which you can try to put together yourself if you're up for a headache.
Killing enemies rewards experience and currency that can be used to upgrade your character's stats and CyberTech (mechanized bodyparts), as well as to unlock new weapons, PSI powers and cybernetic implants. As you progress through the game, you can really feel how all the tiny upgrades come together for a huge boost in power. When you start out, your character can panic at the mere sight of a monster and gets his legs broken in almost every gunfight. After many hours of progress, you control an unstoppable death machine that jumps and teleports through the world, leaving even the strongest enemies at his mercy.
One of EYE's strongest points is the visual design. Set in a futuristic cyberpunk world, the artstyle looks surreal and mysterious. It's easy to see that this game took inspiration from works such as Blame! and numerous others.
The leveldesign is great. EYE has a rather small number of maps you'll encounter during the single-player campaign and can revisit for side missions at any time. They are large and nonlinear, with many different paths and corridors, and have unique themes and styles. The maps play more like "arenas" than traditional maps. When you're dropped into one of these for a mission, you're often required to find a far away objective while fighting off an endless number of constantly respawning enemies. This can be very annoying and even frustrating for newer players, but for the more experienced, it keeps the gameplay fresh and adds a lot of replay value. The detail put into these maps is impressive, especially given their size.
However, the size and nonlinearity of certain maps can make them difficult to navigate. New players may find themselves aimlessly wandering in circles while fighting off the respawning enemies for an hour or more while trying to find that one mission objective with no idea how to get there.
The game gives you access to a vast arsenal of tools to deal with your enemies. You start out with a number of weapons, and can unlock more from vendors after you've upgraded the necessary stats or completed certain research projects. Most weapons feel and sound satisfying and are fun to use, but once you progress to the later levels and start encountering enemies with armor, you'll notice an imbalance towards the few armor-piercing weapons. EYE does have some kind of bullet physics, which doesn't seem to be particularly consistent and can make it very hard to hit moving targets at a distance. Even close up, enemies strafing around you can be a challenge to hit. It feels more like lag and affects just you, but not NPCs.
Once you've sufficiently upgraded your stats and arsenal of PSI powers, you can deal with enemies like a spellcaster, making them explode with your mind. You can also buy a number of implants for support skills that let you cloak, increase weapon accuracy, see through walls, reduce incoming damage and more.
Unfortunately, both PSI powers and cybernetic implants require energy to use, the same energy that is also consumed by running and jumping, and you lack the means to reliably restore this energy on characters that aren't highly upgraded. What that means in practice is that you can use these tools only sparingly for a major part of your character's life while playing similar to a run-of-the-mill FPS, until you get certain powers, implants and CyberTech upgrades, after which you can spam these abilities as much as you want.
When you're tired of killing your enemies, you can start hacking. Hacking is one of the game's main features in the form of a minigame, and you can do a lot of things with it. It lets you open doors, steal money or energy, make enemies explode, turn hostiles into allies to kill each other, and more.
Personally, I found the hacking minigame to be annoying, frustrating even without a high stat in it. And the game forces you to hack on multiple occasions to open doors, or you cannot progress further. Although dependant on your hacking stat, it is still somewhat random in nature, and sometimes the enemy has much higher stats than you, which leads to unwinnable scenarios. Even defeating evenly matched opponents in the minigame can take quite some time, and while you're stuck in the menu, you are fully vulnerable. Since most maps have respawning enemies, you can (and most probably will) be interrupted by an attacker at any time. This is likely to happen even if you find some remote corner before your attempt. A character highly skilled in hacking has the potential to horribly mess with his enemies, but you're almost required to do all hacking before your cloak runs out of energy.
The single-player campaign consists of a number of levels you can count on your fingers. If you only do the strictly necessary objectives, the game is pretty short. An experienced player with an upgraded character can complete the campaign in under an hour, while a new player should be done within a handful of hours, provided he/she doesn't get horribly lost on Noctis aka Mars.
Where EYE really shines is the replay value, thanks to the large arena-like maps with respawning enemies and side missions that can add countless hours of fun. It also is said to be a great co-op and multiplayer experience, though I cannot comment on that because I've never done anything but single-player.
EYE has plenty of both good and bad things about it. However, the bad stuff is mostly of the "newbie-crusher" type, that makes this game somewhat hard to get into because you don't know anything about how it works, or can't find your way around the nonlinear levels, or get obliterated by enemies you don't know how to deal with. Once you learn the mechanics and memorize the maps, many of the issues become nonexistant, while you grow accustomed to others. For someone just picking EYE up, the bad might outweight the good, but the longer you play and the more you learn about the game, the more this balance will shift towards the good. After a few dozen hours I have come to terms with most of the shortcomings and accepted them as features that ultimately make EYE to what it is as a whole.

This really feels like an unfinished game. There's a decent core, but to say that everything around it is unpolished is an understatement.
Perhaps the most important issue is that the game is very unbalanced difficulty-wise. The first level is by far the hardest because you start with no upgrades and just a single forward weapon. The biggest challenge is surviving long enough to gather enough scrap to purchase a side weapon slot (by which point you'll likely have picked up a weapon to fill it) and upgrade the attack speed once or twice. It's unimaginable how much easier the game becomes after that. By the time you've got two forward and two side weapons with upgraded attack speed and maybe even extra bullets (which should be by the end of the second or third levels if you've been selling surplus picked up weapons to the randomly appearing stores), you'll be a weapon of mass destruction and the only danger remaining will be accidentally running into the few enemies that somehow made it past your bullet spam. Particularly bosses which might survive a few seconds so you'll need to shield-dodge past them to be safe.
The second major flaw is the control scheme. Arrow keys, Right CTRL, Right SHIFT, Mouse and the 'i' key? Really? If the devis don't wanna take the time to add key remapping (and they should), they should at least change it to use the WASD, Left Shift, Space and 'E'.
And then there's the inventory/buying screen. Sometimes it seems to buy something as soon as I enter it (maybe because I'm still holding down the left mouse button to shoot.) Sometimes weapons seem to disappear from their slots, and it's a toss up on whether they're really gone or just invisible - gotta go back to the battle and shoot to find out which. Sometimes you sell a surplus weapon and end up selling an equipped weapon alongside it. And there's no information on what buying the Health, Shield and Energy powerups does, plus at least the Health cost is wrong. Says 20, costs 40 or 50 (maybe depending on the ship.)
So once you've somehow survived long enough to get the necessary upgrades (I recommend starting with the Bomber ship which can take way more hits and just needs a couple relatively inexpensive speed upgrades to be more playable) you get the cathartic experience of mowing enemies down as soon as they appear until after beating one level just like any other you're suddenly sent to rolling credits.  But the first level or so is just a chore of frustration.
Also, it took me about 2.5 hours to finally beat the game.  The first 2 hours was idling for cards.   I didn't time the actual winning run, but pretty sure it was way under 1 hour.
Hopefully these issues can get fixed sometime, and then I could recommend the game, but since the Die for the Empire isn't labeled "Early Access", I don't know if the devs are even working on it anymore.

Trauma is a rather unique point-and-click frame-by-frame adventure about life and self-discovery. It is a slow game, with the story told through a series of dreams, which in turn consist of a series of snapshots that the player gets to traverse. There are no people in any of the dreams and they take place exclusively at night, giving the game a creepy, mysterious feel. It feels lonely, and the music does a wonderful job of emphasizing this atmosphere. The narration is mostly uninspired though, and is read in a slow, very flat voice that could have used a bit of emotion. Trauma is certainly not for everyone, but if you enjoy slow gameplay and an interesting story that you have to discover and piece together yourself, I suggest you give it a try. Keep in mind that it is very short and can be fully completed in about two hours, so I would say $5 would be a more reasonable price.

"Heavy is good, heavy is reliable. If it doesn't work, hit them with it"
And oh, how heavy is this game.
Fristly, i'd like to say that i watched an entire PT on this game before buying it. Don't take my 8 hours of GP seriously.
The essencial about this game is covered pretty much everywhere, i won't go over it again. I'd like to add, however, that calling it "batshit crazy", "old tech", "flawed gem", "a mix of deus ex,warhammer 40k" or whatever is to sell this game short. I will discuss about how this game plays and then about how it feels.
The gameplay itself is quite simple. It is heavy and reliable. No fancy cutscenes, no quick time events, no nothing. mechanically wise you can buy this game for its face value, there is nothing hidden here. Or at least not in the game itself. You see, this is very true to the 90's fps in this sense. Wanna take cover? you have to actually move yourself behind the wall. Wanna dodge something? good luck with WASD keys. Wanna hit a moving target? (oh they move fast) Gotta train it for good, and the game gives you all the time in the world... for training at least. This game requires some very raw skills kinda forgotten since modern FPS style. If you are 25 YO or older, you already know where i am going with this, if you are younger, this could be a very intresting experience.
Some say this game is not an fps, but an RPG with fps elements. Maybe, maybe not. For all i care this is irrelevant. What matters is that you will end up shooting sooner or later. And shooting here is so tight that i could lick my guns to polish it with a blanket after each mission. It feels so damn good! i had actually grown emotionally attached to the guns i use often, hell, i might even start giving them names. The AI has an attention span of a golden fish, true... they are♥♥♥♥♥♥ But somehow this doesn't bother me. It actually makes the game play nice.
About how it feels: heavy, solid, yet... oniric.
It is very half-life ish when we talk about feelings here. You know, that brutal immersion those games offered us. The way you interact with the world helps a lot in this sense, but there is something more about it. The level design, the neo-noir main approach and the art style walk the lore talk, it feels coherent. You feel a growing confusion about what is happening, you feel so... alone. This provides a most unique immersion for the player, and if you are a social freak like me, you will end up addicted to it very quickly and very strangely. This feeling when you are sneaking around to find some advantage and you spot an enemy. "oh, so this is where you stand... now- where are you going?". This game gives you all the time in the world, and it feels... yeah, it surely feels. In some aspects, this is better here than in, let's say, DE:HR or even than MD, being slightly pushed back by the forseeable AI.
Tl;DR: If you are a millenial or older, this neo-noir Diesel punkish looking game feels strangely familiar, and it just might warm your heart with it's cold dark atmosphere.
ps: don't try to make sense out of the main plot. There is none to be found.
