I picked this game up a couple of days ago and decided I'd give it a go yesterday. 7 and a half hours later, it was 3:30 am and I didn't want to turn this off. I'm getting older and my body doesn't like staying up that late anymore, but damnit if it wasn't worth it.
Grimlore have made a great game here, and I truly hope it doesn't get lost in the admittedly large pile of fantastic games that came out this year (especially on the Switch). This one deserves a play through for any RPG and RTS fan. There are sections where I honestly felt like I was playing a modern spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate, then it would switch to an RTS level and the base building felt fresh with its more realistic supply routes and resource types in the area. I couldn't just spam a dozen units out of a barracks in a pinch - I had to wait for supplies to be delivered from another sector first. Certain sectors will even have abandoned canoes or boats that, if you build an outpost and then a fishing hut, your workers will start using to go fish out on the water. It just makes the environment feel a whole lot more real and organic.
Speaking of environment - this game is achingly beautiful. I think that's what brought me back to my Baldur's Gate days in certain levels. The isometric verticality of the cities and environments is so well done and the art design and environments are gorgeous. As some others have said, however, the character models do look a little bland and don't stand out enough. This is especially the case in RTS mode when you're battling with your heroes and an army - I think that's part of the reason they went with the highlighting in blue option, instead of designing over the top and giant-sized heroes that would stand out. I do appreciate the realism of that, but the character models still lack a bit of...flair, as the owner of Shenanigans would say.
I personally don't find it odd that Doug Cockle is voicing one of the main characters in this game - I mean, he's a top notch voice actor - did anyone really think he would only work with CDPR going forward? He performs very well in this title as well. In fact, all of the voice acting I encountered sounded wonderful and mostly genuine, even if some of the lines of script may have occasionally let down the image.
In summary - I'm so glad this game came along after many years in development. There aren't many titles that scratch this particular itch this well. This one genuinely does both of its defining genres a great service and I would recommend picking it up asap! Even now, at full price! What are you waiting for?

This game isn't for everyone. Had I not gotten the code from a friend as a gift, I would have never downloaded the game. And, in fact, I got the code, redeemed it, and couldn't be bothered to download and play it for several months. But recently I installed all the games that I'd gotten for free, or as part of bundles, and not yet played. Trauma was next on my list to try.
Now that I've finally played it, I definitely recommend it, with caveats.
I've heard the game described as an interactive film, and that's a fair description. I've always been intrigued with the idea of interactive films, and well-executed artsy projects, so that wasn't a turn-off.
As you get deeper into the game and discover all of the available gestures, and begin collective all of the available alternative endings, it's easy to get sucked into just how accurately the game depicts a dream state. It has an elusiveness and a believable unbelievability. Some of the animations and transitions are mind-bogglingly perfect. And once you collect all of the alternate endings, you get the alternate alternate ending, which provides an "oh snap!" kind of reveal. Perhaps not a surprising alternate ending, given the nature of the game, but a fulfilling one.
Collecting some of the photographs does require some tricky maneuvering, given a lack of direct route, but careful use of all available gestures will get you to them.
Overall, I recommend the game. Is it short? Yes. Is it for everyone? No. Would I pay full price? Maybe not. If I had money to throw around and price wasn't an issue, the game is certainly worth every penny for what it achieves artistically. When it comes to replayability, and the length of time it kept me engaged, and the amount of money I actually have to throw around: I probably wouldn't personally pay the full sticker price. But, get it as a bundle, or get a discount, and it's definitely worth a playthrough.

This is a game that's purely about exploration, but has nothing worth finding.
There are some novel mechanics for navigation and opening (metaphorical) doors, and there are some neat visual things, and there are a couple barely poignant poetic moments. But there's no information, no story, no emotion that gets uncovered that isn't just straight up boring. You'll discover a hidden photo with a memory like "I remember this one time I when I was stressed out." The whole game is aggressively devoid of meaning or interest.
The whole game is a set of scenes that you discover things in, and there are a couple different things to find in each one that resolve the scene differently. The scenes are set as dreams, so they're a little bit surreal but mostly just boring, and they're narratively unrelated to both eachother and the so-called "story" of a woman who was in a car accident.
The closest thing to a game mechanic is discovering gestures and using them to unlock new paths. It's pretty insubstantial, but it is actually rather satisfying to revist an area you've already been to and find a new resolution by using a gesture that was central to a different scene you played later. But again, that one neat exploration element is spoiled by the game having nothing to reward you with except the pretentious, poetic, and incoherent musings of a depressed Werner Herzog wannabe.
I literally can't remember how this wound up in my Steam library, maybe a Humble Bundle, which is good because I couldn't recommend this game at a price any higher than free. Only try it if you're looking for a textbook example of the kind of pretentious gameplay-lacking indie game that everyone makes fun of.
P.S. Steam didn't count the first time I played, so my played time is higher than it says, but it's still very short.

As someone who dislikes many forms of puzzle games, I can't say that Kami is a game within my interests. Still, since it had a very unique aesthetic, I decided to give it a go.
Visually, I've got nothing to add. The game is beautiful, and it also fits the general aesthetic. The music is also good, enhancing the aesthetic, but not much in terms of immersion or gameplay... to me, anyway. Still, it's cool!
The puzzles are my problem. The first puzzles, I enjoyed! They were elegant, simple, and could still twist your brain a bit, when you found out that the most obvious solution wasn't the most efficient. I liked that. 4-6 moves was cool. The puzzles were also visually well put together! It's a gimmick, but it's well made nonetheless.
The problem, for me, comes with later puzzles, where the patterns turn into chaos, and moves going as far as 19. Without hints, there are waaaay too many possibilities with very few seams where one could start. (I'm mentioning the last level) Thankfully, the hint system helps a lot! It's also limiting, since you have a daily limit for it... Roots from mobile, I guess. One hint per level, later on, is ideal, since at least you know where to start.
All in all, it's just not my type of puzzle. There doesn't seem to be any real algorithm to solve it, and there barely are rules of approximation, later on. Initially, yes, sure. But later on, the levels are too chaotic for my taste. It's a matter of patience, at that point.
The levels have 2 solutions. One, is perfect, with the given number of moves. The other one, is "ok", where you have ONE additional move. It's impressive how much of a difference that one move makes!
Perhaps it proves how ingenous the game can be. It's just not for me. It's like sliding block puzzles. I hate those!
The concept is simple, and it starts well! If it seems up your alley, go ahead! It's just not for me.
The premium levels (free on this version!) were a cool gimmick, but the middle set, in particular, had very obnoxious patterns. They were so similar that it was almost impossible to identify anything in the puzzle. The other were conveyed properly, though.
The solution is often awkward, not following any teaching of the game early on or anything. Good to pass the time, I guess.
If you want a game where you can roll through the levels with only grenades equipped, this is it.
This certainly isn't Dawn of War I

I would highly recommend Styx: Master of Shadows. This game is one of the most unique and excellently crafted fantasy universe and storyline I have ever experienced. It's advanced-medieval style, creature design, character clothing and inclusion of such elements as flying ships and vast bottomless pits is extremely comparable to the series of novels, "The Edge Chronicles", by Paul Stewart and Chris Riddel. Although intended for a younger audience similar to Harry Potter and Percy Jakcson, the series far surpasses them with its intriguing, mature, and sometimes macabre universe and story. Its dark, and masterfully crafted illustrations help propel the written text to higher planes of wonderous excellence It is most certainly a book series that would be better enjoyed by an adult audience. I can not say for certain if Styx is influenced by The Edge Chronicles , but the similarities are there. If you enjoyed either the game or the book series, I would most certainly recommend the other. Or, if youre simply interested in a fascinating fantasy game, I would recommend Styx: Master of Shadows.

I saw this game at Betacon and was immediately thrown back to my old Amiga rpg's (like someone else said, Eye of the Beholder, one of my favorites).
It's fun to play, a nice retro experience.
Pros: swift graphics, easy to navigate, lots of bag space, good character display (inventory, stats, talent, etc), FUN - even though it's a bit one-dimensional play
Cons: too much treasure - really, it drops too much treasure, making the levels too easy. That is somewhat offset by ridiculous boss fights - way too much hp.
I think it should be a little more balanced:
Normal mobs should only rarely drop 'rare' items, and they should drop less items. Even though you have lots of bag space, you're currently tossing stuff left and right.
Bosses should be about 10% easier, and normal mobs should hit a little harder making getting through each level a bit more challenge.
I think there should maybe be a bit more 'quest' involved instead of just 'kill x number of y'. I realize the game isnt really developed to include a quest line, but something like that would be a bit more fun (find a certain treasure, somewhere in the next 5 levels maybe?)
All in all a nice game, well done, and I want to support indy developers. Thanks for creating it. I had fun, spent hours doing it. Worth the $10. Keep up the good work.

Styx is a very likeable character and I hope to see a better designed sequel in his future, but unfortunately for his debut appearance Styx's creators put him in the deep end of hardcore stealth gameplay by handicapping him with his abilities and giving his opponents a massive boost in offence with sheer numbers.
I recommed only for willing supporters like myself, I do not regret my purchase.
However if you are looking for a stealth/combat game I highly recommend Dishonoured, Hitman:Blood Money, and the old Thiefs 1-3.

This is what I would consider the Medea of indie games.
It has an amazing story, a beautiful art style, and enthralling music. The boss fights are truely some of the best I've seen in a long time. There is one problem, though. Being in my books the "Medea of video games", it shares the exact same problem Medea has. The beginning is amazing, the middle is enthralling, and all the way up to right before the final boss, it is a generally good time (I found the final "giant" boss to be quite dull, and the Ken boss fight wasn't great, either, but at least they were both enjoyable). The problem is, though, the final boss fight is, sadly to say, mediocre at best. Compared to the others, it seems stiched together at the last minute. You beat the final boss with no satisfaction, more just a feeling of relief that you don't have to deal with his annoying attack patterns anymore and it's all over, only to realize that it is then followed by 3 platforming sections (2 of which are, like the final boss, more annoying then enjoyable). Though, all of that said, I can easily say that this is one of my favorite video games of all time (I love Medea just the same), and I would recommend it to anybody that likes platforming games (word of advice, it strays a bit more towards the frustrating / difficult side of platforming in some times) and to I believe all people I know!

Right off the bat, I’ll say you as the player will either love this atmospheric exploration game or it’ll really wear on your patience fast. It can be mind-numbingly slow, confusing, and the controls are tolerable at best. There is almost no gameplay beyond exploration and collecting to speak of. Still, I do recommend this game very highly to exploration lovers, role-players, and players with active imaginations. For these people, I promise this game will have a lot of the things they enjoy in gaming.
Honestly, while I do highly recommend this game as stated above for open-minded players and exploration lovers. Personally, I found this game initially to be rather boring and hard to get into. As I tend to play more direct story driven and action-oriented games. Yet, I decided to give "The Path" the play time I needed to honestly judge it. Out of sheer determination fueled by the other good reviews. Which generally said the game would get better if given time. For which I can say was true in my case. I slowly started to get into this game as my predetermined notions of what makes good gameplay faded with each step I took into the dark woods. I quickly realized this game almost requires at least an hour or two to really judge it. Due to the game’s slow pacing and subtle influences.
None of the game’s storyline is directly forced upon the player and is instead left to them to find and figure out. While initial gameplay as stated above may leave the gamer lost and confused. Once they do discover their story oriented purpose in the game, either through sheer luck or logical deduction. Story-driven events will start to play out more often and the story should start to become clearer in their minds. Leading to the player’s enjoyment level most likely increase. As in my case, once I got that (ah-ha!) moment I started enjoying myself.
I have on purpose been rather vague with the details for those who do not like spoiler reviews so far. But for those who would like more to go off of. When deciding whether to give this interesting game a go or would like to just know more of what’s really going on. The following two sections go into more descriptive detail. The first covers the gameplay elements and “generically” describes the goal of the game. The second further down one: describes the goal of the game in-depth and does contains some direct story spoilers. Each section has a tag with a warning label for those who rather avoid spoilers. If you choose to read on or not thank you very much for taking the time to read my review. - Vekcrim
--- WARNING: Gameplay related spoilers below ---
This game is ultimately very dark and twisted. From the start, you’re given two important choices to make. One which is obvious: Which of the young ladies would you like to play? The other, which is subtly hinted at: Is your chosen maiden going to be a good girl by following the given directions without deviation or is she going to venture off the beaten path and explore the dark woods?
So logic would dictate initially you, of course, would obediently follow the directions you’re given and go straight to grandma’s house without deviation, right? Oh, how obedience in this game is so overrated. All you’ll get for your goody-two-shoes effort is a whopping “D” rating as your character arrives to sit at the bedside of her dead-looking grandmother. While the words “FAILURE” is plastered across your screen. Before the game unceremoniously plops you back on the character selection screen. Yup, the game wants your little Miss to be a disobedient minor. If you hope to receive anything above a “D” rank and some acknowledged “SUCCESS!”
Now if you’re girl does like to venture on the wild side and decides a little trip in the woods would be fun. Things are going to get a tad dark and atmospheric. As the game’s bright and cheery visuals turn quickly into a dark and eerie wooded locale with some lite horror elements introduced to set the mood. Also, to make things more interesting within mere seconds of leaving the path you’ll be completely lost and find yourself walking in circles never to see the path again. Sounds like fun right? Well yes and somewhat no.
Wondering the woods lost is basically the initial core of the gameplay. As the girl explores she’ll come across random items and some limited interactions with other characters. Which is intended to give the player hints and imagery to build upon to develop their own personalized interpretation of the game’s story. Which not surprisingly will make the initial experience very confusing. Borderline leading to some players to rage quit out of frustration and boredom.  As they will be most likely waiting for the game to give them a purpose or at least a goal to work towards. Something the player may gain either within a few minutes or may take upwards of an hour or two to figure out. If they stick around long enough. Depending on a little luck and a lot of patience.
After the player finishes his or her first character’s playthrough in the woods, either by coming to a key event or staying lost and running out of time. The goal of the game kind of becomes clear to the player to a certain point. Which is to lead each girl one-by-one to their horrible demise. For which the player receives higher ratings depending on how many items they found and if they located the girl’s personal key event. I did say the game was dark and twisted.
--- WARNING: Contains story related spoilers ---
As I mentioned above the player is rated on whether the player choices to collect items and if they find the girl’s personal key event. By now I'm sure you've most likely figured out from the game visuals, mentioned grandma reference and the fact that the girls all wear red. This game is based on the Red Riding Hood Fable. So the key event the player is ultimately looking to get the best rating is to locate the other main character in these stories besides Red and Grandma. The big bad wolf who wants to eat the young maiden. Pretty obvious huh, if you think about it.
Yup, what you’re now thinking is correct: the player’s ultimate goal to get the best rating is to systematically hunt down the wolf and sacrifice your poor maiden to him. With each girl’s experience in the process being unique and the wolf being a little different for each of them. Due to the girls being of different ages and having their own personalized perspective of the events as they encounter them.
As the player finds the beast(s). They get to watch some unique cut-scenes of Red's and the wolf's initial encounter. Some being more entertaining than others. Before being taken to just outside their grandma’s house and allowed to enter it. Although, this visit is not as visually cheery as the good girl’s visit. Each character gets their own twisted nightmarish version of the house to briefly tour. Before the player is shown their girl’s fate in the form of multiple image stills depicting a gruesome death by the big teeth and claws of their wolf. Followed by the player receiving a chapter completion prompt with that elusive “SUCCESS!” they were looking for and an overall higher ranking.
Afterwards, the player is returned to the character screen to select their next victim. With the deceased girls no longer being present alluding to the horrors that befell them. Now what happens, when only a few girls are left or better yet; none? Is there something sinister going on behind the scenes. Maybe something to do with the memories and visions the girls saw. Well, I'm going to leave that’s for the player to figure out; enjoy! Thanks again for reading my review/overview.

I cannot recommend this game in its current state.
Why?
There are several reasons. First off, there is absolutely no story at all.
Okay, so the game is designed to be a dungeon crawler, but in my opinion there should be at least some kind of story and questlines. Now the quests are kill number X of enemy type Y, and the same "quests" pop up at the list all the time.
While I like the simple turn-based combat system, the game lacks enemies. "Okay, I killed a level 8 Goblin. Again." -- Next floor. "Okay, I killed a level 9 Goblin. Again" .. So basically you're fighting the same damn enemies every floor, that simply get a level increase every floor. It gets extremely boring, extremely fast. This is absolutely horrid. The game isn't in early access anymore.
Okay, so you create a party of four (4) characters in the beginning, like many other RPGs. You get four classes, that's fine. But oh, you unlock new classes AFTER you finish some floors? On paper this sounds nice.
However, the implementation is awful. You cannot make any more characters after the start. So how can you get the new classes? Starting a new game? ... NO. You have to buy them from the Tavern. Still sounds ok?
Well, the thing is.. the characters in the Tavern are randomized. So, if you want the new class.. you have to refresh the thing (which costs of course) and the damn button doesn't even always work! ... Well, if you don't want to pay, the only way to refresh the damn tavern is... PLAY FLOOR 1, return. Check if the class is there. No?
PLAY FLOOR 1 AGAIN. Return. Class is there! Ok! .. Well, I wanted a female version and the race is wrong. So, no.
PLAY FLOOR 1 AGAIN. Return.. class isn't there.. REPEAT. AGAIN. AGAIN. AGAIN. AGAIN.
When you finally get the damn class you wanted, with the RACE you wanted and GENDER you wanted...
You have played the first damn floor like a 100 times over. Fighting the same damn enemies, for a millimeter of XP bar.
Niiiiice. So you get the point, every time you want a new character you have to do this. Every new class unlocked, you have to do this. It's absolute bullcrap. It's tedious, boring and so-oh repetitive.
And the thing is, even if you manage to get the new class you wanted with the right setup --
The new character is likely much much lower level than the rest of your party, that you started with.
Ok, so what to do? Of course if you don't care, you can just take the low level with you and hope it doesn't die. (Yeah, and if a character dies, it loses its gear, plus you have to pay for resurrection.)
But, if you want it to get to the same level as the rest of the party?
You have to go SOLO PLAY.. you guessed it.. FLOOR 1, get the XP.. REPEAT. Then if the character gets strong enough, you can move up and keep soloing until its the same level as others. Seriously, more and more grinding the first levels of the game. Just to get a new character?
So yeah, this game is horrible at its current state.
I advise you to NOT buy it unless these things make a little more sense.
Even on sale this feels like a ripoff.

I can't deny that this game has some very fantastic mechanics, the art style is just AMAZING for one, the tech tree brings variety into the game, will you fight your enemies with explosive rocket launchers that can damage your turrets, or will you go full god like and have powerful blasters behind them with buildings that increase their range, damage, ammo capacity, firing speed and decrease reload time. Or maybe you just think "I can do SO much better!" well, sadly you can't have a tower that shoots, but you DO get a tower that SHOCKS the titans as they come into range with a click of the mouse, and add multiple ones together, and you got yourself a FORCEFIELD that will kill anything on your command!
But maybe you don't wanna see towers shoot the titans from far away, maybe you wanna send DRONES in that get up close AAAAND personal, starting with tiny droids that mass produce very quickly and shoot faster than the basic blaster (Puts that blaster to SHAME), then going to BIGGER droids with bigger guns that act like a TANK for the tiny droids, but thats not all, upgrade the droids so the tiny ones have a better weapon and the bigger droids? OH boy lets say they get a WHOLE new weapon (Im not gonna spoil it, but lets say this weapon is DEADLY against anything really that doesn't have armor)
With 5 planets to battle on (Earth, Moon, Mars, Saturn and Titan), the fighting never stops until you defeat the final boss on every planet leading to titan, each planet holds a new variety of titans, earth has your standard titans, moon moves onto armored titans that might force the blasters blasts to be defencless, so you gotta get better ones, mars has ghost titans that are unnoticable by regular blasters (Unless you get that certain upgrade that allows that to happen), so you must use the special shock towers to kill 'em, saturn has FLYING titans that will drop bombs on your towers, crazy isn't it? Titan however, has titans that will SHOOT your turrets from afar, as if titans dropping bombs from above wasn't bad enough, titans shooting your towers with armor will be your biggest problem.
Again, the dificulty IS harsh, i mean this game will full on throw EVERYTHING at you every new level and the game kinda says "Ok, so you got this thing, kill it, ok? Ok, have fun with that" each new level, to a certain degree where it feels like its screaming "HEY BTW WE GOT THIS NEW THING THAT YOUR TOTALLY GONNA HATE! HAVE FUN!" all the way to the last level where it just says "Well you know we can't be bothered to google the definition of mercy but were pretty sure it means you need to prepare yourself (before you rek yourself)"
Yes i PROMISE there will be rage-quits, this game isn't exactly all easy otherwise i'd rather not review this game at all.
I top my hat off to puppygames for creating a game that has variety and really pumps some love into a genre that i consider dead now (and tower defence games are my favourite :> )
HOWEVER, i have to give 1 VERY big problem i have...

This is one of my favorite indie games!
You control this flying ship which speeds up when you fly downwards and slows down when you fly upwards. So you have to use momentum and your surroundings (like cannons and bouncy platforms) to your advantage. It feels really nice to glide through the levels with your ship.
Now let's get to where the game really shines:
. Almost every level has multiple ways to beat it and there's a lot of hidden trophies. The levels are pretty varied, some are like puzzle where you have to find the right order to push blocks and unlock switches, others are about finger dexterity, where you navigate your ship through narrow corridors and evade moving hazards.
I also loved the speedrunning aspect of the game, every level has a highscore table where it shows you how fast you were compared to everybody else. I made it my goal to get into the top 1000 of every level and I had a lot of fun figuring out the fastest way to beat each level.

Whatever you may say about this game, I for one consider this a game to swear by... no wait, I meant at. This is a game to swear *at*, repeatedly and profusely as your fingers grow numb and your eyes become bloodshot.
This is a game about cutesy momentum-propelled sentient spaceships, where gasoline does not exist and you must rely on cannons and bouncing pads and other assorted devices to keep your spaceship avatar afloat. Though the the graphics are lighthearted, the game itself is a cruel stern mistress, demanding more and more of your fine motor controls and keen reflexes. In later stages, just one degree of rotation or one millisecond of hesistation can mean the difference between glorious victory and ignoble destruction.
Fortunately, this game has an easy mode, so beginners can have checkpoints and unlimited times to retry a stage and hit the goal. On the other hand, this game features normal and hard modes as well, for the player who demands maddening challenges to triumph over. The game's levels are actually short, and the game can be finished within a day, assuming you finish all the stages in one go. But if you enjoy unforgiving games and testing yourself to beat momentum puzzles as fast and as perfectly as you can, then definitely give this game a go!

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

The Path is centered around six sisters, each one a different Red Riding Hood that the player can take control of on the walk to their grandmother's house. Players are originally instructed to stay on the path on the way there. Upon reaching grandmother's house, players are treated with an eerily empty house, a mysterious rocking chair, and a pale old woman in bed with a stuffed wolf lingering nearby. Or, should they stray off the path, they encounter objects that inspire their chosen character to relive unpleasant memories. Gather enough of these memories and your character will encounter the dreaded wolf.
Unfortunately, what could have been an intriguing exploration game with a unique underlying concept is rendered more trouble than its worth by poorly designed gameplay. Each character you play as seems to move slower than the last, causing the game to suffer from terribly boring stretches of walking that seem to be taking you no where. The forest has very few noticeable landmarks or interesting sites to discover. I often found myself walking for long stretches of time, encountering absolutely nothing of interest. On top of the drearily slow pacing, the moment you start to feel like you're moving a little bit faster the camera swings to an inhospitable angle.
Overall, the Path has a pleasantly creepy vibe to it. The music is often discordant and mixed with child-like singing and chanting. The air is foggy and the forest is dark. The hallways of the grandmother's house are large and imposing and there's a sense of foreboding whether you stay on the path or adventure off of it. The memories you find are unnerving and just a little bit haunting. In terms of atmosphere, the Path is a clear winner. However, the poor controls make even turning your character clumsy and awkward. The game quickly becomes so tedious that it loses what charm it originally had going for it.
There's something to be said for the relaxation that comes with a good walking simulator. Many people debate over whether or not these type of "artistic experiences" qualify as true video games, but I believe that laid-back games that focus on exploration are just as valid a media as high-action platformers and shooters. As a genre, walking simulators often rely on some of the underlooked aspects of a good game: character, environment, and atmosphere. However, they are, first and foremost, intended to be played as video games and, as such, are required to maintain a certain level of playability that the Path fails to achieve.

As an art game, this game truly excels. Its very beautiful and has a lot of charm to it.
The best moments in the game for me were my first playthrough with the little girl. There's something to be said about running headlong into a forest as an innocent little girl. I came across a couple random objects and curios throughout my sprint into the unknown. Then I met the girl with the white dress, chased after her for a bit, then hand-in-hand we went through the forest, until she brought me back to the road. I then went to grandma's, and she was there in her bed. To my surprise, nothing "bad" happened. It was an interesting experience.
The worst moments in the game were mainly technical issues. In certain areas the character you control cannot run, making progress annoyingly slow. The camera will also get stuck on occasion, or just have a bad angle. I once passed through the door of a shack, and got stuck inside it, forcing me to quit. The game is also heavily cryptic, making it very hard to understand whats going on. I eventually got bored of the forest, not finding enough to keep me invested, and quit. When you do find something, all you get is a quip from your character. Not really worth the time.
All in all, its certainly worth it to try this totally unique experience, but its will strain anyone's patience soon enough.

I wanted to love this game so much because it has a beautiful world, great gameplay style, good ambient sound... it does a lot of things right.  But it's marred by a thousand small issues that make it a pain to play.  It sucks but these issues make the game more bothersome than its worth, at least to me.  For example, there are times when you are met with a challenge, and something glitches so that you can't do what you want.  Some of the hideouts in the game are inaccessible because of poor hitbox placement.  It kills me when I see small bugs like that ruining my gameplay experience.  Another issue that irks me is sometimes an enemy will stumble upon a fallen comrade and slip into a nonstop loop of calling for help.  It's funny the first few times but it did start to bother me after a while.
I've had issues where I kill an enemy in just the right spot for me to do it stealthily, then when the kill is done, the guy's body glitches and flings itself a few feet forward, warning all the people in the room of my presence and ruining my careful plots.  In a stealth game, I love trying to plan my route and carefully kill targets, but glitches like this destroy the experience for me.  I don't know whether this game was rushed at the end of development or if the devs just didn't care to clean up the bugs.  Either way, it's *just* enough of a problem that I'm going to stop playing.
If you can deal with issues like these, please play this game.  It's a wonderful experience.  I just can't handle it the way it is right now.

Great old school dungeon crawler. Create 4 characters and recruit 2 more. Turn based combat with a sense of preserve the more powerful abilities for when you really need them. Good gear selection often makes you consider which item will help which character the most. Boss battles add some difficulty to break up the grind. Decent monster variety - I was pleasantly surprised when I killed a slime and it split into baby slimes. A mix of default class skills and new abilities that can be purchased or unlocked with the talent tree. Global stats add one more reason to keep dungeon diving. Doesn't seem to be a way to heal or use abilities outside combat, but it seems balanced to take that into account. Little snippets or lore to provide some story.
Overall, a little rough around the edges - some of the tooltips could be improved, no way to see acquired abilities outside combat, the UI is a little bit clunky, enchanting isn't well explained, but everything is definitely good enough to not get on my nerves. Has many of the quality of life improvements that I've come to expect in newer games (tooltips, equipment comparison, autosave, reasonable inventory management) while having that older game vibe. Seems like the dev is responsive to comments and updating regularly.
Pretty mindless and the music is bad enough to turn off and listen to your own tunes or a podcast or something. Definitely scratches that grindy dungeon crawler itch.

Fun sci-fi tower defence
The story is somewhat simple. Basically, aliens (titans) are invading earth and it's your job to stop them.
Gameplay revolves around classical tower defence cliche's with sum bonuses. Basically there is one campaign to play and you unlock levels as you win them. The aim is to protect your factory from being destroyed. You have a limited number of towers you can place on the field, in order to defend your factory (which has limited health). When your factory is destroyed you immeditely lose the game. As you win each level, the money you earned gets tranfered to the next level. Furthermore, as you progress though the story you earn points which you can use to buy new towers, walls and other buildings. There are a variety of towers available including lasers, plasma, support anti- air. All towers will have limited ammo and will have to spend time to recharge again. Towers may be upgraded when clicking on them and spending resources (ie. money). You collect money by building resource gathering buildings. there are a wide variety of enemies including (strong-weak) land and air units. In some levels you will be facing a boss which requires clever placement of towers to destroy. You can aslo call upon limited abilities to assist in the defence such as bombs and fire-rate boost. defeated enemies may drop money or abilities to use later. The game lasted me 12,7 hours so it's decently long, plus you can replay levels after you beat them.
Audio serves the game well. Weapon fire sounds vary between lazers and other weapons. The sounds also help invoke a strong sci-fi, yet cartoony feel to the game (ie. less serious), Other sounds such as alarms are clear and crisp to help warn you of attacks at your base. Dialogue is spoken through text boxes only and there is no audio.
There is also a survival mode besides the campaign which tests how long you can last.
If your looking for a good tower defence game get this NOW!

This game was so terrible that I was driven to write about it here:

This company should be ashamed of themselves for releasing a product so terribly far from complete.  The number of bugs, the fact that the minimum requirements are considerably less than  my pc but I still had to turn everything to the absolute minimum to have any framerates at all...
Constant clipping issues from everything, whether it moves or not, regardless of graphics settings.  Crashing out of the game entirely.  Locking up on the load screen (you can go make tea and read a chapter from your favorite book while waiting for the loading screen under the best of scenarios).
I play multiple other games with as high or higher requirements listed than this game, with absolutely zero issues on any of them, no drop in framerates, no crashes, and I can run other programs in the background while playing.  With this game, I have absolutely everything else shut down, and it still struggles to run.
The interface is clunky, and not intuitive at all.  It has been a long time since I've had to go do a lookup on a game just to figure out how to open up a character screen.  Actually, I've NEVER had to do that for a game before.  For those wondering, F6 will let you back in to select your skills if you closed the screen because you were being attacked while picking them.
The most frustrating feature that I found was that you cannot select your heroic abilities to be set on "auto cast", so you will forever be micro-managing every single unit against the computer.  Think about that for just a moment.
This game was gifted to me by two of the dearest friends that I've ever had as an early Xmas gift, and now I have to face them and tell them that they need to request a refund on it, because I got tired of it crashing my computer every time I played it.
Perhaps one day companies will stop getting people like us to pay to beta-test their products, but I doubt that I'll still be gaming by then.

First of all, I want to say if you are interested in playing this game, don't let my opinion blindly turns you away from it. What I write is only meant to inform you of my opinion of the game. I hope it can be useful if you are on the fence about it.
I have always wanted to play this game ever since it was up as pre-order due to the art style and the premise, but when the game was actually released, the reviews are very lukewarm so I waited for it to go on sale. Which was probably the best decision I made.
I'd say it's a 5/10 game. I really wanted to love this game but I had a meh experience with it with some occasions of being extremely annoyed by the story and mechanics. After experiencing the game first hand, I personally won't recommend anyone buying it full price. I didn't completely regret giving the developers money for their hard work, it but I feel a bit betrayed for my time invested. However, please try the game if you are really curious, I'm sure you will enjoy some aspects of it. Here's my reasonings for the things said above:
Overall, the way the game is presented is different than a lot of other visual novels and I think that's very refreshing. I love the mature character design, despite all the girls being pretty girls, they're still very believable in terms of appearance. In fact it was the main thing that got me interested in the first place. The art style is mature and the visual is generally pleasing. The backgrounds are kind of reminiscence of Makoto Shinkai's work although not of the same level. The music is generally nice although forgettable. The only one you won't forget is the thing that plays when you are exploring. It's such an annoying earworm after several hours.
The story starts off with a mystery that is engaging and for awhile I was very interested in knowing what's going on. I was looking forward to unravel the mystery. If I were to play only the first half of the game, I would 100% recommend it to my friends. And that's where the problem lies for me. The story and characters gets really really lame and boring halfway and near the end. All the build up for really weak payoff. The endings are weak and I was legitimately disappointed.
Also I think I got the "true" ending on my 2nd playthrough and it wasn't at all satisfying. The characters are also very boring and or annoying, the exception being ♥♥♥♥♥ and Snappy, even then they're still not that great. Also the main character is an absolute jerk/bully. I did not enjoy playing as Takayuki.
The other strange thing is mechanics. The game is presented as this leisurely game and the story is kind of presented the same way. But then you are presented with the investigation mode where you question the characters a la Ace Attorney to give you information. It almost shamelessly tries to be Ace Attorney all the way from the music to character reactions. Which completely disjoint the experience from the peaceful and realistic -literally- everything else to this whacky Phoenix Wright cross examination. Some characters get so out of character too during this part. Also Max mode is such a useless gimmick and an annoying waste of time.
Overall, it was not the worst game ever, but for me the bad parts outweights the good parts. It is a personal opinion first and foremost. I can't diss this game because for the first 5-6 hours or so I legitimately had fun and engaged, but that turned disappointing past that hour mark. I can't recommend this game due to the disappointing endings and strange experience overall.

A "We couldn't get the rights to WH40K so we called it something else" game.
Run around in the bleak cyberfuture clad in stylized knight/samurai armor. Brings your guns, bring your drones, bring your cybernetic legs and bring your magic to kill loads of enemies across the galaxy. Ranging from drug-addled lowlife to the most elite soldiers in proper armies.
The game has a branching storyline with different endings and different levels will be seen depending on the route you take.
These levels themselves are usually very big and open. Requiring backtracking, sidetracking and generally exploring it as you complete objectives.
They are also sprinkled with characters to talk to and take sidequests from. Usually a fetching or assassination quest.
Enemies spawn continuously and will literally never run out. Not that you will run out of ammo anyway since enemies specifically drop ammo for the weapons you are using most of the time in addition to the few armories on the map. Big lockers where you can pick new equipment during a mission.
There's a decent selection of guns that all feel satisfying to shoot but are rarely actually much different from eachother. There's also a few drones, both stationary and mobile to help you, swords for close combat and a selection of miscellaneous items such as grenades, medkits, armor and of course the ammo itself.
You manage your inventory in a grid style. You have pockets quite literally everywhere. Shins, thighs, lower and upper arms, a bunch of belt slots and then your back. Pistols fit on the belt anything larger fit on the back. The rest are just for those small misc items.
You will have to manage your weight as well, getting a penalty to movement speed the more you carry.
Which leads me to the next part, stats. Yes you heard that right. E.Y.E is a FPS/RPG hybrid in which you level up and allocate points into your stats. There's a lot of them and you will have to specialize from the start if you want to use the late game gear due to stat requirements. At the start you pick three genes that determine how much of a bonus or how bad a malus each stat get then you get to roll the dice until you're satisfied.
You will also get to perform research (which takes an absurd amount of time later on) for new gear or raising the limits of your cybernetic upgrades. These just give you a flat bonus to something. Legs make you faster and jumpier, arms make you stronger etc.
TL;DR (and me getting off track)
Run around and shoot baddies as a supersoldier in the future.

Rating: 6/10 ("Slightly above average")
This visual novel makes me wish there was a "neutral" option as opposed to simply "recommended/not recommended".
Recommended for: People who enjoy VNs. I wouldn't recommend it for your first VN as it can be a bit slow and boring in places; I don't think it can capture a first time reader's attention.
My playtime is 14 hours. It took about 10 hours to clear the first route, so the remaining 4 is for the rest of the endings. Skipping dialogue I'd already read, of course.
The art is very good, very high quality. Music is decent but forgettable.
The atmosphere feels very calm and serene despite the subject matter. There really isn't a sense of urgency apart from certain endings. Selecting/clearing a route is very easy: simply select only the first options in letters and you will get the first ending, only the second options for the second ending, etc.
The game tries to be more interactive than most visual novels  by giving you options to "Move", "Ask", "Check", access "Inventory", "Think", use "Guidebook", and "Smartphone". At worst, this feels unnatural and unnecessary. At best, it's a fun option during investigations (which I'll get to in a bit). There is a feature called Max Mode which you use in certain situations, usually investigations, to say the right thing. It feels a bit like the game is trying to emulate Danganronpa in that way.
Investigations take place in each chapter when you have to confirm the identity of Aya's friends. Most of the time, it is quite simple to select the correct options, but occassionally there is trial and error to it. Luckily you only actually have to complete them the first ending you get; after this, there is a "skip chapter" function which is best left until after you reply to a letter.
The characters are, for the most part, decently written, with some questionable aspects to a few like Nozu/Chibi (why on earth did he ___? it doesn't really make sense). Takayuki, the protagonist, is passable, but has moments of being exasperatingly dense and coming off as simply a trash human being. Taking advantage of someone's phobia to force them into a panic attack in order to get information...really?
Overall, it was an adequate experience. Some of the endings were unsatisfying, but the "true end" makes up for it, mostly.

This is how KAMI works:  Click on a square to assign it a new color, and all connecting squares of that color will change too.  Change it to the color of squares near that group, and you can change those squares next move too, as they're now the same color.  Do this until the whole area is one color.
There is a surprising amount of depth to the game, but I didn't have a lot of trouble with it.  Also, the last 9 "premium" (free expansion) levels seemed to be random garbage.  Even so on a couple of those levels I got UNDER the perfect score, which seems like it shouldn't be possible.  Maybe those levels weren't very polished.  I feel as though a bigger playing area could have added some needed challenge and enabled more varied puzzle designs.
It's very pretty too, but I wouldn't pay 4 bucks for this.  Get it on sale.

I believe the three strongest points to cover on this game are its story, gameplay, and replay value.
STORY:
An interesting and creative universe is one of the most strong features of this title, which isn't terribly common in stealth action games. Your choice of player character is a fascinating specimen in of themselves, and often can be amusing to behold as he bumbles through the narrative. The actual plot itself is somewhat weak, however, and leaves you wanting to see more of this fascinating world.
GAMEPLAY:
WIth a few exceptions, the game is generally go from point A to point B. The strength in gameplay here is the sheer variety in what you are actually able to do, to deal with the various obstacles in your path. Actual combat in this game is weak and a generally poor way to solve your problems, but that is very much the point -- you are just a goblin thief. You are small, scrawny, and generally fragile -- but very skilled, and crafty. Enemies can overwhelm you quite easily (and some cannot be fought at all) , but the game offers you a good amount of tools for outsmarting them.
REPLAY VALUE:
The game also offers numerous awards for completionists-- running a mission without killing anyone, without setting off any alarms, collectathons, and secondary objectives. Replaying missions is necessary for completion of all of the challenges, which can help completionists, but I believe most people would simply play through the story and put the game down for good.

Nimbus is a lot of fun and very pretty, and it's basically just as challenging as you want it to be. There are a lot of optional levels, you can configure how you want the checkpoints to work, and your time records don't unlock any content or anything so it doesn't matter if you don't care about trying to accomplish them.
However...
If you _are_ interested in time records, be aware that Nimbus has one enormous bug: it bases its records on how much time elapses in the real world between the beginning and the end of the level, rather than how many game ticks pass in that time. So depending on how powerful your computer is, falling through the same vertical space without pressing any keys may take you anywhere from 4 seconds to 30 or more. Lowering your resolution and turning off graphical effects can help with this on some of the levels, but these are not adjustments you should be forced to make to fix a gameplay issue.

An incredibly slow, occasionally frustrating platformer with charming aesthetics.
If you want a very slow game with some tricky platforming elements, you will probably enjoy Pid, but the pacing and method of maneuving (toss the beams) struggled to keep my attention.
PROS:
-Art style is endearing.
-Levels have a variety of platforming elements.
NEUTRALS:
-"Dispensers" are oddly designed and seem pointless, especially since the same items are dropped by enemies and found throughout the levels anyway.
-Collecting stars seems just as pointless as the dispensers. It seems the stars are finite, although there is no HUD to track if you've collected them all or not (and you spend them on consumable items..??).
CONS:
-For a platformer with some tricky setups, the games "toss a beam and float through it mechanic" leads to some very looses controls at times. It would have been much better if the player could control the actual landing point of the beam instead of it just being a set distance in front of you (this requires a bit of practice just to learn where the beam lands, and in a game with already poor pacing it really struggles to keep the player engaged).
-Incredibly slow gameplay.  Looking at the achievements, less than 15% of players have beaten the first boss....probably because they got bored...
-Slightly floaty controls (not bad, but they aren't tight).

Honestly, this Dawn Of War and all it's pieces along with the first Dawn Of War. Are forever going to be timeless favourites.
Countless hours are guranteed to be spent customising and building your forces up.
However from the things I've seen and read in regards to the third are leaving a reluctant feeling towards it, which is unfortunately a shame as it seemed the games took a seriously wrong turn from that point.
Now, with Dawn Of War 2 it seemed to have a complete overhaul to combat compared with the first.
The first allowing you to create a HQ of sorts and amass armies of 20-30+ as you worked through the campagin or skirmishes in real time strategy style.
With the second you control much smaller forces, to be precise "Commanders" and their squad (Up to 3) along with the combat being completely different.
Dawn of War 2 introduces cover mechanics on a far greater scale and much more destructible enviroments. This meant you had more options to choose when deciding what to do on a mission, take the shorter and more exposed route but risk being wiped out? Or send a squad of scouts ahead on the route with cover? Sometimes the use of explosives would be permitted to break down a wall and create a new route, but the general use was taking out heavily fortified bunkers with an artillery strike.
Dawn Of War 2 introduced a new threat to the universe which was also the main campagin for this game. The Tyranids, an endless and near infinite invasion of alien beasts. Feeding on everything in their path to spread and power the hive. Even whole universes would fall to the swarm.
This threat to the Space Marines were as ever deadly just as the Necrons were in the first. Numerous sub-species of Tyranid meant you had to carefully adapt for each mission, the same can be said when facing Ork or Eldar. Choosing whether to adapt more to the heavy armor of the enemy with plasma and explosives or to become a force to be reckon with by using your own heavy armor - Dreadnought Included.
Also fear not if you loved the Chaos, they are still here in this game and even have their own campaign. At this moment in time I'm still going through it so I shall not comment on that part.
I could probably carry on writing what could seem as rabble, but honestly. If you loved the first game and do not mind a bit of change, then I would still recommend this game to you. Stand strong Space Marine.

Here's what I wish I'd known before I got into this story.
A single playthrough of the story is 20-30 hours long, and there are only five decision points in the entire story (six on a second playthrough). Seriously - this story is LONG. Stop for a moment and try to imagine yourself clicking through a story, line-by-line, for twenty hours. If you flinch at the thought, then just look for the highlights on YouTube instead.
There's no way to measure your progress through the story. I didn't know how long it was supposed to be, so it felt like being on a bus ride without knowing how many more miles are ahead of me - will I arrive at my destination in a half hour or in eight hours? Around hour 10 I lost my patience with it and I started going through the story as fast as I could - speed-reading a few lines per second (which isn't very difficult) - and I managed to get to the ending in just over 14 hours total. Occasionally I got a screen that says "extend the little wings which fly in the sky highly." That's a chapter stop, and I didn't realize this at first. I would have enjoyed it a lot better if the chapters had titles or numbers to help measure where I am in the story.
This story feels like it wants to be an anime. There's easily enough material and music here for a full 26-episode season. But, at the same time, the story really doesn't need to be this long. It's a slice-of-life thing between a college boy and several girls, all of whom are well-defined with strong personalities and quirks. (There's also a duck with a hat.) It's a pleasure to get to know the characters, but lots of scenes are drawn out past the point of tedium.
There are three high points of the story. One is the recorded dialogue: EVERY LINE of dialogue (other than that of the protagonist, Aoi) is voiced in Japanese, and the voice actors are good and put an anime level of inflection into their delivery. If you want to learn Japanese, it's interesting to compare the spoken Japanese with the English text translation - and there's a scrollback log that lets you re-read and replay previous lines.
The second high point is the artwork; the backgrounds are brightly colored, and the characters are beautifully drawn, with changes to eyes and mouth giving a little bit of animation from line to line. Animated transitions between scenes are a nice touch. And the third high point is the music - the background songs are distinctive without being annoying, and there are two "theme songs" which are presented like opening- and closing-credits videos when you reach them in the story.
It's also nice that the story is fairly realistic about how much time, effort, and training it takes to build a glider and get it into the air. It gets points for not skimping on the detail here.
I heard that the English version of the story was censored clumsily, so I installed the "Restoration Patch". Once I figured out how to get it working, it worked reasonably well, though I still had a few problems with bits of artwork sticking around after they should have disappeared. Even with this patch, the story suffers from poor translation in the second half (the words and sentences make sense, but I can't figure out what anyone is doing or why). The patch also restores the hentai scenes - and let me just say, don't get this story just for the hentai scenes. There are two tame topless scenes in the first half (you can probably find the artwork online), and then in the second half (I did Ageha's route) there are three sex scenes that seem completely out of place, pushing the characters to suddenly become a whole lot more adult - but I guess that's the point. Fine if you like that sort of thing, but a little weird.
A general map of the story:
First half = building a glider and flying it to the clouds. When you reach the first "music video" you're about to the middle of the first half, and the first decision point isn't long after there.
Second half = one year later, putting the Soaring Club back together again, and pursuing your chosen romance.
Overall, despite the nice touches, I'd have to recommend against this story. It's sweet, but I'd say it's just not worth spending this kind of time and focus on (for me at least). The characters just aren't deep enough to deserve this amount of story time. I've gotten a lot more out of stories that have been a lot less of a time commitment.

It's tough to recommend this game unless you really REALLY like tower defense games.
Going through my backlog of games, I started playing Revenge of the Titans which I got from a Humble Bundle years ago. At first, it was kind of neat. The art style was simple and kind of cool, the music was decent (in the end levels in particular, there's this really good ambient track), there was a little bit of humour in the campaign, and it seemed like there would be a lot of variation in enemies and weapons as you level up. But several hours in and the gameplay flaws really began to show.
- There are maybe 3 very distinct enemy types. There are tons of enemies in this game, but they pretty much vary only by things like "oh, this guy moves faster" or "oh, this guy has more armor" etc.
- Level after level, the grind shows itself. Same gameplay, pretty much every single level. (Other than when you need to use the Capacitor, a specific weapon used for a specific enemy type.) There's never any variation, or anything that makes you scratch your head and plan something out. And the art of each level pretty much varies only by colour.
- There's loads of weapons and gadgets to unlock and use, but you'll most likely end up using the same combination of weapons for every single level once available.
- Campaign is started on the hardest setting by default...and it's mind numbingly easy.
Most of my play time was spent grinding for the last few achievements (which was honestly the one thing that kept me going.) So, I'd give it a 4.5/10. It is a decent game for being so cheap (especially from a Humble Bundle) but again, only if you are desparately wanting some sort of RTS/TD game can I give a full recommendation. The developers also seem really nice too, and are active on the discussion forums, which is a plus.

I think the best way to describe this game is to call it a mod for garry's mod. That is what it feels like to me.
Positives.
1. Fast paced action oriented gameplay.
2.It's free.
3. It more or less requires teamwork to actually get anywhere unless one guy can manage to rush forward by sheer luck alone.
4. If you can get a good team the game works well and has a decent balance where the classes work off each other well.
Negatives.
1. It's far too easy to get overrun. If you stay in one room or area for more than a minute you have basicly ♥♥♥♥ed yourself over. While it is true that a group could hold out in a room, since the zombies never stop spawning you aren't really helping yourself. Holding up only works on the lower difficulty settings. Too many zombies. Because of the way this game works, because of the guns you have and because you are going to get seperated from your team. It becomes far too difficult early on.
2. The weapons are unbalanced. I'm not sure if this was done to get us to relyon our teamates but the guns are not very good. If you are playing support it's practically impossible to actually defend yourself against a mob of zombies. You will not do enough damage to take out the group at any point. Shotguns are painfully slow to reload, if you get a group larger than the ammount of shells you can have loaded at once you are ♥♥♥♥ed. This is a bit weird really since the game more or less encourages you to rush but it doesn't really give you any weapons you can outright rush with. The closest is the sniper which does enough damage but if your aim is even slightly off you'll find you might also be screwed.
3.The game relies on some amount of teamwork but you'll rarely get any teamwork. For some reason, most of the servers I joined simply resulted in people running way the ♥♥♥♥ ahead and everyone trying to catch up. It's more or less impossible to solo this game so running ahead helps no one. If you run into a large group you are kinda ♥♥♥♥ed unless you have some teamates with you but most of the time they will just abandon you first chance they get. Add this to the fact that many of the people who are playing don't speak the same language and are usually younger and you have a problem.
4. There are a lot of kids and non-english speakers playing this game. Look if someone doesn't speak english that is fine, the problem is if I need to communicate to you i'm going to have a very hard time doing so. Even the kids who speak english aren't really much help. I've run into very little screaming or anything like that. However I have run into people that don't seem to understand the fundementals of the game and just try to hold up in a room.
I think there is potential here for something really interesting but some improvements needs to be made. Since it's free I recomend trying it just because there is enough here to be entertaining and frustrating.

When I bought this game I was on an adventure game kick and an indie game kick and steam was scrathing that particular itch at the time. The game appeared to be an interesting little indie adventiure game based on running through mazes, collecting clues, solving puzzles, etc. all while telling a rich story, through gameplay and abstract symbolism. It was supposed to ba a tale of a woman who, while in a quasi-concious state, unravels the story of her demise and/or recounts the regrets in her life, ultimately finding a way to acheive some sense of inner peace or resolve some internal conflict; perhaps while having an out of body experience as she dies or edges closer to death. All this seemed interesting to me as an adeventure game player and I was excited to unravel the mysteries of this womans life and what exactly had happened to her. WHAT I GOT, was what appeared to be a slideshow of random industrial and urban set pieces that resembled something you might be shown by a friend who just went on a walk with thier first DSLR camera. The story was so abstracted and boring, and there were no puzzle elements or really any clues to find at all. You can beat the game or more accurately "complete the interactive experience" in about 20-45 min by simply moving from frame to frame and clicking on everything. The word game doesnt really apply as there is no challenge or any sense of completeing anything at the end, its more of an activity center for manic depressives. Threre seems to be no resolution of conflict (nor any conflict in general) in the story, and even if there were its conveyed so poorly and in such a boring manner that I couldn't have cared less anyways.   Moreover I feel especially cheated for buying this for about 6-7 $ US expecting to be puzzled and challenged for at least the better part of 7-8 hours, only to then "finish the experience" in under 30 min, with no recourse for return or exchange. Do yourself a favor and do not waste any money on this "interactive experience", which was clearly designed by people who thought it was so edgy, unique, indie and deep (when it is none of these things) that it could rest on those laurels without anything resembling what would be objectively considered a game. Some might say that Dear Esther could be given the same criticism, however DE is a much richer experience, immerseive in its beautifully exectued graphics and sound desgin which (with a little help from headphones and a dark room) can transport the player into the setting giving them a large sense of immersion. DE is also short hoever, I feel I could explore the island of DE for hours (and have) and there is more value in it to me based on the immersive experience it creates. While DE is not technically a game it IS a well crafted "interactive experience" the mystery surrounding the letters and clues you find on the island are abstract and cryptic enough not to spell everything out for you, but are engaging and keep you wanting to search the island in an effort to discover what happend and why its important. Trauma on the other hand fails as an "interactive experience" as much as it does as a game. The choice to move from boring still to still and mediocre sound design make the experience wholly non-imersive. The story is also so abstracted, disjointed and boring that by the end you dont care what is going on or why, thus you have no insentive to continue "coimpleting the experience". Trauma fails miserably as a game and even more so as an "interactive experience", if you are intrigued by Trauma, dont bother and buy Dear Esther instead becuase clearly more love and care went into making it and it is a much richer experience on the whole.

Imagine you arrive to listen to some kind of musical production. The stage is a little too small. The lighting is a little too bright. An accompaniment begins; it is serviceable, maybe even has some good moments although it frequently veers into the distinctly unimpressive. You wait in anticipation for the star of the show. But the backing track just goes on and on.  Every now and then, a performer steps up. Maybe they are here to really kick off the show! But no. They just perform another mediocre little routine that, after a brief moment of promise, fades uninspiringly back into the drone. There is no star, no performance to make this worth spending your night and money on. You leave unsatisfied with an empty experience.
And that is pretty much my experience with SpellForce 3. There is no part of the game that is actually exciting or compelling to engage with. Where there are interesting concepts, the follow-through to make them that "star" is without fail not just slightly but entirely lacking. I feel that Grimlore did not want to commit to fleshed out or engaging systems on either the RTS or RPG side; a mistaken compromise that results in an empty frame of a game without meat on its bones. Far from the "perfect blend of RTS and RPG", it feels like the developers didn't have a clear and well thought out direction in hybridising the two genres which consequently brought down their whole effort.

Welcome to the Shrouded Isle, where ignorance is a virtue, and kindness is a crime. As the high priest, your responsibility is to perpetuate the centennial tradition and appoint community members in charge of the monthly cultural events, such as book burnings or flagellating of sinners.
At the end of each season you will also need to pick a Sinner to sacrifice on the public square, thus appeasing the Old God. Don't worry it won't be too hard: everyone is a sinner! You'll just need to make sure you have enough evidence.
You have one job and it sounds easy: making decisions and appointing people. But every decision has consequences. The community is bound together by very strict social constraints, and balance must be upheld. Let your obedience or fervor drop below critical levels and society will collapse, as well as the Old God being angered! You must also maintain favor with the 5 major houses, or face rebellion.
Appoint someone you know to a job and you can calculate the effects on balance. Appoint someone you don’t know however, and you will find out more about them. It's all about fine tuning and taking risks.
The Shrouded Isle is short, but has quite some reply value. You'll fail at first. A few times. The game doesn't have full tutorials but relies on the player to figure out how Society works; a plus in my book.
The bi-chromatic graphics are gloomy and fitting (you can pick from 5 color schemes).
The music is also appropriately dark and atmospheric.
The most chilling aspect is the societal critic, which gives you a full insight on how backwards religious communities thrive, without an ounce of preachiness or moral highground. The Shrouded Isle will take you back to the Middle Ages, and make you glad you weren't there in person.

I understand that the patterns were used to add to the difficulty, but it wasn't for me.
Other than that though, the game is perfect (in my opinion, of course), and the level of difficulty is just about right. I definitely recommend KAMI and I look forward to trying other games created by State of Play.

EYE is like a nightmare that you do not want to wake up from.
As alien as it is alienating, EYE offers an experience like no other. You take the role of an secrete militant religious organization that calls itself EYE. Due to plot reasons, you wake up with no memory for unspecified reasons.
The first thing you may realize is that the controlls were probably made by Marsians and the tutorial consists out of clips from Youtube videos explaining basic commands. It doesn't help that much of the text is poorly translated from french. After making your way out of the tutorial  cave the game allows you to pick your equipment, using inventory system. The game allows all kinds of builds, from Street Samurai to Psychers, to Snipers and Heavies.
A notable shoutout is to the guy who came up with the hacking system, which is a riff on classic JRPG combat, which essentially means that the object you are hacking has as much of a chance to take over your body as you have to do their. Essentially, when you hack into a door, the door hacks into you. You may posess hacked soldiers and use them for stealth manuvers.
After loading up every square inch of your body you may begin to power through the gangs of raiders and spacemarines located in a dull industrial area. If you haven't noticed, you also have psychick powers, which allows you to create astral clones of yourself, as well as push enemies away from you, shattering their ribcage.
The interaction between all those different systems created a fascinating dynamic, which keeps one hooked for hours on end.

What happened to Fumino Aya? (Japanese way of introducing is the family name first, then the given name)
Btw a nice play on words as Fumino Aya can be also read as "Fumi no Aya", which is "Letter from Aya" or "Ayas letter".
Aya is a penpal from 15 years ago who suddenly stopped writing to you. But then you find a unopened letter from her, in which she states that she has killed someone and can`t write to you anymore. You`re confused. What does she mean? Why have you not seen this letter 15 years ago when it arrived? And why is this "new" letter missing a post stamp?
You decide to look for Aya and travel to her hometown where you find a vacant lot instead of her home. You learn that there was a fire 15 years ago, which burned the house down. But why is everbody mentioning that Aya herself is dead already 25 years? And what about those "ghost sightings" of Aya after her death? Who wrote those letters to you?
Is Fumino Aya really dead?

Trauma is a casual Point-&-Click adventure game but with a slight twist. In the game, you play a young woman exploring her dreams shortly after a car accident that kills her parents and hospitalizes her. The dreams serves as metaphors for her life, exploring her childhood, her time in college, her relationship with her parents, and her feelings on her life. The dreams sequences are made up of real life photographs, which are nothing short of breath taking, arranged in a way to create a sort of segemented 3D environment. While this seems like it would lend itself to some interesting puzzles, it does not. In fact, Trauma lacks puzzles, however, instead favoring a drawing mechanic.
There are four drawings in the game (Lift, Catch, Drain, Cut) and each one allows you to interact with cetain objects in each dream to unlocks different endings. The drawing mechanic, however, is not deep, at least not mechanically, and serves more as a tool for exploring the metaphor of a dream.
Overall, the game is intesting. It's beautiful, does some unusual things and ends up touching upon certain things that most games fail to.

This game has some promise to it, but I can't recommend it as it is.
The basic gameplay is alright, and I like the theming for the different classes. The best gear adds to basic stats (for example, +damage done, +max HP) as well as adding skills to your deck while they are equipped (such as +1 temporary counter next physical attack card).
The problem is that certain builds straight lose to some monsters - try being a barbarian against a troll who regenerates 25 hp a turn, but also hits really hard.  He's weak to fire, you see.  Not that you have ever had a chance to take a fire card.
Aside from that, the difficulty curve is really bad for a proper roguelike.  You literally can't build a good enough deck to have a shot of winning without grinding gear and fame across multiple heroes.  The meta-progression elements here are less well-executed than in, say, Rogue Legacy or Dead Cells.  Because I expect that I would have to grind many playthroughs that would end in getting trounced at level 9, then again at level 12, or some such, I have no interest in continuing to play this game and can't recommend it.

So much potential - such a great concept, and *almost* fun!
Unfortunately, the difficulty spikes that often plague genuine rogelikes are, in this game, a total loss for the game as a whole.  Obviously, punishing RNG is somehow fun to some people.  Some few masochists.  But in this game, I can't find it fun.  In fact, it ruins any fun I was having.
To be clear to the developers, it's just not cool to inevitably end up in a match-up -- in every playthrough -- that just isn't possible to defeat with your current class.  It's not a matter of skill - suddenly, the only matches I can pick are two over-leveled enemies that can kill me before I can set anything up.  What a waste of the first and/or second dungeon's card hoarding!  What a waste of time...
Suggestions: Either give me a better option (start over the dungeon?), or give me a game option for "casual"/softcore that allows me to die and stay in the game.  Sure, call me out on it: mock me as a weenie, keep me off the leaderboard, block my achievements, but save me from the RNG gods and the STUPID difficulty spikes!
What a waste...
Edit: It *is* addictive.  I may have to change my rating, a few hours in.  The "retry" upgrade *does* give you a couple more retries, but I still think that the final level is too difficult for fun.  Even once I have a "perfect deck" in my mind, there are "hard counters" in creature types.  If you diversify to hedge against hard counters, you end up with a crap deck.  If you specialize, you inevitably get cornered against a creature that it absolutely can't beat.  That's not fun.  I'd be down for a more casual version, but I guess that makes me the wrong audience.
