What this game does well:
It has an artistic, non-concrete story that is somewhat creepy.  It is an interesting jumble of snippets from semi-related events.  The story, to me, felt more like seeing the shadow of an event, and being unsure what it really was.  What does it mean?  I believe this obscure feeling is quite intended, and is the main drive of playing the game.
What this game fails at (miserably):
Being a game.  The game doesn't just make you walk slowly around.  It makes you walk SLOWLY around.  Too slow!
It would be different if the graphics and music were a cool experience.  But they just aren't.  It's rather ugly.  The best part of the graphics are the scrawls and doodles that pop up on the screen, kind of like after seeing a bright light for a second.  But the trees, the characters, the ground... they all just look terrible.  If the game is working so hard to be artistic, they really need to consider the visual and auditory effect they are getting across.  Although, I understand that art can be whatever it wants to be... but I don't believe they were capable of improving the visuals.  If they were producing photorealistic scenery in other games, and then they decided to shoot specifically for this ugly style, then I'd say they made a bad choice, but accept their choice.  However, ToT has basically proven that they are not visual artists in the realm of 3D graphics.  Perhaps a case could be made for the color choices being well done, but it feels like such a small victory when one girl's buttcrack is a line awkwardly drawn on the back of her character.......
The sound was closer to getting across an effect, but I think they just didn't know how to get the effect across quite right.

This is a good little game.
The sound is good, the animations and graphics are simple but work very well for this game.
There is a feeling of progression here, since you get to keep loot and unlock skills for the next run.
Your starting deck depends on what class you pick and they are quite different in their strategies. There are a couple of different routes you can take by having different equipment and picking up different cards during play, but the basic gameplay strategy is to reduce your deck to fewer good cards with great synergy.
There will be plenty of hard decisions along the way, that will impact your deck, or perhaps your future runs.
All in all, the deckbuilding is not spectacular, since you can not set up your own custom starting deck, but have to pick a class with a premade starting deck, but there is definitely still enough here to be fun, and you get to customize the deck a bit, by unlockables, once you start gaining fame.
I also like how thematic the cards for the enemies are, for instance Medusa has Medusas gaze cards, that can turn your cards into stone and Vampires have fly, steal card and life drain cards.
Different enemies poses different threats and have different strengths and weaknesses, which of course will make good or bad matchups, depending on what class and what strategy you focus on.
The gameplay is fluid, quick and addicting, so I recommend this game.

The art style is FANTASTIC. That is the only positive game element to be had here. Save your money and stay away, regardless of the pandering reviews from what I can only assume are people who have never played tower defense games before. I mean hell, if it wasn't for the art style this thing wouldn't even survive on Miniclip.
The game feels like a continuing list of bad design choices, a case study in what not to do in a tower defense time. When I complain I feel like a lecturer in basic game design: "encourage strategic play", "present consistent rules for your game world", or maybe "release without game crippling bugs and advancement locks". It's bad enough now, but be greatful you weren't playing when the campaign tech tree was locked and you'd be forced to menu-delete a game when an armored enemy type showed up an you had no units capable of damaging it.
Almost every mistake (as I'm coming to call them, because I honestly don't think any of them were actually thought through properly), is at once trivially annoying and long term game breaking. Manually resetting and time consumingly repicking your tech tree to deal with new enemy types every level may seem simply irritating, but gradually emerges into an overall expectation that you pick the "right" tech tree that enables victory, and all others will fail by default. Having to painfully micromanage your reloads is grating, and eventually ensures that every strategy will be limited to your clicktimes and not your strategy, dooming any kind of open-world defense. And the rediculous armor and repulsion systems vex you piece by piece as your weapons and equipment become obsolete, before finally running the final, game destroying flaw: you will not lose when your defenses are overwhelmed, you will lose when the charming little boxlike enemies have countered every possible defense and your entire list of defensive options have become obsolete.
It's like the equiptment they give you is just a taunt of what your strategy could have been: oh hey, here's a rapid fire turret. Too bad it does no damage to enemies after level 4, when they all have armor. Hey, check out these repulsion buildings to herd the enemy into chokepoints. Sucks that every other enemy after level 6 has become "intelligent" and will simply run up and eat them. Laser weapons? Armor reflects them - useless. Slowing razor field units? Can't be used with the anti-armor explosive guns, which destroy all your own buildings, including your own defenses, because apparently future scientists drink too much coffee to understand friend-foe ID. Similarly, saving up money in the campaign feels rewarding until you find out that the game raises the difficulty with your cash level and thus it's advantagous to avoid any kind of strategic spending. RotT plays like a cod game, where every interesting idea gets thrown out within ten minutes because it happens to be too fun and interesting to keep using.
I like playing tower defense games because of the evolution of your goals and the resource management involved. I'm not sure I like playing them when resource management is a menial clusterf*** and the evolution of methods is only happening in the enemy forces. I've never had a tower defense game where I've felt so much like *I* was the computer, and the enemy forces were actually the human, getting to play adaptively against me with all the strategy and choice-making I was missing. Playing like a bot isn't a good feeling. I do not recommend playing like a bot. I do not recommend this game.

Similarly, the extra abilities you can unlock in the game are all useful or entertaining, but are underused.  An added disincentive is that by the time you unlock everything, the game is over and you don't get a chance to play with your gadgets.

Gunpoint is a stealth puzzle platformer. You play as a freelance spy who takes various jobs in order tries to solve a rather complicated murder case. Your main tool in solving the levels is the ability to rewire various electronics such as doors, alarms, switches and even enemy guns.
The pixel art visuals are passable but not particularly impressive.
The sound effects and music are fairly basic but get the work done.
Most of the levels are built around your ability to rewire objects and often this needs to be combined with more traditional stealth to solve the levels. This was fun enough, but unfortunately most of the levels are fairly simple affairs. I would have liked to see bit more complexity with the level design.
The game also has various extra gadgets you can buy. The early ones are pretty much essential, but many of the later ones are rarely useful or required. It would have been nice to see some more depth here too. There's also a rather pointless upgrade system for your abilities.
Most of the levels are quite easy and simple. Some of the optional objectives are slightly trickier at least.
The controls are passable with a mouse and keyboard. I wasn't a big fan of the jumping controls, however.
The game has some pretty good and genuinely funny writing. The noir-inspired story is decent too, although a little bit too convoluted for its own good.
Gunpoint is a decent enough game with solid writing. I would have liked to see better level design, however, and the pixel art isn't very impressive. I would still recommend Gunpoint, especially if you like stealth games.

Fun game to play. If you've played DoW, then this second iteration might not be your cup of tea. Reason being, is that base building is foregone entirely, and while generally more lore-friendly than Soulstorm that had various allied factions fight each other for no apparent reason, it's more akin to a top down squad based rpg than an rts.
Micromanagement is the skill that you will mostly need. Providing troops with cover, reviving them, healing, deploying grenades and other gadgets, that kind of stuff. Maneuvering around the battlefield is fairly intuitive, and the AI does a good job at both taking cover and returning fire, all while throwing a nade or two.
I do find that the game needs some time-slowing feature to allow for more intense battles be controlled better. I don't like heavy micro, but I certainly can do it. Unfortunately, every boss battle is very intense, requiring non stop commands to evade special attacks and artillery strikes. Intensity in boss fight is amazing, generally speaking, however when all you can do is dodge attacks and have no time to set up a counter offensive, simply because by the time your guys have cleared the blast area, another one is coming, things can get infuriating pretty fast.
This aside, graphically the game is pretty and offers plenty of gore. Limbs flying off and corpses blowing up into tomato paste. Explosions are very well done and are satisfying to watch. And so is combat in general.
Sound-wise, weapon shots, explosions, vehicles, crumbling buildings, everything is top notch in the sfx department.
As for the story, it's pretty good, concidering the style of game this is. I won't spoil anything, but just know that Aurelia (the Blood Ravens chapter homeworld) is a pie a lot of races want to take a bite of.
Mechanically however the game suffers a little bit by having no ingame way of remaping your controls. It is possible to edit a text file but that is not something most people would want to dable with or bother for that matter. This means that if you want a QWER type skill usage, you'll have to do some tinkering with the keybinds file. And you may as well do it, since some skills are in places they don't belong at all. Medkits are M, Nades are F, exiting buildings  is U, you can imagine how quickly your hand will have to jump around different buttons for basic skills. This is not a problem in and of itself, but when paired with the fact that you have 4 squads that have to be controlled simultaneously, all with a different skillset, things become much more different as you'll have to jump around alot. For example, you press 2 for your tac team, F for a nade, then 4 for your scouts, D for a satchel charge, then they get low, 1 for Commander, M for medkit. and so on and so forth.
It's very easy to confuse your orders. If you press 3 by mistake, or haven't gotten used to which numbber accords to which squad, you may give an irrelevant command, or waste some ability/equipment. Not a big deal, but there are some problems with the customization of the control scheme.
Anyway, if you can get this game on sale, defo go for it, worth your money. If you get the Master Pack on sale, then defo go for it.

I do like the option of accepting quests (though they seem very limited currently, like 'kill 5 imps next trip'), and of returning to the town to recover and try some upgrading.  It does end up with a rather grindy feel, though, even with being able to choose to re-enter at levels other than 1 every time.  And venturing in to the ever-changing tower has quite a bit of appeal for exploring, even if it seems fairly limited so far.
Inside the tower you only run in to enemies when opening new rooms.  You never know what's behind the door, a tough or easy fight or something else.  You also won't know how much health and mana you've recovered until you step in to a fight, and can't do any preparation outside of combat.  No potions are involved.
Misspellings are not rare.  Character generation, you get to create 4 out of a potential party of six, is very limited.  A very limited number of headshots.  Species doesn't make much obvious difference and there's very little information.  The only time armor rating for characters can be found is when entering the tower, for instance, and limits on what a class can equip aren't shown...you only find out when trying to equip.  There's very little or no explanation about how most of the mechanics function.
There also appears to be some bug(s).  Some of the level 5 traits aren't available to select despite appearing to meet the criteria.  Locked doors you can find keys as loot on enemies, but I've yet to find how one is supposed to open blocked doors.
To sum up, I'd say that Darkest Dungeon does most everything Zavix Tower does, but far better.  It just has that much darker theme.  Zavix looks more like traditional D&D style adventuring, but the execution still needs a lot of work.

My feelings on Istrolid are...Conflicted. This game has a lot going for it: Simple, streamlined graphics that will run on any computer, good ship construction capability, fun combat, (for the most part), a decent "Campaign" mode, multiplayer support, and a fun challenge mode. Because of these good factours, it's a great little game on the surface. That being said, upon further inspection, and several hours of gameplay later, There are some aspects of this game that simply do not stick well with me: I have no idea who this game is supposed to be for! Those who want agood RTS will be disappointed at the poor controls lack of real goals other than "claim all the circles on the map". Those who want to design great looking ships of various size classes will be sorely saddened by the limit of parts to $1000 worth...and in a game in which a single part may cost between $10 to $100 each, that really isn't much at all. Because of this, you're limited to making Cruiser-sized ships at the largest, in a game which desperately needs Capital ships and even mobile battle stations. To fix this issue, I suggest the developers remove the $1000 limit and let the players build what they want, no matter the size! The challenge would then be waiting for the ingame money to build up in torder to build such colossi while also protecting your bases. All in all, there are the elements of a great game here, the developers just need to remove the monetary limit, add more parts to the ship creator, and improve Gamemode variance and controls for the fleet.

This game is about maintaining the balance between three groups of resources with needlessly complicated UI. That's really it. As a cult leader, you investigate your citizens, pick advisors and then tell them to do things, so resources from the first pool can go up and down. By picking them some families will love you, some not so much, which will change their sympathy towards you (second pool). Then you have to sacrifice your citizens to make your dark god happy, which will change your relationships with the family of the sacrifice (second pool), make some waves in the community (first pool) and decrease a potential number of advisors (third pool, although I sometimes saw families without killed members, so maybe they recover somehow). Every random event and your decisions will do exactly the same - change at least one of the three pools. It's fine for one, maybe two hours, but after that, the main loop becomes boring, especially since descriptions of your actions are mostly the same. At first, you read them, then you look only at numbers and click "skip", like in many other similar games.
I mean yeah, it is fun to pick between scold a guy for too fancy and potentially dangerous dressing, or convince everyone else that it's a great new addition to the community, but it is just fancier stat change, triggered by a person described in only two sentences and two very mechanical traits. It is just too hard to see the characters as something more than portrait, name and short description.
The fact that your advisors have random traits makes this game a bit unfair. What is the point of recruiting someone to increase community's faith only to find out that his negative trait decreases faith? So now you have to use someone else with a trait that increases faith, even if his or her action has nothing to do with it? And since advisors can be picked only from specific families you have to be extra careful who you sacrifice to the dark god, so you would not end with people not suited for their job. But half of the traits are hidden and/or uncertain, and you can inquire only one person per family per turn, so there is a very small field for conscious decisions making here. You just do not have enough information for anything better than guessing. And when that is your best option, then the rest of the game could be just a random coin flip, cause what is the point? To balance the stats for twelve turns? Where is the fun of balancing something that you do not have full information about?
I dig the atmosphere, the art style, and the music, and I understand this is an indie game, but there is just too little too simplistic content and gameplay to keep me interested. Not for 10 dollars. I get this game with Humble Monthly and I am pretty sure that for full price I would be a little pissy about it. For now, I am just bored and disappointed. And yes, I could try to finish it at least once, but the game show me everything after first half hour, so again - what is the point?

Where to start... ok. I want to like this game. I do. Stealth games are hard to make well and the idea of playing as a little gobbo is cool. I laid down 7 bucks during a sale for it and booted it up.
Graphically it isn't bad. It's stylized like the Fable series in a way, but slightly less elegant; it has a more gritty look. I have a couple of frame drop issues (mainly when I look outside) but that is more than likely due to my laptop's strength. There are a few clipping problems, especially with the dagger when Styx is pressed against a wall and the camera can clip into the walls as well if you manuever it during Styx's wall-hugging. Lip syncing with Styx is on spot for the most point, but then the humans... well. Honestly it's bad. It isn't Godzilla dub-over bad, but it is definitely noticeable.
The game opens with a cut scene trying to immerse you in the world and it fails rather badly. They go on and on about this amber and the Heart of the Tree and how it's an infinite source of power but never mention for what. Magic, ostensibly? Or is it also used as currency? Styx is captured right away and interrogated... well. He isn't really pressed for info. He just spills the beans, really, which I found odd. He is speaking to some Lord that has barely any conext for you to care about and then you're thrust into a... memory? Or is he telling the story of how he got there? It's VERY unclear. Whatever, the game can still be great even if I don't like/care about the story.
I hope you enjoy (poorly written and hammy) dialouge because Styx never EVER shuts his f****** mouth.  To make things worse, his voice actor is awful. This may just be me, but I honestly find his voice grating. He tries so hard to add depth and cynicsm to Styx by emphasizing his curses but it just gets obnoxious, like a middle schooler trying to be edgy. Not good. At all. And when I say he never shuts up, I mean it. The developers decided to shove EVERYTHING down your throat by having Styx say it to himself repeatedly and it really kills the immersion and any chance you have to like the character. Oh, and Styx also will never stop whining about his headache, either. We get it, game. His head hurts because of the tree or something; wee.
The controls aren't bad, though there is some weirdness with movement (I guess this has more to do with the character model floating over edges, I suppose). I finally get Styx's dagger, which apparently is super cool and foreign according to some guards, but it's seriously just a knife. That's it. So you get the knife and the game shows you how to silently kill. You sit there, holding down a button till you can muster the strength to kill him, fine. Standard stealth game fare. Then they thrust you into a combat situation... and this is where I felt like an idiot for buying this. It's a bunch of quick time events. It is beyond bad. It's stupid, it's tedious, it's slow and everytime you get into open combat you sigh out loud; not because you've been caught, but because the combat system is absolute garbage. If everything else with this game was golden and this combat system was still used I would pan the game just for that. It's seriously that bad.
THEN there is unlocking doors. Instead of having some sort of skill based mini-game or something more creative, the game has you stand there and hold a button while Styx shoves his finger in the lock and looks around like he's having a siezure. It's stupid, it's boring, and it adds nothing to the game. Take it out. Bad, developers. Bad. No treat for you.
Lastly, and this may be just me, the fall damage seems VERY liberal. I understand having fall damage in the game, it makes sense. But this acrobatic little gobbo would die if he fell off your back porch, it seems.
Overall, Styx could've been cool. I'll finish it and pray to Posiedon it gets better, but there are SO many things fighting against it. I don't know if I can grit my teeth through anymore unlocking sequences or "combat" QTE's. If you still want to play the game I encourage you to wait for it to go on sale for less than 10 or 8 bucks.

I think we've all gotten off at the wrong bus stop at one point or another, and the experience can be anywhere from annoying to positively harrowing. In Pid, your little spaceboy Kurt falls asleep on a bus and ends up on a planet of robots, where the buses haven't been running for 300 years. In his journey to find some way off the rock, he comes across a shining gem that creates pillars of levitating force. But someone isn't happy about him having it, and sends a veritable army of robot minions to chase him down.
How's that for a puzzle platform hook? Pid compliments its children's book premise with appropriately soft pastel visuals, collectible stars, and goofy characters. The presentation is the real stand-out here, making each level appear inviting and mysterious and charming all at once. The soundtrack is both subdued and peppy when it needs to be, and there's some cute writing on display with the NPCs and cutscenes. It's really everything you could ask for in an indie platformer.
The lavish charm makes the game's intense difficulty all the more jarring when it starts smashing you against spikes and explosives. Pid wastes no time in wasting you, pitting you against tiny platforms and precise timing puzzles in the first hour. The levitation is a clever gimmick done well, but you'll have to master it in a hurry to survive. You'll also gain a number of supporting abilities and items including bombs and super jumps that will need to be used to their fullest. Stars you find are used to replenish expendable abilities, but even if you're completely awful at the game you shouldn't run out.
Levels abound with secrets, but by the time you reach the city they'll likely be too frustrating to sniff out. I kept running into annoyances like secrets you only get one chance at, spoiled by checkpointing or unscaleable heights. The clever and colorful bosses offer yet another source of frustration, since they have very long lifebars and patterns but you can only take one or two hits before dying and starting the whole thing over. There are challenge rooms beyond the lengthy story mode as well, but even the very first set required pin-point precision to complete, let alone get the par or challenge time.
I wish I could recommend Pid without reservation, I really do. I adore everything about how it looks and sounds. But it suffers from that most common affliction among indie games, a poor difficulty curve. I still say it's worth a try, because if you have the time to devote to it you can surely overcome its challenges. Just don't go into it thinking it's as friendly as it looks.

As it seems in the video game world, games heavily carried not by it's gameplay but by it's story and experience seem to be on the rise.
The Path is one of these games.
Extremely simple controls, as all you're given the option is to walk. In order to interact, you release the forward key. Gamers who are easily put off by a slow-pace, lack of action, and/or lower end graphics, I suggest you stop reading now, and shop elsewhere on Steam. However if you're a fan of exploration, experimentation, and a psychological approach on the horror genre, then by all means, keep reading.
This is in fact a horror game, despite the lack of actual jump scares or a monster chasing you. The Path is unique that instead- you're chasing the monster. Play one of the six sisters who is tasked to bring your sick grandmather some wine and bread, but by all means, don't stray off the path- or so, as the game warns you. Despite the game's warning, you won't be rewarded unless you go on the path less travelled and go in search of the sister's wolf, unique to her. To avoid spoilers, I will break down the experience without actually delving into the story outside of;
There's little to no voice acting. There's limited reading as each sister makes a remark on each object you do come across, as well as meeting her wolf. This minilmalist approach helps you get into the mindset of the sister, and what personality drives her to her decisions. Once meeting the wolf and finally arriving to grandmother's house are you treated with discovering the consequences of growing up and a bookend to that sister's story. Much like a silent film noted and influenced with a mix of an independent arthouse and a creepy horror film, enough is left unsaid to allow the players attempt to connect the pieces together. This leads to deep discussions creating webs around the game of everyone's different but meaningful and personal experiences.
The Path is ultimately unique, memorable, and gorgeous in concept and haunting in it's hidden messages. This game is not for everyone, but for those who've fond memories of finding an old book to dust off to read of the dark fairy tales of once ago. This game is for those who can handle strong adult themes that can unrattle those sensitive to graphic truths of the real world. I bought this game the first year it came out, and even today I find myself going back to it. Well worth my money, and time, over and over again.

In the grim darkness of the 41st Millennium, there is only war. Well war, a glitchy AI, spotty difficulty, and some iffy game design choices, but let’s stick with just war. Dawn of War II is a game which differs massively from its predecessor, focusing on more of an ARTS feel rather than a typical RTS like those before it. Rather than emphasizing strategic base-building, the developers pretty much removed it entirely. Rather than focusing on massive battles between large squads of opposing forces, the population cap and squad size were shredded and the battles now involve no more than a handful of men. As you may expect from a community so passionate as that of Warhammer, this divided the community straight down the middle. Some absolutely condemned the shift as a direct affront to the emperor himself, while others found the change most welcome and were promptly executed for tech-heresy. As you can tell I tend to fall into the former category rather than the latter, though don’t mistake me, Dawn of War II absolutely has its strong points. I think that while there are definitely points in favor of Dawn of War II, during my time recently replaying it on a tougher difficulty, the problems protruded much more than I had previously noticed. I’ve had many an opinion of Dawn of War II throughout my many playthroughs of the campaign and time spent in multiplayer, but I finally have settled and made my decision: I don’t believe that Dawn of War II is a game worthy of your time. There’s many reasons for me coming to such a decision, and as a massive Warhammer 40K fan I certainly don’t want to be warning people away from Dawn of War II, but there are just too many unignorable flaws for me to say otherwise.
Dawn of War II has massively increased the focus on a single-player campaign over the previous game, making for a much more memorable experience. Dawn of War I’s campaign was fantastic, seeing you duel chaos sorcerers, massacre ork warbands, and just about watch your planet be consumed. Dawn of War II has similarly awe-inspiring moments during its campaign, with massive clashes against a tyranid hive fleet, doing battle against an eldar farseer, and defending a hulking forge-world from an ork warboss. The story itself fantastic, with twists that I genuinely wasn’t expecting, which is rather surprising to find in an RTS game. Problems arise when you can’t experience that story because of persistent flaws in game design that litter your travels: problems such as a braindead AI and some questionable campaign map designs. The AI has moments where it simply doesn’t function, I would tell my soldiers to move and instead they chose to sit still and have a four course meal, three of which were bullets. This isn’t nearly as bad of a problem on normal and easier such difficulties, as you can brute force your way through most of the missions, but as the difficulty rises, so too does the AI’s incompetence. As with Company of Heroes 2, Dawn of War II uses a somewhat confusing cover system that locks your men into positions near objects that can shield them. So when you tell your men to move, they’ll move to the cover points nearest to where you told them to go. Your men move into cover on their own, sounds fantastic right? Not even close. This causes all sorts of problems, as there have been multiple occasions where I’ve tried to move a squad into an area and instead they go just about everywhere except where I wanted them to. Sometimes, soldiers will ignore heavy cover and move into light cover for no reason other than the AI figured that your soldiers’ dead bodies would make better cover than solid rock. Not only does the cover system cause glaring problems, so too does the level design. Many levels throughout the middle of the game, when you begin truly fighting tyranids, are littered with monster boxes which spawn unlimited hordes of the monsters. Were this a true RTS that would be less of a problem as you could always build more units, but here in this ARTS hybrid abomination you’re only working with about a dozen men, with no ability to spawn more, only to reinforce existing squads to full strength. While you can teleport in more men to replace those lost, it’s just a shame that the developers couldn’t manage to teleport in a decent AI.
Like a space marine with no eyes, Dawn of War II is more or less hit or miss with its difficulty, missing much more than it hits. I’ve played Dawn of War II’s campaign before and thoroughly enjoyed it, however as of late I’ve went back and tried a playthrough on a tougher difficulty, finding it to be the exact opposite. Many missions in Dawn of War II’s campaign end with you having to fight some kind of themed species boss, such as a tyranid hive tyrant or an ork mekboy. These fights are all the exact same, with some kind of melee boss chasing your men around an arena for five minutes until you finally bring the abomination to its knees. Dawn of War II has the same problem that games like The Division or, to some extent, borderlands tend to have: bosses are too bullet spongey for them to be any sort of enjoyable encounter, instead just being frustrating and drawn out. This is made exponentially worse as dying forces you to restart the entire mission as opposed to reloading a save or anything of the sort. Combine these frustrations and you have a recipe for such frustrating mission design that you’re going to be forced to repeatedly fail missions just to grind levels for your soldiers. What strikes me as especially nefarious about Dawn of War II is how the difficulty so rapidly ends up spiking, going from being challenging, but rewarding, straight to being absurd and leaving you feeling as if the cards were stacked against you from the start. So almost halfway through the campaign your missions get exponentially more difficult, your men start feeling weaker, and your patience is bound to be wasting away. This sounds like a problem on my part. Pride, if you will, and too much of it for me to get over just dropping the difficulty down a notch or two. I could absolutely see that being the case were it not for one simple little note: you are unable to change the difficulty after you’ve started the game. Seeing as the difficulty only spikes about halfway through, that means that you’ll invest a bunch of your time into one campaign, only to find yourself both unable to progress and unable to drop the difficulty, almost forcing you to start over. I find it baffling that this was ever seen as a good idea, as it’s forcing an ultimatum upon the player: either grind for hours and hope to get lucky, or start all over. This is extremely saddening to me, as the story is so engaging and a few of the more set piece missions are actually fantastic, but that’s irrelevant if you’re unable to get to them in the first place. That’s not the only good thing about Dawn of War II either, being able to outfit your own space marines is so much fun, deciding what role you want each of your squads to play, and this would be perfect were it not for such a braindead AI.
Dawn of War II seems to have a common theme: every time I find something I truly love, it’s held back by either the AI or the artificial difficulty: often times both.

TLDR: It's a somewhat engaging story with definetly flawed gameplay mechanics. Certainly not a game to write home about, but worth a play if it's on sale. 20 bucks ain't worth it.
Pros:
- The storyline doesn't grab you initially, but develops a modest hold on you. I can't say I was enthusiastic to see the conclusion, but it was okay. Ending a bit lackluster and abrupt. The last act is definitely hurried, which juxtaposes roughly against the relatively relaxed pace of the rest of the game.
- It's a nice approach to a walking simulator. It can feel as if it's an open-world. Kudos on that part.
- Can truly imitate the confusion of the detective genre, at times pleasantly and at times frustratingly so.
- Graphically, it's okay. Nothing to write home about, but okay.
Cons:
- The game can feel like a frustrating scavenger hunt.
- Driving, like most games, is poorly executed. Traveling from A to B - especially, when you need to backtrack - can feel insufferable.
- The narrator's voice acting feels as if it was a cold read without any understanding of the story and where you are within that story.
- Lots of Dad jokes
- While the tile music is catchy, it quickly becomes annoyingly repetitive. So the same with the rest of the very limited music.
- The separate locations often have little atmospheric depth. It's more about what you find in the locations, with the notable exception of the mechanic.
- The wolves are no challenge, even when you're only fighting with a crowbar and outnumbered

Kona's an interesting game. On the surface it's a mysterious "walking simulator" (I use the term without derision) with some light survival bits. There's a lot that makes it quite special, though.
It's one of the only games I've played that accurately captures life in a blizzard. The snow falls correctly. Sounds are muted aside from the crunching of the snow and howling winds. Visible distance is about ten meters. I don't think this is a small achievement, considering this is an indie game. It does a better job at capturing a blizzard than massive games like The Division.
I could take or leave the survival bits, but they didn't detract from my experience so don't let that turn you off. Kona is an engaging short story about a small town in northern Quebec that is full of mystery. Well worth playing.

I'm really glad I bought this during the Summer Flash sale, because this game is really really bad. If you don't have instantaneous reaction times, the best you can do is delay an inevitable loss. The controls are unresponsive and half the time I'm throwing my sword away when I want to lunge.

I actually found the game strangely charming. Sure the movement feels a bit clunky and the game is pretty thin on substance, but if you're just looking for something to sink hours into for no apparent goal, then this could well be the game for you. Despite its down points, you'll find yourself going through floor after floor, although this is mostly just so you can reach a checkpoint and not have to go through those levels again.
Pros
+ Casual pick-up and play
+ Charming graphics
+ Strangely addictive
Cons
- Repetitive
- Bad sound effects and soundtrack
- Frustrating inventory menus
- Messy UI
- Lack of any real goals

CULT SIMULATOR - unsurprisingly heavy going...
This is very much a personal, critical response to a game I really wanted to enjoy. I'm not trying to dissuade anyone from playing it, or discourage the developers, but I just felt like sharing my experience.
BACKGROUND:
I love board games, interactive fiction, narrative-based games, and horror/B-movie themed games. Games like Elder Sign, Betrayal at House on the Hill, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and Tales of the Arabian Nights are some of my favourites.
The aesthetic of The Shrouded Isle appealed to me very much, with the deductive gameplay promising nice replayability too. I was very enthusiastic about the combination of gameplay & stylistic elements promised here - but after a few half-games, and one complete playthrough, I feel no desire to return and pursue any of the other endings.
Why? I just didn't find it easy to enjoy. Which surprises me, so I'll try to describe why.
MY ISSUES:
At its core, The Shrouded Isle is a stat-balancing game with some deductive reasoning and risk-taking. Gameplay-wise, you will select a combination of advisors, call upon them to change the stats, sacrifice one, and repeat. There are some other decisions to be made, but mostly you'll be trying to keep your 5 main stats (and the associated houses) content for 3 years - broken into 4 seasonal turns each.
This really became fatiguing to me for several reasons. The initially-impressive colour schemes start to really grate after a while (though you can switch mid-game for some relief), a complete playthrough lasts way too long for me in this kind of replayable game (1-2 hours), and there is simply too much information onscreen at once (lots of small, important text to keep track of).
The narrative elements, descriptions, and occasional side-quest decisions are wonderfully atmospheric at first, but they just end up being skipped through as the stat-management mechanics emerge and the descriptions start to repeat. This is my biggest problem - as I love to take my time and imagine stories taking place in games like this. But it all started to blur into one for me.
The idea of forming a story with the fragments of characters' behaviours, and insights into their personalities, was so appealing to me at first. But unfortunately, the mechanics of the game and the narrative descriptions seemed to get in each other’s way for me. I couldn't enjoy the story building or character development, because it essentially distracted from the task at hand - stat management - which was itself made difficult by the presence of so much text onscreen. It's a real catch-22 for me.
SUMMARY:
Hats off to the designers for creating a game with a truly unique visual style, gorgeous art, and intriguing concept. The music is very distinctive and evocative too. I certainly don't want to discourage the developers - I applaud the focus on narrative, imagination, and emergent storytelling here. I would love to see more experimentation with these priorities in games like this. I also think this would make an insanely good boardgame, with each player controlling a house for example and the characters/traits on cards.
Personally, I just found some issues with the interface and the flow of play that prevented me from getting engrossed in either the story or the gameplay - I found myself in an uncomfortable stasis between the two that was hard to enjoy. I think I would enjoy it a lot more if there was less characters to manage, and more opportunities to get acquainted with them.
If you're curious, like stat-based strategy games, and find the theme appealing, it's sure worth a look for €10. I would certainly recommend taking your time playing this - perhaps even taking physical notes on paper to aid with the deductive part. If the moody tone appeals, and you can be patient with the gameplay, I'm sure it can be a very engrossing experience.
If it's all a bit heavy for you, I might recommend the hilarious Reigns as a similar game that I enjoyed very much. It is leagues lighter in tone, text, and complexity, but it manages to build little stories, characters and worlds effortlessly, despite the simplicity of play.

I will play pretty much any WW2 game on the market.  This...is not one of the better ones.
There are a lot of reviewers saying that the game is unbalanced, and a couple saying "oh, you're just using the wrong units!"  Having spent two hours and plenty of experimentation on the first mission thus far, I can tell you - it's not the units, it's the balance.  My biggest issue with the game is actually the extreme lethality - you're annihilating the enemy's units every turn, but they're also annihilating yours, and it's mostly a matter of who can spawn more fresh units onto the field faster.  So it gets very grindy, very quickly, as you build a mess of new stacks, hurl them at the enemy's airbase (which is apparently located in a bunker, as opposed to the nice neat (and more accurate) mechanic of Panzer Corps where you roll a tank in and capture it), do a little damage, wipe out the enemy nearby, get wiped out by their counter-attack, lather, rinse, repeat.
Because of this, you have no real incentive to preserve your own units - knowing that the next force to come over the hill is likely to blow them away anyway - so you just sort of fling them around mindlessly.  Manage supply lines?  No need, no one's lasting that long anyway!  Which sort of defeats the purpose of a strategy game.
Maybe if it were getting more polish, or if there weren't so many better options on the market.  But it's sitting in a genre that's already saturated with good titles.  No reason to pick this one up.

I am planning to play it again sometime. My impressions so far aren't the best. It has been a long time since I played it, but I still wish to give my opinion on it.
I've tried feeling into it, but it didn't work too well. This game tries to deliver some emotional narration and story, but it didn't strike me. It rather felt pretentious and weakly executed.
You are moving through some dreams or memorized pictures of a woman after some car accident while restoring at a hospital. It could have been a dreamy, surreal game but felt too simple: You move through photos of real-life places by clicking around them or (as seen in games like "Arx Fatalis", "The Void" or "Black & White") by drawing symbols on the screen which you first discover in somewhat hidden areas of these photos.
The photos were distorted with warped lightnings and all to give them some surreal feeling. However even I as a layman can tell that this is something you can probably easily do with Photoshop, or by making mistakes when taking these photos you would otherwise want to avoid. Then there are a few rather simple CG animations put in these photos. And cutscenes which didn't feel >that< bad but which are real-life footages, more often than not close-ups of a female actor pretending to be unconscious for most of it giving some hints towards the meanings of her dreams as well as her restoration from the accident. I didn't like her voice actress too much. I had some feeling of boredom and apathy listening to her. Perhaps this is how someone in such a situation would sound like, to give some feeling of emptiness and aimlessness, but this is naturally nothing one feels drawn to, and in combination with the rather simple gameplay and general "sterile" feeling of this game it somehow added to me feeling the whole of it to be lacking.
So, I don't know, the concept sounded interesting, but there really isn't too much to do in this game. Navigating through warped photos isn't exactly something that takes a massive effort game design-wise I guess, and as simple as it sounds so it did feel when I played it. Not exactly bad, but far from being impressive either. I think there could have been a lot more to do with this topic, seeing some woman questioning aspects of her life and identity could carry power and meaning, but it felt rather superficial as this woman was partly dealing with things someone probably could get over very early in one's life like chasing fake dreams of stars or those dictated by leading figures in one's life. This is something I can't sympathize with, as it has some touch of immaturity I cannot really relate to anymore.

In the days of WW2 the combined allied forces faced off against a ruthless foe. A force which sent dozen of allied units to the gates of Hades with little effort. Battalions of tanks, squadrons of aircraft, sqauds of infantry and fleets of ships were all reduced to rubble. An enemy created by the gods to leave nothing but chaos, madness and destruction behind. A force which knew no mercy, showed no mercy and expected none in return. What is this force you ask? Game Balance...
On the surface, Tank Operations: European Campaign may seem like a decent turn base RTS game set in WW2. It is not until you actually start playing the game that you find that things are wrong.. very wrong.
Plot is cliche and nothing you haven't seen before. You play as the American forces during World War 2, sent to the European front to defeat the Nazi occupied Europe.
Gameplay is unbalanced. In the campaign, you start of with a few starting units. You can build new units such as infantry, tanks, aircraft which will become useable next turn. As a turn base game, your units have limited 'moves' each turn. You can create new units like infantry, tanks, aircraft etc via buildings or ships. Some units also have special abilities (which need recharging afterwards) such as improving sight or damge. One of the my biggest gripes (as mentioned previously) is balance, which is shown by the fact that your units do pittiful damage, compared to enemy forces. To demonstrate this, in the first mission I had a two fleets of ships. I sent my landing force composed of tanks and infantry into the beach head. I immediately targeted the coastal guns to help defend my navy. My units did abissmal damage to the gun, but I thought it would be ok after I shot at it with my ships. After doing the later and ending my turn, the coastal gun (which somehow managed to survive 3 tank shots, 1 infantry attack and shots from 3 of my battleships) regained most of it's health (WHY!@!) and it along with a handful of tanks and infantry managed to decimate my force. By mid way I had lost most my ground forces, my aircraft badly needed repairs and my navy were being blown up to smitherines. Yet, I still was unable to eliminate a SINGLE coastal gun. This was honestly quite frustrating and made playing a chore rather than being fun.
Sound is decent, if mediocre. Weapons (ie. tank, ships, aircraft fire) sound decent, but nothing special. Music is forgettable. Voice acting is quite poor.
Graphics arent that great. I personally don't mind the artstyle in these kind of games. However, the lack of animations (while moving) is quite cheap.
If you are looking for a fun, challenging and FAIR game, look elsewhere.

Styx is currently one of my favorite games to play. Most negative reviews talk about the difficulty of the first fight, but it's actually rather simple, as you don't block, but rather parry. From what I've gathered, after the patch, the game is now much more forgiving when it comes to grabbing ledges, but will sometimes do things you don't want it to do; such as automatically making Styx move onto the top of the ledge rather than hang from it.
The game truly is very interesting though, as it's not quite as forgiving as other stealth games when it comes to the actual stealth mechanics. When first starting to play, I find that it's very important to pay attention to everything that you're told in order to truly learn and understand the game. I have yet to run into any glitches or anything of that matter and find that whenever I'm caught and/or die, it's always my own fault, rather than the game mechanics. All in all, I really enjoy the game and recommend it for anyone who likes stealth-based games and/or anyone who wants to find a game that can really challenge them to analyze their surroundings and think on the fly.

As far as WH 40K games go, this game and its associated expansions are basically God-tier.
First, I want to touch on the overall aesthetic of the game. It does a great job of bringing the WH 40K universe to life in a way that really hadn't been done before its release. Most of the tone is set by the dialogue and over-the-top voice acting (did I mention this game has Steve Blum in it?), which is actually a positive in a sci-fi universe where everything is absurdly overdone. This game really feels like it's being authentic and deferrent to the source material itself rather than just piling in a bunch of references, and it's no coincidence that the Blood Ravens went from being an invention just for this series to one of the most popular space marine chapters in canon.
In gameplay terms, this game is unoriginal, but still very fun. It relies heavily on other the Company of Heroes series, which really shouldn't be a surprise given that both games were produed by Relic and THQ. That's why I can't really fault them for unoriginality in this regard: sure, the gameplay is something you can get elsewhere, but Relic knew what they were doing and they did it well. This reliance on Company of Heroes style combat also gave this game the odd distinction as the only game I can think of in which space marines ACTUALLY USE COVER, which if you're at all familiar with the lore and tabletop game, you know they HAVE to do in order to survive (I know cover got nerfed a bit in 7th edition with widely available 'Ignores Cover,' and I haven't checked much into 8th edition, but I digress).
Anyways, this game gets a solid 9/10, become Force Commander Hair Gel and lead your SPESS MEHREENS to glory today.

Pid is a game with a lot of great ideas, but poor execution makes it frustrating to play.
Being a platform/puzzle game, Pid demands precision jumps and skilful use of the central game mechanic - the ability to lay beams that propel Kurt, the player character, away from the surface they are fixed on. Unfortunately, poor controls let the game down in this department. Kurt routinely 'sticks' to the end of the beams, making it difficult to jump off the end of them. Poor design of several puzzles exacerbates the problem, as many puzzles and boss battles are timed, and leave no margin for error. The result is controlling-smashing levels of frustrating in many of the puzzles.
This is all the more disappointing because of the excellent game concept, graphic design, animation, sound and music, which help bring the simple but engaging story to life. Each area has a unique aesthetic and introduces new game mechanics, which ensure that the game never becomes routine or old. Each new challenge requires skilful use of the skills and abilities you have accrued so far.
I can only recommend Pid if you have considerable patience to look past its flawed controls. Be prepared to spend 30% of the time enjoying the calm ambience of the game's better-designed areas, 10% of your time working out the solutions to the more challenging puzzles and areas, and 60% of your time wrestling with the terrible controls and dying over and over again as you try to get past a challenge once you have identified the solution. If you are willing to take on this frustration, then the game is definitely beautiful, original and occasionally offers some thought-provoking puzzles.

I wish I could hit the Recommend button more than once.
Within the past several months, I've been getting progressively more interested in Visual Novels, and when I saw that this one came highly recommended on Steam and that it was even on sale as well, I decided to pick it up.
I was not disappointed.
This is by far the longest Visual Novel I have ever played myself, with the first route taking just over 25 hours (no skipping, no auto, watching through the 3 cutscenes in their entirety), so considering I only paid 9 dollars for what turned out to be over 50 hours of playtime to complete all routes...I definitely got my money's worth.
I would recommend this VN to everyone, those new to them like myself and also those with more experience with them. Every single route tugged an entirely different heartstring, and none disappointed. If I had to rank the routes in order of how much I like them (which for me, is a Herculean task), it would be as follows:
3-way tie for 1st: Kotori, Amane, and Asa
Strong and close 2nd: Ageha
Last but certainly not least: Yoru
The artwork is fantastically done and the music....is by far the strong point of the novel. Each emotional/touching moment is paired with a song, and these songs do an AMAZING job of evoking the right feelings for their respective scenes. You can check them out on Youtube...my favorite tracks are "A New World," "Morning Glory," and "My World."
In short, I HIGHLY recommend this game. It will make you laugh, and then it will tug at your emotions. If you like touching stories about high school kids finding love for each other and the sky, then go for it. I would even pay full $15 price for this, considering how much content I got out of it.
I was on the fence about doing the whole Restoration patch to put the sex back into the game, but after playing through all routes I found that I didn't really need it to stay interested in the characters/story.
One final note: some of the translation can be a bit wonky at times, but it didn't take too much away from the story, and it didn't happen during the highly emotional parts. If you can look past that, then I would say pick this novel up. You won't regret it.

I love this game. When I have a limited amount of time to play games, this one has been my go-to, just to see if I can get farther up the tower before returning back to town to sell off all my goodies.
It's a dungeon-crawler with fully customizable party members, which is one of the best features. I'm not a very melee-centric player, so having the ability to fill my backline with mages or priests as my discretion is a nice touch.
Gameplay can feel a touch grindy, but it's expected in this sort of game. There are bosses every five levels, and they are ridiculously hard to beat if you haven't been leveling up your abilities and getting better equipment. It feels rewarding to open a chest full of goodies, and even more satisfying to look at the ability list of your party and be able to decide what to upgrade first.
You can also fight monsters at your own pace, which is great for me because I've never been great at fast-paced combat.
The only criticisms I have currently come from the lack of a tutorial or explanation at the start and the repetitive music. There were a few instructions at the beginning of the game, but it mostly expects you to figure out gameplay quickly on your own, which isn't the case for everybody. I figured most things out on my own, but I always feel like a bit of guidance for new players is always a great feature.
As for music. Eh...it could be better. It's mostly just background noise to me. The sounds and cries of the enemies are all the same as well, to expect to hear the same screechy grunty noise when you defeat an enemy often.
Otherwise, it's a great game that I've gotten a lot of enjoyment out of! I finally defeated my first boss and look forward to duking it out with stronger enemies!

If My Heart Had Wings (commonly refered to as "kono sora" in japanese, i think) Is really deep. It has a diverse array of characters that makes replays feel less like "alternate endings" and more like "alternate universes" kind of like fate/stay night (IMHO). I really liked how heroines that you dont choose dont just fade into obscurity, or (worse) suddenly dissapear, leaving readers to go "what was that person for anyway?" on any single playthru. It makes it feel like the game is less about "the life and choices of protagonist X" and more about "the Soaring Club". That said, I dont mean that the routes are as drastically different as they are in Fate/Stay Night; they are _distinct_ but not as jarringly different as routes in F/SN are.
There are less "choices" (i.e. branch points) than i expected, which was actually kind of nice, it made me feel like i could more sit back and read the story and get immersed in it rather than constantly have to figure out which choice raised the flags for the heroine i was aiming for. Some people will undoubtedly find that this makes the game more linear and feel like they have less control over the protagonist, more of a story, less of a dating sim.
That said: I played the "limited edition" version on tablet first, found the "collect wings" thing to be BS since it took so long,  breaking the story into chunks that were too short for the amount of time you had to wait in between each chunk to even get a feel for the story (i played for 10 min, and then ran out of wings, then spend 3 weeks mining for wings, once a day, every day and then played one long chunck, which got me... maybe 25% into a single play thru? maybe.
Soon the steam version went on sale and i said "screw this imma play it on PC, even though i was also thinking "this is exactlty the kind of game i want to play on the bus or during lunch, on my tablet T_T ). The steam version... its... its good, but every so often, you hit a section where you just KNOW something is wrong. The context suggests one thing and the dialogue says something... different... I _GET_ that its because the edited the lines to make it an all-ages version and that what was edited was deemed "too suggestive" or "innapropriate for younger audiences" but for me, i found it incredibly jarring and immersion-breaking. I dont know if its possible to edit things to the point where its not jarring, but well... when a character is obviously talking about breasts (from context) but the dialog is suddenly about "big eyes"... its well.. it feels like driving down a straight road and having someone suddenly pull the e-brake for a sec, and then look at you like "what? why are you looking at me all wierd for?" this was exacerbated by the fact that i know enough japanese to KNOW that the character says "breasts" not "eyes"....
I tried to apply the "restoration patch" to the game, and... somehow i ended up with no vioce acting? Not sure. Im trying to fix it now, but not even a "clean reinstall" seems to work. theres probably some file left over that im not finding to delete and its causing errors. Some places have said the restoration patch does not fix the dialog, and only adds the sex-scenes back in, and it might wreck the CG and the scene replays, but... i want my voice acting first, so i havent gotten to the point where i check that stuff yet.
Still: 8/10. would buy again.
would be really nice if i could play it on table tho.... Need more japanese visual novels on mobile plz.

Incredibly flat and boring, terrible as both an RTS and RPG. Mostly plays like a cheap Warcraft 3 knock-off, and won't hold the attention of even the most patient player thanks to a generic and lackluster story alongside its sub-par RTS gameplay.
Gameplay wise, it is notably too fast where it should be slow, and too slow where it should be fast. When in combat with AI, it quickly devolves into a tower defence game as even a difficult AI merely spams units as fast as possible.
Unfortunately, the control for your own units is nowhere near precise enough for such rapid-pace combat, and you are stuck with the choices of either A) Allowing your units to chase down hostiles freely, which will often lead to them being kited back into the enemy camp due to how hard it is to track your own units, or B) Not allowing your units to move at all, which I'm sure you can guess is a terrible idea.
Additionally, most units are constructed in groups of three, and each individual unit takes multiple population points - Usually an even number - Despite the population cap being a multiple of 5. Thus, you will almost always be missing multiple units even with 4 or 5 free points.
Outside of combat, the game moves painfully slow - In the campaign it encourages "Exploration" of large, mostly empty maps using slow-moving characters. Additionally, it lacks many basic features for an RPG, such as fading walls in interior spaces, and NPC navigation is patchy at best, making the whole experience needlessly tedious as well as slow.
The story is an incredibly generic fantasy setting - I can say with confidence that I've played two other games this year with the same premise. The story will have you bored out of your mind within a few hours, but unfortunately, the game itself isn't fun enough to make up for it.
Overall, it feels like an early-access indie RTS, and is definitely not worth the $50 price tag. 3/10 with extra points for the game's graphics, which are a solid strong point in an otherwise weak game.

I might as well get this review over with so that potential buyers (like yourself) understand what you are going to get yourself into.
You are a High Priest in charge of a isle community and it is up to you and your decision making before the 3 years are up when your god returns around at that time. Sounds easy right? Well, not really. This game overall is challenging. And not for the patient sort. If you don't fulfill certain requirements, the game will be over...If any of the traits or houses go under. It's game over. You need to REALLY understand that this game DOES NOT. Hold your hand. You- and you alone have to make the decsions that will have a lot of impact in the isle community. Each advisor you appoint  will have strengths and weaknesses that other advisors of the particular house may not like. So for example one person might have a 10+ in ignorance in one house but also has a negative -10 in Obedience that can affect another house's relationship and it's overall 'trait meter'
You can use inquires but the game doesn't give you a whole lot of them. Inquires help you reveal the house member's strengths and weaknesses. Major vices are one thing you have to really look at. And major strengths are something you should really look at as well. If you sacrfice somebody that has a major strength in favor of someone else's vice. Just so you can appease that particular house and it's particular set of trait? Your doing it wrong. In fact, it's considered 'game over' from then on out. Use them very wisely. Study the strengths and weaknesses wisely. And before you ask. Sadly each 'new game' the house randomly switches the pro's and con's around. Everything else is the same. But the advisors 'traits' might switch around.
The art-style is cool and music is nice. Simple not over-the-top.
This game is really made for the thinking gamer and NOT for anyone else but those kind of gamers. If you are that sort of gamer. Then i recommend this game for you.

I tried hard to like this game as it looked really promising and I thought it was just a matter of getting used to it, but in the end my recommendation is to avoid Styx unless it is on sale and you are really craving for an infiltration game. It's not a bad game but there are too much design flaws that makes it dull and tedious after a while: I'm only 10 hours into it and I already want to rush it without caring about secondary objectives, not even talking about bonuses such as relics and gold coins.
Update: I've finished the game after about 28 hours. It's worth one run for the story, a few secrets which are fun to find, but this is it: for sure I won't get back to it, too tedious. So my rating & review is unchanged except for the conclusion.
The main problem is that the shadow mechanics are broken: sometimes you sit in plain light and the guards won't notice you, sometimes you are in the shadows under cover and the guards will spot you. The designers added a shoulder tattoo that tells you when you are in the shadow, but this is not helping a lot since you have to walk into the zone to know for sure. I died an incredible amount of times because of this broken mechanism. This is really annoying as you are supposed to be a "Master of Shadows".
The second big problem is that the patrols are not so predictable: sometimes the guards will change their routine for no visible reason. It seems there are some scripting there. Also the designers introduced arbitrary difficulty by putting for instance 3 guards watching each other in a tiny room, which leaves you with very little options.
Then there are all those - not so - little bugs: when you kill a guard, the body will fall in an unpredictable manner. It happened quite often that the guard bounced back 4 meters away, thus making noise and alerting all his friends. A lot of jumps will just lead you to a premature death:  the controls are quite clumsy (I'm playing with an XBox controller on PC) and it's hard to spot the paths on the walls.
There is also some silliness in the design:
I was a bit too harsh when I wrote this review: the game is overall enjoyable, I had some good time with it, but you have to be prepared for some frustrating moments. The game is just not worth 30 euros.

I should preface this with a few comments.
1. This is the first squad based strategy game I've played.
2. I didn't play the original Dawn of War.
3. A friend got it for me entirely for the coop.
Those out of the way should let most people ignore my review since it may just be my lack of lore knowledge or squad strategy not being a genre for me.
I didn't like this game much at all. I found it really boring most of the time and the strategy feels absent altogether in my opinion. You get multiple squads but can only pick 4 to bring. If you're playing coop each player gets 2. The first player gets the short end of the stick since as far as I can tell you're required to bring the force commander as your initial squad. This makes being first player even worse.
The squads can do multiple things but they're so clearly geared towards one role it's hard to break. For example the squad commander seems to be melee, I leveled mine to be able to use missle launchers but he then lost the ability to use any of his commander items gimping him horribly. Gear conflicts sometimes too, there's a special armor set that lets you use special weapons but completely removes your ability to use the normal ones and some accessories like grenades.
Your squads special abilities can use 3 resources which just feels unneccessary. Some skills use energy which regenerates naturally, some use ammunition which you have to find crates to replenish, and other still use a special deployment mechanic that lets you deploy them more often depending how many of a certain building you've captured in maps on that planet. The last one is the worst of the 3. You can only cap one building each time you play a map even if there's multiple on it, also because it's tied to the planet you're on your uses fluctuation wildly as some planets you'll have 3-4 uses then you'll go to a new planet and only have a single use.
Related to that last bit I hate the rate at which they recycle maps. You will play multiple missions on the same map so the scenery quickly becomes repeatative. These "missions" are basically start at one corner and kill everything till you reach the other corner. I know it's an RTS like game but having to take objectives and hold them or even something like create distractions to draw main forces away would be nice, but no you just run face first into all the hordes of enemies you see. Which is the last issue I take with the game in that it's "strategy" doesn't exist, you use guerrilla warfar exclusively. Run in and kill as many as you can, once you're about to die hit retreat to go to the nearest beacon thing you captured to summon more troops, then run in again, repeat till you win the mission. The only real choice you have is which beacons to grab which isn't much of a choice since grabbing the closest one to the objective is a no brainer.
All in all I'd recommend skipping this if any of this sounds like a red flag to you. If you're a fan of the genre or the franchise maybe you'll get more out of it than I did.

There is still a spooky atmosphere and sometimes you might catch yourself sitting there for a moment and thinking, “That is creepy wow okay” but never should you feel threatened or scared by anything that happens. "There is one rule in the game. And it needs to be broken.”

An okay game. It isn't fantastic but I believe I got my money's worth at $7.25 on sale. Did some of the easy achievements just to see if I missed on anything important. Nope.
PROS
1. The Goblin-sized Realism
It makes sense for a medium sized goblin (Rakash) to be able to duck into holes, hide behind crates, squeeze into hidey holes, hide in the darkness etc.. It feels more logical than a full bodied human crouching into vents or hiding behind a wall.
2. The Armour aka Skins
I love the design of the skins on the knights, the captain, the apothecarist, the elves, the crossbowmen (including the crossbow and cyclops suit).
3. The Elves
I love their radar sense of smelling Amber. Although it doesn't work when you're overhead, the sixth sense gives an different form of difficulty to the game. While they are basically the same human model, I consider them different due to this radar sense. They can detect you even if you're standing behind them or behind walls. I lump templars, knights and every other human as one group as they share the exact same methods of detecting you e.g. listening, line of sight and bumping into you.
4. Clones
I love the way you can use an alternate self to trigger traps, activate mechanisms and cross grilles. Quite interesting to feed "yourself" to the orcs so that you can move through. I was hoping for more "clone-and-you" combos though.
5. Orcs
I love the part where they can reach out of their cells and grab you. So interesting. I was hoping to find a way to release rampaging orcs into the castle. Sadly, most of the orcs you deal with are tamed guard dogs.
CONS
1. Jumping
My main pet peeve. You can't jump well in this game. You have to rotate the camera to find the perfect angle, else you might miss a critical jump. You can't jump downwards at an angle. This makes the game feel like a jumping simulator instead of a stealth game. This might be because I'm playing on a PC and using the keyboard instead of a controller. But if it is, it's a horrible port.
2. Grips
My second pet peeve. The developer in charge of setting the grips was horrible. You can't shimmy, you can't grab hold of places you want to reach, you climb up onto braziers, you autoclimb almost every other time you grab a grip, you have to slow move to properly drop off an edge else you fall off, you can land on book shelf edges where you can't shimmy and you can't shimmy at a 90 degree angle turn.
3. Enemy Vision Upgrade
The dumbest thing I've seen so far. Instead of a cone or an arc of vision, I got an useless pointy line sticking of their face.
4. Invisibility Upgrade
If you get the permanently invisible upgrade (not moving while invisible) and you're in the path of an AI, the AI will become shocked and pause. He will recover, bump into you again and the whole cycle repeats.
5. Tokens
Gives you Skill Points(SP) to upgrade your skills only if you collect ALL of them. Couldn't you just scale it so 1 token = 5 SP? Collecting Tokens is reminiscient of how Thief Works.
6. Querberus
I was expecting someone to make you Amber potions or weapons. He did absolutely nothing except give you an easy "talk-to-me-and-I'll-move" stage. Then he got killed by Styx.
NEUTRAL
1. Combat
While others have been giving the combat system a short shriff, I'm quite satisfied with it. This is a stealth game after all. However, I do not like the system of engaging in a parrying duel. As a stealth fighter, he should be trying to avoid any form of combat, especially the dueling. This form of fighting is reminiscient of Dishonoured.
2. Spit Sandball
Knocks out torches and pisses off orcs. These 2 things work but I was hoping for other uses like knocking out the lamps and braziers.
3. Zone Repetition
I'm a bit divided on this one. What I like about going through the zone backwards is the ability to find other hidden areas
SUGGESTIONS
1. Clone and you combos
Styx whistles (X on the keyboard), lures the enemies over, clone activates a mechanism, something bad happens to the enemies. E.g. Styx hides in a grate, whistles, enemies comes over, clone activates a mechanism, trap activates, enemies die. Styx whistles using vetriloquism to make it sound like he's in a cell (This is unique), enemies are lured to a cell, clone activates a mechanism, enemies are trapped in said cell (alive).
2. Spit Sandball
Use it to blind your enemies, use it to extinguish lamps and braziers (not the large ones).
3. Ropes, Chains, Flags
I see so many ropes, chains and flags. Pity you can't use them in the game.
4. Clones
If you summon a clone and use Amber Vision, the clone dies and you lose the amber for summoning it. Normally, unsummoning a clone returns the Amber. It's quite silly as you might want the clone to see things in Amber Vision.
5. Replay Value
I realised that I did another walkthrough just to see if there was additional story/fluff. I believe it would be interesting if the relics or coins had some special story or meaning. This would enhance the game by leaps and bounds. Currently, coins and relics only serve as Skill Point conduits.

An excellent example of an artful video game that uses interactivity to engage the player and enhance the message of the story. Inspired by the tale of Little Red Riding Hood, the player chooses to play as one of six children each given the identical objective of visiting their grandmother in a cabin in the woods. The game gives the simple instruction of staying on the path to grandma's house, but the player is free to disobey this command, abandon their duty to their grandmother, and instead venture into the forest where each girl's unique "wolf" awaits. The Path is about the inevitable human curiosity, the obliteration of one's innocence, and the consequences that follow. It is deep, it is beautiful, and is a great example of what video games are capable of as an art form.

I wasn't really expecting much out of this game, but in the end it really surprised me with a fun, albeit hard, stealth experience. There isn't anything super original in terms of the stealth gameplay, but it's got a fun storyline that follows Styx, the worlds first goblin, in his quest to steal the heart of the worlds tree. Most of the voice acting for the NPC's isn't the best, using generic English accents and only a few lines of dialogue each, however, the voice actor for Styx is pretty good and does well with delivering Styx's sarcasm and cynicism while still sounding like the gruff old goblin that he is. The game also sports a simple yet effective upgrade system for your 3 skills: clones, invisibility and amber vision (similar to Assassins Creeds eagle vision). When going through levels there are main objectives, side objectives and insignia objectives. The first 2 are self explanatory, but the insignia objectives are where the game adds some replay value. Each level has 4 objectives that will get you bonus upgrade points: doing it without alerts, within a certain time limit, stealing all the coins and without killing anyone. This means you can go through the level and explore everywhere and find all the coins, and do it another time as fast as possible, or even try to do it fast, with no kills and no alerts. You DO NOT have to do all of them in one go, in fact it would be pretty much impossible. Once you've done the objective for that level once, you can replay it again (as many times as you want) to get the others.
CONS:
PROS:
All in all a fantastic stealth game, lots of stealth, and you get punished if you get impatient or make a wrong move, just the way a stealth game should be. I don't like number based systems of rating since there are to many aspects to fit into one number, but I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who loves a solid stealth game or even RPG as the story is also pretty awesome even if it does seem cliche at the beginning ;) ( play it and you'll know what I mean). Slight ledge issues and combat aside, this game blew my mind seeing as I bought this without expecting much.

I get that Tale of Tales was trying to tell us a story in an original way, but they don't seem to have an understanding of the importance of immersion. I know a lot of people have played Super Meat Boy and loved it. I also know that many people have not even heard of Nimbus. Do yourself a favor. Check it out.
If you liked Super Meat Boy, then you should like Nimbus. It's in the same category of game, in that it's an action platformer with puzzle-y elements.
It differs from Meat Boy in that you have to keep up momentum. Generally this means that, while you can slow down in Meat Boy, you can't here. There are easier levels and harder levels (and impossible ones), and I've found that I get the same sort of satisfaction from beating a level in Nimbus that I did in Super Meat Boy.
I don't want to compare the two games too much, because there are a couple giant differences. The momentum thing is one. Another is it's a fair bit more puzzle-y and less twitch gameplay. Also, I really like the art style. The 2.5D cutesy affair really remind me of Yoshi's Story, which is another game worth playing.
Check it out. Hopefully you'll like it.
