This game is mastery. It's become my all time favorite sidescrolling platformer, and I'm sure it'll rank highly on your list too. This game has impressive 3D graphics, though the game operates in two dimensions. The level design is excellent, and is made so few new features have to be formally introduced, but are rather taught to you subtly. It follows many major, yet basic, game design rules modern games often fail to address. Artistically, this game makes me squeal with joy. The lighting engine is brilliant. I especially enjoyed the outdoorsy bits, where it was very open-wordly. This game has a very simple premise, yet introduces new concepts consistently, even till the point where it introduced several major features in the last level. The bosses are clever, and require dexterity, as well as problem solving skills, as the rest of the game is. One of the biggest things about this game is its impressive co-op integration. Storyline-wise, NPC speech never addresses the second character, which is a bit of a shame, but gameplay-wise, it's done amazingly. With a second player, each player has less maneuverability, but together new tasks can be accomplished. It's a nice trade-off, and yet, none of the level design has to be changed for it to operate. I've played through the game almost two times now, and that filled 25 hours. Even now, I still have challenge rooms to complete, and easy and hard mode for new depth. I'm excited to continue this game, and would argue that it supplies a minimum of 40 hours to a player as dedicated as I am. I would give this game a solid 9.5 out of 10. Excellent game.

Warhammer 40000: Dawn of War II is a tactical RTS slightly spiced up with RPG elements. Game is based on an infamous board game, which originally is set in a milky way.
During campaign we play as small task force of Space Marines, fighting various enemies, be it countless numbers of sectoid tyranids, high tech eldars or hordes of orks.
Campaign features fully working coop mode, so I completed the game together with a friend of mine and tbh I find it really enjoyable.
Each mission has long philosophical discussion which shows every character's personality. Story itself, despite being filled with cliches, has quite some interesting plot twists. Now, as I mentioned before, DoW2 features some of the RPG elements - each squad you control has personal leader, who has level progression and set of special skills that you can use for own advantage. For instance Tarkus and his tactical squad can be useful to draw enemy fire on himself and clear enemy structures by throwing grenades at them. Cyrus and his scouts can become invisible and provide intel about enemy forces, etc. Every hero has several equipment slots, such as armor, weapon and "slots for tactical items". Some items that your character wears give bonuses, such as additional health points, or some passive bonuses to other squads etc. Tactical slots are usually filled with stuff like various orbital airstrikes, turrets, stun grenades, explosives etc. (said Tarkus has grenade at start, but you can take it away from him and give it to any other character). Each character has several styles of playing. For example you can give your character an RPG and turn his squad into tank destroyers which, in turn, will become vulnerable to infantry attacks. Another example is whether you give one of your squads jetpacks and let them jump from above, stunning enemies, or whether you will give your squad teleportation ability, thus having totally different style of gameplay. Some of the items (such as jetpacks&teleports, for example) are bound to only one squad and can't be used by anyone else.
Another shootout to RPG (in a good way) is boss fights. Yeah, as soon as you reach your final destination, you'll have one of them epic boss fights, where one giant mofo would try to smash your tiny strike force.
One more important thing that's worth mentioning: There are 6 squads in total, each with unique abilities under your control, but you can land on a planet with only 4 of them, leaving 2 other squads behind. In fact that sort of adds bit more thoughts to your tactics.
Gameplay revolves around your task force being deployed on a planet and assaulting checkpoints, at which you can heal wounded soldiers and order fallen ones, filling your squad with fresh members. It may sound a bit boring, but maps are large and unlinear, so what might sound boring is, in fact, one of the things I personally liked in this game the most. You can build up your personal path to your destination point, be it large passage on the left, or, perhaps, you will flank the enemy from the right? Or both? Or even clear whole map? (tbh thats what me and my friend did in most cases, lol). It's all up to you and your imagination really. By the end of the map you'll see your stats for the level. Game will rate how aggressive, fast and careful you were during this mission. For example if you spent 40 minutes and wiped out 91% of enemies, while losing only one squad of yours, you'll score with 5 stars for your agression, 1 star for speed and 4 stars for caring for your people.
Besides main missions there are also side missions. As you've probably guessed, they aren't as descriptive and interesting  as main storyline, but sometimes you can get quite valuable items for completing them, be it armor, or a brand new shiny gun.
So, as we've done with pluses, it's time to hit on game's issues:
-Let's start with actual "squad selection". As I said, you can deploy only four squads out of six, which leaves other two behind. Unfortunately squads aren't too balanced, so you'll quickly find your favourite ones and will stick to said 4 squads for whole game. For instance when playing through campaign, me and my friend stopped using Cyrus straight after being able to use other squads.
-Side missions. Not only they are short on briefing and dialogues, but also quite repetitive, which makes them quite annoying closer to the end of the game.
-Bugs? Yeah, usually game runs smooth, but I've encountered several sync errors on loading screen, right after mission end, which led me to disconnecting from the party and having to restart whole game, wtf? One time we even ahd to replay whole mission!
-Boss fights. Haha, I just described them as a plus and here I am, saying that they're bad. No, in fact boss fights are cool, but my problem here is f#cking HUGE amount of HP and DMG they have. In the end of the days you constantly end by running from boss and when finally caught by him, retreating to last checkpoint and filling your squads with fresh troops, because boss wiped out all of them in a matter of seconds. I think it would be way cooler to restrict retreating during boss fights, but in return, decrease bosses' hp and dmg. Idk, just my thoughts... Overall it's quite playable.
-Maps being repetitive. As I mentioned above, all maps are quite unlinear. And OF COURSE that means you'll have to play on each map for at least two times! Now, I wouldn't really mention this if side missions would offer new maps or something but basically, most of them take place on same levels with just different goals, e.g. DEFEND instead of attacking, hence why you get bored of them quickly. Speaking of defense maps, I just don't understand how did relic manage to make ALL of them defense maps feel so similar. Different planets, weather, times of the day, still feels like one same map for some reason. Maybe it's just me, though, idk...
-Campaign features full support for two players, cool right? Well, and you know what ain't cool? SAVEGAME SYSTEM! I played the game as guest so that campaign we've completed TOGETHER with a friend of mine is saved on HIS pc, while MY efforts are... Well, left behind? not like it's hard for my friend to share savegame file, but still, was it so hard to introduce proper savegame feature for second player?
-Campaign is cool, but main problem is that it covers only space marines' adventures. So by the end of the game you just left with feeling "oh, so that's all? But I want more!" I mean, remember StarCraft: BroodWar with every side having separate campaign, featuring different plot and showing the story from different angle? Or Warcraft 3? Or old C&C's? Peperidge farm remembers! Enjoy only one campaign and that's it.
-Closer to the end of the game you start feeling a bit ridiculous cause enemy has full squadron of tanks, thousand of infantry units and all you've got is... Yeah, still same 4 squads of brave marines. Sure, you'll be given Dreadnought ( "sort of" vehicle). A nice addition to your strike force, but game still gives you that actual real life "feeling" of being very underpowered. I understand that this feeling is exactly what Relic was trying to give us, players, but it just doesn't feel right. They chose totally wrong approach. I'll try to elaborate my point regarding this in other separate reviews for Chaos Rising and Reribution addons, but yeah. I still think it ain't right...
HOWEVER! don't let game's issues decide for you. All that pile of text I made below "issues" part is just a small drop of problems in the ocean of fun you'll probably have while playing with your friend (especially if you'll be communicating via microphones). A huge thumbs up to this game because nowadays there's not much games which can provide you with so much fun! Oh and yes, there's also multiplayer available! Not gonna lie, I'm not pro RTS player, so I'm not the one to judge game's multiplayer balance but still, game's definitely worth a try! ESPECIALLY in coop!

This was very interesting to play, its basically a mix of an interactive slide show of images with a bit of point and click gameplay, but with a interesting art design behind it. They are pretty much real life photos, you can tell just from the screen shots. Its like looking at an abstract gallery of someone else's mind-scape. You bascially play different dreams (about 4) that have different outcomes depending on what you do in the dream.
So what I like about it is the interesting style and design it went for, the concept of the game is very cool which is looking into the mind of someone recovering from a horrifc accident as she travels into her own mind as well as her memories.
Also the soundtrack is fantasic, whoever made it should be given alot of credit for really creating an intense atmosphere while playing the game, the intro song is really good and the slower melodies really strike a cord in me, I don't know why but the soundtrack is ideal for the overall theme and tone the game wanted you to feel.
But is it a fun and interesting game to play? Its a tough call because this is very much an art project kind of game, while I think its good and interesting (I love point and click games after all), I do feel that at some points the message of the game gets lost and the game is very, very short. I would have liked to see this kind of game expanded more.
I think its an interesting project, a little pricey, I got this on sale but still a cool concept, I like the idea of traveling into the mind of someone and discovering as the character also discoveres things they didn't realize at first.
So if you like that kind of concept and are willing to try something VERY different from the usual point and click, then give this a try.
I would give this game a  6.6/10

Before I start off, I'd just like to point out that I have a thing for artsy games. I know that some people may not like these sort of artsy games, but this is my honest opinion.
In TRAUMA, you play as a woman who survives a car crash and is trying to make sense of her dreams as she recovers. These dreams are captured in a series of polaroid photos, which you navigate by clicking on details in the photos or drawing gestures. These gestures are what you use to perform actions - for example, you can catch a ghost by drawing a head shape. There are four endings to each level - one intended, three side endings that use the gestures found in other levels. There are also 10 or so collectable photographs inside each level, providing for deeper insight into the woman's life and a cute little timewaster if you've found all the endings.
I strongly reccomend this game. It reminds me a bit of Dear Esther in that both are exploration-based and are both about car accidents. This game is one of those that have deeper meanings to what is presented in each level; I'm discovering more and more interpretations for the respective dreams as I play more. There's also the entire beauty of it all - hundreds of photographs stitched together and edited to form a fluid experiance. Oh, and did I mention all the mind♥♥♥♥ parts of it? Naturally, being set in a dreamscape, this game is bound to have a few (read: many) cutscenes that are going to blow you away with the sheer imaginativeness of it all. It may not for you, but it certainly did for me.
It's really evident that Majewski put in a lot of effort into creating the best game he possibly could, and although it is a bit short and lacks achievements/tradingcards, it's an utterly fantastic game that I would say is worthy of your time and money.

I do like this game...however I do not like it as much as I thought I would.  Its not to say its a bad game, oh no no no, its actually pretty decent, just I feel it suffers from some oversights.
Basically you have to defend your base from the oncoming hoards of Titans, using what ever you have researched and are available.  Ok simple enough.  You get an icon showing the direction the hoards are coming from and you build accordingly.  Just on some missions, during my play time, I find that an all important hoard direction marker is actually hidden/obscured by my HUD, which lead to my defences getting demolished because I didnt see said marker.
But really...tis a minor gripe, if annoying.  The actual gameplay is pretty simple, just point and click to deploy your stuff or click and drag for multiples, so nice and easy to get your defences where you need them/want them to be.  Research is pretty easy to understand with icons showing what needs what to be available, though the game does tend to recommend tech to you if you havent got it, so it kinda takes it out of your hands a bit, by basically saying " you need this, not what you are currently thinking "  Though you can ignore that.  But it does offer you respec points for your research so you can get what you want within you resorce point limit at the time, so thats a pretty useful feature.
Graphically I like it, its a nice and different style to see.  I particulary like how the Titans are designed, especially the sub-bosses.
But one other thing that gets me is the price.  I would not pay the £7 it was advertised for.  Fun fact, I recieved a 90% off this game coupon from Steam by crafting a badge, so I had it for 70p!  So what I would do, if this game interests you, is get a coupon or wait for it to come on sale at around 33% off at minimum and then I would say its worth it.
Not a bad game, just a few little issues and a bit over-priced, but it is alright.  Should cure your Tower Defence itch for a little while.

There is no real interesting things about this game, it is shallow and all you do is watch stat bars move up and down, you can save yourself money and just open up a spreadsheet and "play" this game there. I uninstalled and got my 1GB back.
The core gameplay is there are five bars (Ignorance, fevor, penitence, obedience, and discipline) and these must be kept above their minimum by the end of the game. Each house represents a different bar, the player needs to choose a person from each house to represent them every three months. Characters have different positive and negative traits, these traits can effect the other stat bar they are not a house of.
Then you have your personal reputation with the five houses - drop too low and they rebel (game over). So, pick a character from every house, and choose whether to use them each month (locked in for 3 months), you can select 3 people, selecting less than three people increases their bar and house rep more.
Then at the end of the three months you kill one of them. If you exposed a big negative trait (scholar, poet, imaginative, etc) through enquiry or actively using them then select them because it has a less detrimental value on your bars and reps. Then the hosue you killed somebody from, you should just actively use somebody from their house and not kill them again the following season.
Which traits and events you get are luck (RNG) based too.
The game is super shallow, all you do is balance stat bars, it is seriously not worth $10, if I had not got this in a Humblebundle then I'd have requested a refund.

This review is for people who have played the earlier spellforce games.
UPDATE: After about 25 hours logged. The game is a fun RPG with lore spellforce vets will recognize. However, the RTS rework is garbage. I don't like it at all. It's still a fun game, but it's not as good as the previous Spellforce games.
TLDR: The game is fun, get it. You will enjoy it. However, the RTS side has some changes I'm not a fan of.
I'm 5 hours in and I've gotten a taste of both the RPG elements and the RTS elements.
PROs:
-Spells are much easier to cast and target thanks to the Click'n'Fight system. I really like it. Much easier than previous Spellforce games to get the right mob targeted or to get the right allies healed.
-Voice acting is great, story is interesting. The lore from the old games is mentioned. I'm enjoying it.
-I've been happy with the skill tree's and hero development.
CONs:
-The changes to the RTS system are not my cup of tea. The need to control and manage territory and a little cumbersome. I prefer the old style free for all. It seems like different territories will perhaps have different resources and the resources are somewhat shared across territories. It's just not what i'm used to.
-It looks like the goal was to simplify the RTS side so you don't have to manage the workers so much, but I liked managing the workers.
-While it doesn't break the game, it doesn't feel like classic spellforce RTS. I'm hoping I get used to it as I play through.
Nice idea but perhaps a serious head trauma would help me enjoy the game more

Finally, a hero we can all identify with. He is just a normal person-like we are-and is doing what he loves-like we do. He represents the everlasting battle, which goes on between personal passion and societal norms.

Kokurase - Episode 1 is a short quirky roleplaying game developed by galanti and published by fan favorite Degica. What I personally like about this game is it takes the RPGmaker system we've come to know (and depending on who you are love/hate) and gives it a new spin.  In order to complete this game, you'll have to consistently switch between 8+ different characters, all at different locations doing different tasks, to complete one unified goal. It's a genuinely interesting system that helps bring life to a sometimes stagnant game engine. The artwork is absolutely gorgeous, it's sort of simple to call it "anime" because its incredibly stylized and has a nice edge to it.
It also has components similar to other logic collecting games like Phoenix Wright, where you have to recall statements/ideas that you heard previously into new conversation. This makes every moment of dialogue more meaningful, and gives you more reason to pay attention. Not that you'll have any trouble keeping focus, the writing is charming and quick witted.
Overall this is a really loveable game with interesting game design mechanics, and I'm excited to buy the DLC when it becomes available.
But for now, download this game, its free!
Added: Episode 2 is out!

A review with minor introductory story details.
If My Heart Had Wings (Kono Ōzora ni, Tsubasa o Hirogete) is a visual novel centered around a group is students in the soaring club, a school club primarily focused on aviation. Surprisingly there is more than romance to this story as the main objective of group is to fulfill the dream of flight. I wasn't expecting to listen to several detailed explanations of glider aerodynamics and construction but I found them interesting. The story itself is mostly light hearted and humorous but at the same time has dramatic, emotional moments.
Visually, this visual novel is very pleasing. The art is done very well with many vibrant colors and gives a unique look. The soundtrack is spot on when it needs to be and very tame during normal sequences. In the settings menu allows a lot of customization, such as pausing the game when it is off screen or even changing the announcer's voice to any of the characters.
Unfortunately, the game does suffer censorship and certain routes will seem less developed than others. Translations will be a bit cringey at times with americanization. I'll be blunt and say that the censored version of this games acts like sex doesn't even exist. It's painfully obvious when they tweak a scene to skip an eroge scene in the original. I personally recommend using the 18+ restoration patch to have better translations (just skip the eroge scenes).
My Opinion on the routes:
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Kotori - The best route. Clearly the most developed and gives the most satisfaction when reading.
Amane - The next best route. Fills in a lot of details that are unexplained in other routes.

- There are a total of 5 routes + 1 bad end.

Achievements will be locked if you decide to use the patch. There is a Steam guide that shows you how to apply this patch if you need help. Do note that there are separate guides for Windows 7 and Windows 8. If you're interested in applying this patch, be prepared for lengthy eroge scenes with voice acting. You have been warned.
- Originally released in May 25, 2012 in Japan.

This was a fun little game.  Not very long, not overly complex or maddenly difficult...just a nice little journey though a trauma victim's memories and impressions.  Gameplay is essentially point and click for navigation, and you learn to create these "symbols" (performed with mouse-based gestures) that have generic purposes (e.g., directional controls) and in some cases can be used in less-than-obvious (but usually clever) applications.  A modicum of replayability is achieved via multiple solutions/endings to each chapter, and by finding all of the "polaroids" thoughout.
If you're worried about bang-for-the-buck, then get it on sale like I did.  Take a look at the screenshots to see if you like the photographic art style.  It's certainly not for everybody.  But if you're looking for something simple and explorative, a touch psychological, with some light puzzle elements, then it might be for you.

Gunpoint is like DEADBOLT without all the things that make DEADBOLT a great game and with all the things that make Gunpoint a great game.
But seriously, Gunpoint is a 2D stealth game mainly revolving around a simple idea: What if you could rewire the level? For example, you can make a light switch near you turn off a light somewhere else in the building, and then make the light switch made for that room open a door somewhere else, so on, so forth. You must make your way through levels by using clever ways to trick guards into helping you.
Gameplay-wise, this is a gem. If running around in a stealthy manner, stealing data and rewiring the level (sometimes, with hilarious consequences) isn't enough for you, you also have rocket-propelled pants that will have you knocking down guards and smashing windows. Most of the puzzles are right in the sweet spot - they take some while to figure out, but no walkthrough is needed. Adding to that, every level has multiple solutions.
The story is not really all that great. The dialogue and characters are really funny and well-made, but the plot is sort of what you expect from a silly detective game. Don't let that stop you though - the witty dialogue makes up for that. The main problem with the game is the fact that it is extraordinarily short, meaning around 2 hours for completing the campaign and 4-5 hours to get a 100% completion. The game is over before you know it, but if you want to, you can try out community created levels or see what happens if you choose different lines of dialogue.
The music was enjoyable, but not all that memorable or great, and the graphics really make the atmosphere that you want to see in a stealth game taking place in the modern world.
For any fellow completionists out there, this game has pretty easy achievements and 100% completion should come naturally within 4-5 hours. Too short if you ask me, but if you only care about increasing the percentage then this is for you, I guess.
Overall, it's a nice little game, I recommend getting it for the gameplay and jokes, although you might be really disappointed in the length, so perhaps you should get this on sale.

It took me a long time to get into this game, but the end result is still disappointment. I really like the Blade Runner meets Deus Ex (original) vibe this game was going for. For starters, the brouzouf system is pretty awful. It's like the souls from Demon's/Dark souls - it does everything! Too much, as a matter of fact, for me to care considering how expensive all of the research, personal upgrades, weapon unlocks, etc. are. The starting weapons are a little too good, IMO. Because after grabbing a farming map and unlocking a few of the weapons, things like the TRK (?) sniper rifle are still just completely dominant in terms of accuracy and damage output.
Another item is the checkpoint/saving system. One moment, it's saving after certain missions; the next, it's not saving throughout the course of a level I invested about 2 hours in. IT'S RIDICULOUS THAT THIS IS SO INCONSISTENT. Just put in a damn quick save button/manual save option.
Side problems, I cranked the brightness way up because during underground levels, I couldn't even see enemies without the EYE vision (more often than not, way too zoomed in to be useful with any scoped weapon).
If you are major into grinding and farming games, I guess you'll like EYE. If you want a game with a tight feeling to all of its elements, this definitely isn't for you. It requires a lot of personal motivation to figure out what is going on and enjoy.

Ok before I begin this review, let me tell you that the 33 hours i spend on this game is ONLY ON THE MAIN STORY, I bet you can tell that I am heavily immersed in its story. Anyway lets get on to the review.
Story: Now since this is a review I will try my best to not spoil much for some of the people who planned to get the game or haven't started on it yet. My Heart Had Wings story focused on a highschool club by the name of the '' Soaring Club '' which consist of the characters Aoi ( Main Male Character ), Kotori ( Main Girl Character ), Ageha ( Childhood Friend ), Amane ( Leader of the Soaring Club ) and later on Asa and Yoru ( Twins ). There are different routes for this VN but I will only talk about the main story ( Kotori ). Kotori your typical tsundere character but with a physical disability, she loss her use of her legs due to an accident. Our main male character (Aoi) also suffered a physical disability, his knee has problems that prevent him from continuing his passion from cycling. At first Kotori hates Aoi but since Aoi is able to understand her due to their losses, as time goes on Aoi managed to make her gradually open up. But enough of these 2, lets talk about the Soaring Club. The Soaring Club undergo many losses and sacrifices, whether it is emotionally of physically, each member suffered through different events that occur in the VN and you just became so immersed into story that you to see them overcome their problems.
Visuals: The visuals of this game is absolutely stunning to the eyes. Every scene was drawn incredibly well and coloured with bright and vagrant colours. However, in 3D glider flights scenes, the glider itself looks ugly and old.
Animation: The animation was very well done as well. During glider scenes, there are some scenes with shaking screens or even when the glider was about to took off. These kind of scenes have some kind of an impact to the reader as they allow them to experience what the characters are experiencing.
Sound: My god. The sound themselves fits every scene well. No matter what kind of situation, whether it is good or bad, the sound themselves just made the scene so much better.
My Final Score For My Heart Had Wings is 9/10, This is a very good VN that worth every penny and time. (P.S sorry if many of you find this not helpful, this is my first time writing a review.)

KAMI is an attractive well-presented and simple puzzle game.  To solve each level you must select areas to fill continuously with a colour (like the paint bucket in MS paint), doing this a number of times to have the entire screen one colour to complete the level.
Highly original and learning curve is not steep.  Some later levels are very difficult however.
It doesn't take too long to make your way through a majority of the levels, so game-length is perhaps shorter than most similar puzzle games.  Some have compared it to LYNE which seemingly has no end.
Overall, recommended because it's a unique and refreshing take on the puzzle genre, well-presented and colourful.

After the success of Hearthstone, dozens of digital card games have been released, such as
, which is a hit in Japan, but few developers have bet on the single player format. The Nerdook Productions studio is one of those who decided to create a card game totally made for single player:
, a game that along with
is, in my humble opinion, one of the best options to play alone.
Monster Slayers is a card game with a dungeon crawler theme and roguelike elements, such as permanent death and procedural generation. However, the game also has a progression system in which it’s possible to unlock upgrades for future runs. One of these upgrades is the option to have two more tries before the run is over, so the game becomes a bit more forgiving.
The gameplay consists of exploring dungeons to find the boss of that area, defeat it, and proceed. During the adventure it’s possible to choose two support characters (called
”), who offer special abilities that can be used from time to time. Also, you’ll need to defeat monsters, make deals on altars that offers a great benefit at the cost of a great loss, eventually choose some free extra cards from other characters, buy items and gear, sometimes find a healer who can also delete some of unwanted cards from your deck and rest under the bonfire in the best Dark Souls style.
To win a run you’ll need to go through three dungeons, chosen randomly. In the first two you’ll need to recruit a support hero and you cannot change them later in the same run, so choose well. Already in the third dungeon you’ll find the final boss: Harbinger, who will require you to make the most dirty tricks to succeed, so always have many support, defense and chain cards on your deck. In fact, Rogue is the best class to learn to play, just because it already starts with a lot of chain cards, so it's great to at least help you unlock some upgrades quickly.
Even offering a gigantic range of different cards, the strategy that works best is to delete weak cards from your deck and have several cards that generate chain reactions and adds defense – keeping your deck only with a few powerful cards. This doesn’t mean that other strategies don’t work, but this is the most reliable and it’s the one that will guarantee you victory most of the time. Remember that during the first runs you’ll need to focus on unlock upgrades for your next characters, so you can have a chance to beat the game. At first you will die quite early on, but after getting some upgrades, the game gets fairer - not easier, but more balanced.
More than counting only with your chosen cards to win, you also need to keep an eye on the best equipment you can find along the way. Although you can buy armor and weapons, it’s perfectly possible to beat the game only with the gear you find through the dungeons, so you can keep your money to heal HP and buy other cards.
When you defeat the final boss you can continue playing in survival mode with your victorious hero, and you also unlock Legendary Mode, which is harder, has a new end boss and makes you lose all your gear when you die. Speaking of extra content, the six additional classes that are included in the
are basically secondary classes of the standard ones. These new classes are unlocked after you win a run with the equivalent basic class, but if you want to unlock all classes right from the start you can get
. Honestly it’s not much needed, since the new classes are not necessarily stronger, but different.
Inspired by
, the Peter Whalen's game that opened the doors to him to work with Blizzard to create Hearthstone later, Monster Slayers  has an immense responsibility: to offer a fun game full of depth . The good news is that this game honor his inspiration and is even more fun, detailed, complex and addictive than other Nerdook Productions games such as
and
. If you enjoyed Monster Slayers and want even more variety, the Fire and Steel expansion offers six more traditional classes, two experimental classes, new cards, two new biomes, eight new enemies and four more bosses. Either way, with procedural generation, every run will be different always.
Finally, despite being a completely single player game, 'Monster Slayers' also has its competitive side with the inclusion of the Steam leaderboards, where you can compare your best scores with other players. The game also saves your progress in the cloud and has a bunch of achievements.
* Easy to learn and difficult to master
* Fun and addictive
* High replay value
* Extra challenge for those who want a more hardcore experience (Legendary Mode)
* The game starts completely unbalanced and only becomes balanced when you unlock several upgrades
* The strategy of keeping your deck with just a few powerful cards is practically the only viable

A buggy and broken mess of a game that does enough things right to make up for its plethora of problems. A game with a plot so ridiculous yet fascinating when you get invested, with characters that can come back to life as the plot demands. EYE should not be nearly as good as it is.
If you've never touched this game before, or you've tried to and hated it, try finding yourself a nice guide on character creation and abilities. Before long, you will become a walking tank with electronic warfare capabilities, invisbility screens, psychic powers, and carrying miniguns, small nuclear cannons, or a revolver that can kill God.

It has an ambigious and kind of meta storyline, which is fine, but this game feels...I don't know if this is the right word, but unpolished? If they made a sequel that was more polished it would be an amazing AAA game. I give props to the crew who made this game, I heard it was a very small group and given that fact it is a pretty solid game. As you level up, trying to get certain items, researches, tech and spells can get very grindy. Once you play through the game a few times it feels kind of short, especially when you learn the "shortcuts" in each mission where you can skip most objectives. If they made it so there were more twists and turns in dialogue and actions (not too much but some more), more variety in endings and missions, and put in more customizability to guns/spells/tech/hacking, it could be amazing. I hope they make a sequel, even if it is only a spiritual successor (seeing as...well you will know what the ending(s) are when you play it and understand why I say it would have to be a spiritual successor)

People, this was a rare gem of a game. For those that prefer using their brains and thinking through a variety of options to weigh their final effects in game play, well...Styx is nothing short of a blessing. I found the the world of Styx fully formed and simply beautiful by way of atmosphere and design, really stunning. The game play is just fine, all the complaints about not being able to accomplish fine motor skill events is simply not correct. The gameplay is quite long, and whereas the scripted dialog is too slow and immaterial, it only appears for the briefest of periods and very infrequently.
What does make up the vast majority of play time is a thoughtful challenge that requires one to set aside even the most developed "run and pillage" tactics and, instead, think about how to accomplish something by NOT breaking things and face to face bang and slash. Its a solid change of pace that asks a simple question to the player "have you got anything above your shoulders more than what got you through the last dozen FPS games you have been playing?" Some do, and to those I would say Styx was a standout game that once ended left me wondering how long it will be before somebody else actually builds something NEW. For those that liked PORTAL, for those that liked SWAPPER or TALOS, well it is nothing like those in gameplay and very much like those in the great satisfaction found in cerebrial concentration.

Shotgun Legend closely imitates the original Legend of Zelda, and you already know what that is, so let's talk about the shotgun. What makes TLoZ's combat distinct from its successors is the combination of a short sword and grid-locked movement. Fights are a unique kind of scramble for position as Link tries to get right up to the enemy to line up hits, without getting into a vulnerable position himself. Swapping the sword for a shotgun is an effective twist on the design that gives Shotgun Legend its own feel despite how it follows Nintendo's design in other places. Because of the gun's wide spread, you still need to get in close to deal the most damage, but the ability to deal decreasing damage at increasing range allows a lot more flexibility in how enemies and encounters can be designed. Shotgun Legend fully exploits that flexibility with some of the more deviously challenging room layouts I've seen in this genre. It's gaming comfort food, but has enough distinct ideas to be worth checking out.

Nidhogg is a somewhat unorthodox one on one fighting game. I would compare it to a mixture of Speed Runner and Bushido Blade. Basically, the aim of the game is to kill your opponent dead by stabbing them with your sword, breaking their neck, or throwing them into an abyss. After first blood is drawn, your goal is to advance through the slightly jump-and-run-y levels through several screens to the goal. Your opponent, however, will constantly respawn and try to stop you so he can get the advantage and make a run himself. This, coupled with the fact that you only have one hit point, makes for very fast and intense duels.
You are limited to a small, fixed moveset which however covers all tactical eventualities, and since both duelists are exactly equal, it makes for a game that is mostly determined by skill, positioning and awareness. It's very much a game of action, reaction, counter-reaction. Curiously, this puts it into a 'sweet spot' of thinking - think too little, and you're not prepared for your enemy's maneuvers. Think too much, and you're liable to become blind and vulnerable to a simple tactic like 'roll under the sword and  leg sweep'. I have found myself on the receiving end of a neck snap too often because I tried to force a parry. It takes some time to get used to, but once you're in the flow, Nidhogg gets immensely fun.

One of the most frequent criticisms of The Path is that it's not really "a game". And it's not. If you want a capital-G Game, look elsewhere. But does that need to be a criticism?
What is it, then, if not a game? It's an experiential marvel. The only game I've ever seen with more atmosphere than The Path is the similarly un-game-like Dear Esther. While the theme of Little Red Riding Hood is so incredibly overdone in interactive storytelling circles (though few have made it to commercial release), The Path has an interesting enough take on it to be worthwhile. The characterisation is superb, although you have to search for it and even then it's expressed in a very minimal fashion. Each of the girls is likeable but flawed, and, without wanting to spoil too much, each one is ultimately undone by her flaw. While not a game in the ludic sense, interactivity does play a vital part of the experience, creating a sense of "discovering" the story and also creating emotional resonance by making the player complicit in sealing the girls' fates.
The negative sides of the game are that sometimes atmosphere takes precedence over technical considerations. Sometimes the text that's communicating the story is illegible because it doesn't contrast strongly enough with the background, and sometimes the game just gets too dark to see what's going on, which I guess is supposed to be scary, but just ends up being frustrating.
I can't recommend this without qualification, because it's not for everyone. Indeed, that's one of its strongest points! If you're interested in something that isn't quite a "game" in the traditional sense, are willing to put effort into engaging with it rather than having everything neatly presented to you, and your narrative sensibilities tend toward feeling rather than thinking, it's definitely worth a look.

It’s a few years since I first came across The Path, by Tale of Tales but, on re-entering the fictional world of the sisters, I find the game has lost none of its appeal.  Originally released in 2009 and loosely based around Red Riding Hood, The Path was intended as a different kind of video game with an emphasis on partaking in a narrative, rather than being structured around quests and conquests.  However, I feel there is an element of strategy involved as the player is graded according to how many objects they find, how many of the secret rooms they unlock in Grandma’s house.
Game play is deceptively simple.  You give a basket to one of the sisters and they leave home with instructions to follow the path to Grandma’s house.  The whole point of the game is not to do this, to wander through the forest where you interact with various items, collect flowers and objects.  As each sister meanders through the dense woodland, there are items and places specifically for her.  However, the player commences with no idea of what to look for, so there is a great emphasis on exploration.  In my opinion, much of the game is about unlocking the personalities of the sisters.  They are all different, although the stylisation and method through which we unravel this is systematic.
Each sister can meet her nemesis during her travels, but the guise of the wolf is different for every individual.  When these situations occur the player can only watch as the scenario unfolds.  After this event, the girl is transported to Grandma’s house and her journey through this domain depends upon what she has collected and encountered on her travels through the forest.  Here, each sister is upon a path pre-determined by her previous actions.
The Path can be described as a psychological game with a distinct horror edge, however I would argue there is more to the game than just this.  For instance, there is a definite attempt to blur the boundary between fine art and the video game.  One only has to watch the leafy tendrils growing around the games title as each sister begins her journey, to experience the surrealist arrangement of Grandma’s house and the cubist demise of each sister.  In addition, the music is haunting and the sound effects well judged.  One aspect of the game which I feel encompasses the horror element is what happens if the player causes a sister to run.  This is especially effective in a darkened room with the sound up.
The Path is a game to experience at your leisure.  It is a much slower paced game than any other I’ve encountered, but as the emphasis is on participating in each sister’s journey, the pacing works well – this isn’t a game to be rushed, its one to lose yourself in.

Kona is all about the location, exploring, finding things to photograph and read. Discovering what happened to the residents of the village.
When you are outside the game does a good job of directing you to points of interest without actually telling you where to go. I was about half way through before I remembered I had a map. The map shows your current location and direction you are facing as well as where you left the car and other places you know about. If you still manage to get lost you can follow your own tracks in the snow to go back the way you came.
You can enter peoples homes and cabins (some are locked, but spare keys are always nearby), search through their drawers and cupboards, take their things, read their diaries, look for clues as to who they were and what happened to them.
Your findings are automatically summarised in your journal, which I would suggest you not read, it feels like some of the detective work is taken away and done for you and all you've been doing is walking around picking things up.
The journal does serve as a way of tracking progress with placeholders for things you don't yet know giving you some indication of where you should go. You do not need to complete everything before you can finish the game. Once you have reached the end of the story you cannot go back and look for anything you may have missed without starting a new game.
The survival aspect is mostly limited to staying warm, campfire sites are scattered around and most buildings have a stove. Heat sources also serve as save points and stay burning once alight. You have med kits and painkillers, also cigarettes which were still healthy in the 1970s.
There are some encounters with wolves which you can feed, scare, kill, run away from or try to avoid them altogether.
There is one puzzle (with the wheels and wires) which I managed to solve by accident that looking at it afterwards didn't make a whole lot of sense. I recommend solving that puzzle to get the snowmobile key if only because I can't think of any other game I've played recently where you get to drive a snowmobile.
In the end, the story was a bit thin and the ending was disappointing. It felt like there was a rush to tie it up and give the player reason to leave the area. But I had fun getting there.
Notable bugs:
Same full screen bug that many Unity games have on Linux, with same solution.
Resolution is set to 1920x1080 by default and does not scale to fit the screen, use the keyboard to navigate the menu and increase resolution.
At one point the game stopped translating documents into English, after a save quit and reload the translations returned.

I'll leave a quick review after getting this from Humble Bundle, never having heard of this game before.
The Shrouded Isle is a bit like a board game where you have an Xcom style rules foundation beneath a strongly Cthulhu-themed kind of CLUE spin on top. That's honestly the best way I would describe it.
You are leader of a cult town, and the game has 12 seasons over 3 years. In those 3 years, you have to keep the town running successfully while also sacrificing a person every season. Depending on how well you do at this, you will get one of 6 endings, some good and some bad. I got one best ending and one worst ending after about 7 different false starts, all while this game having no tutorial whatsoever; I was able to figure it out just from the choices you can make while playing normally.
By the end of it I had learned the key part of victory: if you want the best ending, you need to investigate each of your town members until you find the 7 you are supposed to sacrifice, and sacrifice them while still keeping your town in order and (relatively) happy. That was the main challenge, and I must say it was fun to pull off. The gameplay is streamlined and efficient, with a single play lasting from 15 to about an hour max. You can save whenever you want and come back too, or even just walk away and it will wait till your next action, so this is great for people who need games that can be paused or put down.
The graphics are not very complex and have a unique monochrome kind of style, and unlike other reviewers, I am actually perfectly fine with that. It's obvious this game worked with a small budget, and the simplified graphics do a great job of selling the game. I'm sure it may have been better if they had invested more time and money into a wider palette of colors, but it works great with what it has.
For people who dislike simple graphics, town management, or a Cthulhu theme, maybe try another game. If you are willing to see how good fo a cult leader you can be in a well balanced, fun little town management game, give this a try.

I just think a lot of stuff in the game looks bland.
Gameplay: Gameplay was simple and fun to play occasionally. It's not one of those addicting games that you play daily. The online was surprisingly fun. I wanted to unlock all the parts on easy then beat the campaign with those parts on hard. But that plan didn't work out the way I inteded. Make easy difficulty easier and hard difficulty harder. I also dislike the limit of cost for your ship. It made it frustrating to express my creativity of space ships if I couldn't even make a big one with the space they provide you.
This game is easy to pickup but also easy to put down. Very fun to play with a friend and it can be a very peaceful way to spend your time. I suggest this game to anyone who likes to be creative and strategic.

To be blunt, What's Under Your Blanket is nothing more than a tongue-in-cheek jerk off simulator with terrible Paint quality graphics.
The game is comprised of five levels, and five sub-levels. During the main five levels, your objective is to play with "what's under your blanket" while avoiding getting caught, setting your blanket on fire, and breaking your bed. You must achieve your goal within two minutes by quickly clicking on your blanket to fill up your jerk-o-meter. The faster you click without interruption, the higher your multiplier climbs. The higher your multiplier climbs, the faster your jerk-o-meter fills.
Every now and then a family member, or special guest for the current level that you are on, will interrupt you. If you get caught, or set your blanket on fire from jerking... I mean clicking too fast, it's back to the beginning of the entire game for you. I might also mention here that there is no save function, and no pause menu. The escape key will also immediately close your entire game.
The five sub-levels are simple arm wrestling competitions, and barely favor a mention whatsoever. They're thrown into the game for filling the void of an otherwise empty game. Just click away until you finally win.
Don't get me wrong. I had a laugh my first playthrough of What's Under Your Blanket. However, when I revisited the game for a second time to clean up the achievements I missed the first time, due to the fact that they were broken upon the launch of the game and have only been recently patched, the humor was gone and I was bored... stiff. *badum tsh*
Truly, games such as this are destined to end up on places such as Newgrounds... but Steam? It's hard to fathom that this title made it to the actual store front. I'd like to preface this with saying that Spellforce 1 was the game of my childhood, and so there were some heavy expectations, but there is also likely to be some bias.
So, here are some pros and cons:
+ This game is absolutely gorgeous, to the point where more or less every single scene could be made into a poster. When I first saw the extremely brief snippets of gameplay that the devs showed about a year or so ago, I didn't believe that would be the final game. The final game is just as good as these snippets, if not better.
+ The story is incredible to me as a fan of the series. Spellforce 1 was a clunky as hell game, but underneath all that the story was actually fairly interesting. This builds on that lore in a massive way, to the point where almost every other mission blows my mind in some way.
+ In comparison to the first game, the gameplay this time around is significantly faster. I was worried that this would equate with linearity, especially with the first game being so surprisingly open-world and with so much backtracking, but I was happily proven wrong. This game is certainly more linear than its predecessor, but it definitely opens up.
+ I shouldn't have to say this, but no gamebreaking bugs in the slightest. I had one single crash in the 10 hours of game when I was travelling between zones. The game gives you 10 autosave slots plus however many manual saves you'd like, though, so the crash wasn't a big deal.
- This isn't perhaps a problem for me per se, but I think the gameplay could have been made deeper. Gone is the fairly robust RPG system from the first game, replaced with a much simpler one that allows for only 6 abilities per hero instead of the 9 that first game offered. This is a shame, but the gameplay is overall good, so it's not a dealbreaker. Also do not equate this to me saying that the game is casual. Not at all. In fact I think there is a lot of comparison to be drawn with Company of Heroes, and that's the sort of level of RTS you should expect.
- I have an NVidia GTX 1080 alongside 16GB of RAM and a decent i5 CPU, so I can't really complain about my machine's performance. Even so, running this game on ultra does cut down a few frames when there are a lot of units. I can't not hate the graphics, because they're beautiful, but I can see lower end PCs struggling with this game, which would be confirmed by other reviews.
- No Dwarves. With only three factions I am sad to see no Dwarf faction... There is at least one Dwarf so far, so I'm slightly happy, but DWARVES ARE THE BEST. I feel like there is space for the Dwarven faction, too, since on the worldmap you see what could easily pass off as moonsilver ore. I have a sneaky feeling (and hope) that they will be added at a later date. The story does admit that there are 6 'intelligent' races, which as SF1 notes are Humans, Elves, Dwarves, Orcs, Trolls and Dark Elves. One or two more factions to spice this game up a bit wouldn't go amiss.
I would love to gush all over the lore now, since the one person who shares my love for SF1 hasn't bought this game yet, but I will refrain from that in public. Might get arrested. This game is brilliant though.

The game looks interesting and the gimic of moving around from photo to photo while using magic symbols to interact with the game's world has some potential. The art and photography is appealing, especially when it suddenly does something weird, like suddenly sucking up a random billboard or shattering a ghost. It's imagery is a strong aspect.
It's just that it has no overal point.
At best, the game is cryptic. At worst, the game has nothing to say. As a jaunt into someone's dreams and psyche, you'd think you'd come away learning a great deal about that person, right? I couldn't find any value to that assumption. Most of the details given about this woman's identity as a character don't ever appear to connect. She went to Uni, she went to a coffee shop once, she had a teddy bear.
Why should I care?
It doesn't necessarily connect or amount to any revelation about the character. There's no real coherrence about this towards any real goal. It's just weirdness from beginning to end. I'm sure it's the point; to allow for your own interpretation of what to make of all this but I struggle to find that satisfying. It doesn't seem to justify it's own existance by offering any conclusion to take from the journey made.
Perhaps this is meant to be from the point of view of the Doctor tending to this woman? It would explain the tiny amount of information we gleam from her dreams and bits of information from them, only to have the game end abruptly.
What drags this still lower in my opinion is how boring the gameplay is.
One of the larger flaws is how entertaining the game is. The 'puzzles' are no more advanced than find a thing and perform a special symbol on it to get something to happen. Nothing amounts to anything more than just an alternative ending. That also seems to be weirdness for weirdness' sake. If you learn what does what and what will only work with what, your only challenge is to spot what looks interactive and what isn't. This is not all that hard either. If you can be bothered, you'll breeze through this within an hour and a half.
If you like weird things, you won't feel too bad if you get it during a sale. Otherwise, it's not that remarkable. For a flash game this bland, it feels overpriced. Go play one of the weirder looking things on Armour Games. It's free and likely more entertaining than this.

TL;DR: Interesting concept, but incredibly pretentious and barely a game.
TRAUMA's concept is interesting: Exploring surreal dreamscapes, and gradually learning ways to interact with them, allowing you to later go back and experience previous worlds in a different way. Each dream can be "solved" in several different ways.
Unfortunately, the execution falls well short. The dreams are tiny, static environments, and confusing to navigate. In fact, you can't "walk" at all; you have a series of pictures, and you draw glyphs on the screen to move around. This may have been forgivable in the mid-90s, but this game was made in 2011! Every screen can have a half-dozen different exits, depending on how the writer was feeling that day.
There are no puzzles to speak of. Each dream is "won" by drawing the right glyph in the right spot. You're treated to a small animation, a line or two of voiceover narration, and the next dream is unlocked. If you solve a dream "incorrectly" (i. e. by using the right glyph in the right spot, but a different glyph than the one you "learn" in the dream)... you're treated to a small animation, a line or two of voiceover narration, and then told to go back and do it correctly. Whee.
There's a collection sidequest - pictures hidden in each dream - which is nice if you enjoy pixel hunts. It takes about twice as long as the game itself and adds 5 seconds to the ending cutscene. These 5 seconds tell you exactly nothing new about the protagonist (her every other line is "everything is still terrible") and only serve to make the ending slightly more depressing. It took me less than two hours to finish the game, about half of which was pixel hunting.
In short: TRAUMA has paper-thin gameplay, the writing is cryptic-for-the-sake-of-being-cryptic and highly pretentious. The dream concept is interesting, and the game has a memorable moment or two, but in the end, it is overwhelmingly flawed. Unless you're extremely desparate for any sort of adventure game at all, no recommendation.

This game is a bit confusing at first, however once you take the time to sit down, read dialogue and learn the mechanics it is an amazingly fun fps/rpg. EYE is like a Russian Warhammer 40k mixed with ShadowRun, CyberPunk 2020 and D&D. You're in the future running around different planets in medieval armor, have cybernetic enhancements and magic all at once. The game is not forgiving for failure at all. If you fail to hack even a door or a bank dispenser you can be counter hacked giving you a sort of Laughing Man esque face over your screen. To get rid of this you have to then hack yourself. If you die, which is quite easy if not paying attention to your stats and ammo, you can get permanent wounds which reduce your stats. When single player isn't enough you can play the campaign in coop up to 32 players. The only downside is that there is no Friendly Fire, unless you backstab a friend with a melee weapon or give them a Medkit Overdose. Overall the game is very fun and a beautiful work of art once you get into it and soak it in.

Fourth Update: (Fudging spelling ;..;)
Further clarifications and added suggested fix from the comments.
TLDR:
The devs seem great, are very responsive, helpful, they take feedback and probably tried their very best to make this game. I have nothing but good things to say about them based on my experiences, regardless of my opinions of the (basically) finished game.
That being said:
DO YOU LIKE THE SPELLFORCE UNIVERSE?
Give it a try when it's on sale, the story seems very good in my opinion but the gameplay isn't deep enough to entertain you I think.
(Subjectivity is a thing though.)
ARE YOU NOT INTO THE SPELLFORCE UNIVERSE?
Probably don't get this one. The gameplay is pretty flat as an RTS and pretty flat as an RPG. Unless you're really into the story, you'll probably get bored.
IN-DEPTH REVIEW:
What I expected when I bought this game was a warcraft 3 style RTS with RPG elements and more emphasis on custom characters.
If you have the same expectations then I'm afraid you'll probably be dissapointed I think.
Gameplay:
The RTS gameplay is very basic and not very complex. As a big fan of RTS games, I wouldn't recommend this game as an RTS. It's perfectly adequate and functional, but very simplistic and with little variance. RTS fans probably won't feel their RTS cravings satisfied with this.
There isn't enough units or buildings for there to be any differences in play-style or base-building.
There's 1 infantry, 1 spearman and 1 archer per tier, but there's only 2 tiers of the basic units.
There's a third tier of 3 elite units that tend to be situational in my experience. (healers, siege etc.)
There's 1 siege unit with no options. You'll basically always be building the same units in the same order.
Bases are limited in space and buildings need staff, which is also limited.
The end result is that each region you occupy will only have maybe 3-4 buildings tops due to not being allowed more staff than that.
These things come together to form a very linear and non-creative base building situation.
You'll always be building the same few buildings, in the same places and for the same reasons. There's no real unit or building variety at all, you'll always have roughly the same unit compositions and you'll be using them the same way every time.
There's no real management of the base to speak of, you just build the resource buildings, build a barracks, build units then send them to attack and that's it. There's no creativity to be had with it.
As an RTS, it encourages you to just get out there and attack/conquer your enemies rather than building and managing your base and economy, which I feel is a mistake as management and base-building is the bread and butter of RTS games.
If you're looking for an RTS like Warcraft 3, Cossacks, Age of Empires etc, this likely won't satisfy you.
The RPG elements are well done in general, there's a lot of character to everything you see and everyone you meet. There's inventory/equipment/stats management for a whole party of hero characters. Imagine a simplified Pillars of Eternity.
The story itself seems very good as far as I have experienced. (which is about 2-3 missions ATM.)
If the awkward and simplified gameplay doesn't bother you too much then you'll probably have a great time with it regardless.
I feel like they tried to merge the RTS and RPG genres, but just didn't quite manage to iron out all the things that clash and don't work together.
Especially in an RTS game, it's incredibly important that the player feels like they can quickly see and digest everything within the camera's immediate view, but this game's maps just weren't designed for it. You have to constantly rotate the camera to see things.
That kind of camera is good for an RPG, but not for an RTS. Having to rotate the camera even just once to see a scene clearly is awkward and cumbersome during RTS gameplay, and just makes you feel like you don't have a grasp on what's in front of you.
The keyboard shortcuts are also very awkward due to the merging of genres.
Hero abilities get bound to QWER-ASDF-ZXCV by default, which looks intuitive on paper until you realize that a lot of RTS stuff now has to be bound to non-intuitive keys instead.
The building menu is K instead of B for instance, and the Attack-Move order is G instead of A.
Rather than having all your heroes be always "selected" and binding half your keyboard to their abilities at all times, it would've been better to just have access to the spells of the first hero selected through the QWERT keys. Heroes can easily be bound to hotkeys for whenever you feel you need to use someone's particular skills.
I also found it incredibly hectic to manage your party during combat while you're also trying to manage the army around them, especially since a full party can require you to keep up to 12 hotkeys with individual uses in mind for your hero characters alone. (And that's ignoring the required attention to your heroes' positions and statuses so you don't just go firing off hero actions blindly.)
The skill trees also feel lacking in my opinion, there's basically just 6 skilltrees (3 fighters, 3 mages) with a few simple entries in each tree and next to no varience. There's only 1 offensive spell for each element, so all mages will have basically the same loadout because there's just nothing to choose. You can choose if you want to build a mage, archer or warrior, but you'll end up building the classes the same way every time you do. An archer will basically always end up the same, and so will a warrior and a mage.
Overall, Spellforce is a bit of a mess.
Both the RPG and RTS elements end up suffering from the same problems due to the awkward fusion between genres. In the end, it just becomes an adequate but simple RTS, and an adequate but simple RPG, with a lot of stuff that doesn't work well with the other genre clashing all over the place.
It's not a bad RPG, it's not a bad RTS, but it's very shallow gameplay and you probably won't get your RTS or RPG fix playing this game.
With that in mind, I cannot recommend it at full price.
If you're into the Spellforce universe then these things probably won't bother you much.
If that's the case then I'd say get it on a sale, for the story content mainly.
If you're not into the Spellforce universe, like me who was just looking for a cool RTS, you will likely get bored with this game fairly quickly.

5 Years on and this is still a fun, unique title that belongs in the library of people who are fans of RPGs, Sci-Fi/Fantasy and FPSs.
On the subject of genre, you will probably have to be a fan of all three to enjoy this title. The story and a number of the gameplay elements live in the sci-fi/fantasy realm, from optic camoudlage to 'Psi' powers which are pretty much magic. The majority of the gameplay though, sits firmly in the realm of FPS, but with a lot of RPG elements from levelling to upgrades.
Story wise, this is a psychological, sci-fi dystopia story, with metaphor and a small amount of 'mind f**king', that may have you questioning the world you find yourself. The story isn't very complicated, but nor is it overtly spelled out for you or particularly well told. I love a good story in a game, even if it's to the detriment of the gameplay. I would not say this is one of those stories that kept me riveted.
But now we're onto the best bit, the gameplay. The gameplay is largely excellent. You have a variety of weapons, turrets, and other tools at your disposal that all work in typical FPS style. Instead of being limited to an arbitrary number of weapons or a weight, you're limited by the space in your various pockets and holsters in a system reminiscent of Deus Ex; a minor caveat to this is that carrying a great deal of weight will impact your movement speed. In addition to various tools, you have a variety of skills which vary from hacking to stealth, from X-ray vision to enhanced jumping. You also have access to a second set of skills, your 'Psi' powers, which are essentially magic spells that convert matter into energy, transmute enemies, or deal damage. Both, of these skills require resources that regenerate over time, so depending entirely on them will be tricky.
In addition to skills that you can learn, you can also enhance your stats in a classic 'levelling' RPG style, these stats can impact your skills, speed, endurance, and allow you to unlock new weapons and skills. There are actually 3 ways to increase various stats, firstly through gaining experience, secondly through cybernetic upgrades that cost currency, and third through research, which is unlocked through looting or other research, it requires both time and currency to research, but there are other benefits to research.
In addition to shooting, and levelling, you have one other major skill to master, hacking. While you can get through most of the game without touching this mini-game, utilizing it is often advantageous such as taking over the 'cyber brain' of your opponent, turning them into a minion, or deactivating turrets from behind cover, or even acquiring extra currency.
Though sometimes you will be forced to shoot guns blazing, other times the game gives you so much freedom to play your own way, through cyber-warfare, stealth, sniping, or continuing to shoot everything.
The death penalty in this game involves running the risk of acquiring 'scar tissue', which permanently weakens your character, opperating counter to the stats you gain while levelling. Since you're more likely to die on difficulties above your ability, this effectively penalizes the inexperienced yet bold, which may not be the best decision for a video game since sitting in your comfort zone is usually considered less fun. Scar tissue can eventually be removed and prevented through research, a research I consider 'mandatory' as this freedom allows you to experiment, push the boundaries of your skills, try new ways to tackle problems on subsequent playthroughs, and allows you to more freely use Psi powers, the strongest of which have the risk of causing a scar when used.
Speaking of subsequent playthroughs, the game features what is essentially a 'new game+' system, allowing you to take your now much stronger character through the game again, perhaps to try a different ending, perhaps boosting the difficulty. Alternatively, you can revisit previously unlocked areas to complete randomized extra objectives, this can allow you to do additional 'levelling' or see newish content. All in all, this stretches out the longevity of the game a little, but with finite content and a relatively small number of areas to explore, don't expect to sink as much time in this game as some others.
One minor annoyance is the enemy AI, which almost exclusively resorts to charging toward you and attacking with no real sense of self preservation or tactics. Enemy spawning is near endless at times (dependant on your settings), which can serve to further increase the feeling that enemies are nothing but expendable cannon fodder, reusing the same smallish number of enemy models over and over, which over time gets a little boring.
If you get tired of playing solo, this game also features a co-op mode, your experiences will of course vary when going online. 5 Years ago, it was a little tricky to get going, and I have not tried it since. If you do struggle, make sure your router and firewall correctly forward/allow the necessary ports.
Graphically, this game still looks better than a lot of small-studio / Indie games that are arriving on steam, despite being over 5 years old. Perhaps some things feel a little too-shiny, but that's a personal preference, not really a complaint.
Overall I recommend this game and think it has stood up well to the ravages of time. It is a shame that few games have tried to capture the audience that this game managed to.

Weak recommendation.  This essentially copies Dream Quest--not just concepts, but many specific abilities and cards--but Dream Quest is a good game to copy.  I feel Monster Slayers does some stuff better but other stuff worse.
Monster Slayers employed an actual artist! But Dream Quest does a great job of making info on keywords, stats, cooldowns, etc. all available when you want it, while Monster Slayers does a pretty poor job of this.
Both games require you to spend several runs unlocking advantages before you have a serious shot at winning, but Dream Quest's are achievement-based, whereas Monster Hunter focuses more on just playing a long time.  Monster Hunter also seems to have more vertical power growth, which made the first dungeon of future runs start to feel trivial after only a few runs.  And when you beat Monster Hunter, you lose the items you used to do it, so it requires ongoing grinding to replace them (whereas in Dream Quest, once everything is unlocked, it's unlocked).
Dream Quest classes grow differently but start pretty similar.  Monster Hunters classes seem to start with more differences and acquire unique cards faster.  Also, Monster Hunters has several cards that can be used in multiple ways.
Some days, I felt like I had to make 5 runs on Dream Quest before one of them got good enough card options to make a viable deck.  Monster Hunters seems more consistent and overall easier.  (Note:  This may not be apples-to-apples, since I started playing Dream Quest before they added easier difficulty settings, and I have not unlocked Monster Slayer's "legendary mode".)
Just a gut feel, but Dream Quest strikes me as more finely-tuned, whereas Monster Slayers feels like it lets you get into degenerate cases (such as playing your whole deck every turn, or killing the final boss in one round) more easily and with greater impact.
(Note:  I played Dream Quest on iOS, and most of my play with it was a long time ago.)

Gunpoint is a 2D stealth strategy game told in the world of an old-school noir detective novel. Think Deus Ex meets the Maltese Falcon.
In the not-too-distant future of some European city, guns were made entirely illegal. Now, weapons manufracturers are congealing on the shadows to introduce their products into the underworld. You play an intrepid yet apathetic detective who gets wrapped up in the police investigations and the shady corporate workings of this new black market.
What to expect:
-Witty and irreverent pre-mission dialogues. You can choose alliances or betrayals of your police comrades and your untrustworthy business ties. There seem to be a number of alternate endings.
-Main missions themselves involve infiltrating secured buildings containing lucrative secrets needed to advance the story. Your detective can jump massive distances and cling to nearly all walls and ceilings. With upgrades, he can break through windows and knock down doors or shoot guns.
-Security guards will shoot on sight. In order to access the necessary areas, you need to tackle and disable guards one by one. Or just shoot them with your very loud and distracting gun.
-The ability to hack most electronic systems remotely. From anywhere on the map, you can disconnect or reconnect electrical circuits to your whim. For example, there is a light switch connected to a ceiling light. If you so choose, you could redirect that switch to connect to a locked door. Then, every time you flip that switch, the door will open or close. You can connect a door to a light. An elevator to a sound detector. Establishing or cutting the right connections is key to solving Gunpoint's puzzles.
-Art style is pixels. Music is sleazy and noir. What else were you expecting?
Gunpoint's idea is straight-forward. Classic detective tropes surrounding hacking and stealth strategy sequences. Those strategy maps, however, are slightly challenging but always fun.

It should say something about this game when I tell you this is the first review I've done on Steam.
I've been a big fan of the stealth genre since back in high school, starting with Splinter Cell and blossoming with Thief: The Dark Project. Unfortunately true stealth games are pretty rare. This is one of those rare games. So here's my opinion of the game.
Story: The story is pretty unique, with a well-crafted setting and at least a few good twists and turns. It may be a tad hollow at times, but everything ties together by about the halfway point. The only issue that some may be disappointed with is that many of the cutscenes are played out with still artwork slides accompanied by the voice actors, a pretty dated style by today's standards. But the talent and the quality of the art make it acceptable, and after the first couple of cutscenes, I ceased to even notice. After all, Thief used the same method and it got the story across perfectly.
Gameplay: I found it, for the most part, masterful. The stealth tactics necessary to survive are your most effective weapon by far. The shadows are truly black, and leave everything dark instead of the more common shadowing represented by a blue that leaves it nearly as easy to see as in broad daylight. Which is a major pet peeve of mine.
There are plenty of methods of quietly eliminating your foes, but often at a risk. The AI is fairly intelligent, with enemies capable of communicating and working together with each other. Once in a while they may get stuck, but it's rare and never ruined it for me.
As a side note, the game does require a good bit of time to progress, and plenty of patience is needed to complete each stage.
Combat: I separate combat because this may annoy some people. It took me a while to get the hang of it, and I quickly learned that if you end up in direct combat with someone, you probably made a major mistake. It is clunky, and you can only engage one enemy at once. It leaves any other enemies the chance to strike you down with ease. I'm convinced that this was intentional, however, representing Styx's physical weakness and requiring you to stick to the shadows. It completes the challenge necessary in a stealth game, which is not to get caught. To me this is refreshing, since it's been so common in recent years for stealth games to be mostly combat games starring a unrealistically powerful warrior masquerading as a stealth game.
Environments: The environments are quite beautiful, with many details and several ways to progress throughout. Unfortunately, many stages end up being recycled. While the patrols change significantly and new areas will open up within them, it is probably my biggest problem with the game. However, I never felt that is was such a problem that it lessened the fun factor for me.
So, to summarize:
Pros:
-Good story
-True stealth gameplay
-Intelligent enemies
-Several abilities to slip past or trick your enemies
-Well-constructed environments
Cons:
-Recycled stages
-Odd combat system
-Challenge may be too high for some more casual gamers
So, like I said, this is one of the best stealth games I've played. It's one of those rare gems that deserves recognition and I would definitely recommend anyone that enjoys a good sneaking, andrenaline flooding challenge. It's worth the full price.
