An excellent old-school action-adventure in the vein of the original Zelda.
You have your primary weapon - the titular shotgun, and find a number of secondary weapons and passive equipment along the way.  While the shotgun's range isn't too bad, it has a pretty large spread so you want to be relatively close to your target for maximum damage.  1-2 close up shotgun blasts will take care of most normal monsters, or you can keep picking away at the enemies' invisible healthbars from the relative safety a few meters grant.  Most of the secondary weapons require ammo, that randomly drops from enemies, and can also be bought from some vendor or replenished for free from the occasional ammo station.  Regaining lost "hearts" (HP) works the same way - loot drops, vendors, health stations.  As you progress, you also find heart container (max health) upgrades, ammo capacity upgrades, and shotgun upgrades (adding additional pellets to the shotgun blast).  You can switch secondary weapons by cycling through them while playing, or from the inventory screen which pauses the game play so you don't get hurt while picking the best weapon for the current situation.
The map is open world, littered with monsters and dungeons.  Plenty of secrets in both the map and the dungeons, most of them blocked off by obstacles that require a weapon or item found in the dungeons, so it's best to note down where you come across the (quite obvious) obstacles so you know where to revisit later.   The monsters respawn after you move a few screens away (not sure how many, maybe 4-5), but the cleared obstacles remain cleared.
The vendor at the starting location has a compass costing 10 coins (drops from monsters).  You should buy it quickly, as it gives your character's relative position on the minimap for both the overmap and the dungeons.  However the actual dungeon rooms/features will not be visible until you find the dungeon's map somewhere inside, and the overmap features will not be visible for quite a while longer.  Again, note taking would be encouraged, though there's no real need to actually draw a square-by-square map of your own like some games pretty much required in ye olden times.
The game controls great with the Xbox 360 pad, so I never tried the keyboard controls.  One thing to keep in mind is that this is
a twin-stick shooter.  The only direction you can fire your weapon is the one in which your character is facing, and the only way (as far as I know) to face in that direction is to move in that direction, which adds a level of difficulty when trying to blast nearby enemies without colliding with them and losing health.
There is a hardcore mode, where you only get the one life and if you die it's Game Over.   I did not even attempt it, considering how many times I died on my play through.  In non-hardcore mode, if you die, you get sent back to the save point.  There is only the one save slot, but that never presented much of a problem to me.  Save points are placed at all dungeon entrances/exits, health & ammo stations, some in-dungeon transitions, and whenever you find an item/upgrade.   If the save is made when your health is too low, reloading it will bump you up to 3 HP or about half your max HP, whichever's greater.
I had a lot of fun in then 5.5 hours or so that it took me to complete the game.  I did miss one passive item and a few ammo upgrades along the way, hunting them down without a guide would probably take another hour or two, and I'm not enough of a completionist to do that.
Honestly, I'm not sure why Shotgun Legend still in Early Access - I played it from the beginning to end without encountering any bugs.

This is the first "Early Access" game that I've purchased, and I had some reservations about doing so.  "Early Access" to me indicates buggy and/or unfinished games, that I would basically be paying to be a playtester for.  I can gladly say that this is not the case with Shotgun Legend, and the game is fully completed, and I haven't encountered any bugs during the four hours that I've played the game.  That being said, on to the review of the gameplay:
Let's start by getting the obvious out of the way.  This game is "heavily influenced" by the original Legend of Zelda, to say the least.  That being said, it manages to do something unique with the formula, including some fairly creative powerups and combat strategies.  If you're a fan of the original LoZ, then you should have no problems jumping right into this game.
While there are many similariites between the two titles, Shotgun Legend offers a new take on the Action-RPG combat by equpping the protagonist with a shotgun instead of a sword.  This allows you to attack enemies from farther away, while decreasing the amount of damage you depending on how far away from the enemy you are.  While this might not seem like a huge deal, it complelety alters the way that you play the game because it is no longer a simple hack-and-slash mechanic that you're dealing with.
The game provides a very basic concept for a story during the intro, but this becomes more fleshed out as you advance and find various notes left around the world that add more to the game's backstory.  All in all, it provides a fairly interesting plot to go along with the basic LoZ exploration concept.
I picked this game up during the Winter Sale for $.49 today, and I honestly didn't have high hopes for it.  Gladly, I have been proven wrong, and have already put 4 hours into playing it.  This is one of those games that you want to keep .playing and advancing in when you start it.  I highly recommend it, and since the game offers trading cards,  you can pick it up for the $.49 sale price, and most likely make back most of, if not all of your money by selling the cards.
Here's a quick breakdown of the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
- Borrows heavily from the original Legend of Zelda, while paying homage to the same
- Heavy on exploration- lots of secrets to be found, and doesn't hold you hand throughout the whole game
- Replacing the sword with a shotgun offers a unique approach to playing a familiar action-rpg
- Secondary items are creative and help to enhance the different ways in which to play the game
- Despite being an "early access game," offers a complete game, that seems to be free of any major bugs
- Very cheap, especially if you can get it during a sale
- Offers Steam trading cards, which can potentially get you back all or some of the money you spent on it
Cons
- Difficulty spikes with some of the dungeon bosses.  While most are fairly easy to beat after learning their pattern, ther are a couple that really ramp up the difficulty
- As someone with red/green colorblindness, I sometimes got killed because I failed to see a bat that blended into the background, or because I couldn't tell the differece between a normal enemy or its poisonous (green?) counterpart.
All in all I definitely recommend this game, especially to any Legend of Zelda fans out there.  I've played many ROM hacks of the original LoZ, and this game manages to do what most of the don't- introduces something fresh and avoids becomign stale and repetative.

Pid (Planet in Distress) is a platforming/puzzle game made by Might and Delight. I was lucky enough to get it from a Twitter Giveaway. I feel not enough people have played this truly amazing game, It features a unique art style with kooky looking characters and world, The only game I feel it bares resembles to is Little Big Planet for the PS3, PSVITA. It has great level mechanics, with the inclusion of a tool which allows you to place beams which will lift you up (similar to Light Bridges from Portal 2), this makes for most the puzzles in the game, to aid the player on his journey he can get items using Stars he collects, Items Include things like Armour, Bombs etc.
But also along the way there are hidden items, called memories which are souverniers, from playing the game, they seem to be very well hidden as I haven't even found one yet!.
One thing I really love about this game is the soundtrack it is amazing! really sets the mood, from the slow jazz at the beginning of the game to the catchy melodies later on. A concept I find really intresting in this game is there are sort of stealth elements to it, some enemies will if they detect you cause you to die, this makes more stratergy as to when to time movements, which leads me on to my next point, Pid is Hard, the puzzles aren't to hard but some of the platforming bits require movements which are done in a window of only seconds.
Once you have finished the story the game also has some other content, such as CO-OP, Challenge Maps and the Leaderboards to see how fast you can finish the game.
The only problem I have with the game, is at times it can feel a little repetive, I feel should there be a sequel, maybe adding more power ups or something would spice it up.
So In conclusion even though I was given this game I would happily pay for it, and I recommend you do as Might and Delight are making some excellent indie games.

Anyone who saw my previous review would know it was less than stellar mostly because of the microtransaction model, but there have been a lot of changes since then. Yes you still have to build up the town to get full functionality but you do so with either gold or medals gained from quests, which replaced the shards.
Good points:
The game is easy to learn and get into, especially if you've played oldschool dungeon crawlers like Wizardry or Bard's Tale. But even if you haven't the tutorial does an adequate job of explaining how the dungeon works.
Sometimes a new character shows up at the end of a floor and you have the option of recruiting them or not, but unlike tavern recruits they cost nothing.
Some new classes are made available by progressing through the tower, once you pass the appropriate floors they'll be available without having to spend anything to unlock them. You'll still have to pay to hire them at the tavern just like the standard classes though, unless you manage to meet one in the tower.
Every 5 floors passed in the tower gives you the option to start at that floor instead of all the way back at floor 1 each time you enter.
Bad points:
Dead characters lose all their equipment unless you focus on upgrading the Church, but to be fair characters only die if you wipe and that's actually a bit hard to do unless you get careless and try to do a floor you know you aren't ready for yet.
The price seems a bit steep at $14.99, but that's what sales are for.
All in all a fun game, if you like loot based dungeon crawlers give it a try.

I give the game kudos for its eerie soundtrack and artwork that evokes an aesthetic wholy appropriate for the theme of the game and its Lovecraftian inspiration.
However, the gameplay is severely lacking.  This is not a game of strategy, but a game of luck.  Everything is randomly generated each time you play, from the cult members' various vitrutes and vices to the actions that they take when selected each month.  There is a lot of guess work involved, and you can make some fairly educated guesses as to which members might have a major vice.  However, if you cannot get the game to actually reveal that vice (which, again, the action of revealing the vice is random) then you are out of luck.  That type of gameplay simply isn't compelling.
Another issue with this game is that it does an extremely poor job of explaining itself and how to play.  There is no tutorial and limited instruction from the game.  I watched a few videos on YouTube, which did help quite a bit, and after a few short plays I had a much better idea of what to do.  No, it's not hard to go watch a YouTube video, but I don't feel I should have to look to outside sources for rules and instrucitons for playing a game.

I've yet to survive more than two seasons, and often I quit and restart after the first, because it's so clear early on whether you're going to be successful (lucky) or not.  Frankly, I don't think it's worth spending any more of my limited gaming time on this game.

5 Years on and this is still a fun, unique title that belongs in the library of people who are fans of RPGs, Sci-Fi/Fantasy and FPSs.
On the subject of genre, you will probably have to be a fan of all three to enjoy this title. The story and a number of the gameplay elements live in the sci-fi/fantasy realm, from optic camoudlage to 'Psi' powers which are pretty much magic. The majority of the gameplay though, sits firmly in the realm of FPS, but with a lot of RPG elements from levelling to upgrades.
Story wise, this is a psychological, sci-fi dystopia story, with metaphor and a small amount of 'mind f**king', that may have you questioning the world you find yourself. The story isn't very complicated, but nor is it overtly spelled out for you or particularly well told. I love a good story in a game, even if it's to the detriment of the gameplay. I would not say this is one of those stories that kept me riveted.
But now we're onto the best bit, the gameplay. The gameplay is largely excellent. You have a variety of weapons, turrets, and other tools at your disposal that all work in typical FPS style. Instead of being limited to an arbitrary number of weapons or a weight, you're limited by the space in your various pockets and holsters in a system reminiscent of Deus Ex; a minor caveat to this is that carrying a great deal of weight will impact your movement speed. In addition to various tools, you have a variety of skills which vary from hacking to stealth, from X-ray vision to enhanced jumping. You also have access to a second set of skills, your 'Psi' powers, which are essentially magic spells that convert matter into energy, transmute enemies, or deal damage. Both, of these skills require resources that regenerate over time, so depending entirely on them will be tricky.
In addition to skills that you can learn, you can also enhance your stats in a classic 'levelling' RPG style, these stats can impact your skills, speed, endurance, and allow you to unlock new weapons and skills. There are actually 3 ways to increase various stats, firstly through gaining experience, secondly through cybernetic upgrades that cost currency, and third through research, which is unlocked through looting or other research, it requires both time and currency to research, but there are other benefits to research.
In addition to shooting, and levelling, you have one other major skill to master, hacking. While you can get through most of the game without touching this mini-game, utilizing it is often advantageous such as taking over the 'cyber brain' of your opponent, turning them into a minion, or deactivating turrets from behind cover, or even acquiring extra currency.
Though sometimes you will be forced to shoot guns blazing, other times the game gives you so much freedom to play your own way, through cyber-warfare, stealth, sniping, or continuing to shoot everything.
The death penalty in this game involves running the risk of acquiring 'scar tissue', which permanently weakens your character, opperating counter to the stats you gain while levelling. Since you're more likely to die on difficulties above your ability, this effectively penalizes the inexperienced yet bold, which may not be the best decision for a video game since sitting in your comfort zone is usually considered less fun. Scar tissue can eventually be removed and prevented through research, a research I consider 'mandatory' as this freedom allows you to experiment, push the boundaries of your skills, try new ways to tackle problems on subsequent playthroughs, and allows you to more freely use Psi powers, the strongest of which have the risk of causing a scar when used.
Speaking of subsequent playthroughs, the game features what is essentially a 'new game+' system, allowing you to take your now much stronger character through the game again, perhaps to try a different ending, perhaps boosting the difficulty. Alternatively, you can revisit previously unlocked areas to complete randomized extra objectives, this can allow you to do additional 'levelling' or see newish content. All in all, this stretches out the longevity of the game a little, but with finite content and a relatively small number of areas to explore, don't expect to sink as much time in this game as some others.
One minor annoyance is the enemy AI, which almost exclusively resorts to charging toward you and attacking with no real sense of self preservation or tactics. Enemy spawning is near endless at times (dependant on your settings), which can serve to further increase the feeling that enemies are nothing but expendable cannon fodder, reusing the same smallish number of enemy models over and over, which over time gets a little boring.
If you get tired of playing solo, this game also features a co-op mode, your experiences will of course vary when going online. 5 Years ago, it was a little tricky to get going, and I have not tried it since. If you do struggle, make sure your router and firewall correctly forward/allow the necessary ports.
Graphically, this game still looks better than a lot of small-studio / Indie games that are arriving on steam, despite being over 5 years old. Perhaps some things feel a little too-shiny, but that's a personal preference, not really a complaint.
Overall I recommend this game and think it has stood up well to the ravages of time. It is a shame that few games have tried to capture the audience that this game managed to.

With titles like these I'm reminded of the so-called golden age of FMV gaming, brought on by CD-ROM drives. Horribly clunky, dysfunctional pieces of puppetry and grainy video. Okay, I'm making this all sound awful, aren't I? Well, what I meant to say is that perhaps personal computers are fast enough these days to make those approaches plausible. Maybe we didn't hate those experimental games, but the fact that the technology to run them properly didn't exist? No more macroblocky and grainy 64-colour video and sluggish screen transitions. Trauma is short but lovably dreamlike -- and not at all hindered by the technology onto which it is born, unlike most of its 1990s relatives. Trauma is also bleak.

The Shrouded Isle is a really entertaining act of balance, where every action has benefits and consequences, and you are constantly pushed to make decisions that will put you in a tricky situation. The team has done an impressive job of creating the perfect equilibrium wherein you're always on the edge of disaster, shifting problems from one area to the next, while simultaneously keeping in mind longer-term goals and criteria for winning.
The learning curve is fun - the game doesn't explain every interlocking mechanic to you, but you are brought to discover each of them very organically. I reveled in the cruelty of certain mechanics when they were revealed to me.
I also find a lot of pleasure in replaying the game now that I fully understand it, thanks to a hefty amount of randomization. It's a good way to spend ~1h focusing my attention on tactics and detective work, and has a lot more personality than, say, Solitaire or Minesweeper. :P
Your mileage may vary, but this is a great game for the type of person I am and how I like to spend my leisure time.

After purchasing this title, I was a little worried, as I had sunk fifteen bucks into a title I knew nothing about, and the title I played prior to this, Nekopara, had slightly left me famished for more. However, I can wholeheartedly say that in my opinion, If My Heart Had Wings was worth the full price paid, and honestly, I wouldn't have minded paying a little more for this title.
The game's story is substantially written, with me sinking in fourteen (14) hours of reading into only a single storyline. Granted, this time includes the necessary filler and build-up work, but the payoff at the end of the storyline I played was well worth the time put into the title. I can't wait to start anew, and if the game is how it looked to be, go through the other potential storylines. However, at the point of writing this review, there were a couple of loose ends in the story (no spoilers, but the motivation of one of the characters isn't resolved), however I'm confident that as with other visual novels of this nature, this will be explored in other avenues.
Further, I am more than happy to say that none of the plot points are rushed or feel unnatural in occurrence. Such as with Nekopara, where several of the scenarios left me wondering, "Wait, that's it?" or "The conflict's *already* resolved?", this title takes its sweet time developing the plot, characters, and resolution, starting with the introductions, gradually building the stakes and the bonds between Mr. Minase and, in my case, Ms. Habane, letting all of the buildup release in the climax, then winding down smoothly to the falling action, then ending on a sweet, satisfactory ending.
Now, while I might sound like this game is flawless, there were a couple of hiccups that I noticed. In some spots, the translation gives way to some odd text, and sometimes it is downright incoherent or misleading. Further, while the game has a substantial amount of scenarios to scroll through, there are also instances that did make me wonder if it couldn't be cut for the sake of cutting filler.
All in all, however, I must say that this is a title that I will hold as a treasure on my hard drive. With a title like Nekopara, the allure was there, however there just wasn't enough to warrant me to save it on my computer, and to be honest, while it was a nice momentary distraction, I would feel no loss in deleting it from my library. But, with IMHHW, this one deserves to be put to a disc, so that I might save it in a vault to show future generations what a true visual novel worth the silicone is about. My only fear would be that they would make an unnecessary sequel to this title, as it stands confidently on its own merits, but if this should be the case, I would hope that if this is the case, MoeNovel would do similarly to what Circus did for Da Capo, and put it in the same universe, but with enough time passed to mention the happenings of the first run while leaving it untainted. Final verdict is a solid ten out of ten. If you love visual novels, especially of the romatic nature, with strong character development and one hell of a payoff, this is a title you need to buy as soon as you can.

First off, this game has some of the best stealth gameplay I've ever experienced. It draws a perfect balance between the refinement of the modern stealth/assassination genre and the sprawling, complex, natural-feeling maps (and audacious, slightly clunky platforming) of more classic PC games. Very rarely does anything in the game feel unfair or unwieldly, even when the game throws its nastiest situations and most fiendish enemies against you.
While the gameplay is, as mentioned, excellent, the story and setting are where this game truly shines. Many games make a petty show of attempting moral ambiguity - this game absolutely nails it. The plot would be more at home in a particularly outstanding dark fantasy novel. Go in expecting cheesy simplicity, like I did, and the game will throw you for a loop. Wonderful stuff, well told.
My only complaint with this game is that some of the English dialogue doesn't quite flow naturally, obviously having been written by someone who had English as their second language - probably a native French speaker. The voice actors carry it well, though, and make it hard to notice unless you have some familiarity with the slightly awkward phrasing often used by French people speaking English. Honestly, it's kind of a charm point.
Basically, Styx is well worth the price, and the hours you'll sink into it. I truly look forward to more titles set in this game's compelling and frightening world.

One of the best out there. A really fun, and enjoyable deckbuilding game. If you think that it is an indie game and the price is so low... a must buy for me. Amazing work!

Gunpoint is a 2D stealth strategy game told in the world of an old-school noir detective novel. Think Deus Ex meets the Maltese Falcon.
In the not-too-distant future of some European city, guns were made entirely illegal. Now, weapons manufracturers are congealing on the shadows to introduce their products into the underworld. You play an intrepid yet apathetic detective who gets wrapped up in the police investigations and the shady corporate workings of this new black market.
What to expect:
-Witty and irreverent pre-mission dialogues. You can choose alliances or betrayals of your police comrades and your untrustworthy business ties. There seem to be a number of alternate endings.
-Main missions themselves involve infiltrating secured buildings containing lucrative secrets needed to advance the story. Your detective can jump massive distances and cling to nearly all walls and ceilings. With upgrades, he can break through windows and knock down doors or shoot guns.
-Security guards will shoot on sight. In order to access the necessary areas, you need to tackle and disable guards one by one. Or just shoot them with your very loud and distracting gun.
-The ability to hack most electronic systems remotely. From anywhere on the map, you can disconnect or reconnect electrical circuits to your whim. For example, there is a light switch connected to a ceiling light. If you so choose, you could redirect that switch to connect to a locked door. Then, every time you flip that switch, the door will open or close. You can connect a door to a light. An elevator to a sound detector. Establishing or cutting the right connections is key to solving Gunpoint's puzzles.
-Art style is pixels. Music is sleazy and noir. What else were you expecting?
Gunpoint's idea is straight-forward. Classic detective tropes surrounding hacking and stealth strategy sequences. Those strategy maps, however, are slightly challenging but always fun.

This is what I call a progressive rogue.  As a rogue, you die alot so do not become attached to that one character.  But there is progression, that you earn fame which enables you to unlock special abilities to carry over to your new character and companions for the next run.  In addition, any loot you gain or buy from merchants carry over to your next character.  There are about 8 character types to pick from such as mage, cleric, theif, barbarian, etc.  Plus you get an additional two companions which you meet up at the first and second map.
So in this game, you level up by defeating bad guys which earns you a choice between new cards, action points (for attack cards), mana points (for mana), more hit points, etc.  As you open the map in a level, you will encounter monsters to defeat with your deck, captains that grant the chance to upgrade a card or gain more action points, healers to heal, campfires to heal and get bonus, monoliths that grant positve and negative perks, special npc that grant rewards, merchants to buy new cards and equipment, etc.
Each card cost action points and mana points so leveling these up are important.  You have hitpoints.  Equipment grants bonuses to hitpoints, attack strength, gives new cards, percentages to get more potion drops, etc.  During combat, you can be weakend, poisoned, ignited, etc, but you can do the same to your opponents, with each card you play.  There are lots of cards with different effects, from special attacks, buffs, debuffs, magic spells, etc.
You win the card match and open another part of the map.  Once you defeat the main boss in that map you progress to the next map.  After three maps, you meet the main boss, who has  lots of hit points, great cards, and a beeotch to defeat.  I still have not defeated him and I am not giving up either.
I'm rambling.  My advice, if this seems interesting watch a youtube review to get more info as it is better to watch  a video then listen to me ramble

is a tribute to the Legend of Zelda, but instead of Link, you are Eugene, a shotgun wielding hillbilly. Exploration is fun and rewarding, dungeons are challenging, and combat is exciting.
If I were browsing the Steam store, it is very likely that I wouldn’t have taken a second look at Shotgun Legend. Luckily, this game was recommended to me, so I gave it a try. Pid is an extremely charming 2.5D puzzle platformer, but its unforgiving sections in the game can often make for a frustrating time. You play as Kurt, a boy who falls asleep on a space school bus and needs to get back home. Unfortunately the planet he's on is less than willing to let you go. You must dodge clever robots and learn about the planet, which has a surprising amount of lore.
The gameplay has a lot of satisfying controls like precise jumping, but its core mechanic is a superpower Kurt gets early on. You have the ability to place down up to two beams that can carry you like the Funnels in Portal 2. This opens up a lot of solutions to puzzles considering that you can place them down on almost any surface. These puzzles, as I've said before, can get a little frustratng because most of the game a single hit will kill you. And sometimes the beam placement can get finnicky and you get killed.
To top off the great story and puzzling, there's a co op mode that takes Audrey with you. With two people, each person gets only one beam. Personally I think the beams are a power you shouldn't dumb down to force co operation. Instead, either give one of the partners a different power, or just give both partners two beams.
Summing up Pid, it's really fun if you are normally really precise with your movement. The story is engaging and charming, and if you can part with half your power to enjoy the game with another human, then more power to you!

Before you start playing this game, don't be confused, LOCAL multiplayer is really it's strong suit. Now I don't have many hours played on my account, but I've played this game plenty on a friend's, and it really is an excellent game.
It's definitely a game of skill. No outside forces are going to impact whether or not you come out the victor, it's simply you against your opponent, and occasionally taking advantage of your surroundings. The swordplay is easy to get used to but hard to master, and when you snap the neck of an enemy that's on the ground, it's amazingly satisfying. The visuals are a retro style done right, and the music and sound effects make the game come alive. One of the best local multiplayer experiences I've ever had.
However, connections with online multiplayer seem to be giving other people problems. (I don't have experience with this myself, as I've only played it locally) so if this is a turn-off for you, keep that in mind.
If the local multiplayer experience is enough to warrant the $15 for you, go for it. If not, get the game on sale. One way or another, Don't pass up on this game.

I just started playing this game, as of this writing im about 16 hours in so as a new player what do I have to say about it? First of all it is very much like a Minecraft game, but better .... and worse. Second of all bear in mind this is an EA game so there are gonna be bugs.
How is this game better?
1) There are FAR more farming options vs minecraft
2) The graphics are more realistic vs MC
3) There are more tools and weapons
4) More animals
5) More realistic grow times for crops and trees
6) Breaking your leg (literally) takes time to heal (instead of instantaneous fix)
7) Really custom building, with furniture, kitchens, grills, the works!
8) The survival creatures after you arent made up beasts but real ones like boars and bears.
I could keep going on BUT ...
So how is this game worse then?
1) Your head clipping through objects/terrain
2) Really hard to find certain materials (but I think it's a bad seed in my case)
3) Micro-managing how certain things are done. IE grow hemp, turn it into fiber on the loom, then spin the fiber on the spinner wheel and then back to the loom to weave it into cloth, so you can make bandages. If you grow cotton instead you skip the first step of the loom but its still a long process just to make a leg splint/bandage.
4) The "caves" are basically sinkholes, almost a straight drop down in many cases, almost never gradual decline down, thank of a Chasm in MC but only 1/10 as wide if not a literall hole in the ground
5) Cooking meat requires a close watch lest you burn it (this is either a plus or minus depending on how you see it), easy to do on a cooking grill, much harder in a smoker as it only works with the lid closed.
6) You cant breed animals, so no everlasting supply of meat or byproducts like leather.
For the price it's definately worth playing as a MC alternative, I can see this game taking off when it gets out of EA, my only real gripe is that I cant make charcoal and I am forced to use coal for the smelter(finite vs infinite resource). I do look forward to the day I can cook an egg for breakfast rather than kill and eat a whole chicken though,

Nothing's gorily graphic, but nothing leaves much to the imagination either. Both practically and thematically, you are leading these girls to their dooms when you leave the path, but if you don't leave the path, they haven't ~lived~ or something. Anyway. It's by turns heavy-handed and nasty, the writing is more curlycue artsy-fartsy than terribly meaningful, and yet, and yet, and yet. There are some touches. The Path is certainly a different gaming experience. A modern, gothic take on the classic Red Riding Hood Tale that articulates the dark cautionary elements quite well in subtle ways.
The game has but one objective: Go to grandmother's. Upon doing so, this means you've somehow lost the game, so as it turns out, you are actually encouraged to disobey the rules, and adventure into the dark, dreary forest, interacting with objects in the woods, skipping freely, getting completely lost. Eventually, you, as one of six 'Red' girls, will find what represents the Wolf, in one of it's various incarnations.
Upon meeting the wolf, you are taken back to the path, completely desolate and somber as you tread quietly to grandmother's in the rain. There, grandmother's house is no longer a sweet old lady's cottage but an absolute mind-♥♥♥♥ where you die, but you technically succeed in the game.
While the game is completely open to interpretation, and is more art-focused, this reward of defeat, especially after a character has been presumably injured, molested, or otherwise attacked, raises a few questions, considering rather than being able to outsmart the wolf, once you are locked into the animation, there is no way of fighting back. You essentially play 6 victims. Again, this is more of an artistic form of story telling, but it still raises a few questions.
Overall, visually, the game is appropriately sharp and goregous with a bit of an aesthetic to intice gamer-cult followings, and the soundtrack is fascinating and at times intensley dark. With so many themes and theories out there, this is a game for anyone who's looking for a different gaming experience, or for someone starting out in indie gaming. Or, simply for anyone into either gothic things or fairy tales.

This game looks and feels like a freemium mobile game, (albiet one that rips off WoW's art style,) but the mindless repetitive gameplay is far less of an asset to a full PC game where the game needs to sustain your full, undivided attention.
Story is essentially non-existant at this point with big "coming soon" signs, but given the genre, the story is typically an excuse plot, anyway.  You're four random strangers that met at a bar and are killing bigger and bigger orcs for their pies and loot with a slightly higher +something. Oh, and you probably have to do it to save the world because the darn world always needs saving.
Gameplay is paint-by-numbers dungeon crawling. You start with 4 heroes of 4 classes, and you know exactly what four, because they're the same D&D started off with.  You will find absolutely nothing of interest in chracter-building (they are only now even working on having the ability to name your new characters "by popular request") or in combat, which mostly amounts to spamming the basic attacks or the one skill you upgraded to max mindlessly. Skills are purchased for gold, but "talent points" are used to upgrade skills, although the interface for this is (apparently intentionally) terribly uninformative. Given the nature of the game, you pretty much pick one skill you like and max it out.  With one talent point per level and 5 linearly-improving points to sink into each talent, you basically only make a real choice every 5 levels since this sort of game gives zero incentive not to min-max.  Respecing used to cost money or take "quests" but now just takes "quests".
"Quests" in this game are arbitrary things that pop up as you enter the dungeon.  (I'm not sure if I'd praise it for streamlining the process if they weren't going to make quest choice meaningful or not, but I'm sure quest givers are "coming soon" as well.) Given the limited number of ways you can interact with this dungeon, and how you have almost no control over what you fight, the "quests" basically amount to "kill the things you were going to kill anyway, and you'll get some of the special game currency from back when this was freemium".
Loot is pretty much straight Diablo-style.  Common drops have base stats for a given tier, but color-coded uncommons, rares, and yes, even purple "epic" equipment have additional bonuses to random stats.
Dungeons are just a bunch of random square rooms that eventually lead to a stairwell up which, in sheer game logic, gives you the option to exit, as well.  The game claims it has "roguelike" mechanics, but all it really has is procedural dungeon layouts, and even that is moot because dungeons are so featureless that they might as well be drawing "encounters" from a deck of cards, and do away with the concept of space, entirely.
In essence, there's nothing here other games at this price point don't do better.  Look at these other games, which have every feature this game has, plus have more innovative features, plus better game balance, are around the same price, and are old enough to go on sale and be cheaper (Paper Sorcerer is $5 even before a sale, and a far more deep game!):
Or go for
, which realized its rut and actually tried to reinvent itself to a fair degree of success.
For that matter, get a DS or a Vita, and play the dozens of Wizardry clones like the Etrian Odyssey series (at least, past the first game...) or the like where at least being mindless and repetitive is an advantage on a mobile device.

Dawn of war II was a game that I really wanted to work for me, it never did. I spent around $25 buying the Grand Master Collection, only because I am a massive fan of the original DoW. I think what I expected was a DoW with better graphics, mechanics, factions and units. What I got was something I wish, never was.
I got a Dawn of War title that had no base building, fewer factions and units that feel almost bullet spongey. I dont like the art style even though the graphics are not the worst, but the game drops like a rock in terms of performance in some situations and I have a semi decent rig. The overall feel seems much different and has a very slow feel to it, even though it's going for fast paced.
Now I'm not the only one that feels this way, one of my friends feels the exact same, and he wishes the game was more like DoW 1. We where hyped that DoW III had base building but that didn't work out to well either.
I feel kind of alone In this situation because everyone (besides me and said friend) seems to like it. So the point of this is if you're like me and just wanted more of what DoW 1 had to offer, don't buy it. if you don't expect the orignal and you want it for the lore and universe, buy it, you'll probobly enjoy it..
Otherwise I'd definitely stick with the original DoW, and if you already own it, buy one of the many expansion packs/DLC.

The Shrouded Isle is a very intrguing game.  The game is an interstingly managment game where you have five traits and five houses to keep satisfied while sacrficing a villager.
The inqury stage gives 0-2 inquries of virtiues and vices  or reveals of for each family dempending on their favor. Rebellious - 0 Dissatisified - 0 netural -1 satisfied -1 zealous -2
If a family is rebellious and are not placiated be the next season they will kill you.
The other traits are vaues of the town: Ignorance, fervor, discpline, pentince, and obdeience. These traits are affected by the various families though other charchters' vices and virtues affect them as well.
After the inqury advisory selection,there is the task selection, it can be a balancing act of trying to discovery vices and virtues, while raising certain traits. The fewer tasks you assgin the greater the affect of family morale and the increase or decrease the traits.
All of this comes together to quite a challegne to keep from losing in tweleve turns and when you lose you get the feeling like you know how to do better,so you play again.

TRAUMA is one of those games where you can't really call it a "Game" since there's no actual gameplay. It's more like an interactive short film about someone's psyche. It reminded me a lot of Dear Esther, which I also recommended. TRAUMA is a point and click game where you discover the meaning of this woman's dreams, and event's in her life that may impact her dream. It does it's job well, as all four locations feel like a lucid dream.
Keep in mind this game is definitely not for everyone. It's not a point-and-click adventure game in the since of The Walking Dead or Sam and Max. Most hardcore gamers would probably be turned off at the lack of gameplay and deviation from the norm of most modern games.
Even the story itself is pretty vague, most of it is left to the player's interpretation. But it's uniqueness is what I liked about this. If you're looking for something to wrap your brain around, or are just looking for something different I'd say give this one a try.

My only critique is that the game is fairly easy to win, and there's really only one strategy that the game rewards (i.e., try to keep everything in balance). Still, it was a very enjoyable experience and I highly recommend it!

I was extremely excited to see a new take on the first person stealth game through the eyes of a goblin. It was a great idea, awesome graphics, good story. Unfortunately as I started playing I realized the controls were not optimal for the PC but it was still a good layout.
Greatest weakness of the game lies in controllability and common sense. Here are examples:
1. While on the edge of a balcony - you figure Styx being the awsome goblin that he is *should* be able to just drop down and grab the ledge the same way he climbed up with the option of pressing the E. -No it's not possible- Instead he walks off to his doom.
2. I understand he is small... but does he have to get stuck under a small ledge on the wall (possibily even a glitch with the wall) and cannot jump? I mean it's only 2 inches out of the wall.
3. He carries a knife (awesome). Takes more than 2 seconds to slice open a guy's throat. Wasting valuable game time.
4. Controls are slugish and if you're a wall there's a chance Styx can't respond at all.
Sorry guys- played an total of two hours trying to give this game a fighting chance. I can't take it anymore it's just too painful.

If my Heart Had Wings is a romance game about a high school glider club known as the "Soaring Club." Styx has many flaws: dated graphics, clipping issues, inconsistent AI and lame dialogue (story eventually gets interesting, but dialogue never does). This will be enough for a lot of people to dismiss it out right. I did enjoy my time with it a great deal for the following reason: levels are huge and well designed, filled with opportunities for exploration and alternate paths, and enemy placement that requires a lot of thinking to get through. This is where a stealth game must make its stand and it's where Styx shines. For that alone, stealth fans should give it a chance. Also, mechanics are well implemented, with enough variation in your tools to keep things interesting, and side missions and collectibles add to the fact that you'll spend a lot of time on each level. Thankfully, this one also has quicksaves.
Yes, you'll go through each level twice in the campaign. However, you'll start in different points and face different enemies the second time around, so the levels won't feel the same, which is a testament to the quality of its design.
In the end, even considering its flaws (which can mostly be blamed on the fact that this is a budget title), I spent nearly 40 hours completing Styx (side missions and collectibles included) and enjoyed my time with it. Stealth fans shouldn't miss it.

Nidhogg is a digital expression of the innate human instinct to take pointy things and stick them into someone else's gut. The goal of the game is hilariously simple: stab/brawl/sprint your way to the other side of the map and get eaten by a large worm as a reward. Yes, it's that ridiculous.
Yet, this straightforward game design brings to the table an adrenaline-pumping multiplayer experience with its rapid pace and tense back-and-forth action. Clashes between players often end in spectacular splatters of LSD-esque, trippy-coloured blood across the arena, with plenty of laughter in the process.
A perfect way to settle a dispute with a friend or a family member, the only downside to Nidhogg is its price tag, for the game has a meagre 4 maps to choose from, making it slightly overpriced for its limited content. Overall, Nidhogg is a good game, but it should only be purchased when it's on sale. Have at ye!

The Path can be compared to walking in a gallery with ugly modern "art", or listening to some very dissonant "music". Disgusting and revolting, pretentious piece of crap. And no, I don't think I'm missing "the point" of the "game". I regret spending money on it, and if it were possible, I'd give anti-money to its creators (I'd give 20 $ so that they can lose 20 $).
What's the gameplay and the setting? Basically you walk through a boring, endless forest with disgusting colour palette, terrible graphical filters and scratched words with illegible annoying font going across the screen for no reason. There are a couple of cut-scenes that can be triggered in the forest, there's a metaphor for taking risks in life (straying from the path that leads little red riding hood to granny's house), and a metaphor for how life rapes you in the end no matter what you do.
I felt dirty after playing this, I wanted to take a shower multiple times, it was such a disgusting experience. No gameplay, no meaningful story (except for some lousy metaphors I mentioned above), ugly, unpleasant to the senses on a very visceral level, nauseating, pretentious, artsy-fartsy, irrational, waste of time. I even wonder if I should write this review - it may attract attention and make people wonder "is it really that bad", thus making them give money to the creators of this abomination and losing hours of their life on something that cannot be unseen.
Guys, make no mistake, I like indie games, dark games, depressing games, I like intelligent sophisticated games with a message and unique ideas or perspective. Trust me, this isn't the case here, this is the worst "game" I have ever seen in my whole life.

Please note that The Path may not be everyone's cup of tea. It's not what some would consider a "game", but more of a story shrouded by symbolism and is incredibly artsy. If you hate games that are almost purely story driven and more of an experience, then you might want to look elsewhere.
For a person like me, The Path is just the type of thing I love. Not only is there dark and mature themes, but the symbolism is absolutely brilliant if you notice them. I also enjoyed the "Red Riding Hood" theme the game had going for it. After replaying a few times and discussing the story with others, I realized the game is actually very open for a lot of interpretation. More so than I anticipated. The ideas that many have come up with have only enriched the experience for me.
Basically, you have several sisters, each very different from each other, and their goal is to get to grandmothers house to deliver some goods. The rule is to not stray from the path, but it has to be broken in order for the girls to encounter the wolf. If you do not want to be spoiled or have my opinion on the wolves and their interpretation with each girl, please skip the next paragraph.
In my opinion, each girl represents a stage of life. The wolves are an experience that one must go through to grow up. These experiences may be harmful or scarring, but like in the game, the girls get up, wounded, and make their way back to grandma's house. The whole story is about growing up. Letting your curiousity getting the better of you, getting wounded, but growing up a little. The path is a safe life without exploration. There is no harm, but neither do you learn anything. That is why you get a failure screen when you do not encounter the wolf.
As for it's length, if you just buzz through the main task at hand, it is very short and you also miss a lot of added story. Each girl has items and unlockables. There is also 144 "flower coins" to collect if you so chose. In my opinion, the replay value only lasts as long as there is something that you missed, which just to note that the forest is randomly generated each time so finding everything will be a challange if you switch girls or start over. Unless you are the type that enjoys resetting the game and starting fresh repeatedly, you probably will complete the game once and rarely touch it again.

Having played and completed the original Faerie Solitaire, the Remastered version has vastly improved on many problems the original version had. For those considering getting this game, it is very similar to the card game Tripeaks, but with pets to collect and powerups to be purchased and used (with the in-game currency called Pure).
In the original, collecting all the eggs was an immense hurdle and luck-based grind. In my opinion, this was not an enjoyable grind because you were not guaranteed when you would get an egg, if you would get an egg. They have fixed this in the Remastered version by adding a fail-safe to how long you can go without an egg appearing, while greatly improving the drop rate on eggs.
The Challenge Mode in the original was very similar to the Story Mode, just more difficult. The developer has created a brand new Challenge Mode entirely for the new Remastered edition; implementing new mechanics, obstacles, and puzzling patterns to overcome.
The game is having some infrequent crashing issues at the moment (roughly every hour of play), but the creator of the game is actively in the Discussion Forums on Steam reading these crash reports. He/She is also listening to suggestions and feedback, and reply to them with what they think (which is great).
The original does have Steam Achievements while this one does not, but that is a feature which is promised to come soon. I'd strongly recommend purchasing this game for $9.99. I received this product for free because everyone who purchased the original Faerie Solitare before the release was given the Remastered edition -- While it was a fantastic and much appreciated gesture, it played no part in my positive review. I like the game for the game, not because it was given.

Have you ever dreamt of being the head cultist and spiritual leader of a small post-apocalyptic village, working to awaken your great patron-god, Chernobog? Was your dream colored in Lovecraftian greens?
No? You’ve no clue what I’m talking about? Well, I can’t say I blame you.
That's the Shrouded Isle, a game with this exact premise. It’s a bit more complex than picking a villager and ending their life; each one has minor or major virtues and vices, which affect you in positive and negative ways, respectfully. Each run of the game is broken up in 12 seasons–it takes place during 3 years– during which you have to sacrifice 12 of your fellow villagers.
The villagers, there’s thirty of them, and none come from the most distinct genetic material; each is a member of one of five families, whose primarchs control some different suppression apparatus — the Iosefka family is in charge of the fervor in the village by building monuments and spreading the holy word of Chernobog’s imminent return, the Kegnni make sure that your villagers remain proper and ignorant, and so on and so forth.
It’s a game about information, and acting upon it. During each season, you’ve got three months to vote on the activities your cultists make. While you’ve got five councilors — one from each esteemed family on your shrouded isle — you can pick to work on one to three of your councilors’ activities each month; the more the activities worked on, the lesser are the returns for you. It’s a perfectly logical system that allows you to discover more about your villagers’ vices and virtues at only a small cost.
Vices and virtues are also found out by inquiries, of which you will get some, as long as you’re in good standing with the different houses; it’s always difficult to decide whom to use your first couple of inquiries, on account of knowing virtually nothing other than some cursory flavor text, give n to you by the house leaders whenever you scroll over the members of the family.
shroudedisle1
Villagers and the five attributes of the entire village–Ignorance, Fervor, Discipline, Penitence and Obedience–are not the only ones you have to be on the lookout for; each house also has an approval rating that raises when you continually vote for their advisers, and falls whenever you ignore them. Approval also plummets whenever you decide to sacrifice someone; particularly if you have no proof, or even an idea, of an advisor’s transgressions.
‘This might all seem like a lot to follow, and I did have some difficulty making sense of it all during my first game; which is why one of the families quickly rose in revolt, and did me in, thus ending playthrough #01. That said, once I began all over again, it made sense and, in less than two hours, I stood above the precipice, awakening good old ‘bog and watching him as he stretched those holy wings of his.
The Shrouded Isle is all about revealing information one month at a time, and using that information to the fullest. There’s no overarching storyline, when one really could’ve worked quite well.The art-style is good but minimalist, and there are about…eight screens in the game overall, with an additional three-four cutscenes.
It’s entertaining for what it is…but I’m not certain that it’s worth the price tag of 10 euro. That has to be its biggest weakness; the Isle simply doesn’t have enough content. After my two and a half hours, I have absolutely no desire to go back and replay it in its current form; if the developers introduce a content-focused patch, perhaps I will.
The Shrouded Isle is an interesting experiment that’s built around a cool concept, strong aesthetics and ambiance, but hobbled by lack of variety and lacking a cohesive story.
Should you play it? Only you could say that, and I hope to have provided all the tools necessary to help with your decision. Happy Gaming!
PS: I know there are different endings–but I didn’t feel curious enough to spend another few hours unlocking them.

Oh wow, a story! It's mostly for kicks, but at least it gave me a reason to play (as sarcastic as that sounds, I actually mean it. I feel like there was a point to all that).
The research system is fantastic. It may look daunting to the first-timer, but once I got used to it, I started to wish it was even bigger. As it is, it's good.
While I'm sure it's meant as part of its aesthetics, the battle environments always look... sterile and off-putting. I would have liked to see some daytime areas, forests, cities. Maybe more weather effects like rain and snow outside of X-mas. Instead we get... rocks. And more rocks. In pale pastel colors. Add to that an ever-present, pointless dim spotlight effect which makes everything look dull and dim. On every stage. It's a fun game, but borderline unappealing and somewhat hard on the eyes.
I'm not sure if I was playing it correctly, but I had difficulty setting up towers along paths, as creeps would invariably destroy those towers (not including the creeps that specifically go for towers). In any case, it didn't matter in the end, as I found that on most maps I could just make a super defense perimeter around the base and nothing would get past it except for boss monsters, in which case, all that required was a second set of towers attacking the boss right away.
The automatic difficulty scaling could use some work. Once you get the hang of the game, you'll quickly start to rake in funds. But if you do too well (+50k in funds), the game gives you zilch next stage. It feels like it's punishing you for doing well, and even without looking it up, I could tell the game was "cheating" by doing that.
Out of all the Puppygames, I regard this one as the best. It's not frustrating, it's not brutally hard, has a good length, several game modes, and even the stages I failed it didn't remain failed for long.

The Shrouded Isle is a a simple to play, moderately difficult to master strategy game that centers around discovery, and resource managememt. Your resources being virtues, and house loyalty. I am certain one could just ignore the evil God and simply manage the resources and make it through the seasons well enough. But, I don't like playing it that way. I like to track down all the "major sinners". This is more challenging.
The trick to this game is understanding what vices lead to what major sins. When you get the message from God he gives you a target, he also ramps up one of your virtues and forces you to keep that higher than the others. The trick to finding the target is knowing which base vice results in the sin he detests. Each citizen has a virtue and a vice. Some are minor, and some are major. The trick is to utilize the folks with major virtues and eliminate the ones with major vices as the God dictates. So you will want to inquire about the folks with those base vices (like unrepentent for example) and herd them up so you can uncover the major sinner that season. This is while balancing your virtues and making sure they don't get too low.
There's plenty of strategy to be had in this simple little game for for those who like to do simple logic with resource management, it is a pretty fun game. Don't expect loads of weapons and units, it isn't that kind of game. But do expect some fun game play in this simple setting. If you just want to blow through and get to the end you can do that, but if you want to ferret out the sinners while you manage your resources you get a lot more fun out of this game.

Styx has many flaws: dated graphics, clipping issues, inconsistent AI and lame dialogue (story eventually gets interesting, but dialogue never does). This will be enough for a lot of people to dismiss it out right. I did enjoy my time with it a great deal for the following reason: levels are huge and well designed, filled with opportunities for exploration and alternate paths, and enemy placement that requires a lot of thinking to get through. This is where a stealth game must make its stand and it's where Styx shines. For that alone, stealth fans should give it a chance. Also, mechanics are well implemented, with enough variation in your tools to keep things interesting, and side missions and collectibles add to the fact that you'll spend a lot of time on each level. Thankfully, this one also has quicksaves.
Yes, you'll go through each level twice in the campaign. However, you'll start in different points and face different enemies the second time around, so the levels won't feel the same, which is a testament to the quality of its design.
In the end, even considering its flaws (which can mostly be blamed on the fact that this is a budget title), I spent nearly 40 hours completing Styx (side missions and collectibles included) and enjoyed my time with it. Stealth fans shouldn't miss it.

Total rewrite of the review.
I will begin with my own thoughts about the game. The singleplayer campaign is absolutely amazing, wish I had more time to play it during the days. The skirmish is very meh, the heroes are bland and the loot even more so. Wish the loot system during multiplayer skirmishes were a tad more like WC3 where mobs dropped loot/equipment when you killed them rather than running around in the starting gear and only buying potions. Something to give the MP battles a bit more variation. I've encountered a few bugs, but no gamebreaking ones, probably since they're fixed by the time I reach them.
I would personally recommend this game at this moment (12-12-2017) and give the players a few words of warning regarding your own hero: Strength 2h is a waste, if you want to go 2h, the dex alternatives are much better due to the high crit. Strength only gives block which is quite a waste, and casters are generally stronger as the protagonist, especially since all the followers have great personal skilltrees that support their maintrees.
There are a lot of negative reviews regarding bugs on this game, though it was something to be expected. Not a single release of Spellforce has been that playable on release, but every release of spellforce are amazing at their end stages with all expansions and fixes. Generally, games released nowadays have tons of gamebreaking bugs and other problems at release, but the sheer force this game has faced makes me a bit stunned, they seem to lack the devoted fanbase most established gaming companies have. Divinity 2, if you spoke to one character, you were unable to continue the game. The servers totally crashed at release and you couldn't play the perfect Co-op game at release. TW:W2, especially ME... a total bugfest. Most Ubisoft and EA titles are famous for their releasebugs. Betheshda has also gotten quite the bad rep recently.
Games nowadays are huge, especially from a coding perspective, and with publishers biting at their necks, companies really don't have the time or possibility to fix all of those, the worst case being the latest Heroes of Might and Magic.
We as consumers have a right to be angry or annoyed with all these problems, but the main culprits are most of the time the publishers and the gosh darn release dates.
I believe this game will be even better than Spellforce II as a finished product(as I mentioned earlier, spellforce II was horrible at release), and am eagerly awaiting all patches and expansions(or dlc's that it is nowadays).

I gotta admit I gave the Beta a negative review and if I judged the game again from a Spellforce veteran's point of view, I still would. But this wouldn't be fair because for anyone who loves RTS and RPG.... WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR? But if you're a Spellforce veteran like me who even replayed part of the 1st game only a few months ago, you should read the cons and pros first before buying the game. I'm not gonna judge every element due to my quite limited playtime so far, this wouldn't be fair, just some general elements of the game.
Pros:
+ awesome graphics (honestly that's the biggest pro of this game, it really is AWESOME and this game should still look great in 5 years! so please bring some expansions!!)
+ great atmosphere
+ nice music
+ tons to discover and I really mean it. I've spent so much time on maps just to discover every corner for a hidden sidequest or some loot
o not able to judge the story yet, so far it looks interesting (3rd mission)
Cons:
- worker & sector system... by far the WORST thing of this game. you cannot control your workers freely anymore like in normal RTS titles, instead you can construct anytime anywhere but only in your sector and workers will just move there magically to build it. once finished, you can assign a number of workers to the building. you see the workers, but cant control them directly. and if you wanna build somewhere on the map, you first have to conquer the sector (the whole map is divided into e.g. 10 sectors). this whole system feels cheap and gives you artificial limits. i don't want to play the settlers, i want to play AoE!
- sth which also annoys me is Grimlore Games' new interpretation of the Spellforce universe. Since you're mostly revisiting old maps like Greyfell, Liannon and Leafshade, you'd think that you would recognize them.... but you don't. Greyfell is still a city on a mountain but its layout/shape, color of the walls and w/e are completely different. Plus the maps are much smaller, I really wouldnt mind the longer loading times if they were bigger. and then you visit Leafshade which is a freaking jungle with palms and stuff and an elven city. elves living in the jungle? i know they like trees and stuff but usually they live in "normal" forests, dont they? i have never seen in any movie or game elves living in a jungle, they're not amazons... they also behave too much human-like, usually elves are mysterious and proud people but during my encounter in leafshade they behave like drunkards using vulgar language, it's just not very elves-like...
- dwarfs? trolls? dark elves? exist (at least trolls and dwarfs) but can't play them. please bring an expansion, I really miss them, especially the dwarfs. right now u can only play orcs, humans and elves and ull meet some indivuals who are trolls/dwarfs...
- races are sadly quite similiar. they all have more or less the same buildings with some exceptions at the last tier, same goes for the units but everyone has like 2-3 special units. in Spellforce 1 races didnt have any similiar units at all, they were all quite differently. But I guess SF3 wants to hop on the eSport train although I doubt that's gonna work.
- the fighting animations look quite bad. I guess after the awesome graphics there was no more money to implement some decent animations. at least the heroes should have good ones.
After all these cons you probably wonder why I still give a positive review. Well, if you don't know Spellforce 1+2, I definitely recommend the game. If you do, I might wait for the 1st expansion (which hopefully will come) and then decide again. Or wait for a Spellforce 1 Remeasterd if that is ever gonna happen.
Oh btw the graphics are awesome.

Oh my gosh! I love this game! You can play together on public worlds, or by yourself. You can play Creative where building is super easy and you don't have to worry about dying, and being creative is your only concern.
Or, you can play survival and explore and work at staying alive by eating and drinking and not getting killed by bears and wolves and stuff like that.
There are lots of different blocks, which you can make with a block bench. There's furniture, doors, decoration, etc. In the sawbench, some general stuff in the workbench, and clothes, shoes, and accessories in the loom.
You can mine ores, customize your profile (change what you look like), you can wear different clothes, customize your home with lights and furniture. You can plant fruits and veggies, grow trees, etc. You can fly in creative mode, and depending on the settings for single player, you can fly in survival mode, too, using F2. Really, the possibilities are endless, it's all up to you how you live your Rising World life! And you can make as many worlds as you want! Some might be public, some might be private. Some might be creative, some might be survival. You can name your world's whatever you want (not, though, that you cannot rename a world once it's already created), decide on what creatures there are and how likely you are to find ores! And dungeons! Dungeons are one of my favorite parts of the game! In caves you might find old stone buildings, which are dungeons. They might be really big, or really small. I've found some of both. But they all have several chambers, maybe some corridors and staircases. But in each chamber is a chest with stuff in it! And old bones are also a common occurrence.
Anyway, this is really long, but I hope you find this helpful. I highly recommend this game!

The game features a decent campaign with scenarios set in very detailed locations. The skirmish mode and online multiplayer both only have six maps and three races with very slight differences in build order. The interface comes with some handy features, like a larger mini-map that displays resource locations in each sector and single hotkeys used to cast spells from each hero. Resources (wood, food, stone, iron) are automatically gathered from the environment by workers assigned to a particular building; managing the limited number of workers at each building is part of the economic strategy. Upgrading the city or outpost will unlock the next tier of structures and increase the worker population. New map sectors can be captured after eliminating the creeps contained therein; while new sectors can expand resource production, items must be physically transported from one outpost to another (all done automatically), so you can destroy caravans of other factions. Heroes cast spells, gain experience through combat to unlock new spells, and have an inventory to increase stats. Regular units contain the usual assortment of infantry, cavalry, and ranged options. Units die quickly, which gives less time to use spells during combat. There is also a lot of grind at the end of games to eliminate bases, as defenses are cheap and very effective against smaller number of units. Still, SpellForce 3 has some good ideas in the economic side of the game with worker allocation and resource acquisition that, along with the occasional role-playing feature, make it stand out in the real-time strategy genre.

IMHHW is a visual novel that follows the life of a boy name Aoi after returning to his old home town. He mets some old friends and makes some new ones after being given the position of a dorm mother at an all girls off campus house. Throughout the game you make several choices which impact which path you take, as well as alter the ending.
This was my first visual novel after reading Katawa Shoujo. In all honesty I have mixed feelings about it. The introduction and mid-story was very pleasing and kept my interested, but the late-story and ending kind of left me hanging (more so than Katawa Shoujo). I personally don't like open endings because I want to see how things truely ended, but it might appeal to some people.
The soundtrack is amazing, the voice overs add a nice touch, animated cutscenes and images added in to really expand on certain scenes 100% made the game that much more enjoyable.
All in all I'd give it a 8/10, and again the only reason I'm not giving it a higher score is because of my personal opinion on the ending.

As of the posting most of the dungeons are not very complex, by far the best dungeon is the fish shaped one (number 5).  It is less linear than the other dungeons and makes you solve a maze to get through (albeit a simple one).  The final dungeon was difficult but not impossible and it still allowed for more surprises from the developer.
Using a shotgun to fight definitely takes some practice because of the random spread and how it doesn't knock enemies away like swords do in other games.  However the shotgun mechanic creates a good risk/reward situation everytime you engage an enemy.  Another good thing to see is that the NPCs will defend themselves if you attack them.  And it will hurt when they fight back.
When I have seen problems with the game, the developer was quick to fix any issues like crashes or problem areas.  For example I commented that when you get a rim fragment it shouldn't teleport you to the entrance of the dungeon becuase there might still be things in the place you need to collect. The Path is the only game from developer, Tale of Tales, that I thoroughly enjoy. If I had to narrow it down as to why that is, it would be due to the extremely mature themes and musical dissonance, combined with the exploration of the forest. Each item you find is unique to the character you play and, upon discovery, your character will interact with the object and an image will be superimposed over the screen, as if it were a memory.
There are six characters in all, each with their own unique locations and encounters with the wolf. Once your encounter with the wolf has been made you are left on the path, in the pouring rain, heading for your grandmother's house one last time. Upon arrival your character experiences their final nightmare and you are returned to the home screen to choose the next playable character.
The music and sound design is what becomes most dissonant in The Path. The off-tune choir of girls singing, mixed with an assortment of synths playing to heavy chains clanking in the background. It's all very unsettling.
The Path focuses on very serious themes without directly implying what has happened. If you find the topics of♥♥♥♥♥♥and child abuse horrifying then I advise you not to play this game. Nothing explicit is shown, it is merely suggested. It is up to you to put the pieces together.

So, I love old school dungeon crawlers, starting from days of the Wizardry series and Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord.  I've played every American Wizardry game and many of the Japanese ones.  I've played the old school Bard's Tales and Might & Magic games.  I say that so as to give you perspective on my review.
Visuals: These are always hit or miss for me.  I have a growing dislike of 'photo-realistic' graphics in games, so the slightly old-school/cartoony feel of the graphics is just about right for me in a 3D game.  Some of the animation is a little rough, but not in any way that detracts from the game for me. 4/5
Gameplay: For the most part this game is what I long for in a simple, old school dungeon crawler.  Explore the dungeon(Tower), kill bad guys, get loot.  There are, however, some downsides.  These, mostly, are centered around the free-to-play aspects.  For instance, inability to create a full party from the start, having to buy more bag space, etc.  These are not deal breakers, but they go to a trend in gaming that I don't like, false dificulty.  Challenge me with gameplay, not pay walls.  That said, those things haven't yet become game breaking or deal breaking, and can also be purchased with the in-game gold, which is a nice option for those of us that don't want to pay for micro transactions. Another thing I miss/haven't encountered are puzzles, secret doors, or some of the other standard Dungeon Crawl tropes.  If they are in the game, i just haven't found them yet, otherwise, i think the game misses out on something. I give it a tentative 3/5, 4/5 if the microtransactions remain unneeded to progress in the game.
Music/audio: I just stopped playing a few minutes ago, and I can't recall either the music or sound effects.  That could be because they aren't memorable or because the only thing I can hear is the sound of my sick elderly cat wheeze/snoring beside me.  ?/5 until I can play without the old windbag next to me.
Overall: The game is great fun, but definately has the Early Access feeling of an unpolished game.
