Dawn of War 2 is a tactical-action title that almost holds its own weight with the help of the excellent Warhammer 40,000 backdrop but is not without many flaws. I'll focus on the problems during my review and close with why I was close to giving it a positive rating.
First off, let's clear that this isn't a real-time strategy game but a real-time tactical one. During your missions, you're not allowed to build units, change equipment, gather resources, etc. Whatever little real strategy there is to it, boils down to "should I grind some more or fallback to my base to recover and redeploy" - the kind of thing you're faced with when you're in a dungeon in an JRPG deciding if you better go back to town or drive forth. Safe to say, that's not real strategy but a barebones layer on top of what is extensively an action game in our case here.
That being said, the tactical aspect of the game, which is beyond doubt the core gameplay for DoW2 is also really shallow. I've heard the cover system, garrison system, retreat system, minimal deployment and other things being highly praised for this game but however I don't find any of it particularly interesting, engaging or challenging. This is my first foray into the franchise and I started playing on hard and I've failed a mission once so far, everything being as easy as a walk in the park for me. Whatever tactical merit is here boils down to using your unit's abilities at the right moment and that's about it. Some specific cases and boss fights go a step beyond that but, even though they're spread well enough to keep you entertained, they're all forgettable and formulaic.
The UI is a bit of a mess and largely mouse driven. Using the keyboard is helpful but in a limited way as each ability is assigned its own key instead of your current MOBAs and MMOs QWER fixed layout - meaning that either you'll have to remember dozens of key presses or (like me) just a few favorites and restrict yourself to using those most of the time, which seems to does the trick. It's a shame though since with different loadouts there are dozens of abilities on the game and I'm always ignoring those in favor of passive bonuses since I just know that I'll never wrap my head around all the options available at any given point between the four squards the game offers per mission.
On top the shallow-but-fun tactical clickfest, the mission design is very awkward. Defense missions make a bit more sense but for the majority of the game you'll be infiltrating areas and trying to reach one or more objectives. What makes it so odd is that the entire map could easily overcome you 10-to-1 but even with the future technology of the 41st millenium or psychic link of tyranids and eldars, they still will let you take the map at your own pace while you (repeteadly) fall back to recover your troop strength from time to time - not only that but if you fall back, your enemies won't even bother to follow pursuit, meaning that approaching one objetive by coming in, killing a few, retreating to heal then killing another few ad aeternum is not only a viable but also necessary option much of the time! It's hard on your suspension of disbelief and it's mildly insulting to the 40K lore that drives the game.
Outside the main gameplay which are your tactical-level, real-time, fast-paced missions, there is also a more turn-based gameplay out of combat, which is processed in days. You can think of it as a predecessor to the modern XCom titles (without the base-building aspect) or Starcraft 2's single-player mode where you mostly configure your units and choose which missions to go next. It's pretty barebones but it works fine. The story, characters and voice acting is passable but don't overstay their welcome either, being mostly a breather from the action phase. The cutscenes and overall presentation of the game is well to my liking but those players used to latest generation graphics may find it outdated at this point.
The missions are mostly repetitive and as you can see there are few highlights to mention overall on this game. What are the high points here then? First, it's a good enough game and is very entertaining despite not being terribly inspired or well executed. Second, the Warhammer 40,000 setting in itself is a huge boost for the game in general, which is obvious by how solid the game feels between units, factions, lore, themes, etc. I'm a long time fan of the franchise and even though this doesn't give me a full 40K boner, it is, if nothing else, a mediocre translation of the vast source material and it's renowned fame into a fast-paced, somewhat shallow action video game.
The main reason why I'd recommend this game for is, if you, like me, can get it on a Steam sale  for 75% off with both expansions included. That's the type of value you just can't argue with if you think you can play through the entire thing - base game and expansion. It's definitely enjoyable enough to binge on for a few hours at a time. Would I recommend it at full price? Absolutely not.

The Shrouded Isle is a a simple to play, moderately difficult to master strategy game that centers around discovery, and resource managememt. Your resources being virtues, and house loyalty. I am certain one could just ignore the evil God and simply manage the resources and make it through the seasons well enough. But, I don't like playing it that way. I like to track down all the "major sinners". This is more challenging.
The trick to this game is understanding what vices lead to what major sins. When you get the message from God he gives you a target, he also ramps up one of your virtues and forces you to keep that higher than the others. The trick to finding the target is knowing which base vice results in the sin he detests. Each citizen has a virtue and a vice. Some are minor, and some are major. The trick is to utilize the folks with major virtues and eliminate the ones with major vices as the God dictates. So you will want to inquire about the folks with those base vices (like unrepentent for example) and herd them up so you can uncover the major sinner that season. This is while balancing your virtues and making sure they don't get too low.
There's plenty of strategy to be had in this simple little game for for those who like to do simple logic with resource management, it is a pretty fun game. Don't expect loads of weapons and units, it isn't that kind of game. But do expect some fun game play in this simple setting. If you just want to blow through and get to the end you can do that, but if you want to ferret out the sinners while you manage your resources you get a lot more fun out of this game.
If you've ever "rubbed one out" this game is for you, plus it's fun, you really feel the "panic" of being caught. It's cheap, so why not buy it?

Styx: Master of shadows has you playing a goblin in a stealth action setting similar to thief except minus the stealing things part and plus a lot to murdering everything. The storyline is interesting and the devs do a good job with pushing the narriative along which is mainly what got me through the whole game. Also the MC has a very tongue-in-cheek sarcastic view of the world and the dialogue/monologue has it's own brand of dark humor.
The stealth element of the game is absolutely central to the gameplay to the point where if you are discovered your chance of survival is very low especially if it's by two or more enemies. Normally in most stealth games this is not much of a problem because enemies are spaced out and have non-overlapping patrols, but in this game you will find areas to be VERY crowded, making traditional duck and weave navigation somewhat problematic. One of the mechanics, cloning (in which you make a duplicate of yourself with limited abilities) assists with this somewhat and even offers the chance when upgraded to set lethal traps for enemies. However, I found myself using it most of the time just to alert guards and get them to chase it so that I could pass areas in a reasonable amount of time. Most of the other abilities are somewhat useless. Invisibility costs A LOT of amber to use and only lasts a short while, and the combat skills are really only useful in 1v1 situations and don't help against hardened enemies like the knights or elves. So basically, you either pull entire rooms using your clone (easy & fast) or try and systematically eliminate targets until the way is clear (very very slow/difficult). Overall though, the crowdedness makes it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to stealth missions.
Speaking of the enemies, the AI is very quirky and patrols seem very easy to glitch. Sometimes a path that an enemy takes 3 times in a row suddenly differs on the 4th for no apparent reason. I would think this is a feature except it also does things like teleport around during alerts and some enemies will even get stuck in corners or between objects indefinitely (for no reason!).
The levels in this game are pretty huge, which seems like a truly impressive feat at first until you realize you spend the second half of the game backtracking all the way through them which I found to be kind of boring and a bit lazy design-wise. That being said, the overall design is nice and I would enjoy them more if it weren't for the last beef I have with this game: the controls.
Controlling your character in this game can be a literal nightmare if you decide to go running around in high places. Targeted jumps to wall sconces work maybe 80% of the time and if you don't have your camera and directional tilted the exact way you will miss by a fair margin. Performing safe falls (e.g. lowering yourself until you are hanging by your hands and then dropping) is almost entirely guesswork and you may find yourself accidentally climbing all the way back up, potentially exposing yourself to danger. Also the corner turning is very awkward and the corner kill feature isn't very obvious as to what distance you can do it at (more guesswork). Simply put, the controls for this game, while adequate, can be frustrating as hell in tense situations where every second matters.
Anyways, I _would_ recommend this game to someone if the devs were to fix the majority of my abovementioned gripes. Maybe even a fan-made patch could do it. In its current state though, I would recommend giving it a pass unless you are a die-hard fan of stealth games.

My morbid mission seems simple. Keep my village in shape (aka cowering) for three years (twelve game turns) so that we can appease the demon Chernobog and be ushered into the apocalypse whilst in his favour. The end is nigh, and as cult leader I must decide which villager to sacrifice each year. Sometimes that’s an easy choice. This young Cadwell was an artist, polluting minds with her creativity and we simply cannot have that. Sometimes I have only a few minor transgressors to choose from, yes, he asks too many questions and ugh, she seems to be sympathetic to others whilst this one likes reading books… but is that really punishable by death? Well.. someone has to go and I’m certainly not going to kill the Sadist, he’s working miracles!
You have to work out a delicate balance. You must keep each house happy or they will revolt, you must keep your five important stats balanced and of course most importantly, you must ensure you follow the dark whispers that Chernobog utters. Ignorance, fervor, discipline, penitence and obedience, you can’t be a good cult without all those in abundance. This is a dark, brooding and depressing Lovecraftian management simulation. The art is a simple monochrome aesthetic in three hues, each more ugly than the next. Delightfully ugly though, which really describes the game throughout. The music is jarringly appropriate and the overall atmosphere is one of evil and malevolence. That’s pretty impressive considering this is a 2D text management game with three colours and almost no animations. My 4 month old son is not very well at the moment and his grizzling cries as we sat together playing this game (another game for my “one handed mouse gameplay list”) added beautifully to the ambience.
Each turn has you choose 5 advisors from each house. From these five, someone will die. They will also be the ones who take actions for this turn so you must choose a careful balance to ensure that you have advisors who can meet your current status needs and to be sure to have a worthy sacrifice afterwards. Each house member has a perk and a vice – randomly generated. These start out hidden, then you get an idea for the category they’re in and finally unlock the specific trait. If your reputation with that house is high enough, you’ll get the option to discover a trait from someone, otherwise they can be randomly discovered whilst taking actions. After choosing your five, you begin the turn. You now have three months and must choose between one and three advisors to take their house action each turn. The aim is to balance everything perfectly – your stats and your reputation, through the months and years, whilst discovering who has the most murderable traits. What fun!
It does have one major flaw; a single game should last about an hour. You can complete the game and not “win” (get the good ending) and then start again, but once you’ve won once or twice and discovered most of the vices and experienced the events, this is going to have little replayability. With RNG involved, it’s possible to die a lot in the first year – or get a combination that makes the game seem easy. Getting “lucky” in this game could actually drastically decrease your playtime. I enjoyed the challenge at the start, but having played it for a few hours can get through one game quite quickly now.

One of my new favorite stealth games. The stealth gameplay is solid and the level design is well thought out. It would not be an exaggeration to say that there are hundreds of ways to complete each section. You are given the tools to complete each area, but how you choose to do so is completely up to you. The story kept me interested all the way through, and for those that have played Of Orcs and Men you'll enjoy to learn the backstory of the goblins and Styx.
The Goblin difficulty level can be a bit frustrating, but it is definitely satisfying when you do everything right. As stated before, there are many different paths you can take, so if you find one isnt working out repeatedly you can always think of some other approach. I'd reccommend playing it on that difficulty, as the action combat really isnt that great and I'd rather just die and load my game than have to deal with it.
Adding to the depth of the game is the skill system. As you progress you get points that can be used to unlock skills that are all fairly useful. You'll find as you go on that certain skills really mesh with how you like to play the game and you'll be using them frequently.
As you near the end of the game levels do become reused. I was disappointed with this at first, but the layout and type of npcs are radically different the second time around. I ended up finding paths I didnt even know existed as I tried to maneuver around the level. I never felt like I was just repeating the same thing like in other games that do this back tracking.
All in all it's a very fun game and I'd reccommend it to anyone that enjoys stealth games that actually WANT you to use stealth, unlike some of the games that have been released in the past few years under this genre.

Puppygames develops an awesome tower defense game which changes the elements of your traditional TD. The awesome research options between levels, harvesting of resources, and the variety of tools to change alien tactics creates a unique experience between each level.
Revenge of the Titans, obviously you know the name as you are looking at this review. This game offers an interesting differentiation onto a typical Tower Defense game; enemies destroy your towers and the idea is to block the path rather than create a route. The world is being attacked by an alien species from Jupiter’s moon Titan. The name of the game seems to make me believe maybe we attacked them first? But yet again there is no real story other than the world is under attack and you are chosen to lead the defense force. You not only defend the earth, but you progress through the solar system defeating the alien scum at each planet until you finally arrive to Titan. Each planet has about ten levels, each which offer new bosses and pose new challenges that keep you on your toes.
The towers are upgraded by placing upgrading towers adjacent to towers. This is interesting as you can place multiple add-on towers adjacent to a tower to create rapid fire towers, or even long range sniper towers. The difficulty curve seems rather perplexing, with little explanation onto how to play this game can seem rather difficult till you figure it out. The game is incredibly entertaining, once you figure out the general gameplay you can really get into this game. You are given one upgrade point per level which you can use to customize your defense force. With about 73 upgrades and only 50 levels means you cannot research every possible option. The game allows you to respec after each mission, which allows you to manipulate your towers to achieve optimal defenses for each level. When playing the campaign make sure you remember that your money transfers between levels (and your towers automatically sell returning funds from the towers). This information is useful, as you can start saving early making the later levels easier. If you mess up after beating a level and lose too much money you can go back replay the level prior to it and fix your mistakes. This allows you to bring a better end result and alter your starting cash in the next mission.
Revenge of the Titans is an epic tower defense game that drives in new challenges and creates new concepts not seen in previous games of the same genre. The campaign is long and difficult, on the standard setting, but you can make it easier at the drop of a hat. Each level requires you to respect in order to take advantage of alien weaknesses, but this makes each level dynamic and unique.
Pros:
+Fast paced tower defense game
+Upgrade screen allows for between match tactic customization
+Transfer of funds between levels means how you play the level before impacts the later levels
+Power-Ups transfer between levels, so you can easily stack them. (I for example used none of my abilities until the last level to make the final boss incredibly easy).
+Great difficulty curve, if you are a beginner you can significantly reduce the difficulty to ease up the levels.
+Gameplay from prior levels transfers to the next level, meaning you must play tactfully throughout the entire game.
Cons:
-Poor tutorials, by the time you figure out all the nuances of the game it’s already over. (I for example didn't realize that levels don't start until you place your first mineral extractor until level 48 - this would have been useful to know early on)
-Recommended upgrades seem rather worthless (it’s better to just rush barricades)
-Not a traditional tower defense (there is no maze building, and to upgrade towers requires add-on towers which can be hard to space)

Don’t judge a book by its cover. While it may look like a flash game, Monster Slayers is charming and extremely polished. There isn’t a story, so to speak, but an end goal: defeat 2 legendary monsters (depending on which areas you choose) and then a 3rd—the Harbringer—to prove yourself a true Monster Slayer.
To do so, you must first create your hero, choosing their class—6 starting, and 6 more that can be unlocked by defeating the Harbringer with the classes that preceded them—and appearance from a list of presets. It’s a nice touch, but like the game says, you won’t be alive for very long anyway.
That will be true at least for the first few runs when you start the game. You are given the choice between two random locations from 6 possible, each has their own list of monster, which dictates how you’ll need to approach them. The Elderberry Forest, for instance, has spiders that inflict poison and can force you to discard cards from your hand with their webs. So hitting them hard and fast is in your best interest. If you’re playing a less damaging class, you may want to upgrade your cards before attempting this area.
Selecting from one of two possible locations actually adds a layer of tactical strategizing as you learn the enemies found in each area and how best to deal with them during your runs and plan accordingly when you enter the location. It gives you the option to plan your run a little better since you'll know what you’re up against.
Locations are divided into interconnected areas, each of which tells you exactly what you'll encounter— enemy, altar, shop, treasure—within them. You have to actually visit a node to reveal the ones adjacent to it, so you’re able to uncover as much or as little of the map as you’d like depending on where you find the boss room, denoted by a crown. There’s a risk versus reward here that regulars of roguelikes will be familiar with: do you stay and try to get gold and equipment at the possible risk of dying or being rendered too low on HP to face the boss or do you conserve your HP and make a rush for the boss and risk being flattened?
Even something in between those two options may result in being overwhelmed sooner, or later, so choose your battles!
There’s a lot of on-the-fly decision making involved in this game. Altars allow you to sacrifice something—Mana, starting AP, a tactical advantage such as adding junk cards to your deck or more powerful cards to enemy decks -- in exchange for a benefit like a powerful card, quick cash, greater HP, and the like. Whether these exchanges are worth it or not is entirely up to you and accepting one could easily alter the fate of your run for better or worse.
Treasure rooms give you the option to choose between a card or some gold. The card is chosen at random, so sometimes it's better to just take the money to potentially spend it on something better later down the line. Equipment carries over and isn’t specific, so if you feel as though your run isn’t going to last much longer, it's probably best to spend you feel as though your run isn’t going to last much longer, it’s probably best to spend your gold is lost.
Shops give you the option to buy and sell equipment and buy, delete, and upgrade cards. You can’t change equipment during a run, but successful or not, you’ll be able to keep them. Upgrading costs 20 gold the first time and rises incrementally from there; same with deleting. Upgrading allows you to increase the effectiveness of your base deck, meaning that you can’t upgrade cards found during your run. Deleting cards from your deck is a useful way to remove weak or junk cards from your deck so that they won’t clutter your hand. Some cards have no effect other than to take up space when you draw, so it's in your best interest to delete these.
Allied units like captains and party members that you didn’t select this run will offer a combination of the above. Some will give you a card and others will train you to have more starting AP—it all depends on what you choose.
If there’s an enemy in the next area, you’ll be shown their name, level, and how much exp you’ll get from defeating them.
Combat is where you’ll be spending the bulk of your time. Battles are fast-paced 1v1 affairs during which opposing combatants draw a hand of cards and play them in turns. The number of cards you can play depends on your mana and action points, both of which regenerate automatically. The higher the card level, the more AP they will cost, so keep that in mind if you rush upgrades early on.
There are 4 types of card: Attack cards which deal damage and use AP, Magic cards which deal damage and use MP, support cards which allow you to choose their effect and/or do damage based on condition (like number of cards in your discard pile or number of cards of the same type used that turn), and interruption cards, which activate automatically when the conditions listed are met.
The enemy A.I. is pretty intelligent and will keep you on your toes, chaining together attacks, wearing you down with status ailments, and negating your purity deck with blocks their programmed play style dictates.
After battle, you’re rewarded with the experience shown before the fight. If you level up, you are fully healed, so it’s in your best interest to plan when you’ll level to a degree. Each level, you have the option between a mixture of upgrade/delete a card, add AP/mana/HP, or get a new card/equipment.
Every five levels, your hand size is expanded by one, so at max level you’ll be able to hold 6? It’s important to balance your attentions as you level; having a deck full of strong cards is useless if you don’t have the energy to use them and vice versa.

If you're a fan of roguelikes, Monster Slayers is a great game for beginners and veterans alike. It's satisfying to progress, even if that progress is slow; one run at a time. Multiple classes with different play styles with 6 additional classes to unlock by beating the end game make for a lot of replayability and the quick combat makes it so that you can pick this game up and put it down at will.
Highly Recommended.

It's not often a digital card-battle game feels exciting, but Monster Slayers nails it with the wonderful art style, super-simple gameplay mechanics, and watching your character battle monsters each time a card is played. Strategies start to become clear the more a specific character is played, allowing you to efficiently build a winning deck.
Speaking of strategy, there are a variety of enemy types with their own play style, some are fast chain hitters, counter-attackers, life leechers, and some mimic your exact deck! Monster Slayers keeps you on your toes and constantly tests your deck, but don't worry, the game gives you plenty of opportunities to tweak it.
Collecting cards to build a winning deck each run is fun, addictive, and super-rewarding. With the addition of loot and that "just one more run" gameplay loop, Monster Slayers is a rad roguelike with great replay value.

I've put in almost 30 hours on Monster Slayers, and I think the game's extremely fun for the price.
You pick a class and enter a randomly-generated dungeon where you find, upgrade, and delete cards to build a better card game deck.  There are some stats that determine how many powerful cards you can play a turn and how hard you are to kill, and you can find RPG-style loot items that augment your character.  It's a little like Hearthstone or Guild of Dungeoneering, but with more RPG elements.  Because you can have a very small deck of cards, you can get a lot of control over combos, and yet the random looting elements mean you can't always build the same deck every run.  If you like card battle games, there's a good chance you'll like this one, too.

Let me just open up with a bit of a confession: I absolutely LOVE building starships! I just cannot get enough of it! This game allows me to construct my own fleet and order them around like a real star-fleet commander. This game has no shortage of strategic depth, but it's also not overly heavy-handed with it. The main strategy boils down to what kind of fleet will you construct. Will you create a variety of smaller ships, like scouts, fighters, interceptors, and bombers? Or will you invest in some heavier ships, like cruisers, battleships, and destroyers?
The art style is very basic, but that's far from a bad thing. Every ship is just a bunch of rectangles, squares, and triangles. Everything's really easy to discern; at a glance, you can see that the enemy frigate is mostly armed with missiles, for instance. The simplistic art design makes this game run well even on unimpressive hardware.
My verdict? 96/100. A few of the weapons could use rebalancing (*ahem
ahem*), and it still has a few bugs, but aside from that, the game is great! Considering it's free, I'd definitely snatch it up!

Out of the many modes in this game, my favorites are "Escort" and "Annilation". In Escort, you are either on the side that has to escort a tank and kill all the other players or try and destroy the tank while killing the players trying to escort the tank. Annilation mode is basically just a death match played in numerous levels (mostly a big freezer room) that people like the most.
Guns are also a pretty big part in the game. When you reach (I think) the level; First Class Private, you get a great gun that you'll probably use until you level up to a high enough level where you can buy new and more powerful guns.
Leveling up in A.V.A. is yet another great and important factor in this game. You basically just complete rounds that earns you XP and (like RPGs) you level up. When you reach level Sergeant, you get kicked out of the level 1-5 beginner channel and now have to play the level 1-10 Beginner channel or the open channel.

This is a pretty, minimalistic puzzler. You have a rectangular grid with squares painted in various colours and only one action - to repaint any contigous area into a new color. Given that, your goal is to have only one colour left on the board, and that in as few moves as possible. The first couple of levels are very easy, and then you are given more colours, and less obvious shapes on the board. But the difficulty progresses nicely, and there's a built-in hint system if you are stuck.
Actually, playing this with a mouse seems a bit inadequate, this is a perfect game for touchscreen devices. And it is - go and play it on your phone or tablet. It's also a perfect choice when you only have 15 minutes to play. As well as pretty enough and innocent enough to fool someone into thinking it's a wallpaper or some kind of screen-saver. So maybe office-safe too!
Go play it, it's worth your time.

Firstly, the hours recorded here are only what I've played online, there are plenty of offline hours and I haven't finished the game yet.
Initially I was on the fence about this game, to the point where I wanted to request a refund. The ledge detection can be off and the duelist comat system is limiting. However, as I played more, I found these things actually worked for the game, because Styx is a weak goblin, who is only good at sneaking around, setting traps, backstabbing and knife throwing, so I actually found that I've found the character to be more immersive in this way.
Most of us have played Assassin's Creed. Well Styx is not a super Assassin, he's a survivor, he stalks his prey not because the mission forces him to but because it suits him.
The turning point to enjoyment for me was saving my game a lot, dropping boxes on people, poisoning and learning that if one way is difficult, choose another way and Styx has multiple pathways to his objective. This is not Dark Souls, where you go one way you die and then go another way you die.
The giant roach creatures are ahnoying but, tuned my timing, I haven't met elves yet but I can imagine they'll tune something because they can smell you. Knights are tough, but not tougher than falling objects.
I do recommend this game, admittedly, not being a stealth fan, but often enjoying stealth stories I played on easy, other wise I'd get frustrated probably, but you always go back later and say why didn't I play this on a higher level.
Any way, I'm enjoying this game.

This is a really fun and unique indie game.
Being someone that enjoys Photography, I really enjoyed this. It’s a kind of point and click game, a woman who is in the hospital narrates her thoughts and you search and explore her dreams looking for answers and picking up little collectables along the way that give you extra little pieces of information about her life.
I really like the style of this game, the scenes are made up of photographs that you flick between and it uses a few photography methods which I thought was quite clever. For example it uses low shutter speed methods to show movement in the photos and ghostly figures.
(Low shutter speed being where you take the photo but it carries on taking in light through the lens, so if someone were to jump into the photo while it was still taking in light, it would pick up the light reflected off of the person. Hence pictures of “ghosts”)

If only had this developer more money b/c it's obvious that they really know how to make a true stealth game. Vast levels a la the original Thief trilogy. The level design may not be as interesting as in the father of the genre but everything is perfectly explorable without any cutoffs which would prevent you from backtracking.
has a handy arsenal & abilities at his disposal like balls of sand/invisibility, and all of these are perfectly usable in every mission. You won't end up using them only once like it happens in some other games. Verticality of all the areas is giving you freedom in how to approach challenges the game puts before you. There's still some trouble in the jumping but I don't think it was anything critical; just had to quick-load now and then. The story itself is quite good; also the ending was satisfying in my opinion. The way it is told isn't entirely fascinating (especially the cutscenes, they
horrible) but it uses concepts like over-hearing conversations which made me more immersed -- the story was told as I was playing the game. On the other hand, the tasks you're given are truly enjoyable. Not once did I find anything repetitive, even after the game started to reuse (almost ALL) the levels after mission #4. There's a big variety in quests like escorting somebody to a safe place, assassination, following a key target, pickpocketing... And there are always new adversaries coming your way as the story progresses. The game is funny at times, and does a great job of making you interested in its lore too (unfortunately there wasn't much to find out). To sum it up, Styx is pretty much the best stealth game of 2014. It does things right. Having bigger budget, I believe it could be simply spectacular.

Revenge of the Titans is a 2D tower defense game with RTS elements developed by London-based studio Puppy Games. As in all tower defense games, your goal is to halt the oncoming horde of enemies by strategically placing defensive towers that destroy them. In this case, humanity is being attacked by aliens coming from Saturn’s largest moon Titan.
The campaign spans 50 missions across 5 locations (Earth, The Moon, Mars, Saturn and Titan). After you’re done with the 10-hour campaign, you can spend more time with the game in the Endless, Survival and Sandbox modes. There’s a good amount of content here. If you’ve played a classic tower defense game, Revenge of the Titans will feel pretty familiar. However, what separates this game from the usual suspects are the subtle yet profound base building and resource gathering elements found in traditional RTS games.
Every map starts with just your base which you have to protect from the Titans. Then you have to build factories that mine crystals in order to make money to be able to purchase other buildings and towers. You also have additional buildings at your disposal such as shield generators, cloaking devices, reloaders, etc. All of these can be unlocked over time in the research screen before every mission. After completing each mission you are awarded with a single research point. Apart from buildings and towers, you can research technological advancements which bring their own benefits to the table. The great thing about the research system is that you can re-spec the entire system before each mission. This enables you to try out different tactics and you will need certain towers and abilities when facing a particular enemy.
Enemies come in a pretty large variety of shapes and sizes and certain missions also throw huge bosses at you which can be very challenging. Certain towers are good for certain enemies, that’s where the research screen comes into play. You need to pay attention as to what types of enemies are coming so that you can choose the appropriate towers and technologies otherwise you’ll have a pretty hard time finishing a mission.
The game will also randomly distribute power ups and cash bonuses during missions which you will need to manually pick up on the map within a limited time frame. There’s also a tower that needs to be used against a certain enemy that you have to manually control. Coupled with the base/add-on/tower building, the situation can get pretty hectic at times and certain elements such as the power up pick ups simply come off as an artificial way to increase the action. It impeded on the strategic element and just feels needlessly overbearing.
That said, Revenge of the Titans nails the addictive and tactical core that makes tower defense games so satisfying. And with the RTS twist, it manages to differentiate itself which is really important as the genre is becoming increasingly crowded. It’s a good title for newcomers and veterans alike.

First off, I would like to say this will be a long review that is both fair and pretty detailed without being a novel so bear with me.
MY INITIAL THOUGHTS
For a player that hasn't played since SpellForce 2 Original release (no expansions) I find this game to be a fantastic experience. Gameplay (despite some tiny flaws and bugs I have noticed but I'll explain later) is nearly perfectly executed, the storyline and deep lore poured into the campaign only a few missions into myself is already enough to warrant my attention to finish the story. This is a game worthy of my olden days of Warcraft 3 LAN parties where my roomates and I would play for hours killing computers, each other and talking about ways to improve each other while laughing. This is Warcraft 4 to some extent to me but without Blizzard's hectic development.
MY FLAWS WITH THE GAME SO FAR
As of release when I write this after a solid 5 hours on Twitch streaming, I can say the bugs are few but kind of apparent. Pathing, though improved since beta, is still a problem especially for bigger armies. Bugs with hero deaths in the campaign and autosaving have led me to be stuck in a loop of Defeats despite no reason to be defeated as my hero died but others were around to revive. Only six skirmish maps, despite their beauty and deep strategic depth on release is kind of weak. Multiplayer is still somewhat laggy but I won't complain too much because it was vastly worse in beta. All in all these bugs are very annoying but I am sure will be patched and fixed as time goes on.
MY FAVORITE THINGS OF THE GAME
Not everything in this game is bad. This review is positive for a reason and as such I have a few solid points I personally love about the game. To start, the game offers a fun and yet simple skirmish mode that begs to be praised from the younger predecessors. Combat is bloody, fun and fast and punishes mistakes while rewarding those who know how to position their armies and use their heroes strategically. The campaign as I stated is deep and stuffed full of lore that is building the world for SpellForce: The Order of Dawn; the first game of the series of which this game prequels. Geralt of Rivia's voice actor (Doug Cockle) brings life and a grizzled narration to the story's dark storyline and helps to immerse you in the missions. The environments, maps, co-op campaign and wide-open doors of the developers seems to be showcasing that this game is definetly worth its price of only $50 USD. Does it need polish still? Yes. Is it broken and full of bugs? No. Is it fun and worth it? Absolutely!
TL;DR - SpellForce 3 is a worthy title of its namesakes and is a powerful new contender for the supposedly dying RTS/RPG genre and I will be enjoying it for awhile and think it would be worth it for sure on sale for you to check out yourself! If you still aren't sure about it, check it out on Twitch where people like myself are streaming it for your enjoyment and whether its worth your purchase. Thanks for reading, folks. Kerrigan Out.

This game has more than what meets the eye.  From the other reviews I am sure you have a good idea of what game this is, but I am here to talk about the depth of the gameplay.  I know for a lot of card game fans and rogue-like gamers out there this is important.
The game can seem to get boring after you find yourself discovering everything.  After you seen the cards, beat the boss, played the rogue class, farmed some items, maxed out talents, etc.  But, you haven't tried legendary mode.  This is where the real game begins.
Legendary mode is much much harder than normal.  It is still relatively easy if you are playing rogue or wizard with card draw on mana charge (those two are just very fine tuned class).  But if you try to beat legendary on any other class I would say it takes some commitment and stratgizing.  You will have to maxmize the full heal you get on every level up.  You will have to pick a choose fights carefully.  It becomes a game of efficiency.  You will start to remember which enemies have which cards.  A nice part of the game is that you have one deck.  The enemies have tons of different deck.  Means are pitched against a dozens of different playstyles with one playstyle that you tune and adjust.  This leads to optimization and dealing with counters.  Any realisitc deck that you can obtain there is ALWAYS a counter deck to it (a little rng factor too to spice thigns up).  You will likely to run into one of those counters, and if you are caught off guard without planning for it you are likely to lose and it's game over.
Just for some examples you have enemy decks that excells as the game goes long.  Enemy priests that cloggs your decks with curses and puts perma-dots on you.  Or decks that excells as the game goes long but also if your deck is thin, like medusa which turns your cards to stone and you find your self rapidly running out of cards.  Undead knights have anti magic and combo breaking abilities, as any enemy with the "Enough" card (end the turn if six or more card is played) shuts out combo decks and decks that cycles through.  Enemy mages and rogues are deadly if you don't have the means to handle the bursts.  Enemy rangers that are guarenteeed to go first meaning you will take a good chunk of damage.  Enemies that just cancles your cards and tickle you down slowly.  Enemies that utilizies poision that if enough will kill cycling decks.  Enemies that doesn't give a ♥♥♥♥ how much defense you have and just blow you away with damages and are backed up with their own high health and stats.  Merceanaries (mirror deck of yours) that may forces a stalled match if your deck outheals the damage it can potentially do.  And the harbinger that you have to plan your whole end game around.
You have to deal with all these things with the gears you equip, the gold you find, and the deck you build.  It is a changllenging task, but a fun one.  I currently have only 6/12 classes to have beated the legendary mode.  I am placed currently 4th in the world in terms of total fame and I think my hours reflect as well as legimitizes my assesment of the gameplay on the difficulty it is IMO meant to played at.  So if you are worried that this game wanes out or gets too easy, I assure you that will not be an issue.

I was a little wary of all of the positive reviews at first, but let me say that this is a game that really does grow on you.
When I first kicked-off the game I had a basic knowledge of the NES Legend of Zelda games, but I found myself dying a fair bit, more than I expected. And it wasn't until I persisted and got to the first dungeon (after having died a fair bit in the Level 4 dungeon without realising it!) - that I began to understand what the game was about.
Suffice it to say, that as a tribute, this does indeed check all the right boxes. It's still in early access as I write this, but I was lucky enough to be able to talk to the developer as I was playing, and provided a little feedback, and he is adamant that he takes all feedback into consideration, which to me is already a win.
I have currently gotten to the point where I am in the final dungeon, which in its present state is only three rooms, but this is actively being worked-on, and I am told will be done fairly soon, at which point I would love to come back and try again.
All of this said, there are a couple of points I hope are addressed in the near future:
- Smart Bomb / Wave Cannon sound effects are a lot louder than expected, and can put folks off, I have found.
- When I originally walked through the evil forest to get to what I thought was the next dungeon, I found I was mistaken, and getting back was a nightmare, as every time I died it reset me back to that dungeon. Cue 20 minutes of me desperately trying to make it out alive..! Not sure whether I should just suck that one up though...
- Final Dungeon location is not immediately obvious, nor was the hint to its location (which I never found, but was told about)
- Grid-based movement is a little cumbersome when fighting enemies in tight corners, but not sure how you could get around this.
- Some respawn locations are right on top of enemies, so when you restart with three hearts, unless you are moving and shooting immediately, you often lose some health.
Other than that, a very enjoyable title, and one I fully intend on playing again when it has been finished!

Okay people, when the developer handed me a free copy of this game for review for exposure on my Youtube channel, I looked at it and the price tag of $9.99 USD with a feeling of "pffft.  Legend of Zelda huh?  Right!  ...$10 huh?  Really??"
Watch my first impressions review and experience with this outstanding retro style game HERE:
Those doubts after my first livestream first impressions have been more than erased by the sheer amount of FUN this game delivers!  This game feels and behaves just like you'd expect a Legend of Zelda shooter to!  It's awesome fun, and a lot of that fun, much like an old school Zelda classic is exploring the world, the dungeons, and figuring out how to best defeat all the different monsters and bosses that you will encounter.

Super Meat Boy meets roguelike.
In Just Get Through you play as a dude who gets lost in a ancient temple and needs to escape it by going through portals while evading deadly traps. As you get further the levels get longer and harder, introducing new types of traps, and every few levels you can upgrade your character.
The gameplay is pretty simple - you can run around, sprint, wall jump and throw dynamite. You can use it to destroy traps and create a faster way to the exit, but you need to be carefull - if you're careless with the explosives, you can find yourself unable to complete the level.
Just Get Through offers a variety of different game modes, for example the classic one where you need to get as far as you can, night mode in which the levels are dark and you need to use torches and flares or coin run in which you can pick up money and spend it at certain spots.
Levels are randomly generated, but there's also a level editor. If you prefer hand made levels you can find a big variety of user created ones to play.
Summary
+well made platformer
+endless amount of randomly generated levels
+a lot of game modes
+level editor and levels made by users
-simple graphics (but they have their charm)
-frustrating at times
8.5/10

The Path in an arthouse exploration/horror game where you control one of six girls as they make the trek to grandmother's house. You're told to stay on the path and avoid the wolf, but if you do what you're told, you don't get to experience anything this game has to offer.
The Path is a mystery that needs to be unraveled. As you explore, you find more things and learn more about each of the girls, and you may bump into the "wolf". For each of the girls, meeting the wolf is a life-changing experience.
The game is a very interesting mystery and an engaging metaphor, but when held to the normal standards for a video game, The Path is severely lacking. The controls are completely awful. The aesthetic is nice, but the actual graphic quality is pretty poor. The sound is odd, which is fitting for this game. The gameplay is slow. Really, really slow. You'll need a lot of patience.
The game description on Steam should be taken seriously. This game is not for children.
The Path is definitely not for everyone. Pick it up if an arthouse title with difficult metaphors interests you, but if you're looking for a fun game, this is not it. $10 is probably a bit much; wait for it to go on sale.

Video showing off game:
The Shrounded Isle is a management game where you are spinning many plates: You must keep 5 families happy, maintain 5 major traits above a threshold, AND find the major sinners in the families to sacrifice to your god.
Every season you choose an advisor from each house and for 3 turns you can choose from 1-3 of them to do as they will. The less advisors you use, the stronger they affect things and the stronger impact on their house. You also learn more about the advisors as they work. Are they virtuious or one of the major sinners? After 3 turns, you must sacrifice one of your advisors, which will have repercussions and bonuses if you do it right. If you're in good standing with a house, you can make inquiries to learn more about advisors before you pick them.
Then you do it all again until you fail to balance everything, or survive to the 3rd year. The ending is dictated by how many sinners you sacrificed.
Visually the game is quite distinct and the music is a great brooding tone.
Balance; having played lots of management games, I found the game challenging at first. But once you get a good handle on the game, you can perform pretty well. I was able to finish with all sinners sacrificed and got the "best" ending. But it was down to the wire, which made it an exciting time.

I'm the vaunted leader of a tight-knit community of demon worshippers, choosing from among my acolytes to select my most vital inner circle. Time is running short. Our dark patron awaits our devotion, and he speaks to me--personally--in the dark realm of my dreams, where my fragile mortal mind can come closest to appreciating his messages. He commands me to prove our worth by burning out the sin and corruption in our community. His return is coming soon.
Cannily, I suss out the innermost flaws of my little flock. I ask devotees to spill the secrets they've learned, tattle on each other, and point fingers. I use the authority of the circle to put people to the test, granting them power and then silently observing what they do with it. Each season, I mark one for death.
On the night of the end of summer, with fall's tint not yet creeping in among the trees, he came to me in my sleep and bade me obey him: find the artist among my people, who threatens the careful ignorance I've cultivated in them, and kill her on the ritual table. I use all my skills to identify the threat, and...
...I can't kill her right away, because her family already isn't happy and if I sacrifice their daughter they'll rebel.
The heart of my dissatisfaction with The Shrouded Isle is the odd mismatch between its atmosphere and its gameplay. The basic game functionality is about managing a set of ten meters. Five meters are the qualities of the worshippers (ignorance, fervor, discipline, penitence, obedience) and five are how happy each family is with you. Each family member (there are 30) has a positive trait and a negative trait that determine how they affect the five quality meters. Choosing to use someone from a family will make the family like you. Choosing to kill them will tank their happiness score. So the gameplay comes down to managing the meters to keep everyone happy enough that you can kill the people you need to without pushing any family into the critical "rebellious" zone, and without dropping any quality meter into the critical red zone (either is a game over).
That strategic gameplay is engaging for the short time the game takes, but it feels out of step with the game's core idea  of managing an arcane cult. A lot of artistry (though by that I mean quality, not quantity--the art is good but there's not actually that much of it) goes into getting you into the role of the cult leader, but then the game obligates you to make *strategic* decisions instead of *role-playing* decisions. You can easily be penalized for doing the thing that makes the most sense in-universe, which is a bit of a pet peeve of mine. If the game set things up differently, and made it clearer that your grip on these families isn't so tight in the first place, I could more easily forgive it, but I didn't get that impression.
It's also rather short--I had to try a few times before I got the hang of the game, but if you know what you're doing from the get-go you could probably finish this in less than half an hour.

I've probably played close to 100 Real Time Strategy Games and Role Playing games, and they are my two favorite genres by far. My two all time favorites, Baldur's Gate 2 and Age of Empires 2, have just had a beautiful next-gen baby, and her name is SpellForce III.
UPDATE!
This year has featured some great RPGs but with really disappointing stories, starting with Mass Effect Andromeda, but SpellForce finally broke that trend, the writing in this game is truly a work of art. So many twists and turns in the first mission I have no idea where it could possibly go from here. It's a very original and unexpected story, the kind you can't even expect from The Last Jedi.
UPDATE!
Introducing an RTS campaign with the most character development I've ever encountered, and the best writing. Early in the game, the second mission to be precise, I was faced with a very difficult decision and nigh brought to tears. I haven't encountered a decision so hard so early since The Witcher 2. Ironically one of the most prominent characters of this game is voiced by Doug Cockle (voice of Geralt of Rivia A.K.A. The Butcher of Cidaris) Yet this game features much more complicated RPG elements than the Witcher 3 ever did.
Play an open-ended RTS campaign with an adventure style world that you get to travel freely through as you do quests and build a base and conquer other bases all at the same time, while enjoying dialogue options and branching decisions, complete with beautiful environments. Explore goregeous wilderness and the most ♥♥♥♥ing epic castle I've ever seen in the history of fantasy!
There's a world sprawling around it and as you expand and get bases started on each map, you can travel between locations on the map Dragon Age style and do various quests in each one. As you get to know the characters led by Geralt as they try to quell a rebellion. Command armies, maneuver formations of pikemen, swordsmen, cavalry, archers, mages, support and siege units around your heroes as you micro-manage their abilities.
Expand your economy as you fish, hunt, mine, smelt, chop, extract and purify the natural resources of a fantasy world. Send your heroes on quests to explore, hunt monsters, collect items, various types of equipment (weapons, armor, helms, shields, rings, amulets, consumables, etc.) and most importantly, clear spots for more base building! Ah base building! A classic and essential RTS feature that I haven't seen in a new game in years.
As you expand your army and empire and upgrade your soldiers, so too, do your Heroes level up. The ability trees of this Real Time Strategy game put Mass Effect and The Witcher to shame.
In the only skirmish game I've played I spent a while figuring out how to expand and collect resources. It's a very strategic game, and very micro-intensive. Resources are all forward and it requires a well planned balance between economic development and expansion for acquiring those resources but also the Soldiers and heroes required to find and hold the resource spots.
When I finally got a siege army going I took out a couple of an Easy AI's outposts and he had a huge formation of infantry that I chased down and butchered with archers. I was thinking "ye easy AI indeed" but then my archers got pincer attacked from behind by two cavalry formations while my heroes got out-microd at the front of the fight. Rip my whole army, but it was an amazing experience and I learned an important thing: This so called "strategy" game aint just throwing that word around for funzies, this is some hardcore♥♥♥♥♥♥

"Real" stealth games don't come along very often these days since it's more profitable to play it safe and add in optional combat elements, but every now and then one comes along like Styx. This is a game more like the old Thief games, where if you get caught it's effectively quickload time because your chances of escaping a fight alive are fairly slim. It feels a bit budget at times for a $30 game, mainly in the graphics and voice acting, but the gameplay is solid enough that I didn't mind. The game is seven missions long, but each mission is split into 3 or 4 somewhat large areas which each have a main objective, a side objective, and 10 gold coins per area (so 30 to 40 per mission), so it has a fair amount of length to it. You get experience at the end of each mission to spend on skills, with bonus experience rewards at the end of each mission for not killing anyone, not being seen, finishing the mission in a certain time limit, and collecting every gold coin in the mission. You have a few special abilities like being able to make clones of yourself or temporarily turn invisible, but they're heavily limited and the main focus is on traditional stealth.
The only real problem is that the game lacks a real motivation to actually do the bonus rewards - you already end up with at least around 200 experience per mission just for completing them, and the rewards only add 20 each. For the rewards like not being seen and not killing anyone you might just get those anyways (though I can almost guarantee that you won't bother sparing anyone in the final mission, because after a few seconds of sneaking around elves you'll be ready to slaughter every last one of those beady-eyed hellspawns), but the time limits are usually around an hour less than my final time and seem to be based around speedrunning through the mission instead of exploring to look for items, and the coin challenge is an all-or-nothing deal, so I'd almost guarantee you won't actually get it on your first run of any mission if you plan on going for any of the other rewards. But at the same time, just like I didn't criticize Thief 2014 for not forcing you to steal gold, I don't really mind it here either, because at the end of the day you'll steal everything you see anyways because it's just fun to do it.
Overall Styx is the type of game that just sets out to do one thing and does it pretty well, and while it could definitely be better it's just nice to see a game with a budget that caters more to purist stealth fans. I think $30 might be a bit high, but if you're into stealth games it's worth getting sooner or later.

Monster Slayers is a single-player collectible card game with rogue-like elements from indie developers, Nerdook Productions, who previously developed well-known indie games, Vertical Drop Heroes HD and Reverse Crawl.
In Monster Slayers, you play a hero on a quest to defeat three powerful monsters in order to join the legendary Monster Slayers.
Gameplay is presented side-on, in two dimensions. The upper portion of the screen shows the action in each battle, using cartoon-like sprites with basic animations, while the bottom section shows your hand of cards and various statistics, gauges, and other useful information.
The battle graphics are great and fit the sense of humour and general feel of the game to a tee. Card graphics are big and easy to recognise, and the always-available tooltips fill in any information that you might not remember just from looking at the card name and graphic -- very useful for a beginner.
When you're not in battle, the dungeon and 'world' maps are simply presented and work well. In fact, the interface in general is very easy to use and I didn't ever find myself not knowing how to do something.
Graphics options are non-existent, but the game should run fine on any modern hardware.
Sound and music also fit the game very well. The music seemed to me to be sort-of comically jaunty, but full of doom as well, much like the game itself, and although it gets repetitive, playing on and on for hours, I didn't find it annoying.
Sound effects are fine and consist of all of the sorts of things you'd expect from a fantasy-battle-based CCG. They're well normalised and I didn't need to adjust relative sound and music volumes from their defaults.
There are some voices in the game, too, and personally I loved these, though one of the female character's "Hello" when encountering friendly NPCs in the dungeons very quickly got on my wife's nerves. If you find one annoying, though, there are many more to choose from when creating your character, both male and female.
Monster Slayers plays similarly to a single-player computer version of Magic: the Gathering, or any of a host of other fantasy collectible card games, but with a wicked sense of humour.
You start the game by creating a character of one of the six provided classes: rogue, ranger, knight, barbarian, cleric, and wizard. When you select your class, the humour in the game becomes evident, as there's a special note below the character name: "Don't spend too much time here. This hero will be dead soon."
The first time you play, the game provides you with a short tutorial dungeon, before putting you on the world map screen, from where you can select one of the Northern Valley's treacherous dungeons to explore. Entering the dungeon, you're shown a grid of connected rooms, each one of which holds a random encounter. When you first enter, you can only see the four rooms around you, but as you defeat monsters or encounter NPCs, more of the dungeon opens up, until by the end you will most likely have explored every room.
Most often the rooms hold creatures to battle -- the type and level of which is displayed to you before you enter the room -- but when you first start the first and second dungeons each game, you'll also be given a choice of companion, each of whom has a special ability with a cooldown. Other than battles, you'll also encounter merchants, trainers, healers, and a number of other non-deadly, or even friendly, NPCs and objects, many of which award you new cards.
When you do enter a room with a creature, though, the battle card game begins, and this plays like many other CCGs, with the goal being to wear down your opponent's health to 0 while not losing all of yours. There's a bit of a twist, though. Although your hand is often only four cards, many cards perform an action (e.g. attack or healing) and then draw another card, so, particularly for the rogue class, you may end up using double or even triple the number of cards in your hand on a good turn.
Some cards use action points, which are limited and refresh each turn; some cards use mana, which is limited and carries over each turn; and some cards use neither, and are essentially 'free' to use. The main difference between the characters is the cards they have in their card decks, with each one being geared towards a certain style of play. Rogues churn through cards fast, with lots of redraws; knights easily build up lots of defence ('block') and are good tanks; and barbarians are happy to burn their own health and then rely on regeneration to recover, in order to do increased damage to their enemies.
Defeating an opponent earns you gold and experience points (XP), but any health you've lost carries over with you to the next battle, unless you visit a healer, or, importantly, go up a level. Each level of monster is worth five XP, so kill a level two monster and you'll earn 10 XP. This is important, because one of the basic tactics of the game is to carefully plan your battles in order to level up when you most need to regain your health. Levelling up also normally gives you a choice of character improvement: an extra Action Point, a new card, or a card upgrade, for example.
Dungeons are procedurally generated and the game has perma-death, so when your character dies, off you go to start all over again. All is not lost, however, as you keep a small percentage of your gold, all of your items from the 'party inventory', and, importantly, you earn fame points. When these reach enough for the next rank, you gain a point to spend on a permanent improvement. These include deck changes for future games, stat increases, and a range of other benefits.
Each dungeon has a boss creature. Defeat three of these and you've fulfilled your Monster Slayer quest and, I assume, completed the game. Simple, right?
There are a few things I didn't like about the game, but only a few.
Firstly, I've clicked the 'Sell Junk Items' button from the inventory screen far too often and it's sold off equipment that I wouldn't have called 'junk' at all, with no way to recover it. Make sure to use this button only sparingly!
Secondly, the companions, while a nice addition, are not really used to their full potential. This is certainly a deliberate design decision, to focus on the main character, but it seemed like a bit of a wasted opportunity, with such a good range of companions and only a couple of improvements available for each.
And lastly, Monster Slayers is too addictive by far! I think it must be a digital narcotic.
Note: according to an update on the Store page yesterday, there are now also six more classes to unlock by completing the game with each of the six starting classes. Oh no! That's even more reason to keep playing.
Pros:
+ A great sense of humour
+ Very good use of rogue-like elements
+ Most excellent fun
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Could do with more
- The 'Sell Junk Items' button sells good things, too
Monster Slayers is very, very good. If you enjoy CCGs, and you like rogue-likes, you should buy it. Now.

This here is a nice little card based Rouge-lite game.  I got it during a sale, I think it cost me about half price or so.  But even at 10 bones you get a pretty decent value for your money.
Visuals:  A pretty basic visual style, but the art is nice.  Cards all have a nice little image.  The characters are all cute and detailed.  Animations do the job, although I recommend setting Fast game mode to speed things up.  3/5
Audio:  Nothing to write home about.  The music is alright, but nothing that gripped me, nor did it prevent me from shutting it off in favour of my own music.  Sound effects do the job, as do the voices.  2.5/5
Gameplay:  Pretty entertaining.  Pick a class, choose your equipment (if you have any), pick a dungeon, then pick a companion.  After that you get to navigate a map.  You have to proceed through 3 dungeons total, with each getting more difficult.  You heal, get a chance to change equipment, and cooldowns reset between dungeons.  You get to see what the encounter will be prior to clicking on a room, so you can plan ahead to some extent.  Rooms consist of monster encounters, NPC's, treasure (more cards or cash monies), merchants, campsites, and alters.  A good mix of things, and it allows you to play however you choose within reason.  Early encounters seem to be pretty easy once you've amassed a nice selection of gear to equip.  But in the second and third dungeon the difficulty can amp up pretty quick.  However, rarely did I feel like I was dead on the map selection screen, with no way to progress without dying.  RNG is definitely a factor, but that is to be expected.  The Alters, in my opinion, are rarely worth the price for what's offered.  Campsites are nice, with a risk/reward situation of increasing some stats if you keep gambling, but you can lose all rewards as well as the chance at healing.  Overall, I found the gameplay to be addictive.  The "one more run" mentality set in, which means I view it as pretty sucessful for this type of game.  I still believe there may be some balancing issues, particularly in longer runs, but I also believe that the dev is trying to work on this.  In the short amount of time since release, there have been several rebalances and tweaks, as well as an expansion released with additional classes for free.  4/5
Overall, I recommend this game as a nice little time-waster.  It's not the deepest game, but it's fun.  You can tell the dev put alot of heart into it, and continues to do so after release.  I have not complaints with the game, and I believe it will only improve with more patches as well as DLC both paid and free.  If a Rouge-lite dungeon crawler with some light deck management, give it a shot.  I doubt you'd be disappointed.  4/5

Kona is a solid adventure-style game with an interesting mystery and a colorful cast. It does that rare thing in game stories where none of the characters are purely black and white, even the worst of these people are at least relatable. Like many 'adventure' games, the focus is the story and the gameplay is peripheral, but said gameplay integrates with the rest much better than others, with a focus on survival in a deadly blizzard and combating natural, and unnatural creatures.
Survival is touted as one of the game's main features, but I feel this is where the game is weakest. Surviving the deep, Canadian cold is a challenge, but only so much as the time and distance between places where you can warm yourself. I was swimming in supplies to start fires, to the point I think there were more logs, matches and fire starting kits than snow!
There is a light amount of combat against the aggitated natives, and I'd say this aspect is done well, as you have a few weapons and other means to dealing with hostiles. Animal lovers rejoice as I completed the game without actually killing any living creatures. However there wasn't enough of this combat to really make it more than a momentary distraction, not a major gameplay element.
The exploration is one of the more fun aspects of the game, as you have free reign with your truck and the enviroment is big enough to feel wide and open, but not so huge as to not know where to go. There's plenty of items to find out in the woods, as well as more details about the game's mysteries, not all of which I found in my first run.
The game also touts some horror elements, and while there are 2 or 3 GREAT atmospheric horror sections, there is no real pay off. There are dangers, but they are all disapointing.
Kona took me about 3 days of playing, with about  3-4 hours each sessions. And I took my sweet time exploring the enviroments. It's short, but just at that level where it's still worth a purchase.
If you are into story-centric games, I think you'll enjoy this one. If you're after survival or horror, I think you'll enjoy the atmosphere but beyond that you'll be disapointed.
Lastly, this game is steeped in Canadian culture, to the point I've been calling it 'Canada; The Game.' But considering how much fun I had, and how much more of the game I wanted when it was over, I say we kickstart and purchase more game set in the frozen lands of our Northern Brothers and Sisters!

Gunpoint was an enjoyable experience and rather satisfying considering its rather short length. The gameplay is fluid, only if you the player are skilled. I am not skilled so there was a lot of floundering around however when I was playing the game well, utilising all the tools at my disposal I realised just how much depth the games mechanics have. However for some odd reason the difficulty of the game fluctuates from sit back and spend 10 minutes strategising and formulating a plan to "really, thats it?". Arguably the last two levels were dissapointing, being relatively simple and more an example of quantity rather than puzzle quality. However the sheer amount of guards and mini puzzles in the last level allow  the mechanics to shine and we see just how hectic this game can get mechanically when pushed.
The length may deter some but the game is worth it for the price. The music in this game is passable. One or two tracks stand out but nothing you will find yourself humming later on. The writing is most likely going to divide players. I took the zany approach and made my character a gun wielding psychopathic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, resulting in some of the funniest dialogue I have read in a while. However I know that this writing will come of as random for the sake of random for some. It is possible however to play a straight and narrow character with no shenanigans if desired.
Overall Gunpoint was a fun distraction, you will most likely beat this in one sitting and unless you enjoy challenging yourself replaying levels for times then the replayability isnt really there. There are some alternate dialogues depending on the ingame choices but not much besides that. But the pixel art style, dialogue, story and combat makes this a worthwile indie title to play on a lazy day. I give gunpoint a 2.5 out of 5.

- The fun comes from trying to reach minimum moves. You're not going to like this if you're content with just finishing puzzles.

Istrolid is a custom-build kingdom, a model-kit on steroids, the heaven of Bob the Builder.
It's a challenging game, but I found most of the game to be a little dry. Why?
- The game doesn't introduce the building mechanics very well--At all, actually. I had to spend some time figuring out how to place things, rotate them, and then how well my ship would operate.
- The gameplay is a lot of point-and-click with minimal strategy. One mode is currently available, and there's nothing that really makes me salivate about playing the game.
- Many features, too little tuning. What I mean is, many parts, but there is too little depth too them.
- The battleground is pretty bland with minimal artwork (Although the artwork that is there looks fantastic and should be expanded upon)
- The AI has brawn, but apparently little brain.
"Well, then--" You might ask, "why do you recommend this?"
=
- Customization is easy and you build your fleet down to scratch
- Physics are entertaining and easy to understand
- The battlefield is open for many adjustments: (Obstacles, background, more gamemodes, lore, etc)
- The battle can get hectic, whether you're using a battlecruiser holstering many weapons, or miniature ships equipped for fast support. Lots of activity, and exciting to watch.
Sadly, while I have played only a few hours, I feel like I've already found all that the game has to deliver. I look forward to an update that greatly raises that bar.
Cheers! And good luck devs.

This is a very hard game to quantify into a catagory, genre group or ranking. Not truely a game, but not enough of an indie classic to be called "art"; to me it stands on its own as a psychological examination of life and what it means to mature from childhood to adulthood for the six sisters of this thriller/horror interactive piece.
You have one objective: get to grandma's and do not leave the path. But you have no choice but to leave the path to truely experience this game.
This is NOT a game for people who do not have patience. There is a hell of a lot of backtracking and blind searching as you uncover the clues of the characters, their habits, personalities and innocence. A completionist run for a single character can easily take away three hours while you listen to the same eerie music over and over, challenging your mental memory and the occassional flashes of the trail you've left behind while getting hopelessly lost in the forest.
Compared to a similar indie "art" game, To The Moon, this interactive title is certainly very similar in the amount of love that the development team put into this piece. But unfortunately the message isn't as clear as it could have been without being a completionist or cheating and hitting GameFAQs for a plot synapsis.
As an art deco title, it's a game that must be played at least once in your life. English Literature and Psychology Majors will get a real kick out of this title, as well people with an interest in slow-paced thriller and horror games. But other than that recommendation, think really hard before you purchase this title if it isn't on sale: it is a difficult one to recommend to casual and mainstream gamers.
I lean on the said of "yes" because I really appreciate these types of games. But then I'm a student of psychology.

Although the levels are randomly generated, which might seem like a recipe for cheep gameplay, the game is surprisingly fun and has a good difficulty slope. One of the biggest worries one might have with this game is that the enemies would sometimes spawn in inconvient places, making for annoying gameplay. This, however, is not the case at all, and that has everything to do with the way it's enemies are designed, as all of them, with the exception of few, are either not lethal 100% of the time or in motion, meaning they can always be affectively dodged. As you climb the levels, more and more  enemies are introduced, and all of them, at least that I've seen, bring something new to the table. What starts as a very simple game with minimal challenge slowly evolves into this extremely challenging game with levels that are basically labrinths with clusters of enemies and spikes that sometimes seem almost impossible to beat. Every so often there'll be a part of a level that is impossible to get past in the state you are in. For example, maybe there's a part of a level that requires TNT when you don't have any. However, it doesn't feel completely unfair because chances are, you had the oppurtunity to get TNT, but you chose a health upgrade instead. But the best quality the game has is easily how addictive it is. Every time you see the death screen displaying how many levels you got through,  it always feels like it's your job to try again and best yourself.
Pros:
+ good difficulty slope
+ addictive
+ well designed enemies
+ good controls
+ satisfying power-ups
Cons:
- sometimes impossible levels
- redundant game modes
