I like, and feel I got my money's worth out of this one on release day.  It's a game of managing tradeoffs, which I enjoy.  It's sort of a mashup of the mobile game Reigns and the boardgame Mystery of the Abbey.  I didn't particularly enjoy either of those, but smoosh them together like Shrouded Isle does and you get something that's fun.
If I had to pick a group of people this would appeal to, I'd say "boardgamers who enjoy picking apart the systems of thinkier Euro-style games."
It's very dry, in terms of presentation and player interaction.  But there are folks, and I am one of them, who hear "it's dry" and their ears perk up.  The turn to the speaker, interested, and inquire "Dry, you say?"  If you are one of those people, give this one a shot.
It's more-ish, in that when a game ends I find myself wanting to try another, but I don't see myself playing it for like 50 consecutive game-hours, either.  I expect I'll play it for a bit, put it down, and come back to it very occasionally for a game here or there, and that's fine (already got my money's worth, after all).
I've run into a couple of display bugs, neither very serious (release day, remember); they didn't lessen my enjoyment of the game in any way.  Hitting shift-B in-game will allow you to report bugs while sending a screenshot and debug logs -- something I found out from the forums but don't recall seeing mentioned in-game.
The art is--unique.  You're getting exactly what you see in the screenshots here -- sparse art in color palettes I can only describe as "unsettling."  I like the art and don't ever want to see another game using this art style, if you will pardon the contradiction.  The soundtrack is appropriately moody but not something I'd listen to on its own.  It has a vibe that reminds me a bit of György Ligeti's work.
So, yeah, overall I enjoy it and recommend it, but I think it's only going to appeal to folks with specific tastes.

Pros:
+ Very engaging, addictive game
+ Easy to just turn on and play for short bursts
+ Challenging; you really have to plan out your strategy, and even then it may not pay off
+ Real sense of accomplishment when you root out a Major Sinner
Cons:
- The system could use a lot of balancing, in terms of difficulty. You're juggling five different aspects of faith, as well as the approval of the five families, and the deity's approval. The problem is, taking the difficult route (in terms of finding traits) and just using one advisor per month may get your +10 to that aspect, and +5-15 to another aspect...but their sins take away 10-30. Using all 3 advisors can mean gaining 40 or so points between the various aspects, but losing as many as 90 points. And then you have one month to recover whatever was ruined, and you may end up with an advisor who takes away from the very aspect you're trying to recover.
- Only one difficulty level. See above. While the challenge is fun, I've gone through 40-50 times without ever making it the full three years. There are too many balls in the air, and the downsides of each action are significantly more than the upsides. I would almost say it needs to be reversed, with virtues adding 15-30 and sins taking away 1-15; as it is, there is very little chance of 'winning' except for hitting the exact sweet spot concerning RNG.
+\- Color scheme was nauseating; this has been fixed by the latest patch, which added other color schemes.

A breath of fresh air. The original Spellforce games were unique in their way and while the gimmick of those (third-person zoom in) is absent for good reason, the blend of RPG and RTS remains. The graphics are excellent and performance is rock-solid for me but it's the art style that really makes this. It has that classic Baldur's Gate feel to it and maps and cities appear to be massive in scale and feel alive and interested to explore. The voice acting is excellent throughout and is what weirdly stands out the most I feel.
Shout-out to the devs for setting up such an excellent interface. It's been a long time since I had a game where I couldn't think of a critical missing UI feature.
Gameplay-wise it's not going to be for everyone. There's a certain slow pace to both the gameplay and the initial progression. Sector-based gameplay is a bit odd as is the resource management but I'm hopeful that this improves further in the campaign. And while the overall quality appears to be excellent, you do notice a few small things that indicate that this might not be a full triple-A title and that some minor details were rushed through (voice lines not matching text, some repition in city NPCs if you really look for it, MC gender references).
All-in-all, definitely recommended. It's perhaps a sad indicator of the state of gaming that I'm this amazed by a well-developed game that's breaking new ground and marrying old-style RPGs and RTS features together into a wonderfully weird cocktail.

The game is borderline OK, perhaps even good for an indie effort. The story and visuals are nice, but be prepared to endure some severe flaws in the product. First, even after two patches, the game is very buggy on OS X (crashes, hangs, needs commandline argument tweaks to start). Second, while the game's design is generally polished, there are some critical design failures in some places. In particular, it can be pretty hard to see when you have successfully highlighted an item for interaction, as the crosshair is just a white dot that is easily mistaken for snow or shine on a reflective object. Also, the mechanics for running violate all laws of biology, gaming and common sense: when you are in danger and get stressed, you become LESS, not MORE capable of running, which also makes certain sequences needlessly frustrating. The main character must have some severe genetic defect that causes adrenalin to have the opposite effect.
Finally, a minor observation: the 3rd person narration, particularly with that voice, does not go very well with the detective/horror atmosphere. It would have been better to have the main character comment about his exploits in the 1st person (not necessarily with the most cliched Chandlerian monologue, but still...)

I purchased this game almost three years ago because I thought it had some potential. A game that focuses on building without the zombie survival silliness that was popular at the time was right up my alley. But, there wasn't much of a game yet and a lot of jankiness, see the awkward animations in the trailer for example, so I put it aside for another day.
Unfortunately almost three years later, and nothing much has changed. There's still no game there, and what game there was may have even become worse with the addition of survival elements like hunger/water meters and hostile animals. I think this is due to a lot of the gameplay features being quite shallow. Like crafting for example. There is a whole page of crafting stations and most of them do the same thing. The ones that don't, like the smeltery, add unnecessary complexity and time wasting. Yet smelteries work in the same way as Minecraft's furnaces where you stick in fuel and ore, and get ingots. Risingworld's only difference is that you have to stick in fuel and ore one at a time. Which as you imagine gets tedious and adds nothing to gameplay.
On the possitive side Risingworld has quite powerful building tools. If you are a hardcore builder type this might be worth it for you.
In summary Risingworld is missing the simple gameplay systems that interact to create interesting and complex behaviours you'd expect in a typical sandbox game.

A marriage of Super Meat Boy and Spelunky if they met on the Gameboy Color. A fun precision platformer full of tricks and traps with randomly generated, fully destructable levels. Light character-progression offers a diet rogue-lite meal. Includes a level editor and in-game level browser full of clever user-generated content. Daily and weekend runs. Lots of game modes that offer a twist for everybody. Steam leaderboard support, tight responsive controls, and thrilling gameplay.
Some of the collectible palletes in the game are downright ugly. I wish there was a way in-game to see what palette is in use and disable it from the rotation without guessing from the endless pages in the main menu. Finding "broken" palettes (ugh). There is little 'push' for the player beyond competing against your own scores or on leaderboards, so you must be score-driven to get the most out of this arcade platformer beyond a certain point.
Wall-jump and blast your way through treacherous traps and roaming robots in a series of procedurally generated, fully destructable platforming dungeons. Highly recommended.

I've noticed a lot of negative reviews lately, across all indie open-world games, so I decided to write a positive one here.
Rising World was received very well by the community! It opened up several new doors that open-world games hadn't seen before.
This is a very fun game, and I used to play it together, with my brother and sister.
It requires you to do everything, which was taken as a positive, at least when people buying games on Steam were optimistic, and looking for new aspects. For example, you have to put each ore in the furnace, add coal, then light it. After a while, you can take out the ingots.
When you chop a tree, you have to pick up the logs. You can chop the stump afterward, as well.
These were considered positives. I still enjoy those aspects of this game. That what makes it Rising World.
The terraforming is like no other. It is amazing! You can make insane mines/caves, and then build your own scaffolding/walkways.
When you go mining, the ores blend so well with the rock they're next to, it just feels realistic. There aren't sharp edges - here is iron, here is stone... it's not like that.
Rising World feels really nice! The graphics are pretty good, too.

I recommend this game and encourage you to play it for yourself.

Classic-style, loot-based dungeon crawler that feels more like a phone game, complete with microtransactions for gems. The game itself, in spite of its simplicity, scratches the right itch for quick-access RPG elements when you don't have time to navigate a 3D worldspace to get to your objective. When my rogue got one-shotted on the first floor, stuff got real. The turn-based combat is challenging, and makes you appreciate every single hp. This game certainly deserves a place in its niche.
Upon perusing the in-game cash shop, you'll find the standard slate of $1.99 to $59.99 gem packages that we've all come to loathe. Nothing kills an RPG chubby faster than an in-game cash shop. It breaks immersion every time I have to employ my self-discipline to deny myself the luxuries of bag space, rezzing my heroes, hiring new ones, etc. However, if you can shrug off the temptation, you'll probably love this game.
For PC, there are quite a few titles out there that can deliver a similar experience, minus the cash-grab. If you need a good game for a low-end PC, Forgotten Realms' Baldur's Gate comes to mind, which has even been improved upon as the genre has matured.
To the devs: You're on to something potentially amazing. A clean RPG experience will always have an eager market. FTL and Terraria (BtP) are amazing, timeless games because every player stands on equal ground. Please drop the microtransactions, put a price on your hard work, and rebalance the cash shop rewards into the game as part of its progression. With your current monetization strategy, I can't recommend this title to anyone I know.
************************************************************
************************************************************
Edit:
I've been informed that the cash shop will be shut down, and the game will be released as a paid title. This is a terrific decision - the traditional monetization model is one that we can all get behind without feeling guilty about impulsive purchasing. Game was free the first time, and I will gladly buy again upon release.

Revised review (2016-07-02):
***  Review of paid version based on evaluation key given by developer ****
The game has fared well from the updates given to it since I last tried it - lots more content and variety of things to encounter. Still plays great - responsive and looks decent. Dungeon floors are randomly generated each time you enter the dungeon. The microtransaction features have been removed, making for a much better experience.
Game play has been better balanced - you have much better survival odds now, so running out of gold is not so much or a problem as it was. Now it is the case of several things to spend it on and having to decide which is best, rather than spending it all on reviving your lost characters.
Documentation is still lacking and the tutorial is very basic. Both are supposed to be in development, and willbe welcomed when available. The interface has some tool tips, but lacks others - presumeably will be added as the game is polished.
The changes are postive enough that I have to change from a maybe to a recommended with the current version. I do hope it gets completed (and it looks to as the developer is still very actively working on it!) - it is a nicely done roguelike.
Original Review (2016-03-14):
It looks pretty decent, has low hardware requirements, and has such great potential that I really want to recommend it. Unfortunately, it appears to be designed as a requiring microtransactions to make any real progress. Documentation is lacking (tutorial hasn't been created yet, but is promised; there is no manual to explain which key does what; some routine things in othergames don't happen here - eg can only heal or regain mana in combat.)
When you go into the dungeon there is only 1 way out (other than every 5th level - maybe, I never got that far) - and that is through the morgue. Unfortuantely, characters cost 100x level gold to revive, while with a starting party you can expect to have to clear 15 to 20 rooms of monsters to earn 100 gold. Sadly your mana and health will likely run out in about one third that many rooms (or less if you run into higher level monsters...) meaning you are only going backwards unless you buy gold or crystals to revive dead characters...
If there was an alternative to yes and no, I'd choose it. The game is still in early access, so it may well change before final release. I'll try again at that time and update my review afterwards.

The cast and crew include some veterans of Seinfeld's long-running NBC sitcom Seinfeld, including writer/producers Feresten and Robin, and actors Michael Richards (Seinfeld character Cosmo Kramer), Patrick Warburton (Seinfeld character David Puddy), and Larry Miller (who plays the title character on the Seinfeld episode "The Doorman"). TRAUMA is an experimental non-game. You're navigating the subconscious of a woman who has been severely injured in an automobile accident. The dreamscape is presented as a storyboard of compelling photography. Imagine MYST with a camera.
The game teaches you navigational mouse gestures as you advance through the four non-linear chapters of the story. There are goals and nine Polaroid photographs to collect in each chapter, but no compelling reason to collect them. The goals are a framework that encourages you to explore the landscape of each chapter.
TRAUMA is not fun, but it is interesting. If you like experimental gameplay, you may enjoy this. There is a prologue video (the accident); I wish it had an epilogue, as well. A final shot of the patient waking up, or dying, or *something* would be a welcome final chapter. But as I write this, I realize that perhaps that is the point. TRAUMA tells the story of Life, Interrupted.

At it's most basic, The Shrouded Isle has you using randomly applied traits to keep balance between the houses.  Each season has you picking five people - one from each house - and putting them to work for you.  Based on their traits, they may raise obedience, fervor, ignorance, etc. - or lower it.  You learn a bit about each of these people as you play and at the end of a season you have an important decision to make - which one is a sinner and needs to be sacrificed.  After all, you're a High Priest and your god expects something!  Sometimes you may get tasked with raising a certain trait, sacrificing a specific type of person, or other mini-quests.  You'll also encounter various people from the houses who may have problems they want you to solve (such as a son getting arrested).
Graphically there isn't much to The Shrouded Isle.  And that's a good thing.  It looks great the way it is and the minimal design adds a certain charm to the somewhat dark nature of the game.  Personally I found the soundtrack to be pretty good, too - especially for a small indie title.
I really have very little to say that's bad about the title - the price being the only real issue.  While the game is enjoyable and I didn't mind paying it, it may be slightly steep for some folks for the amount of content.  But that aside, I easily recommend this game if you're into strategy, hidden identity, or other similar type titles.

Gameplay is fairly straightforward - you pick one advisor from each house at the start of each season, then use up to three of them each month (three to a season) to balance out the 'virtue' levels of your village.
Each potential advisor has one virtue (which will boost one of the bars) and one vice (which will drop one of the bars). Hidden amongst the advisors are eight who have unforgivable vices that you're trying to hunt down and sacrifice at the end of the season.
Alongside this you're also balancing out your reputation with each of the houses, who tend to get annoyed when you sacrifice their people or fail to consult their advisor. Let a house get too annoyed with you and your career (and life) will come to an end.
On the whole it's a nice little logic puzzler / deduction game. Presentation is good - the monochrome grows on you after a while (and you can switch between three colours). Music is nice and atmospheric, with each house having it's own signature tune.
The game generally takes around 45 - 60 minutes for a full three year game. There's no save feature, although it's not really needed - it's the kind of game you can dip into while listening to a podcast or have an hour to spare.
Varied enough to keep you interested throughout the campaign. After that there is multiplayer if that's your forte

I find this game a bit shallow, at the very least at this point on release. Basically you have several meters all running down based on who you choose during the three turns / months per season. The game is fundamentally one very similar to concentration, with villager virtue / vice instead of number / icon matching cards.
Layered on top of that though is two states of unknown, the first is where you haven't seen a virture or vice, and the second when you know which meter the virtue or vice affects. Kind of like learning what suite a card belongs to in a memory game, then next time learning what the number of that card actually is.
The various kinds of virtue and vice are cosmetic really, primarily there are three increments of value per virtue or vice, with the greatest value having the most impact. Which is to say for virtues they are the best villager for increasing the related meter, and for vices they are one of your specific 9 traitors.
It's got more kinship to the game Werewolf in that aspect, as each villager is rather like a role card and there are traitors in your midst to be killed off each turn / season. They're just targets though, sitting there to be killed. Granted if you actively used them before realizing who they are, then you've been draining your meters at a much, much faster rate than normal.
It doesn't really sound all that uninteresting, except guesswork is punished in this game. If you can't point and show that a traitor is obviously a traitor then the family house they come from becomes especially irate, draining the meter faster than normal to penalize guessing. Which isn't necessarily so bad, but you *also* don't get the meter bonuses for killing a traitor either so you get double shafted for guesswork.
After awhile you can basically know what a villager / card is with high certainty, although it is hard to guarantee anything early on when you know practically nothing of the playing board. Yet the guesswork will punish you for trying. The other issue to deal with is that RNG can end up with some houses rather loaded with traitors, and even if you miraculously uncover them all, killing them in a row is punished because the family house will riot if you sacrifice from them twice in a row, or more.
You can try to reach the end of the game without going out of your way to kill the traitors, and simply use the most optimal vilagers to maintain your meter balance. The game is in a sense more about how many of these traitors you can kill before the timer runs out. Completing the mysterious voice's commandments can actually end the run, as the meter threshold immediately gets shifted and might put you in a situation where you have too many meters to balance in one season.
Which is odd since, there isn't an actual bonus for killing the specified traitor over the other ones. Killing all 8 other traitors first doesn't cause you any unexpected problems, either. So success may be best achieved by avoiding the voice's tasks and eliminating the other traitors first. I don't know if the game's ending requires you to follow the voice's commandment's only though, and avoid killing traitors before the appointed time. Frankly that's a lot of RNG to wade through for not much gain, IMHO.
Oh, and the mix of virtue and vice on a villager doesn't seem to have much in the way of restrictions, so you can end up with some runs where you can't find a villager to give you an even break on points. Others you might find three houses have villagers that actually give you more overall points to your meters, and in the early stages of the game. Town events also aren't particularly common or interesting that I've found.
Closing note:
I don't strongly feel this is a game that shouldn't be recommended given what you get for the price it is on sale for.
However, I do feel the consumer should have a good idea of what you're getting into as this isn't a very high replayability game.  Somewhat similarly simple games like Werewolf have more lifespan because they are social games where the group of people you play with affects gameplay the most dramatically, and what happens on subsequent playthroughs could change dramatically despite the relatively bare and basic game framework.
As this is a single player game, I rather reluctantly give it a thumbs down as there simply isn't that much ground to tread with the content provided.  The price is about right, but it would probably be best to still be warned that the depth is shallower than it may appear to be.

I'll admit, Dawn of War II cames as a bit of shock to me. I rushed out to buy this game right away because of how much I loved the first Dawn of War series. When I got this one, I was surprised to see that the mechanics had been totally changed and the campaign is basically a squad based action RPG. Which, I'm fine with. The game was a lot of fun and well worth a playthrough. But calling this game an Real-Time Strategy game would be EXTREMELY misleading. Even calling it Company of Heroes reskinned for Warhammer 40,000 isn't very accurate, because Company of Heroes incorporates resource management and base building.
Rather than dwelling on what this game isn't, I want to focus on what it is. It has a compelling story, great visuals and a very interesting leveling up system for your team. While the battle interface isn't fluid, it's managable and allows you to keep track of your team in chaotic firefights. The bosses usually require varied strategy to defeat, and you need to consider your loadout carefully before each mission. Going up against a tank boss without equipping Avitus with a missile launcher will make the battle much harder. A word of caution is that I experienced frequent frame-rate drops during battles. As I can run Doom 2016 at maximum settings without so much as a stutter, I have to believe that the problem has to do with the game as opposed to my machine.
I didn't play much of multiplayer. Mostly I did the arena survival mode, which was a fun little time waster. Be warned, however, expect to get yelled at... a lot, by other players in this mode for not holding up your part of the battle. I understand that there's a skirmish mode in this game, but its pretty lackluster and shallow. Multiplayer seems to largely be an extension of that.
Overall, I'd recommend this game if you want to try an ARPG that uses RTS elements. I've logged a lot of hours on this game through multiple playthroughs and I don't regret it at all. If you're looking for the spiritual successor to Dawn of War, look elsewhere. This will not satisfy the RTS itch you're trying to scratch.

3 Hours in edit:
I've lost prematurely a few times now and earned one bad ending, and at this point I think I have a good idea how of this plays.
Put simply this is a game of deduction and risk-management. To survive you must appease all five Houses while also maintaining five pious traits among the population — if any of these 10 things falls below a threshhold for two turns in a row it's game over.
With any decision affecting many of these things at once, you must juggle many variables in your head to hedge the outcome. For example, you may strongly suspect a person of embezzelment but have insufficient proof. Having them work during their time as advisor may expose their vice and result in a profitable sacrifice, but also may not, in which case you'll need a failsafe sacrifice from another house with a petty vice (like shyness). At the same time employing the embezzler will unavoidably damage Discipline, encouraging you to recoup the loss with another more virtuous advisor from your Discipline-centric House, which at the same time will help repair lost favor from killing their family member last season, and on and on... With the razor-sharp balancing you'll find yourself thinking of every detail to make things work.
It's a very unique system with a board game feel to it, engrossing to the point where I quickly forgot I was basically just clicking through menus. People who expect tactile gameplay should stay away, but people who like puzzles and strategy should enjoy it.
It's not without a few (very minor) rough edges though. For instance flavor text gives very strong hints at a person's virtue/vice. This is a nice touch but at some points it makes things painfully obvious — I once had an event that singled out a person for influencing the public by making paintings, but for whatever reason it was still left to me to discover they were an artist through rote espionage. If I'd sacrificed her before jumping through those hoops the masses would have been unconvinced.
Still, that's a trivial complaint compared to the whole experience. If you're into puzzles and you like the art style, I wholeheartedly recommend it at the current price.

Let me start off by saying that this is is a great tower defense game. This is more difficult than many of the other tower defense games out there, yet easycomers or young children should not fret since their is an easy campaign in addition to the normal campaign. The game also features an endless mode, a survival mode, and a sandbox mode. The missions are non repetitive and usually include new maps with new spawning locations. The graphics, at times, can be beautiful, but are often hindered by the game's dark atmosphere. There are many things I found that set Revenge of the Titans apart from the other tower defense games. For starters the game places you in the game with a base that you must defend and roads leading from the spawn areas to the base. One would assume the enemies would follow these paths? That person would be wrong as the enemies travel along the path only to increase speed but swiftly disengage the path to attack nearby towers or form a direct path to the base. You heard me correctly, the towers are destructible, easily so in fact. The towers must also reload ammunition, slowly I should add. All these things add to the difficulty of the game, yet I am thoroughly pleased as this adds unique challenges and situations and surprises to the game which allow the game to remain a fun challenge, even after hours of playing. This leads me to the research screen. After each level, the player is rewarded with medals and a research point. The player can then use the point in the most advance research screen I have ever seen in an indie game. This screen feature a myriad of choices and subcategories. One fault i must find is that although the player can research towers, these said towers can not be upgraded, other than the placement of other upgrade towers nearby that can also stack in boosting power up to 4 times. After an hour or so of gameplay, I am throughly pleased with this game and recommend that others pick up this game if on sale, as I find some difficuly in justifying $9.99 for a game which resides in the overflooded quantity of tower defense games on the steam marketplace. Unless you are a large fan of tower defense games, I find that picking this game up for less thatn $5.00 is a sweet spot, as I was able to use the %75 off coupon to receive the game for $2.49.

A very simplistic hidden identity game. Each villager has a Vice and a Virtue. A Vice is a detriment to your village's resources, and a Virtue is a buff in addition to the villager's House action. So, you might have someone whose House rewards Penitence, with a Virtue that rewards Ignorance, and a Vice that penalizes Devotion. As you assign villagers to actions, you slowly uncover what their Vice or Virtue is. You also increase their House's approval rating, which provides another means of discovering Vices and Virtues.
The payoff of discovering the hidden Vices and Virtues is twofold: You can make more efficient resource gathering decisions, and you can also figure out the best villagers to sacrifice to your god, who wants to root out particular Vices over the course of the game.

I'll probably give it a few more plays to grab achievements and experience more of the choose-your-own-adventure story prompts. Kitfox Games' The Shrouded Isle is a management game in which you are the cult leader of a small village, drenched in Lovecraftian lore.
To appease the slumbering old god Chernobog who watches over your village, you have to sacrifice one villager every season. The game plays out over the course of three years and can come to an early end should you fail to meet the requirements of either the gods or the villagers, or even both. You have multiple ways in which you can fail, for example I decided to side with one family over the others, resulting in one of them drugging me and presumably killing me, thus ending the game. Another time I was unable to keep obedience levels high enough and was thus forcibly exiled, although with the possibility of the old god potentially wiping out the town and even the whole world, maybe that was a good thing...
The five families that govern the village make up the core gameplay, you will never be able to effectively balance their satisfaction levels but if they end up rebellious and you end up unable to please them by the end of the seasons, then it will result in death, as mentioned previously.
Each family is in charge of one of the factors you'll be managing throughout the game. They are in charge as follows: Keggnis, ignorance, Iosefka, fervor, Cadwell, discipline, Efferson, penitence, and Blackborn, obedience. They all have a certain amount of power over the town such as the Blackbornes being in charge of the guardsmen of the village and the Caldwells being the wealthiest merchant family.
These families will frequently accuse each other of potential sins, sending you letters asking for assistance in the matter, the first one I recieved was a younger Blackborn informing me of her mother writing letters to an 'uncle' outside of the village, which is strictly forbidden. I chose to publicly reward the young Blackborn, shaming the mother but raising my reputation with them. Then there was the time a Caldwell was accused of theft, which she surprisingly confessed to, despite knowing that it was a sin worthy of death, however she was great at raising penitence so I kept her around until she was no longer of use.
Each member of the families has a chance to have a virtue or vice, effecting how they go about punishing potential sinners. This is all procedurally generated too, so no playthrough will be the same, there's always something different. Sometimes you end up with a family member who has nothing but vices and vice versa, heck you can even rename each individual family member, making each run feel more unique.
Depending on the satisfaction level of the families, some will let you inquire about a family member up to two times to discover any hidden traits or fully uncover any already discovered ones. You're then required to choose one advisor from each family for each season, decide which one gets to carry out work for one of the three months of the season, and ultimately which one to sacrifice.
This was the part where the game forced your hand, if you weren't able to discover a truly sinful trait of any of your chosen advisors, then the villagers would be none too pleased, feeling it unfair that the chosen sacrifice had made no transgressions. Even worse, if you chose a member of the same family two seasons in a row, then they would be furious, a surefire chance to make them turn against you.
Artistically, the game has some absolutely gorgeous design. The only comparison think of for it is Darkest Dungeon, but stripped of colours and relegated to only two tones, out of the three different colour palettes the game presents you with. Personally the default palette suited me.
From time to time, Chernobog whispers to you in your dreams, demanding that a certain factor be increased or the sacrifice of a particular individual. Of course being an old god he just has to be vague, not giving you the name but instead the trait of the person whose lifeforce they desire.
Being procedurally generated, you're bound to see the same events and traits pop up time and again, but this is really the only drawback I can think of. More varied events could fix that.
For a short game, and for the low asking price, The Shrouded Isle is an easy recommendation for me, if not for the beautiful art style alone. Even more so if you're a fan of management games like these, or if you just love the works of Lovecraft.

As a French Canadian myself, I found this game to be incredibly immersive and wonderful.
I played it in its native French language and was delighted at the authencity of the accents and patois used in the dialogue. Of course that goes without saying since the studio that made this game is from Quebec.
(If you understand French, then I highly suggest you go to the options and make the switch for better immersion)
The game itself was very fun as a light survival/heavy exploration genre where you try to piece together what happened to a very small village in the north of Quebec in the early 70s.
Since this is an exploration/survival game, there is a gathering and crafting element, however the gathering isn't annoying and the crafting only occurs on certain objects or places, not on your person, so it's more fluid that way.
It's clear that this game was crafted as a labour of love because it is filled with tiny details that just make the world so believable. All of the items and details you see in the houses, the shop, etc are all period accurate and even gave me nostalgia for a decade I wasn't even born in.
I would say the only downside would be how they handled loading areas.
For a game this immersive, freezing in place and seeing a standard circle logo animation while waiting for the next area to load can really take you out of the game in an incredibly forceful way. I understand that the developers are working on making the loading smoother, so I hope they manage to do it because that's really all this game needs at the moment.
Kudos to Parabole and I can't wait to see what else they do with this game and I hope they make it a series.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of the Indie Action game Just Get Through. Just Get Through was released on Steam on January 30, 2015 by Developer/Publisher Retrific.
(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
Great fun to be had here for under $5. Highly replayable. 4/5
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
This is a great little indie game that may have slipped by you last year. Just Get Through me is kind of an interesting little game. It's tons of fun, has plenty of game modes and can become heavily addictive! The randomly generated levels are fun enough on their own, just trying to get through (as the title suggests). You plot your way through the course and avoid the traps to get to the other side. You even have dynamite to help blast away traps/walls. There is also a Daily Run, that is the same for everyone and you can compare high scores both globally and across friends. Chart your runs, your high scores, and have a blast. The graphics have a fun retro feeel (you can even unlock different color schemes!), the gameplay is simple and fun (and controller supported too!). This is a great little gem that may have passed you by in 2015. It's already a great deal at under $5, and in the upcoming Steam sale this could be one of the better bargains. 4/5, worth it for sure.

My "review" as a solo player.
AKA: Things I like, things I don't in my singleplayer experience.
FYI: Haven't finished the game yet. Still playing through! Definately deserving of a positive review and definately worth playing.
Things I Like:
- Multiple factions that look different, have different units and abilities and different campaigns. USA, Germany, Japan, Russia, Britain. All the main players!
- Units have inventories (even individual soldiers and vehicle storage). You can pick up enemy weapons, ammo and gear, you can have units run out of ammo, allowing for some battlefield scavenging and logistics like no other game I've played.
- Some campaign missions have different objectives to the old capture and push forward. Some are infantry focused skirmishes, some are even defence missions where you have to hold out for a certain amount of time before the enemies stop coming and your reinforcements come. Opening more of the map for you to counter attack, retaking your overrun positions and taking the enemy outposts!
- It's realistic and historically accurate in terms of weapons and vehicles as far as I know. Very cool. Unlike CODWW2. Which is something I like for sure.
- Being able to repair even the enemy's vehicles and use them as your own! Very cool to have some Brits take a German Tank and not have to worry about wasting the points buying a tank.
- As a certified 'turtle strategy' champion, I can confirm that it feels good to reinforce positions in this game. Lots of defence options including mines, barbed wire, sand bags, tank traps etc.
- Battles are long and take time. I like this because short battles wouldn't have that sense of warfare like the larger ones do. Also, with this being the only singleplayer mode, it would make the campaign seem very short if the map was just a small square filled with tanks like something out of War Thunder.
- You can play as each individual unit too! The 'Direct Control' feature makes it play like a top down shooter, like Asteroids if it wasn't old as hell. Of course, you can also pan the camera to a more third person position, but the camera doesn't follow where you aim. This feature, however, has been super useful, unique and fun!
Things I didn't like:
- Playing maps that had the same objective. A lot of them, at least to begin with, you are tasked with taking objectives. If you take a set of 3 objectives, you get more units and the enemies send a wave at you. I remember being quite disappointed when I got stuck on a mission, decided to see what other campaigns are like and was met with the same scenario with a different location and factions. The minimaps are all too similar in those missions with the objectives in slanted rows of 3 all the way up the map. If all of the campaigns are anything like the USA campaign, then that means I would have to play about 3 of these in a row before getting something new, and even then, they could just feel like a reskin of the ones I've played. I'm not sure. I haven't finished the game as levels take quite a while.
- Units being locked to what mission you are on. E.g. There is a mission for the USA where it's more infantry focused, so you have different types of infantry units that aren't included in the regular battles. I don't care if I don't need shotgunners in a long range battle or Officers or a special forces team, but it's wierd that I had to play half-way through the USA campaign just to see them for the first time. Maybe it's for historical accuracy. I'm not sure.
- Expensive tanks being destroyed in a single hit, despite being hit from the front. That's never fun!
- I don't feel rewarded by completing missions as much as I should do. In the last 10 minutes of a possibly hour long level, you can just tell you're gonna win. All you get for that is a window saying congrats, with your losses and theirs and some Steam achievements. If I've killed 3 times as many of their units and destroyed 3 times as many of their vehicles, you'd expect more than that! I think this could be improved upon. Maybe a system of upgrades or unlocks for your faction. Maybe this is where they could add those Officers and shotgunners in.
- Not many modes. You got skirmish missions (I've been calling it the campaign because you can't choose map or factions or teams like other 'skirmish' modes I've played. It's just missions in a set order.) and that's it. Wish there was more.
That said, this game is great.
They have had a sequel out recently, but I heard a rumour that it doesn't have a singleplayer unless you buy the 'Airbourne' DLC. If that's the case, I probably won't get that. At least, not at full price.
Anyway, if you liked Company of Heroes and maybe wanted more depth and a longer experience, or if you liked Commandos but wanted it on a larger scale, then I can definately recommend this for you!

I happenned to randomly discover this game and Oh Boy I already love it.
First the graphics appealed to me for some shady reason, but the cherry on the cake is that you can choose between three color patterns [Yellow / Green / Purple] depending on your tastes and eye sensitivity, which keeps this oppressive and really neat atmosphere.
Edit - After playing for quite a bit with the purple colors I see everything in yellow on my screen, odd but neat.
As for the game itself, I had a few concerns, like the longevity, the gameplay or the story, so I'm going to address theses points one by one.
- Longevity, my first run lasted 2 seasons before getting overthrown, considering you need to reach the end of three year, I can assure you, this will be awfully challenging, but in a good way, you need to be goddam crafty and anticipate ahead.
Edit - I made it after two years I think ? Now the game tells me I need to survive 11 years ? Unsure what's going on but the balance is easier to handle than I previously thought, the side objectives now are tricky.
- Gameplay, it's really simple and yet so complex : You pick 5 household heads between the 6 available per household (30 in total) each season to form your council and you sacrifice one at the end of said season.
The thing is, each one of them have perks and quirks affecting the outcome of the Discipline, Ignorance and so on scale balance.
I don't have to say that when one balance or some household affection gets too low, you get a bloody game over.
- Story, there's barely any of it in the way that people are used to, the events happen within the town depending on the actions of your council and actually brings you in a deviate way a mental picture of the town, I heard there was multiple endings and so far I saw some little dreams aswell exhorting to do this or that.
Overall, an amazing game simply because of it's atmosphere, cunning plays and the Iosefka / Bloodborne reference in it.
Also the fact that you can chill infront of it without any timer pressure is really relaxing and allows to treat it like a side game that you can hop on and off if you do desire without any constraint.

If Cyberpunk is currently your thing and Half-Life's Source Engine has always been your thing: then I think you are probably going to find E.Y.E. Divine Cybermancy to be a very interesting game. If a Cyberpunk, FPS/RPG, with some of the most ♥♥♥♥ed up achievements aren't enough to entice you to play this game, then I don't know what will.
My friend is a really big Cyberpunk fanatic and one day, he started showing me his progress in the game and I have to be honest - the Source Engine was noticable (almost straight away), but I feel like that isn't a bad thing, since it adds unique features, such as: a few RPG Elements (Levelling-Up, Research/Skills and Stats, Purchasing Item...), Psi Force (A variety of mental/phsycic powers: sort of acts as the games Magic system),
Not only is it a Dark Cyberpunk world, but you can get really cool Augmentations/Upgrades for your character! (Enhance your Vital Organs, Limbs, Nerves, Skeleton, Natural Resistence and much, much more).
The GENERAL combat system is what you'd expect from a Source Engine-based game, however; the extra features, selection of weapons, qwerky stat system, Psi Force abilities and the option to enhance your body with augmentions, just makes the combat a lot more vercetile, than any FPS or RPG that I have ever played.

Trauma may seem deceptively simple at first: it's a flash game about exploring the dreams of a girl who's been through an accident. It will probably take 30 min to an hour to finish the main path, yet there are hidden secrets and alternate ways to end a dream.
Trauma is all about exploration and is very light on the challenge. It plays like an out of body experience. The main puzzle is navigation through a set of mouse gestures. The girl will narrate the dream logic as she recognizes signs from her real past. Each dream has a core dilemma that needs to be solved.
The light gameplay is more than compensated by the depth of story ideas. Through each dream, you start knowing more about the protagonist and by the end, symbols start falling into place. The dreams are interconnected; you will find recurring ideas, and some solutions are applicable in more than one situation.
Trauma is best played right before bed. It will make you think about the stuff that goes through your head at night.

Its gameplay is very focused on stealth, although there's plenty of ways to finish each level. If you like frontal combat you'll find this game very challenging and difficult, but even if you alert the enemies you can always go back to a semi-stealth gameplay. This doesn't mean that you must always be silent or that the enemies are unbeatable -you can always get to defeat most of them if you want to or just stay in the shadows and be a quiet boy. Every mission can be replayed to accomplish all main and secondary goals, visit all the corners or just do things in different ways.
The level design, graphics, overall atmosphere, special effects, voices, music and sounds are all excellent. The cutscenes are very artistic and don't interfere too much in the pace of the game.
The gameplay is not totally flawless but it is very good; you won't be banging your head against the wall, Styx always goes where you want him to go. He doesn't get stuck nor moves when you want him still. You can always choose what skills to improve to match your own gameplay style. The frontal combat is a little bit strange and Styx feels slow when trying to run from a bunch of guards but again, stealth is the name of the game and that is not really a problem.
I recommend this game if you like good stealth, dark stories, good parkour and exploring different paths to get to the same goal. By the way: there are no stupid sidekicks, no foolish minigames, no upgradeable weapons, no non-sense vendors or stores along the way, no funny costumes, no princesses to save and no... no female characters at all (strange but true).

Not only has Cyanide Studio been the sole provider of proper Games Workshop Studio properties, after their CEO (Games Workshop) went nutters and gave the license to nearly everyone with a buck and a development team after Relic (RIP you glorious ♥♥♥♥ers) went under, they've taken the ball and not only rolled with it to it's natural RPG conclusion, but have excelled at it.
Of Orcs and Men, where you are first introduced to Styx and the mythology they've established, is a welcomed breath of air (in a stale monogamous relationship of mechanics that are supposed to mirror story, that is the current character driven action adventure of copy paste)
Styx is a story told in a 3D world in which you are free to move in any typical action-character game, however what sets this apart is the experience given by Cyanyde Studios from their previous (and held in high esteem with this reviewer's opinion) games - Namely, Game of Thrones & Of Orcs and Men - that focus (and streght that carries) on the character instead of the mechanics.
Styx is a goblin. Possibly the worst goblin and only goblin, Not only is he (possibly) the only goblin, but he like us were created without seeming purpose, and the search for said purpose is the main drive - and proper plot - of this story.
While the gameplay mechanics reinforce the frailty of our shorter-than-short protagonist (antagonist?) is the main selling point, what really drives this game home, is the EXCELLENT writring by Cyanide, that has proven time and time again that they can make a true character driven game - aside from their yearly pro-cycling installment (which by the way, also is hallmark)
You are the assassin Styx, through and through, which is a rare thing to say these days.
Cyanide has come a long way since the '12 installment of Game of Thrones (which again, was a really good story for Fans of the series) and they show no sign of stopping.
Personally, I could do with more stories from the ultra-cynical-only-out-for-himself-trick-or-die-goblin Styx, and maybe if we're lucky. the Bloodjaw clan.
Make no mistake however, these games are - unlike the Telltale Games variant which might be classified as interactive novels - full-blown video game (camera over) shoulder to shoulder, and I could not be happier about that fact.

A Indie styled platformer with some unique mechanics and a decent story arc. It keeps gameplay fresh by introducing new alterations to the levels that force you to use your tools in different ways. The bosses, while typically looking pretty great, are the most tedious parts of this game. Between those and several indiana jones-esque running levels, the games dificulty level not only curves up, but ANGLES up. A few hours in and it goes from a somewhat casual game to meatboy like brutality. Only this isn't meatboy, your controls are super floaty and the tools don't always go where you expect them, making you yell obscenities at your screen. The ending and final boss left me unfulfilled for the 10 or so hours I put in. Still a decent game, but I wouldn't be surprised if tons of people start this game and then abandon it when the dificulty spike leaves them throwing a controller into the wall. Not reccommending it due to that, but it is well made, didn't crash, and I played through it to completion, so clearly nothing offended me so much to quit playing.

I tried very hard to like this game but I just couldn't. It feels dated and clunky. The combat system is a joke, it's basically QTE without any prompts. It consists of clicking 1-3 times at the exact right moment and hoping that you don't get struck while in the kill animation. Stealth kills involve holding your foe down. letting him squirm for an arbitrary amount of time before you decide to stab his face or break his neck. I understand wanting to make stealth kills take a little longer to be riskier, but why make me hold down a button and put a guy in an arm lock for 5 seconds? Why not just make the kill animation a longer than the "loud" kill?
The "parkour" was also very clumsy. You'll miss ledges you should be able to grab I had one where my hands went higher than the ledge but he wouldn't grab it), and as many people have pointed out, you can't turn corners while hanging on a ledge. There is also little incentive to not killing everyone in the area. There are "treasures" scattered about, and to find them you'll need to murder everyone in sight. This encourages exploration I guess, but with such a poor combat system and illogical (and time consuming) stealth-kill system, I really didn't want to explore and kill everyone.
Finally, the story had potential. It looked like it would be dark and gritty, even creepy. I can handle slow exposition, but my problem here was that there were numerous failed attempts at humor in a game that should have been more serious. Or at least, actually funny. Styx just looked like a dummy, and I don't care to play a game as a dummy.
In the end, I got a refund. This has been done WAY better before.

The game has some exciting ideas and presents some really cool plot hooks, but honestly fails to deliver on any of them in a satisfying way. I initially bought the game because the setting and driving mechanics really pulled me in, but really the driving never really advances into anything more than filler time in an already short game.
The survival aspects similar to The Long Dark are fairly mild. Heat becomes the only meter you ever really need to worry about and most of the time that just serves to prevent a roadblock until you get an item to fix it or provide a sense of urgency. I played through the entire game never managing my stress or health until the very end.
The writing of the plot really just tried to hammer everything in and the mystery aspect of the story really fell apart. The clues leading up to the big reveal just were not enough to solve anything yourself and when you finally figure everything out, it's too obtuse to have ever hoped to figure it out yourself. The plot runs along multiple threads, but when they come together, only one plotline really has anything to do with the big mystery. The others just explain small details.
Overall, I can't back the cost for a 5-7 hour game, especially when I really felt like even that time was more than it needed.

This is a 4-star/4.5-star game that was completely ruined by its terrible, terrible, terrible, stupid ending sequence.
Obviously, I put my time in on this game.  I played for far too many hours before the game was complete because I thought maybe I was just missing part of the gameplay.  (I was playing The Long Dark beta around the same time, and the Kona beta seemed to have more of a story in place.  Those elements, however, were isolated but connected just enough to make me think I was just missing something, so I kept looking for more.)
I put the game aside until it was complete.  Having explored much of the basic area already, when I returned, much of the environment was well-tread due to my play during the beta.
Here's what I enjoyed about the final game:
-  frequently clever, funny narration (not The Stanley Parable, but within the detective genre context, witty)
-  great journaling tool
-  the snowmobile (the absolute highlight of the game)
-  parallel storylines, both of which were engaging
***SPOILERS BELOW***
After finally exploring all the locations south of the ice wall and collecting as many clues as I could find, I headed north, presumably to investigate the victim's cabin, collect any remaining clues, and solve that mystery.
Abruptly, the story-driven game I had been playing for 14-hours turned into a bullsh*t boss stage.  The investigation was over.  The story was over with a quick Scooby-Doo summary of the game-long mystery.
The controls are not at all set-up for the fast-paced shooter horrorshow mini-game that followed.  The ghost wolves are not easily dispatched as the targeting system lacks the accuracy to make it an enjoyable challenge.  Running with the gun is a bit of a hit-or-miss proposition.  Even though I searched everywhere and collected everything, I had nowhere near enough ammo. Reloading took forever.  No opportunities to restock vital supplies.  Awkward and frequent pauses in the action to use first aid/painkillers.  Frequent deaths, and completely repetitive.  No idea where to go, how to get there, or when it might end.
These can be fantastic qualities in a game like Alien: Isolation.  It's a terrible quality in a journal-and-evidence collection game.
It is possible that I could have reconfigured all of my controls to make the action-filled experience more enjoyable (and successful), but I don't even care.  I didn't buy this game to have a first-person shooter experience.  I wanted an experiential, cerebral mystery, set in the snowy far north.  That's the game I was interested in playing when I bought Kona.
The end sequence was a complete failure.  I'm guessing it ocurred for one of two reasons: (1) it was a lazy solution to storytelling that ran into a dead end, or (2) the game's creators wanted to build their portfolio of programming/development skills.  Either way it was incongruous with the entire story and look/feel of the the rest of the game.
I couldn't be more disappointed.

Es el año 1970, al norte de Canadá, una tormenta azota el pequeño pueblo de Atamipek Lake. Somos un detective casi retirado llamado Carl Faubert, quien viene en busca de un cliente para ayudarle a encontrar a los culpables de cometer delitos contra su propiedad. Recién arribando al pueblo el asunto se sale de control, y vemos como una serie de eventos nos sumergen en la intriga de un sinfín de preguntas sin resolver.
Kona logra atraparnos desde el inicio con una excelente narrativa, una trama llena de misterio y búsquedas de objetos; a veces los mitos son mas que leyendas, y el invierno es implacable…
Jugabilidad
Lo mejor de Kona es que nos da la libertad de explorar la mayoría de lugares del mapa sin un orden específico, hay algunas partes donde no podremos ir puesto que necesitaremos de algún abrigo para repeler el frió o de una moto-nieve para llegar a lugares lejanos con mucha nieve, pero en general, tenemos libertad de ir donde queramos.
Al comenzar el juego llegamos a un pueblo que parece desolado (esto lo confirmamos al avanzar), todas las casas están a distancias largas una de otra, tras descubrir la escena de un asesinato, inicia nuestra aventura detectivesca y  vamos a los primeros rompecabezas del juego (que son súper sencillos). Más que rompecabezas, se trata de buscar objetos escondidos, necesarios para poder seguir adelante con la historia, conforme encontramos cosas importantes (pruebas, objetos, notas) vamos rellenando una libreta de notas que Carl carga consigo.
La primera impresión en Kona es lo bien lograda que es su atmósfera, estamos en un área muy fría, y todos los detalles son tomados en cuenta, el esfuerzo puesto en la ambientación rinde sus frutos, a pesar de que no es una bestialidad con respecto a gráficos, Kona logra meternos en la experiencia fácilmente, la sensación de desolación y de que algo anda mal se siente en la atmósfera, te la trasmite eficientemente.
Pero en ese sentido no es perfecto, su mejor característica se ve opacada por tiempos de carga sumamente molestos cada vez que entramos a una propiedad, apenas cruzamos el portón de alguna casa, un circulo comienza a dar vueltas en la pantalla mientras se renderizan los objetos de la propiedad (la casa, graneros, garajes, etc.).
Jugamos a Kona yendo de casa en casa a lo largo del pueblo, todo el mundo parece haberse esfumado y en cada hogar siempre hay una historia que escudriñar, alguna pista para seguir, o algún descubrimiento macabro sobre el cual tomar nota para investigar.
Utilizar el teclado y el ratón se siente bien. La experiencia con mando, (control de Xbox 360) no es mala pero podría mejorarse, manejar el inventario con un mando puede tornarse algo frustrante.
Mecánicas
En Kona no hay muchas cosas nuevas, tiene un sistema modesto de crafteo –que sólo se centra en los objetos necesarios para la historia, por dar un ejemplo –LEVE SPOILER: vamos a encontrar un imán, después, adelante en el juego, encontraremos una cadena pequeña, uniendo estos dos objetos, creamos una cadena-imán que nos sirve para alcanzar un ítem que se encontraba en un rió congelado –FIN SPOILER.
Debido al frió Carl podría desorientarse o perder la concentración, lo cual hace que corra menos tiempo y posteriormente baje su salud, hay que ponerle un ojo a este detalle. Adentrarse en las zonas boscosas bajo una ventisca puede afectar el bienestar del personaje, lo bueno (y lo aburrido) es que rápidamente en el juego podemos hacernos con ropa muy acogedora que nos quita esas preocupaciones de encima.
A lo largo del mapa se encuentran fogatas, o las estufas y  chimeneas en las casas del pueblo, sirven como fuente de calor y también se guardar el progreso del juego cuando nos acercamos a ellas. Estas fuentes de calor siempre están apagadas, y necesitamos madera y cerillos para poder encenderlos, lo aburrido acá es que ambos objetos necesarios (o todos en general)  abundan mucho en el juego y pocas veces sientes alguna presión con respecto al apartado de supervivencia.
La recolección de pistas no requiere de mucho ingenio, pues todo lo tenemos a la mano literalmente, dentro de las distintas casas del pueblo hallamos muchas cosas para investigar, y uno de las características principales de la trama es la “habilidad” que tiene Carl de revivir hechos que pasaron en algunos lugares, como flashbacks donde él puede ir a un momento especifico y ver algo que paso en ese lugar, lo cual aporta datos importantes o información en nuestra búsqueda.
Al inicio del juego invertiremos mucho tiempo en nuestro vehículo, yendo de aquí para allá buscando el siguiente punto de interés que continúe avanzando la historia, El auto de Carl tiene la función de puede ser utilizado para guardar objetos de interés una vez nuestro inventario (la mochila de Carl) esté completamente lleno.
Gráficos y Sonido
Visualmente no es sobresaliente, pero no podemos negar que la ambientación y la atmósfera son suficientes para que nos metamos de lleno en la experiencia de juego (hasta que llegamos a los tiempos de carga mencionados al inicio).  Lo jugamos con los gráficos al máximo con un Core i5, 8gb y una GTX 1060 de 6gb, con pocas caídas en los cuadros por segundo y algunos dientes de sierra –en el vehículo.
El sonido es muy bueno, escuchas el viento, el crujir de la madera en las casas, los pasos sobre la nieve, lobos a lo lejos que nos ponen alerta, todo está muy bien. La banda sonora es excelente.
Un punto alto es la narración, con un excelente trabajo de voces mientras la narrativa del juego se desenvuelve, con un narrador omnisciente que nos relata como Carl vive esta aventura.
Conclusión
Kona es un juego imperdible, lástima que los tiempos que tarda en cargar los sectores del mapa nos sacan de concentración en la inmersión que se alcanza de manera muy natural. La historia es entretenida, con cosas que hacer,  lugares para explorar (cavernas, senderos nevados, etc) y el deseo de saber qué es lo que está pasando desde los inicios de la partida.
Conducido por su narrativa, Kona ofrece un juego donde la aventura y la supervivencia se unifican para poner a prueba nuestros sentidos de detectives. El juego es desarrollado por el estudio independiente Parabole, de Canadá, tiene un precio de $19.99, tiene una nota media de 4.5 estrellas en Steam.

Kami is serene yet engaging. It combines a beautiful esthetic with simple efficacy puzzles to a very satisfying effect. The puzzles are easy to complete, but they present a challenge by encouraging you to use the fewest moves possible. I find myself doing the same puzzles multiple times because I am determined to find that perfect move set.
The visual style of Kami is simple and elegant. Using a combination of complementary colors, you strive to turn your puzzle into the singular hue of your choosing. With each click, squares of folded construction paper flow out from the selected location, slowly turning the puzzle into a satisfying uniformity of color.  The game does not restrict you to any specific move limits, and instead will continue to be playable well beyond the recommend move goal. This freedom allows you to simply play with the colors; folding and shaping your paper until your heart’s content.
Kami's music is a beautiful rendition in a traditional Japanese style. The game gives you the option to play the music during the puzzles or you can leave the music off and solve the puzzles in near silence. Aside from the music, the only sound during the puzzle is that of folding paper which accompanies each of your moves. This makes for a mesmerizingly tactile experience.
The simple design, beautiful colors, and comforting sounds add together to make an elegant and relaxing experience that calls to me at the end of a stressful day. For the measly price this game requests it would be a shame not to experience this little slice of peace and beauty.

If you consider buying Rising World, you should inform yourself about it first. This is not different to other things - you wouldn´t buy a TV, car, etc. without first reading the Pro/Cons before, right?
Rising World is a game in development, in Alpha stadium. That means it is incomplete and every update can change the whole game experience.
The content of the game is currently "limited" to building. Why i set "limited" into paraphrases? Simply because the game is yet incomplete and still, in my opinion, the best building game out there.
It has (yet!) no hostile NPC, no electricity or mechanics, almost no survival feature (only basic hunger / thirst). And still i tell you it is the best building game out there - why?
When you start Rising World you start off with choosing your randomly generated world. With different biomes (grass, forest, winter, mountain, lakes, desert, etc.) that have a beautiful graphic.
The light effects, day and night cycle, weather effects (sunny, foggy, rainy) give it all the feeling of a living world.
Some animals (hostile and neutral) do their business around you.
But thats not all. You start crafting a tent, a fire place and feel like a nomade. When you adventure futher you build some crafting tables that allow you to build a wide variety of differently textured blocks with many different shapes. Some furniture, decoration items, different lights (fire and electrical) and tools.
So far not exciting enough? Well, then have a look at the system of planks, beams and logs. You simply craft them from wood but can change them in size - and texture (via console).
While the normal blocks can be placed like in any other crafting games too the planks and beams are objects that can be rotated, resized and placed in any way you can image.
You make them tiny and rotate them - craft a vase, a table, a grandfather clock, a spinning wheel, ...
Make them the size of a block and place them freely like you need
Make them huge and rotate them to build your round tower, tubes, etc.
Don´t feel bound to a certain grid - just work with this amazing planks and  beams system. And save your masterpiece with the blueprints - or download those others provide and use it in your own game.
This system is it what makes the difference to other building games i know. Its flexibility and nearly limitless application possibilities.
Whats for the future?
The next update will bring some more weapons and especially - character models that can be adjusted individually. Also the survival features will be improved.
The character models will be the basis for the next update - bandits, pirates, traders, hostile npc...
And after? Horses, Trains, Breeding (a plug in already allows this!), electricity....
Red51 is a passionate developer. Not the fastest - but for a good reason! Being mostly alone working on the game and having to depend on freelancers he does an awesome job about this game already and, at least for me, he has my trust to bring his vision into reality with Rising World.
Have a problem? Just post on forums and he will answer, if the community doesn´t do it before.
His vision for the future is to raise Rising World to a new level. While currently almost completely a building game he wants to make it a game with each 33% for Building, Survival and Exploring.
And the best thing is - nearly all features in the game already can or will be individually adjustable. You love Tigers but hate Bears - no problem! Just check out these nasty Teddys.
You love building but survival is not your thing? No problem - creative mode and easy switching is no problem.
Is everything so great about this game? No. It isn´t. Currently i feel very lonely in this game. No matter if single player or multiplayer.
Due to the missing challange of survival and hostile NPCs most people really focus on building on their SP games or on private servers.
I sometimes feel too lonely and even though it tickles me to build another fortress or huge mine i retreat and play something else - waiting for better times (next update).
Taking a break from the game doesn´t mean though it´s not good anymore. I just accept the fact that the game is in development and not complete yet.
And that sometimes means to do a break and play something else - always lurking in the dark to wait for the next upate with....
No. Sorry. Way too many crappy wanna-be games like this on Steam. But there is one good thing about this game - you don't have to bother with the refund.

Kotori is a passionate girl who's legs are disabled and therefore has to move around in a wheelchair. she was the most passionate about the Soaring Club as she was in love with the sky after reading Isuka's( Amane's BF from before Isuka had an accident with the glider years before) flight log left behind in her room at The Flying Fish Manor. She constantly drove to succeed in making the glider perfect but unfortunately she could not fly the first one as she could not use her legs. In the second year though she was able to with the help of Amane drawing designs for a cockpit which required only her hands to use and she was over the moon. she constantly strove to do things that everyone else could but her family when they found it did not approve and tried to whisk her off home out of a sense of protection for their disabled little girl. however thanks to a secret SOS sent to the main character, Aoi, you ride your bike at full speed to convince her dad to let her come back and show him what Kotori has been able to achieve and fly on the Morning Glory with her by your side piloting the glider with her new disabled person cockpit.

Great fun, good music to keep your mind immersed. Nice basic features. Explosive terrain, perks all based on the basic gameplay yet each varied enough to stay interesting. Choose one from three [randomly rolled to choose from] each time you choose.
You can play nice and fast or good and slow. Varied traps and good controls [very light complaints and I put controls #1 on games that are above decent.] Incredible replay unless you just plain don't like the game. Daily runs if you feel like boosting the competitive aspect.
Really a good pure platformer. Blow up terrain, watch out for traps, stay alive until you die.
Basics: Get to the portal each level, anyway you can or want. Each time the level gets harder/different. After [2-3?] levels you pick a perk from a pool of three chosen at random.
More TNT? Slower wall slide? More HP? Faster movement? Faster movement gain faster? TNT explosion on impact? More TNT totals? I'm sure there are more.
No enemies I know of, so the traps while have their own [certainly not easy at all!] danger, it has a depth of certainty so dying is quite often your own fault. Though again, not easy since you need to react if you fall and need to dodge or move fast. Perks help and you can/must use all your advantages.
Complaints: I think Four choices should be given from perks. Not to make it easier but to make the random levels a bit more balanced with more abilities to choose one from. Sometimes you just can't go on because you die from not knowing the next level will require more of what you don't have.
Also, the traps could use more umph and maybe a touch of Super Meat Boy's meatiness/blood. Some also just are unfairly unthreatening so you die unfairly not knowing how or when you'll die from something. [One trap looks like a rock outcropping but it kills you on contact?!]
There's more but overall the game is very good and focused, could use refining and more punch-to-the-gut impact with the danger/traps or double edged perks that are really good and really bad at the same time.

I've only played the common route and one character route so far, but here are my impressions:
Positives:
- Setting/Plot: The setting is very believable, but still novel and powerful. This is without a doubt the game's strongest point. The various climaxes of the game, when the action really came together for the Soaring Club to do something amazing, never failed to give me chills and inspire a big emotional response.
- Visuals: the sprites especially are very high-resolution, well-drawn, and unique. I'm admittedly not that knowledgeable about visual novels, but I haven't previously seen one that does varied zoom levels for the character sprites. This game gets a lot of mileage out of that technique, and the sprites always look good while they play these tricks with them. Backgrounds and movies are also great, but the care taken with fine details of the character sprites really steals the show.
- Character design: I find the characters to be varied and interesting, especially the first 3 heroines (I maybe didn't get enough time with the two who appear later to feel much connection with them; maybe this will change when I play their routes, though). The heroines have very distinct, personalities, and are also very independent; they don't depend on their relationship with the main character to define themselves (a common  problem in visual novels, IMO). Admittedly, the heroines all fall into pretty common visual novel tropes, but I don't really view this as a negative so much as an inevitability.
Negatives:
- Translation: The translation for the common route is actually great. I noticed very few odd turns of phrasing, and very few grammatical and spelling mistakes, and only one translation that was simply bizarrely wrong (the repeated appearance of a phrase like "Then, on the first day of summer", when it was clearly inappropriate and clearly didn't match the vocals).
That said, the translation for the one character route I have so far played (Kotori's route) was frankly appalling: about half of it suffered from one of:
- very poor English (dialogue that would certainly not have been spoken by a native speaker)
- out of character (wording did not fit for the character)
- nonsensical in context (perhaps a single sentence was translated independent of everything around it, or without the context of the visuals and voice acting? At any rate, it was sometimes clearly wrong, even with my poor grasp of spoken Japanese)
- incorrect translation, or failing to correctly capture the mood/emotion of the context (again, even with my poor grasp of spoken Japanese this was very obvious at times)
I would recommend the game as an excellent visual novel, with the caveat that you have to be willing to bear with a terrible translation awaiting you at the end of the game, where the most emotional scenes await. I found that frankly very disappointing, after the earlier parts of the game were so much better-done. I'm holding out hope that it was just the particular route I chose that was terribly translated, and that others will be better when I go back to play through them... One odd thing I noticed was that it was perhaps the first 2/3 of the character route that were especially poorly-translated; the last 1/3 of it was back on track and reasonable. I can't really say whether the problem is going to be so prevalent in other character routes.
