Across my entire games library, there is no title I am able to call more confusing than E.Y.E. I've long sat on the fence between calling it the most incoherent trainwreck of a game I've ever seen and the one of the absolute best RPG shooters I've ever played. As the thumbs-up on this review suggests, I usually fall off the latter side of the fence.
E.Y.E. is many things, but, as stated, it is an RPG at its core and an FPS at heart. These labels, however, hardly do it justice. Between its rich feature list and innumerable player statistics that can all be taken advantage of as one pleases, E.Y.E. is a game that can practically be played any way you want.
Want to throw on heavy armor and rampage through levels with a minigun? Go for it. Want to strip down to nothing, grab a power sword, and speed through maps at 400MPH like it was Hotline Miami? Your call. Want to grab a shotgun, leap ten stories into the air onto the head of a cyberdemon, and pump your way through his skull? Entirely possible.
Between character builds, weapon loadouts, personal playstyles, and the robust, unique hacking minigame, it would almost be entirely correct to say that there's little you
do in E.Y.E. Every part of the game can be played cooperatively - or competitively - in multiplayer to further demonstrate the beautiful chaos of the games' overwhelming array of options.
There is simply no way to properly explain E.Y.E.'s story and atmosphere. Even those people - such as myself - who have finished the game to its fullest extent still struggle to understand it. It is best described, albeit insufficiently, as every dystopian sci-fi universe in fiction smashed together and explained by a frenchman on 400 tons of LSD via Google Translate. And that's just the tutorial.
E.Y.E. is dark, depressing, and its story will make the game feel hopelessly futile in the end - in a good way. Its lightless levels require permanent flashlight usage and often are so dark that even the flashlight is useless. Its music is pure brilliance that, once again, demonstrates how unnervingly powerful the game is despite its inexhaustible list of quirks.
The quirks, however, aren't all good. It's clear very early on that the game may as well have been made exclusively in a shed after happy hour as it runs on Valve's Source engine, relies on Half-Life 2 content in a surprising number of places, and features models that run the gamut between professional quality to downright goofy.
The prior mention of a frenchman on 400 tons of LSD is likewise accurate. E.Y.E. is the product of a French indie studio with a limited translation budget, leaving much of the text - its primary means of story dialogue - terribly confusing, at best. Strange mission objectives and complex level design can sometimes exaggerate the effects of the poor translation to an extreme and hold up gameplay.
Questionable weapon balance, random drop-influenced player upgrades, a tutorial that often seems insufficient for most new players, and sometimes obnoxious on-screen messages all contribute to how E.Y.E. can often seem like a steaming mess. Some systems are completely discarded as the game progresses and some statistics end up entirely useless, leaving balance in yet more disarray.
After I'd finished with E.Y.E., however, it left a mark on me that has since changed my perspective on games and dystopian environments. It's made me wonder why so many big-budget games with more experienced and less-pressured staff have been little more than drops of rainwater compared to the ocean of potential that E.Y.E., in all its indie-to-the-bone glory, is.
And I
can't find my legs.

I'm a stealth lover so I'm really trying to love Styx. But it's hard. It does several things right, I absolutely love the character! I'm so sick and tired of Vin Diesel in every ♥♥♥♥ing game. But here's a fun, interesting character in an original story.
The climbing mechanics is actually well designed, as in the idea is great, but the implementation leaves to be desired. When you are hanging from a hook, for instance, the camera positions itself in a way that you can see surrounding climbing options and moving your direction keys shows you where the jump key will take you. It's pretty clever! but that's as far as it goes. Say a guard is getting close and you want to climb down the ledge. Well, to do that you have to fall off the ledge, quickly move towards it (the usual jerking back and forth we are used to do in platformers) and then it grabs the ledge. But that's not all! if you do that he will climb back up automatically, defeating the whole point. No, you have to press jump and hold in order for it to keep holding the ledge and not climb back up. Another annoying thing in the platforming mechanics is ledge movement, it doesn't turn corners, it doesn't follow slight changes in height etc.
Oh well, platforming is awkward but not game breaking in my opinion. The level design is the problem I have. Now, I praise the open ended nature, the multiple paths, it's exactly what lacks in today's stealth games (including Thief4). So they got that going for it. But it's the wide open spaces I don't like. Since we are talking about stealth, let's see how Thief approached level design. Corridors and small rooms. You could sit in a dark corner and study the patrol routes of the local guards. Every now and then you had open spaces and these were the dangerous parts. When you are in the open there are way too many variables to keep in mind, you never know how many guards are around you, it's too big! let alone who has the angle to spot you, and the distance, and your visibility. I keep getting spotted by people I have no idea where they are! At any point you can spot a dozen guards moving around. It's absolutely overwhelming and goes against what makes stealth gameplay fun.
Maybe this is one of those games where stealth is not supposed to be your first option, instead you have to cause mayhem or kill the guards silently, I don't know. The open spaces certainly seem to support that, but that's not how I tried to play it. And I do believe games have right and wrong ways to be played. I could be playing it wrong, just like my buds used to try and assault Lord Bafford's mannor using the bow and arrow and I would laugh at their feeble efforts.
Since I have to pick between yes and no, I'll go with YES just because I think more people should try it. It's interesting, different, and I might just not be for ghost stealth players like me.

Lets give a brief review of Kona (spoiler free)
Kona is a survival game, with slight horror elements. The term "Horror" should be used more loosely here, because most of it comes from a uncomfortable atmosphere, and less from typical horror experiences like monstrositys or jumpscares.
We start off as a private investigator named Carl Faubert, and our job is to investigate a vandalism cause, fined by Mr. Hamilton. Hamilton is a rich english man, who settled down at a really small village at Lake Atamipek, and he kind of owns the whole place.
Thinking this is an easy job, we travel to the place and unforseen events happen, wich seem to involve a lot of townsfolk...
While beeing a survival game, the aspect of "Survival" falls a bit short. We got three meters, we have to watch: Stress, warmth and health. While the stress and health meters are easy to maintain at top, with cigarettes (for stress) or medikits (for health) the warmth meter is the one that draws the most attention to it. The whole place is surrounded by a heavy snow storm and therefor the player is close to freezing all the time. As soon as you enter different locations you can warm up by firing up little fireplaces. But you have to carry the necessary tools for that (matches, firestarter and logs).
Except of that, everything goes down to investigation. You are gathering clues, to get answers to certain questions. Every place inhabits its own clues, and some are pretty tough to spot. Other require problem solving skills, since the game also has little puzzles.
While the game starts of pretty slow paced and quite relaxing, you can feel an incoming climax building up. And damn, the final act delivers for that!
TL;DR:
Kona is a sweet little game, with a lot of secrets and a backstory that is NOT told to the player. You have to discover it all by yourself. The narrator of course gives you a lot of "TL;DR" information about documents you find, so you wont have to read through all of them. The detail in this game is amazing, especially all the work put into the documents. The developers did well in generating a very own universe, that is incredibely close to reality.
Pros:
- very interesting story-telling, by letting you discover everything by yourself
- uneasy atmosphere, that keeps you strained to the very end.
- really great climax, that solves everything and maybe gives you answers you didnt expect
- good controls, feels mostly intuitive and easy to use
- puzzles are mediocre, only a few existing, but they are mostly entertaining
- every person has an own story to tell, and you feel connected to them
- replayability is there, because of all the little secrets that you might've skipped
Cons:
- slow ramp up, feels a bit "boring" the first 1-2 hours
- sometimes a bit irritating, especially hints that have no narration
- you have to make up the whole way yourself, there is no guidance, wich sometimes leads to a bit of frustration
- health and stress meters seem to be mostly redundant most of the game, you dont even know why you got them
- no "real" saving option, you get autosaves all the way and can save by your own, but only the last 10 saves will be displayed
Over all this is a great game, that is somewhat different from other games in this genre. A great ending, a slow start. Can definately recommend this game for every fan of "horror" mystery games, because that experience is different.
I also (oh who would've thought?) made a series of Videos about that game, with a normal playthrough. Without any knowledge beforehand, so i missed a lot of secrets. Going to upload 1-2 more videos showing a bit more of it.

Kona is a casual exploration and survival game with a few puzzles and a focus on narrative. It is set in Canada during the 70's and you get to explore a large open town. You were hired as a detective and you must meet your client, however there are obstacles in the way preventing you from doing so. You begin to uncover more story while struggling to survive against the harsh freezing snow storm.
- Kona is a beautiful game. The visuals are vibrant and cheerful and the snowstorm is pretty realistic. There is a lot of snow everywhere, so luckily it looks good, and the snowy trees look great. I appreciate the small details such as leaving bootprints in the snow, and the fact you can actually see your legs when you look down. These small details help a lot with immersion. The town is large so there's a lot to explore. The house and cabins you explore are full of small details and actually looked lived in, and all look unique, so that alleviates repetition. Overall, Kona has great visuals that help immerse and elicit feelings of freezingness.
- The main menu greets you with some beautiful music when you start the game. Throughout the game environment, and in your car, you can find radios which you can turn on and play music. This is a nice little touch which was pretty cool. The music of Kona is really good, as is the sound effects. The sounds are realistic and help immerse you in the world. Also, the voice acting is particularly good too and the narrator did a great job. Overall, this game has really well done audio.
- The initial goal of the game is to meet a client requiring your detective skills. However, a snow storm starts and you begin to witness anomalies. Due to certain obstacles restricting your path, you must explore an open town to find tools and answers. You have a car which you can drive around the town, but most places are exclusively accessible by foot. Exploring can be dangerous as you encounter wolves, and freeze to death or lose sanity. Starting fires will warm you up and regain your sanity, however starting a fire requires using your finite supplies, so there's some strategy as to when and where you should start a fire. I was pleased with the exclusion of hunger/thirst meters, as this makes the game more casual. Throughout the town, you will come across buildings like gas stations or cabins. Sometimes there's puzzles to complete such as figuring out how to start a generator, so you can move a car lift to retrieve a crowbar. There's always a lot to interact with and the narrator helps keep you on track. Overall, Kona is an engaging game which keeps you entertained.
- I don't usually care for stories in games much, but Kona has a really unique and surprisingly well executed story that keeps you intrigued throughout the game. You must uncover the mysteries and find all the evidence along your journey. But soon you realise that something strange is going on. Overall, Kona has an interesting and intriguing story.
- The game runs smoothly and bugs were mostly absent. However, one major criticism is the frequent, and long load times. They jarringly pop up out of nowhere, and pull you out of the immersion. Maybe it would be better if the entire play area was loaded at once, or loaded dynamically.
- I have to praise the UI design, especially how the map works. It's really awesome and more games should do this.
If you're looking for a great exploration game with a good story and proper gameplay, then I would highly suggest Kona.
I give this game a 7.5/10 - a very well made and detailed survival exploration game.

Kona puts you in the shoes of private investigator Carl Faubert in the backdrop of 70’s northern Canada. He comes to Atamipek Lake to meet a local wealthy industrialist, William Hamilton, to be recruited as his personal bodyguard. But things go wrong right from the get go when he reaches the deserted town and starts seeing things he know shouldn’t be there.
Kona is essentially a survival game with detective elements mixed in it. To survive, you need to build campfires and iron stoves while fending off wolves and moving from building to building and unlocking new areas. Kona maintains a creepy atmosphere throughout the length of the game while not being nerve wracking or going fully survival horror.
The narration is solid and is told with a pinch of dark humour which provides a breath of fresh air from the many other survival games with essentially no story whatsoever. The way the narrator tells the story is also right on the money and it weaves a strong narrative grip on you during the game.
Kona has you going from one place to another in pursuit of more clues, and more often than not these places will have places for you to warm up and supplies to take. The truck is essentially the only of way of travelling aside from foot and it acts as both as a container and as a protection from hungry packs of wolves. The game also has a slight tendency to lead you off roads and into the woods where you might spend a good lot of time trying to find your way through them.
You also keep a journal which helps you in keeping record of the investigations and making you feel like a proper detective. What differentiates Kona from the bunch of other survival games is the excellent atmosphere, strong narrative structure and the detective elements inserted and mixed brilliantly with the survival elements.
Not everything is good with Kona with the huge load times really breaking the immersion at times. The game also reuses a lot of its assets and you might start to feel a little bored from seeing the same environments time and time again. Even though it is out of early access, the game still has its fair share of bugs and while they’re not game breaking, they can certainly distract you from your adventure. The enemy variety is nothing more than wolves and the combat leaves a lot to be desired. The game also has supplies thrown at every single place you are and that makes you feel like you don’t need to scavenge for the materials.
And while these are minor nitpicks, they do impact your time with Kona and you might not see the brilliant atmospheric game which is hidden behind these issues.
Reusing of assets aside, Kona is a brilliant looking game which provides an excellent backdrop for your adventure. The environments are lovingly crafted and the sense of isolation is present in every frame of the game. The animations of Carl himself are also very well done with subtle little touches to his regular movement and those really pull you in the game.
While the soundtrack is subtle considering the nature of the game, it compliments perfectly the atmosphere of the game and the sense of isolation through its sound. There are a few audio issues but they don’t really distract you away from the game.
Kona is a superb survival game which is different from the stream of other games of the genre in a very unique way. It has a strong atmosphere, gripping narrative and wonderfully executed detective work. There are a few nagging issues which might pull you away from the game but if you’re looking for something which provides you with a really tense atmosphere then Kona can be right up your alley.

Orion is a science fiction visual novel developed and published by Cylight Studios. You are Sam Acacius, a bright young teenager living on the Orion station with your older brother. One day you receive a terrifyingly cryptic message on your holopad stating that the section of the space station that you reside in will be destroyed in just days. What will you or can you do to prevent this tragic circumstance from happening? Can one person truly make a difference?
Since most of the visual novels that I've read to date have been fantasy based or occuring in present day I was very thrilled to finally get my hands on a V.N. with a science fiction theme. The premise in Orion is intriguing but somewhere along the storyline I seemed to lose interest in this novel and I just didn't find the protagonist to be very likeable as his personality rubbed me the wrong way on more than one occasion throughout the narrative. I must also mention a glaring flaw that I found with this V.N. which is that the quicksave or save function...DID NOT WORK! That's correct you can't save your progress in this visual novel through normal means but after some experimenting I finally managed to find a way to save. After starting the V.N. up you have to begin a new game each time then from there you will be able to load up an archived quicksave...how in the heck is anyone supposed to know that?! This is something that shouldn't even be an issue with ANY visual novel or game at all?! Over the course of a few months, I started this V.N. three times but always quit reading when I realized that I could not save. Nonetheless, after figuring out a way to save my progress after the third time...I finally managed to finish this V.N. to completion. Needless to say, after all of this my opinion of this visual novel really began to wane.
Visually, Orion looks great with it's manga-inspired artwork and beautiful coloring. In fact I think it was the terrific art that first caught my eye with this V.N.. The dialogue is also voiced quite nicely as well even though I prefer non-voiced visual novels. I don't remember coming across any typos so if there was any then they were few and far in between which is excellent. Also, the sound is capable and there are even some ambient noises for immersion but the soundtrack itself is not very memorable in my opinion. To summarize, in the looks and sound department I found this visual novel to be in the above average range in it's great presentation.
Sadly I got a bad ending with my first...er...technically third playthrough with this V.N. since I FINALLY figured out how to SAVE the novel. I know that I keep beating a dead horse about this and you can't see me right now but I am facepalming...no...double facepalming again at the moment, just as I'm writing this, over the mere thought of that "save" fiasco. I guess you could say that the "bad" ending complements quite nicely the "bad" impression I got of Orion because of the problems that I've had with it. With that said, there are a total of nine endings available so maybe one day I might try another read but at this point that's highly doubtful? As far as options go, there is a CG gallery and an original soundtrack but no Steam Achievements or Steam Trading Cards to collect. Not saying that these things are present in this V.N. but typos, short length or horrible artwork I could overlook but not being able to save is just unforgiveable. In summary, even though I found the story to be interesting, Orion's other flaws left a really bad impression on me so I don't recommend this visual novel to anyone.

The writing is horrible. Whatever story this game does have is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and sloppily executed. Some of the dialogue regarding forgiving certain people is so ‘horrible fanfic’ level and terribly unrealistic with how easy the ‘forgiveness’ part is dished out with no tension, conflict, doubt or even remotely trying to talk about the subject at hand before granting the forgiveness.
The plot is very rushed, barely giving you the time to get to know any of the characters or the politics of Orion at all, before launching you headfirst into a convoluted story where all of the side-characters refuse to properly explain anything at all. You know, in stories like fantasy and sci-fi, the backdrop is half of what makes the story interesting. Not properly showing it off is a huge mistake.
There’s just too big of a difference in skill between the CG artist and the character artist. One makes the characters look like adults, the other makes them look like tall children (or like a ten-year old with breast, you know, that girl bully). It was the CG’s that made me think I was going to play an adult character, only to find out afterwards that the MC is a minor. In fact, I didn’t even realize that the character art and the one in the CG were the same person at first and kept waiting for this boring child to get off the screen so the ‘real story’ could start. I really don’t like young adult stuff, not now that I’m an adult. I prefer to play as an adult, which given the CG art I thought I was getting in this game. My mistake.
To be honest, I didn’t care about a single character in this story and started skipping through the story just to get to the endings, which were equally unsatisfying. Not a single ‘ending’ ever showed the consequences of your actions. (Well, maybe the bad ones kind of did, which is why they were only slightly more entertaining than the rest of the story.)
This is a huge fail as a writer. You want your readers to stay engaged in the story and connecting to your characters, not skipping ahead and thinking they don’t give a damn if the whole space station blows up right now. Ideally, you also want to write a satisfying ending that shows the resolutions and the consequences thereof (not skipping over them!), whether that ending is ‘good’ or ‘bad’ (aka ends happily or unhappily).
This game failed on all three. It even failed on the art. Of course, there’s always going to be some differences between the character art and the CG art in a visual novel. But here, the differences were so great that the character weren’t even (or only barely) recognizable between the styles. Do I really have to spell out how bad that is?
The bullies suddenly becoming Sam’s friends is some higher order BS. I’ve been bullied, alright? They don’t just stop on a whim, no matter what you say to them. Virgil felt like the author’s self-insert, guiding you along to the ‘true path’ (the ending they wanted), while resetting if you’re on the ‘wrong’ one before even letting you properly see where that path and its consequences would lead. Because of the way the 'endings' were done, it ultimately makes any 'choices' you make feel empty and meaningless, since you're in essence always heading for the 'true' ending and any of the other 'endings' aren't really an end at all. You also don’t want your protagonist to come off as a whiny brat, that generally doesn’t endear them to your readers.

I wish I could recommend this visual novel. It had sone great concepts, the music and sound design are decent, and there was so much potential. The voice acting is also fairly good. I hold a particular fondness for Virgil. But the endings are dissatisfying, especially the true one. Its execution started off fine, and I commend the alternate solution Sam comes up with, but shortly thereafter it rushes straight to the epilogue without showing how things went down, which is just lazy and poor writing and totally anticlimactic and disappointing. Most of the characters felt flat and not very well fleshed out. There also should have been more reflection of the MC's ability to retain memories across timelines, like unlockable extra lines as you finish more endings. I also have a complaint about the artwork. Many, actually. Mari's sprites make her eyes look really weird due to the art style. Sam's sprites make him look way younger than he's supposed to be, in a way that doesn't match how the CGs DO manage to accomplish making him look his age. Also the differing art styles between the sprites and CGs are much more distracting than anything else. The same character looks way too different between the two art styles, creating a sloppy production effect.
All in all, this visual novel had too much potential flushed down the toilet due to sloppy writing and execution. I don't regret playing through this but it is not worth full price. Only buy if it's severely discounted or you receive as a gift. Or if you have a huge boner for plots that utilize timeline shenanigans and like sassy AIs who've mastered the art of sarcasm.

I've played this game in beta (hence the free tag) and out for a rather long time... probably longer than you will and I certainly have to recommend it.  It's fun, plain and simple.  You choose a character, get a couple companions, kill a bunch of enemies, level up your cards, delete some, replace some, attach some equipment to your character, die, and repeat until you succeed!  It's a rogue-like card game.  What more can you expect?
One of the best aspects of the game is that it's both a simple and complex rogue-like.  It's easy to get into, incredibly easy, in fact, but then you have to carefully manage your cards based on your needs.  Pick a mage or cleric?  Focus on your mana gains early on.  Going rogue?  Chain-chain-chain-chain-backstab-death.
You've got to think ahead to know what you need and don't need.  Knowing what cards you'll get at different stages helps.  Knowing what enemies you'll face in what area helps.  Knowing what your character excels at helps.  Basically, knowledge is power.  Play for an hour or two and you'll start understanding this.
If I was asked what the worst aspect of the game was, I'd have to say... luck, I suppose.  Luck can really break you in this game.  Whether you were unlucky in your companions, your cards, the people you met, or the enemies you're faced with.  It's to be expected in a rogue-like, I think, but still... a bit misfortune can be a real killer.
Overall Score -- I'd give it a 9/10.  It was good enough to make me play for nearly 60 hours, after all.  That's like... $0.10 per hour of entertainment.

Just Get Through is a 2D platformer with randomly generated levels that combines fast paced gameplay with roguelike elements to create an enjoyable experience. As a fan of platformers this was a game I wanted to get my hands on as soon as I heard about it and I'm certainly not disappointed.
+Nice and simple pixel art style
+Randomly generated levels means you'll never play the same level twice
+You collect colour palettes which let you change the colour of the game and there's quite a few to collect/choose from
+Fully destructible environment
+A variety of different traps waiting to send you to your death
+You get checkpoints in the levels which becomes particularly handy for later levels
+As you progress through the game levels become more complex and more challenging
+Every so often you get an upgrade which helps you with a certain gameplay mechanic such as increased jump height
+Full controller support including the ability to rebind controls (which you'll definitely want to do)
+Dev is quite active in the forums which is nice to see
+There have already been a number of hotfixes and updates just over a week since launch
-Very occasionally levels are impossible to complete which is due to the levels being randomly generator
Verdict:
8

Men of War: Assault Squad  is a real time strategy "Blitzkrieg" type of game, where you get limited amount of troops to finish the mission. Since you do not have the ability to build a base like in most other strategies, Men of War provides some challenge at higher difficulty settings if you try to finish it quick.
The story is based on 2nd World War events where you try to fulfill different objectives to gain some advantage for your fighting side. The campaign is seperated by single missions that do not have any connection to each other, besides some story description. The story is supported by some details about the events that supposed to have occured during WW2. The gameplay consists of only managing your squads and units that you receive to finish the mission, alongside using some special functions like air or mortar strikes, that fulfill your weaponary. More squads and special attacks are ordered by the points you gathered through fulfilling the objectives during one mission.
The combat itself is simple but some missions require micro-management to use your units in most effective ways. There are some different types of equiptment that units can use, so adjusting to different objectives and situations helps with progression. If taken slowly, the game does not offer much challenge since you can always re-draw units, heal them up and re-capture strategically important positions or simply camp for more points to produce a real huge army that simply rolls over the enemy. At higher difficulties howerever, the amount of units the enemy throws at you gets challenging so you have to micro-manage your units even better to not let them die in vain. Sadly, the AI (both of the enemy squads aswell yours) is simply broken sometimes. Units run at each other without shooting, or your units standing next to enemy and both sides do not shoot. The AI almost never re-draws units so if you have enough units to capture a point, you can be assured that you will kill all enemies along the path aswell.
The graphic and effects are far more enjoyable than in most Blitzkrieg games, especially compared to the older Men of War titles. The interface has been adjusted for the better aswell and you can modify some of the UI for better squad management. Most of the actions provided are still somewhat needless, but since you can simply more them out of the center of the UI, they do not disturb much like in previous Men of War titles.
The whole progress of the game is still done by slowly fulfilling the objective inside single missions, but it feels satisfying in Assault Squad to finally move few meters on the map. The battles are packed with some action, the town and other surroundings do look destroyed and impacted by the fire fights, so the progress inside single missions feels good.
The audio gives a nice feedback during the battles where the biggest fire fights happen, where the heavy weapons and tanks are placed. The music provided a nice background sound without being too intrusive. The immersion during the missions was definetely on a high level in Assault Squad due to combination of visual feedback from the battles aswell audio feedback from the gun fights happening mostly on multiple places at same time.
Men of War: Assault Squad is an enjoyable blitzkrieg type RTS game and will most likely gather your attention for at least few missions. It is quite fun to fight in each single mission since the environments do change a lot and you get to destroy some towns and farm along your WW2 progress. I would recommend higher difficulty settings for some challenge since else you roll over enemies rather quick with some gathered ressources.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Bought and played it simply because: For the Emperor!
Although this game is categorized as a RTS game, it is more of a squad based tactical RPG. Unlike the first Dawn of War, this game has no base building and unit building elements in it. So, this is a sequel that is quite different from its predecessor, but that’s not to say it’s bad, it’s just different. Fans of the typical RTS genre that usually involve building a massive army then proceed to steam roll the enemy might get somewhat disappointed. But in terms of the campaign story and the squad based gameplay itself, it is still a pretty good game that can stand on its own.
The single player campaign does have a decent plot that allows you to explore more of the Warhammer 40,000 universe, in addition to having great characters and stellar voice acting. Also, we are finally introduced to another faction from the Warhammer 40,000 universe, which is simply another deadly enemy of the Imperium: the Tyranids – the devour of worlds!

So far, I've found this game to be pretty enjoyable.
When you start a new run, the randomly generated levels will be small and have few obstacles... as you get further, you'll have to navigate larger, more confusing levels, with more frequent deathtraps of ever-increasing variety.  At first it's just sawblades and spikes, then turrets, wall-mounted shotguns, little death robots that patrol back and forth along the floor, etc..  After that?  I'm not sure.  It gets pretty challenging after a while, and I'm not good enough yet.
To help you along the way, you have an arsenal of dynamite sticks that you can throw to destroy parts of the level and the traps.  You can also choose an upgrade every few levels to increase your health, dynamite capacity, jumping height, wall grip, etc.  You will also occasionally find chests that unlock new color palates to make the game look more colorful and interesting.
Jumping can be a little frustrating, since the game will only let you jump off a wall once before you need to jump off a different wall to keep going up.  It's a design choice and I respect that, but it's a bit hard to get used to at first.  I also have a couple of small issues regarding gamepad play, but the Dev has already said that he'll work on resolving that.. so it's alright.  I still give the game a recommendation.  For $5 it's worth it for me.

I like the direction it's going. I really do. The only real issue I can see so far is its early stage of development. When you are constantly living in fear of the "Falling" glitch, that's something to be said for a game that tries to be so immersive that it plays you the song of your respirator's people.  If you don't know what I'm talking about, I'll explain... You have to constantly listen to your own breathing.
Oh, you meant the game-breaking and ever-lurking bug? Why, that's when you hit terrain funny, or the edge of such, or the game just gets a wild hair up its♥♥♥♥♥ and decides that you aren't touching ground. You can 'float' along, stuck in the falling animation and gaining digital momentum,  until you manage to trigger either the same or a different bug, which forcibly helps you meet the ground directly under your boots, at terminal velocity. For me, it happens about once every hour. Could be more, could be less, and I often forget to save. That... is what makes this game unplayable in its alpha state for me. That one bug.
Does that mean I say the game sucks juevos grande? No, of course not! Like I said, I like the direction it's going.  I like having to care for the suit and all your needs, (power, water, oxygen etc.) and feel it's a nice touch to differentiate it from other block-mining games, as well as giving the term 'SURVIVAL' its meaning.  The enemies, once you find them, I couldn't help but laugh at when I glanced through the forums and first found their lairs. The crafting system, while not very intuitive or flashy, works well, (I'd recommend mentioning to people that turning on a forge while holding it will kill them... and a better guide of what to do to advance your tech wouldn't go amiss. Particularly iron. Maybe some sort of mission parameters and planned actions tab on the PDA, like proper space missions. Could even tie in the milestone achievements in-game to it.) As with all early-access games, especially alpha-builds, this thing needs work. A lot of work. But... if this all pans out right, I got a good feeling about it.
It's tough... but I'm gonna say I DO recommend the game, not for what it is now, but what it looks like the dev wants it to be.

Kona is an Adventure/Survival game set in Canada (more precisely Quebec) back in the 70s. Its key strengths are the constant
factor, which pervades every bit of the game until the end, and the
needed to proceed with the game and its puzzles. Right from the start, the game captures the player’s attention with beautiful images of wilderness (from which a sense of freedom springs up). The protagonist is a private detective named Carl whose employer is in a small Canadian village and has work that needs to be done. As soon as he moves forward to reach him, things go with a twist and everything changes (and not for the better). The player will need to appeal to his/her survival instincts and quickly look around to survive. As the game progresses, more mysteries come up. These mysteries need to be solved through careful surveys of the village and its surroundings (e.g. to obtain a key item it is required that the player collects some other items that are spread across various locations). Beyond mere “fetch an item to get another” missions there are puzzles like the “Secret Project” one (you’ll figure it out what I mean once you’ll get there). And of course, there are journals which tell the story of the folks living in the village and their conflicts with each other. From these papers the player will understand the psychology of each character (i.e. the weak, the greedy etc.). Another fun aspect of the game is that you get to decide whether you want to travel on foot or by car but if you decide the former you won’t be able to have a mobile deposit of stuff nor halt the cooling of your body temperature (due to the extreme cold). That’s an interesting choice is it not? Another thing that I absolutely love about this game it’s the personal journal in which the protagonist jots down notes whenever interesting stuff is found (I think that during my first playthrough I didn’t find everything that was out there, this brings us to the next topic). Has this game replay value? Why, sure! Mainly because it’s hard to track down every single interesting clue that is lying in the cold and the blizzard doesn’t make things easier. The cold can be fought with fireplaces or radiators, places that to a lone wanderer such as Carl are safe havens. Basically, the players will find themselves crossing distances from one fireplace to another and solving puzzles/investigating ordinary or strange phenomena and (another satisfying thing about all of this) taking photos. Carl is a clever detective, and any detective worthy of this title will carry a polaroid. In absolute certainty, I can say that this game does a good job showing the realities of harshness and the evil that lies within the human soul.
Kona is a game with both great introduction and middle phases but ends way too abruptly for my taste. I find the ending somewhat a little too brusque because I thought I could explore more parts of the map. However, I do recommend this game because it’s grand. Even though, I am inclined to tell anyone who is going to play it not to rush to the end: take it slow and explore, read the various journals and enjoy the game fully. I think that the entire Kona community would appreciate a second episode that would answer the question: "Where is the Wendigo now?"
Thanks for reading.

Even if you got this for free, as I did, it's not worth your time.
Great atmosphere and environments, sylistically pretty, endearing characters. Occasionally well paced, with a well thought out learning and difficulty curve (I found this only to be true early on and in the factory area).
Terribly sloppy and imprecise control for what they want you to do.  Much of the game design is centered around exploiting the crappiest aspects of the control scheme to create challenge.  Boring, repetetive enemies with little to no character.  Often times, the play areas seem too open ended, with much of the game taking place on small platforms out in the open, making the game feel disjointed and since the penalty for failed exploring is so great, pointless.  Very long for a game so lacking in fun, clocking in at 12 hours to completion for me.  I did not have the trouble with bosses most are reporting, and only found the last boss in the backstage area to be truly garbage and cheap.
I can't tell if they wanted this to be a punisher or not, as it seems to be mostly hard because of the design being often centered on making you battle the control to get what you want.  After more consideration, I do think they were going for a punisher style game, but they got several things wrong.  Most punishers really on precise control and overwhelming difficulty with progress gained by learning patterns and pitfalls.  This game adds an unacceptable level of randomness to an already slimy control scheme that makes me question the intentions of the designers.
Had I known the miniscule amount of enjoyment and satisfaction I would have gotten coupled with such a high level of frustration, I seriously, absolutely, 100% would never have played this.  I hope this dissuades at least one person from wasting their time and sanity on such refuse.
If you must play, don't explore, and don't seek out the secrets.  Just get to the end of each area as quickly as possible.
Hopefully, the developers will do something better with their obvious talents, but the lead gameplay designer needs to go take some classes.  Unfortunately, the high sales of this game have perhaps convinced them that they made something of merit.  Shame on you guys for releasing something so obviously intended to enrage people.

I love stealth games, ever since Thief the Dark Project / Hitman. This game is really worth picking up if you are into stealth games. It like a hidden gem on Steam. I did not even notice this until I saw the picture of Styx, who I loved in 'Of Orcs and Men'. After 5 hours of play here's what I think.
The Level design
- The levels are so super open which is great when compared to most stealth games these days (Thief 4 anyone?) There are multiple paths to take to your objectives, ranging from roof rafters to air vents to just sneaking behind people into the main doors.
The voice acting
- Oh my days I love the voice acting. Styx sounds so bad♥♥♥♥♥ I'm pretty sure it's the same voice actor from their 'Of Orcs and Men' game. The guards sound like characters out of Fable, but in a good way. And the minor mannerisms that Styx has when you choke out a guard or assassinate somebody is so good! You can even hear him sigh sometimes in a way that makes it seem like for him it's "just business as usual ..."
No need to kill (thus far)
- Apart from in the tutorial where they teach you the combat mechanics, thus far I have no had to kill anyone. I only assassinate them cause it's fun!
Note: The combat is pretty much a quick time event. I dislike quick time events but the game is based around Stealth and I tend to reload once I'm spotted. So for me the basic combat isn't such a big deal.
Music
- It's pretty cool at times although it can get a little bit repetitive.
Jumping / Movement in-game
- I'm writing this as a thing! Mainly because Thief 4 made me feel like I was a cardboard box! This game is not at all like that! I can freely jump from rafters to ledges and if I judged my distance properly, I pull off a sweet / silent leap. If I got it wrong, then I go splat into a tiled floor and die. It's amazing! You really feel like a small, sneaky git, nimbly moving around huge armour glad guards.
Level System
- I've only had time to level up once thus far. But it seems really good how they did it. You get to pick from tree's kinda like Skyrim but much more basic. You can pick skills to cater to your playstyle. I'm going down the Stealth and Kill tree's at the minute. The skills you are able to unlock are not numerous but they are really really useful and impact the game in a large way.
Performance on my PC
- I'm playing on a Geforce GTX 560 TI on a pretty old system whenever it doesn't freeze up.

A cool game, but sadly has too many annoying little things to be actually considered great game.
All enemies have ranged attacks, which makes the actually ranged enemies somewhat pointless. This is of course to make fleeing harder, but they could have just made the enemies faster and more agile.
Outside of scripted events, it is impossible to get enemies to attack enemies of different faction, which stops you from using some more interesting stragedies to get rid of opposition.
Once detected, the game forces you into combat. By forcing, I mean that if enemy steps withing few feet of you, your camera is actually forcibly turned to face them, This is unacceptable in a stealth game.
Then there are the smaller things like slightly unintuitive controls, not being able to turn corners while moving on ledges. not being able to kill enemies when they have noticed you, even if they would not be able to parry your attack and sometimes not being able to kill enemies cause they are leaning on a fence, even though you are standing right behind them.
All in all, great story, but the gameplay has too much little issues.

I wish we had a neutral, thumbs-sideways option.
The UI is attractive, the music and sounds are pretty good, and the voices are okay though uneven. The backgrounds are clean and distinctive. The sprites are well-drawn, and some of the CGs are nice. The story ideas are fairly interesting.
Here's why I'd give Orion a neutral if I could. As I frequently point out in my reviews, if a game is supposed to tell a compelling text-based story, that game needs an editor. Not just to find typos ("tume-jump"), but also to find changes in tense (between present and past in the narration), misused words and mixed-up idioms ("worried sick of my absence"), redundancies ("I hurry quickly"), and non-sentences caused by missing words ("What kind of trouble will adding something completely unexpected?").
The art creates problems for the story, too. The cartoony sprites conflict with the serious CGs and undermine the dramatic tone of the story, so you never quite get a feel for what's at stake. That conflict also contributes to confusion for the reader regarding characters' ages, especially that of the MC.
Other reviewers have pointed out the rushed nature of the story, and how a failure to set a seemingly unimportant flag early on creates false choices later; I agree that the results are illogical and frustrating. And the true path cuts away from the most important actions the MC needs to take, skipping to three months later--that's not much of a reward for the reader.
Ultimately, I've seen better in indie VNs--but I've also seen much worse. Orion has some aspects that are worth experiencing, but they're not worth going out of one's way for.

Orion is a little strange for a visual novel. It features above-average voice acting and beautiful CGs. For a visual novel to have decent voice acting is usually a sign that it is a Good Visual Novel With A Budget.
I'm not so sure if Orion actually qualifies as good, though. It has many intriguing plot ideas, but the execution of said ideas is very poor. The average scene in Orion is as follows:
1. Meet a character
2. Learn some background information
3. [2-5 minutes later] PSYC! Plot twist, none of that information was accurate.
4. Virgil laughs
5. Repeat
There just isn't enough time for the first round of information to feel like the norm before a plot twist is attempted. I felt dazed and unsure of if anything anyone said could be trusted, and the impact of the twists were severely diminished because I ended up never believing the established information in the first place.
Due to its rushed and poorly executed storyline, head-scratching (and not in a good way) path to achieving the true end , and general incoherence, I can't recommend Orion UNLESS you are solely interested in the voice acting.

Summary: despite its flaws I really enjoyed this Visual Novel. It was a nice surprise and better than I expected.
The idea of a Sci-Fi Visual Novel was appealing to me as it combines two media that I like. The story turned out to be solid and interesting and I liked that the main character had realistic personality and emotions rather than being caricatural. On the downside the other characters, with the exception of Virgil, and the setting were a bit underdeveloped in my opinion. We get enough information to understand the context of the story, but at times giving us information on Orion in small impressionistic touches is detrimental to the immersion as the world doesn't feel fully real. This keeps the story moving nicely but I think it would have benefited from taking some time to flesh the world out a bit more.
Another insteresting aspect is that the choices you make during the game do have an impact and result in four completely different branches. However, for each of those branches there are two different endings, and which ending you got from your choices seemed a bit random to me. I did get seven out of the eight endings very easily without using a guide though, so they are not difficult to get. It just doesn't really make sense sometimes, and I am not sure the story needs all those 8 endings (maybe four would have been sufficient). Also the endings did seem a bit dry and lacking something, but this might be because they are not really endings. It all makes sense in the end, when you get to the ninth ending. But even that one feels a bit dry.
One strong point of this Visual Novel is the art. The music is good and fits well with the story and the background art is very nice. All the characters are fully voiced in English and the quality of the voice acting is quite good. But above all I really loved the CGs.

I love the combat but without having friends over, it doesn't have a lot of replay value. The bots are pretty challenging to play against but with so few stages it gets old fast. The single-button combat is very tense and super fun though, so I'm torn about the game. I guess I just wish I had an excuse to play it more.

I was impressed by the beautiful art (kudos to Badriel), but also by the protagonist being an actual character with personality. The voice acting really sold the emotions and even fight scenes. I suppose the setting itself isn't super unique, but the time powers are interesting and Virgil's pretty awesome.
Now to the gameplay/replay. The short version: it's a Renpy with lazily designed flags and endings, although this lack of control ironically matches the theme of it being difficult to control the timeline. The long version: The four paths are accessed by specific choices, while the endings are determined by flags. Based on personal experience and the walkthrough, these aren't the good flags based on points; it seems like everything has to be exact to get the good ending. This is what we call "fake difficulty", where the game gives you choices that don't actually work so it feels either counter-intuitive or broken (unless you're already familiar with these types of VNS). An opportunist could say that it matches the theme of not having total control; and the good endings do feel satisfying with the aforementioned acting. It's just a shame that they give you a "gameover" message even on the good endings to push you to unlock all the endings.
Overall, I enjoyed this experience quite a bit after getting it on sale. I just can't recommend it as a game at full price. Grab it when it goes on sale, and don't try unlocking all the endings at once.

--- A Poorly Designed Touhou Clone ---
From the design, menus, facilities, controls, this game doesn't hide its identity as a pretty blatant Touhou clone.
Not that the fact that it's a Touhou clone made me don't like it. The reason I don't like the game is because it's badly designed.
Good things to note are the game is very generous with its extend, where 1ups are simply item drops. The game drops 3 and more of them per stage. Plus, with correct settings, the game can manage to keep its 60 FPS. The lack of Vertical mode for display is disappointing, however. But it can't be helped. The game doesn't have any Replay or any sort, but the game lets you Stage Practice. Not too bad.
The root of problem for this game is the Stage design and the ship itself. For one, the ship is very slow, even without using Focus (Equivalent to Laser Shot in Dodonpachi games). It will be fine if the normal shot itself is very wide, but it isn't. It makes aggressive play unviable. Secondly, the Focus shot itself. It's a lock-on type of shot and oh boy, it's impotent. It's lock-on range is very skewed to the front. the fact that this shot's power is practically the same as its main shot doesn't help, either. Not only that, the game is very stingy with Bombs. The Bomb is a charging type, similar to Ikaruga's homing lasers. But it doesn't fill quickly at all! The game fills bombs quickly with item drops, but one use of Bomb depletes all of the Bombs. That removes your defenses!
The worst of all, the stage design is bland. Not cinematic, not fast, just bullet spraying with cheap enemy placement that aren't designed for a slow ship. And the bosses are even worse. They're bullet sponges with cheap bullet patterns! Especially the ones with big, long bullets without any warning what so ever! It makes the game a test of memorization. Granted, one of the keys to 1cc shmups is memorization, but making the patterns cheaply kill you is simply not fun.
This game is competent as a program. It's stable, it's playable, and it doesn't crash. But might as well as playing this game as an example of how to make a badly designed shmup.

This isn't one of those games that you sit down and click away with one eye open and half a brain engaged -- this game is HARD. Not hard like impossible for bad reasons, or stupid puzzles. You're marooned on Mars with no support, no other people, and no plan but to survive. How easy would that be in real life? And you have an entire planet to deal with, and explore. You have to change Mars itself into Earth using pretty much nothing as starting equipment. It's a long, long process and you have to really THINK about what you're doing the whole way. This game isn't for the average 6 year old IQ who just wants to blow stuff up. You have to build and maintain everything you need to live, keep it all topped up, hope you are able to grow enough food to survive, bust your butt to ensure you can get enough fuel to just keep from freezing, keep the air flowing, and keep every bit of lichen, or bacteria, or shrub alive in conditions harsher than anything Earth has to offer. Making Mars into Earth isn't easy, but man is it worth it.
Absolutely a must for any cyberpunk fan!!!

I\'ll be honest: I received this game as a joke from a friend, but despite its many flaws, E.Y.E. has really managed to grow on me. Sure, it requires traversing many clunky menus. Sure, the hacking interface is a pain to look at. Sure, the lore is all kept in an \"archives\" room of your base and all in text. Sure, the game has a tendency to spawn in waaaaaaayyyyy too many enemies. Sure, the game doesn\'t explain its various systems (especially mental well-being) very well. Sure, I haven\'t even listed probably half of the problems this game has.
Despite all that, though, there\'s something kinda charming about this game. I know it gets called \"Deus Ex on crack\" a lot, but it\'s not a bad analogy. The levels are (for the most part) very open-ended with multiple ways to complete your objectives, much like in Deus Ex. The difference here is that there\'s even wonkier gameplay and a vaguely Oriental aesthetic.
Overall, I\'d say E.Y.E. is a game worth checking out. I might be hesitant to buy it at full price, but if you\'re interested in an open-ended, Deus Ex-like experience and don\'t mind something that\'s a little rough around the edges, pick this up during a sale.

King's Bounty: The Legend is the first game of the King's Bounty series where you take a role of an adventurer that with the right combination of troops and magic is going to save the kingdom from its doom. The game is an RPG with turn-based strategy combat style.
The gameplay in KB:The Legend consists of traveling through the world map, getting quests and gathering troops and then fighting enemy forces in a turn-based hex-strategy styled battles. The combat is really similar to Heroes of Might and Magic, however you are not going to build castles or a kingdom here and instead travel through a huge open world. The story is quite simple - you are the treasure hunter for the king and discover after a while a plot against the kingdom by evil forces and you are obviously the only one that can destroy them. The gameplay is however very fun in King's Bounty series and it is enjoyable to be able to traverse the land almost free (sometimes a quest or a strong army blocks your progress) but since the world is so huge, you mostly have different possible locations where you can go to. There are a lot of different factions that can offer you forces so you have a lot of choice depending on what strategy you enjoy more in battles. The classes offered are also quite distinguishable so it is even fun to play through the game multiple times with different classes and armies.
I would say it takes a while to learn the combat in this game since there are so many different troops that have their own skills, effects and with some mods even gather experience and level up. For playing on higher difficulties, that definetely offer a great challenge, it will require to know which troops the enemy has and how to counter them, which army is stronger against other faction, etc. It is great fun to find these things out, especially if you continue later the series.
The graphic has its own style in this game and while some others are flashy and colourful, others have a darker touch to them. It looks a bit comic-phantasy styled but fits the game really well. The interface is looking really cool in this game, every menu including the options have some cool things about it and are always simple to use. It took me almost no time to get to know which buttons to press for different menues and how to use them.
The progress is described by how far into the game you proceed by finishing quests, fighting enemy armies and leveling up your hero (and with mods your troops). When you hero levels up you definetely feel stronger since you get more skill points aswell can hire and command more troops. Competing for a top place in the list is also a fun challenge that you can try to take on.
One of the few games that I had audio on through most of the games - the music is really enjoyable and the sound effects give you some hints about your whereabouts aswell effects during the battle used. As you can see on the number of hours player, I enjoyed going through this game already multiple times due to great immersion into becoming the spell-swinging, rage using battle commander.
King's Bounty: The Legend is a great start for a great series and it definetely is an enjoyable and fun RPG with strategic battles. It will appeal to Heroes of Might and Magic fans, aswell RPG fans aswell turn-based strategy fans. It has great unique comic-styled touch to it, nice music, a lot of choice regarding armies and spells to use aswell great feeling of progress. If you enjoy the first few hours, it will most likely suck you in for long time.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

This is probably the hardest platformer I've ever played, and I A+'ed all but a few of the dark levels in Super Meat Boy. The problem is that Pid isn't fun hard, it's just frustrating and annoying. Controls are awkward and inconsistent, and the checkpoint system is dreadful (invisible checkpoints everywhere, so if you fall into one while failing a difficult platform puzzle, now you have to start from a different place and if you complete the puzzle you have to make it to the NEXT checkpoint to save your progress). This is the first game since the NES days that I actually considered quitting because it was too hard.
Granted, I played on Normal difficulty because I didn't realize that Easy was specifically patched in because of complaints at release. I could've dropped down to Easy, but was too proud. But if you go into this expecting a nice chill Metroidvania, as I did, then you're in for a big surprise (not the least of which is that it's not at all a Metroidvania, whoops).
One especially frustrating thing is the lack of a level select. There are some secret areas that I wouldn't mind going back to, or puzzles I would like to figure out, but instead you're forced to complete them as you go. I did do a couple of the challenge rooms, and they are a fun way to do some tough puzzles without having to play through the game.

Pros:
- Interesting setting (Canada, October 1970)

Kona is an enchanting game with an immersive open world that captures the imagination. Set in Canada in the 1970s I can best liken the game to the Television series “Twin Peaks” with it’s bleak and mysterious environment. I was quickly drawn in with the beautiful landscapes and well balanced storyline. I had no idea of how immersive the atmosphere Kona actually was until I found myself having a virtual heart attack during certain parts of the game when something unexpected happens. I generally dislike narration within games but here it is well executed and there would be something missing without it.
As a fan of open world or sandbox type games where I am not restricted in my options Kona offers great choice. You can explore the winter wilderness or the homes of ordinary folks (and some less so) in pretty much any order you choose. Seeing the stuff of every day life develops a sense of “normality” to the game which increases the impact of the unexpected when the visions and ice related drama’s come into play.
Game play is not overtly complex but rightly so. FPS players might become frustrated with the apparent repetative "travel to location, find stuff, take pictures, read journal, repeat", but then this isn't an FPS game (well not really). If you are willing to loose yourself in the storyline and enjoy exploring It has an (almost) noir feel without seeming too cliche. This game is storyline driven and as the player progresses an evident escalation increases feeling of unease.
The visions add depth to the environment and do not feel dislocated from the game as I originally thought they might (having seen the odd youtube video before purchase). The need to stay warm, keep your head are interesting game mechanics I haven’t come across before. These stats were not so annoying that you keep dying every 5 minutes but enough to make you think before you go outside.
Less appealing was the conclusive end which I will not spoil for those who might consider a purchase. I will say that played this game on a laptop well equipped to handle powerful games but I found the end laggy and the controls too sluggish for the FPS style finale. Consequently I dropped this game before I completed it and this is a rather telling admission. The ending seemed inconsistent with gameplay utilised elsewhere and whilst a great climax to the storyline it felt predictable and frustratingly difficult.
Load times were irritating as walking/driving across a bridge or area of land could trigger a spiralling load screen icon which detracts from the immersive feel of the game. That said on my machine they were only between 10-15 seconds which is notable but not the end of the world. Sound continues during load times which can be irritating when riding the snowmobile. With respect to the Radio's found in every location I'm undecided as to whether this adds to the game. Certainly the track playing is errie (as is the repetition of the same track) but I wonder if more could have been made of this in a "Life on Mars / Ashes to Ashes" kind of way. There certainly was scope for it.
Ultimately I find myself thinking that this kind of game is exactly the kind of game that I enjoy playing and for that reason I can forgive the conclusion which frankly is only a matter of taste at this point. Whilst Kona feels a little short (I got to the end in 1h 30m!) I thoroughly enjoyed being immersed in the wilderness and found myself wanting more! I’m pleased to hear that this is one in a series of games and eagerly anticipate the sequels as/when they emerge. Thanks Parabole for a great game.

Full review:
KAMI is probably one of the more unique puzzle games that I’ve played as of late. The game has you folding paper, origami-style, to solve puzzles. The game’s title is the Japanese word for paper and I still have no idea how to pronounce it (I’ve been saying it like ‘CAM-E’).
The method used to solve each puzzle is why this game is so unique. Each puzzle starts you off with a square sheet of paper, much like origami, with this piece of paper being covered in small triangles of varying colors. Your objective is to make the entire sheet of paper one solid color in as little clicks as possible.  There’s a color palette at the bottom of each puzzle and its your choice in deciding what color the end result should be, with that hopefully being the color netting you the least amount of clicks.
When you click on any triangle in the puzzle, any other triangle of the same color connected to the clicked triangle will change into the color you have selected. This is a bit difficult to explain, so I encourage you to look at videos, etc. This color-changing mechanic is accomponied by a neat-looking animation as well, which I would describe as a sea of paper-folding triangles.
The game’s major fault lies in the amount of content offered. I wish there were more puzzles to do, as there’s only 63. The game is $4 (on Steam) though, so that may be the reason. I ran out of puzzles rather quickly, although that can probably be attributed to the fact that I went for the bare minimum ranking in each puzzle, “okay”, instead of opting to go for the “perfect” ranking in each. There is another ranking as well, known as “fail”, and I’m sure you can figure what that means on your own.
The game’s difficulty curve is fantastic. Slowly increasing, but not to a completely frustrating point. If you’ve got time to kill, then I highly recommend KAMI. Although it may be short, it’s well-worth the unique experience. Oh, it’s also worth mentioning that the game does not fully display in widescreen, but instead has some rather thin black bars to the left and right. No idea why it wasn’t optimized for widescreen, wish it had been.

The only thing that might have made it better, and this is entirely subjective and debatable, would have been to get further into the mind of the character.  There are a great many subtle queues that enable the player to relate to the character, with the game mechanics being worked into this relationship in an ingenious way.  However, when I had finally found every little thing in the game, I didn't feel particularly close to the character.  Of course, that may have been intentional.
The mechanics of the game are very reminiscent of a game called The Void, even down to the look of the symbols as they are drawn, but that's not a bad thing - The Void was a creative masterpiece that way and I love the interface.
I highly recommend this.

Orion: A Sci-Fi Visual Novel is a fully voiced interactive visual novel revolving around a protagonist with time-warping capabilities. There are 9 total endings (1 is hidden/true ending) that vary quite a bit.
I definitely enjoyed the voiced narration and soundtrack. The artwork has a Western illustration style with plenty of Sci-Fi elements (as opposed to the traditional animu) and do a great job portraying the story. One major gripe I have about this game is the rather abrupt and shallow endings. I really wish there would have been more detail or follow up of each ending. They were clearly designed in order to help you (as a player) gain information in order to understand/discover the true ending.
Traditional VN options are present: text speed, window size, skip commands etc. Full save and load states are supported alongside qs/ql.
I enjoyed my playthrough of each ending (~2 hours total). There aren't that many VN's on Steam anyways, so this is definitely worth a shot.

I like short visual novels if they feel self-contained, not like a piece of what should have been a larger story. The setting and characters in
feel underdeveloped; when characters go from friends to enemies or vice versa, it doesn't have the emotional impact it should, because the reader barely knew the characters in the first place.
The choice structure is interesting, with an in-story justification for the choices and multiple endings. But there are a few occasions where if you don't have the right flags to reach a particular ending, instead of hiding the unchoosable option, the game just ignores your choice without any feedback. Took me a little while to realize this was a deliberate design choice, because it feels like a bug.
The true ending, which takes about two hours to reach (Steam didn't record my play time correctly), might have felt like a satisfying conclusion if I had a better sense of the relationship between the characters -- a better reason to care about them -- but instead it's just anticlimactic.
The voice acting is quite good, and I love the CG art (although it clashes badly with the more cartoonish character sprites). But overall
is dull and unmemorable. Even at a lower price point, I couldn't recommend it.

Men of War: Assault Squad is a wargame that focuses on World War II, and the five major players: America, Germany, the Commonwealth, Imperial Japan and the Soviet Union. I have so far experienced some of both of the Commonwealth and Imperial Japan campaigns and I have come away pleased with what I have experienced. Engaging, and challenging enough even on easy difficulty, it tasks the player to grapple with so many different soldiers, artillery and armored vehicles.
It can quickly become overwhelming on your first try, with so many different buttons, each soldier having individual inventory, and weapons being flung all over the place. There are a lot of different buttons, but thanks to the solid UI, it's easy to find your way around. It's exactly what you'd want from a tactical game, with easy to reach buttons for different ammunition, gear and grenades.
It is difficult at some points when you are faced with three heavy tanks, rolling toward you backed up with a compliment of infantry and maybe a flamethrower.
But that's what your own defences are set up for; the artillery guns, the Anti-Tank rifles, and the infantry hiding in the alleyways or the dense bushes; they are waiting for the tanks to expose themselves, and, with some luck, they will shoot true, and the heavy machinery will be down, allowing your mortars to move up into the streets and fire on the enemy control point, and with a cunning pincer movement, suddenly your infantry have the enemy flanked, and another point is yours.
One problem I can see is that the gameplay can get quite repetitive; I feel like I have seen a significant portion of the game already, and only played significantly as two different factions. I will likely pop in and out of the game to finish missions one by one, instead of trying to slug through them, because they do typically take some time, especially against a determined defence. Maybe, though, I still have some learning to do.

5 routes in. Updated this a bit.
The game is short if you're a Skip Jockey. If you're a "do a route now and then" kinda gamer like me, I think the length is fine.I take my time reading VNs so be warned it will likely be shorter for you.
Considering the cost of a movie ticket, I think the price is fine. Voice, art, music, writing and sound effects cost money and this is well done.
This is a visual novel, not a point and click or sim. Look it up if you haven't "played" one before.
This is sci-fi not otome. I can only read so much fluff before needing something to chew on.
Its a VN with 9 endings with several choices along the routes. I'm noticing there are main branches and others just give bits of flavor text. Some routes are definitely more detailed and its not intuitive to get to some of the parts that divulge major character backgrounds. The flow of the choices and what you get from making them are the only area I can pinpoint for mixed feelings, that not intuitive, not quite satisfying at times part. Not sure if its a "when you do a route amongst the others" mechanism that starts bringing things more into alignment or that I just stumbled on vague for the first two before getting more into it.
I won't talk about the storyline or plot, as going through it is the most fun of these VNs and I'd hate to lose an "Oh!" in the midst of playing to a review without enjoying the set-up within the VN, especially with a short VN.
Voice acting, sound and music give a premium feel that really go the extra step for immersion. Its a tough choice between Cyrus and Louca being my favorite characters. Voice, writing and character are just such a good mix, but it took a bit to get there. Still, "NO! Keep eating." had myself and most of the folks in the room chuckling. Voice acting isn't over the top, good tone for the characters and were nice for the feel of the game. Really glad to see more of the VAs from other VNs I've enjoyed.
Art was split with sprites being more cartoon art (which I happen to like as a nice change around all the anime style I also enjoy). CGs have a much more graphic novel feel (what I read when not in VNs) with a good use of color and lighting to add to drama / feel. The backgrounds felt more a mix of the two styles. They had a good level of detail and some added to the feel in a more cinematic way than just showing a kitchen, bedroom, theater. i.e. characters interacting in the background making speeches or crowds of people shoving around. Would have asked for more of those. Kudos to the background artist for playing in both styles and working to bridge some of the disconnect that using such opposite styles in a single game can cause.
Writing... I have to go through more routes. Not like I need it to discuss, but I WANT to go through more routes, which tells me its good. They're tackling 2 tough things in this story: 1. Time travel and all the trip-ups, intricacies and just literary physics you have to keep track of for plausibility. 2. The only voice really telling the story is a 16 year old clueless boy, who's purposefully been kept in the dark about everything his entire life, and is describing things in the first person. In the telephone game, this means you as the reader are even more clueless.  It manages to be intriguing and frustrating simultaneously which I guess is part of that immersion thing again.  I'm assuming this isn't the writer's first VN or if it is, I admire your "go bold or go home" self. Nothing like skipping the bunny hill and going straight for the black diamonds.
I'm off to learn more of the story. I know there's a lot hidden and I hope the majority makes it into the light through Sam's eyes.
I may update this review if things change, but I'd say it comes in next to "Octave Higher" for me which means some good depth of work, world creation and concept and in the upper ranks of VNs I've tried, especially for indie.

Personally, I greatly enjoyed this game. It's on a large enough scale to properly allow for tactics such as flanking and strategically placed artillery, but still remains small enough that you can generally avoid being overwhelmed by the amount of things you need to pay attention to.
Another thing that's enjoyable is how damage is handled. Although individuals soldiers have a health bar, everything else in the game instead works on a critical system. Although a single penetrating shot can destroy any vehicle, you can also destroy the engine, turret, main gun, and tracks/wheels of vehicles if you ca't reliably penetrate, or possibly even damage crew through spalling.
Also enjoyable is munitions. Units don't simply deal arbitrary damage infinitely, but instead rely on using the proper weapons from a limited supply. Soldiers can use grenades to flush enemies out of difficult to assault positions or disable enemy vehicles, and cannons must properly choose between AP and HE rounds depending on the target. And any unit left to fend off a hoard or making constant assaults must be resuplied by the unarmored and easily destroyed supply trucks.
However, the game isn't perfect. The fact that different nations had different tanks means that some missions can be a bit imbalanced, either for or against the player (for example, the Stug III Ausf. G will ofetn show up as an early german armor, despite being very well armored and with a good gun. It will easily beat most of the eraly game tanks unless you manage to flank it, since it has no turret).
There is also no campaign, but rather just a series of skirmishes. Although the units and enemy will sometimes change frome on skrimish to the next, the first three skirmishes for each nation can get kinda same-y. For that matter, the fact that the skrimished follow the exact same pattern between every nation means they all get same-y, even the fourth (defense) and fifth (sneaking/limited resources) skirmishes.
Also, online play is no longer possible. I don't do much multiplayer usually, but be aware if it's something you enjoy.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed the game. If you like RTSs and enjoy realistic damage instead of just health bars for everything, as well as a need to actually use tactics instead of just blobbing or marching endless streams at the enemy, you should definitely play this game.
